#1,323
Chapter 35: A Visitor's Guide to Brockton Bay - The City is Very Safe and Friendly​


"—have been confirmed through observational data compiled by Dragon. The Simurgh did, in fact, exit Earth orbit on a seemingly uncontrolled course some time in the late evening of yesterday. The cause and potential purpose of this event has yet to be determined, although Chief Director Costa-Brown had this to say—"

"Gotta be a lie," said a customer in the diner to his friend. "We all know it's one of those long cons that thing likes to pull. Has to be."

"But what if it isn't?" his friend shot back before launching into wild theories for which Jaune lacked the context to understand.

It's a common occurrence ever since he sat down in his booth, really. He'd follow most of what was being discussed by the other diners, then an odd word or phrase would slip in to throw him for a loop, making him lose the thread.

Still, he got the gist. The general feeling in the restaurant was one of unease, whether from the distant news that was the change in behavior of an Endbringer, to complaints closer to home of the curfew imposed on the city. Another bombing took place last night, hitting a homeless shelter in the Docks. Elsewhere, ABB gangsters clashed with a squad of soldiers, requiring Protectorate cape support to help break the stalemate.

Somehow, through it all, life went on.

Jaune rubbed his neck, cracking it from side to side to work out the kinks. The hotel their team stayed in was a pretty nice one, but the bed didn't compare to his mattress. Was that a condemnation of the hospitality industry in Brockton Bay, or praise to Academy City sleep technology? Hard to tell.

Spotting the waitress coming around with a laden tray, he offered her a smile, getting a flustered giggle from the fifty-ish woman in response that surely would make her children cringe to no end were they present. It's nice that she's stopped staring askance at him, at least. What was wrong with ordering four different dishes? He needed the gains.

"Here you are, sweetheart." The woman placed down the plates one by one, each piled high with omelettes, sausages, salads, and pancakes. She also passed over an extra dish filled with milk. "And here, for your darling cat."

"Meow meow meow!"

The perturbed look returned to the waitress's face, and Jaune did not blame her. The meows hadn't been actual meows, but spoken words. After a brief stutter, the waitress seemed to decide that her mind had played a trick on her, and left while shaking her head.

Escha broke out into actual meows, this time the felyne equivalent of laughter.

"Not tired of that yet, Escha?" Jaune asked with a smile, directing his question towards the phone on the table rather than at Escha herself. To the outside observer, the scene would pass as him speaking to a person on the line. Slightly rude in this setting, but it worked for their purposes.

"Never!" declared the felyne in glee.

Since learning of otherworld cats and their idiosyncrasies—the inability to talk or walk on two legs, and so on—Escha had developed a new game of blending in without blending in, with the pair of them waiting all morning for somebody to call her out. So far, nothing. People saw what they wanted to see.

Jaune pushed one of the plates over to Escha, because a bowl of milk did not a healthy Palico make. Then, boy and cat dug into their meal.

Between bites, Esha asked, "So what are we doing today?"

"I'm not too sure on that, myself."

The world didn't move at their pace, no matter how much he wanted it to. The wheels of bureaucracy were advancing in fits and spurts, with the heroes tied down to various responsibilities as they awaited approval for a concerted operation alongside him and New Wave (who had jobs or schooling occupying their schedules). The villains, meanwhile, cited their own priorities, meaning that a push against the ABB wasn't going to happen yet, if it did at all today.

An idle thought had occurred to him, of whether these guys realized that their private lives could end at any moment due to an errant bomb, rendering everything they do moot. Tattletale claimed it would be fine before she departed this morning. He couldn't say he agreed with the sentiment.

And, well, why must he?

"You know what, let's the two of us go look for trouble."

There had to be some good they could do.

Escha raised her fork aloft. "Aye-aye, captain!"

After they finished their breakfast, and paid, they left the diner.

On the way out, Jaune unhooked his Panacea Poncho from the coat rack, putting it on over his button-down shirt. For a brief instant, it blocked his view.

When his vision returned, Lisa was right in front of him.

Jolting in surprise, he cried, "Whoa, Lisa, don't sneak up on me like that!"

There was this long beat where Lisa (and it's Lisa, not Tattletale, because one did not mix cape names and civilian guises) seemed to just stare at him, face completely blank, to make him instinctively worry that he had messed up.

Then she grinned, and all was well again.

Well, besides an obvious problem.

"Sorry, sorry. I thought you saw me. Where are you…" Her eyes flicked down to Escha, lingering a bit. "...two off to now?"

His hand came up to rub the back of his head. "Nowhere in particular, I guess? I just thought she and I would walk around, maybe keep an eye out for the ABB. That's not a problem, is it?"

"Oh no, course not!" Lisa hurriedly waved her hands.

"Great. I was worried it'd cut into your plans. Are you done with, ah, whatever it was you're doing? Want to come with us?"

"Sure thing, I'm totally free." She giggled. It sounded off to both Jaune and Escha. Too sugary sweet.

He leaned down a bit, and asked, "Are you alright, Lisa?"

"Me? Just fine. Copacetic."

"You're what?" A bewildered Escha pulled a face.

"Good. Excellent, " Lisa amended.

Jaune and Escha shared a glance.

"If you say so," Jaune said with a shrug. He searched his pockets. "Hey, check this message I got from the heroes."

He tossed her the Company scroll.

As ever, Lisa became fascinated with the device as soon as she unlocked it. She hid her inexperience well, slamming a finger on one of the app icons with confidence.

Thump.

Lisa dropped to the ground, unconscious.

"Man, it's been a while since I've seen that. How nostalgic," Jaune said, retrieving the scroll.

A little mean, too, but she's the one that attempted to trick them first. In his book, one prank invited another, adding spice to life.

Clearly, the fake Lisa—or rather, the Lisa that belonged to this world—disagreed with the notion. Once she awoke a few minutes later, she chose to beat a hasty retreat rather than linger, leaving the bemused pair of Jaune and Escha behind. She hadn't been kind about it, either, leveling a number of accusations against him on her way out, most having to do with him somehow cloning her body for reasons ranging from nefarious to sordid.

Lisa… Lisa could be nasty when the mood strikes her.

She could have been smarter, too, and Jaune wondered what her plan even was. Did she think to fool him so that he might spill secrets she can use to one-up the Lisa on his team?

He mulled on that possibility, and nodded. Yup, that's her, alright. With a dash of overconfidence to convince her that she can paper over the flaws in the plan with attitude and audacity.

Adorable.

"Jaune, Jaune, what's that building?" Escha asked to interrupt his train of thought.

He looked down at her, walking on all fours next to him, then followed her gaze to a large, multi-story complex on the other side of the road, massive banners advertising special deals plastered on the windows.

"That's a mall. Like a market, but everything is inside."

"Can we find trouble there?"

A solid maybe, going by the soldiers manning the entrances. They resemble the Atlas guys that came to Vale for the Vytal Festival, armed and serious. For the ABB that was trying to aim their attacks at civilian centers, a mall would make a tempting target, hence the presence of the guards.

"I suppose it can't hurt to ask if they need help—" He spotted a person armored in blue and silver walking out of the mall to talk to the soldiers. "Nope. Nope, nope, nope."

There was an alley to his right, and Jaune ducked into it at speed, Escha on his heels. Making certain, he didn't linger, but crossed to the next block over before continuing down the sidewalk.

Escha nudged his leg. "You knew that guy. Who's he?"

"Armsmaster," Jaune almost spat the name. "He's a hero, but don't let that fool you. The guy is ruthless. Skilled, though." As much as it hurts to admit. "Come on, let's head somewhere else. This place is well-protected enough without us."

However, Jaune soon encountered a problem. Street after street they walked, and the best he found were a couple of punks spray-painting gang signs on a wall. This area of the city seemed a touch too safe, with soldiers posted at all semi-important buildings, along with the occasional hero—some he recognized, some he did not and might be out-of-town assistance—touching base with them before hopping in a truck and getting driven off elsewhere. The comics always portray life like there's a mugging on every corner, but here, there was barely a peep.

Escha didn't mind the quiet, though. She had a thousand questions for everything around her, curiosity running on full overdrive as she flitted from one interesting object to the next.

"How do 'cars' work?"

"Er, there's an engine in them that burns fuel, which gives them power to move. I don't know much more beyond that."

"There's people in that box!"

"That's television tech. The people in it are actually in a different place, and the image is sent to these devices so people from far away can see them at the same time."

"Like signal flares?"

"...Exactly."

"What's ice cream?"

Gasp!

And so, not long after breakfast, they were eating again. Jaune sat on a park bench, chocolate ice cream cone in hand, watching Escha take a tentative lick of the vanilla ice cream cone she held with both front paws. It seemed a nice, safe flavor for a felyne, better than chocolate at least, because he still wasn't certain to what extent their appetite differed from regular cats.

The first taste, and all the fur on Escha's body bristled. Her eyes grew wide as saucers.

Translated to human? Ohoho.

"Good?" he asked.

"It's the most delicious thing I've ever tasted…" she whispered in reverent awe.

She opened her mouth wide to chomp down on the ice cream in one bite, before recalling his warning about brain freeze, and instead began furiously licking the cone with her tiny tongue. The ice cream cone spun and spun, whittled down on all sides at an amazing speed. Amused, Jaune offered a bit of his ice cream, and laughed at how her head followed after the cone as he pulled it away, trying to get in one last lick before the treat moved out of her reach.

It was worthy of a picture.

Snap.

A felyne with a glob of ice cream on her nose, get.

Call it luck or irony, but that was how trouble found them, while they were having an enjoyable time and minding their own business.

As they finished eating their ice cream, a figure descended on the park from the sky, resplendent in white and gold. With her back to the sun, cape fluttering, Glory Girl appeared a vision of divinity, larger than life. She also didn't look happy with him.

"You know, it's not a good idea to wear a skirt and fly," he said, gazing up at her.

Now, she really didn't look happy with him… then Escha rushed at her, begging to be taken into the air, and Glory Girl forgot his existence altogether.

Huh. Maybe he'd start throwing the cat at all his problems.

"You're not off the hook," Glory Girl said later, as they watch a windswept Escha work on her second ice cream cone, purchased for the felyne by their new guest.

Jaune rolled his eyes. "For what?" he argued. "I'm not going to attend a family meeting when I've already told you that I'm not related to you guys! And how did you find me, anyway?" Did he have a stalker?

Glory Girl answered by flipping open her phone, a clunky monstrosity whose ugliness was pasted over by cutesy stickers. The load time for the 'inter'-net offended him on a base level.

A picture of a boy talking to a cat, inexpertly taken, filled the screen. A swipe, and it now displayed security footage of them outside an appliance store, Escha smushing her face to the glass. While standing upright.

"The PHO message board found your cat, and I recognized your face in the photos." Leave it to the eternally online to uncover any and every detail when nobody else could. "They're debating between her being a Case 53 and a biotinker monstrosity." Escha snuffled her nose at the accusation, and Glory Girl immediately changed her tune, gushing over her. "Oh, but I know you're not, cutie! You're the most adorable cape in the world, yes you are!"

Escha scooted further away from the strange lady.

"So you were trawling the net for cat pictures," Jaune concluded. People truly were the same in any universe. In this specific case, it's another point of similarity between her and him, though Jaune refrained from telling the girl that. No need to encourage her delusions.

Glory Girl made a so-so gesture. "More like the thread showed up when I was on the lookout for new capes in the city."

For you, she meant. Oh damn, he did have a stalker.

"Well, you've found me. You can go home now." Please.

She frowned, turning her body to face him. "Uh, like hell I will. I've got questions."

"I already said—" He was cut off by Glory Girl seizing him by the front of his poncho.

The heroine froze as a blade tickled her throat, with Jaune holding a flashbang in his other hand, ready to slam it against her face. Below, Escha brandished a boomerang, summoned for her by Jaune.

Slowly, Glory Girl retracted her fingers. "Heeey," she said in a soothing tone. "I wasn't going to do anything to you." Neither of them moved, and she could detect the wariness radiating off of them. "I'm serious! Do you think I beat up random people for the hell of it?"

"I can't say, because I'm not from around here," Jaune reminded her. He returned his sword to his Pocket, and Escha got back to the important task of eating her ice cream, boomerang laying within reach. The disappearance of Crocea Mors caused Glory Girl to do a double-take.

"Is that a part of your powers, or Tinkertech? Or—wait, no." She closed her eyes, opened them, refocusing. "I was trying to find you, because you're consorting with villains! Explain yourself!" she ordered.

Jaune considered replying with a simple 'no,' rethinking it as he realized that probably would end in a battle. He settled with, "Brockton Bay is in a time of need, and some of them aren't that bad."

"Are you kidding?" The words were almost a yell, as Glory Girl's face warped into a snarl. "Brockton Bay's problems are because of villains. They've been ruining this city for literally years!"

"I feel like there's a number of them that are a little too young to have contributed to that," Jaune pointed out, thinking of the Undersiders.

She ignored the comment. "Do you know what they did to Lord's Market last year? Seven people dead, and Hookwolf got away with it scot-free!" The frustration bled through in her voice, made even clearer as she pounded a fist on the backrest of the bench. The wood cracked.

Escha scooched over another inch.

"And those Undersiders—"

"What about them?" he asked, a touch sharply. Most of the group meant nothing to him beyond a face, but Lisa was once included in that team and he didn't care for the hostility he was hearing.

"They robbed a bank two weeks ago! The psychos took dozens of hostages and put poisonous spiders on them to keep them compliant! It's sick!"

…Lisa, what the hell?

"I mean, there has to be a reason for that." He waffled a bit. "You're probably misunderstanding it." Weak, as far as a rebuttal went, but he lacked proper information to argue the point further.

She scoffed. "Sure. Totally an overreaction on my part." Needless to say, sarcasm. "Grue clocked little Vista in the head. Bug girl stuck a knife against my sister's throat. That Tattletale bitch? She shot me. And the utter crap she kept on spouting…" Glory Girl mimed a strangling motion, before the tension in her seemed to just cut out, and she slumped back in her seat. Long, golden hair fell to cover her expression. "Idiot doesn't know what she's talking about."

The words were out of his mouth before he could reconsider them. "Heh. She'd disagree with you there."

And, oh, did that set Glory Girl off. She shot him a glare that made Jaune curious if maybe she had laser vision to go along with her flight, super strength, and invincibility, because she looked like she wanted to set him on fire.

"Ugh! I'll bet that you've met her, haven't you?" She gave a spiteful laugh. "Was it the spandex? Did you get pulled into villainy by her ass?"

"I've talked to her," he snapped back. "And I'll admit she can be"—he searched for the appropriate term—"an experience." Yeah, that sounded about right. "But she's helped me a lot, and I know for a fact she could be quite sweet behind the words she says. They're… walls."

Between her and other people. Between her and the world, the situations she couldn't handle. She threw a whole tirade at him the day they first met, and it had taken him many a night of lying in his bed, thinking, to understand that she was terrified of him in that moment. There were reasons for the things she does.

Sometimes. Mostly, she was just being annoying for the sake of it, he was pretty sure.

Glory Girl stared at him for a while without speaking, and when she did, her voice had grown colder. "How long have you known her? You're talking like she's your friend or something."

He could tell it was a loaded question. Circumstances like these called for a lie.

But he just plain didn't want to.

"She is."

Glory Girl had her fist up, and Crocea Mors was in his hand. Only the resounding boom in the distance stopped them from coming to blows.

She looked from him to the rising smoke. A growl, and she floated into the air. This meeting was over.

Except, she hadn't left yet by the time he put on his domino mask. Her eyes blinked in astonishment as a cape appeared to settle over his shoulders.

"You're helping out?" she asked, incredulous.

He sent her an odd look. "Yeeeah? There's probably people caught in that explosion so of course I'm going, what are you, dumb?"

"Fuck you," she shot back. Then, with less hostility. "If you're serious, I can fly you there. It'd be faster."

Jaune weighed the option against his rocket boots, deciding that it'd conserve the boots' limited flight time.

"Deal. Let's go."

He placed a domino mask over Escha's face (Glory Girl nearly died then and there). After they were ready, she looped her arms behind him as he held Escha in a similar grip, and lifted off. If their weight bothered her, she didn't show it.

The three of them zoomed over the rooftops at an admirable pace, faster than a car and completely bypassing traffic, people, and every other obstacle. Their vantage point allowed Jaune to observe the location struck by the explosion, with an eye for powers or gunfire—he found none. The culprit messed up, thankfully, because the damage took place outside on a rather sparse street.

Half a block away was a school. It could have been so much worse.

That didn't make the scene he arrived to any easier. Amidst the ongoing fires and wreckage, he saw the victims. Some were already dead, shredded or thrown by the force of the blast. Others wailed, or whimpered, or shouted for assistance.

There were civilians milling on the scene, and one police officer. Except for the latter, none seemed sure of what to do until they spotted their group touching down, at which point the civilians all cleared the area.

Wait, what?

He didn't have time to question it. Glory Girl acted as if that was normal, flying over to the police officer, then to a half-destroyed shop after a quick exchange. There, she began moving the rubble at the entrance to gain access.

Left to his own devices, Jaune summoned the stimpaks and jars of healing potions he brought along on this trip, sharing them with Escha before they split up and got to work.

Nobody would call what he did proper triaging. He ran from body to body, blabbering a rushed explanation to each person as he jabbed needles into arms. People in bad shape received two. Those that looked too far gone got one anyway, just in case they were alive and that made the difference. When he ran out of stimpaks, he bought more from the Marketplace—Lisa would understand.

The process repeated for ten or so victims. As he applied medicine to a woman covered in tattoos, he heard Glory Girl speak up behind him.

"What's that you're using?" She floated closer, her approach silent, watching the process over his shoulder with interest.

"Stimpaks. Drug that stimulate regeneration." He thrust some into her hands. "Check for other people that need them."

Emergency vehicles began arriving. Police cars, PRT vans, fire trucks, ambulances. Once the EMTs mustered the nerves to approach him and he gave them a run down on the stimpaks, they hurried to direct him toward the worst cases. Soon, those that could be saved all had a shot, or were covered in green healing fluids. Those that couldn't…

Well.

"As far as we can tell, the ABB attacks are random," Glory Girl explained as they watched the various ongoings from the sideline. "There's no predicting where they'd strike."

"See why my proposal makes sense?" Jaune said, leaning on a street light and distracting Escha with scritches. "Waiting around, responding to the threats after they act… the heroes are wearing themselves out. I half-suspect that it's part of Bakuda's plan to keep them from bringing the fight to the heart of the ABB. They need more reinforcements than just the trickle of capes coming in ones and twos."

Glory Girl tch'ed. "I know that. The Protectorate knows that. But…" Her lips pressed together in a thin line. The prospect of allying with villains displeased her.

With a groan, he threw her a bone.

"Look, you don't have to like it. Don't even think of it, as I told you all. You're working with me. Just me."

"Compromises." She spat the word with venom, then shook her head. "Whatever. I'm not the one deciding these things, and I'm not gonna ruin it, either. What I can do is ask you about this." She held up an unused stimpak. "Are you the one that made them?"

He winced. "Not the maker, so I can't really tell you the recipe, sorry."

"Oh no no, that wasn't what I was asking, I get that Tinkertech isn't easy to replicate. I was just—" She caught him about to raise an objection, and her mind raced ahead to the correct conclusion. "It's not Tinkertech."

"No."

In an instant, she was in his face.

"How do you know that? Where did you get them, then? I—why didn't you bring this up yesterday!?"

"There wasn't a good chance?" He avoided her wide-eyed stare, able to guess the thoughts behind them.

Indeed, Glory Girl looked like she had many unkind things she wanted to say. Still, what she did voice aloud was, "Would you be willing to share a sample of this? It could be a game-changer if my sister or the PRT manage to figure out the chemical formula."

"Sure. I don't mind." He indicated the stimpak she was holding. "Consider that yours to keep."

She stared at him, agog. "Wait, hold up, you're not asking for a price?"

"...I could have charged for it?"

Glory Girl studied him with a careful eye, gaze roaming up and down as if it would unlock his thoughts to her. Finally, she slumped her shoulders.

"You're an idiot," she said with the air of having discovered a great truth.

"Oi."

Her boots left the ground. She moved through the air with an ease he envied, turning to look back at him. "I'm not wrong." There was a bright smile on her face. "And it's not a bad thing. You're an idiot."

"Yeah, well, screw you." Truly, a masterful repartee.

She stuck out her tongue. "No way. We might be related. Uncle Neil got very cagey when I asked him about illegitimate children."

Welp, there went any hope of him convincing her she's wrong. "That's… quite a landmine. I hope it isn't causing too much of an issue in your family."

"We'll have to see," the girl admitted, rising higher. She jabbed a finger at him. "You're not off the hook, either."

"You said that before."

"Still true. You might have good intentions, and might even be a hero, but it'd be better if you stopped hanging around villains. They're going to drag you down to their level."

With that, Glory Girl waved them farewell and, in a blur, flew away.


-o-​


Back in civilian guises, aimlessly they walked.

Over the course of an hour, Jaune and Escha found no other emergencies in their vicinity. The ones they do hear of were already long over by the time they reached the scene.

Lunchtime came around, and the pair started dialing back from a state of combat readiness, steps slowing, eyes wandering to the storefronts and other interesting sights. For a meal, Jaune picked out food from multiple places, anything that seemed to have caught Escha's fancy, getting them as takeouts to eat while on the street.

All the while, he somewhat expected the question. It was still a surprise.

"Jaune?"

Munching on popcorn, he answered with a simple "Hm?"

"Do you really think Lisa is a bad person?"

He looked down. Escha was avoiding his gaze, walking with her head down.

Jaune sighed, and vanished the bag of popcorn away. "Why do you say that? Don't take what Glory Girl tells you to heart."

"I'm not!" Escha denied at once. "But…" she trailed off. Glanced at him, found him looking back, and returned to staring at the sidewalk in front of her. "N-Nevermind."

"Hey, I don't mind talking this out." They were coming up on an intersection. By some nebulous instinct, he pivoted on his heel to take the turn, using the chance to lean down and brush his hand through her fur in encouragement. That gave Escha the push she needed.

"I like Lisa, but she's a villain."

"Well, you knew that."

"But I didn't know know. I thought it was like pranks, or stealing fruit from the market so the seller chases you. Everybody does that at least once."

Jaune couldn't help it, breaking into chuckles. What a world the felyne lived in.

"While that is quite dastardly, Escha, it isn't villainy, and definitely isn't supervillainy." He collected his thoughts, wondering how best to explain. "I can't say I know much about this world, but from the comics I've read, superheroes and supervillains are catch-all terms. They're names. Labels to note who's on what side. The words themselves don't make you a good person or a bad person."

"But a lot of the villains are bad. Lisa even said so herself!"

Another turn, one he hardly paid attention to. He was finding it difficult to disagree with the sentiment Escha raised.

The fire lady had been a villain, no doubt rotten to the core. Attacking Beacon required a mind monstrous beyond comprehension.

Except, the White Fang were there, too, and he heard they used to be peaceful way back when. Had they been hiding their villainy before? Or did they hang out with types like the fire lady and that's how the turn to violence began?

And Jax, dear Jax. The guy that he turned into a shishkebab. Even long after, Jaune didn't know for sure what was going on in that psycho's head. He had a perfect life at Beacon, a shining future of fame and worship awaiting him, and he decided to turn his gun on everybody. Playing at hero one moment, becoming a villain the next. Did his head crack?

All told, it painted a bleak picture. Villains were an awful lot, and corrupting forces to boot. A thief, a fraud, a cheat he may be, nobody had ever called him a villain, and he did not wish them to.

Lost in his musings, he passed a street sign, and almost dismissed it until he did a double-take. The name was one he vaguely recalled. Casting his gaze at the surroundings, he blinked in confusion for a little while, before recollection dawned.

When it began was hard to say, but his feet had guided him down a familiar road. Lined by nondescript office buildings, it nevertheless stood out from every other street in this city. Not the details, he was hopeless there. The shape, the angles of the buildings, those were harder to change.

A look to his left, a look to his right, few cars were in sight. He stepped off the sidewalk and onto the road.

Finding the spot was a task and a half. He strolled back and forth, working off the memory of a rather tense and hectic time, one not made easier as passing cars distracted him with their honking horns.

The view did it, in the end. He stood on the median strip, and from there the long, long road stretched all the way to the coastline, letting him see the blue ocean. And it all came roaring back.

That day was hell. He still mustered a smile.

"I think we would have to ask Lisa about it before we make up our mind," he said to Escha, shading his eyes as he peered at the horizon, "because saying that villains are bad would be fairly accurate, but not always true. Not here, at least."

For a day, heroes and villains had fought side by side to protect a city. No divide in between, they were simply people, entrusting their backs to each other as they stepped on the line to defy the world that wished for them to die. As it should be.

Then, the story had turned completely on its head.

He pointed down the street. "A hero died there, and he was no better than the beast he set out to slay. He's not important."

Taken aback, Escha stared up at him with a silly look of confusion. "Wait, was that it?" she asked, dissatisfied with the complete lack of details and tension. Jaune threw back his head, and laughed.

"Short story, huh? Well then, let me tell you a second one." He pointed at his feet. "I met someone here. You wouldn't think her a villain if you ever hear her talk. Yet, she was. A villain braver than any hero, good and kind. She and I made an amazing team, and we hunted a monster together."

That, Escha reluctantly agreed, counted for something. The greatest of bonds were forged by monster hunting. The bigger the monster, the better.

"So that's the girl you tried to mate with last night?" she asked.

He balked. "I did not try to mate with her!"

For a cat, Escha sure can look skeptical. "I dunno. You were like Logy whenever he tried to flirt."

Ouch. "Oh, come on, you wouldn't blame me if you were ever in my situation."

Escha scrunched her face, unconvinced. "I like Lisa better," she opined.

"Ha! I like Lisa, too, but Sundancer… you'd have to meet her to understand."

When it came down to it, despite all she said, Pyrrha did not believe in him, not really. His own partner couldn't trust him at the finish, playing a trick to send him away.

He had to go to a whole new universe for someone who didn't dismiss him as a weak, pitiful creature. Who truly saw him as a companion, willing to laugh and cry, fight and die, by his side.

How did it take a villain to grant his fondest wish? What a treasure for him to have found.

The only sun for him.


Author's Notes: What I didn't show was Jaune instinctively striking the Praise the Sun pose at the end.

Yang Xiao-Long. Never in the running. Lost anyway.

Chapter 36: A Visitor's Guide to Brockton Bay - Go Out at Night, It's Fine​


Girl That Won't Shut Up POV

Door code today was 495632. My lucky number as of two seconds ago.

The side entrance, nestled within a nondescript alley, unlocked. The interior was brightly lit.

Alarm pad override HB62A83. Idiots changed it weekly instead of daily.

No blaring alerts. Stillness reigned. Then, shadows moved along the wall, the accompanying footsteps silent.

There's so much empty space. That's just unfair. God, we need a bigger home—base. Not home.

The whisper of footsteps passed a door. Returned.

Let's not risk it. This will do.

The door opened, then shut. Nothing inside the room but crates and boxes.

Next guard change is in… about four minutes. Bleh. Too long to do nothing, too short to kick my feet up.

Soon, the sound of people outside the door. They fade in the distance.

…flying cabbages… what kind of insane—oh! Right on time. Here we go.

Another door, remote-locked. Up in the corner, a blinking light. Elsewhere, a man watched the camera.

I know what you did to your father. Your mother and siblings could, too.

The door opened without prompting. Anything that needed saying had been done hours ago.

Hehe, it didn't go to waste this time~

A long corridor stretched on, wide enough for ten marching abreast. Meant for mass intake of civilians in an emergency, before conversion to current use.

I'm getting an urge to skip along this hallway. Better not, though. Next door code is 302755… wait, or was it 104246? 483920?

The door loomed large.

Fuckfuckfuck—oh, there's no lock.

The sound of palm meeting face. A sigh.

Just gonna… not mention this part at all in the retelling. Have to show him my cool side.

A turn, a flight of stairs down.

The corner should work. Angle of approach, previous footprints, yeah, here's good.

A cloak snapped out to form a screen. Colors warped, blending in.

Now you see me, now you don't. I'm magic. Ha.

Heavy boots on concrete. Multiple figures ascended the staircase. Eyes behind helmet visors skirted over a spot mere inches away.

Buh-bye. Suckers.

The cloak went back around delicate shoulders.

Should be a straight shot, now.

A slight vibration passed through the hall. Somewhere below, a muffled roar.

What is—ah, the Travelers' last member. That's gonna be so annoying to handle. Sooner he or she is out of town the better. Bitchdancer, too.

One final door. A deep breath. Fingers danced on a keypad. The locks disengaged.

They call me Bond. James Bond. Or maybe I'd be the femme fatale?... I would make a phenomenal femme fatale.

The door slid aside, then closed shut. The ambient hallway sounds cut off.

A tall, skinny figure sprang to his feet. Nobody was supposed to enter without his say-so.

"Who—!?"

"Hello again, Coil. I win."

Completely, and on my own. All I ever needed was more time, just a little more time, to put you in checkmate.

The other person moved his hand, revealing a firearm. A gunshot rang out.

"I'm also bulletproof."

...Owwwie.




Evening arrived, and along with it came communications from both sides of the law. They were ready, come what may. The push against the ABB would commence tonight.

Jaune waited for the villains to begin trickling into the small courtyard hidden in the shadow of an office building, leaning on one of the artsy, geometric tables that were scattered about the area. Faultline's crew got there first, almost an hour early. Their reason became apparent as the woman gravitated at once towards a frolicking Escha, proceeding to ask her an endless series of questions that didn't make much sense to Jaune. She brought with her four capes, and given the lack of orders, they wandered over to the spread of donuts and muffins he had laid out.

What? It didn't kill to be a good host, even if Tattletale made fun of him for it in her texts.

Of the four, the neon-orange man was the most outgoing, introducing himself as Newter whilst taking a bite of blueberry muffin (*shivers*). He declined a proffered handshake, citing that his skin contained hallucinogenic properties potent enough to down an elephant. His teammate, a blobby and shell-encrusted cape called Gregor the Snail, accepted the gesture in his stead. There was also a waifish young woman—he mistook her for a teenager at first—swaddled in green robes who didn't speak, and an actual teenager tending to her, dressed in a thick red bodysuit. Labyrinth and Spitfire, were their names. A reality warper, her allies boasted, and a... a fire spitter. Oftentimes, it's written right on the tin.

Gregor opted for a cruller (a sign of good taste, that), and Spitfire coaxed Labyrinth into munching on a vanilla frosted donut (childish tastes, plus a caretaker, hmm).

Not long after, a squad of men and women in professional gear trooped in. Reminiscent of Hound Dog, they donned black body armor and tinted helmets, and wielded assault rifles enhanced with various futuristic attachments. These newcomers claimed to be mercenaries hired by Coil, which rather put Jaune in a state of alert, but he relaxed when they gave no indications of attacking. It seemed, for the moment, that they were all on a side.

One thing he noted, the mercenaries were exchanging a furious conversation among themselves in hushed voices, centered around the screens of their phones. He counted three times thus far that their members turned in his direction. Tattletale may be interested to hear more about this.

They refused snacks. Their loss.

Next up were the Undersiders. Their leader, Grue, strode into the courtyard with powerful strides, cloaked in darkness. The insect-masked Skitter followed on his heels, head swiveling to observe each person present and, if Jaune was not mistaken, to check out Grue's rear. The local Tattletale met Jaune's eyes for barely two seconds before she hid behind Skitter. A girl wearing a dog mask snarled at him, three dogs marching at her feet. Bitch.

He still refused to believe that was her actual supervillain name. Tattletale had to be joking.

The last member rounding out the Undersider, Regent, made a beeline for the donuts to grab a custard-filled and a chocolate frosted (indulgent, decadent even), balancing them along with his scepter. He didn't take any back for the rest of his team.

A thunderous rumble, like a car engine but ten times louder, brought activities to a halt. Everybody prepared their armaments or powers, and faced the direction the noise came from, which meant Skidmark scrambled in a panic for cover when he and his Merchants, Squealer and Mush (or was it Moist?), made their appearance. The man took the slip-up with ill grace, huffing and puffing at those that dared to look at him from then on for too long. Their group, too, passed on refreshments.

That little episode was soon forgotten for Jaune, because the next person to arrive was Sundancer. Her ballet training showed in how she walked—good posture, her steps light and elegant. She looked rather nervous at the number of people here, and avoided going near the mercenaries, shrinking away from their guns. The suns decorating her black bodysuit glinted under the courtyard lamp to draw the eye.

Oh, and her team accompanied her, the Travails or whatever. Trickster, Bally, Jean Sis. They were… shapes. Wearing clothes and stuff.

"Do you guys want anything?" Sundancer asked her teammates, indicating the boxes on the table, and she gave a heavy sigh as Trickster promptly left to a corner for a smoke. "Guess I'll just get him a blueberry muffin or whatever, then. Ballistic? Genesis?"

Oops. Well, he got close.

"Jelly donut," said Ballistic (no opinion in particular).

"Can you see if they have anything cinnamony?" asked the very un-gorilla, very wolf-like Genesis (clearly a sophisticated and intelligent person). He recalled Tattletale mentioning her being some sort of shapeshifter.

Sundancer nodded, and split off from the group. She stumbled a bit upon noticing that he was looking her way, but nevertheless approached the table, saying a polite hello to him and the members of Faultline's group sitting on the benches. Spitfire passed her fellow pyro girl a paper plate, which was quickly loaded with a blueberry muffin and a jelly donut. She plucked a custard donut next (modest, sweet, brave, kind, funny—wait a minute) then checked over the choices for Genesis's request.

Jaune coughed into a fist, drawing her attention. "I already ate the cinnamon muffin, sorry."

"Oh..." she murmured under her breath, and fidgeted. "Um, thanks for letting me know."

"Take a cruller. Those are tasty."

More fidgeting. "I actually figured I'd leave it, since there's always somebody else that wants the french cruller."

That term jogged a memory. He remembered Sundancer using it in relation to his name. And now, to indicate food. A versatile word, french. He would like to know its meaning one day.

"Fair point," he replied. "The thing's delicious, and I've seen fights break out over it." Because people in Beacon understood that ceding the best food on offer didn't win them esteem from their peers, it just meant ending up with the worst food. "Lucky for you, Gregor here already had one."

Gregor nodded, translucent skin wobbling in an unnerving manner. A Case 53, his physiology and appearance deviated from the norm to an extreme degree. Thankfully, the man hadn't held it against Jaune for needing a while to become accustomed to the uncanny sight, and turned out to be quite a conversationalist.

Pointing at Sundancer, Jaune continued, "Which makes you the 'somebody else,' and this"—he pointed at the donut in question—"free for the taking."

That got a small laugh out of her, and Jaune perked up hearing it. Since she was still looking around as if searching for another person who might object, he took the box of donuts and raised it toward the girl.

"Come on, nobody will mind."

His heart sank seeing the hesitant manner with which she reached out a hand. The Sundancer he knew, by the end of their short time together, was a person that could be decisive when dealing with him. She wasn't afraid to show her unreserved side hidden under the meekness. This Sundancer…

"Um, is something wrong?"

Jaune shook off his malaise, and plastered on a smile. "Of course not."

Whether she believed him or otherwise, she left soon after to rejoin her team, where she proceeded to be bombarded with questions, more teasing than prying, from Genesis. Curiously enough, Genesis ended up with the custard donut. Sundancer had kept the cruller (modest, sweet, brave, kind, funny—stop that) for herself.

"You know, I think that went pretty okay," Jaune said aloud to the table.

"Dude," Newter replied through a mouthful of food. He had gone for seconds, holding a muffin with his tail. "I have better conversations than that with the cashier from my usual convenience store."

Jaune glared at Newter. "Yes, well, we all have to start somewhere. It's an improvement over yesterday, at least."

"Literally anything would count as an improvement over yesterday, and I doubt you've made up for it by bribing her with food."

Seeking support elsewhere, he turned to Gregor. "You saw what happened, didn't you? I'm doing great, right?"

Gregor pondered on it, looking up at the moon.

"A fruit not eaten, becomes fruitful in time," he finally said in his rumbling voice.

"...What does that mean?"

The man patted him on the back. "Better luck next life."

Ouch.

In truth, he didn't know what he wanted, or expected, from this. The Sundancer standing before him today was a different person from his friend. She's someone who never fought by his side, and shouldn't matter to him.

Yet, different people they may be, the two girls shared their past and their thoughts, so he was certain of one thing: the Sundancer here wasn't happy. Not with being a villain. Not with working for Coil. Not with this violent life. If he had to point towards a reason for why he still insisted on trying to talk to her, it would be that. She wasn't his friend, but she needed a friend.

"Soooo, are you just gonna keep making moony eyes at her?" Newter asked.

Spitfire scolded him, "Leave the guy alone! I, for one, think it's romantic!"

"No, he's got a point," Jaune said, sighing. "There are bigger problems to focus on for the moment. We're not here to socialize."

Even if it did look exactly like that. Perhaps the presence of catering had gotten them to let their guard down, or maybe it was the fact that none of the various groups here were direct rivals to each other. Whichever the case, people have begun branching out of their respective teams, conversing to while away the time. It started out formal, full of subtle posturings as Jaune witnessed at Somer's Rock and imagined was the norm. That didn't last long, however, and he would hear a joke here, a complaint about rent there. On an unspoken accord, they were all easing the pretense of supervillainy, and came to resemble regular people living in the day to day. The scene was, he thought, almost harmonious.

Ignoring Skidmark pitching a drug to Trickster who looked done enough to consider violence, of course. Plus Bitch glaring at one of the mercenaries and cracking her knuckles, having overheard an unfortunate remark. There's also Skitter doing… whatever she's doing with a whole big cloud of bugs while speaking to the person next to her, Sundancer, who seemed to be hyperventilating. And—

Okay, so it was more harmony in chaos, but the sentiment stood. He hoped this continued on during the upcoming operation.

Jaune checked the clock on his phone—adjusted for local conditions—then scanned the crowd for Tattletale, a bit worried by her absence. 8PM was the agreed-upon time for the meetup. The villains would soon start to ask for details of the game plan, and only she possessed the full scope of that. He'd rather avoid the awkwardness of telling people he had no real clue of what to do or where to go.

His eyes caught a flash of purple amidst the crowd.

"Tattletale!" he called out, realizing a tad late that the native version was running around. It turned out to be a needless worry, because he ended up with two Tattletales in front of him.

"I should have worded myself better."

"Yup. That was dumb of you."

"Totally."

How nice. They've put aside their differences to gang up on him.

"Alright, I guess it doesn't matter, since you"—he waved a hand at the local Tattletale—"are probably going to help coordinate things." From experience, it was the place on the battlefield where she shone brightest.

"Bomb disposal, too," Tattletale chirped. "We gotta make my little sister earn her keep."

Was that the lie today, pretending to be a long-lost twin sister? He supposed it's an easier notion to swallow than talks of clones and doppelgangers.

"Cut the bullshit," the local one spat. "I don't have a sister."

"So far as you know~," Tattletale singsonged. The other signs, like how she rocked on her heels and failed to suppress a smile, piqued Jaune's interest.

"You seem happy. Did something good happen?"

Her eyes softened as she looked at him. "The very best," she replied with surprising honesty. "I'll tell you about it later."

At that time, he'd have a few questions to ask her, too, about a tale of bank robberies and spiders.

Tattletale cast her gaze across the courtyard. "For now, let's deal with the night ahead."

"Sounds good," Jaune agreed, and provided his report. "Everybody's here and ready to go, except there's something up with Coil's mercenaries. They're all in a tizzy, and I think it has to do with us."

She shrugged. "No need to worry about it. I know why. Like my copy here, they've just received new orders, is all." After checking that the mercenaries weren't paying attention to them, she pulled out an unfamiliar phone and waved it before Jaune's face.

Her counterpart made a strange noise at the back of her throat, alternating her gaze between the phone and Tattletale at a rapid pace. Presumably, she recognized the device, and had not banked on seeing it in Tattletale's possession.

"That's right, better put all those nasty little thoughts aside, missy, because you're not getting paid to find our weaknesses anymore."

The local Tattletale flinched at that comment, before faking a grin. "No clue what you're talking about. I'm just a sweet, playful thief-for-hire. No schemes here. Promise." The whole time, her eyes remained rooted on the unfamiliar phone, the girl's mind no doubt racing by now.

"Uh-huh. Glad we're on the same page," Tattletale drawled, sounding snide. With a snicker, she then turned to him, fiddling with her personal phone. A melodious ding rang out in his pocket. "Here's the list of addresses I want the heroes to hit up. They're numbered in sequence, and I've even marked them out on a map for you. Remember—"

"Don't give it away all at once."

"Good, you remember. They might get cute if you hand over the whole list right off the bat. Leverage is important."

He rather doubted the heroes would stoop to that. A certain person might try, but there were a dozen others to rein him in; Dauntless, in particular, appeared willing to play ball. Still, Tattletale tended to worry no matter what, so he accepted her advice with a simple nod.

"Wait for my signal, then start passing out the locations. Blame me if they ask—say I'm deducing it as I go along. Keep in contact. It's best if we can have both sides moving at the same pace."

"How should I divide the hero teams? I'm not that familiar with their powers."

"Leave it for them to figure out, they have more experience there. Stick with whoever is their leader."

He grimaced. "Armsmaster."

"Maybe. Or the Protectorate could recognize that he's not a people person at his core and is better off on the front line while putting in D-Dauntless—bahahahaha! I can't! I just can't!"

As Tattletale—both Tattletales, actually—laughed their hearts out, Jaune pinched the bridge of his nose. Gratified as he was that someone else held a poor opinion of Armsmaster, the very real possibility that he'd have to partner with the man loomed large before him, and he would have appreciated helpful instructions on that front. It didn't seem to be forthcoming, though.

Once her mirth subsided, Tattletale got back into it, guiding him through the routes that the list of addresses would form. She intended for a two-pronged offensive, with teams leapfrogging over each other to knock down the major ABB strongholds and bomb caches at a blistering speed. It's a loud, straightforward strategy, and for a good reason.

"Whoever gets Lung or Oni Lee after them, call in. I'll let you know which villains I'm sending, or what heroes I need from your side. The instant you see those two bogged down, disengage."

Because at that point, a direct assault on Bakuda wouldn't stand the risk of the ABB's other capes making an entrance. Lung's powers involved transforming into a dragon, his strength ramping up over time. At his peak, he dueled Leviathan. They did not want him tossed into the mix at a critical moment. As for Oni Lee, the ABB's second-in-command was a teleporter. Enough said there, really.

Either one would complicate the situation. Remove both, and life becomes simpler. It'd be their team, their allies, Bakuda, and a whole lot of bombs. See? Simple.

Tattletale tapped her chin in thought. "Am I missing anything? I don't think so…"

"In that case, you handle things here and I'll head out to meet the Protectorate," he said. Taking out his phone, he placed a call to her, then hung the strap around his neck, turning the volume down low to prevent eavesdroppers. It would allow them to communicate throughout the attack. "If you need me, just shout."

As he departed the courtyard, Jaune swung by the table he was sitting at, and grabbed a couple of unopened donut boxes.

It paid to be a good host, after all.


-o-​


The mustering point for the Protectorate was located within the ground level of a parking garage, just across the street from where the villains met. They were waiting for him on the far side of the facility, a distance at which they couldn't see or hear well should any errant criminal cape decide to draw attention by activating their powers. Thus, a veneer of separation existed. The shining heroes weren't working together with the dastardly villains, they only by chance happened to hang out in the same general area without knowing. Plausible deniability was a wonderful concept.

Not to say that every single hero agreed with it. As he walked under the flickering lights, Jaune counted the number of frowning faces, finding it just shy of half. Much of that ire has shifted towards him, once they heard the steel of his boots ringing out on the concrete. He kept up an affable mien, not letting it get to him. They were allies.

He meant to head towards the heroes he identified as their leading figures based on yesterday—Armsmaster, Dauntless, Miss Militia. Except, a blur zipped across the space to cut off his path. Glory Girl was in the building, and she had other plans.

"Yo," was all he managed before the smiling heroine grabbed ahold of him. In a matter of seconds, he found himself facing a different set of superheroes, Glory Girl landing beside him.

The common threads of white, tight costumes individualized by personal themes and complete lack of masks tied these people together as a team. The distance between the members denoted closer relationships. Two sets of parents, two sets of children. It didn't take Jaune more than that to place them, though the presence of a familiar pair of siblings cemented their identities as the independent hero team New Wave.

Laserdream and Shielder looked a lot healthier than they would a few weeks from now. They were, he knew, wonderful and brave people, and he gave a small wave of his hand to acknowledge them. Shielder returned it, while Laserdream studied him with an inquisitive air.

"Everybody, this is the guy I've been talking about." Glory Girl flourished her hands at Jaune, presenting him like a prize.

Under their scrutiny, he did the first thing that came to mind.

"Anybody want a donut?" He held up the colorful boxes he brought along like a shield.

They were seized at once by Glory Girl as her just dues, with the heroine zeroing in on the store's special 'birthday cake' donut (showy, attention-grabbing). It's a mess of sprinkles and frosting that smothered the dough under their weight, and she scarfed down on the sugary abomination with relish as she passed the boxes on.

While his offerings made the rounds, one of the older women stepped forward. She declined a pastry, instead signaling to the Protectorate heroes. After receiving some unspoken form of assent in return, she focused on him. "Huntsman, right? A pleasure to be working with you. I'm Lady Photon—Sarah Pelham, out of costume." She extended her hand.

Jaune shook it. "Capitalize the M, but yes, that's me." Why do people keep giving him side eyes over this? "Happy to help out." He hesitated. "Should I…"

"Oh, no, please don't think you have to give your real name," said Lady Photon, anticipating his question. "It is simply the belief of New Wave that capes should be open about their identities, and I understand that many do not share that sentiment." She then smiled. "Although, I must admit I'm surprised to see you're not wearing a mask."

"Or a costume," added Laserdream, eyeing his poncho and jeans. She has yet to notice the smudge of strawberry frosting (whimsical, or perhaps eccentric) on the corner of her lips. It brought to mind of smeared lipstick, and lent her an erotic air.

He probably shouldn't mention that in front of her mother, though.

"The cape looks pretty, but it does kind of get in the way," he explained. "I reckon tonight calls for hardier clothes."

The outfit he wore yesterday was made for the stage, and a few good hits would tear the flimsy fabric to ribbons. He hadn't fancied the idea of giving everybody a free show.

"As for the mask, I've got nothing to hide. And on that note, my name's Jaune Arc."

Lady Photon's smile grew decidedly warmer. Behind her, a wave of consternation passed among the Protectorate heroes, who had been paying close attention.

That's right. No secrets here, folks.

A little part of him whispered that by revealing to them what seemed a startling revelation, they wouldn't think to ask about other minor details that were far more inconvenient. He didn't much like that part of him and, as he often did, ignored it.

Glory Girl chose this moment to chime in. "What did I tell you? Me and him are two peas in a pod, he has a forcefield, he dresses like Amy, and he even thinks like us! Tell me with a straight face he's not from our family!"

Unless her family was filled with duplicitous liars, he doubted it.

The older generation exchanged glances. They would be of an age with his own parents, Jaune estimated. In their forties or so. All blonds, and the women shared a distinct resemblance. Between the four of them, the lack of relation to him was quite noticeable, in his opinion.

"Ehhh, I don't know, Vicky," Laserdream said carefully. "I can sorta see what you're seeing, but none of our relatives have the name Arc."

"He might have kept his mother's maiden name!"

"I didn't."

"Quiet, you. That statement can't be proven, so it's not valid evidence. Of course, we do have one easy way to decide this." Adopting a honeyed lilt, she called, "Oh, Amy~!"

The person that shuffled out of the group, munching on the last morsel of her glazed donut (mild, inoffensive, sort of sticky), didn't seem to belong. Not to the Dallons, and not to the Pelhams. Rough brown hair peeked out from under her hooded robes. In contrast to the confident demeanor displayed by everyone else in her family, she walked with a slouch, trying her best to hide behind the red scarf wrapped around her neck. She wouldn't maintain eye contact with him, instead sending furtive glances at his face, at her feet, and at the corners of the parking garage. All in all, this girl gave the impression of someone dreadfully fretful and dour.

He cocked his head as he noticed something about her robes. A white base decorated with red crosses, the design fit the Panacea Poncho he was wearing to a tee.

Oh, dear. This was Panacea, wasn't it?

"For the record, I bought this poncho on whim," he quickly pointed out. "It was raining at the time, and I needed something to help me keep dry. I've never heard of her before in my life."

A victorious grin bloomed on Glory Girl's face. "What you call a whim is actually influenced by a bunch of unconscious decisions you're making in a split second. That's a pretty well-known facet of human psychology. Think about it. There are probably dozens of brands you could have chosen. Why did you pick a design that is specific to Panacea, arguably one of the most recognizable capes in New Wave? Hm?"

At this point, it was quite clear to him that Glory Girl had already made up her mind and was searching for confirmation in the littlest detail, discounting every contradiction that arose in the process. Even his silence was taken as proof, and she gleefully waved for Panacea to come closer.

"Show her your hand," she ordered. "Amy's powers let her understand a person's biology in order to heal them. With skin contact, she can read you down to your DNA, and match it against another person. Me, for example."

He gave the unassuming Panacea a second glance. That sounded powerful. Perhaps not in direct combat power, but it was perfectly geared for a doctor trying to suss out hidden injuries and illnesses. Some diseases were hereditary, weren't they? Could she detect them? Could she heal them?

Such capabilities, and they were going to use her as a glorified paternity test.

Meh. Fine with him. As far as he was concerned, this would bring the farce to a close. He felt a little bad for Glory Girl, since her desire for family carried with it a sense of innocent endearment, but that didn't prevent him from obliging the request, reaching out.

But then, as Panacea tried to take the offered hand, he pulled back. Their proximity had allowed him to note a most concerning stain on the sleeve of her white robes.

"Why do you have blood on your clothes?"

Panacea looked down, and groaned. "Damnit! I just had that washed." With a rueful shake of her head, she said, "Don't mind it. I was handling an emergency case before this."

He winced. "Ooh. Bad?"

"I don't want to talk about it," Panacea said, rather curtly.

"She's being modest," Glory Girl cut in. "The appointment was requested by Alexandria herself!"

She bragged as if that should mean something to him. His cool demeanor, borne of ignorance, seemed to impress the New Wave heroes.

Seeing it as a challenge, Glory Girl continued, "And, oh man, bad was underselling it. Apparently, Amy said they found the victim way late, so—"

"Vicky, quit it." Panacea sharply admonished. "It's not his business."

"Oh, come oooon."

"Enough, Vicky. Let your sister work," said Lady Photon.

A scowl stole over Glory Girl's face, but that lasted only until Panacea seized Jaune by his hand. The act proved a sufficient distraction for her to forget the earlier line of thought, since she was dying to know the answer to the mystery that was him.

He was expecting glowing hands, glowing eyes, an electric shock or two, anything to denote Panacea activating her powers. Nothing so dramatic took place, insofar as he could tell. The healer just stood there, observing his palm while Glory Girl flitted back and forth around them, unable to contain her eagerness.

Then, Panacea pressed her lips into a thin line, frowning at him. She waited, and when he didn't react, she spoke up.

"Drop your forcefield."

"...Pardon?"

"Your forcefield is in the way! I can't actually make contact with your skin, you need to bring it down."

He glanced to the side. His free hand came up to scratch his cheek.

Sheepishly, he muttered, "I can't."

"What!?" cried Glory Girl.

"The only time it breaks is after I'm beaten within an inch of my life."

There was a beat of silence.

"And we're not doing that," he added before Glory Girl could get ideas. The way she deflated suggested she was thinking exactly along those lines.

However, her smile returned in record time. "Wait, wait, wait." She flew in front of him, finger pointed right at his face. "Are you just saying that? Like, you can shut your forcefield off any time, but you're pretending you can't because it would prove me right?"

Aaand now people were coming around to Glory Girl's view all of a sudden, because he looked absolutely suspicious for sidestepping a conclusive, 100%-accurate test. Through the phone slung around his neck, he could hear the sound of laughter.

"I can show my family album."

"Then why don't you?"

Because he couldn't be sure what details people would glean from his scroll, or just the scene of his family' living room. Because he didn't need a hundred prying questions leading to the conclusion that he was an alien from outer space.

He couldn't win.

Burying his face in his hands, he asked, "Can we please just focus on dealing with the real reason we're here instead of your wild delusions? You know, Bakuda and bombs and all that?"

"Sure thing… cousin."

It was almost a relief to rush into battle.
