#2,520
Chapter 41: A Lazy Day, in Between​

Jaune laid on his bed, staring at the ceiling. In the wake of an encounter with the Outsider, it's only natural for a person to ruminate upon the past, present, and future, questioning the whole of their worldview.

…In truth, he has had ample time in the dream to do that and also spent the first ten minutes after waking up mulling over the same, along with the heady subjects of life, love, and the universe to round out his soul-searching. He got some great stuff out of it, too. Quippy lines that would make people's heads spin.

It's been about an hour since then, however, and his head was mostly empty at the moment. They were well into the morning by now, past time that he should start being productive.

There's just one little problem.

"I don't feel like going anywhere today," he said to the room.

Honest words pulled together to form a rather callous statement. His world hung in a precarious balance (probably) and he's the one person that could save it (probably). He dreamed of being a hero, and heroes don't rest in the stories.

Up on her bed, Lisa groaned. "Saaame."

Escha likewise gave a tired meow from her perch atop the cleaning robot puttering around the room.

It's nice that he wasn't alone in this.

"Want to stay in?" he asked.

Another groan, and another meow. He took that as their yeses.

-o-​

For breakfast, Jaune made crepes. A nice, uncomplicated dish to fit most palates.

Light shone as his fingers came in contact with the pan on the stove, in which a thin sheet of batter merrily sizzled. He noted with some chagrin that the him of yesteryear would not have committed such a mistake; the motion used to be far more smooth before his Aura was unlocked, its protection leading him to grow careless around the kitchen. Before the sensation of heat could cause him much pain, he pinched the batter and flipped it over to cook the other side. Once that had turned to a golden brown color, a flick of the pan sent the crepe cartwheeling through the air to join a stack of its brethren on a plate next to the stove.

Escha, crouched atop the counter, set aside the spoon in her paws to pick up a marker. She wrote on a piece of paper, then held it up to display a number.

An 8 out of 10. Not his best but not bad, either. Escha must have taken off points for the slight wobble in the flight path. Jaune accepted the score with good grace, performing an elegant bow to the judge. His lips quivered in suppressed laughter.

The felyne held no such reservations, giggling at his theatrics as she returned to the very important task of licking clean the spoon of its leftover cream. It's hard work, because Jaune made sure that a lot had stuck on after he finished whipping up a bowl of the stuff.

In his household, years ago, a spoon like that would have sparked a war among seven girls and a boy, each one deeming it as a wonderful treat. That became six girls and a boy when Saphron moved out, then just the girls as Jaune developed a knack for making the dish. Today, Escha enjoyed the prize by default, happily lapping up the cream as she watched him pour the next dollop of batter into the pan.

The point then and now, of course, was to distract hungry gremlins from the bowl of cream stowed in the fridge. Funny, how some things changed, while staying the same.

"Hey, Jaune?" Lisa called over. "Can I ask you a question?"

"What's up?" Jaune answered. He glanced behind him. Already at the table, Lisa had the Company scroll in her hand with the laptop set in front of her open to a spreadsheet. He recognized it as the one to keep track of their Point balances, going by the three columns of figures running down the page. (There wasn't one for Escha as she saw no need for it, her interest in what the Marketplace could offer starting and stopping at the pictures of fishes.)

"Why are we short on Points? It was at seven hundred last I checked."

Jaune winced. He knew he had forgotten something.

"Oh yeah," he said, affecting a carefree tone to try and play off the coming rebuke. "I bought a couple sets of stimpaks. Remember that bomb that went off downtown I texted you about? There were a bunch of people hurt by it. I was going to tell you, but then the whole mess last night happened."

Lisa didn't respond right away, and he could imagine her upset face looking at the back of his head as he kept cooking. After a bit, he heard her sighing. Computer keys clicked and clacked as she typed in the adjusted figures.

"Next time, tell me earlier. I need to know this stuff in case we have to make purchases in an emergency."

"I will, no worries," he quickly agreed.

"I'm serious. It could put us all in danger."

Another stab in his conscience. "Yeah. I'll do better."

"Make sure you do," she warned one final time. "Now, putting that aside, how do you feel about selling that big EMP bomb Bakuda made?"

"I'm all for it. There's really no situation I can see where I'd want to set it off, so the faster it's gone the easier I'll sleep." The device claimed too much space in his Pocket, but taking it out risked the chance of a detonation that would wrought destruction on a civilization level. Keeping it was not an option in his mind.

"None at all?" she asked. He was glad to hear that a teasing note had returned to her voice.

"It may surprise you, Lisa, but I don't plan on holding an entire continent ransom."

He felt a tug on his sleeve.

"Jaune, Jaune! We can ask for all the yummy fishies in the world!"

It's official. Escha was evil.

"Let's maybe not," he said, weakly. "I'm happy to buy you food whenever."

"Wouldn't work, anyway," Lisa added, eyes on the scroll. "Says here the bomb is unfinished. It's functional, but looks like you got to Bakuda before she managed to boost the range. This can only reach the city limits at most. What a shame; the completed version would have been worth a lot higher."

Jaune laughed along with Lisa's joke. Or rather, he laughed by himself.

…She was kidding, right?

The EMP bomb vanished from his Pocket to render his many concerns moot, bringing their balance to a whopping 9,600 Points. It drove him to giddiness seeing the number that high.

He also wondered who needed that level of armaments. Their foe would have to be great, indeed. Were there planets full of killer robots out in the multiverse? (He tried very hard to not think about the possibility that they just sold the bomb to a megalomaniacal supervillain; the chances of that were remote, he was sure.)

They continued on down the list. Most of Bakuda's other tinkertech explosives went the same way as their bigger cousin. The Tinker possessed a cruel streak, having designed the bombs in ways that made Jaune queasy. Entries in the scroll detailed the myriad effects of her work, from one that caused skins to fall off bodies to another that boiled people from the inside. He asked Lisa to keep the conventional explosives, the two or three devices that created a big fireball and nothing more exotic beyond that. Otherwise, the Points balance swelled further as his Pocket emptied. It bumped them up another 1,700 Points, all told.

Jaune paused his cooking to trade victory high-fives with Lisa and Escha. From a single trip, they've passed the ten thousand mark in one fell swoop.

Next up were the rifles. He had Lisa to thank for their addition. After seizing control of Coil's phone, she had arranged for delivery of the shipment, hence why a crate was sitting in the alley upon their exit. They shot lasers, which he admitted was pretty cool, and the pew-pew noise spoke to his very soul. However, their firepower underwhelmed him; the laser guns were a bit more effective than regular guns, that's all. Cleaner shots that burn through flesh, hampered by limited ammunition. Most of their value on the Marketplace came from aesthetics, by his reckoning.

Since nobody on their team was particularly enamored with the rifles, they decided on selling the lot. That netted them an extra 2,500 hundred Points.

But, that was not the end.

"You want to sell the halberd?" Lisa asked to confirm. "Not gonna hang it up on a wall as a trophy? God, I'd love to watch the look on Armsmaster's face if he knew."

"You know, now I'm kind of tempted." A dark thought crossed his mind. If the guy still has a face. "Ah well, the Points mattered more for us at the moment." Not to mention, he already had a memento in the collection of pictures saved on his scroll featuring their team striking various poses with the halberd, so it's no big loss letting go of the physical object. There were also a few bad memories associated with it that he'd prefer to not be reminded of everyday. "Do it, Lisa."

With a soft ding, the halberd faded from reality, and they became 3,200 Points richer. Lisa recorded the full balance based on the usual 1:3:1 split, with adjustments for the amount Jaune spent on his own which he had no leg to stand on to complain about. The end result was greeted by pleased smiles all around.

"I do enjoy seeing numbers go up," Lisa happily chirped.

The last crepe came off the pan and, buoyed by the good mood, their breakfast began on quite a high note.

Crepes could be either savory or sweet. Jaune preferred the latter for a lazy morning—it set the tone right. That meant cream and diced fruits (strawberries, bananas, and apples) to accompany the meal, with each person filling the thin pancakes to suit.

The fruits were less fresh than he would have liked. Living on the frontier, he had grown used to nearby farmers coming around with basketfuls of the choicest picks from their harvests, the stuff that people gifted to their close friends and neighbors before the rest got shipped off to the big city. These were… good enough, for a meal he whipped up on a whim. The centerpiece was a kiwi-looking fruit from Astera, which Escha insisted that both Jaune and Lisa taste. The tartness paired well with the crepe.

It did make him smile to see the cream was a big hit. He wouldn't call it a family recipe, more a regional thing with everybody in the settlement following the same basic steps. Still, every happy little hum his companions gave as they ate boosted his hometown pride.

A plate of shredded cabbages sat next to the other dishes, there for them to snack on so they could squeeze out every last Experience Point for their adventurer cards.

By chance, Lisa was looking at her card as she bit down on her crepe, and she struck upon a fortuitous discovery related to the leveling process. The flour and strawberries did nothing of note, but she earned a few points to her next level when she ate a slice of the kiwi. 'Bioenergy', 'soul', whatever people called them, there was an overlap somewhere that translated their properties, and it cemented Jaune's determination to seek out tasty dishes out in the multiverse.

Of course, he doubted the finest cuisine could beat the simplest method. It turned out that he was a higher level than the others, now. Lisa and Escha measured at level 3, a result that came about from the cabbages they've been consuming. He, on the other hand, clocked in at level 6. The guild receptionist back in Axel, Luna, informed him that killing foes yielded better points than food. Evidently, that included more than monsters—people were fair game.

He didn't quite know how to feel about the fact that a life could be reduced to numbers on a piece of paper, recorded as some sort of stepping stone to a prize, like one of those punch cards that would get him a freebie at shops he frequented often. To complicate matters, he harbored misgivings on if these levels were worth pursuing to begin with.

The skills gained from the cards worked in odd ways, ill-defined and limited. Yes, [Sense Rabbit] was a perfect ability that anyone anywhere could benefit from so long as killer rabbits continue to roam the land. [Markmanship] might be synergising with the gunlance, albeit he found it difficult to tell whether the sense of certainty he got when he aimed the cannon was due to the Skill, or just plain skill. It didn't guarantee a hit. He definitely can miss his targets, seen during the fight with Lung and Armsmaster; good aiming couldn't stop opponents from moving around.

And then there was [Set Bait Trap] to round out his current repertoire. What did it do, and how did it work? He had no clue. Certainly, the cardboard box propped on a wooden stick tied to a large strawberry he had arranged on the table possessed all the elements of the skill. The baited trap was set.

Yet, the bitterbug Escha retrieved from the terrarium was sitting near it now and the big, blue beetle showed no interest in taking the bait. For all intents and purposes, the Skill bore zero effects.

He tried poking the bug. It crawled a little further away in the complete opposite direction of the box. Beyond that, there appeared no visible developments to either the trap or the bug besides causing Lisa to scoot her chair to maintain distance from the insect, thoroughly creeped out by its skittering limbs.

That disgust reminded him of something he had been meaning to ask her.

"How come you're no good with bugs, but were okay with spiders?"

"Eh? What do you—" She stopped. Green eyes flicked up from the laptop screen, looking over at him. "Where did you hear that from?"

He dusted off the last bite of his crepe, and gave a shrug. "Glory Girl brought it up that the Undersiders sicced a bunch of spiders on people at the bank you robbed."

"Of course she did. That idiot loves to run her mouth."

Trying hard not to frown, he affected casualness. "Did it really happen?"

"Yes, it did," she replied without the slightest pause, and observed him carefully.

"Lisa…" He searched for the best way to put this. It's important that Lisa didn't think he was accusing her. Whatever else, he considered her his friend. "What the hell?"

Nailed it.

The girl rolled her eyes, putting on a little grin. She sat straighter in her seat.

"Hmm. I'm sensing some discontent. Did Glory Girl put nasty ideas in your head about mean, old Tattletale? Personally, I wouldn't have gone to a person with an agenda if I wanted to hear an honest take." She raised up her hands. "But, I mean, that's just me. You might be different."

Ouch. She's all kinds of prickly today.

"Look, it's not that I'm believing other people—"

"Aren't you?" she asked, a tad shirty.

"I'm not basing my entire opinion on it, is what I'm trying to say," he amended. "But I am curious." He held up his hand, pinching the thumb and index finger together. "Maybe a tiny bit concerned, too. There was mention of hostages."

Sitting on the table, Escha nodded along with him. Nervous, she nibbled on her crepe, employing it as cover to hide her face behind.

Lisa closed her laptop. "Alright, fine. Let's have this conversation."

A brief moment passed in silence as she regarded him with a cool air. Her nails tapped a rapid beat on the table.

"I want you to consider a hypothetical," she began.

"What does this have to do with the spider thing?"

"Humor me. Assume you're going into a fight. Now, you have the option of using your Aura, or you can pilot a giant robot to do it. Which do you choose?"

Jaune pondered the question as he assembled another crepe for his plate, spooning a couple chunks of apples atop the thin pancake and adding a dollop of cream. He didn't start on eating it, instead leaning back in the seat.

Either option sounded like a trap, but the giant robot offered a breadth of destructive potential that he couldn't match on his own.

"I'd take the robot."

"It doesn't come with a manual," Lisa added, causing Jaune to falter.

"Ah. Well, okay, that's a little more complicated, then."

"Because you might lose control of the robot, right? Better to rely on Aura than risk it?" Lisa continued in one breadth. "What people don't understand is that Skitter can achieve complete, total control over her bugs. Bugs for her are like Aura for you. She can make them reenact a ballroom dance, were she so inclined. Got that?"

"Can she—"

"Yes," Lisa declared with utmost certainty, despite [Blank] ensuring his thoughts were a closed book to her. "Within her range, insects become an extension of her mind. They can't do anything she doesn't want them to." Suddenly, Lisa snickered. She slapped a hand on the table before pointing at him. "But that's not the real issue for you, is it? No, it's about me."

"You're the planner," Jaune said, confirming the deduction. "If Skitter wanted to use venomous spiders and take hostages, that had to run through you. You wouldn't make the mistake of overlooking it."

"Flatterer. You give me too much credit." Lisa feigned shyness, squirming from side to side. She dropped the act in the next second, speaking fast. "I did give Skitter the okay, to tell the truth. Do you have black widow spiders in your world?"

Jaune nodded. "If you mean the ones with the long, creepy legs and that red hourglass on their backs, then yeah. We don't get them around my region, but I've seen them in movies. They bite people."

"They do, they definitely do. So, answer me this. In what cases are they deadly?"

"Every case," he said at once.

"Bzzt. Wrong. They have, like, less than a one percent mortality rate in my country."

Jaune balked. "Wait, what? No way! They're some of the deadliest spiders out there!"

"Yes way," asserted Lisa. "Movies push the story that they're sacs full of venom leaping at your face, but black widows pose a danger mostly to children and the elderly, people who are already pretty off-limits when it comes to a bank robbery. And I took that into account beforehand. We were at the bank on a school day, at lunch time. Older folks like to go in the morning when the lines are shorter, because a lot of them can't wait on their feet for that long. Children don't have a reason to be in a bank at all, and especially not during school hours. The plan was designed so that the chances of anyone getting hurt is so remote, it's nearly impossible." She sat back in her chair, plucking a strawberry and popping it in her mouth, a grin still present. This time, of satisfaction.

On the one hand, what she claimed sounded reasonable. He could follow the steps in her logic. On the other, he lacked a frame of reference to determine if that's true or not. He didn't go to banks.

A look at Escha earned him no help. She didn't seem to know what a bank was in the first place, her behavior indicating a cat that was thoroughly lost.

There was a spot of cream on her nose. That, she understood, and it has begun to occupy much of her attention.

"Glory Girl was so freaked out about it, though," Jaune said, just to have something to say.

Lisa shook her head. "Black widows look scary and have a bad rep. That's exactly why Skitter brought them, and why she told the people inside the bank how 'dangerous'"—she formed air quotes—"the spiders clinging onto them were, so none of them would think of trying stupid heroics. Because 'everybody knows' that black widow spiders are absolute killers. They weren't in any real danger, it was just—"

"Fear, like playing ghosts!" Escha exclaimed, perking up with a relieved smile on her face.

Jaune stared down at his plate. He took a bite of his food, not quite tasting it. "Fear, like the Grimm."

Lisa quickly raised a finger to object. "More what Escha pointed out. It's a valid strategy." She fidgeted when he didn't agree. "It just makes sense."

"Against an enemy, I guess," Jaune said. "Not a civilian."

Spreading terror among the populace? There's a very real reason the White Fang were so reviled. Fear in one's heart summoned fear in monstrous forms.

The girl leaned forward, palms on the table. "Did you think people were actually scared? They were gonna go home with a story to tell, none the worse for wear, and they knew it. Cape fights are a show, and the money we stole would be taken care of by insurance. It's all theatrics."

"Bakuda's victims would disagree with you."

"Bakuda is an outlier. She's legitimately insane."

"She's still a cape. It can't be fun and games as you claim when a city might get blown up whenever."

"No, you don't get it," she argued. "A lot of capes aren't in a good headspace, but they're better than her. They understand the rules to this game of cops and robbers we play. At that bank, do you know what would have inspired more fear, and been deadlier?"

"More spiders?"

"Hehe!" She clamped down on the unbidden laugh. "No, silly man. I'm talking about guns. The weapon that the vast majority of bank robbers prefer to use when committing their crimes. You make a spider bite someone's face, they'll probably survive and fight back. You shoot someone in the face, they die. If we had gone that route, I guarantee you the response from the authorities would be different; they wouldn't have messed around with sending in the Wards team. In their eyes, we were playing kiddie games."

"I… Okay, I can see that. They can't be crazy enough to send a twelve-year-old into a hail of bullets," he said, thinking of Vista. "Although, Glory Girl told me you shot her."

Which meant a gun was involved.

"Shot once. At a girl with a forcefield that can take a bullet. I knew how her power works, and tailored my actions accordingly. In any other circumstance, the gun would have stayed in my purse. Hang on one moment."

She opened up her laptop, and Jaune heard her fingers dancing on the keyboard. A final click, and she turned the screen around for him to look.

After a while, he spoke. "Lisa, what am I looking at here?"

"My gun. At least, a similar model," Lisa answered, her smile widening.

Jaune studied the stubby object again. He hesitated to call it a handgun, as it was smaller than the hand in the picture with an almost nonexistent barrel. To his knowledge, a rough measure of the caliber placed it between puny and laughable. It wouldn't kill a Grimm even after a hundred rounds.

"That's your gun?" he asked, incredulous.

"Sure. Uh-huh."

"I'd be more scared of the spiders than that."

"Right? It's not good for much except to make someone think 'Gun!' and then panic. That's the entire point of it!"

"Fear," he repeated, but it lacked the previous sensation of a pit in his stomach.

"Shock," Lisa corrected. "A jumpscare, if your world has the concept of horror movies."

"We do, but…"

He didn't really have an idea of where he was leading with that. The image of the weapon simply failed to register as a threat. Even without Aura, he was confident that he could take on someone armed with that gun.

Lisa waited to see if he would continue, before replying, "There are rules, and I'm always mindful to toe the line. If anything, it's Glory Girl that broke it. She pulled my arm out of its socket that day. I had to pop it back in before I could make my escape." She caught his wince. "Yeah, it wasn't fun for me, and waaay overboard. The whole debacle came down to Glory Girl taking it too seriously. She acted like the Undersiders used Grimm to rob a bank, when it was just bugs. It's stupid."

Despite himself, Jaune gave a small laugh. Put that way, he had to agree that it seemed excessive. One was the reason why people cry, and sleep with the lights on. The other was considered pests at worst. There's no comparing the two, beside the spider Grimm that lives in Vacuo.

"So… Are we okay?" Lisa asked.

He composed himself, and leveled a serious look at her. "Please, don't ever think I'll be fine with taking hostages, even as a charade."

"Yup. Never would. I'm not that kind of girl anymore," she assured him.

"Then—"

*Thud*

"Ahhh!"

He, and Lisa, snapped their gazes to the box that was now sliding every which way on the table. Escha's cries emanated from within.

The box soon reached the edge, and went over to take Escha along with it. Between her paws, she held a strawberry. The fruit had tempted her before it did the bitterbug, it seemed, thus springing the trap.

A brief silence followed, before the pair still sitting at the table burst out laughing.

"Yeah, we're okay," Jaune said, before getting up to check on the felyne.

After making sure that Escha was unhurt, which was rather perfunctory considering her Aura, their day continued on.

Plants needed watering, and insects needed feeding. Both had survived well during their absence, sheer vitality overcoming the shortfall in sustenance. That did not save Jaune from rebuke, of course, and he received quite a lecture by Escha as he helped her tend to her garden.

Lisa, meanwhile, worked on the analytical side of things. Leveling up the adventurer cards had granted them skill points. They've agreed to save them up for the moment, since the abilities available at this time were of dubious use. The increased stats fascinated her, however, and she insisted on setting down benchmarks so they could estimate their future progress, which translated to a bunch of graphs on the laptop.

Jaune assumed she was doing actual work, and left her to it.

Training took the better part of the afternoon. Besides the usual conditioning and combat skills, he added the beginnings of ground-fighting to the mix. Where to strike, what to watch out for, and the like. There were no spars on that front yet, to Lisa's great relief. (She complained enough about the regular sparring, anyhow.)

It culminated in the first ever ranking tournament among their team. They kept it light, with Jaune going very easy on the others—literally, strapping one hand behind his back. Even then, he restrained himself to gentle shoves, simply testing out his companions' defenses to see where they stand in their training. Lisa and Escha went at it with more seriousness for their bout.

Lisa lost that one. She accepted the defeat with the grace she was known for.

Evening arrived, and it was decided that their newest member would get the first movie viewing in her life. Escha had no real clue of what they were talking about, but was eager to experience it.

Lacking popcorn for snacks, they made do with cabbages.

…Lisa sent him into the kitchen to scrounge up a spread of cheeses and meats.

Anyway, as darkness fell outside the window, Jaune turned off the lights and sat down on one side of the couch, Lisa on the other. Escha chose to plop herself between them. On the table before them rested the laptop.

The opening scene played, and from then on Escha was hooked. With an open-mouthed smile, she bounced on the cushion as she followed the story, paws waving up and down in uncontrolled excitement.

Neither he nor Lisa were familiar with the movie, but she told him a few minutes in that it's 'basically Mulan in space'. Whatever that meant, he enjoyed it. The animation style was charming, the songs were catchy, and the plot that was shaping up resonated with him. He's all for a story where an ill-qualified nobody defrauded their way into an army, learning the relevant skills on the job to shore up the gap and, presumably, grow into a hero by the end.

Hell yeah, he was rooting for the girl on the screen.

And giant robots were cool. Let's not forget that.

At around the midway point, where events were taking a dramatic turn, he peeled his eyes from the movie to look at Lisa.

"I've been meaning to ask," he said quietly. "Are you better now?"

"Hm?" She turned to meet his gaze.

"Yesterday, when we were talking over the phone, you became kind of… off. And once we met up, it looked like you had been crying."

He expected a scoff, maybe a biting retort. He froze as Lisa gave a long sigh and rested her head on his shoulder. Her legs curled up onto the couch.

"That was because I lost my powers."

"What!?" he yelped.

Below, Escha shushed him. She hadn't paid any attention to the conversation.

"Then I got it back," Lisa added, to give him pause.

"Oh. That's… good?" Jaune settled down a little. It still seemed a matter that warranted a lot of panicking, but the girl's calm demeanor threw him off. "How did you lose it in the first place?"

"Well, I always thought the migraines were a result of using my brain too hard. That's the prevailing theory for Thinker headaches," Lisa explained in a murmur as she returned her gaze to the movie. "After I turned on [Blank], I didn't get them anymore."

"I know. You were over the moon about it."

She nodded, though their position made it look more like she was rubbing her cheek against his shoulder. "It was amazing. That whole day in Brockton Bay, I let my power run free for every little thing. I used it nonstop, just because I could."

"And when did it shut off?"

"I… I'm not sure. I didn't realize it was gone at first. It felt like normal, you know? But then you asked me to help with Lung, and the details kept slipping my mind. I looked up, and suddenly I couldn't tell what the people surrounding me would do next." She shivered. "Scariest sight I've ever seen."

Jaune turned off [Blank].

Lisa giggled. "You're fine. By now, I can read you like a book no matter what."

"Is that a good thing? I don't feel like that's a good thing."

"It is."

For his peace of mind, [Blank] came back on.

"So, what does it mean?" he asked. "You said you got your powers back. Is it just on the fritz, then?"

"What does [Blank] do, Jaune? What is it built for?"

"It prevents mind-reading."

"Not exactly right, but close enough. It doesn't matter much, because the question we should be asking is this: by whom."

Lisa's migraines faded away after she activated [Blank] for herself. What did that imply?

"Oh, boy," Jaune muttered.

"Mmhm. People believe that Thinker headaches are failsafes to prevent our brains from overheating. I'm starting to suspect that they're wrong."

That her power was not hers alone. That someone or something else had a hand on the lever. Until that ceased working, in which case they resorted to the on/off button.

"I'm still figuring out the reasons why the migraines occur, and why my powers came back. It's a bit worrying, but I'll deal with it."

"You could—and this is just a suggestion—you could shut your powers down for good. That'll solve the problem."

"Can't. It's what I bring to the table."

"That doesn't matter. You're a part of this team, with or without it. You understand that, right?"

"I know," she replied with a tiny grin. "I want to solve this mystery, though. Maybe there will be an answer waiting ahead to explain everything, and a solution. So, I'll stick with it."

Faced with that determination, Jaune could only say one thing.

"Got it. Let me know how I can help."

And with that, all was settled. For now.

The pair returned their attention to the laptop screen. What fears and doubts they had, they pushed to tomorrow so that they may enjoy the night. Perhaps it's a foolish, short-sighted notion. Sue them, they were young.

"...Are you going to keep your head like that?"

"Yep. You have comfortable shoulders. Problem?"

"No, no. I've heard that said before. I'm just starting to wonder if I haven't picked up two cats instead of one."

Her hand lightly batted at him.

"See, that's not really convincing me otherwise. Escha, you agree, don't you—"

A furry paw slapped over his mouth.

"Shoosh," Escha said. Her eyes were riveted on the movie, filled with wonder.

Jaune and Lisa shared a look, and smiled.

Chapter 42: This is a Drinking Travel Story​

On the first day, they rested. On the second, they prepared.

On the third, bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, they were back at it again. A new world awaited.

-o-​

Danger Rating 0. What did that mean? Well, they wanted to find out.

Here, it meant a bright blue sky and the sparkling sea. It meant cheerful passersby and smiles. Jaune sat on the concrete balustrade dividing the road from the water, eyes shut as he leaned back to enjoy the warm breeze; the temperature was perfect for shorts and a t-shirt. He listened to the ocean waves crashing onto shore, his breaths matching to the rhythm.

Despite how vulnerable he appeared at the moment, nothing in the surrounding environment tried to attack him. The people walking by were content to leave him be, with neither street toughs nor inquisitive lawmen deciding to accost him on such and such pretext. In fact, there were not even raised voices to ruin his mood, the sound of pedestrians a murmur compared to the cawing seagulls. It's a far cry from the sort of raucous din that one got in a city like Vale.

Almost an hour in, and he has yet to find trouble.

How peaceful.

Hearing a sigh next to him, Jaune cracked open an eye. Escha was also squatting on the balustrade, stretching her body luxuriously as she enjoyed all this open air so unlike the box that was their quarters. She looked twice as fluffy as usual, her fur whipped up by the wind.

"What do you think, Escha?"

"It's shoooo relaxing…" Escha answered, her little tail swishing at a lazy pace.

Jaune gave a light chuckle. "It is. It really is. I've been waiting for the other shoe to drop, but I'm starting to think it never will. Would you want to live in a place like this?"

Escha placed a paw under her chin, mulling over the idea. She panned her gaze across their surroundings, noting in particular the fishing boats far out off the coast and the ample shades provided by the palm trees lining the street.

"I don't see any monsters," she said. "It's weird."

"Good weird or bad weird?"

"Good!"

The clues were there. People didn't go armed and ready for a fight to break out. Ships traveled the ocean unopposed, with not a single cannon in sight. These big aircrafts would arrive from other lands, and they were plagued with a distinct absence of Nevermores, dragons, and other nasty beasts.

And if he needed confirmation beyond what his eyes could see, then the newspaper by his hand was it. The articles were in Japanese, so he had to rely on a text-translation app on his phone to turn the random lines he scanned over into understandable words. The haphazard way he went about it meant that he missed huge segments of details, but he got the gist.

The newspaper reported on heavy topics like which team won the baseball game last night, the alarming prevalence of college drinking, and the state of the economy. The world news section spoke of troubles in far-off lands with a sense of detachment, urging humanitarian aid and an 'international response' as the solutions. No mention of sending in the Huntsmen/capes/adventurers/espers, no warnings of Grimm/Endbringer/cabbages/memetic virus.

Danger Rating 0. A little corner of the world, at peace.

"Okinawa, huh?" he said half to himself, looking out across the wide sea as sunlight glinted off the water. "Grand blue, indeed…"

"Ja~aune, Es~cha! I'm back!"

The pair twisted in their seats to look behind, spotting Lisa waving to them as she crossed the street.

And it was Lisa, rather than Tattletale, because the girl had swapped out her costume within five minutes of their arrival—it would have stood out too much. In place of the skintight bodysuit, she wore a light jacket over white camisole, plus a long skirt. With her hair in a bun, the ensemble rather lent the impression of a sweet, modest girl from a well-to-do family.

Well, she was rich, at least.

"Did you manage to pawn off the coins?" Jaune asked. They still owned a good supply of the gold coins to fund their travels, not to mention the gold bar.

Lisa directed a sly grin at him, and held up her hands. Two thick sheaves of paper bills spread out, decorated with stylized borders and art; the number '10,000' was printed on the front-most bill.

"Who do you think I am? It went off without a hitch, of course," she bragged. "They think I'm either a lucky tourist that found sunken treasure, or CIA—a secret agent," she explained for his benefit. With a smug grin, she began fanning herself with the sheaves of money. "I haggled for us a pretty nice rate, so we're living the good life today."

"Nice!" Jaune cheered.

What was the point of going to a Danger Rating 0 world? In a word, house-hunting. They needed a base, a world they could retreat to where they face little risks to their lives. This was their first chance to experience one such place.

That said, while safety ranked among the chief considerations, it was far from the sole factor. Ready access to daily necessities and food counted for a lot. Comfort and peace of mind, too. Living mattered.

Lisa put it best. Remnant didn't need a neurotic husk of a man, stolen of hope and joy. A person like that… might never reach the finish line.

With a shudder, Jaune shoved those dark thoughts aside. Now was the time to be happy. Everyday was a time to be happy. He put on a smile, and swung off the balustrade.

"Well, no sense sitting around. What's our next step, Lisa?"

"I asked the guy from the pawnshop about places to stay, and he pointed me to a rental agency. I went there and flashed some cash to book us a house for a few days. It's a few miles down the coast. We'll grab a taxi there."

Finding a taxi cost them all but a minute. The area had a dozen of them lying in wait for tourists like their group, pouncing upon them the moment they stepped up to the edge of the sidewalk. They piled into the backseat, with Escha feigning normal cat-ness from then on, and away they went.

The entire drive, Jaune had his face pressed to the glass.

Cities—plural—dotted the long, curved coastline, and he marveled at their construction for they never seemed to have an end. The neighborhoods may grow sparse at the outskirts, but homes lay scattered deep into the forest and mountains, with not a single defensive wall to be seen. The nearby islands had been populated, with boats docked in piers or hotels rising high above the trees. Civilization continued on as far as the eyes could see, unbound from borders. From fear.

It's beautiful.

All too soon, they arrived at their destination.

The place Lisa rented pressed right up against a small beach, with a footpath leading from the house down to the water. Jaune stepped inside to a comfortable space that could have accommodated a few more people than just him, Lisa, and Escha. The design featured a great deal of white—white tiles, white walls, and so on. Clean and tidy, it lacked the lived-in feeling of a real home, but he supposed it was suited for guests seeking a short stay with no fuss.

Escha bounded up the stairs to explore the second floor. Jaune followed her to find the felyne in one of the bedrooms, bouncing up and down on the bed. That left two other rooms for the taking, and he picked the larger one for himself. Lisa was sure to protest, so he staked his claim by pulling some of his belongings from his Pocket and dropping them about.

Once that was done, he returned to the first floor with Escha on his heels. A quick run through the kitchen and a storage room, and their exploration came to an end to put them back in the main living room, staring through the glass of the wide patio doors.

"There's a pool here!" he exclaimed. It's a small one, meant more for relaxation than serious swimming. Even so, he couldn't remember the last time he had been in a pool, and could hardly wait to jump in.

Lisa, who was lounging on the couch and browsing the inter-net with her phone, read his intention the instant he reached for the door handle.

"Hey now," she called out to him. "Let's leave that for later. I want to head into the town."

"Oh? Anything you're looking for in particular?" he asked.

Lisa shook her head. "Just to check on prices and goods. You can tell a lot about a country by what's available for people to buy. I'm reading up on headlines and things, but a firsthand look will help me get a better sense of day-to-day life. There's no guarantee this world doesn't have problems."

Right, because they've visited multiple Earths and witnessed wild divergences between them. Lisa's knowledge might well not apply, especially if they considered that this was the other side of the planet from her home.

"I'm down for that," he said, nodding. "We've been cooped inside for days, and I'd rather not sit around any longer than I have to. Are we walking?"

"It's not far. There's a market, like, a couple blocks over and a shopping street near that."

He should have known it wouldn't be so simple. By the second hour, checking prices had become Lisa browsing clothing racks for deals and trying on outfits, and it occurred to Jaune that his companion was simply indulging in her hobby, with him present to carry her bags—a task in which he excelled due to his dimensional pocket. All the space he managed to make was now slowly filling up again, with additional bags sitting by his feet that Lisa had in no uncertain terms warned him to keep his eyes off of.

Years of experience allowed him to take it in good stride, better than Escha at any rate.

"Jaune, I'm boooored…" the felyne said, wiggling on her back as she laid on a chair.

Jaune reached down and rubbed her head. "It's just a little longer."

"You said that twice already!"

He averted his gaze from the accusing glare, knowing full well that Lisa would be at it for hours yet. She was at the back of the store, talking to the clerk in an animated fashion, presumably about fashion. She wore an unguarded expression that he thought suited her. It softened her features.

Spotting him looking, Lisa gave a small wave of her hand. He returned the gesture, and when she raised a pair of jeans, her head cocked to silently ask his opinion, he showed a thumbs-up. Satisfied, she made for the fitting room.

"What was different about those pants?" Escha asked curiously. "It looks the same as the last pair."

"Bigger holes, bigger tears, more fraying at the knees," Jaune listed out.

"Oh! So it's cheaper!"

He held up a hand to stop her there. "Now, I didn't say that. If this is anything like home, that pair of jeans would sell at a premium."

The idea threw Escha for a loop, and she stopped fidgeting to ponder this over.

"I dun get it…" was the conclusion she arrived at. She stared up at him, expecting him to explain.

He, simply, shrugged. No fashion guru, was Jaune Arc.

(Well, that wasn't really the truth. Nora once mentioned how the tears and frays told a story. That they insinuate. What, he never asked, but the way Nora waggled her eyebrows in Ren's direction while saying that told him enough.)

Lisa exited of the fitting room, the pair of jeans slung over an arm. She dropped it in the pile of clothing marked for purchase, and left the task to the clerk while she rejoined them. Her outfit had changed, the skirt switched with shorts to give her a lively air.

"Oh. My. God! This place is such a find!" she gushed. "I can't believe some rinky-dink shopping street on a tiny island had so many good choices!"

Jaune laughed, and said, "I am a bit jealous of it. My hometown had—has three clothing shops, and we thought that made us the fashion capital of the region." The sheer breadth of options on display here was best compared to that in the city of Vale, which he maintained beat out Earth on overall style and uniqueness. Pricier, though.

Lisa nodded. "Brockton Bay isn't at that level of pathetic ("Oi!"), but a bunch of the malls closed down over the years. Everybody does their shopping on the Boardwalk, and their selection is never that great. I didn't realize how bad the clothing industry has gotten until now. It always seemed normal even before I dropped by the east coast."

And wasn't that telling? A spot outside the island's main city, an island that by all accounts numbered just one among many that formed the country of Japan, could afford to ship in premium goods. Meanwhile, the America of Lisa's universe had gone for years with inferior merchandise, long enough that it became the norm.

An Earth like this held promise. It's a treasure trove in a very mundane sense.

The clerk finished bagging Lisa's new clothes. Money exchanged hands, and Jaune moved to pick up the lot while they chatted. Seeing him walk to the door, Escha clambered off her chair; she made sure to stay on four legs to give the impression of a normal, albeit large, cat. Eager to leave, she shoved against the heavy glass door to nudge it open.

Jaune felt a tug on his clothes, pulling him up short.

"Where are you going?" Lisa asked when he turned back.

"...Out?" he said with a touch of uncertainty.

Lisa went around him, planting her hands on his back and pushing him away from the door. "Nuh-uh, we're not done. It's your turn now."

Jaune frowned, and dug in his heels. Lisa came to a sudden stop, unable to budge him.

"I don't need new clothes, I've got plenty."

"How are you gonna swim without swim trunks, genius? Go naked?"

Instantly, the clerk was by their side, adding her strength to Lisa's in order to push him deeper into the store.

"I would be happy to help you! Please, come this way. We have a new line of top-branded, competitive swimwear that would be perfect for you."

"Oh?" Jaune asked, somewhat curious.

"Yes, it is a highly efficient style engineered to minimize drag and reduce space in your luggage."

That, admittedly, sounded convenient. "I guess I can take a look."

With a piteous meow, Escha let go of the door. She flopped on the ground, and laid there motionless for the next hour.

For… reasons, Jaune rejected the swimwear choices recommended to him, and opted for what he thought was more his style. White trunks with printed palm leaves in red, reaching his knees—the latter a firm requirement despite vehement protest from all corners.

Much of their afternoon was spent at the fish market where Escha, that shameless cat, performed an immediate about-face. She insisted that they linger at each market stall to take in the scent of the fish on offer, meowing in protest should they try to move on before she could study in great depth the choicest cuts of that day's catch. Any offer of free samples must be accepted, the wares tasted and reviewed.

Felynes possessed a wider range of expressiveness than normal cats, and Escha stretched that to the limits, directing soulful eyes that should never have been possible toward the shopkeepers. Those who proved magnanimous in feeding her were treated to darling purrs that strung together in what almost sounded like music.

It was. In a reverie, Esha had by accident broken into a rendition of her 'I Has Fish' song. People overlooked it, since cats couldn't sing.

The market made good money on them that day, as Escha clamored for Jaune and Lisa to buy pound after pound of fish. By sunset, Jaune once again found his Pocket filled near to the brim with clothes and tuna, prompting a trip back to the rental house to stow them away.

A fish tank set against one wall featured a number of tropical species in varying sizes and hues, adding a splash of color to the wooden tones of the shop.

The restaurant seemed popular, because in a span of ten minutes since their arrival, it grew from a few scattered groups of customers to a boisterous crowd. The room became so loud that Jaune nearly missed the waiter setting down their food, the clatter of plates lost in the din.

It's a stark contrast from the polite demeanor of pedestrians they pass by throughout the morning and afternoon. He preferred this, in truth.

"Japan sure is different between day and night, huh?" Jaune commented as they began eating. The local specialty turned out to be a braised pork belly dish, stewed in sauce and cut into cubes. They seemed nice.

They were college students in an engineering program, and for Jaune it was a fascinating look at the civilian life he could have led. There's a splendor to the pursuit of higher learning, where one delved into the mysteries of the world among like-minded fellows. According to Iori, the classes taught them far more than basic facts and figures. It has helped them to value hard work and discipline, along with the development of creative thinking. Exams, a word that always brought dread to Jaune, were to them an exciting chance to put their skills into practice.

Too late, the thought had been planted.

"They do have this easy familiarity between them," admitted Chisa.

Aina chimed in, "They're both blond, too."

"So is he." Lisa pointed at Kohei. "And blond hair isn't that uncommon overseas. We're not related!" she insisted, to deaf ears.

So far as the other boy was concerned, this one tidbit has put them on the same side. It seemed younger siblings were a menace no matter which world they exist in.

As for Kohei…

"She's his little sister… but she doesn't want to be… they're not blood-related?... unforgivable…"

Welp, he didn't need super-intuition to understand that. Their haphazard excuses had struck the boy in a critical weakpoint (fetish).

Lisa's face was one of disgust, and the girl whirled on him. "Your nonsense is putting the wrong idea in people's heads. Fix this!"

"How?"

"By forfeiting your life!" shouted Kohei, leaping for him.

Jaune put out a hand to seize him by the throat, stopping him in his tracks. Kohei's rage transformed into confusion as he tried to escape only to be unable to budge Jaune's arm. After a short and futile struggle, the boy dangled limply off the ground.

"I changed my mind," Kohei managed to croak out, and Jaune put him down.

He glanced at his surroundings in order to see what the reaction to the sudden outbreak of violence would be. To his surprise, nobody batted an eye, accepting it as normal—natural, even. It cast doubt on Lisa's claim that people on Earth were a lot gentler in how they interact with each other than on Remnant, and raised his score for this universe by a couple of points. The kind of world Lisa described as ideal sounded a tad boring.

The boy quickly shook his head. "Nope, I'm good. No problem with you at all. Uh, but you might want to keep an eye on Kohei. He's what you Americans would call a backstabbing son of a bitch."

Lisa's protests that she was neither a little sister nor harboring romantic thoughts once again went ignored.

Jaune tensed as Kohei stepped up to him.

"I challenge you to a Peek-a-Boo style contest. The loser will give the title of older brother to the winner—" A hearty slap from Iori cut Kohei off, and he amended his words. "The loser will face punishment."

In the background, the rest of Club Peek-a-Boo stopped what they were doing, and roared their approval for this bold challenge.

He was starting to really like this bunch. They reminded him of Beacon.

"I accept!" he answered with just as much enthusiasm.

"Then—!" Two cups landed on the table beside them, filled to the brim. Kohei grabbed one. "First comes the oolong tea! Bottoms up!"

Jaune didn't question it, taking his own cup and downing the drink in one go.

His vision blurred.

He next regained consciousness still standing before Kohei. Only, they weren't where they had been mere moments ago. No, they've moved to the center of the restaurant, encircled by a crowd. The people around them were chanting as one, counting down.

"Whuh? What happened?"

"Heheheheh, you absolute fool!" said Kohei. He had a fist chambered behind his back. What for? "PAB-Style 'oolong tea' is a blend of vodka and whiskey."

What part of that is tea?

"If you want to blame someone, blame your naive self, lightweight. This battle had already begun!"

With that, Kohei launched his fist.

Instincts took over, and Jaune retaliated with a punch of his own, a sharp and textbook blow that can lay a civilian out in one shot. He doubted Kohei could see it, let alone block.

Yet by some unknown method, the other boy dodged the hand with barely an effort. Jaune could have sworn the boy had not even moved, like it was Jaune who missed. There was no time to think about it, however. He braced for Kohei's attack.

"My paper beats your rock!" Kohei crowed in triumph, the fingers on his hand splayed wide.

Jaune needed an embarrassing amount of time to reach understanding. The battle he had been challenged to, that he almost knocked a person's teeth out in, was nothing more than a game of Rock, Paper, Scissors.

Iori emerged from among the spectators, and handed him a cup.

"Sorry man. You lose the round, you drink."

He peered into the cup. "This isn't 'oolong tea' again, is it?"

"Haha, no way. During a contest, we prefer to use Spirytus instead."

Jaune confirmed that the color was different. Reassured, he took a sip… and spat it back out, coughing and hacking.

"Yeah, Spirytus is a lot stronger than our oolong tea," Iori continued. He patted Jaune on the back before walking away, neatly dodging the cup Jaune attempted to press into his hands. "Good luck. I have my own match to get through, so let's hope we meet on the other side."

"I can't drink this! I think it peeled the skin off the roof of my mouth!" He gagged as he saw Iori snatching a bottle from a table to fill a cup for himself and gulped it down like water.

Across from him, Kohei smirked. "How weak. You're no big deal after all. Heheheh."

The boy strutted back and forth before the crowd. Believing that he had already won, Kohei basked in the cheers raining on him from every corner. The fact that he used an underhanded trick did not faze him, or the spectators.

The sound of drinking interrupted his swaggering. Kohei turned around to see Jaune upending the contents of the cup down his throat.

It was no easy task. The liquid burned as it traveled to his stomach at the same time that it seemed to shoot straight up to his head. He could smell nothing but the stench of the alcohol, and it was impossible to stop the tears streaming from his eyes. He had never tasted a drink so foul.

Calling it quits wasn't in the cards, though.

Finally, he pulled the cup away from his lips, holding it upside-down to show there were only drops remaining. The crowd roared his name.

Jaune swayed as he sneered at Kohei, who no longer looked as confident.

"He still has to strip," Kohei said.

"Strip! Strip! Strip! Strip!" shouted his fellow club members.

They're kidding, right? Strip RPS? The restaurant would never allow that.

Jaune revised the sentiment after spotting the owner at the counter sharing drinks with two massive dudes. Who were naked. A number of spectators were likewise missing pieces of their clothing. They showed no qualms at the state of undress. The only people to stay fully-dressed were Lisa and company sitting at the table, with none beside Lisa losing their composure.

Well, okay, then. This was normal around these parts. Just what kind of universe had he fallen in, he wanted to ask.

Although, it sure was hot in here. The AC must be malfunctioning. Removing his shirt wouldn't feel like a punishment in this heat, would it? More a reward.

In one smooth motion, he tugged the hem of the shirt over his head and peeled it off. Afterward, he sighed in relief.

Kohei looked at him oddly. "You could have just gone for your shoes, or your socks."

"Oh, that's a good point," Jaune said, a slight slurring in his voice. He kicked off his shoes, and removed his socks.

…Wait.

"You are a cunning opponent, indeed," Jaune praised his foe, and hiccupped.

"I feel like I'm bullying you. Are you old enough to drink?"

"Are you?" Jaune accused. The sheepish look on the many faces around him spoke volumes. "Whatever, that's enough talk. You picked this battle and I'm not backing down! Rock. Paper. Scissors!"

The second round, he was ready. The strong alcohol may be throwing him for a loop, dulling his reflexes, but this was still the reflexes of a person training to slay monsters. A person that has sparred against some of the best fighters of his generation.

As Kohei threw out his fist, Jaune analyzed each minute movement of the fingers. The human hand only had so much range of motion. For this game in particular, the pinkie and index fingers were the key tells. If neither moved, then it's rock. The index, but not the pinkie, meant it would be scissors. Both, paper.

Jaune grinned as his scissors met Kohei's paper.

"Damn!"

"Heh. Too easy."

Thus began his glorious comeback. The third round found him facing a swaying Kohei missing his shoes. Experienced drinker or otherwise, 192-proof vodka—and wasn't a number to make his liver sob in utter terror—was a sledgehammer that pulverizes the concept of alcohol tolerance. He's pretty sure it's not supposed to be drunk straight.

"This stuff is stronger than Everclear. There's no way it could possibly be safe for consumption. Oh god, Jaune's drinking something worse than Everclear," Lisa muttered to herself from the sideline, confirming his suspicions. The girl had a hand pressed to her temples, and she was shaking her head as she watched their contest.

Escha patted her on the leg in reassurance. Perhaps her keener eyesight had let her see through Jaune's tactic.

The third round went to Jaune, and so did the fourth. There was no stopping him from then on. His opponent had not the fortitude to withstand the successive drinks. Reduced to a rambling wreck of a man, Kohei lost the final round facing the wrong way and donning a single sock, which a kind club member stripped for him.

Jaune punched a fist into the air, celebrating his victory.

A sharp voice cut into the moment. "Not so fast, Jaune Arc."

Two club members were pushed aside, and between them strode Iori. The dark-haired young man wore a serious expression on his face, and the steely gaze of a warrior met Jaune's own blue eyes.

"You have defeated but the weakest of the Heavenly Four. Now I will take you on."

Jaune looked Iori up and down… then quickly up again.

"With what? You already lost."

Fresh from his own bout of Strip RPS, there remained not a stitch of clothing on the other boy. Iori peered down at himself, and his eyes bulged out.

"When did that happen!?"

Jaune left the other drunken idiot to it, scanning the crowd. "Alright, so I guess I won that match by default. Who's next?"

"Ooh! Ooh! How about me~."

The woman that emerged from the crowd was older than him by a few years, and she was drop dead gorgeous. Like, pretty-as-Pyrrha level of beauty. Her dark, wavy hair fell to her shoulders, and she had a figure that one may call enviable, with breasts that strained her t-shirt and a slim waist.

"You're in their club?"

She nodded cheerfully. "Mmhm. The name's Azusa, and I'm one of the senior members. I love Strip RPS!"

Before he could respond, Jaune felt hands gripping his shoulders. In a flash, Iori and Kohei dragged him into a huddle.

"Jaune, I might have a problem with normies like you, but this is serious," said Kohei.

"She's a tough opponent," Iori chimed in with his analysis. "A veteran of this game. But between the three of us, I think we have a shot."

Jaune stared at the other boy. "Again, with what?"

After all, he was the only one with any clothes left to play.

Iori immediately latched onto his leg, the last speck of his honor nowhere in sight. "Oh come on, you have to. You have to!"

"Please, I will forgive you for having a little sister. Help us strip Azusa!" Kohei bawled, arms wrapped around Jaune's other leg.

Taking pity on them, Jaune said, "Alright, alright, I'll do it. Just stop groveling while you're naked! Hell, stop clinging to me while you're naked!"

And that, was how Jaune found himself standing across from a ravishing beauty, gearing up for a match of Strip RPS with her.

He studied the woman, seeking the source of her confidence, a reason for why Azusa stood unguarded and laughed unreservedly. It's a maddening task, futile in the end. She waved to her friends, blew kisses at handsome men, and gave every indication that she knew she would win.

What was her game? Where lies the secret weapon to secure her victory?

The countdown reached zero, and Jaune's hand descended without him ever figuring out the mystery. Given no recourse, he fell back on his old tactic, giving his utmost effort.

His rock met her scissors.

"Hang on, I won?"

"He won!" yelled both Iori and Kohei. The two of them jumped on Jaune, whooping and hollering at the top of their lungs.

"I knew I could count on you!" said Kohei, the one that tried to kill him.

"Glug, glug, glug. Ahhh, that's some good Spirytus!" Jaune said softly as he strolled down the street.

Lisa winced and shushed him. "Keep it down, people are probably sleeping by now. And that's water you're drinking." She adjusted her grip on his clothes. "Fuck, you're heavy."

"I'm not!"

"Heh, yeah, you're noooot. You're sweet… is that the right word, sweet? Why is sweet good, but the other flavors bad, anyway? It doesn't really make sense."

"Uh-huh. Doesn't make sense at all. Now, how about you just focus on putting one foot in front of the other. We're almost there. Escha, can you take his water bottle and toss it in the trash can over there?"

A white blur pounced on him, robbing Jaune of his precious treasure. It darted away into the darkness before he could react.

"My water…"

"We'll get you more," Lisa soothed him as she towed him along.

They reached the rental house without incident. As Lisa fumbled for the keys, Jaune swayed in the breeze, humming a song under his breath. He caught a glimpse of the pool in the back.

"Let's go swimming," he suggested.

"I—huh, you're thinking it's a pretty nice night."

He nodded, glad she had read his mind.

They've landed on a tropical island, in a world where days of peace carry on and on. How wonderful it would be to watch the stars and the sea tonight, and think of nothing but how pretty they were.

Lisa pondered the idea for a moment. "That sounds like fun. What do you think, Escha?"

"You two go," Escha said, yawning. "I wanna go to bed."

"Awww, have a good rest then, sweetie." She scratched Escha under the chin, then turned to Jaune. "I guess it's just us. Give me a bit to grab my swimsuit, and we'll meet by the pool?"

The door opened, allowing entry. Escha padded inside, bidding them goodnight as she climbed the stairs. Lisa followed her up to get changed. She left the door open for him.

A short while later, the patio door slid aside.

Lisa walked out under the moonlight. She looked up at the sky, and a million stars shone upon her to take her breath away. They reflected off the dark sea and from here it seemed as if she stood on an island in the depths of space.

Her gaze lowered to the pool, and she sighed in fond exasperation as she saw Jaune already there. Light steps brought her to the edge of the water. Kneeling down, she smiled softly at him.

Lisa then rapidly blinked her eyes, before shouting.

"Why are you naked again!?"

Interlude: This is a Lewding Story​

The shrill cry woke Jaune from his dozing, and he opened his eyes.

With his elbows resting on the edge of the pool, he tilted back his head to look up at Lisa. At what point did she approach him, it's hard to say. His thoughts had been elsewhere. Framed by the moon, she's pretty as a picture.

The wide-eyed stare somewhat ruined the effect, of course. Composure, gone. Cheekiness, gone. She's almost shy, and it's an interesting look he wouldn't mind seeing more of.

"Cute bikini," he said.

"Um. Thanks," Lisa stammered. His casual attitude seemed to have thrown her further off-balance. "Nice, uh…" She stopped talking.

He gave a small laugh, and said, "It's not like you to be speechless, Gossip Girl."

"It's not like you to be naked," she squeaked.

Jaune looked down.

Ah, yes. She shouted something to that effect, hadn't she? Well, here's a mystery for the ages. Why, oh why, was Jaune Arc going without clothes. Of the two people present, none knew the answer. Since he didn't want to admit that, he mustered all the cunning he could access at the moment to ponder on the best way of explaining his perfectly normal circumstances.

Jaune spread his arms wide.

"Look, it's no big deal. Why do people scale mountains? Because it's there. Why is a man naked? Because it's hot. Some reasons aren't that complicated."

A much better answer than 'I can't remember what I was thinking, or if I even was.'

His words shocked a giggle out of Lisa. "My, do you become profound when you're drunk," she teased.

He pinched a thumb and index finger close together. "A tiny bit drunk."

"Not from where I'm standing, silly man."

A silence fell over them after that. Under the night sky, boy and girl gazed at one another. Each wondered of how to proceed from here.

The stalemate ended as an odd gleam entered Lisa's eyes. Slowly, her lips stretched into a shark-like grin that set off alarm bells in Jaune's head. She tended to show that face to… he didn't want to say prey, because he didn't like thinking of himself as prey, but if it quacks like a duck, then…

Quack, quack! thought Jaune.

Unaware of his deep introspections, Lisa idly mused, "No big deal, huh?"

Before he could ask, Lisa brushed back a stray lock of hair and lowered herself to sit on the edge of the pool. She dipped her toes in to test the temperature, and after finding it ideal, let her legs sink into the water.

"Ooh, it feels pretty nice." There's a strange cadence to her voice, an attempt at a breathy whisper that came out stilted and taut.

What he would have said in reply died in his throat as Lisa slipped a hand behind her back.

She held that position, nervously chewing on her bottom lip as she observed him. On Jaune's part, his eyebrows were trying their best to meet his hairline. To him, it looked rather like she was about to—
