#2,962
Chapter 45: The Man Who Stayed​


The soldiers of the Empire have taken to watching the sky.

Common doctrine would see scouts ranging inside the forest and infantrymen covering a tight perimeter around their camps, and called it a day. The problem for them was, none of that mattered when faced with Jaune's response of hurtling through the air at breakneck speed to bypass it all.

A few times, it worked in their favor. A whiff of his presence early on, and the whole platoon would be back in their trucks, the convoy long gone before his arrival. On this occasion, they received mere seconds of warning. Knightly helmet turned upward, a soldier spotted him at the very moment he dropped down on the forest clearing.

Jaune must admit to an overeagerness that caused a wide grin to break out on his face, for the camp was an artillery position, to boot. He's been searching for these guys for the better part of two days; they had grown cautious after he took down the previous artillery batteries.

That was two days in which the last cannons of the East Europan Imperial Alliance's 705th Battalion—the invaders, the enemy, Imps, them—assailed Yuell at all odd hours, raining fire upon old and young alike. Well, not anymore.

The quickest among them unslung their rifles. They managed to squeeze out a couple of potshots that missed wide. By that point, he had chosen his target between the five cannons. The firing team stationed there had enough time to scream, then he was upon them.

He slammed into the gunner operating the handwheels of the artillery piece, crushing the man against the controls. His foot then kicked up to feed a second soldier a superheated jet of rocket exhaust just as the spotter on the other side of the cannon traded his binoculars for a sidearm, bringing it to bear. A shadowy hand grabbed that man by the head, pulling him forward to smash his face against the inches-thick metal of the cannon barrel. Crocea Mors appeared, and Jaune proceeded to lay into the rest of the team.

Around him, the camp awoke in a flurry of activity. Shock troops rushed forward to buy time, and after the last person within Jaune's vicinity fell, they opened fire to push him into cover; the cannon was just the right size to hide his bulk, and the bullets pinged off the steel without piercing through. Behind them, military trucks left running all this while raced toward the other cannons as the gunnery crews scrambled to prepare the equipment for travel. It's a tactic they've refined on the third day—yesterday—of fighting, having lost all of four and half of another platoon to the combined effort of Jaune and the Yuell militia. The guiding principle centered around a concept that caused Jaune's lips to curl in distaste whenever it came to mind: the survival of cannons and tanks were paramount, the lives of the soldiers less so.

He let them carry on. Better that they retain a measure of hope for escape. It kept their forces split, making them easier pickings.

Also, the last time he tried annihilating the trucks right off the bat in the thinking that it would force the soldiers to surrender, it trapped everyone there with him and they had chosen instead to throw themselves at him in a suicidal charge. That mess culminated with one insane fool setting off grenades in close quarters to rip away a big chunk of his Aura. Let's not do that again.

Hiding behind the cannon, he heard a small *tink* as an object hit the ground next to him. Looking down, it's a hand grenade bouncing end over end, its shape of a clump on a stick reminding him of candy apples. Before the second bounce, Jaune threw out a hand. His fingers brushed the explosive, allowing him to vanish it inside his Pocket. It then rematerialized with his grip loosely-wrapped around the handle, and he tossed it back at the Imperial soldiers. A loud boom was accompanied by the screams of both those caught in the blast and the survivors witnessing their allies go down.

"Noooo!" a soldier shouted. "He was such a good guy!" His voice cracked at the end.

Jaune winced. He preferred it when they just swear and tell him to go die. It kept things simple, and gave them the image of cruel, cold men who knew what were getting into with this war so he didn't have to think about issues like some among the soldiers sounding awfully young and holy were there a lot of them that won't go home after the events of the last few days because—

Their fault. They shot Tattletale, and attacked the city. People were dead due to their invasion.

An officer barked an order, directing the soldiers to ignore the wounded and focus on their target. Whatever their feelings on it, discipline took hold and the Imperial squad resumed their careful approach toward his position. Yet, with their numbers depleted, the wall of bullets grew scattered, unable to maintain the steady rhythm that would pin him down. Jaune seized that moment to sprint out of hiding. [Third Arm] pulled him low across the ground, shield up to catch stray gunfire.

The distance between him and them closed in a blink, and the soldiers' formation promptly fell into a messy brawl with bullets flying every which way as they chased a blur. His Aura and his shield provided a defense against their guns, but speed proved the best protection of all, and he used every method available to him—rockets, Void magic, and in some cases plain old Huntsman physicality—to bounce from place to place. Imperial armor was as effective as wood when meeting his blade. In the span of seconds their ranks underwent another precipitous drop. Red scattered in the air, and stained the grass beneath their feet.

In the confusion, a lucky shot clipped him on the hip. With a grunt, he rotated with the motion. The Imperials must have thought that was the battle won, must have found a limit to what they could believe of the reports from those who faced him and lived to tell the tale. The first note in a ragged chorus of triumphant cries passed through the clearing that then stuttered out as he continued on, a swing of his sword slicing the person responsible in two.

Between the eye-slits of their helmets, Jaune watched hope die. The last to fall was the officer, an unfinished order on his lips.

Beyond them, a change shifted among the firing teams and drivers. Ropes and hooks dropped from their fingers, the artillery pieces left to lay abandoned on the ground. Trembling hands took up rifles. One man raised a lance. They understood that there's no chance to escape with the cannons, and orders were orders. Their lives for bits of gears and metal, even if they had not a plan in mind for victory.

Jaune gave a shout. They answered in kind, terror-stricken and despairing.

Five minutes later, only one person remained standing within the clearing, and the artillery cannons of the 705th Battalion fell silent for the last time.


-o-​


Jaune observed the forest, alert for Imperial soldiers looking for a rematch.

When it came down to the wire, with death before their eyes, some of them had indeed admitted to themselves that they loved life more than they respected orders, but who could say? They might have rediscovered their courage after a bout of soul-searching in the woods, or received reinforcements from the rest of the battalion. A part of him wondered what fate would befall them should they reach their allies. From what he had heard of the strict and traditional-minded Empire, their military seemed the type to take a dim view of runners.

In any case, the battle was won, and all that's left was to wait for his allies. They were sure to appreciate the gifts he prepared for them.

At his feet, laid piles.

First was a pile of ragnaid canisters, capsules filled with a ragnite-derived healing agent. They functioned akin to stimpaks and healing potions, with a startlingly similar effectiveness; wounds that would have killed a man in another couple of minutes if left to bleed were sealed in moments. Precious as gold in these times of rationing and intercepted shipments, the doctors heading up efforts to treat casualties of the Empire's attacks, the Coalhearths, had asked him to keep an eye out for them.

Then there's a pile of firearms, which his fingers itched to sell off. With the latest ability he purchased from the Marketplace app, it'd be but a press of the button. The clunky machine guns and antiquated rifles carried low price tags, however, and could do much more good in the hands of the Yuell militia. Marina told him that weapons training was a compulsory subject in Gallia's schools, so each extra gun was a civilian that could now join the defense.

(Well, that wasn't completely true. The taciturn woman had muttered all of five words before losing interest and pushing that guy with the lance, Walter, forward to explain in detail.)

And finally, he had a pile of three wounded men, tied up with their bleeding staunched. He couldn't say it was the best idea to leave them alive, nor did he think they would thank him when they wake up. Yuell's militia members harbored a deep, unabiding hatred for the people that murdered their neighbors and invaded their home. It might end up with him needing to step in. He'll have to see how things pan out.

The handheld radio hanging on his hip crackled to life.

"Spotted you. Approaching now," said the scratchy voice of a young woman.

Jaune raised the radio to his mouth. "Got it. How did it go on your end? I'm glad you're okay!"

There was no response. Typical.

He heard the squad of Yuell militia before he saw them. Bushes rustled and the armor pieces strapped to their uniform clanked as they moved over the uneven ground. Then, blue shapes emerged amidst the green and brown of nature, following the trail that the 705th's trucks had taken to get here. The squad of ten or so people approached at a slow, careful pace, their guns poised to shoot at the first sign of Imperial red armor. Their faces below the hard helmets brightened as he waved to them.

The smiles did somewhat dipped once they caught sight of the carnage, with most of them turning green as a result.

He spied a flash of movement at the corner of his vision. Turning there, he met the inscrutable gaze of Marina. The woman melted out of the surroundings from a different direction to everyone else, a hunting rifle propped on one shoulder and a radio strapped to her hips. Her footsteps were silent on the grass; they glided past stray leaves, touching not a one. The hunter of wild game showed better training than the actual town militia members, and looked quite comfortable compared to how she was in the city.

It was harder than pulling teeth, but he found out that Marina lived in a cabin miles deep within the forest. The woman had been in town trading the prey she hunted for supplies that day the Empire launched their attack, and threw her lot in with the garrison when those guys came under fire. By this point, she's an official unofficial member of the city's defense.

"Well?" she asked, brushing her bangs out of her eyes.

Well what, lady? Jaune tilted his head, a vaguely blank smile on display as his mind raced to decipher that cryptic question.

Marina gave a pointed look at the indents in the ground marking the spots the artillery pieces used to occupy, then she cocked an eyebrow.

"The cannons?" he guessed, receiving a minute nod of the head from her. "I took care of it. They're gone, gone, gone and the Empire's never seeing them again."

One of the militiamen, a young man Jaune hadn't gotten the name of, seemed unconvinced with that answer. It's hard to blame him since the scene lacked any signs of the broken and melted pieces of metal that would come with blowing up the cannons. The young man opened his mouth to inquire further, and earned an elbow to the ribs from Walter standing next to him, who then gave Jaune a thumbs-up. As someone who had been accompanying Jaune in bringing the fight to the Imperial forces, Walter had learned by now to just accept things at face value. After all, a magician did not reveal his secrets.

Setting to work, the squad fanned out. Roles were divided up, with drivers climbing into the trucks while the others combed the grounds of the camp for spare ammunition boxes and useful supplies. Walter was assigned the unenviable task of rifling through the pockets and knapsacks of the fallen soldiers, confiscating bullet clips, boots, personal effects, and so on. Many couldn't help delivering swift kicks in passing to the captive soldiers, though they left it at that.

In a short while, they had all the loot stacked on the trucks with the captives none-so-gently thrown aboard, and everybody grabbed seats for themselves. One by one, the vehicles began to move, forming a single file line.

Jaune hopped on the last truck, where he sat with his legs swinging off the back. He could have flown and it would be faster, he supposed, but this method conserved the battery of his boots. Also, it's just nice to be around people.

The forest clearing grew smaller and smaller in his view until a turn obscured the blood-soaked ground altogether.

Through the woods, over meadows, and onto roads, the convoy traveled back to Yuell. A jovial mood accompanied them, buoyed by victory—one unmarred by casualties on their side, at that. A flag of Gallian colors flew above the lead truck to denote their allegiance for the lookouts posted in the city, blue and white with a simple design of a unicorn's head.

The journey proceeded without impediment, soon putting them at the outskirts of the city. There, Jaune parted from the convoy while they carried on. Their destinations were in the same general direction, but the way he entered the city couldn't be on the back of a truck, because…

Because…

The people of Yuell have taken to watching the sky.

The first person to notice the trucks told the second, the second told a third, and the news spread like wildfire. In the neighborhood surrounding the university where the population had concentrated, men and women, old and young poured out onto the streets. Their eyes twinkled with an eager light as they turned their gazes upward.

Someone shouted, pointing at a rooftop. A gasp was heard.

Jaune made his entrance, seeming to bound over the building in one effortless jump. A few people still screamed even now, their minds insisting that gravity would take hold to splatter him on the street. That turned into awe, the sort of pure astonishment where one's eyes opened wide and their hands flew up to cover their mouth, when Jaune leapt again despite never touching down. Alternating blasts of his rockets allowed him to stride above the crowd in a series of hops, giving the impression of a man out for a jaunty walk on thin air.

Reaching the center of the avenue, he hovered in place. Looking from face to face, he waved to the people watching him, turning in a full circle. It's important that they see.

"Our counterattack…" he called out in a loud voice, then paused to let the moment build.

His audience jostled forward, craning their ears and waiting with bated breath.

He spread his arms wide.

"...was a success!"

The street erupted in jubilation. Jaune threw his head back, and his laughter rang across the sky. Keeping one rocket extended to retain altitude, he angled his other boot. It brought him into a slow revolution, bobbing him back and forth through the air in a motion that almost mimicked a waltz.

"One more day," he continued. "One more day is ours!"

The crowd below was roaring now, echoing his words as a chant while he danced above the avenue. Many followed his lead, with partners snagged at random to start an impromptu celebration. Jaune breathed easier, seeing the joyful expressions on their faces.

He lowered himself to the cobblestones, and was nearly bowled over as people gathered round. Pelted with voices from every direction, he couldn't hear much beyond a babble. Some had tear tracks on their faces, and were among the ones screaming his name the loudest. None cheered harder than the children who clamored and climbed onto him. They perched on his shoulders or his outstretched arms, miming the wings of birds as if they would take off at any moment.

Their parents didn't even try to scold them, and in fact were just as keen to approach. They reached out their hands, striving to touch him.

It… It wasn't slaps on the back or handshakes, exactly. To him, their actions seemed to bear a reverence that bordered on… well, he didn't know what. Like how people would look in a church, maybe?

Jaune scanned the crowd. Among them, he saw even more of those homemade charms than yesterday. The citizens of Yuell have fast taken to the practice of wearing kerchiefs, armbands, talismans, and the like, dyed in the same red-and-white ambulance theme of his poncho. Others copied the mark of the Outsider tattooed on his hand, thinking it his personal crest that would help them avert disaster in some small way.

Belief, and magic. Belief of magic. A wizard, great and terrible, has come for Yuell in its time of need. His miracles were myriad and potent, astounding all who witnessed him. He flew through the sky, healed the sick, and fought evil wherever he roamed. In their eyes, there was nothing he couldn't do.

It's a show, a sham. Jaune had no better clue of what to do than they. Yet, it was necessary because victory did not end with the enemy's defeat, and a war was turning out to be a lot bigger than one battle.

Once more, he cheated the world, and it was his greatest lie to date. A lie he could almost be proud of. To give hope as only a Huntsman could.

Before long, he decided it was time to go. With a smile, because he must always smile, Jaune motioned for people to make room, and once they were at a safe distance, he fluttered his fingers in farewell and blasted off.

One street over, he landed on the ground to fall into step with Marina. If he startled her, she hid it well, with her strides proceeding at the same pace up the road.

"Yo," he greeted. "Did the others leave for the garrison?"

"Mmhm."

"Are you heading to the university, too?"

"Yes." Then, after a beat, she added, "It's loud over there." Marina jerked her head to indicate the direction Jaune had come from. The noises made by the spectators of his little performance could still be heard at this distance.

"Heh, yeah. They were pretty excited when I gave them the news. I tried doing this thing again, where I sort of spin"—he demonstrated by twirling on the balls of his feet—"in the air. They took it well. I didn't think that many people would know how to dance. You should join them."

"That sounds… not me." She had needed a second to think of the right words, which Jaune rather suspected in the young woman's case equated to the shortest words.

He replied with a bright laugh. "You never know. Have you actually tried? It's fun."

"It's useless," she countered. The pair crested a slope, and the entrance of the university came into view, lying across the wide intersection. The wrought-iron gates were open, with one gate tilting off its hinges.

"I don't think so," Jaune said. "Everywhere I go, people know what dancing is." He pushed his hands into his pockets, leaning back to walk with an easygoing gait. "If it was useless then why does it stick around?"

Her eyes narrow for a brief moment. "I meant that it won't help."

Won't stop bullets. Won't win the day.

"You're thinking in practical terms. It's, you know, the spirits and whatnot. People have to believe they can live. Sometimes, that makes the difference."

Upon entering the campus, Jaune swiveled his head this way and that to admire the sights. Even with the damages from artillery fire, Yuell University retained a sense of elegant pomp. Marble columns lined the exterior corridors, each walkway wide enough for a car to fit. Ornamental fountains, shut off to conserve water, depicted unicorn herds in gallop. The statue of the founder stood proud at the center of the front lawn, and around it were three craters marking where the Empire's cannons had missed their target.

Through the windows, one could see hallways filled with paintings, from scenes of nature to important personages that have studied within its walls. One particular wing seemed dedicated to portraits of Gallia's rulers, the House Randgriz, which culminated with a painting of the present-day Archduchess Cordelia sitting on her throne in full regalia, the scepter in her hand resembling a spiral-shaped spear.

The highest bell tower had taken a hit to crumble one side, but the bell survived. The headmaster made a point to have it rung every hour per schedule. Ostensibly, as a show of Gallian defiance against the Empire. Jaune translated that as the man wanting a way to look dignified while still thumbing his nose at the invaders.

"I guess it's a bit like this place," Jaune said, half in thought. "Sure, it has some of the hardier buildings in town, but that hole in the roof is a pretty good indication that it's not that tough. If safety was the goal, this isn't it." At a window, there was a flash of blond hair, and purple. His pace quickened a tad. "The bells, the flags on the towers, the music they put on last night… Those are the reasons why everyone flocked here after the shelling began." He waved to passersby, and they waved back. Students of the university worked side by side with townsfolk to move supplies and build barricades, fortifying the defenses further. "The people, too. Doesn't it just make you feel better being near them, being aboveground, instead of huddling alone in a basement? We're all in this together, and we can make it."

That last part was the point of his rambling, something to say to lift Marina's spirits. She needed hope like everybody else, the curt demeanor notwithstanding. As he strode inside the building, he turned to see if it had an effect.

Then, he started searching his surroundings.

"Marina? Where'd you go?" He looked up, down, left, right; there was no dark-haired sharpshooter in sight. Jaune scratched his cheek. "Like a ghost, that one."

It later occurred to him that he must have looked insane to passersby the whole walk through the front lawn, talking at length to himself.


-o-​


The meeting point was a lecture hall tucked in a corner of the campus, ideal for its lack of sightlines with possible firing positions outside the city. Jaune nudged the door open, and sidled inside to find everyone else already present, deep in discussion.

"Look. No, look." Tattletale slammed a hand on the table as she addressed the person opposite her. "If the line is broken, then the Empire would have sent more than one battalion and this place would be sacked to hell and back on the first day!"

Set between the podium and the bench rows, the table hosted a map of Gallia. Figurines in blue and red were placed on its surface to denote the last known positions of the various armies in the conflict, forming a line that split the country in two.

Up north, the line was uncomfortably close to the capital, Randgriz. With a path through the flat Naggiar Plains, plus numerous sea routes, the Empire had amassed a formidable force along that front to batter the Gallian defenses. As old newspapers tell it, the Imperial Army used to be even closer to Randgriz, until Gallia's hero (they had a hero!) succeeded in a gambit that pushed the invaders back across the river. The subsequent counteroffensive by General Damon and the Gallian Army drew the line they saw today, and see-sawed in a deadlock so tenuous that it's said a single battle could well decide the fate of the entire northern front.

Down south, the Gallians were having an easier—for a given value of easier—experience holding the line. The Kloden region remained a firm blue, centered on a place named Castle Gassenarl. They're responsible for much of the momentum behind the forces protecting the southern half of the country, which included Yuell. It helped that the Barious Desert provided a natural barrier to an invasion, barring that one time at the beginning of the war where this exact type of thinking almost cost them their capital as the Empire rushed their troops through the desert to strike at the heart of Gallia... but people tend to gloss over that while talking to Jaune. In any case, the roles reversed once the war became one of attrition, with the Barious now keeping Empire supply lines lean and fragile. It's a section of the front that many consider as secured, the cities behind it safe from depredation.

The red marker set next to Yuell said otherwise. That figurine denoted an incongruous conundrum amidst an otherwise simple state of affairs.

An old man faced down Tattletale from the other side of the table. The commander of Yuell's garrison, his fighting days were long over with his aged and shaky hand gripping onto a walking stick. Of course, a large part of that shaking was due to anger, with the old man appearing ready to brain Tattletale with the cane.

"The Imps are crafty," said the commander. He used his walking stick to move the figurines, shifting the line westward so that another swath of Gallia fell under Imperial control. The marker next to the city stayed in place, but now spoke of a greatly-changed scenario. Yuell was the front. "We are facing a continued application of their attritional tactics. With their numbers, the Empire can afford probing attacks to test our defenses. We need the Arc here to project strength. If they determine that we are weak, their true force is sure to—"

Tattletale cut in, shaking her head. "They sent what they thought could sneak through the gap and still get the job done. The structure of Gallia's military isn't a secret. They would have known that most of Yuell's able-bodied was conscripted in the national Militia with your armory gutted to support them. That's why they sent a platoon to take the city at first. Yuell didn't warrant anything bigger than that."

She punctuated the statement with a sweep of her hand. With the way her sleeve covered all but her fingertips, it looked more comical than impressive.

The girl had dressed down in period-appropriate clothing after it became clear that they would be staying for longer than a day, and looked quite demure this afternoon in a white summer dress, her hair tied up with a purple ribbon she had gotten from somewhere. She also 'requisitioned' a Gallian-blue militia jacket for herself so people would know she's not a civilian, and therefore would take her words with the seriousness it was due. It's unfortunate that the garment sat rather large on her slight frame.

Still, people did listen. She occupied an influential role in Yuell's decision-making, based in no small way on her connection to him.

"Now is the time for aggressive action," she insisted. "Jaune is doing better work out there than he would be sitting around to guard the aristocrats. Ignore what they tell you for once in your life. You should be organizing the volunteers. Put the guns we looted in their hands and post them on the barricades. This leaves Jaune to run wild which will end the problem quicker, without him having to rush back to the city like two nights ago."

Jaune suppressed a shiver. That raid was too touch-and-go for his taste. The Imperial troops had punched a line almost to the university by the time he arrived on the scene.

He looked to the third occupant of the room. Marina must have gone ahead of him, because she stood in a corner with a bored expression; it didn't seem like the others noticed her yet. The woman had been there that night, holding off Imperials from a sniper's nest on the bell towers. If she had an opinion about the current situation, she was keeping it to herself.

"That's how we win. Defense, and offense," declared Tattletale with a tone of finality. She crossed her arms, and sent the commander a challenging glare.

The old man tossed an immediate rebuttal at her. "It's not that simple. Military training is a compulsory part of our education system, yes, but the majority do not keep up with it afterward in their everyday life unless they are a member of the garrison or pursuing careers in the armed forces. Their skill with firearms is rusty, as is their knowledge of squad tactics. Not to mention how they'd fare with the physical demands of battle. The amount of time it'd take to bring them up to fighting shape… It is sad to say, but our remaining citizens are unprepared for the rigors of war."

Tattletale glanced toward him at that moment. She averted her gaze a split second later, but by then he had formed a good guess at the reason for the eye contact.

Jaune sighed under his breath, stamping down on the surge of guilt. Their little team of otherworlders were no better prepared for the circumstances they've stumbled onto than the locals. Of the trio, he was faring the best. (That's the problem, really.)

With the small acknowledgement of his presence, Jaune stepped forward to join the group. After a beat of hesitation, Marina followed suit, scaring the hell out of Tattletale in the process as she realized the woman had been inside the room this whole time.

The first thing the commander asked of him concerned the state of the handheld radios, an attitude which caused Jaune to scrunch his nose for how it reminded him of the Imperials. The old man relaxed once he and Marina had shown the pair of devices to him.

He could kind of understand where the old man was coming from, even if he didn't like it. The handheld radios were precious equipment, newish technology that saw the light of day a mere two or three years ago and happened to revolutionize warfare as a result. The bulk of the inventory manufactured by Gallia during that time went to the Army and the drafted militia units. The local garrison owned just that one pair.

"Wonderful," the commander said. He caught the look in Jaune's eyes. "Begging your pardon, your grace." His head dipped in apology, as Jaune tilted his head at the moniker and sudden tone of servility. "Your life is paramount, of course. It is just that such an obvious thing does not bear wondering, unlike the mundane objects our poor hands make. If it pleases you, may we know—"

"They won," Tattletale interrupted with a roll of her eyes. She hurried around the table toward Jaune. "No casualties on our side or he'd be a lot more glum. No issues or he wouldn't have waited for us to stop talking. He managed to hit the artillery, exactly as I told you an hour earlier when they went quiet. Whatever, that's not important." She gripped him by the arms… then took a moment to straighten his collar and brush at a grass stain on his shoulder, before gripping him by the arms again. "The insignia on their uniforms. What were they?"

He simply said, "The 705th."

The girl broke out in a big smile at the news. She bounced on her heels, studying him in detail to make doubly, triply sure of the truth. That vision of innocent joy could only mean one thing.

Tattletale whirled around. "I told you. It's one battalion." She held up a finger, wagging it back and forth at the commander. You know, to be extra smug and rub it in. "One."

"You cannot be certain—"

"I am. Every single platoon we've seen is from the same group. The rag-tag offensive they're putting up points to a unit stretched thin over a wide area." She leaned over the map, humming a triumphant tune as she moved the pieces. The original line was reestablished. "It's a strike force that snuck in. No more, no less."

The old man gave Jaune a glance before studying the map. "...If it is as you say, they would be meeting with resistance in every direction," he said in a slow and deliberate tone, ceding to the idea. "Hence, the decentralization of their platoons."

"Exactly. Unless these other two towns"—Lisa tapped on the dots marked Braeden and Asnein on the map, northeast of Yuell and closer to the front—"have fallen, they can't move unopposed. We have no reason to turtle up."

Jaune chimed in. "Well, we don't know how many soldiers they still have. I'm a little concerned about that."

"Judging by how their attacks are slowing after each engagement? Half-strength, at best," Tattletale replied. "A few more days and we got this in the bag."

That's days of people dying, plus Tattletale and Escha living under the pall of war. Jaune mulled on it, his eyes darting across the map.

"We really can't retreat? Pull everyone back to a safer city?"

The old man answered, "There's no telling what the conditions will be on the road. An Imperial attack in the open… I shudder to imagine. That is not to mention those who would refuse the order." His hand squeezed down on the head of the cane. "Yuell has stood for four hundred years."

Jaune got the sense that the old man would be one of the people staying.

"I'll bet they're looking out for that, anyway," Tattletale added. Her finger slid over the page, connecting a line from Yuell to the closest city down south. "I have confirmation that this road is unguarded. See something odd?"

"Nnnnn-no."

"You skirmished with Imperials troops here, and here. Why are they stationed on either side of the road, you ask? It's a trap. They were waiting for us to run."

"Alright, that's out, then," Jaune said at once. No need for a mess like that on his plate. "What now?"

"It depends on what my scout reports." Tattletale checked the clock. "We'll have to wait a bit, though. There's a good ten minutes before she's scheduled to check in."

That gave him and Tattletale a moment to themselves, and she wasted no time pulling him into a corner of the room.

No, not for that. Unfortunately.

"What's the haul?" she asked.

"There were five cannons, and I sold the lot for 5,000 Points. It's—"

"Getting smaller," Tattletale finished for him while giving a pout. "Damn, it was at 2,000 per cannon last time. The supply and demand theory is becoming more and more probable. That changes my plans a bit."

The prices offered by the Marketplace for loot turned out to be no static thing. The emerging pattern suggested that further sales of the artillery pieces would meet with diminishing returns at some as yet undetermined milestone.

"But for it to fall by half," Tattletale muttered in dismay.

"I think it's the sexiness factor," said Jaune.

The artillery pieces might be modern tech in this world, sure. They were hopelessly outdated by the standards of his Remnant where airships strapped with railcannons roamed the sky above the Vytal Festival, let alone whatever universes were out there that produced portal technology and interdimensional marketplaces. Lacking fantastical effects, they were just clunky and antiquated guns, but bigger. Mass-produced goods could only carry a hardworking businessman (looter) like him so far.

Tattletale sighed. "I hate that I can't tell you you're wrong."

"Oh please, you do that even without an excuse."

"Huh. Good point. Jaune, you're wrong."

He stuck out his tongue at her, and she mirrored him in kind.

A few minutes past the hour, and a phone rang. All eyes in the room focused on the device in Tattletale's hand. (Some more than others, and with barely-disguised fascination at what was considered another 'miracle of Arc'.)

Most days, Jaune would be the one on the other end of the line. Since he had passed his phone off to somebody else, he listened in alongside Tattletale.

"Long-range recon asset, report," Tattletale ordered. Her lips twitched with suppressed laughter.

"Ma'am, yes ma'am! Agent Blackdog, reporting!"

Because, clearly, the last thing any Imperial spy tapping in on the meeting would imagine after hearing the name was that they needed to be on the lookout for a white cat. Escha had taken to the role with enthusiasm, by all accounts having a ball playing secret agent.

Jaune was glad for it, as it got her out of the city where she didn't have to look at broken homes and weeping mothers.

"Listen, listen, I found another platoon!"

Oho? He leaned closer to put his face next to Tattletale, the phone between them.

"I eavesdropped on the commander's tent, and they were talking about how the rest of the batter-lion are coming here from the other villages in the region. They're preparing for an attack on the city tonight to swarm you under cover of darkness!"

"How many people are we talking about here?" Jaune asked.

Escha paused. "Erm, I don't know. He just refers to them by platoons—there's six. And nine tanks."

"Artillery?"

"None!"

He left Tattletale to continue the debrief with Escha. A plan was forming in his head, one he didn't need his partner to think of. When the call ended, Tattletale took one look at him. It told her all she needed to know. She smirked, indicating her agreement.

The Imperial forces wanted to attack Yuell? Well, they can't do that if he attacked them first!

Jaune punched a fist into his palm. He was going to break this tide come sunset, once and for all.

His team will be home before the weekend.
