#3,039
Chapter 46: Players, and Pieces​


All of a sudden, Jaune's not feeling so hot anymore.

"How many of them are there?" he murmured, peering out of the foliage through a set of binoculars.

Inwardly, he thanked his allies who had convinced him to advance alongside them in a stealthier approach. Diving headlong into the scene before his eyes would have caused him a spot of trouble.

A small spot of trouble, his ego insisted. Teeny-tiny.

Sunset's light has cast the world in an orange glow, and the long shadows of faceless soldiers stretched across a ground which rumbled with their combined footfalls. A small clearing in the forest had become a huge tract of flat land by the efforts of the 705th Battalion, too large for them to use it all with tents laid out in rows and a chain link fence running around the perimeter. With a mere couple of hours to their assault on Yuell, the soldiers were out in force to complete the preparations. They went about their tasks with rifles slung over their shoulders, or set near to hand. Officers ran to and fro, barking orders that were promptly obeyed. Progress could be tracked by the way everything seemed to grow tighter over time, the different squads shifting closer and closer to each other.

"Two hundred, maybe closer to three hundred," one of their scouts estimated, a bit stunned by the sight.

"It looks like three of the platoons are just infantry," Walter added his observation. Kneeling beside Jaune, his lance was placed on the ground. "No tanks, no artillery, all numbers."

And quantity, in a certain light, has a quality of its own. In the absence of tank maintenance crews and firing teams, the infantry platoons filled out their ranks with a few dozen additional shock troops whose job was to spray bullets at a target. Compared to that, Jaune's side had mustered most of the town garrison for the operation, and still fell short of one platoon. He was a force by himself compared to people here, and even then he must admit the disparity was a bit much.

He contemplated donning his armor set for this one. It's bulky and slowed him down a tad, meaning he couldn't avoid the hits as well as before, but the innate protection of the Rathalos armor would ensure his Aura didn't sink like a stone under the hail of bullets waiting in his future. Chip damage was the death of a Huntsman.

Jaune blanched at that last thought. Yeah, armoring up sounded like a nice plan.

"What are we doing, boss?" asked Walter. The rest of the militia also looked to him for an answer, and Jaune realized not for the first time that earning the reputation he now held brought with it a great pressure. They believed him wise, for his victories. Frantically, his mind raced to analyze the situation.

"You're not going out there, and you aren't splitting into separate teams," he said, adamant. "With their numbers, they can overwhelm your positions no matter what you try, and I can't be everywhere at once. They'll keep me occupied and take you out squad by squad."

"Wait, are you saying that…" Walter trailed off, hesitant to finish the comment.

Jaune nodded. "It'll be on me to hold their attention while you rain down fire on their heads." Awe met his declaration; they could not imagine overcoming one-versus-three hundred odds (and neither can Jaune, to be honest). A sweep of his hand and ammunition boxes appeared on the ground, joined by a selection of Imperial machine guns. Most of the militia have witnessed him breaking the laws of physics on the daily, so it passed with muted reactions. "Keep a constant barrage on those soldiers and maybe you can trick them into thinking we have a lot more people on our side. It'll make them wary of getting near you."

Mica, a recent recruit to the town militia, retrieved one of the guns to check its condition. As he nervously fiddled with it, he said, "I don't feel so good about this. There's too many, and—"

"And we have Jaune Arc on our side," Walter replied. "He's worth a thousand of them!"

A surge of pride welled up within him that he just couldn't stamp down. It emboldened him to take charge, and he shifted to place himself between the two men, cutting into the conversation before an argument could start, or worse, someone loses their courage.

"Stick to small goals, and they'll add up to victory," he advised.

A wisdom he learned from Tattletale, it's no more than what he was doing with his trips to other worlds. Some challenges sounded insurmountable, the battle impossible to win, until they were broken into little pieces so that one's mind could wrap around them.

"We're here to remove their tanks from play, first and foremost," he said. "Those are the biggest threat to the city due to how much destruction they can cause. After that, it's a matter of scattering the soldiers. Disorient them, scare them, force them to lose heart so they can no longer even contemplate an attack on Yuell. With that, it's our win."

And just killing the tanks could make that happen. Morale was a fickle thing.

As for the tanks themselves, they sat at the center of the camp, engines idling and ready to fire to full power at any moment. Arranged in a ring, their formation turned the radiators inward to minimize exposure, pointing to some awareness that a base this large always ran the risk of discovery, and an attack. Sandbags were stacked to block the gaps between the tanks, further protecting their weakpoints with the operators for the vehicles leaning on the sandbags as they chatted to while away the hour.

With a good shot, a lancer might be able to strike true at one of the vehicles. The odd-shaped rocket launchers weren't that accurate, however. Those tanks were going to be on him to deal with.

"Marina?"

The woman, heretofore dead quiet, gave a nod and raised her new sniper rifle looted from Imperial hands. "I will cover you."

Marina's no planner, hence her silence all this while. She nevertheless excelled at her own field. In that simple phrase Jaune heard a promise, and it steadied his nerves like nothing else.

He had reliable people at his back. What was there to fear?

As the last sliver of sunlight lowered below the horizon and darkness overtook the world, the camp was alerted to an intruder entering the perimeter.

A suit of armor, which many Imperial troopers mistook for one of their own brethren at first for its crimson red color, rammed through the chain link fence. Its last-century aesthetics threw further confusion over the matter. None knew what to make of it, until one of the officers made a decision and ordered his troops to stop the trespasser—he didn't correct them when they aimed their firearms instead of trying to subdue him.

A bullet struck Jaune in the stomach, and but for a grunt he barely slowed down. He stuck close to the ground, and a blast of pale fire under his heels with each step he took threw him forward at a speed he was hard-pressed to match on his best day. His hands held both the shields of Crocea Mors and Red Rook to form a protective cocoon.

The camp was awakening in a furor by now. Soldiers from all directions began firing on him.

To them, he was a faceless thing, a tank in human form that shrugged off their attacks as if they were toys. On his part, Jaune sent a rare prayer to the Outsider that his defenses held. The white glow of Aura testified to the effect borne by the repeated impacts all over his body that even his shields couldn't fully prevent. Pitting his momentum against that of their onslaught was a contest he would lose in due time.

Silver lining, he didn't need to win. He had a goal, and reaching that was all that he needed to do.

The Imperial soldiers realized this, also, as it did not take a genius to notice he was set on a straight course to the tanks. The operators scampered to their feet in response, and hurried to climb inside before he got there.

A single word galvanized their efforts to a fever pitch, screeched by a panicky soldier in a tone of utter terror. A cry that was taken up by a hundred throats.

A name for him.

"Valkyria!"

"Valkyria! It's a Valkyria!"

Coming in fast, Jaune sprang high in the air. His shields switched with a rifle, and he wasted no time opening fire on the figures swarming over the tanks to keep them away from the hatches. Despite his one-handed grip and haphazard aim, the rounds miraculously found purchase in their targets, puncturing through the inadequate armor they've donned to pierce the flesh beneath. Further support from within the forest sent the tank crews scrambling for cover.

One of the tanks was almost ready to go. Half its operators laid bleeding on the metal exterior, but a skeleton crew of two managed to enter, with one of them reaching up to shut the hatch.

Close to two hundred pounds of person and armor landed on the man with both feet, and the two of them dropped into the hole together. Jaune found himself in a cramped space filled with levers and dials… and a whole lot of red as the man below cushioned his fall. The noise of their fall and the subsequent screams of a man whose bones had been ground to a pulp alerted his partner, who spun around to come face-to-face with Jaune. Behind the Imperial helmet, a pair of blue eyes the exact shade of his own widened in surprise.

The soldier voiced the beginning of a question as his pistol cleared the holster. It turned midway into a gurgle when a length of sharp steel slammed through his chest. The light in those blue eyes faded to a dull shine.

The stench of death quickly filled the enclosed space, blood and waste and complete foulness to make Jaune gag. He tolerated it to pan over the controls. Plans of turning the tank against its allies was soon quelled by a lack of understanding for what all the buttons do.

He tried pulling a random lever anyway. The main cannon fired a shot that exploded something in the distance. A shiver ran up his spine.

"That was amazing! Almost seems a waste to do this," he said, summoning the Company scroll. A couple of taps led him to the correct menu. Time for a magic trick.

From one moment to the next, the steel ceiling was replaced with an open sky. The floor beneath his feet fell away, causing him and the two bodies to drop the short distance to the ground.

Around him, a hush. The Imperial soldiers had no frame of reference for what had just occurred. Although they would not see past his full-face helm, Jaune grinned. They were going to flip.

He dove to the side, and slapped a hand on the adjacent tank. Peeking at the screen resting in his other hand, he caught a new entry popping up. Nobody else counted as being in possession of the vehicle.

Perfect.

That tank, too, vanished into thin air, and he could practically read the thoughts running through the minds of his opponents. The battalion only had nine of the things, and they didn't grow on trees.

He burst into motion, and his previous spot exploded in a cloud of dust with how many guns shot at him. The nearest tank had people climbing on its side, and Jaune wasted no time setting upon them. The operators tried to cling to whatever they could grab, but their strength was no match for his, and he ripped them away from the vehicle. One almost made it down the hatch before a shadowy arm reached in after him, getting a firm grasp on his ankle to drag him kicking and screaming from safety. A piteous moan of dismay followed the disappearance of the third tank.

A roaring engine signaled the end of his selling spree. He jumped onto the other tanks to meet shut hatches after shut hatches, the remaining crews succeeding in putting at least some of their people inside.

With the easy avenue closed to him, Jaune switched gears. The tanks represented genuine threats now rather than opportunities, and what do you know, the radiators were fast powering up to extreme temperatures, exposing their critical weakness. He rolled off the tank he was on and into the center of the formation, the roiling heat of the surrounding radiators akin to a breeze within his Rathalos armor. Having gained a measure of reprieve from the gunfire chasing him, he looked around to consider his next steps.

Shooting a gunlance shell at this proximity sounded like a bad idea, so he activated his boots and jumped high above the camp. A tinkertech bomb landed on the ground in his place. It went off a short time later, forgoing simple incendiary effects to spew outright lava across the area. The lava encountered the radiators, and melted through to touch the ragnite fuel coursing within.

Fireworks bloomed in the night. The explosions rocked the camp, with not a single tank spared from destruction. Burning shrapnel rained on the soldiers, slicing apart the disciplined formations and setting tents aflame to light up the camp in a malevolent glow.

That… that was a lot more than he intended.

He didn't have time to linger on it. His pause had given a soldier the chance to line up a shot, and a lance's warhead clipped him on the shoulder, thankfully not detonating then and there but still spinning him end over end. Unbalanced, he lost control of his rockets, the steady hover becoming an erratic struggle to stay aloft. The subsequent fireball at his back slammed him into the dirt with a resounding crash.

A boot stomped on his neck a second later, then a booming echo deafened his ears as the soldier standing above him unloaded a rifle round to the back of his head.

"D-Did I get him?" the man stammered afterward. He sounded like he couldn't believe it, shell-shocked by the preceding series of events which defied any conventional logic.

"Owwww…"

Bang! The rifle went off again, mostly on accident, to double-tap what should have been a dead body. Even that didn't work, and Jaune shoved away from the ground, throwing the soldier on his back as he stood up. His sword appeared to hand, and he swept it across the man's throat before he could pull the trigger a third time.

A glance at his surroundings, and the sense of burgeoning victory wash over him. Morale among the Empire troops had plummeted after the latest display. In their eyes, what stood in front of them might as well be an immortal monster sprung from legend. They held onto their guns as one would a teddy bear, for comfort rather than as a means to kill their foe.

As he advanced on them, one of the soldiers cast his rifle into the dirt. His shoulders drooped in defeat. Jaune accepted it as a signal of surrender, and rushed past him without a second glance to deal with the next opponent.

A pair of arms latched on to him, to give him pause. Jaune turned his head toward the culprit. The soldier he thought had surrendered was staring back in hopeless despair, holding him down for his allies to shoot.

"Die… please, just die…"

In answer, Jaune seized him by the visor and tore him away, shifting on his heels to use the man as a shield to block the incoming gunfire. The soldier shook and danced to the rhythm of bullets, his eyes fixated on Jaune in a numb fear until the end. His body was then tossed to the side as Jaune continued to advance on the others.

Yet, again, he felt another pair of arms, these wrapping around his waist as its owner tried to tackle him off his feet. He bashed the pommel of his sword against their head, denting the metal helmet. The second soldier fell limp to the ground.

Jaune couldn't check on his fate, because following in the two men's footsteps were a dozen more, their rifles and machine guns given up in lieu of knives, or pistols for some. They charged at him to bring the fight to close-quarters. He couldn't guess what they were thinking as it resulted in their allies shooting them by mistake. Consternation grew within him as none of them paid mind to that, nor did they slow their steps as Jaune cut down the nearest ones with ease.

And then it ceased to be with ease, as behind them still more soldiers took up the tactic. They crashed over him as a tide.

He struck out in every direction, facing no shortage of targets. The ground soon turned slick beneath his boots, and crowded with the bodies of the fallen.

Problem was, the space to swing his sword was fading, the distance between him and his opponents shortening until the soldiers were pressed right up to him, shouting in his face as they drove their knives into his armor, seeking purchase in a gap. One jumped on his back, attempting to pry his helmet off. His allies piled on, stacking their weight to crush him.

He lifted the ones above him, the six or seven men, and threw them aside. Near instantly, their fellow soldiers replaced them in greater numbers, leaping on while screaming and screaming and screaming in utter terror as all they wanted was for the monster to die.

And then, darkness began to fall despite sunset having come and gone. The moon above was hidden piece by piece, sliver by sliver, by the Imperial soldiers stacking one atop another until he was unable to see anything around him. He pushed and pulled but found no give. They had blockaded him on every side to the point that their knives were pressed into their own flesh, and they just wouldn't stop screaming!

The rocket boots hummed at full power, and lifted him not an inch from the ground. Surrounding him was a stifling heat, along with the stink of a hundred bodies. He gasped for breath, and choked on the shallow air. His foes had built a coffin for him from their own lives.

An ugly epiphany reared its head. The 705th Battalion had, quite by chance, stumbled upon a method to kill him. A burst of fear roared within his chest. He didn't feel so invincible anymore.

People weren't as dangerous as tanks, he had deemed. What a dumb thought. Who was it that built those machines in the first place?

How was he going to get out of here!?

Desperation drove his hands. A tinkertech bomb appeared in his grasp.

The radio on his hip crackled with static, and it was the most beautiful sound he had ever heard amidst this world of unending cries. A familiar voice followed, scratchy from disuse.

"Hang on, Arc!"

At the edge of his hearing, gunfire erupted. Mixed in with the sharp ratatat of Imperial machine guns were the booming cadence of a sniper rifle, and the screams all around him took on a different pitch—shrieks and sobs filled with pain that preceded parts of the human coffin growing still.

He shoved and shoved and shoved, and this time something gave. A ray of moonlight shone through a gap, returning his sight to him. He threw a punch at a soldier's face to send the man reeling, which widened a space just enough for him to squeeze through. He promptly activated his boots, and Jaune rocketed out of the hill composed of shouting, thrashing, dying men.

A bullet glanced past him, fired from beyond the tree line. He was certain it's an accident. His allies had been pouring gunfire down on the pile of soldiers in their effort to rescue him.

They were now also fending off the approaching squads of infantry who had pinpointed their location. That danger passed as Jaune hit the Imperials from the back and tore their formation apart. He wasn't in a kind mood, tears pooling at the corners of his eyes as he struck out at those that caused him to experience such a fear he had never known. Refusing to let them get near, he summoned guns to hand, blasting away in blind panic—his marksmanship made up for the shortfall in cool-headed focus. Tinkertech explosives added to the chaos, half his stash wiped out before he realized it. As the last gun clicked empty, he fell on them with his lance, the wide sweeps of the weapon throwing people every which way.

Anything, to not endure that hell again.

In his haze, he spotted a man far at the back of the fight, outside an ostentatious tent that spoke of wealth… or command. Dressed in different garb from the common soldiers, epaulets and medals festooned his uniform, he was talking quickly into a radio set.

The tiny part of him not drunk on adrenaline told Jaune to aim for that one. A sniper rifle round claimed the officer's life before he had gone more than three steps.

Jaune slammed a button on his radio, and shouted, "Nice shot, Marina!"

"Mmhm."

It occurred to him that he was coming around to the Gallians' way of thinking. The Imps were the enemy.

The loss of that officer brought with it a collapse of the last vestiges of discipline, and despite their superior numbers, soon the battle was all but over with the broken-spirited Imperial soldiers hightailing into the darkness. The Yuell militia swept into the camp, and with Jaune at their head, they rooted out the last pockets of resistance, driving their foes into a decisive rout as they shouted in victory at their retreating backs.

In the end, it was just Jaune and his allies remaining in the camp, staring off into the woods. The Gallians seemed half-stunned at the thought that they were the ones to hold their ground, and stood there in a blank silence unsure of what to say. On his part, Jaune vanished the armor that had turned uncomfortably warm over the course of the battle, and sank to the ground in relief.

Someone else dropped on their rear to join him. Jaune and Walter exchanged a look.

"That…" began Walter after a time. "Did we win?"

Mutely, Jaune nodded. The other man leaned back to stare at the empty air, an open-mouthed expression of wonder stealing over his face.

"You really are magic," the man said.

Laughter bubbled up Jaune's throat at that, and it's a sentiment shared by Marina nearby from how the corner of her lips was twitching.

A simple statement which encompassed far too much. They have done it. The bad dream which has hung for days over Yuell—

A bright flare shattered the night, the projectile screeching as it traced a line from the ground to the sky. At the zenith of its ascent, it burst into light to illuminate the area.

Silence followed in its wake. The budding celebration died with a whimper, replaced with uncertainty.

"What was that?" asked one of the Gallians.

A horrible suspicion whispered poison into Jaune's ear, squeezing his breath to a shallow wheeze. He sprang upright, and walked a few shaky steps away from the group so he could take flight.

What he spied from that vantage point was the gleam of moonlight over cold steel, a thousand flickers in the dark that joined together to form a long line stretching to the far distance.

Headed here.

His heart quickened its pace, working to a thundering beat.

The officer with the radio, and the flare. One conclusion emerged above the other possibilities.

"Dammit, Tattletale… You said it was one battalion."


-o-​


"One battalion. One," stressed the commander, as the university building shook from the latest artillery bombardment.

It went to show that old people were not above metaphorically kicking somebody's teeth in.

Tattletale huddled on a seat beside the map of Gallia, chewing on her lip as she glared at the figurines. They no longer painted a neat picture. With the new development, there's too much uncertainty to trust it as anything other than base supposition. Two new markers had joined the one resting beside Yuell, signifying two additional battalions… thus far. Their agent behind enemy lines was still spotting movement from the north and east, pointing to a constant flow of reinforcements for the days ahead.

Lying flat on the lowest of the lecture hall's tiered benches, Jaune stared at the ceiling through tired eyes. The nights of troubled sleep were getting to him.

"What is going on?" he wondered aloud. "Why didn't you see this coming, Lisa?"

Tattletale whirled around on her seat, her face thunderous.

"My deductions don't just appear from the ether!" She jabbed a finger at him. "I need information, and for the most part that was coming from the rank and file soldiers you captured."

And from questioning the captives, she had extrapolated their responses to read the intentions of the people above them. In a well-oiled machine of the military apparatus where the chain of command prevailed, that could in theory allow them a straight view to the top.

Of course, there was a limit, and they thought they had accounted for tolerances, the difference between the competency the Empire projected and the reality of their organizational structure. No army was perfect, but an image skewed to the boots-on-the-ground perspective should still provide insight into the minds of the individuals in charge of the war.

But there was a mistaken assumption here, wasn't there? They took for granted that, at some level, every soldier would hold to the overall thrust to the Empire's strategy. That their movements and goals reflected the aims of their superiors, and those superiors to their superiors.

"There weren't supposed to be reinforcements, so far as the soldiers knew," Tattletale insisted. "If help was on the way, their commander wouldn't have pushed so hard. They were getting desperate for results, and even thought they might lose. How was I supposed to know that the idiot was afraid of the other battalions showing up?"

Results mattered above all. An officer seen as incompetent could well find himself removed from his position for his failings, or even placed in front of a firing squad if his actions were egregious enough. That practice went double for the East Europan Imperial Alliance which has held on to its martial traditions, and prized military acumen as a sign of good character. For the man that could not take Yuell despite bleeding half his forces dry, it must have felt as if the war was lost.

Tattletale had read him right, up to a point. Yet, war was a game ultimately played several levels above the likes of them in this room and the commander of a battalion. What they saw as victory or defeat was so very small.

The girl slapped a hand on the table, rattling the figurines. "It's not my fault. It's not!"

Silence greeted her outburst. Jaune and the garrison commander were each embroiled in their own thoughts, contemplating the what-ifs and wherefores of this situation teetering on the brink. Looking back, there had been mistakes aplenty, avenues whose risks now seemed trivial which they could have taken had they warnings of the threat lying in wait for them.

Finally, Jaune spoke.

"…It is a little your fault."

"Oh, fuck you, Jaune!"

The tock-tock of a cane rapping the ground interrupted their quarrel. The old man looked at Tattletale with disapproval for her rudeness to a fine personage as Jaune, to which she rolled her eyes and crossed her arms in defiance. He then slumped down in a chair where he sat rubbing his temples.

"You did better than most," the old man admitted to Tattletale. "Better than I, and men I've known. I have had the pleasure"—he sneered—"of serving under many a commander who couldn't find their bottom with their hands."

Tattletale sat straighter. "R-Right? All of you have me to thank—"

"It is still no excuse to lose your head!" the commander continued, and Tattletale shrank back, wincing. "War is chess played blindfolded with missing pieces. We never have all that we need, or know what the future holds. The decisions being made in this conflict… they are settled in faraway places. It is the lot of Yuell, of us, to make do and survive these choices." His eyes softened. "Remember, that we should have fallen days ago."

Jaune heard a sniffle, barely audible. By the time he peered closer, Tattletale appeared no different from usual.

Another artillery shell shook the windows.

"Lisa, what's your take on that?" Jaune asked. "I figured they would be marching on the city at this point."

She shot him a catty look. "Oh? Sure you want to trust my judgment?"

"I always do, even if I complain. You know that."

A small grin grew on her face. She kicked one leg over the other, and held her chin as she studied the map. Jaune walked over to stand beside her chair. On the other side of the table, the old man leaned forward, waiting to hear what the girl had to say.

With a delicate finger, Tattletale flicked a figurine set next to Yuell to send it bouncing away.

"You wiped out the 705th. That's a pretty good message to leave for their reinforcements. They would have found the camp, and saw the destroyed tanks… the commander… the dead. Before they can do anything else, they need to understand what the threat is that could destroy a battalion."

The survivors would be interrogated, the scene investigated. Jaune imagined what conclusions they'd draw from the tales of fantastical powers and destruction all around, of a night that had flipped upside-down where the few defeated the many.

"Smoke and mirrors, or perhaps not," said the garrison commander. "These newcomers would have a hard time deciding which is it, and won't move until they are confident of avoiding a similar fate. These bombardments—"

"Are there to keep us contained," Tattletale finished for him. "Meanwhile, they're setting up, digging in. An attack is inevitable."

The old man nodded. "Just not now."

Thus, the city settled into a disquieting peace. Plans and suggestions were thrown about in each subsequent session without a resolution as Yuell adopted a wait and see approach to mirror the Empire. With so much attention on them, the possibility of evacuating the populace once again fell out of favor, while efforts to fortify the town pressed ahead with renewed fervor. Likewise, raids into hostile territory were reduced to a near stand-still as the militia encountered the challenge of how to send out a force that was sized both to sneak beneath notice and enact meaningful damages on Imperial positions.

Well, besides Jaune, and his problem was that he could never range far from town due to the prospect of an assault on the city occurring at any moment. After two unsuccessful attempts to ambush a battery of cannons, Tattletale ordered him to rest.

And in a way, life went on.

"Where do you want this, Claudia?" Jaune called out in the early morning hours, a barrel filled with potatoes on his shoulder.

The woman he was addressing turned around. Noticing the weight he carried, she hurried to clear a space among the nearby crates and boxes, and watched with interest as he lowered the barrel to the ground.

"Thank you very much, sir—I mean, Jaune," she said afterward.

He nodded, then looked over to the counter where others were distributing food to the general population.

Rationing was in full effect for Yuell, although most would admit that an unofficial version had begun months before he got to this world, with prices of goods shooting sky high ever since the war commenced to limit what people put on their dinner tables. While money no longer held the same importance to life in these siege conditions, a new issue arose considering the city hasn't received a new shipment of food for almost a week and won't for the foreseeable future. Yuell had already depleted their food stores to unprecedented levels in order to support the national military forces, leading to a shortage that now threatened to fall into outright famine. Measures to stretch what they had on hand became a matter of course. Hence, the daily lineup for a share.

He watched, and saw too many hungry faces. Too much fear that infects from one person to the next.

"I'm… going to the back."

Before he slunk away, he caught an excited look crossing the worker's face. She also bade leave and hurried toward her colleagues. Whispers passed between them, with furtive glances thrown at him as he ducked around the corner into the warehouse.

Nobody tried to follow him anymore after the first few times, meaning he didn't have to be careful bringing out the Company scroll from his pants pocket. His fingers danced on the screen. A translucent box materialized in midair, heaving with cargo.

A minute later, Jaune exited the warehouse. On his shoulders rested two stacks of coarse, woven bags filled with rice grains. Cheap as dirt to the Marketplace at a measly five Points each, they provided better cost-effectiveness than most other options available to him, and he added them to the pile of food slated for distribution today.

He said nothing, and the workers asked no questions. People were curious of the man seemingly scrounging up sacks of food from thin air every day, but they did their best to not pry into it too hard. Of course, there's a smattering of grumblings from those who believed that he had been hoarding it to seek wartime profits. The argument went nowhere far, undercut by him demanding no money and also drowned out by the support he enjoyed from the populace at large.

The additional supplies weren't enough to resolve the food situation, and served as tasteless fillers for the stomach. The point to them was to soften the blow, and Jaune made sure to smile at each person in line as he passed them a cup or small bag filled with the grains to take home.

"Boil it well, okay?" he said to the siblings Hans and Greta.

They spoke together, ""Yes, Jaune.""

"Good." He turned to the person working beside him. "Magari, can you get them breakfast? Three plates, please, not two. Their mother is at that table over there."

"..."

Jaune didn't think he would meet someone less inclined to talk than Marina Wulfstan, but Magari proved him wrong. That girl had been present every morning to help distribute food and still hadn't said a single word directly to him. He would have assumed she had a problem with him, except she would nod and do everything he asked. She was willing to put in the work, at least, and he did his best to show that she was welcome here.

Hans and Greta received the cooked food meant for eating here, and after waving to Jaune, they rushed into the crowd toward one of the outdoor tables set off to the side of the distribution site. A woman—their mother—was there to welcome them, praising them for how helpful they were being. A pair of crutches leaned against the wall behind her.

The shelling had taken one of her legs. Falling rubble, he heard. Ragnaid, like stimpaks, had limitations.

"Well, well, well," a familiar voice piped up.

Jaune turned his head to the sight of Tattletale, the girl sporting a grin.

"Heeey, Lisa… Shouldn't you be at the university?"

"I was, yes. But then I had to wonder where you were." She cut into the line to stand in front of him, drawing dirty looks that faded once people noticed the Gallian-blue militia jacket she was wearing. Her nails rapped a beat on the wooden counter.

"I could have sworn I asked you to rest," she continued.

"It didn't feel right doing nothing," he said with a sheepish shrug of his shoulders. "Come on, Lisa, I'm passing out food not running marathons. This isn't exactly strenuous."

Tattletale narrowed her eyes at him in a playful glare, maintaining it for a few seconds before giving an exaggerated huff.

"Yeah, yeah, go figure." She cast her gaze across the counter. "Well, since you're here… Feed me," she demanded, cutely tilting her head.

He barked a laugh. "Sure! Go sit down, and I'll bring you something in a bit." He then leaned forward to whisper in her ear. "If you prefer, I can buy a dish from the Marketplace. What we have here is pretty simple fares."

Tattletale considered it for a moment, then shook her head. "I'll have what everyone's having. Solidarity, and all that."

She left him to it, spinning on her heels while fluttering her fingers at him. The girl soon commandeered a table for herself next to the one occupied by Hans and Greta, where she chitchatted with the pair's mother.

Returning to work, Jaune found a plate intended for Tattletale of boiled potatoes and two pitifully-thin slices of cured meat, plus bread, already waiting for him. He gave the person who prepared it a grateful nod.

"Thanks, Magari. I'll get it to her later. For now, can you help me serve that group there? They've been waiting for a while."

Magari looked where he pointed, and froze for a second before rapidly nodding in agreement. The girl set about readying plates of food with a pep in her step that Jaune didn't think she noticed, while he wrapped raw ingredients for takeaway in old newspapers.

The people he referred to shared the same dark blue—near black—hair as Magari. The patterns on their clothes, like the two ribbons she wore, indicated a common heritage. He had heard the word 'Darcsen' thrown around, often in the kind of tone that made him frown. In his personal experience they were unfailingly polite, if a touch too deferential toward him at times.

After one too many of them bowed to him, he tried reciprocating the gesture to the next person he handed food to. The bug-eyed look he received was hilarious. Worth it.

He got Magari to smile. Also worth it.

About ten, fifteen minutes later, he made a second trip to the warehouse to restock via extradimensional delivery, then bade leave from the group. Plate of food in hand, he circled around the throngs of people to reach Tattletale's table.

Concern grew as the girl stood up to meet him, the earlier friendliness she showed while speaking to the mother of Hans and Greta gone from her demeanor.

"Jaune, can we talk?"

That line never boded well. He put on a smile.

"Okay, yeah. You want to sit down?" he offered.

She didn't take the bait. "No. This is better done in private."

With that, Tattletale stepped to the side. This revealed the glowing forms of Hans and Greta, the oblivious pair of siblings laughing as they played a game of pinching each other, their mother watching on in wonder.

Ah.

Dammit, she found out.

"You sure you don't want to chill here?"

She grabbed his sleeve. "Come on, ya goof."

Tattletale led the way and they relocated to an ornate iron bench in a familiar courtyard, under a myrtle tree in full bloom.

This little corner of the city had remained pristine, and as Jaune sat waiting for Tattletale to speak, he gazed at the scenery with an odd sense of peace—nostalgia, even. It's almost like nothing has happened and they were still living within that first hour where this world held such wonderful possibilities.

The clatter of a plate being set aside drew his attention. Tattletale had ceased picking at her food to focus on him, and boy did she look unhappy.

"What the hell are you thinking?" she asked in a biting tone.

Now, that's a question with a hundred answers he could give her the runaround with. He even had a couple choice quips to turn it back on her. That wasn't quite fair to Tattletale, however, because she worries. How could he blame her for that?

"It's funny and you might laugh," he said, growing somber despite his words. "I'm thinking that I don't know what I'm doing, so I'm just doing everything and hoping something works."

Tattletale cocked her head to the side but remained quiet, listening. He supposed she could tell he was taking her seriously… or maybe she's giving him the shovel for him to dig his own grave.

"Everybody's banking on me having a plan to win, but the Empire is big. Way too big. Planning to defeat an entire Kingdom is ridiculous."

"Doable."

"For you, maybe. Does it require resources we don't have, by the way?" The scrunch of her nose indicated yes. "That's the problem. The Empire is big, and the solution needs to be just as big. I can't do anything about it." He ran a hand through his hair. "So, I'm thinking smaller."

"Kinda obvious there. We got two or three battalions on our doorstep to contend with."

"Smaller. Tick-tock," he hinted.

Tattletale frowned, and leaned over to look closer at him. Her eyes widened.

"A day!?"

Jaune grinned. "Sounds possible, doesn't it?"

"Sounds stupid, more like!"

A fair take, all told. Jaune shrugged helplessly.

"Turns out sheer numbers make for an overwhelming advantage. Who knew? I'm limited to working with what I have, and that means handling the challenge that's more on my level."

"And that involves giving Aura to those kids… so, what, you're making child soldiers?"

He blinked. "Hah?" The word registered, and he furiously shook his head. "Nonono, I'm doing that to help them survive the artillery strikes. That's causing more deaths than the Imperials' tanks and soldiers. I figured some defense is better than none."

"I remember you telling me that giving Aura to others will drain yours." Tattletale rubbed her temples, and gave a frustrated sigh. "That's the opposite of resting."

"A small amount, and it grows back," he said. "And there's the chance to get it to spread. One person gives Aura to two. Two gives to four. Four to eight. On and on, until the whole city has them."

"Doing that would cause so many issues to this world, it's not even funny…"

"That's the world's fault for trying to kill these people. Think small, Tattletale."

In truth, it's an unrealistic plan with many points of failure. But then, he was throwing solutions at a wall in order to fend off a foe hundreds or thousands of times bigger than him. He's allowed to be a little ridiculous.

For example, the idea to evacuate the populace through the portal. Leaving aside the logistics of arranging a city-wide conga line, the finite space of the apartment would prevent him from fitting many people inside, and would mean abandoning everyone else.

Tattletale didn't take his advice well, and was groaning into her hands now. "And that explains the food you're buying." Oh great, she caught that, too. "We can't feed a city, you idiot!"

"Forever? No." For a while? Perhaps a different answer. There's a time to teach people to fish, and a time to just get food in their hands.

"It's a waste of Points," Tattletale snapped back. She raised her head to glare at him. "At this rate, we might as well call it quits before we get hit by the artillery and die as paupers, Jaune!"

He flinched. "Can we… not go just yet?"

"Fucking—" Tattletale was working up into a furor, shaking in anger as she hissed, "Why are you doing all this? Why even care? They don't…" Here, she faltered. What she wanted to say, she couldn't, and so amended, "They're nice people, but their whole country is at war. In the long run—"

"In the long run, we're all dead," he said, causing Tattletale to freeze mid-sentence. She stared at him, her gaze uncertain. "That's the world. That's life."

He reached over to pick a flower that had fallen on her hair, holding it up to his view. He twirled it between his fingers to admire the vivid purple shade of the petals, and took in its scent.

"The lofty goals are nice and good, but each day we're alive is another day won. To me, this is worth fighting for."

They both looked up as explosions rocked the area.

"Imperials are at it again," Jaune commented in a casual tone, a far cry from days ago.

"Yeah…" Tattletale performed a stretch. "Nearest shelter?"

The answer was instantaneous. "Bakery."

Everybody in the city had learned to memorize the best places to hide.

Conversation put on hold, they got to their feet, and set out at a brisk yet untroubled pace. Running in a panic could lead to accidentally diving face-first into a blast. One lived longer by maintaining calm, along with firm footing. Tattletale even remembered to take her plate of food with her.

The door to the store was left unlocked, intended for this exact scenario. As Jaune ducked inside, the radio on his hip crackled.

"Jaune!" shouted the voice of Walter. "Imperials on the horizon! They're launching another offensive, and I see tanks!"

He cursed, and turned back to the door. Tattletale motioned him to stop and continue to the basement. He hesitated for a moment, but listened to her in the end.

The radio activated a second time. "More from the north!" Then, as they were descending the steps to the level below. "South, too! It's an attack from three directions! I… I… Jaune, what do we do!?"

Jaune raised the radio to his mouth. Tattletale snatched it out of his hand, speaking in his stead.

"Bunker down. The artillery is there to cover their approach. We're scattered all over the place, meaning it's no use going out to meet them, so get to safety and be ready for a battle immediately after the shelling stops. Pass the word along to gather at Rendezvous Point B. We will regroup there to organize a response."

The clipped, authoritative tone of her voice broke through the militiaman's agitation.

"Yes, ma'am!" he cried, and they could almost imagine the salute he was performing from that answer alone. Silence followed on the radio.

Jaune and Tattletale both slumped against the basement wall, sliding down to sit on the floor. The darkened interior of the room made it impossible to see further than a couple of inches, leading them to draw closer. The building shook and rattled as they waited for the shelling to end.

After a minute of utter quiet between them, Jaune spoke up. "You know, we haven't been alone in a while, huh?"

"Yeah," Tattletale answered, chin resting on her knees. "It's been a long week. They kept us pretty busy."

Always with a raid to conduct, or a strategy meeting. If not those, then they were dealing with the fallout of damages to the city, and attempting to raise morale.

He couldn't help but laugh. "How is it that the first chance we have to relax together is during an artillery bombardment?"

"Pft!" Tattletale covered her mouth. "Oh god, that's so messed up."

"Right?"

In the dark, they leaned on each other, snickering at the joke that was their life.

"Tattletale?" he said afterward.

"Yeah?"

He idly tapped his fingers on the wooden floor, collecting his thoughts.

"I don't like war. I really, really don't like war."

Tattletale didn't answer for a time. He felt her gaze on him, her breath tickling his neck.

"Then, would you leave it here?"

Jaune closed his eyes and tilted his head back until it hit the wall, thinking on the question. Behind it was a suggestion, that they could run and never look back. Abandon the city, go home. Travel to new universes and shove the memory of what happened here to the corners of their minds.

He was sure he could forget Yuell, in due time. But to consider the question…

"Not this one," he said, without a lie.

Lisa reached over, and brushed his cheek with a gentle, soothing hand.


-o-​


Nearing on midnight, Jaune sat upon a bell tower ledge and gazed out over the meadows of Yuell. It used to be a picturesque scene, now marred by the crisscrossing tank tracks.

He heard a loud boom, and watched as part of a house collapsed—its support column had been taken out. The occasional artillery shell was still hitting the city even at this hour, though it's more a psychological ploy than a true bombardment. People learned quick to sleep through the sound of a bomb. More than three in succession was the signal to wake up.

His head turned toward the northern side of the city, and he exhaled a resigned breath at the state of it.

The incursion by the Imperials lasted for the better part of the morning and early afternoon. Their three-pronged approach led to Yuell's forces being split in order to blunt the offensive, with resistance a slapdash affair of militia and civilians mounting the barricades built throughout the week. It bought time for him to take the field, but casualties were… high, as a result.

The Imperials were seeking to draw out the fight, as it turned out. The platoons attacking the south and east had grouped close together, and naturally he had sought to counter one after the other, leaving the northern skirmish to fester. That third force wasted no time carving out a foothold, fortifying it with further reinforcements from the rear until a swath of the city bristled with machine gun emplacements and tanks.

Tattletale wasn't happy with what he did to dislodge them. Went a tad apoplectic, in fact.

Eh, she forgave him once she saw it in action. He was only one person, and more power to him did not always overcome a challenge because he was limited to one place at a time. At least, unless he had clone powers or something, but that was outside his means.

Come noontime, the Yuell militia had taken to the field to startling effectiveness.

It proved the right call, and he would fight anyone that said otherwise. After all, the city managed to survive the battle with the pitiful amount of ready combatants on their side, although a large part of that was due to the collapsing morale among their enemy's ranks.

Victory was won by scaring the hell out of the Empire. With flash and glam and magic the likes this world has yet to see.

Still, lights remained in the forest, miles out. The invaders refused to give up, and were creeping ever closer as they narrowed down the specifics of his abilities.

Nothing for it, he'd do his best. He had a few ideas for that anyway, to keep ahead of the curve. Tattletale will hate it.

A yawn escaped his mouth, telling him to head for bed. It'd likely be a better sleep than the previous nights. He climbed back into the bell tower, and before descending the staircase, he looked up past a hole in the roof.

"Good night, Marina."

Above, the young woman gave a hum in response.

The situation for Yuell did not improve in drastic fashion the next morning, nor the days thereafter. News of Empire forces arriving to swell their numbers dampened the spirits of the city's defenders. Escha ranged far and wide, reporting contact at all hours. Each new offensive, they hit a little harder. Each raid, they tried a new strategy. Everyone could sense it in the air, they were building up to something.

By now, none could deny the truth. The war front has come to Yuell.

And yet, the city held. Through day, through night, it held.

It was in this vein that Yuell approached the end of the second week, having grown accustomed to a new normal. But then, as they woke up one morning, Jaune and everybody else found themselves standing at the edge of the city, watching on in awe.

The road to the city was cast in sky blue, pounded flat by footsteps.

The long procession marched at an uneven pace; no lockstep soldiers were they. Their uniforms were grimy from battle and travel, yet were unmistakable to the eyes of the citizens. Many of the newcomers were waving enthusiastically, with the people of Yuell returning the gestures with hesitant ones of their own, their minds disbelieving of the sight.

At the forefront of the procession traveled a tank, the treads rumbling over the dirt road at a human's marching pace. Its angled plating and flatter shape set it apart from the blocky designs Jaune had encountered from the Empire. Colored in Gallian-blue, a white flower was painted on its turret. A few soldiers were hitching a ride, lazily lounging atop the tank.

Most noticeable of all was the white cat squatting on the tip of the cannon. After reporting of their presence, Escha had joined them in the trip back to the city.

The tank came to a stop before the crowd. The first of the marching men and women to arrive rounded the war machine to stand on either side of it. They cradled their guns on their shoulders, showing cocky smiles.

With a squeal of metal the tank hatch opened up, and a young man emerged from the interior. He took a deep breath of the fresh air and wiped the sweat off his brow, ashy brown hair fluttering in the breeze as he enjoyed the moment in the sunshine, before realizing the many gazes directed at him. Giving a sheepish laugh, he climbed down to the ground.

Behind him, Jaune caught a glimpse of a girl with dark-blue hair poking her head out of the tank.

The young man walked up to the city, correcting his course once he noticed Jaune standing further to the front than the others plus the way the people of Yuell were looking to him for their cue. He stopped in front of Jaune, and held out a hand.

"Uh, hi—" The young man cleared his throat, and straightened his back. "I mean, I am Lieutenant Welkin Gunther of Squad 7, Gallian Militia 3rd Regiment… Nice to meet you."

Overhearing the polite greeting that he couldn't help but tack on, his subordinates chuckled and shook their heads. They appeared to be unsurprised by his behavior.

The front has come to Yuell, and so has the hero of Gallia.
