#3,197
Chapter 47: The New Front​


When couriers from Yuell brought news of the city beset by Imperial troops to the Gallian Army, its leaders thought the southern front had experienced a collapse and thus scrambled to fortify Randgriz from an assault they were certain would be imminent. In the process, they gave Yuell up as a lost cause. After all, it's been days since the messengers left the place with an artillery bombardment ongoing at the time. Good luck withstanding that.

When the attack on the capital never manifested, and Gallian high command instead received missives of Yuell not only standing but striking back against the Empire's army, everyone threw around praises along the line of 'plucky Gallian can-do spirit' and such to hide their sheer puzzlement as to the how. Sure, these new couriers told them an answer, except that was instantly dismissed as fanciful nonsense.

Then, they noticed movements behind Empire lines. Units that were bolstering the northern front seemed to be shifting southward, bypassing the central region to reach a destination even further below. Imagine the surprise of the generals and strategists as the answer they got from spies embedded in enemy territory matched what they've already heard. It shook these men to the core, let alone the rest of the country once somebody in the know blabbed their mouth.

Denied by some, hailed by others, one word traveled across Gallia at the speed of journalism.

Valkyria.

Now that warranted a response.

Squad 7. Squad 6. Squad 4. Squad 3. Squad 1.

The military mustered the nearest troops available that they could spare, and reinforcement for Yuell came in the form of a contingent sent by the national Militia, civilians drafted in times of war to support the professional Army. They may not be career soldiers, but they counted as five platoons' worth of able-bodied men and women that Gallia had deemed ready for battle, nevertheless. Veterans in comparison to the local volunteers, they've been blooded on the battlefield for months. The contingent boosted the effective number of Yuell's forces beyond the wildest expectations of a city that had in all honesty thought itself abandoned by the rest of the nation, and were a welcomed relief to its citizenry.

Of course, given the state of Yuell in regards to food reserves, looming threats, medical emergencies, the general trauma accumulated through facing the enemy alone without help for days on end among a whole long list of other issues, a celebration wasn't exactly on the schedule. After receiving a brief summation, Lieutenant Welkin Gunther had passed on the order: go, go, go!

The ensuing hours passed at a frantic pace. A field of tents sprang up in the shadow of buildings on the university campus to provide quarters for the influx of soldiers, and from there the officers sent their forces all over the city to where they would do the most good. Their medical personnel went to support the doctors working under the Coalhearths. Trenches, holes, and barricades meant to deter Imperial offensives were assessed then improved on, with extra hands pitching in from the common soldiers to expedite the process. The engineering corps lent their expertise elsewhere, calculating angles and planting charges before commencing their plan to collapse a series of buildings on the outskirts, blocking off roads and gaps with the rubble. Yuell finally had a wall.

That one… earned them less favor with the residents of the city than their other efforts. A lot of people didn't share Jaune's outlook on the comforting nature of a nice, big wall twice taller than his height, and complaints sprouted to dampen the earlier optimism. The Imps were bad enough, seeing their own side wrecking the city drew forth an uglier feeling. Some also resented the fact that they were drained close to dry of defenders and food at the start of the war, only to get attacked when they were weakest by the very enemy that the military was supposed to protect them against. Grievances building for weeks or even months met an outlet, and began to spill out.

On the soldiers' part, the incoming Militia seemed to have expected a livelier response from Yuell for providing the help they were seeking, except for every person happy to have the soldiers here, there was one or two that kept muttering about how they were doing just fine without it, going on about Arc this and Arc that. The constant comparison would be bearable if half the things said weren't clearly tall tales.

Caught in between, soldiers that hailed from Yuell returned to broken homes. They found a worrying number of faces they knew gone, the ones left behind looking at them as if they were outsiders.

Also there was, like, three different cults that have sprung up in the time they were away. What was the deal with that?

In any case, this abrasive attitude came as very little surprise to Tattletale and, encouragingly, Welkin Gunther. With both sides each having their own way of doing things now being told to work together in a tense situation, it would lead to friction as a matter of course and could go bad fast. Integration was a priority.

The answer they arrived at involved a mission. One that would remind everybody of their true enemy while ensuring long-term operationality for the Gallian Militia in the region.

Those artillery batteries had to go down.

So, as soon as they had some halfway-decent defenses in place to guard the city, Jaune immediately set out to do what he did best. Robbing his targets blind and selling off their possessions to enrich himself.

"Yo ho ho, I do love the pirate life," Jaune said as he checked his Points balance. Around him, the Imperial outpost lay in ruins.

A whistle pierced the air, hanging low in pitch then switching to a sharp high note. Recognizing the signal, he stayed peaceful as the bushes rustled nearby. His allies soon emerged with guns at the ready.

Half of them had the muzzles of their rifles pointed to the ground. Having worked with him on the regular, they knew what they'd find. The other half swept their weapons back and forth, following ingrained protocol to secure the perimeter. They behaved with a level of snappy competence that was absent from the Yuell garrison, and the occasional disapproving look leveled at the locals spoke enough of their opinion. To the real troops, Walter and his colleagues were green as grass.

Jaune hid a groan as one person in particular swaggered right up to him. Of the Squad 7 detachment tagging along, Corporal Brigitte "Rosie" Stark was the cockiest of them all and she chafed at the idea of him leading the operation. In her words, they should be leaving it to people that knew what they were doing; a fresh-faced farm boy had no place in command. Big words for a city slicker in their twenties, as if either of those qualities made her any better than him.

And also, not a farm boy. Jaune Arc was a frontier man, thank you. Sounded way better.

In any case, he somewhat understood where she was coming from. It was a hostile world facing them right now, and a wrong move could spell death for one's fellow soldiers. Nobody wanted to serve under an unqualified leader in these circumstances. Still, experience was relative. He, and the people fighting by his side this whole time, have reduced artillery hunting to an art form. Not that the corporal believed it.

"Alright, where are the cannons?" She gave a pointed look at the indents in the ground by their feet, and cursed. "Tell me you didn't let them get away. We needed those blown up!"

"I handled them," he assured her, displaying a thumbs-up and his brightest, most confident smile.

She huffed in exasperation. "Great, well, we're going to have to do a search. Maybe that'll tell us which direction the Imps took them."

The smile dropped, and he pursed his lips in displeasure. The corporal thought he was lying.

"No, I meant that I got rid of the cannons," he said. "They're gone for good and won't bother us again."

"Kid, you ran maybe ten seconds ahead of us. There's no way you managed anything."

"I flew."

"Uh-huh. Sure you did. I didn't see it."

Behind her, a large and grizzled man raised his finger, then thought better of it and returned to his task, giving Jaune a shrug. Sergeant Largo Potter held a similar sense of condescension as his squadmates about Yuell's garrison, though in his case he had caught Jaune blasting off into the sky while Rosie had been busy sweeping their rear for enemy flanking maneuvers.

Jaune motioned at the battle's aftermath strewn across the outpost as his rebuttal.

Rosie crossed her arms, a stubborn set to her jaw. "Good job tossing grenades around," she grudgingly praised. "Messy, but it made our job easier. Still doesn't mean the cannons are destroyed. We need confirmation beyond one person saying 'trust me', you get me?"

That would be easier if there was any trace of them left. Gone meant gone. Jaune looked around the area, then swiped a bloody helmet off the ground. He fished the Company scroll from his pants pocket once again, holding it out of sight.

"Watch this." He tapped the entry for the helmet on the inventory page.

Rosie blinked as the headgear that couldn't protect its owner vanished into thin air. The thing was worthless to the Marketplace, but it demonstrated his point and he got to enjoy the sight of her circling him multiple times while mumbling about how it must be a magic trick. The following minutes were spent with the corporal demanding that he perform the same act over and over with random objects so she could spot where he was shoving them (which he maintained was just an excuse for her eyes to linger on his rear), until Marina stepped out of the woods to interrupt the argument.

The young woman behaved no friendlier to Squad 7 than to anybody else, and ignored them as she walked toward him. A long case hung over her shoulder, the sort that was used to store musical instruments and the like. She looked between Jaune and the corporal, ultimately deciding that he was the person to report to.

"The stragglers are… dealt with." She glanced back and rubbed the case with her hand, the gesture almost affectionate. "And I found more."

His posture sharpened to alertness at the news. "Where? And how many?"

"Southeast. Thirty," Marina answered promptly. "I saw tents... and crates. They're hidden under camouflage netting. No…" She indicated the empty space that the artillery pieces used to occupy.

"That sounds like a supply depot," Rosie remarked. There was a gleam in her eyes, matched by Jaune. A silent agreement passed between them to put their current antagonism on hold. Their looter souls were burning bright.

"Jaune," Walter called out, having overheard. "Why don't you stick with us this time?"

He cocked his head. "You sure?"

"Come on, hotshot. It's safer with us covering you." The man didn't mention that it would mean greater danger for everyone else, and Jaune didn't bother trying to dissuade him or the others anymore. They've made it clear that they were willing to fight by his side, come what may. Walter cracked a smile. "Let's let the newcomers watch how we work."

Rosie rolled her eyes. "Yeah, yeah, show us what you yokels can do. Promise I won't laugh at you."

Jaune and Walter shared a look. Grin mirrored grin, full of giddy anticipation.


-o-​


The camp blazed red as beams of light sliced through the supply depot.

Imperial soldiers fell where they stood, smoking holes in their bodies cauterized by heat. Those still alive scrambled to hide behind whatever defensive positions they managed to reach and leveled their guns in the direction of the attacks. Try as they might, however, they could not spot their assailants and, unable to mount a proper response, they had to fire blind at their surroundings and shouted in the chaos for orders.

Deep within the forest far outside the range of enemy weaponry, Jaune and the Yuell garrison aimed down their sights. In a calm and methodical manner, they let loose a new volley. Another set of screaming voices thereafter cut short.

Jaune cradled the rifle on his shoulder, and turned to look behind him.

The Squad 7 troops stared back, jaws hanging open.

"We should be done soon," he said to them, then tapped Walter to get his attention. "Looks like we've thinned their ranks quite a bit. The rest aren't about to come out in the open, so I'll go and flush them out for you."

The other man nodded. "We'll cover your approach."

The rifle Jaune was wielding swapped for his sword. The two NCOs, Rosie and Largo, realized his intentions as Jaune rushed ahead of the formation. They sprang forward to try and grab him, shouting in a panic for him to come back. The unperturbed Yuell militia waved them off and continued laying down gunfire while snickering to one another.

Most of the soldiers didn't even notice him when he entered the camp, too concerned with their own safety. The one person shooting at him was in turn zapped by a red beam that burned away a chunk of his shoulder before Jaune ever got there. Sprinting past the injured man, he charged at a wall of sandbags, swiping at the people hunkered behind it with his sword. They recognized him by his face, his clothes, his weapon. Running was better than dying, and they scurried out of hiding.

The fastest soldier made it three steps before eating a red beam to the side of his head. Jaune carried on, crashing into the Imperial soldiers to throw them every which way as he trusted his people to handle the runners. Complete misses rarely occurred, and if it did, a second shot would finish the job.

The mop-up operation ended within five minutes.

And as his allies rejoined him, Jaune watched those from Squad 7 walking in a stupor. Their eyes were locked onto the guns carried by the local militia—Jaune's answer to the conundrum that was the defense of Yuell.

Gallian tradition typically led to manufacturers painting the wooden gunstocks in the blue of their flag. It was a calling card, an affectation that denoted patriotism in one's own home. These rifles were colored in green, and composed of metal from end to end. They bore a clunky appearance which was common among current machine gun designs. The shape didn't quite match Gallian or Empire craftsmanship, however, although the golden double-headed eagle etched on the side suggested Empire origins to raise a few eyebrows.

Then there was the most important detail about them. The fact that they shot lasers.

Faced with overwhelming numbers wielding superior arms (compared to his allies), Jaune had stopped to consider his options. The issue all came back to Points. A power that would allow him to defeat the enemy battalions cost too much for his budget, whereas the affordable abilities lacked the strength to turn the tide. Moreover, the Imperial strategy of splitting their forces neatly countered the equalizing potential he brought to an encounter. He couldn't fight on multiple fronts, nor summon a bigger army to match them soldier for soldier.

What he could have done, was to make the troops at his disposal better.

It began with modern arms, the Earth equivalent of the assault rifles used by the Atlas military. When that failed to stem the Imperial advance, he moved to super modern; bigger clips, faster rate of fire, and so on and so on. Then, he made the jump to the outright futuristic, and there magic was born.


Lasgun
Universe: 40K
Standard issue arms for the Imperium's lowly grunts.
Cheap, weak, and replaceable. But not worthless.


From one imperial army to another, a laser bolt to the head. Jaune found it apt.

A lasgun was accurate at ranges beyond the weapons of this era, the individual shots hampered only by the human ability with equipment flaw a near non-factor. The laser maintained its straight trajectory until the point it dissipates, while recoil issues became moot due to the nature of the technology. The beams punctured through the thin armor of the Imperials' uniforms like paper, and roasted the wounds they left in flesh. Wielding these, battles turned into one-sided affairs where Empire soldiers must cross an unrelenting hail of gunfire before they had a prayer of hitting anything.

The best part? Rechargeable ammunition. Tattletale noticed the half-spent 'power pack' supplying the gun had replenished a charge while exposed to sunlight, and later heating it near a fire achieved similar results. The rifles were in essence a one-and-done purchase.

Add a few extra power packs on top of that, and he ensured close to zero downtime on his side in an engagement. A rain of lasers was no hyperbole.

Lasguns were just plain unfair. Even Tattletale admitted that he couldn't have chosen better, despite the ongoing contention between him and her over the loss of Points.

"What are those guns?" said Sergeant Largo in awe.

"The Yuell special," Walter answered proudly. The man loved his lance, but he had jumped at the offer for a lasgun to supplement his loadout.

"That… that doesn't explain anything!"

"You should be dead," Corporal Rosie interjected. She was looking at Jaune and shivering. "I saw bullets hitting you at point-blank range. Why aren't you a bloody smear spread across the ground? Are you really—" Her eyes were wide, breaths coming short.

"Magic?" Jaune finished for her. He let the word hang in the air for a moment, before laughing. "I know, I know. It's not a great answer, but how about we leave it at that? Explaining would just make things more confusing."

"And you can fly?" the corporal asked in a small voice. The earlier attitude had faded, she sounded far less cocksure.

He hopped onto the air, and hovered there. "Tada~" Landing on the ground, he said, "So, you got to see what we can do now. I hope you can report to your lieutenant that we aren't helpless. Let him know that we'll go over what my troops and I bring to the table once we have some free time."

Among the Squad 7 detachment, backs stiffened and glances flitted between one another. It seemed Tattletale was correct, something she will be happy to hear. Welkin Gunther had directed his subordinates to investigate them.

Oh, it probably wasn't out of maliciousness. The question of how Yuell managed to cling on against dire odds needed answers, and the lieutenant was better served seeking trusted accounts in lieu of rumors. Strangers told lies. (Jaune would know.)

A flash of blue light passed by him, whipping up his hair. A scream, and Jaune turned to see an Imperial soldier falling to the ground. He had been trying to sneak away and now clutched the bleeding stump that remained after the shot took his leg.

"Got the officer," said Marina through the radio.

"Nice work, Marina. Thanks."

While Walter and another local militia member hurried off to secure the wounded Imperial, Jaune turned to wave at the young woman who was still hiding in the shadows of the trees. She signaled back with a gesture that he didn't understand. Propped on her shoulder was a long, oddly-shaped rifle taken from the case she carried everywhere nowadays. Electromagnetic coils lined the thin barrel, and it bore a handcrank on the side of the gunstock. A scope sat atop the entire assembly for long-range accuracy.


YCS/186 Gauss Rifle
Universe: Fallout
What if gun, but lasers?
Science tackled the hard questions and wrought something truly awful upon the world: the last gun you will ever hold, for nothing else in this wild, wild wasteland of 2281 compares.


Nobody has found evidence that Marina sleeps with the thing in her arms like a teddy bear, but that was because nobody ever managed to catch her sleeping in the first place. The Fallout universe grew more interesting by the day, as along with stimpaks they have developed quite decent weaponry. The Gauss rifle lagged behind in the sheer efficiency of the lasgun, though compensating with higher performance for almost the same cost. It fit better for sniping work, and he had nabbed one for Marina to put to devastating effect.

It also fried the last bit of composure for the Squad 7 soldiers. Rosie seemed to have decided that this nonsense was Largo's problem, throwing her hands up and walking away to leave the older man to handle the matter.

Largo scratched his head, and looked around. In the end, he gave a shrug and clapped Jaune on the shoulder.

"Your team's doing good," he said in a gruff voice. "They're a haphazard lot, but they know how to function as a squad."

Jaune accepted it for the conciliatory gesture it was, and offered the man a handshake. "We had many chances to learn." Battle after battle after battle, until they grew numb. "We aren't here to push everything onto you, we just… need more help."

That, the sergeant understood. Largo returned the handshake with a crushing grip.

"Hey, Jaune? I think we hit the motherload," called out one of the town militia members. She stood next to a crate, the top of which had been removed. A blue glow emanated from within. Not only Jaune, everybody gathered round to check it out.

He peered at the contents. "Liquid ragnite?"

"Same thing over here," reported a Squad 7 soldier.

"Here, too," added Walter nearby.

Ragnite had a wide variety of uses. Processed into liquid form, it burned as fuel.

"This must be for resupplying their tanks," Jaune said. The corner of his lips twitched. "No fuel, no tanks."

Sergeant Largo nodded. "I expect they'd have a number of these caches, but tanks are hungry beasts and this will put a strain on them. They're gonna have to be real careful fielding those."

"Hey, they're not the only ones that need it," said Walter. "Get this home and we could have half a dozen more generators running for days. I'm tired of bathing in cold water!"

That got the attention of the locals and Squad 7 alike, deciding their course.

"Okay, load these and whatever we can use on the trucks—we'll take those, too. Walter, Mica, bring that officer along," Jaune ordered. "Assume that the Imps radioed in about us. I want to be gone from the area before artillery starts dropping on our heads. With luck, that will give away their positions and we can wreck another set of cannons."

For a second time, the camp grew into a hive of activity. Yuell militia and Squad 7 alike raced from place to place, cackling as they returned with armfuls of weapons and food. More than one person was salivating at the sight of canned ham and preserved fruits.

Jaune pitched in, cracking open crates to check for loot. One in particular piqued his curiosity.

"What is this, scrap metal?"

Corporal Rosie paused in her tracks to take a peek. "Tank parts," she said with the certainty of experience. "Huh. Do the Imps anticipate that much repairs?"

"They did lose a lot of tanks here." Yes, he was bragging. "Should we take it with us?"

The woman frowned at the crate for a while, troubled over the sight for a reason she did not articulate. Then, she shrugged and cast her doubts aside. "Might as well, kid. The Edelweiss could always use an upgrade."

They evacuated the camp by the ten-minute mark, the camp was a smoking crater at fifteen. A game of hide and seek ensued through the forest as the nearest battery rushed to have their equipment packed up and away. A sparse stretch of tree outed them, leading to a quick skirmish that ended in favor of the Gallian side. Since their enemy had so kindly bundled the cannons for travel, the Squad 7 soldiers suggested they steal the lot rather than destroy it. Unlike those manning the defenses of Yuell thus far, the Militia platoons possessed enough expertise among their people to put together a firing team that would not blow themselves up.

To cap the productive trip, the group encountered a happy sight on the way back to the city.

"Aha!" Jaune cheered, leaping off the side of the truck he was hanging from.

Heads poked out from the vehicles, curious of the reason for the delay. After realizing what they were looking at, people began hopping down to join him, murmuring among themselves.

Rosie summed it up with great eloquence. "Bwuh?"

A squad of Imperial soldiers lay in various states of incapacitation, dangling above from ropes tied around their ankles or trussed on the ground below. An unfortunate soul was doing the split, legs pulled to either side of the path after springing two separate traps.

Near that man, an empty plate.

"How? What in all of—How!?"

"What's wrong?" Jaune asked, striding toward their new prisoners. "If you have time to stand around, then you can help me get them on the truck."

Rosie seized him by the collars, pulling him face to face with her.

"You put a slice of cake in the middle of the road! What idiot would fall for that!?"

He pointed ahead. "Them."

Advanced testing of [Set Bait Trap] indicated that the skill functioned perfectly well. It just required the right bait and a valid target.

The proof before their eyes was undeniable. The corporal let him go, her hands coming up to grip fistfuls of her hair, looking torn between screaming and decking him until the world made sense again. Behind her, Marina reached out to pat her on the back in commiseration… and became quite uncomfortable when the corporal glomped her in a hug.

He was going to mark that down as a success for Tattletale's plan to integrate their forces. It'd be nice to see her smile. She needed the win.

The convoy returned to Yuell to muted fanfare. Two artillery positions going silent passed with little notice when five others continued to roar, and if the Imperials appeared to have cut short the bombardment, rare were the ones optimistic enough to assume it was due to the enemy trying to avoid alerting Jaune of their location. Still, civilians that happened to be nearby swarmed the vehicles once they saw him, raising a clamor that slowed the convoy down to a crawl. Stolen Empire trucks equating to loot was the mentality he had instilled in the city. Attempting to peek at the cargo made for good entertainment to punctuate an otherwise arduous situation.

The Squad 7 soldiers were surprised at the reception at first, but they took it in stride and joined the game to show off today's catch. The liquid ragnite and cannons earned them praise, the food total adulation. The soldiers maintained a certain level of discipline and refused to pass out the looted provisions, as that was intended for the populace as a whole. Instead, they searched their pockets and pouches for personal rations to somehow manage a sizable pile of sweets between the eight of them—Sergeant Largo didn't count as he brought out vegetables, though that got a number of enthusiastic takers, too. The Yuell garrison sitting beside them couldn't hide their smiles at the kindness.

Their first stop was the food distribution warehouse, where they left a few people to assist in moving the foodstuffs. The Militia had made the very welcomed move of adding their own provisions to what was stored, except that also meant a couple hundred additional mouths to feed in the days ahead, which might lead to the rationing system growing a fair bit more precarious unless they received proper supply lines soon.

For his peace of mind, Jaune dipped inside to add another pile of rice bags at a secluded corner of the warehouse for people to 'find'. The distribution going on outside didn't lack for staff, so he left that alone beyond greeting his acquaintances hard at work there. Magari clammed up as per usual when he addressed her but he hadn't missed her chatting with another dark-haired girl in Militia gear whose face vaguely pinged his memory. They seemed to get along, which was heartening.

With matters here well in hand, he grabbed onto the side of the truck as the convoy proceeded up the road.

The liquid ragnite, artillery pieces, plus assorted weapons and tools found their home at the makeshift logistic hub that the Militia just set up. They were in the process of auditing inventories, and the looted supplies drew appreciation for alleviating some of the biggest shortages.

As it turned out, Corporal Rosie spent time blabbing about the lasguns to one of their R&D techies, resulting in the young man rushing into the street to cling to Jaune's leg and beg for a rifle to study. Kreis or Krief or whatever his name was only relented when Jaune said he'd raise the possibility to Welkin Gunther.

All the while, the Militia soldiers of the various platoons followed him with their eyes wherever he went, observing his every move.


-o-​


"When do you expect the ragnite to be used? Some time soon. Tomorrow? Tomorrow or the next day. Whew. That's gonna be a doozy with you sitting on this side of the battle, huh? Sing well and maybe we'll shove you in the basement where the artillery might not reach you…"

Outside the repurposed classroom, the group of Welkin (he didn't mind first-name basis), Welkin's colleague (a Lieutenant Faldio Landzaat of Squad 1, who did mind), the garrison commander (rank: garrison commander), and Jaune (The Great and Terrible Wizard of Yuell, Bow Before His Might) listened in on the interrogation. Lacking the one-way glass and soundproofing of the movies he knew, they had to improvise, and have stacked their heads one above the other as they peeked through a gap in the door.

"She's…" began Welkin.

"Amazing? Insightful? In her elements?" Jaune suggested under his breath. "Adorable, with how she keeps dancing around like a girl on her birthday?"

"Really arrogant."

Fair take, mister Gunther. Fair take.

"And yes, she's doing a great job," Welkin added. "I have yet to understand how. Most of that conversation is coming solely from her and those comments look to have been pulled out of empty air, yet the reactions of that officer support her conclusions."

"...Let's talk tanks, since that's on your mind…" Tattletale continued on the far side of the room, oblivious to the conversation in the peanut gallery.

"How accurate is she?" Welkin asked.

Jaune thought on it for a minute. "More right than not. She does her best when at her own pace, with a lot of data."

"See, Welkin?" Lieutenant Landzaat said with a teasing lilt. "Even on the battlefield one must never rush a lady, let alone in romance. You should pay attention."

Welkin accepted the ribbing with an indulgent smile. "The migration period for the cerulean scarabs intersected with an unseasonal cold front. Such a rare occurrence had to be documented!"

The two men talked like long-time friends, with stories and jokes only they understood. Jaune paid as much attention to them as he did the interrogations, jotting mental notes to relay back for Tattletale later. Thus far, they seemed a reasonable group that knew when to be flexible, with Faldio the more personable of the pair and Welkin the subdued thinker. Neither had demanded for the locals to hand over authority of the city. That boded well for the prospect of cooperation.

The interrogation wrapped up during one of their back and forth. Tattletale dropped a parting quip that caused the captive officer to grind his teeth, and skipped off toward the exit in a good mood. The man would realize he had lost all bargaining chips of value without even wrangling a deal out of Tattletale for his life right about…

"That bitch!"

Now. Heh.

Once Tattletale left the room, he greeted her with a soft round of applause. She preened under the praise, hips cocked and smug grin out for all to see.

"Impressive as always, Lisa. Do you need that guy around anymore?"

She shook her head, and began walking along the corridor. "Stick him in a corner somewhere and leave him to stew. His buddies are gonna add to the story for me. Then, I might come back around with a couple other questions, like why he didn't tell me everything the first time." She glanced over her shoulder at Jaune, striking him with the full force of her devilish smirk. She was a cute one most days, but he'd offer that Tattletale's best look was in the moments before she threatened to bring wrack and ruin to someone's day.

(Sleepy-face Tattletale competed for second place with the utterly flummoxed expression she got when a whole long spew of deductions she was oh so proud of went awry.)

Two doors over sat another classroom, empty but for a soldier roped tight to a chair. He hadn't met Tattletale yet, hence the sneer as she entered his field of vision. The absence of insignias denoted him as a rank and file soldier of little import.

His partner would find something useful. She always did.

He pulled the door almost shut to leave the girl to her work, with a gap for observation. The game began anew.

"Hiiiii~ Were you comfortable? Were you not? Are you thirsty? Really thirsty? How about…"

…

…

"…The Empire has a superweapon," Tattletale declared to the people present at the strategy meeting. The map of Gallia was spread out on the table set between the lecture hall's podium and the bench rows, and gathered around it were the usual suspects plus Welkin and Lieutenant Landzaat.

"What makes you say that?" said Jaune, playing along. Those unfamiliar with Tattletale might just dismiss her altogether, so a hype man slash prompter was an invaluable part of her act.

"The ragnite and excess tank parts you brought back point to a buildup for an offensive," she explained. "That they put the supply depot this close to the city is too risky unless they expect a need for it before we get wind of the location. If that doesn't spell out in neon colors that they're going to attack, then you would have to be blind. The strange part is that none of them from grunt to officer could say for sure what the plan is except for someone from the upper echelons telling them to follow orders. That caginess is suspicious. Clear instructions kinda matter for soldiers."

The garrison commander grunted in agreement. "Only time they don't is when Intelligence gets cute with their ideas." He looked ready to spit on the ground, were this not indoors.

"Precisely. Within the next two days, we can expect to meet a whole fleet—flock?—of tanks."

"They're not boats, nor birds," muttered Welkin, so low only Jaune heard.

Tattletale continued, missing the comment. "These tanks would be experimental ones. Never before seen. At a guess, powerful engines with a lot of finicky and breakable parts. Or." She paused, and swept her gaze around the table. "Or, it's one big tank with the same characteristics, big enough to use the supplies that could have outfitted a herd of tanks."

In tandem, everyone leaned forward. Pandemonium did not break out, but the tension ratcheted up a few notches. Tattletale had seized their undivided attention.

How big were they talking to qualify something as a superweapon? The best estimate by the logistics people had put the crates of spare parts and fuel as adequate for ten to fifteen tanks over multiple battles. Condense that to one vehicle and a single engagement, and they were getting the idea. The very, very worrying idea.

Welkin looked at his colleague. "Faldio?"

The other man held his chin in thought, a finger tapping rapidly on his cheek.

"I… there were whispers of top secret Imperial projects, but…" He stared at Lisa, slowly shaking his head in wonder. "They're called top secret for a reason. We had to send operatives into five different bases to get even a hint of it!"

She gave a lopsided grin. "I'm just that good. So, uh, what are the chances we have more reinforcements on the way that will get here by tomorrow? Because the Empire's big push is coming soon."

Both Militia officers grimaced at her question. They shared a silent conversation that Tattletale eavesdropped on.

In the end, Welkin took the floor. He studied the map, then started to adjust the pieces.

Four red figurines, representing four Imperial battalions, formed a curved line in the forest to the east of Yuell. Welkin added one more in front of them, set on its side—the theorized superweapon. On the city itself he planted a blue figurine for the combined forces of the national Militia and local garrison. Put this way, prospects appeared grim.

The lieutenant then moved along the winding line of red and blue figurines splitting Gallia, keeping most of them where they were but tilting all the markers to face the direction of Yuell, where the line suddenly shifted to incorporate the city. Thus, a new picture was painted of the ongoing war. The Empire contingent on their doorstep has broken through the defensive line ahead of its cohorts, yet now found itself menaced by the Gallians in three different directions. Their position seemed no less precarious than Yuell.

"This, is the state of the war as of today," Welkin explained. He ran a hand through his ashy brown hair, sweat building on his brow. "Yuell has become… important. It is now the shortest path for the Imperials to Randgriz. On the other hand—"

"The area east of it is also the place where Empire forces are weakening," Tattletale chimed in, green eyes flitting back and forth over the map. "The bulk of their army is still concentrated in the northern Naggiar Plains in anticipation of victory there. At a guess, until recently the southern half of the conflict wasn't supposed to be anything more than a holding action to put pressure on the Gallian Army."

Welkin nodded. "The maneuver carried out by the 705th, as originally intended, seemed to have been a gambit with Yuell as the linchpin. Take the city, and they secure a path to the capital; the nearby battalions would thereafter abandon their positions and stream through at blistering speed before the opening can slam shut. Fail, and the 705th should have pulled back to reestablish the stalemate." He mimed moving the pieces on the map to a spot further east, then brushed the imaginary armies aside to leave a blank area. "That they committed to a siege despite the initial failure have opened them up to a counteroffensive they are unprepared to defend against. Each side is currently faced with a threat and an opportunity."

"It all hinges on a single element," interjected Lieutenant Landzaat, dropping another blue marker, set on its side, next to the normal one already sitting on Yuell. He looked across the table at Jaune. "From what we gleaned of his final missives, the commander of the 705th insisted you were a surmountable obstacle right up to the night that you shattered his forces to prove him wrong. Except now, someone on high within the Empire, likely Prince Maximilian himself, believes you are a target worth pursuing to the point of neglecting Randgriz. As for our superiors…" He cracked a smile. "Well, they think you are a unicorn, my friend."

"Meaning?" Jaune asked, head tilted to the side.

Lieutenant Landzaat flicked the figurine representing Jaune, sending it flying at the Empire battalions and scattering them to smash apart the carefully-laid board. "An answer that does not exist. A fanciful dream." In contrast to those words, his voice was bright and reverent. "In short, a Valkyria."

"He is," said the garrison commander, adamant of the truth.

Welkin replied, very politely, "Yes, and the citizens of Gallia fully believe this. At the towns we pass, Yuell is on everyone's lips. There is"—his words slowed for the barest instant, searching for the right term—"intense pressure for the Army to not let this city fall."

"Then, where are they?" the old man asked. Judging by the tightening grip on his cane, the garrison commander suspected the answer.

"Before General Damon is willing to commit to Yuell and thereby open himself up to a possible misstep that could harm his career, he requires proof that it will pay off," Lieutenant Landzaat said with a shrug.

Tattletale snickered. "I knew it~"

"Wait, wait, wait," Jaune interrupted, hands waving as he leaned forward. "Let me get this straight. He wants the victory, before he's willing to work for the victory?"

Lieutenant Landzaat laughed. "Our glorious leader, my friend!"

Next to him, Welkin facepalmed at the frankness his colleague was showing.

A heat was building behind Jaune's temples, anger rising and rising. Someone far off sitting comfortably in an armchair was playing games with hundreds and thousands of lives. With but a single thought, the man consigned who knew how many to die.

He balled his hand into a fist. The desire to slam it on the table, to rage and throw a tantrum, was near overwhelming.

Instead, he turned toward the door.

"Jaune, what's up?" Tattletale asked from beside him.

"There's time yet today to hunt down more of their artillery." He placed a hand on her shoulder, leaning down to look her in the eye. "I'll sap as much of their strength as I can ahead of their offensive. Keep building our defenses up while I'm out, alright?"

Energy that he could spend wallowing in anger was energy that he could be putting to work.

After all, even on the battlefield one must never rush a lady. Or girl, in her case.

Chapter 48: Dreams of Tomorrow​


That night, Jaune once again found a moment of peace atop one of the university belltowers, sitting on the wide stone balcony. A boisterous mood was more his speed, but this suited the late hour.

His act began as a way to boost morale, and a lot of attention came with it. He had not known until later on of the pressure that would arise. Eyes followed him. People called to him. He could see it in them with each new day, how they expected things of him that lay beyond his ability. Still, here, there was none of that. The isolated tower offered a degree of separation from the constant looks and conversations—worship, even—that he got on the ground. He could just sit back and enjoy the night breeze. Sometimes, it was nice to be around people but not have to speak.

He was referring to Marina, of course. She had dropped by a short time after he got here to take up residence on the opposite corner of the tower, where she sat with Escha in her lap, feeding the felyne morsels of food that she had saved from dinner for this very purpose. In between bites, she gave Escha scritches. Good ones, because Escha had her chin tilted up, mouth hanging open in an expression of utmost bliss—life must be wonderful as a cat. Evidence pointed to the taciturn young woman having a soft spot for animals, the cuter the better.

A cloud drifted away, revealing the moon above to cast the tower in its glow, and Jaune could not help but think that the scene was fit for a picture. A pale beauty under the moonlight, Marina had admirers if she ever bothered to care. She preferred the solitude.

These were also the only occasions that his acquaintance would raise her concerns. Among the people in this city to work closely with him, he trusted Marina and Walter the most. They both had good heads on their shoulders and didn't buy too far into his larger than life act. Yet whereas Walter saw no issue speaking straight, Marina clammed up whenever there was another person around so all he would get was business-Marina, the sniper that brooked no nonsense.

She hadn't said anything for a few days. He took that as a sign that he was doing alright in his role, the sentiment bringing much relief. No showman wanted to hear that the jig was up.

The hour went by in quiet contentment. Jaune watched the happenings below for a while, following the Militia soldiers as they strode to and fro. The lights were on at the logistic hub, where the R&D team attached to the Militia no doubt intended to burn the midnight candle pouring over the lasgun. He had traded it for their aid in manufacturing a cache of munitions to his specifics. A forge, some reshaped metal casings, and rockets for Gallian lances had combined to approximate the shells for his gunlance, differing from the design notes only in slight and still workable minutiae—getting those ever curious souls to focus and stop asking questions about Red Rook took monumental effort, but he did it. A stockpile of shells was building up that he planned to cart through the portal when he leaves.

Near the tent, at a dirt lot, artillery pieces seized from the Imperials had been set up, with firing teams conducting drills in preparation of putting the weapons to use. Despite the risks, many among the population hoped to be present for the catharsis of seeing the cannons turned against the invaders.

Over time, his eyes rose towards the far distance to pan across the space beyond the city borders. Enemies laid in wait out there, as they always do. Even Grimmless lands might still carry monsters. His attempts to locate the superweapon that Tattletale claimed the Imperials brought had ended without success. Less than 48 hours, was the window during which they expected its assault on Yuell to manifest.

Despite that, an odd sense of calm dwelt within his chest. He and everyone else have done what they could. At this point, the only thing to do was let the battle come.

Once he had enough of watching the scenery, Jaune got to his feet. Bidding present company a good night, he took the short flight of stairs down to a door that let him back inside the building. Another staircase wrapped around the tower wall, and he descended its worn, wooden steps.

He wasn't expecting anyone to follow him.

"Jaune, Jaune, wait up!" called out a tinny voice above after he had reached the bottom of the stairwell and entered the hallway.

He listened to hurried footsteps growing louder. Escha soon appeared, making quick time as she scampered on all fours. She skipped the last flight of stairs, jumping from the upper landing to the floor, afterward shuffling over to join him in the empty corridor lined with portraits of past Gallian rulers. Jaune placed a knee on the carpet so they were of a height.

"Hey, Escha. Did you need something?"

The felyne smiled at him, but it faded in moments. Unlike earlier, she had grown subdued, fretting with her fur and tugging on them.

Seeing her so unsure of what to say, he continued speaking. "We didn't really have a chance to talk today, huh? Come on, let's hear about your week. How was living in the wilderness? Not too bad, I hope."

Escha emphatically shook her head. "No, no, it was great to stretch my legs. All that space! And the flowers smelled so nice! I found this stream in the woods and there were a bunch of yummy fishes swimming in it, and… and…" The enthusiasm waned, and she lowered her head to look at her feet.

He waited for her to collect her thoughts. She wanted to speak, that much he could discern. Her mouth would open then close, again and again.

Finally, she said, "Why didn't you tell me how things were in the city?"

"Hm?" Jaune tilted his head to the side, not quite certain of the reason for her question.

"I was playing with the kids to keep their spirits up. They didn't know I can understand them, and I overheard them talking to each other about the attacks, about the… the people that got hurt, or…"

Ah.

Now was his turn to mull on how best to phrase himself. Jaune motioned for Escha to come closer. She did so, and he placed a hand on her shoulder.

"I needed you out there because only you could do the job. The information you relayed back to us was critical in protecting the city."

"But people died," Escha said, her voice warbling.

How wonderful life must be as a cat. For the past weeks, the wilderness provided her food and shelter along with a hundred interesting sights. Each day was a day she looked forward to. Never was a gun aimed her way. Best of all, she was saving lives by eavesdropping on their enemies. A real super spy.

Her efforts hadn't been enough. It failed to save everyone.

He moved his hand up to scratch behind one of her ears. "You did more than anybody else can hope for, little hero."

"I-I'm not—!"

Escha scrunched her eyes shut and pushed his hand away, shaking her head all the while. Too upset, she seemed torn between hitting herself and bawling her eyes out.

Felynes were… a child-like race. They gave their trust easily, and from what Jaune had seen, loved nothing more than to frolic. They faced monsters, but have yet to face monsters. He sent her far from the city for that very reason.

Jaune sat down right on the hallway carpet, and patted the floor. Escha sniffled, before plopping down to join him. He scooted closer.

"In Astera, were there Hunters who didn't come back from their hunts?" he asked.

Escha nodded. "Sometimes. We have parties in their memory."

It wasn't death, then, that bothered her so. "They went down fighting, I'll bet."

Another nod. "Uh-huh. Gloriously." For a person who had trouble with longer words, this was one she remembered by heart. "We would tell the story and then toast our drinks to them," she explained.

Embellished, no doubt. It would be a story of what the other Hunters imagined of their fallen comrade's final hunt, full of courage and quippy lines as a warrior danced on the razor's edge. They honored the person, in a fashion, with lies.

It took Jaune not long to understand his friend. Driven as she seemed by curiosity and adventure, a smaller yet brighter wish dwelt within the felyne's heart. Escha dreamed of heroism.

"This isn't the kind of world I wanted to take you to," Jaune said. "It's not a world I would want to stay in. I offered you interesting places, good places—"

"I know what I was getting into," Escha insisted. "You said there would be danger, I was listening back then!"

But war was a whole different beast. On Remnant, there had been two within the last century. Even with Grimm on their doorsteps, the kingdoms could not get along. Yet, it sometimes sounded less than real to him. How could war possibly happen?

He… Unbelievable as it may appear given Grimm attacks and bandit raids, he had to now admit that he grew up in a time of peace. The cities were existing in harmony, or as near as it could get. Dangers abound, but they lurked in the dark beyond the settlement walls; always, driven back within a night. No matter how much Doctor Oobleck carried on and on about understanding the ugly parts of history, nobody enjoyed lingering on such depressing subjects. What he knew of war could fill a thimble. They came from the tales of his ancestors and it was not until recent days that he learned the extent to which his father, and likely his father before him, hid the details. From how they told it, a single person could do everything, and perfectly at that. Protect the people, save the day, win back peace, all at once.

War was way too big for that to be true. He kept thinking after each battle that it would become the final incident to break the Imperials for good. Two weeks on, they were still here. Meanwhile, a lot of people who did no harm weren't, and a voice in his head whispered about how he continued to fall short of good enough—that there could have been a real hero instead of him.

He had tried to spare Escha from that. Tattletale shared his opinion. Even the fight against the ABB in Brockton Bay, which was a skirmish compared to this, had at the time seemed too harsh to expose their felyne friend to, and they strove to keep Escha away from the worst of it.

And he had to wonder, if that wasn't the most hurtful thing he could have done. Escha thought she could do more, and never got the chance.

"A dozen battles were won because of you. That's the truth. You really did help us, little hero."

A flicker of a smile passed across her face, replaced by… well, he couldn't say. He was hardly an expert on the body language of sentient cats.

"I'm going to stay with you for the next one," said Escha.

Determination, then.

"...Are you sure?" He hoped for an answer that was for naught. Escha tapped him on the shoulder with her paw in imitation of his earlier gesture, and gave an imperious hmph.

"A Palico supports their Hunter. No ifs, ands, or buts."

It became his turn to fail to hide the smile. He still preferred she went nowhere near a battle, but that was him neglecting to give her title the respect it deserved—ego all the way down. His mistake, because the felyne spoke the word with pride akin to how one would declare they were a Huntsman. When the time called, there was nowhere she'd rather stand than in the thick of it, even if that led to grief and pain.

"Okay," he decided, and her teary nod said it all.

Then, suddenly, Escha froze in place. Her eyes locked onto something behind him.

"M-Meow!"

A dozen possibilities raced through his mind in the space of a blink. He snapped his head around to see what made her so alarmed. His hands twitched, ready to pull the full arsenal within the Pocket to bear.

A short distance down the dim corridor lit only by the moonlight stood a girl, dark of hair. Dressed in Militia gear, she had a shawl in addition wrapped around her shoulders. In her hands she held a woven basket, thrust in front of her like it was a shield as she startled at his abrupt speed.

"Um. Uh," she floundered under the hard gaze rooting her in place. "I brought bread!"

Having anticipated violence, it took a moment for his thoughts to recompute. Once it did, Jaune recalled that he had seen this person on occasion. Now, that didn't guarantee she was an ally, but the 'small, scared critter' impression she was giving off in waves suggested he may have overreacted a tad. Jaune willed himself to relax.

The girl noted the change in his demeanor, and she offered a hesitant smile. It turned more genuine as he answered with an easy smile of his own. Emboldened, she took a step closer.

"Who were you talking to, sir?" she asked, blinking innocently.

The radio vanished from his belt then reappeared in his hand. Standing up and turning fully around, he showed it to her. She was rather short, he noted.

"Oh, just one of the militia guys. We were discussing tomorrow's plans." Behind him, he heard Escha scuttling off into the darkness. "You're with Squad 7, right?" he asked, changing the subject. "I remember seeing you in that tank. And I think it was you helping Magari at the food warehouse."

Despite an apparent surprise at the fact that he was aware of her, the girl answered in a polite tone, "Yes, that's correct. I am Isara Gunther, Squad 7 mechanic and operator for the Edelweiss."

She finished by bowing her head. The stiltedness of the gesture belied her fluster.

"Nice to meet you, Isara. I'm Jaune."

"I know!" she blurted out.

"Oh. Yeah. I guess that makes sense." He had gotten quite recognizable around these parts, a far cry from the bygone Beacon days of 'you, with the face'.

The girl nodded but did not say anything else. On his part, Jaune missed the timing to continue, and in turn fell quiet. The conversation fizzled out as suddenly as it began.

An awkward mood settled over the corridor. Jaune and Isara Gunther stood there looking like loons as they smiled at each other, their expressions growing fragile with the passing seconds. Above them, the portrait of Archduchess Cordelia, ruler of Gallia, stared at the scene with a judging gaze.

Jaune punctured that silence with a fake cough. "So, you were saying something about—"

"Bread! Here!" The girl stumbled forward, speaking quickly. "Alicia borrowed an oven and baked them for everyone. Uh, Alicia is one of our sergeants, she's from my hometown. I was bringing it to people when I saw you and I thought maybe you would like one, Mister Arc."

He could have done without the sirs and misters, but deemed it better than other epithets the people of Yuell liked to use, and held his tongue as the girl flipped open the cover of the basket. Once filled with bread, it was almost empty by now, the cloth cushioning the bottom covered in crumbs. Jaune studied the remaining loaves of bread, and allowed that they did look tempting. Baked to a golden brown, they were full and fat in shape, still warm from the oven with flecks of almonds decorating the top. He took one, finding the texture pleasingly crispy to the touch. Putting firm pressure on the crust resulted in a sharp snap as it broke under his thumb, releasing a sweet, buttery aroma to fill his senses.

"You know, I can actually see myself buying this." He tried a bite, and his eyebrows rose at the soft, fluffy inside that measured miles ahead of the dry bread he had been eating as of late. The notes of almond added a distinct quality he had a hard time putting to words. "Tastes pretty good. Fantastic, even."

The bread could be a meal in itself, its rich flavors needing no fillings. The first bite disappeared all too soon, and he went for another.

Isara clasped a hand over her chest. "That's great! I'll be sure to let Alicia know."

"Yeah, do that for me," Jaune said absentmindedly, already on his third bite. "Mm. This is so good, I'm glad you stopped by. Really."

By the time the loaf of bread was halfway gone, he was side-eyeing the girl as he ate. She hadn't left yet, and watched him with an expectant gaze.

"Gunther…" he said, searching for a topic to fill the space between conversation. "Any relation to Welkin Gunther?"

Isara brightened. "Welks is my brother." She paused, before adding, "Adoptive brother, I meant. He isn't Darcsen like me."

"Cool."

The girl tilted her head, the question marks above it near palpable. "Cool?"

Oops. The word must not carry that sense of meaning here.

"Great, I meant," he amended, papering over the mistake and hoping she wouldn't mention it, "that you two are siblings. Welkin seems like a great person that would be easy to get along with."

"Is he… cool, then?"

A whole lot less because she asked outright, but Jaune decided against piling onto her confusion the social conventions of another culture and era.

"Sure, I think so. The man's competent and decisive. Your squad respects him as far as I can tell, which is a clear point in his favor."

The last piece of bread vanished into his stomach. He sent the basket a wistful glance, afterward.

"You can take another one if you like," Isara hurried to offer, extending the basket. His stomach shouted for him to accept the deal.

"It should probably go to somebody else," he demurred.

"No, help yourself," she insisted. "We have lots."

Those were the magic words he needed to hear. Modesty tossed to the wayside, Jaune snatched a new loaf of bread for himself. This time, he ate slower to savor the taste. And, to study the person before him.

"Why are you looking for me?" he asked with a deliberately casual air.

The game ended then and there. Isara reacted with a sharp jolt, and almost dropped the basket she was holding. The laugh she then attempted rang with a fake note.

"I… I wasn't… It was a coincidence…"

She was a poor liar. Her eyes practically swam with panic.

"Come on now." He waved a hand to indicate their surroundings. "How do you just happen to wander into a deserted hallway on the third floor of a building this big, unless you hear beforehand that certain people could be found here at night? It doesn't take a detective to figure out something is amiss."

His hangout spot was no big secret. In an emergency, Lisa and the Yuell militia could contact him if they have to. Still, he chose this far flung corner for a reason. People had to go out of their way to end up here.

"Well?" he pressed.

Isara seemed to debate over her next step, her eyes flicking upward for a second in thought. In the end, she sighed and hung her head.

"Was it that obvious?" she said, with the slightest touch of a whine coloring her voice. Imperceptible, to most.

"A little. I can tell a bribe when I see one, and I'm guessing Welkin can too, living with you. And you had that…" He mimed an eager puppy hopping up and down in anticipation.

"I did not look like that, you— you—!"

"Oh my, what happened to 'Mister Arc'?" he teased, falling into old habits. The fierce expression warring with red-cheeked embarrassment was a look he had seen a thousand times over the years, and never went stale. It signaled imminent victory. Or a tantrum that drew in the rest of the house.

Isara came back to herself. She realized what she had done and, more relevantly, the very important person she was speaking to. Her mouth dropped open, mortified. Meanwhile, Jaune's hand twitched with the urge to ruffle her hair.

He stamped down that stray impulse, and said, "Seriously, though. I'm grateful for the midnight snack, but is there something you needed?"

It was odd. The girl fidgeted with her shawl, clearly worried, yet her gaze remained locked onto his. That spoke of intentional practice, and drew a sharp divide to the way she mumbled an indistinct reply.

"Hm?"

At his coaxing, she tried again. "I said, people were talking about you." Confidence grew now that the first sentence was out there. "Everybody had a story of what they saw you do, your… miracles."

He summoned a canteen of water—actual water, not the Spirytus—from his Pocket, and handed it to Isara. She stared at the small container with wide eyes. Tentative fingers unscrewed the cap, and she sipped at the water, shocked to find it real.

"Maybe it's not a lie," she muttered. Shaking off the stupor, she looked back up. "I thought they were exaggerating at first. That it was superstitions and rumors at work. But Magari insisted it was all true, and even became angry with me when I raised my doubts…"

Who did what now? Not the Magari he knew, surely? He still hasn't gotten a word out of that girl.

"...and then Largo and Rosie started telling the same stories after they deployed with you this morning! Those two are as cynical as they come! I…" Jaune leaned back as Isara pressed closer, the meek impression she gave off in the beginning melting away to leave a single-minded focus. "Please, I have to know. Can you truly fly?"

That was easy enough. "Yes, I can."

She stared, but harder.

"What, you don't trust me?" Troublesome gearhead types. Oh no, I have to see it to believe it…

Jaune stepped back to make space. He then bent his knees, and hopped into the air to avoid singeing the carpet. So far, that did not impress Isara much.

It took her a second to realize he wasn't coming down. That was how it always went. People expected the logical thing to occur. Another second passed by as she blankly looked, slack-jawed, at him hovering midway to the high ceiling; the rockets were drawing level with her height, humming with power. Then, it clicked for her, and the satisfied smirk sprouting on Jaune's face settled on a far softer expression.

Because Isara's eyes were like those of the children of Yuell, alight with wonder. They shone with a dream.

He held his position for a little while longer to really impress her, then cut out power to fall back down. The carpet cushioned the sound of his landing, and he sprang up with the grace of a cat to perform a theatrical spin, ending in a bow. Showmanship was important.

"Tada~"

Isara tackled him a moment later, yammering nonstop at rapid-fire speed.


-o-​


The Darcsen had a saying: Look to the sky.

Well, Isara was looking at his boot right now. She had been a lot of things, but apologetic wasn't one of them.

The pair sat on the side of the corridor, along the wall below the portrait of Archduchess Cordelia so that the moon outside the window could better illuminate Isara's endeavor. Jaune had an elbow propped on the carpet, one foot raised in the air and held by Isara, and he briefly wondered how long until the novel concept of taking his shoes off to hit the girl.

He gave it small odds. Isara was deeeeep in a fugue, absorbed in her own world to the point that he sometimes needed to prompt her to continue their conversation. The frustrated pout as she searched her pockets in vain for a screwdriver was quite endearing, though it brought him much relief that she had failed to produce one. That intent gleam in her eyes all but promised a fight should he try to stop her attempts at poking and prodding the boots.

She did, however, have papers and a pencil. Sketches of her ideas, rooted in her father's research, were spread out on the floor around them. They provided him a clear picture as to the reason for her fervent interest.

Aircraft.

The wings and frames Isara drew on the pages were primitive by his standards. Precursors to the very earliest designs, before Gravity Dust ever came into play. To the people of this world, it laid on the cutting edge of technology. Hot air balloons, dirigibles, many innovations have come to pass, but sustained heavier-than-air flight remained an ever elusive and mythical beast. From the sound of it, a dozen different efforts were taking place all over the world, engineers racing to be the one to create the first true aircraft.

"The newspapers from the United States of Vinland reported last year that a successful test flight already happened there, but the two inventors later died in an accident," Isara said, lifting his heel to peek inside the short bell nozzle of the rocket. Jaune tensed his whole body to ensure his toe went nowhere near the activation button. "Then the United Kingdom of Edinburgh said they succeeded until it was discovered that the initial takeoff position was on a cliffside. It worked off of height as much as thrust. The journalist dismissed it as falling with style and I have to agree. A glider shouldn't count." A disheartened frown stole over her face, and she sighed. "A lot of people have started to call the concept a hoax, but I don't know… What do you think, Jaune?"

Jaune shrugged. "I'm no engineer so don't take this seriously." He snatched up a spare piece of paper, fiddling with it as he spoke with greater care than his tone would suggest. "I think a strong enough engine can get you there. Of course, its weight would then need to be compensated with more power, which means a bigger engine, which leads back to—you get the idea."

"Y-Yes!" Isara perked up. "I am familiar with the problem. It was featured during a symposium at Randgriz University, and focuses on the current limitations of ragnite as a fuel source for aviation means. Consensus seems to suggest the use of lighter material, and that is the design concept I am pursuing, but the counter-theory that we should be building heavier holds a surprising amount of merit and I do think that while it isn't possible now, it could lead to a real breakthrough! Wow, you really are knowledgeable!"

No, no I am not, thought Jaune as he folded the corners of the paper. Isara saw what she wanted and filled in the gaps herself, was all.

"What has your experience been with aerodynamic control?" she asked—demanded, even.

"...Bad?"

"Right!? A popular model of thought is that we should mimic the hummingbird design first theorized by a professor in Roeselare that emphasizes rapid wing flaps." Isara scrambled for one of her papers to show him what she meant. "Except the main issue there is the enormous strain put on the components from the constant movement and forces acting on the craft to enact the tight turns as envisioned. Rigid wings do have a place, I feel. It simplifies the construction." She peered at him, eager to hear his input.

Here, he stood on firmer ground, as it were. Employing the rockets in battle granted him a measure of insight on the matter. As he flattened the crease on the piece of paper, he explained, "It's hard to pull abrupt turns, I can tell you that. My best shot at it is to reduce the weight I carry as much as possible then increase power for the boots to the max it can go so I can overcome the direction I was headed in. It isn't perfect, and works better when I'm already at low speeds. Usually, it's not worth it. Wide, circling turns are easier. Less wasteful, too. Wings or no, that should stay the same."

Isara frantically nodded her head, beaming as she copied down his words in her notes. Afterward, she dove right back into scrutinizing the rocket boot with a renewed enthusiasm.

"Can you tell me more about your theories on a metal aircraft?" she asked, sweeping a stray lock of her dark hair aside.

He tossed the piece of paper he was playing with into a growing pile, and picked up another. "Again, not mine. Anyway, the advantage there, I think, was—ack!"

Isara had twisted the boot around, forgetting the fact that it was attached to his foot.

"I'm so sorry!" she yelped.

Strong hands on that one. She was no delicate flower.

"It's fine," Jaune said, waving her off. He sat upright again. "It's fine. I'm tough. I was just surprised."

Isara hunched her shoulders, shrinking down. "I'm sorry…"

He barked a laugh, free and bright, to indicate his lack of ill will. His foot wiggled, inviting her to keep at it. After a little hesitation, she did, this time using greater care.

"You really are in love with flying, aren't you?" he said.

"Mmhm." She steadfastly focused on the shoe, still embarrassed over her mistake. "Welkin mentioned wanting to fly like a bird once, and that was where it started." She huffed in amusement. "I was a kid, and I thought I could build a huge mechanical bird for him by his birthday. I followed the blueprints my father left me. Heh." She laughed into a fist. "Welks almost caught me sneaking a few times into the workshop to try and put pieces together. Then I learned the blueprints were incomplete, and there was going to be a whole lot more work ahead. And… And…"

And as she spent hours after hours on her designs, her mind took off. In her dreams, it became her sitting in the pilot seat, soaring in the sky with her brother marveling from the passenger side. Her goal changed in a small, selfish way, overwhelmed by a yearning she could not suppress.

The years that followed saw her tinkering with all manners of vehicles and machines, striving to build a foundation in the principles of flight. Day and night she spent on her projects, frequently sleeping on the floor of the workshop surrounded by her tools when she struck upon a promising lead. Particularly productive occasions would end with her stumbling to the pantry in the late morning, bags under her eyes as the hungry squirrel masquerading as a girl dug around for food.

Her brother never knew. It'd be on one of his birthdays that he would find out, Isara had decided.

She admitted to Jaune that more than once she laid into whatever she had tried to build with a wrench in a fit of pique. Innovation was often zero steps forward and a month wasted, with nothing to show for it. Didn't help, that news of like-minded individuals reported similar setbacks, further marred by accidents incapacitating brilliant minds or ruined reputation leading to projects losing their funding. The goal of the century, an aircraft flying under its own power, appeared an utter disaster pursued by madcap kooks, facing mockery at every turn. They claimed it was impossible.

Sometimes, Isara confessed, she feared 'they' might be right.

That was, until tonight.

Again, Jaune was no engineer. But one could say that he was something better. A person that believed her.

Here sat a real, 'I saw it with my very own eyes' witness to the idea that one day people could fly. He knew, knew, that her dream would come true.

He held little better than a layman's concept of an aircraft. Yet even that perspective stood decades ahead of anyone else's that Isara could find in Gallia. His clumsy, offhand comments translated to groundbreaking concepts that had the girl vibrating from the bolts of inspiration striking her again and again. One of her sketches in particular has started to bear a distinct resemblance to a museum piece from his world—a success case at that. Years of research, of trial and error and painstaking gains clawed from a thousand failures, condensed in the space of half an hour.

At this pace…

"You'll see it, Isara. This world, from the sky."

Conviction colored his words, causing Isara to sniffle and brush at her eyes.

"I hope so," she agreed. "If we can just make it through this war, if we can—" Burgeoning courage grew subdued. Isara stared outside the window, lost in thought.

How big the war was. How small they were.

It often seemed as though the real conflict was fought elsewhere, by people making decisions several levels above them. Moving those like Welkin and Isara as pawns. Sacrificing them for a victory they would never see. One person's efforts counted as nothing on the stage that was the world map.

Curled in a ball, Isara told a stranger what she could never tell her brother.

Jaune placed a hand on her head, ruffling her hair. "One day at a time, Isara. A small win today, another tomorrow. Step by step."

He showed her the object he was playing with. Folded and creased, a paper airplane sat in his palm. A pile of them rested beside him, fashioned over the hour. They bore tiny differences to encompass all the ways he knew how to make them, and a few that adhered to neither rhyme nor reason but what details he could remember from pictures and videos he saw throughout the years of real vehicles. A badly-shaped Bullhead was among the pile.

"That's what made this."

His lips twitched into a sly smile. The hand in contact with Isara glowed with light.

"And if you can keep a secret, I have something I can do to maybe help your dream."

He released the paper airplane, sending it floating into the dark.

Wherever it may go.

#3,356
Chapter 49: Fake, and Real​


The birds gave it away.

On the last day of spring, hundreds of them took flight at once, causing many people to turn their heads. Of them, Tattletale reached a conclusion the fastest. That was no migratory flight. The speakers mounted throughout the city soon began blaring their warning siren to the population. The Imps were on the move.

Jaune had been working in the city, and he grabbed onto a passing truck carrying Militia soldiers to save himself a trip to the edge of Yuell. Half the garrison got there at the same time he did, the rest were arriving with each minute; everyone had been waiting for this. Tattletale and Escha hitched a ride on the Edelweiss. They assembled behind the wall of rubble protecting the city and used the buildings still standing as a vantage point to observe the situation. Jaune opted for the blown-out window on the third floor of a residence, with his team joining him there.

A flag was the first thing they saw, the piece of cloth dyed in red and gold rising above the trees. Those trees then shattered into splinters as the superweapon came around the hill.

How did they know it was the superweapon? Well, what else would one call that?

"Thing's bigger than any tank I've ever seen," Jaune said. Escha nodded in agreement, her fur bristling.

"Twenty-five, twenty-six feet tall," Tattletale rattled out, eyes pressed hard against her binoculars. "Height of a two-story house. Length, width—it is a two-story house. A bunker on wheels."

"With a whole lot of guns. I'm seeing turrets."

The giant tank burst out of the forest, revealing its full glory.

"And now I'm seeing the cannon," Jaune added. "Holy…"

"Eheh. Yeah. Don't you wish you had saved up for that mech?"

"Couldn't have afforded it, either way."

The turrets were clearly designed so as to cover the all-gray tank from all four directions, set in rounded cubbyholes to allow them to swivel. A person could sit behind the machine gun, kept safe by thick steel walls as they rained bullets on targets that dared come near. A huge fuck-off cannon sat atop the vehicle looking like something that belong mounted on a ship, meant for sea dragon Grimm. At the rear, he spied an extra cannon, an afterthought compared to the big brother at the front. A bulldozer blade churned the earth before the tank, flattening small hills in its path rather than having the vehicle go over top.

The Empire had to respond to the situation in Yuell, and boy did they answer.

"Armored tracks," Tattletale noted, pointing it out for him. Two solid panels covered the sprockets which drove the tank threads, protecting the components from damage. The concept prevailed for the rest of the body, and the tank might as well be a block of steel with the joints and gaps shut tight.

"How powerful is the engine to pull all that weight?" he asked, half to himself.

A voice spoke from the radio Jaune carried with him—Lieutenant Faldio Landzaat's. "Project Batomys! Intelligence reports claim it was how the Ghirlandaio stronghold fell in a night! It's one of the Empire's hidden cards, a fortress-breaker!"

"It's not alone," reported Squad 7's Lieutenant Welkin Gunther. "Enemy tank companies spotted."

They emerged from the forest in a long row, forty or so tanks painted in Imperial red that appeared downright puny in comparison to their leader. The tanks fanned out on either side of the Batomys, matching its pace. One in particular was colored a deeper crimson, its design set apart from the others with sloping armor panels.

"Be advised, the Lupus has taken the field," Welkin said. "General Jaeger's personal tank. Watch for it, I know for a fact its top speed notches in at much higher than regular Imperial tanks."

Behind the formation streamed a tide of military personnel carriers, light-armored trucks each with a soldier mounting the attached machine gun. The combined force rolled over the meadows, eating up the land to leave nothing but barren dirt in their wake.

Tattletale dove at Jaune to snatch up his radio.

"Gunther!" she barked. "Order the hunter-killer teams back to the city, now! Coverage is too tight for them to stay unnoticed. They're gonna get slaughtered before they can fire."

From within copses of trees and shallow grooves dug behind hills, motorcycles shot out from hiding.
