Chapter 59: The One Sure Thing About Life​


Jaune bit down on the meatball drenched in hot sauce and tore it off the skewer. Next to him, Bennett, adventuring youth extraordinaire, did the same. Tears cascaded down their cheeks.

"Sho spicy… but sho good!" praised Bennett past a mouth full of food.

Tongue numb and unable to speak, Jaune simply nodded. The chef had outdone herself. Without modern cooking appliances, to boot.

"Fischl is missing out, wherever she is," Bennett added.

He nodded again, directing his gaze down the road. Unlike the other boy, he had the presence of mind to keep one eye on the girl named Fischl after they got separated. Way, way over there he caught a glimpse of a head of blonde hair bouncing up and down as a rather short individual strove to look past the shoulders of people taller than herself. She had yet to register their absence, and the heavy pedestrian traffic was steadily sweeping her away.

Oops, and it seemed she finally took notice. Her head swiveled to and fro as she scanned the crowd in rising alarm. As befitting an adventurer, relatively new or not, the girl defaulted to action. A quick command sent Oz, her raven, flying off to search for him and Bennett… thus leaving her completely alone in an unfamiliar city, a predicament which soon dawned on her. The image of a confident princess transformed into that of a shy wallflower in a blink, hugging the book she just bought to her chest for comfort as she waited for the sight of a friendly face.

Thump!

And while he would very much like to make his way over there, he had a more immediate concern on his hand. Jaune looked down.

"Are you jinxed, Bennett?"

"Huuurgh! Gack!"

Bennett did not, or rather, could not give a coherent reply, laying in a heap on the side of the road and holding his tongue. One of the meatballs on the skewer had a bite taken out of it, revealing what appeared to be half of a whole pepper mixed in with the ground meat, hot to the point that it glowed. The cook must have forgotten to dice it up into little pieces, so what should have gone into twenty different meatballs had concentrated within a single one.

It marked the third occasion where a mishap struck Bennett in—Jaune checked his scroll—about half an hour. Something something once, twice, and three times.

Was this how Lisa felt while traveling with him, always dreading when the next disaster would strike?

Nah, couldn't be. He was an angel.

After he pulled the other boy up, a few cups of water helped Bennett's lips regain a semblance of their normal size. The pair disposed of the wooden skewers, then once again continued their journey along the thoroughfare. Progress was slow as they drank in the sights.

On the first look, life in Liyue seemed very… very outside. People searching for a meal would find it sold at dozens of wooden stalls, cooked on tiny stovetops and sold right next to the season's latest fashion. Chefs that made it big worked in simple kitchens set in likewise simple buildings, with short tables and chairs put out next to the road. Gambling games were played on the pavement, participants squatting on their haunches. Bards lingered on the periphery of the crowd to recount tales for coins, attracting audiences that clogged up the path. Lisa would probably call it a microcosm of society; Jaune just called it a street.

He crossed under a bridge spanning the road, painted with that same deep red that much of the city favored, and his eyes happened to meet that of a young woman above. She hmphed at him before hiding her face behind a fancy hand fan. The attitude surprised him none, not by now. As a whole, the indoor spaces featured a more upscale atmosphere and bridges like this one connected different buildings together, allowing their patrons to avoid mingling among the scrum of dirty, sweating humanity down here. It did not stop them from watching and pointing, the city a circus with which they found their little amusements.

His attention drifted to a staircase leading upward, and he contemplated the idea of climbing them. The look on that haughty woman's face should she have to share the same air as him provided a powerful motivator. The guards stationed everywhere throughout the city had posted some of their members at the foot of the stairs. From what he could tell, they were never so crass as to refuse entry for people who wanted to go past. Oh no, they simply suggested an alternative route, then let gazes full of judgment do the convincing.

…Eh, whatever. The people up there were the ones missing out. Too far below the true place of power, that palace floating in the sky, yet too high to hear the interesting tidbits and rumors of the street.

"Century eggs! Get your century eggs here!"

"Two of them, one in each arm, each with enormous—"

"Inazuma silks for sale, the first batch since trade routes reopened. Kimonos customized to taste, contact Beidou before she sets sail to put in your order!"

"Break the stone to find the jade, this could be your lucky day."

"...the whole village, I swear it. A miracle that everyone got out before it sank beneath the waves…"

"Outta the way, cabbage merchant!"

"Millennium egg, ten times better than a century—"

Bennett's voice cut through the hubbub, full of liveliness. "Boss, look, they even have gliders!"

Poor Fischl must remain a lost child for a while longer. Jaune adjusted course and followed Bennett to the indicated booth, the other boy practically losing his mind over the rack displaying odd contraptions that resembled bird wings. They were of beautiful craftsmanship, metal frames forged in various designs and the fabric richly painted to resemble the sky at different times of day. The wings measured a little longer than a person's arm span.

One thing he knew right off the bat, there was no way these gliders could fly. The shapes were wrong.

"Fresh from Mondstadt, the best makers on the continent. Each pair tested by an expert Outrider of the Knights of Favonius," the shopkeeper touted.

"That's good enough endorsement for me!" said Bennett, fumbling for his coin bag. "I've been meaning to get a new one. My old set broke after a tribe of hilichurls chased me off a cliff."

Proof that gliders could fall, not fly. Jaune leaned closer to read the price tag. Rapping his knuckles on the counter, he gained the attention of the merchant.

"You mentioned that these are imported?" he asked, receiving a nod. "Bennett, did you check how much it costs?"

"It's fiiine, gliders aren't all that ex—by the Archons, never mind!"

He laughed as Bennett hissed through his teeth at the outrageous price, and patted his back in sympathy. The past couple of shops had taught him a rough idea of the local currency's value.

"That's five times what I would spend in Mondstadt," the other boy lamented.

"Rarity carries a premium?" Jaune ventured a guess, to the emphatic agreement of the man behind the counter.

He had done enough grocery shopping for his parents back home to understand that a specialty from a foreign place often meant limited stock in the local market. Stuff produced in other Kingdoms flew off the shelves whenever the settlement got them. A seller could charge whatever they wanted. Judging by the extra zeroes, the gliders were akin to luxury goods around these parts.

"What good is this thing, anyway?" he asked the shopkeeper. "I have… concerns."

"It depends on the wind, honored customer, but I once saw a young lass leapt off the highest point in Mondstadt, and an hour later I swear she has yet to land. The blessing of the Anemo Archon is keenest felt under two wings, even in these far shores. The freedom of the sky could be yours today…" the man trailed off, waggling his eyebrows leadingly.

Not a bad sales pitch, all told. It piqued his interest because the the man seemed to believe the words he spouted, meaning the contraption deserved its due consideration. And, boy, did Jaune have ideas on that. With the rocket boots, he had propulsion. Assuming a glider worked as advertised, it could give him some proper lift. Combine them together, and the good ship Jaune Arc might then set sail into the clouds.

He fished out a handful of gold coins, displaying them to the shopkeeper. His stash had hit a level where they couldn't be spent willy-nilly, but it was for a good cause so Lisa would understand. Probably.

"If you can accept this in place of 'Mora', then you've got yourself a buyer."

His bright smile faded when the man peered at the coins with a careful eye.

"What strange things," the man murmured, blinking slowly. "Crude make, and they don't shine like Mora. Where did you find them?" Once done studying them, he straightened up and shook his head. "If it is as I surmise, I'm afraid your coins lack the purity found in the work of Rex Lapis. I hold serious doubts about their value beyond simple curios. Keep them, customer."

Jaune clicked his tongue in dismay. Stupid Rex Lapis, whoever they were.

There had to be a quick job he could pick up. Perhaps the Adventurer's Guild needed monsters slain. For the moment, however, he was out of luck.

"Never mind then, I suppose. I'll come by again one of these days," he said. A gesture, and the gold coins vanished into thin air. The trick earned him a round of soft applause from the man, but nothing more than that.

"My wares will be waiting," the shopkeeper assured him, before turning to Bennett. "Now what of you, young man?"

Bennett dithered for a while. In the end, he pulled out his purse. "I'll buy it. Can't be a proper adventurer without a glider, after all."

"A bit of an exaggeration there, don't you think?" said Jaune. He was somewhat of an adventurer type, and he got by just fine.

As goods and coins exchanged hands, Bennett answered, "It tops the list for the most useful tool in our arsenal. You can reach high places, escape from danger, scout for shelter and rivers… Some of my seniors in the guild even go further to call it a badge of the profession." Transaction concluded, he showed off his new purchase, a glider that evoked the image of a fiery sunset. "Wanna see how it flies, boss?"

Color him curious, because he very much did. Yet, Jaune instead hooked his arm around Bennett's neck.

"Hold on there, buddy." A raven alighted on his shoulder, talons raising tingles of electricity where it touched his jacket. The nature of its existence or a warning, Jaune had no intentions of finding out. "I think Fischl has waited long enough for us."

Indeed, the girl's eyes lit up upon their arrival. The lost look on her face vanished, and she rushed over without bothering to hide her relief.

"There you are—" Screeching to a halt, she performed a delicate curtsy. "An eternity I have stood vigil, for my heart knew that we will one day meet again. Boon companions of the eternal night, I greet your return."

"She was worried because you two have been gone for a good while, is what Mein Fräulein meant to say," Oz provided. A hint of blush grew on Fischl's cheeks as she attempted to retain a dignified expression.

"My bad, Fischl," said Bennett.

"Yeah, sorry about that," Jaune added. "We're here now, though. To make it up to you, is there anywhere you want to go?"

Her head rapidly nodded at that. She pointed down a side street, toward the docks. To be precise, at a set of steps leading down below the wharf. While it saw little foot traffic, the people who came from there often carried bundles of goods.

Fischl shifted her posture, her hand making a grand sweeping gesture. "My forbidden eye never lies, and it wove a tale of hidden riches buried in the gaps betwixt. Come, let us walk where few dare to tread."

There was another market located off the main road, and she wanted to pay it a visit. Got it.

She had not been wrong about the 'few dare to tread' part, either. Worn down by decades of use, the uneven steps with their smoothed-out edges almost led to the death of Bennett as they descended the stairs. It put them on a lower docking area with one side open to the sea, the structure above providing a roof. Market stalls hugged the inner wall. The prices were softer down here, the goods on display an eclectic mix of leftover inventory taken from the nearby ships, sold to the stalls on the cheap to free up room before the new shipments were loaded.

The three blonds let out simultaneous squees of excitement. Where others might dismiss this area as a market serving a poorer clientele, to them the whole place gave off the sense of a half-illegal enterprise existing in the shadows, full of secrets and dodgy dealings. The perfect destination for a group of tourists to explore, in other words.

Not long after, the party stood in front of a curio shop (a junk dealer, in truth) as Jaune scrutinized a clunky box. "Is that… a camera?"

Ancient Mistral aesthetics, magic, flying wings that strapped to one's back, and now modern tools. This universe was a peculiar mix of different eras.

Fischl bent down level with him, and gasped as she recognized the object. "It is! Why, you have a most discerning eye. I have not seen one since dear Lumine last visited Mondstadt." She plucked the device, labeled as a 'kamera', from the pile of junk and held it up for a better look. "Alas, a broken thing this is, I believe." The girl released a forlorn sigh. "Fit for no purpose."

That certainly wasn't stopping her from having fun pretending to take pictures of him, Bennett, and Oz with it. Jaune played along, striking superhero poses that floored Fischl for—in her view—their groundbreaking style.

"Want to see something good?" he offered, then broke out his scroll to blow their collective mind. "Scoot in next to Bennett. Now make a victory sign—you don't know what that is? Okay, hold up these two fingers and spread them far apart. You can have it sideways, if you like. Perfect. This is how you take a picture."

Proper photos must always include a victory sign. According to Nora, anyway. Clearly this was the most important thing he could introduce to uplift backwards yokels.

Under the right filter, the two adventurers appeared downright inspiring, and it didn't take much encouragement for them to clamor for more pictures. A scene of herself sitting on the balcony against the backdrop of the blue ocean seemed to light something within Fischl, spurring her to purchase the kamera with the intention of getting it repaired so that she could capture the perfect shot for the historical annals.

Bennett remained of a more singled-minded bent, still spending his money to experience the street food of the docks. Seagulls stole about half of it, but of what he managed to keep, he declared each and every single one a hit. Liyue received spices from all over the world, and they were not shy to use them in their cooking.

At that same junk dealer, Jaune succeeded in trading his gold coins for Mora—albeit at unfavorable rates—after spinning a yarn of diving into ancient ruins to explain where he acquired them. Supposedly, Mora had been in circulation for thousands of years, to the extent that many nations consider it synonymous with terms like money or coin in a similar situation to Lien for the kingdoms of Remnant.

During his haggling, the others moved on. Which was fine, until a bookseller cleared his throat and tapped a sign.

"Please stop reading if you aren't going to make a purchase," he admonished, glaring at Fischl who had been immersed in a book.

In response, the girl turned a bright cherry red. The piles upon piles of literary works she never before read must have been a vision of paradise for the girl, and one she had quickly lost herself in.

"I wasn't…" She faltered, knowing there was no point in denial.

Jaune sidled next to her. "Oh, you weren't," he agreed. Glancing at the sign, he flicked pieces of Mora one by one over the counter that the bookseller deftly caught. "Right?"

The merchant's ire dissipated like smoke. He winked at Jaune, palming the money. "Come again, dear customer."

"W-Wait, you did not have to do that!" said Fischl, tugging on his sleeve. She tried to shove Mora into his pockets, only for him to dance out of reach.

"I told you I was going to get you something nice," Jaune said with a teasing grin. "And on that note, pick out a few more books. I still owe you bribes."

"Compensation," Oz cut in to remind him, sounding amused.

"Same thing, really."

He dropped a hand on the pouting Fischl's head, ruffling her hair to her great protests.


-o-​


The last vestige of the sun had dipped below the horizon. In its place, lamps illuminated the streets of Liyue. Under one such, a group of visitors to the city faced an unprecedented crisis none could have foreseen.

"We're broke," Jaune said.

Fischl and Bennett nodded miserably. Rich in souvenirs and low in funds, they stood in a huddle with him, their three sets of empty palms upturned with not even the lint in their pockets to fill them.

Jaune lowered his hands, and heaved a resigned breath. "I suppose I'll go sell some things."

"What? No way, boss!" Bennett denied at once. "We can't make you do that. No, this is our challenge to face head-on. I vote we look for lost treasures in the mountains."

Sure, let's head into the wilderness at night. Nothing could go wrong.

"That is unnecessary," Fischl said, shaking her head. She eyed the bundle of books and other assorted items in the bag sitting next to her foot. "In lean times, the vaults of the Immernachtreich must open, for its untold fortune exists to grant succor to the worthy who would follow me into the realm of infinite night."

In basic terms, she was offering to resell her purchases. Not much different from his plan, except in his case, he held no attachments to the gold coins floating around in his dimensional Pocket.

"Might I suggest an alternative?" asked Oz the raven. "You could deign to complete your task for the Adventurer's Guild, and be paid that way."

Bennett and Fischl shared a look, the former the first to speak.

"Oh, yeeeah. That was a thing, wasn't it?"

"Not that we forgot," Fischl insisted, with Bennett giving an emphatic nod. She straightened her back, adopting a haughty tone. "You have done well, Oz. I shall reward you greatly for your contributions."

"No need, Mein Fräulein. It was my absolute joy to do so. Please, our destination is this way."

Jaune held misgivings about relying on a bird of all things for direction, but Oz led them true. In no time at all, the party had arrived in front of an ornate building set in its own corner of the main avenue, with bright red pillars framing the entrance. A bulletin board rested near the building. The wooden tiles hanging from it were about the right size for people to write on them, though it seemed no one had. This time of day, the funeral parlor saw no visitors but them.

"Are they open?" asked Bennett. The entrance lacked a window for them to peek inside, but they could tell due to the door made from wood and paper that there was a light on.

"Hard to say. Let me try knocking," Jaune suggested.

He gave the door a series of sharp raps, then stood back to wait. After a bit, he heard a voice that sounded as if it came from deep within the building.

"Come in!"

"Nice," he said. "Looks like we're in business. And them, too."

He headed the group in entering the funeral parlor. Inside, they found a neat and tidy lobby without anyone manning the L-shaped counter. The room was an odd combination of minimalism and ostentation. No decorations hanging on the walls, yet the construction itself was a work of art with intricate wooden frameworks and vivid colors. Sofas of solid wood, sans cushions, were arranged around a low table carrying a delicate tea set.

A wooden screen divided the space, and from behind it emerged a young woman. Her long twin-tails trailed nearly to the floor, chestnut-colored hair tucked beneath a wide-brimmed, flat-top hat that was embellished with a wooden tile and a small branch of beautiful red flowers.

"Welcome to the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor. My name is Hu Tao, the 77th Director of this establishment—Oh me, oh my," she said, taken aback as she viewed their party in full. Her voice held a lively, sing-song cadence. "One client, two clients, three clients! It must be my lucky day."

The young woman—Hu Tao—brushed a stray lock of hair behind her ear. The gesture highlighted her mesmerizing eyes, scarlet irises with pupils the shape of stars. Her gaze found him, and Jaune swore she was looking him up and down.

No, she definitely was, and his ego began to surge upward—

"Let us begin right away."

"Eh?"

Drawing closer, Hu Tao reached within the voluminous sleeves of her coat, pulling out a measuring tape. She proceeded to stretch it across his torso, then the length of his arm.

"Erm, what are you doing?" Jaune asked after a beat.

Hu Tao answered with a soft giggle. "Don't worry. Rest assured, that I have what you need."

She dipped behind him. Jaune turned at the slight touch to his shoulder blades but she was already gone, back to his front.

"I think you have the wrong—" A gentle finger pressed to his lips.

"Shhh. I know. You don't have to say it," Hu Tao sultrily whispered to him. "Come, come. This way."

With that, she spun around and strode away, motioning for them to follow. The coattails of her brown coat fluttered behind her as she walked, a pair of shorts leaving her smooth legs bare.

Jaune exchanged glances with Bennett and Fischl, receiving the same confused look he no doubt wore on his face. Ultimately, the three of them shrugged their shoulders and went with the woman into the depths of the building.

Down a short corridor, Hu Tao slid aside a set of doors to reveal a room twice as large as the lobby. A simpler place meant for hardier work, the wooden floor was rough and worn. Tall, slender boxes lined the sides of the room in neat rows, filling in almost all of the wall space. Without a word, she perused them with a keen expertise before removing one to place on a workbench set at the center of the floor.

"And here we are. I am confident it will be to your satisfaction," she declared.

Jaune looked down at the workbench, appreciating the aged wood construction of the box, sanded smooth. He breathed in the soothing scent of pine. The box was of quality make, sized perfectly for his height. Not that he would call that last one a plus.

No reply was forthcoming from his lips. The silence stretched for a while, until it exhausted Hu Tao's patience. The young woman planted her hands on her hips, directing at him a frown.

"Well? Aren't you getting in?"

Her question woke him from his daze, and he balked. "Am I—no way!"

Hu Tao pouted at the prompt denial.

"Why ever not?"

No, a cute head tilt did not make it any better.

Another look at the box confirmed that he wasn't crazy. Jaune pointed at the thing.

"Lady, it's a coffin. For dead people. I'm alive, thank you."

Hu Tao shook her head in evident dismay.

"Ai-yai-yai, it's the same old style of thinking again. That is no excuse, you understand?" she insisted. "After all, everyone dies."

Was she messing with him? Was it just a thing here? Jaune turned to the others to find that, no, nothing about this was normal business practices. Fischl was flapping her mouth open and shut, unable to comprehend the situation. Bennett sweated as he nervously scanned the rows upon rows of open coffins, many sized for his frame. Only Oz behaved as normal, but he was also a bird.

Undeterred, Hu Tao continued. "Each day you delay is a day you risk a cold, wormy eternity out in the elements. Why, it's utterly irresponsible!" She hugged her arms and mock-shivered, then abandoned the pose to spread her hands wide. "But don't worry, for I am here with the solution for your troubles and with this season's special promotion, if you buy one coffin you now get another one free. Free!"

"For a friend, do you mean?" That was Oz. Even the raven had a limit to what he could bear, skepticism lacing his words.

"Or a mortal enemy! Do they not say that if you seek revenge, dig two graves?" Hu Tao asked brightly. She swung around the table to stand next to Jaune, barging into his personal space to poke at his muscles. "Hmmm. You have the arms of a swordsman, and such an excitable disposition." The poking and prodding intensified, until he nudged her away with an elbow. She didn't seem offended by it, her eyes squinting half-shut, the smile widening. "The kind of young man who may find reason and means for a second coffin. I am sure you have taken many lives. I can sense it on you."

Jaune suddenly felt very nervous. "There was a good cause for it," he assured Bennett and Fischl in a hurry. "They were evil, or trying to hurt kids, or—"

Warm hands held his own. Hu Tao went on tiptoes and tilted her chin up to look deep into his eyes, exuding a silent comfort to let him know he need not fear judgment.

"Do not fret. You aren't just a client, I see it now. I believe there could be a great partnership between us. Imagine it."

He did. "I… I'm seeing a graveyard."

Hu Tao nodded. "Exactly. Me to make them, you to fill them. A greater match the heavens never did create. So, what do you say?"

He'd say that he was very uncomfortable with this line of conversation.

"If he answers with anything but no, then I must warn you that I will tender my resignation," a tired voice interrupted. Shortly, a man appeared at the door.

Jaune had to look up, because the man was taller than him. (Better-looking, too, but he'd ignore that.) Dressed in a classy ensemble of predominantly brown and gold, his straight-backed posture denoted certainty with every step he took. A placid gaze panned across the room.

"Rarely do we receive clients under the light of the moon. It is considered inauspicious. You hail from Mondstadt, if my eyes do not deceive me."

"Yes, that's right, sir," replied Bennett, caught off-guard by the man's casual deduction. "Me and Fischl, anyway."

"Call me Zhongli," the man said with a brief glance at Jaune, likely attempting to place his origins. "Most do, for I am merely a consultant of the funeral parlor. Might you have business here beyond listening to the Director's dubious scheme?"

Hu Tao gave an affronted gasp. "Zhongli! I'll have you know that I am on the cusp of establishing a long-term, sustainable process of outreach with—" She nudged the person beside her with an elbow.

"Jaune," he provided.

"—with Jaune that would reinvent our entire industry. To deem it 'dubious' is giving me too little credit."

"You plan to depopulate the countryside," Zhongli deadpanned.

"Of bandits and other nefarious villains! Think, Zhongli. Many people cannot afford their own funerals, but in this case the community at large will pay through the nose in order to help out. It's practically an iron-clad insurance policy for us, and it won't cost us a single Mora."

Bennett raised his hand. "Uh, I think that's called a bounty, and the Adventurer's Guild already has people who take care of that."

"Quite," said Zhongli. The man sighed. "Please do ignore her, and let me know what you need."

The consultant directed that comment to Jaune on the assumption he was the leader, but as it had nothing to do with him, he just shrugged and deferred to the adventurers. Fischl took it as her cue to search through her belongings, and she soon produced an envelope. The rustling of paper was the only sound in the building as Zhongli opened the letter. A skim of the text and the papers then passed to Hu Tao, whose expression grew more gentle.

"Aiya, it seems I am in for a long trip. I hope I break even, at least," she said.

Jaune cocked his head. "You aren't even thinking of rejecting the job?"

"What a silly notion." Hu Tao began tapping her chin. "Now where did I put my seal?"

Zhongli cleared his throat. Despite the put-upon demeanor, he courteously offered a small box to the director.

"I knew I could count on you," Hu Tao praised, taking the item. She looked from Bennett to Fischl. "So, which of you has the job form?"

Both adventurers blinked blankly at her.

"You knooow, the form that the Guild handed to you with the details of the job and a little square for me to stamp my seal confirming receipt of the delivery?" More silence, and so she added, "Otherwise, you won't get paid by the Guild?"

Fischl jolted. "We won't!? I mean, ahem. Surely you jest, for never in my long years have I encountered this strange practice! I—"

"We usually just report to Katheryne," Bennett explained.

Hu Tao frowned. "Then how does anyone tell if you have completed the task? Oh, never mind. I guess I am simply used to the Liyue way of doing things. Alrighty."

Moving toward Fischl, Hu Tao pressed her stamp to the startled girl's cheek. It left the red imprint of a butterfly within a diamond on her skin afterward that the rest of the party leaned in to study.

"Would the Guild accept this?" Jaune wondered aloud.

"Nope. I just did that because I thought it would look cute on her, hee-hee."

"Oi."

Hu Tao showed him an impish smile. "Not to worry, let's not fret. I'll accompany you to the Guild tomorrow and that should settle the matter. I have business there, anyway." Then, quieter. "This time my proposal will go through, I can sense it. Group discounts. Commission rates. Warranties," she chanted as a mantra.

Jaune and the two adventurers were more occupied with a small detail.

"Tomorrow?" Bennett squawked.

"Yes, tomorrow. The Guild would be closed for the night by this time," Zhongli informed them. "It is no cause for alarm. People often chase Mora, but the secret is that it never runs. Your contract will be honored, I assure you."

"Ahaha." Jaune awkwardly scratched his cheek, avoiding the man's gaze. "Nah, the problem is that we're flat broke."

The sound of a growling stomach brought the conversation to a pause. Once again, Fischl became the center of attention. She hadn't eaten, unlike Bennett and Jaune who had snacked throughout the evening.

The girl wilted under their gazes, but soon rallied, whirling to look at her raven.

"Oz! Kindly conduct yourself as befitting of my retainer!"

Needless to say, nobody was fooled.

Taking pity of her embarrassment, Jaune addressed Zhongli. "Since the Director ("Hu Tao, that's me!") will be going with them to the Guild tomorrow, is there any chance you could advance them some Mora? They can return the amount once they collect their payout."

Food presented no issue, as he could order meals from the Company scroll. Accommodations for the night cost a fair bit in this city, however.

Zhongli held his chin, mulling on the suggestion. "Well, now. The contract between you and the client has been made, the arrangements in place. Yet, naturally, nothing precludes a new contract between us." The calm face then cracked a smile. "In exchange for a sum paid from your future remunerations, a meal and a bed to rest your weary heads. And, more importantly, a fond memory of your visit to Liyue. It is reasonable, I'd say. How about it?"

"We'll take that deal!" Bennett jumped on the offer at once, with Fischl's frantic nods as her endorsement. They both looked to Jaune, like he had any real involvement in this.

"It solves your problem," he said. "Congratulations, you two. You finished your quest."

"Yaaaay, congrats!" Hu Tao likewise cheered, giving them a round of applause that had the two adventurers blushing with pride. "So now that you are staying the night, I have just the place for you to sleep. Ta-da~" She flourished her hands, motioning to Jaune's coffin. "A fine opportunity to test out your future home, is it not?"

The funeral parlor fell silent as the grave. Everyone stared at Hu Tao with dull eyes. After a beat, Zhongli turned away from her.

"I will show you to the spare quarters," he said, and led them out of the room.

"Wait, Zhongli, don't be hasty. I almost had them!"

Cupping her hands like a megaphone, Hu Tao called after the group.

"Remember everyone, we at the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor are always looking for new clients!"

Chapter 60: Mister Teatime​


The moon hung high in the sky in all its uncanny wholeness, ever the reminder to a certain boy that he was far from home.

Jaune stepped out into the night, letting the doors to the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor swing shut behind him. He stopped for a moment, head tilted back to enjoy the crisp breeze, then it was off to destinations unknown. Living on his own schedule had formed terrible habits, a willingness to indulge in the occasional nighttime wanderings and the energy to go with it among them. He fought the urge to whistle a tune.

This late, Liyue Harbor slumbered. The onrush of people had quelled, most returned home. The shops were closed except for the snack bars catering to drinkers—mild and orderly affairs observed with a careful eye by the city guards on duty. It was a quieter side to the bustling capital, peaceful in a way that evoked an image of the city sighing in relief after a hectic day.

Crossing a bridge put him in a section of Liyue built upon an island. The main dockyard was located here, and he spotted some activity still ongoing despite the hour with ships setting out to sea. It seemed to him a foolhardy decision, but perhaps they didn't have sea monsters in this world to deter these intrepid captains. The ocean looked calm enough, at any rate.

He stayed to watch them for a while from the upper levels. Soon, however, his eyes drifted lower to study the stone balcony his elbows were resting on. The tiered structure of this neighborhood suited his purpose.

"Okay, let's see if this works or if I got scammed." It would kill him to have spent that money for nothing. Metaphorically speaking, of course.

Up until Lisa heard what happened, then he might literally die.

A look to the left, a look to the right, the coast was clear. Jaune hoisted himself up before anyone could come around the corner. He clicked his heels together. Flames sparked in response. The subsequent jump took him above the docks.

A contraption of metal and fabric appeared on his back, the straps already secured to him—proper visualization did the trick. A bronze-like alloy formed the frame, forged in a flowing design to resemble the ocean waves. From it extended strips of cloth shaped as long feathers, red in color fading to gold at the tips reminiscent of the early morning sky, of dancing sunlight upon a day in spring.

The slightest wind caused the glider to unfurl. And, suddenly, Jaune ceased to feel the pull of gravity.

He hung there, effortless. The constant balancing game of his rocket boots was missing, the wings on his back bearing that strain as the fires beneath his feet provided power to hold him aloft.

"Well, what do you know…"

The corner of his lips twitched upward, just a flicker that he suppressed. It would be rather embarrassing to celebrate early, only to then crack his head against the pavement in that most classic of landing strategies. That said, he did release the breath he was holding inside.

An errant shift of his shoulder allowed the glider to catch a different breeze. The cloth feathers rustled as he began drifting to the side, and it solved the conundrum of how a person would control the wings. His gaze flicked down to his feet, and he licked his lips in nervous thought.

Nothing for it. He pressed on the triggers of the rockets and braced for it to go catastrophically wrong.

Seconds later, he cracked open his eyes. They then flew wide.

He had passed the cliffs on which the harbor sat. Had gone higher than the tallest building, a pagoda sitting at the top of a waterfall. The sprawling cityscape laid out below him, with little figures moving amidst the scant light of the street lamps.

A bark of laughter tore from his throat. Abandoning the last traces of hesitation, Jaune shot off at full speed, the glider wings on his back folding shut. He built height, using the limited duration of the boots before its cooldown period to get as high as possible, clearing the nearby mountain peak entirely. The rockets cut out at the same altitude as that floating island which hovered above Liyue.

At the very top of his ascent, the moon filled his vision. He drifted weightless for the barest instant in a sea of nothingness. Then, gravity reasserted and he fell back.

The wings snapped into place. He banked to the right in a corkscrew motion, and flexed his shoulders. The glider responded, catching the wind to send him soaring. He let out a whoop without thinking.

The next few minutes, he spent trying every trick he could conceive of. His stomach churned at some of them, but he had no intentions to cease. Spirals, sudden stops, even combat maneuvers to reposition around an imaginary enemy. The world turned upside-down as he performed a wide vertical loop, a feat he had never dared for fear of losing control. Timing it with the rockets coming off their cooldown, he executed a second, faster loop that had him screaming in pure exhilaration as it threw him like a bullet toward the ground. Before impact, the wings behind him spread out to capture the momentum so that he went from a straight descent to sideways, traversing the breadth of Liyue Harbor. Someone pointed at him from below, and he waved to them, overcome by giddiness.

A minute of battery at a time, twenty seconds to recover from the overheat, and half an hour total for it to run dry. The limitations of the rocket boots made it worthless in the eyes of many, a perpetual anchor around his neck that he could never allow to slip from his mind lest he die from a careless mistake. Yet now it met with technology from another world and meshed into a new whole. Working in tandem with the glider, Jaune reckoned he might stay in the air for hours, and go as high as it pleased him.

The world was his, for he could fly.


-o-​


Jaune came in for a landing, touching down at a city plaza. His shoes scrabbled for purchase as he slid across the stone tiles. Momentum bled off with the passing seconds until he was able to shift into a running motion, each stride clearing a wide distance.

A shadowy hand latched onto the pavement, stretching like a bungee cord to slow him further. That finally did it and Jaune managed to screech to a halt, the arm dissipating before it could yank him the other way. He almost fell over then and there, windmilling for balance.

People were watching. He waved to them all friendly-like to play it off, afterward stumbling over to a street lamp to which he clung as his shaking legs refamiliarized with solid ground. With the windswept hair, he looked a mess. Sweat drenched his back, and the muscles in his shoulders ached from a new kind of strain. Gliding turned out to be pretty rough on a person new to the scene, or maybe that was just the many, many ill-advised maneuvers he tried to pull. Still…

"The world is mine, for I can land!" he happily crowed at his success.

"It is an important consideration."

"Right? Man, I should have thought my landing strategy through beforehand and heeey, Zhongli! What are you doing here?"

Although he asked, the answer seemed self-evident with just a quick glance. An old teapot rested on the low table, with a cup placed in front of the tall and slender man who at this late hour was yet dressed in an immaculate suit. The stool set next to the table appeared much too short for him, both knees drawn to his chest in order for him to sit. This teahouse catered to a pedestrian clientele in every sense of the word, even if one would not think it with Zhongli's mannerisms.

Jaune was never one for jealousy… Okay, he was, and the green monster reared its head now. How the other man made drinking tea by the curbside look elegant, he truly wanted to know.

"The nights agree with me," Zhongli answered simply. He raised his cup with both hands, waiting before sipping the contents. "Rumbling thunder portends a storm, but we have time yet. Would you like to sit awhile?"

He hadn't heard any such thunder up there. Still, flying was hard, thirsty work. Zhongli had also been a most agreeable fellow. Calm did not mean cold, and the man played the part of an impeccable host, ensuring the satisfaction of Jaune's party in both meal and accommodations earlier that day—in Bennett's words, amazing. Once he could stand, Jaune walked over to the teahouse, plonking down on a chair and stretching his legs out to get comfortable.

Zhongli smoothly poured him a cup of tea. The man then winced as Jaune knocked it back in one swig.

"You know, that was pretty good. Can I get some more?" Jaune asked.

"...Certainly. Do try to savor it, however. The flavor improves as time goes on."

Jaune replied with a sheepish chuckle, having heard the mild reproach in those words. In his defense, tea etiquette was outside his wheelhouse.

Luckily, he had a ready teacher in Zhongli, who ran through an abridged course for his sake. From the placement of the hands to the proper way of setting down the cup so as to avoid disrupting the mood, it was an entire production that bordered on a ritual rather than the simple act of drinking a beverage. In the end, Jaune scraped by with enough decorum to pass for a country bumpkin fresh from a farm.

Sue him, he had ten minutes to learn.

"As always, the occasion prevails," Zhongli reassured him. "You would fit right in among the flower fields of Qingce Village. Within the Jade Chamber above our heads, they will laugh you out of the room. Yet, you are far more likely to visit the former than the latter."

Jaune nodded, and swirled the cup in a gentle motion before taking the next sip. It was apparently an important step due to something with the water interacting with the tea leaves, and the flavor that would come about.

"You sure know a lot for a consultant to a funeral parlor," he said.

"I merely travel far, and hold a long memory. It is the reason for my contract with Wangsheng, in fact. Knowledge, as leaves, tend to fall by the wayside with the changing seasons."

"And here I thought it was because Hu Tao wanted somebody around to mess with. Not a slight against you, it's my impression of her after—"

"She does."

"Oh." Jaune recalled his experience with the peppy girl. "My condolences. She must be a handful."

"The Director was entirely serious in selling you that coffin, among other things," Zhongli revealed, to Jaune's consternation.

"You're joking with me." He gawked at the other man. " You have to be."

"No, I am not. In any case, let us not speak further of that child. My work day has ended." The two of them drank their tea, with Zhongli noting in approval of Jaune's manners. "Ah, see? You have improved already. Evolve as it may over the years, at its root the practice of drinking tea stems from a simpler age. The rules are likewise."

Jaune made a face, and waggled his hand. His personal experience so far differed somewhat from that assertion.

"I'll take your word for it. Not going to lie, I managed to keep maybe half of your instructions in my head."

Zhongli chuckled. "It is no matter. The goal is not how well one adhered to the rules. Then and now, the reason we do this remains the same. A chance to sit down, and perhaps gain an understanding of those around us."

"Right…"

A short lull in their chat ensued, in which neither spoke a word. The plaza offered a peaceful scenery easy to get lost in, with the stars out and a sea breeze to cool them down. Even as the scant few souls present departed one by one to their homes, they remained to enjoy the moment.

The modern sensibilities of young men everywhere prompted Jaune to kick back on the rear legs of his stool, balancing precariously to prove his debonair attitude. That didn't last long as he soon remembered the lesson taught not ten minutes earlier and revised his posture. The tea cooled during this period, although he preferred that. Cold drinks suited his taste. Like a soda taken straight from a fridge, or 'oolong tea'. Lisa had told him he was a weirdo for putting ice in his hot chocolate.

After a time, Zhongli remarked, "You sigh often."

"Oh, sorry. Didn't realize I was doing that," Jaune said, jolting out of his reverie.

"It does not bother me," Zhongli clarified. "But if I may, what ails you?"

He frowned at the insinuation. "Nothing. Whatever gave you that idea?"

The other man seemed to ponder on it, holding his chin with a gloved hand.

"You lean toward the seat next to you, as if expecting a presence where there is none. You start conversations with the empty air before catching yourself. It speaks of a companion missing from your life."

He stared at Zhongli in mute shock for a brief moment, then his eyes darted to the side. "It must be your imagination. Anyway, I'm fine. More than fine." He laughed. "Have you ever gone gliding? It's amazing."

The man accepted that answer with cool aplomb, drinking his tea as he offered no reply.

Jaune returned to watching the moon. He wasn't going to tell a stranger that he had been thinking of Lisa.

"Would you like to talk about her?"

"...Did I say that out loud?"

"Oh no, but I would think the signs obvious."

Resisting the urge to groan, he said, "You're making it sound way more serious than it is."

It was just that Lisa seemed to be with him everywhere he went these past few months. Always with an advice, an insight, a direction. Now, she was down for the count. Gloomy and waspish, refusing to get out of bed. Giving him the boot, to boot. In her absence, he found his travels a rather uncertain endeavor.

"You do not sound sad," Zhongli observed after Jaune relayed the sentiment.

"It's freeing, in a way."

He walked where he wanted, and did as he pleased. Nothing but his own thoughts guided his path. No sharp rebuke followed in the aftermath. He could concentrate without all the noise. The consequences of his actions fell on his own head, and nobody else.

"But I guess I don't like being alone for long," he said, his shoulders slumping. "It's easier when there are people for me to focus on."

"I understand the feeling well," Zhongli said, nodding. "There are some who say that command is a burden. They are not wrong, yet oftentimes it is the place a person draws comfort. With control, one may believe they can stay the same even as the world around them changes."

"That's not really… It isn't my reason," he denied, a tad weakly if he cared to admit. "And I'm not exactly the leader of our little band. We're partners, more like, and she's usually the one with an actual clue."

"Does she think so?"

Jaune caught the undertones of the question, even without Zhongli voicing it aloud. The idea that Lisa was waiting for him to do something to help her. To give her direction, and step up to be the one at the helm when she faltered.

He balked at the notion. The Lisa he knew would hate that.

But then, how well did he know her, if she wouldn't let him read the book of her life?

In the end, he deflected the conversation down another, less uncomfortable road. "I'm just going to bring back a ton of treasures and see how she reacts. On that note… you've been around, you mentioned. Have you heard rumors of where any are buried?"

His attempt to avoid the subject hadn't gone unnoticed, Zhongli leveling that ever-calm look his way for a beat of silence that stretched on too long. A tiny curl to his lips conveyed the man's amusement.

"Well, now," the man began. He paused to sip his tea, a twinkle in his eyes as he continued. "Liyue has seen ten thousand battles of gods and demons in its long history. Spirits great and small were laid to rest beneath calm, tranquil stone. Many left behind their armaments. Others took on simpler forms as their powers waned. An intrepid soul may find more treasures than they can stomach. Tell me, what manner of riches do you have on your mind?"

Now this was right up his alley. Jaune leaned in, unable to keep the excitement out of his voice.

"Any of them have to do with a 'yaksha'?"


-o-​


Tok.

That, was the sound of the teacup striking the table with a bit more force than was polite. Zhongli had drilled into his head how gentleness was the height of propriety in these matters. The man seemed to have forgotten the very lesson he taught in lieu of a hard, impenetrable stare.

A solid minute in, Jaune ventured to speak.

"Did I say something wrong?"

That seemed to snap Zhongli out of it, and he cleared his throat. "No. No, I simply find it a most intriguing request. For what reason did you—" Mid-sentence, the man's eyes flicked up to the sky. They widened a fraction at what he saw there.

In a blink, an ornate spear materialized in Zhongli's grip, its blade shining golden in hue. Still seated, he drew back his arm and hurled the weapon above Jaune, who was only just beginning to summon his shields to ward against what he had believed an attack.

Jaune turned his head to follow the path of the spear, and caught the moment it met a lightning bolt that crackled with uncontained power descending from the sky. With a deafening roar, night turned into day as the intense light washed over them, and Jaune braced for impact.

Against all odds, no pain arrived for him. His surroundings failed to explode with everything set on fire. He peeked through watering eyes and saw the spear defying logic to hang there in mid-air, vibrating with the force of the electricity coursing along its length. The lightning danced in twisting arcs from one end to the other, redirected away from Jaune and Zhongli to slam harmlessly against the ground. They gouged out the road tiles, and scorched the stone black, but never touched the pair of them.

Finally, it stopped. The lightning dissipated first, unable to destroy the spear.

The weapon fell out of the air and would have bonked Jaune on the head had Zhongli not lunged across the table to snatch it away at the last second. The man dropped back onto his seat afterward. On his face, a wide-eyed look to crack the calm facade.

Shaking, Jaune held out a hand with the palm upturned. No droplets of rain struck his skin. The moon shone over a clear sky.

A shuddering laugh slipped out of him, part relief, part disbelief. "Holy… Of all the luck, huh?" Sweat poured down his brow, and he pressed a hand to his chest to soothe his thundering heartbeat. "Thanks for the save, hot damn that was close!"

'Merely a consultant of the funeral parlor', his foot. The guy diverted lightning with a stick!

Rather than shouting of his feat from the rooftops, Zhongli remained quiet. His gaze was locked on Jaune's, and he seemed to want to speak yet did not have a clue of what to say.

The eye contact broke due to an awakening city. Dogs howled and cats yowled. Windows crash open, the people inside looking out in alarm. A commotion at the other side of the plaza attracted Jaune's attention. City guards were racing into the area, shouting in confusion.

Zhongli quickly banished his spear back wherever he stored it previous, and ducked his head over his teacup to study it with avid interest. A furtive glance compelled Jaune to follow suit, and they played dumb as the guards approached.

"What happened here!?" one of the armored men asked—commanded, really.

"I cannot tell you," Zhongli replied to him. "In the midst of enjoying this fine pot of tea, suddenly there was light. My companion and I did all we could to survive, and nothing more than that. What luck that we are unharmed."

It shouldn't work. It did work. The guard took one look at Zhongli and his vapid smile, and decided that this was a truthful man. Efforts thereafter focused on reassuring the populace, the lightning bolt deemed a freak accident.

Once they had a measure of privacy again, Zhongli spoke under his breath.

"It seems the heavens lend your words credence. A yaksha lies at the heart of your journey."

"Yeah, before that, can we take this conversation under a roof?" Jaune rose from his seat, halting as Zhongli held up a hand.

"There is no need. I am confident it will not happen again."

Thunder rumbled above their heads. Jaune leveled a deadpan gaze at Zhongli.

"You were saying? I think that storm you predicted is coming in."

The man gave a small chuckle and stayed in place. He even sipped from his teacup. The serene, carefree demeanor helped to settle Jaune's nerves, convincing him to slowly lower back onto his chair.

"Some dangers are worth inviting. Now, you are looking for a yaksha?" Zhongli asked with a smile.

One eye on the sky, Jaune shook his head."Maybe? I don't even know what a yaksha is, and are you sure we shouldn't seek shelter?"

"And yet you speak their name. How curious," Zhongli mused half to himself, before spreading his hands. "If you like, I can tell you what little I know of them."

"I guess we're just going to ignore my other question," Jaune grumbled. Spying the trace of amusement in Zhongli's smile, he sighed. "I would love to hear it, yes. Certain, ah, 'clues' are pointing me in that direction."

The man nodded, and refilled their cups.

"This story began," said Zhongli, breathing in the fragrance of the tea leaves, "in the wake of that era where the many gods of Teyvat vied for supremacy. So many fell that the hatred of fallen divinity soaked into the earth, until stone could contain it no more and an unending tide of demons arose to prey upon mortals across the land."

In some dusty corner of his memories, Jaune recalled the stories that started this way. The origin of the Grimm was something none could agree on. In its place, the many fairy tales had offered the answers. He sat up straighter as Zhongli continued on.

"Seeing this, Morax—who some call Rex Lapis—bade a race of war-like adepti that made their home within the mountains for one favor: fight. Fight, so that this land of Liyue shared by mortals and adepti could be one of harmony. So that the hearths of homes ceased to be torn asunder, and families lived to see the fresh morning dew upon the leaves. It is said that this race of adepti went by the name of yakshas."

He had a lead to go on. Jaune didn't pay it much mind, leaning forward in his seat.

"It sounds like you're talking about heroes," he blurted out, one knee bouncing in his impatience to hear more.

The man nodded. "They were. There is a reason why their stories are still told, even today. For those whose lives are measured in the thousands of years, humans may appear so very small indeed, yet the yakshas spilled their immortal blood for them, suffered scars for them, stained their hands of gods and demons for them. Untold numbers of innocents would have died had they but wavered once in their duty."

Eyes falling shut, Zhongli spoke in a slow, soft cadence.

"Alatus. Bonanus. Bosacius. Indarias. Menogias. The yakshas were many, but if you were to ask a mortal in that era, you would hear that there had only ever been five—the mightiest yakshas who fought by the side of Rex Lapis."

"So they're who I need to talk with," Jaune said in realization. "The mountains… I don't suppose you know where exactly they live and can point it out on a map?"

"They are gone."

Those straightforward words doused his blossoming good spirits.

"Gone?" Jaune parroted. "What do you mean, gone? Like… gone?"

Zhongli cracked open one eye. "Words cannot describe how your verses offend me."

"Sorry. Most days, I'm no poet." Jaune lowered his head, contrite, before a detail within the story struck him. "Wait, but the yakshas are immortal, aren't they?"

"Immortal is not immutable," Zhongli refuted. "Even stone erodes with time. To shed the blood of the divine is to carry a weight, and no yaksha could escape this fate. The hatred of the demons slain burrowed into their hearts, imparting a karmic debt for their sin."

Jaune had a bad feeling at what that entailed.

"Of the five that accompanied Rex Lapis, one still walks among the living, tormented by a constant agony. Another forgot his own name, and perished carrying out a final duty. The gentlest gave in to her grief, and her ashes were scattered from the top of Mt. Aocang. The final two yakshas succumbed to wrath, and on a night much like this, brother and sister set upon each other. They fell together beneath the waves, never to be seen again."

"And Rex Lapis let it happen?" Jaune asked, struggling to quell his disgust and anger at the ending that awaited the heroes of this tale.

"He did," Zhongli stated simply. "There is perhaps a lesson there. What I said about control, and change… Duty can become a heavy chain. Grow into your role, but know when to let go. That way, you can always be what they need you to be."

Zhongli took a careful sip of his tea. Keen eyes watched Jaune's face for every detail.

"So, tell me, which of them do you believe is the yaksha you are looking for?"

Jaune gave a considering hum, a hand running through his hair as he leaned back from the table.

"Unless I'm way off here, it looks like I'm headed out to sea."

"Bonanus or Menogias, then? You shouldn't have to journey far from land. By the records, their clash began and ended on the coastline. The exact location is a mystery, but I believe that is a fair starting point for your search. Either may hold the fortune you seek."

Tok. Zhongli set his cup on the tray with the teapot.

"That said, there is no rush. Running about in the dark would do no good."

"Oh, yeah, completely agree with you there," Jaune said, nodding. Bad things went bump in the night so stick to civilization once the sun was down, everybody knew that. "Thanks for the advice, though. The information and the tea, too."

"You are welcome." Zhongli began to rise from his seat. "Now, it is late. I suggest you get a good night's rest. Tomorrow promises to be a busy day."

"I prefer to think of it as productive instead of busy, but you have a point. Good night, Zhongli. We'll talk more tomorrow."

He placed his cup on the same tray, and almost left it at that when a thought struck him. His brows furrowed as he looked at the tea set.

"Hey, Zhongli."

The man paused in the middle of straightening his coat jacket.

"Yes?"

"Before you go…" Jaune scratched his cheek, head cocked to the side. "If you went out for tea by yourself, why did you prepare two cups?"

Zhongli's answer was a small, sad smile.

"We will set out early. The Adventurer's Guild may hold a hint as to our heading."

He could tell a deflection when he heard one. But with that, the other man made his departure. Hands clasped behind his back, Zhongli leisurely strolled down the street, leaving Jaune alone at the teahouse. Jaune stared after him until he disappeared around a corner, pondering the information he was given along with that last piece of news.

"I guess he's also coming along—Hang on a second, he didn't pay for the tea. Zhongli! Zhongli, come back! I'm poor as dirt right now!"
