Chapter 61: When the Sun's Out​


Morning arrived, and as agreed, their new acquaintances from the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor accompanied Jaune and company to the Adventurer's Guild. For a group that relied so much on paperwork and procedures, they were surprisingly understanding about the circumstances. Bennett and Fischl received their pay, plus a commendation for their willingness to make the trek from another nation. The Guild even promised to send more of that type of work their way.

An adventurer passing by had overheard and muttered what sounded like 'those poor gophers'. Jaune was positive it didn't mean anything, because who didn't want to travel and see the world? Part of the pay went to Hu Tao, thus concluding the contract between them.

He would have paid for himself, had he the means. Alas, all that he earned from his stint as a dishwasher last night went right back to the tea house due to a certain someone skipping out on the bill.

Ah well, he owed the guy for catching lightning in his stead.

Also… If pressed, he would admit that he was a little too distracted at the moment to pursue the matter.

"Is this how it always goes?" he addressed the person standing to his side, gaze locked onto the scene before him.

Zhongli placed a hand over his face, and deigned not to reply.

A fair answer, honestly, and Jaune nodded as if the man had spoken. His mind was torn between awe and second-hand embarrassment. For a world without trains, he sure was watching a trainwreck.

"Won't you have a heart, madam? Won't you have a care?" cried the lively, sing-song voice of the young woman who he had come to understand was quite a well-known figure around these parts. Not for good reasons, either.

The person Hu Tao was talking to, the head of the Liyue Adventurer's Guild going by the name of Lan, turned an interesting shade of puce.

"You should not be the one to say that!" she retorted.

Hu Tao blinked, taken aback. "I- I don't quite follow?" She then shook off her confusion, making placating motions with her hands and talking fast. "No, never mind that. I appreciate how you brought it up, because you're right. You are entirely right. Care matters. If your adventurers are to regain that sense of assurance they have lost in this uncertain profession, then they need to trust without a doubt that we hold their well-being at heart. We have to show that wherever they may go, the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor will be standing ready right behind them… and I have an idea on how to prove that."

"Oh, this should be good," Jaune muttered from the sideline. Hu Tao heard him, and she seemed to take it as encouragement. Head thrown back and nose in the air, she declared her terms with the boundless confidence of one who knew they had this one in the bag.

"As an exclusive promotion, our business is willing to give the Guild a trial period. No money upfront. No cost to you. We do not get paid a single Mora until the first adventurer is put in the ground. What do you think?"

With that… generous offer, Hu Tao clasped both of her hands together in front of her chest and showed a beatific smile, soft and sincere.

Lan returned it with a face scrunched up in displeasure.

"I don't have time for this," she spat out. Patience exhausted, she turned on her heels to stalk off without another word.

Undeterred, Hu Tao waved after her.

"I'm glad we're making headway! See you tomorrow!"

The guild head stumbled in her steps, but recovered quickly to hasten her pace.

"An audacious soul, the mistress of death," said Fischl quietly.

Jaune cracked a smile. "That's one way to put it." He noticed her subtle lean toward him, and so moved his hand to gently ruffle her hair. She made no comments beyond pressing her head further into it, reminding him of a cat. Jaune then turned to the funeral director, who was practically glowing with renewed life as she skipped over to the group, her twin tails bouncing and swishing with the motion. "Sorry it didn't work out, Hu Tao."

"That's where you're wrong!" said Hu Tao, jabbing a finger in his face. Jaune tilted away from it, leading the girl to streeetch her arm so she could tap his nose with a black-painted nail. "Negotiations are still ongoing, though they may be long. Many customers are unwilling or unable to voice their needs, leaving it up to me to unearth their true desire if I am to clinch a deal. Today, I managed to get a better idea of Lan, which is why I said that we made headway."

It sounded good, her perspective. It made sense. If he ever decided to enroll in a business course, he'd likely find this lesson presented at some point. Yet, he kept experiencing this strange sense that there was a relevant consideration not taken into account.

Oh yeah, Hu Tao was trying to sell death.

"I wish you luck, then," he said, mostly out of a morbid fascination with seeing where it gets her.

"I don't need luck, silly. Everybody will become my clients at some point, that I guarantee."

As he said, morbid. Jaune shook his head, not quite succeeding in hiding his amusement.

"In that case, it looks like we all got what we came for."

The Yaoguang Shoal to the north would be his heading. One of the fishing villages located there had disappeared beneath the waves a few days earlier, according to the guild head before the kerfuffle between her and Hu Tao. Adventurers dispatched by the Guild were still in the midst of investigating the incident, yet to return to the city. An accurate picture beyond mere rumors remained elusive as a result.

As good a place to start as any, for him.

He glanced over at Bennett and Fischl. Neither showed inclinations of changing their mind and leaving. Having heard his intentions, it cost them no time at all to push aside their own plans of sightseeing Liyue Harbor, wanting to have his back. His mother would call them good kids, what with sharing the sentiment about strangers and friends.

Zhongli acted like he'd be joining as a matter of course, but Jaune was prepared for that already and had no objections. The consultant hid his true strength, and from his previous showing they were prodigious indeed, a veritable dragon beneath his calm exterior. A reliable ally in a pinch, Jaune was sure.

Then, there was Hu Tao.

"Why are you looking at me? Is there something on my face, or perhaps you want to race?"

As for that girl's reason to tag along, who could guess what went on in her head.

"Alright, everybody," he declared in a loud voice. "No point wasting daylight. Let's get what supplies you need, and we'll set out."

Ten minutes later, Jaune decided that he should have been more specific.

"This is what you want to take with you? Not anything else?"

Hu Tao looked toward the coffin, standing upright on its bottom base and given a wide berth by the pedestrians. Then, she looked back at him.

Blink. Blink. "Aaaare you saying I should bring a second coffin? You must be expecting a lot of casualties."

And she expected at least one. No guesses on who.

After all, it was just his height. The very same coffin she offered him yesterday.

Jaune closed his eyes, and counted to ten before speaking a phrase that would thereafter become a common refrain.

"Hu Tao, no. Please, no."


-o-​


The sun shone bright overhead, signaling a wonderful day. For a flower, this would be its last.

Jaune's boot stomped down on the Whopperflower, squashing the living plant beneath his heel. A subsequent stab of his sword ensured it would trouble him no more. With the fight winding down, he cast his gaze around the battlefield to observe how the others had fared.

Liyue was beautiful land, but rife with danger beyond the city walls. People traveled armed and ready for trouble, traders escorted by retinues of guards. Whopperflowers numbered among the myriad creatures that might waylaid the unsuspecting along the road spanning the Guili Plains. Appearing like hand-made dolls woven from giant leaves, they had sprung out of the ground as the party passed by to attack them with elemental magics of fire, ice, and thunder.

Or Pyro, Cryo, and Electro according to how the locals put it. Three among the numerous energies tied to the very gods that ruled the seven nations.

Monsters weren't the only ones with access to the elements. Jaune watched as Bennett set a Cryo Whopperflower aflame with a swing of his sword, his fire magic in top form today, burning hot. The young adventurer truly was reckless, having dove amidst the enemy force in order to engage them at close-quarters. Fine and good, as tactics went—Jaune would never fault that approach. Yet, like yesterday, Bennett's injuries accumulated at a rapid pace as a consequence. Burns crisscrossed his arms from Pyro vines whipping him, flash-frozen by a Cryo mist then zapped with an Electro bolt to create raw, blackened gashes.

The younger boy fought too simply, and suffered for it. His opponents fell regardless, however, so it worked in a fashion. Results were the biggest indicator of success, and all that. Jaune would have words for him later.

He moved on to study Fischl. With the support of Oz, her sense of awareness was a thing of envy. She exhibited good judgment, to aim for Whopperflowers attempting to cast magic, and had silenced many of them before they got the chance to harm him or Bennett. The girl could be a terror if not for her frail strength.

A Whopperflower, granted no chance to wield its element, changed its strategy to rush at Fischl. Made of plants, it was no warrior, except its meager physique actually pushed the adventurer off her balance. Its elation cut short, as did its body, when Jaune sliced it in half on his way past.

"Thank you, Jaune!" said Fischl, spinning to put an arrow into another Whopperflower without missing a beat.

He waved his free hand to acknowledge her, continuing to stride toward Bennett. Seizing a fiery Whopperflower by the neck(?), he swung it at one of its compatriots, the icy leaves of that flower setting alight. The Pyro flower then became his shield against a blast of electricity that rendered it unconscious. Jaune tossed it aside, trading sword for gunlance to pancake the Electro flower.

That left only two Whopperflowers that Bennett dispatched in quick succession, to conclude the battle.

"Whoo!" Bennett cheered. "That was a piece of cake—"

Jaune didn't listen to Bennett any longer than that, diving as fast as he could to the side. A split second later, cloudless skies dropped a lightning bolt on the spot he vacated. A crater remained when the smoke cleared up.

"Heh. It's getting predictable," Jaune mumbled to himself, lying flat on the grass. Bennett offered a hand and he grabbed it to get back on his feet, jabbing the other boy with a stimpak in the process.

Oblivious to the pain of the needle, Bennett said in a voice full of wonder, "That's the fifth time this happened to you. You, not me… I don't think I've ever met someone as unlucky as me before."

Unlucky or lucky, it was hard for him to tell. Two times today, where Zhongli intervened in time. Once in which Jaune was a tad late in dodging and caught a stray zap, losing a chunk of Aura. And twice now that he managed to escape unscathed on his own.

Not too shabby. The key was to anticipate, rather than react.

Of course, a reason behind the phenomena had yet to manifest. Zhongli clearly had a clue but he refused to say it, citing that doing so would doom them both rather than alleviate the matter. That said… In a world of living gods, he could take a hint after the second time. Somebody up there did not like him.

Zhongli and Hu Tao stood waiting a distance down the road. Once Jaune signaled that the danger had passed, they moved up to rejoin the group.

"You are growing used to this," Zhongli praised while Jaune dusted off his clothes.

"I guess 'do or die' is a pretty great motivator," he said resignedly, then gestured to Hu Tao. "And why is she pouting?"

With cheeks puffed up, Hu Tao resembled a chipmunk. Arms crossed, one foot tapping. Yeah, she was mad.

"I knew I shouldn't have listened to you. I knew a coffin would be handy," she grumbled.

In his defense, he had not foreseen divine interference. Sue him. The one silver lining was that it didn't seem to be escalating, so he just needed to keep on doing what he was doing.

And now he had jinxed it, hadn't he?

"There will be many chances yet, Director," Zhongli advised, causing Hu Tao to perk up.

"You're right, Zhongli. It's fated, methinks." She stepped closer to Jaune, observing him closely. "You, Jaune Arc, have a destiny. How else would you survive five lightning strikes, if not to perish for a worse reason." The young woman patted him on the shoulder. "Never you fret, I have you covered."

Jaune looked for help from Zhongli. None was forthcoming. "I'm afraid to ask, but is that a good thing?"

She laughed. "Yes, silly!"

It had better not be another coffin, was all he was saying.

While Zhongli admonished to no effect an unrepentant Hu Tao for her lack of tact, Jaune's attention moved to Fischl. The girl was rushing over, and skidded to a stop beside Bennett. The two adventurers proceeded to give him expectant gazes, bouncing on their heels with the eagerness of puppies.

"How did we do?" Bennett asked.

Fischl did not fall behind. "Has my splendid performance dazzled your senses?"

A 'Geovishap', some sort of stone golem/lizard hybrid, had given the duo trouble earlier. Rending it apart earned him recognition as a mighty warrior in their eyes. Questions soon followed as they sought pointers in order to better their skills.

It flattered him a fair bit. He'd admit that Pyrrha never managed to completely beat the desire for recognition out of him, and rare indeed were the chances for him to stand on this side of things. Of his companions, Lisa hated spending a single minute more on training than what he prescribed, while Escha's physique differed too much for him to contribute in a meaningful way.

Aware that they were hanging onto his every word, Jaune offered his opinion. "Bennett, good aggressiveness. You didn't take a single step back out there." The younger boy beamed. "But, once again, you're still letting attacks land that you're not built to defend against. That you withstood it at all is a miracle, one that's going to run out one of these days."

Why mince words here? He had the personal experience to tell the kid how dumb his style of combat was, since it mirrored his own a year ago. The whole thing boiled down to 'doing whatever', so long as it hurt his opponent more.

As a combat philosophy, it was extremely accurate. Struck at the heart of the matter, in fact. But only up to a point.

Chagrined, Bennett's chipper attitude faded somewhat, and he scratched the back of his head as he accepted the rebuke.

"As for you," Jaune said, directing his attention to Fischl.

The girl gulped.

He poked her arms, eliciting a yelp. His next test was to lift her up by the waist, her legs dangling in the air.

"High! So high!" Hu Tao whispered from behind him, laughing.

After putting Fischl down, he said, "As I thought. Your perception in combat is one of your strengths, as is your teamwork with Oz. There's nothing I can help you with on that part that you don't already know. If I have to note where you fall short, it would be that you are in desperate need of gains."

"Gains?" Fischl parroted.

"Gains," Jaune confirmed. Perhaps he should have expected it from a princess, hailing from another world notwithstanding, that nobody in her castle suggested to her a daily regimen to build up muscles. "Your arm strength could use work."

Fischl took it well, appearing on some levels to already realize the issue, albeit she displayed reluctance at the idea of developing a six-pack that a person could grate cheese on. After he was done, she and Bennett shared a look, and nodded in tandem before turning back to him.

"What should we do?"

"How do we train?"

Admirable of them, but…

"Train?" Jaune said, perplexed. "No, I'm going to solve those problems right here and now. Come closer."

Despite the confusion plastered on their faces, they did as he bade. He understood their bewilderment. Shouldn't the sage wisdom he impart be along the line of training harder and lifting weights?

And while he would certainly say that pursuing those avenues were important, he would also argue that such projects were meant for the long term with small immediate payoff. Advisable, if someone was aiming toward a champion career in the ring. Not so, for ̶a̶ ̶f̶r̶a̶u̶d̶ ̶n̶e̶e̶d̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶a̶ ̶s̶h̶o̶r̶t̶c̶u̶t̶ people on a time-sensitive quest.

"I have something that can help you"—he pointed at Bennett—"stay unhurt for longer, and you"—he pointed again, at Fischl now—"shore up your lacking muscles. Stay still, it won't hurt a bit."

His hands brushed by their cheeks, startling them until they noticed his seriousness. The pair settled down, nervous but trusting in him.

He drew in a deep breath, then exhaled.

"For it is in friendship that we…"

And at the end of his chant, two souls shone bright. The colors matched their elemental magic to a tee, one shining in a light red, the other a deep violet.

Bennett flicked his own arm, marveling at the dulled sensation of pain. From there, the boy moved up to a blade pressed against his fingers, and discovered a complete absence of blood once he pulled the sharpened edge away. Amazing, amazing, he kept muttering.

His excitement paled in comparison to that of Fischl. The girl stared at Jaune with unblinking eyes, vibrating with how high her emotions had soared.

"I knew you were like me!" she squeaked in happiness.

"Yeah? I'm from another world, too. I told you that, didn't I?"

Past them, he saw Zhongli sigh, rubbing at his temples in the manner of one trying to relieve a budding headache. No idea why. Couldn't be his fault.

Abruptly, his view of Zhongli was cut off by a flat-top hat decorated with plum flowers. Hu Tao had lined up behind Bennett and Fischl, hands behind her back, rocking back and forth on her heels. When that didn't get a reaction out of him, she started taking little hops forward, inching through a gap between the adventurers until she was in front of him.

"My turn~" she chirped brightly.

"Hey, now. This isn't a toy that I hand out willy-nilly, you know," he said, frowning.

"I'm delicate and I'm a terrible fighter," she said with pride. "Come on, I wanna glow in the dark! Do you know how hard it is to dig a grave at night in the rain? With all the lanterns doused and lighting them such a pain? And there's not even a fire to keep you entertained? Then the slimes—"

"Alright, alright already, I'll… Hang on, what about the slimes?"

Hu Tao refused to elaborate, merely going on tiptoes. Her head tilted to present her cheek.

"No, seriously, what were you saying about the slimes?"

A solid minute of waiting forced Jaune to accept two things. One, he did not have Hu Tao's patience, and two, he would have to live with never getting a continuation of that story. So, none could blame him when he reached up to pinch Hu Tao's cheek, and pulled.

"Open your eyes. Let's not make this weird. Why do people always insist on making this weird?"


-o-​


About two hours north on the Guili Plains, walking pace, there stood a set of ruins.

Big stone blocks of ancient castles were strewn across the ground, eroded by time. Broken gates and rending tears in the earth dotted the landscape. What remained of the area told of calamity, a war for the ages followed by silence. People did not live here anymore.

It made the movements easier to spot, and oh so suspicious.

"Hilichurls, they have not seen us," said Oz after he flew back from scouting. The raven alighted on Fischl's shoulder as she knelt along with the party in the shadow of a boulder.

"Silly-churl, billy-churl, silly-billy hilichurl~" sang Hu Tao, a hand shading her eyes. "We have a lot of them today. Is there a party going on?"

As the party stalked closer to the ruins, Jaune began to make out a fair few of the figures dancing around a fire, so the possibility of a celebration was there if one were inclined to optimism. The 'hilichurls' ranged in size from short and wiry to looming and lumbering. Shaggy-maned beings, vaguely resembling humans in that they stood on two legs and had two arms. All of them wore masks that hid their faces, and dressed in rags.

"No, that isn't it," said Bennett once they took shelter among the tall grass of the plains. "They tend to stick to way smaller groups. For scattered tribes to unite like this, it's usually the sign of an impending raid."

"And of one who stands above many," Fischl added. "A champion whose violence knows no bounds, that it may even dare to dream of challenging this Prinzessin."

"A leader, huh?" Jaune mused. "One of those?" He pointed to a bigger specimen. These guys measured twice his height at the least, built like Beringels with bulging muscles. Some were scarfing down meat, others shambling around the camp. They barely fit inside the crude tents that the hilichurls had erected within the ruins.

"Mitachurls," Bennett provided the name for them. "Shouldn't be. For a group this big, it's usually a—"

It passed into view. He thought mitachurls looked tough, this one was the big brother to them and encased in a layer of rock armor to boot. Other hilichurls cleared a path for it wherever it roamed.

"Lawachurl," said Bennett and Fischl at the same time.

"A formidable enemy for you, indeed," Zhongli said. He held his chin in thought. "The Wangshu Inn lies a short few hours away, and is likely to be the target. It is well-defended. A warning to them would suffice if you prefer not to engage."

The man studied him when he offered the suggestion, lending Jaune the sense he was being judged. Even without that, he rejected the notion.

"We can take them," he declared.

As he stood up, Fischl pulled on his sleeve to get his attention. "Ah, wait—I mean, do not be hasty, my kindred. A shadow lurks amidst the mountain crags. Hark, it moves."

"Mein Fräulein says—"

"Hidden enemy. Got it. Can you show me?"

Fischl pointed with her other hand at the lawachurl. Specifically, at a lump resting atop the creature's rocky head that Jaune had assumed was an ornament. A closer look revealed a mask depicting a grinning demon, and stubby arms wielding a staff.

"A samachurl. The shaman may drown the world, burn the fields, consume the earth in twisted vines," explained Fischl. "The colors denote an adherent of Anemo. By his will, the air itself shall become our foe, and the winds beneath our enemies' feet would see them move swift as a gale."

Jaune recalled a certain annoying sorcerer in a church, along with the troubles it gave him and a knight named Solaire. Boosting allies was just plain unfair. When done by the other side, of course.

"Okay, we're taking him out first," he decided.

The rifle Ruhm appeared in his hand, drawing curious looks, with him primed to put a bullet at the center of the samachurl's mask via his marksmanship. Yet, he hesitated.

"Fischl, how's your aim? Can you hit the samachurl from here?"

He had students right now. Students! He could make this a teaching moment!

Fischl displayed a startled look for a second at being put on the spot, and looked from him to the ruins with uncertainty. After much fidgeting, her expression transformed into a smirk. The girl flipped her hair, scoffing. "'Tis child's play for one such as I."

"Good. Show us how it's done."

At his nod, she scurried away from the group with eager glee, summoning her bow to hand as she situated on a piece of raised ground. The tall grass still grew there to obscure her form. Even with her standing upright, the stalks tickled her ears.

Fischl settled into a stance, feet shoulder width apart. She took a couple deep breaths to steady herself. Glanced at the group to make sure they were watching. Focused again on her target. Slowly, the bowstring pulled back.

And Fischl spoke.

"Ordained weapon of the darkest night eternal, heed my call."

An arrow of light materialized, nocked and ready to launch. Fischl did not shoot it, however.

"The time is nigh, the gaze of the world falls upon us.

"Release thy seal, as I shall my forbidden eye."

The jewel adorning the back of her dress glowed with an intense light. Sparks of Electro crackled around her. Over time, they coalesced within the arrow, tinging it in shades of violet. The air began to hum with a soft whine.

"To the stars and the abyss,

"Let the judgment of the Prinzessin der Verurteilung descend as a meteor,

"Bringing with it the cleansing peace of the midnight moon!

"Galaxienregen!"

With that cry, Fischl unleashed her attack.

The arrow flashed across the Guili Plains. It followed a path removed from the effects of normal physics, unwavering in its course for the full distance.

The samachurl didn't know what hit him, the arrow slamming home in an explosion of Electro that zapped the shaman to a crisp. The creature was dead before it hit the ground, the body vanishing as wisps of smoke.

In the wake of its demise, an angry roar shook the land, torn from countless throats.

"Nice shot, Fischl! What even is that spell?" Jaune shouted in praise, getting on his feet and trading rifle for sword.

"Could it be?" Hu Tao mumbled from her spot, impressed for a different reason. "Have I perhaps met the versemonger of the north?"

Fischl preened at the look on their faces. "This is a magic lost to all but royalty of the Immernachtreich. I mastered it over the course of many moons."

"Keep at it, you're doing great. Take a couple more shots from here, then you and Oz follow us in," Jaune instructed. "Bennett, you're on me. Let's go."

Bennett saluted, and drew his sword. "Yes, boss!"

Hu Tao sighed and stood up, too. "I'm not exactly keen on violence, but hey, can't let these fellas run amok. I'll help you out." A staff appeared for her, two-pronged tip cast in the shape of flames. It looked more like a ceremonial tool than a weapon.

"I thought you said you were a terrible fighter," Jaune remarked.

"I am," said Hu Tao. Her eyes avoided his own. "…in relative terms."

This little liar.

He mock-glared at her, before grinning. "Ah, whatever. Hey, Zhongli, are you helping out?"

"I am fine here, but thank you for the offer," was the serene reply.

"Your Director is heading into danger, Zhongli!" Hu Tao complained.

"Bodyguard work is not part of my contract."

"...Yeah, I know," the girl pouted.

Jaune chuckled, and accepted Zhongli's answer in good humor, thinking that he'd just have to pick up the slack. With a wave over his shoulder, he charged ahead with Bennett and Hu Tao hot on his heels.

The hilichurls came howling out of the ruins. Their ranks adhered to no order, effecting a maddened scramble across the field. Part sprint and part crawl, the savage gait was above all fast. The distance between Jaune's side and them closed in a matter of seconds, until he could see the etchings on their masks. Some carried crude weapons, some went barehanded. The bigger mitachurl variants favored axes whose blades were massive wedges of sharpened stone.

He continued to maintain pace with the others, a touch ahead to draw the ire of the hilichurls as lances of light passed above him, striking down what foes they could find.

The quickest of the hilichurls—the skinny, wiry ones—entered his range, the first leaping for his throat. A flick of his sword, and it dropped with a thud. Crocea Mors spun a circle, slashing the next from belly to chin. They soon turned to smoke, like Grimm.

The ground started to shake, the bulk of the tribe arriving. The rockets under his feet engaged, and Jaune blasted off over the heads of the hilichurls on a course for the biggest of them, the lawachurl. A second, smaller activation flipped him above the creature.

His sword switched to a gunlance, and he slammed Red Rook down on the lawachurl's head with all his strength—

Boomboomboomboom.

—and followed up with a fullburst that sent fragments of the rock armor flying every which way, kicking up a cloud of dust. The lawachurl came to an abrupt standstill.

The hilichurls' advance stalled out, the creatures thrown off by the thunderous noise of the gunlance. They stared in horror as their leader fell to his knees, then tipped over. Where there should have been a head, a figure armored in the scales of a dragon stood atop the lawachurl.

There was a moment where it seemed the hilichurls would retreat. That passed, as they began to scream and scream and scream. Growls, hisses, screeches—the sounds the hilichurls made sounded like no language, yet it conveyed hate better than words could. Fear, too.

Jaune thought he heard a cry of loss.

Couldn't be.

The body dissipated, dropping him into the center of the enemy force. It proved too great a temptation for the hilichurls. They rushed him, and thereafter the world narrowed to encompass merely what he could reach.

He dodged a blow, ended a life. Grabbed another, used it as his shield. His gunlance swept in a wide circle. Bones shattered to dust upon impact, incapacitating the creatures if they did not die outright. A mitachurl tackled him off his feet.

His face met the ground. He was lifted off it by his leg, only to smash again into the dirt. Up a second time, and he fed the mitachurl a jet of rocket exhaust right as his foot passed the eyeholes of its mask. The monstrous brute roared in pain, letting him go. Jaune hopped on the empty air—once, twice, thrice—to get his bearing.

He spotted Bennett. With all the mitachurls focused on the threat that brought down their leader, the reckless terror enjoyed free reign in carving a path deep within the enemy ranks. The boy laughed when struck by the hilichurls, over the moon as his Aura shielded him.

Fischl was fast closing in, firing arrows while on the move. She aimed for the small ones, wisely seeking to draw them away from the main melee to clear room for her allies.

Jaune then looked to Hu Tao, hoping that she was at least holding her own…

Ah… Um…

Why was everything on fire?

The girl had understated her abilities, her staff a burning stick that she spun and twirled like a circus acrobat. What it touched, it speared and set alight for a double whammy surprise. Flames in the shape of butterflies encircled these poor souls, once in a while exploding to rekindle the fire.

Did she even need him to make a graveyard?

Jaune pushed that matter out of his mind. She could take care of herself, that was the important point. It allowed him room to deal with the squad of big, angry stacks of muscles barreling down on him.

The gunlance returned to his Pocket, swapped out for the shorter sword. Jaune met the mitachurls head on, diving through a gap so that he was among them. The tight confines hindered him none, presenting targets on every side.

He slit the belly of one, and drove the blade up to impale the chin of another. A roll took him under an axe swing, a shield summoned to block a club. A kick from a mitachurl slammed him against the chest of its brethren. Without looking, Jaune stabbed behind himself, eliciting a shriek that cut off with a wet gurgle. [Third Arm] latched onto the one that kicked him, pulling him on its shoulders where he grabbed a fistful of the creature's mane.

The mitachurl shook its head like a dog in an attempt to dislodge him. It stumbled on unsteady feet, stomping on the occasional luckless hilichurl. The wild ride ended when Jaune let go, a rifle unloading a burst through the mitachurl's mask during his departure.

He landed to catch sight of a mitachurl trying to break off so it could attack Bennett. Darting between the crush of bodies, he clamped onto the thing's leg and, screaming with effort, he yanked it back and threw it at another of its brethren.

"Eyes on me!" he commanded the mitachurls.

Also, holy crap how much did he just lift?

"Mine, too?" Hu Tao asked as she skipped past him, bringing with her all that fire she had started in her wake. The grass had caught alight, and she scoured a wide circle in the dirt to break off the path of the flames, keeping it contained in their immediate surroundings.

"Ha! You never told me you were a magician," Jaune called over, fending off a mitachurl so it couldn't take Hu Tao's head off with a punch.

The young woman replied with an offended gasp. "These are the fires of my passionate heart, not parlor tricks! The raging will of a freedom warrior, here to fill Liyue with peace and justice!... Hee-hee, that's me."

So she said, as she exploded a hilichurl.

She sounds like the magical girls from that show my sisters watch. The Maidens, or whatever.

Jaune glanced at the staff in her hand. The girl even had a wand.

Her antics created a fantastic opening for him, however. Where the mitachurls and hilichurls screeched in agony, he walked through the flames unhurt, his armor rendering the heat akin to the summer breeze. He dispatched them one by one, meeting little resistance from foes distracted with the prospect of cooking alive.

Something about him broke the tribe of monsters. Following the demise of the last mitachurl, their tenuous formation, if it could be called that, soon devolved into a rabble desperate to run for the hills. The ones that didn't retreat turned into smoke to join the fallen.

Soon, the only people left standing in the grassy field were Jaune and his merry band, the party cheering their victory.

"A most splendid showing!" Fischl praised.

"I'm not bleeding! Check it out, Fischl!" crowed Bennett.

Jaune hooked him by the neck, and roughly rubbed his head to the boy's laughter. "You did good, Bennett, but don't think I didn't see you take that axe to the face." He summoned a shield he had stolen from a hilichurl, pressing it into Bennett's hands. "Start using this. It'd save your life someday!"

"Right, boss! But, uh… how do I use it?"

"It isn't that complicated. When an attack comes, you block."

"Block… Block… What is this mysterious concept?"

"Jaune, did you see my last shot? Did you? I do believe it was my best to date."

Between the two chirping adventurers, Jaune didn't notice that Hu Tao was gone until she called their names from over by the ruins. Zhongli regrouped with them, walking at a sedate pace, and they followed after Hu Tao into the hilichurl encampment.

He was skeptical of this at first, alert for danger. That sentiment vanished once he spotted the young woman grunting with effort as she dragged a chest out of a tent.

"I found a treasure chest~ And it's all mine~"

Jaune grabbed the handle on the other side.

"You mean, ours?"

Hu Tao snickered, and bit her bottom lip to keep from laughing harder.

"What's in here, anyway?" Jaune asked, lugging the heavy chest over to the rest of the group.

Zhongli provided the explanation. "A hilichurl tribe collects many bits and bobs over the course of their existence. They have an eye for shiny things. Glass, marbles, mirrors…"

Jaune lifted the lid, and everybody but Zhongli piled in for a look. Reflected on their faces was a golden glow.

"And Mora, most of all."


-o-​


"Dibs," Hu Tao immediately said.

Jaune leveled a deadpan gaze at her.

"Oh, look at your face! Don't take life too seriously, hee-hee~" she sang in a carefree voice.

This one wasn't Blonde, but she sure was Annoying.

#5,083
Chapter 62: When the Moon's Out​


Jaune and his party entered a village at the onset of evening, crossing the gate formed of three wooden poles lashed together. Constructed along a freshwater stream, homes ran on both sides of the riverbanks with a single bridge spanning the middle. The people there welcomed them, and their Mora.

One flaw stood out to Jaune in this idyllic scene. The place lacked a wall of any kind, the most token nod to it a fence that marked the boundaries, and while the others went ahead he got the story from a woman drawing water from a well. This settlement established itself not so long ago, decades to the centuries that some could boast of. They built the village first, capitalizing on the ample wild game living in the nearby mountains and the steady supply of lumber that came with the location. Farming followed suit as a matter of course, with livestock later raised in pens next to houses. The wall was an addition they intended to put up over the next few years if they had the time, with the woman deeming the matter as almost an afterthought.

"Sooo." He looked for a good way to phrase it once the villager finished her explanation, his hands occupied with pulling the bucket of water up from below. "It must be rough always fighting monsters to keep them from eating you in the night…"

"Oh no no, could you imagine? No, we have old Fong Sai for that," the woman said, with light laughter.

He frowned. "Just one person?"

That led him down a new, and very interesting, tangent. Safetywise, the village enjoyed protection from a retired adventurer. More than that, a Vision-holder. He dug more into that—obliquely with the subtlety he was known for, of course—and received quite a tale. Vision-holders were unordinary people that one could often spot within a crowd by the glowing gem amulet affixed someplace about their person, plus the way they wielded nigh magical powers derived from an element. Tellingly, all four of his companions carried amulets inlaid with gems that he had assumed were just decorations. He felt rather left out, now.

"Hypothetically, how would somebody get a Vision… you know, if they were in the market for that sort of thing?"

One did not dangle power in front of Jaune Arc, and tell him to keep his paws off it. This was, in broad strokes, the exact plot of how the beginning of Puree Seasoning Maidens or whatever went, just without the weird mascot.

The villager held a hand to her cheek, looking troubled. "I have no idea, dearie. Everybody asked Fong Sai at one point or another, but he would never say. It has to do with the Archons, I believe."

Jaune followed her gaze to spy the adventurer from afar, sitting outside his home. An old man with a quiet demeanor who carried a kind look on his face as he watched life in the village go by. His Vision, a pale blue stone, hung off a necklace tied around his neck and sparkled in the sunlight.

Buying the gem off the man probably wouldn't work, right? Not if gods and destiny and all that were involved? Filing the information away for later, he bade leave from the villager to regroup with the others.

They soon settled at the foot of the bridge, where simple wooden tables and chairs had been laid out for their use. How thoughtful, for it allowed them a charming view of the stream. Fischl in particular seemed taken with the sight, and she spent some time watching the colorful fish swimming amidst the clear water that washed over the smooth river stones, the long tresses of her blonde hair almost dipping into the stream on occasion. Bennett, meanwhile, quickly found himself pulled into a game by the local kids, as he was the most approachable-looking person in their eyes with his rough, down-to-earth adventuring outfit. A pot of tea occupied the rest of the party as they waited for dinner. Lanterns provided light for the area.

The village did not have a restaurant, per se. Rather, it was more apt to call the whole place a communal business as multiple homes pitched in to cook food for the paying guests. Whoever had a free kitchen at the time and knew a halfway presentable dish, and wanted a share of the Mora that Jaune paid to the leader of the settlement. Hu Tao, of all people, helped him to determine an amount that would make for fair compensation. He listened to her since the adventurers from Mondstadt possessed little clue of local prices, while Hu Tao assured Jaune that Zhongli's help would see Jaune passing over his entire share of the treasure chest they found. The consultant to the funeral parlor carried a notorious reputation for airheadedness regarding money, a piece of information that Jaune would have dearly loved to hear twenty-four hours earlier.

Despite everything, the number of dishes still grew to overwhelm their rickety table, and it turned into an impromptu feast once they offered much of the meal back to the villagers so as to not waste the effort and ingredients that went into it. That was the rationale Zhongli provided, anyway. In an oddly strategic move, the generous gesture snagged them the good stuff from the wine cellars—or the clay pots stacked in a storeroom, as it were.

"Psst, hey, what are you doing?" Hu Tao whispered to him partway through the dinner. Up close, the uniquely-shaped pupils of her eyes better resembled the plum flowers of which she seemed so fond than they do stars. They sparkled with mischief, for she had just now ducked her head under the table to catch his sleight of hands.

Osmanthus wine possessed a sweet floral taste, very refreshing and mellow. He had been siphoning some of it into empty flasks taken from his supplies, for Lisa to later try.

"Nothing to worry about," he answered, undeterred by her discovery. To his delight, she snuck a look at their surroundings, then passed her cup over. Hu Tao was joining in on his caper.

"Take this too, if you like. It's plum rice wine, tasty and highly recommended by yours truly."

The two of them snickered as more and more of the alcohol vanished from the table, to the point that it became noticeable and people assumed them a couple of lushes.

"Do at least try to maintain your dignity," said Zhongli in wry disapproval, a hand shielding his eyes from the absolutely deplorable state of today's youths.

Jaune was of the opinion that the guy prone to skipping out on bills had no room to talk. Birds of a feather, they all were.

"Lighten up, man. I imagine that they prefer us this way," he said, waving to indicate the boisterous scene around them.

Over at one table, children—and even some adults—cheered or clapped along as Fischl, aided by Oz, regaled them in a grandiose manner of today's battles. Mention of the hilichurl camp they took care of elevated the group to the status of heroes for the night. Bennett, stuck at the table behind Jaune, was practically force-fed with food that he had been too polite to turn down courtesy of a group of housewives, who commented on his need to eat more and the availability of their daughters. Said daughters surrounded him, flirting with the boy in somewhat futile fashion since most of it passed over his head. (Zhongli, arguably the more handsome of the two, attracted a different set of hangers-on in the form of old men engrossed in discussing the tea they drank with utmost seriousness.)

"Oh ya, dignity is a load of hot air," Hu Tao agreed, propping an elbow on Jaune's shoulder for balance as she leaned back on her chair to look past him at Zhongli. "My dearest employee, let loose a little~ You're going to make those young ladies sighing over you from a distance so disappointed if you don't notice them soon."

The girl said, while entirely missing the gaggle of boys over there trying to catch her attention. Jaune spared her a dry look while accepting a new plate of food, thanking the village girl who handed it to him.

"Well, the point's moot anyway, what with him dressing for a funeral," he said, and gestured at the suit that the other man wore, an understated affair in black betrayed upon closer study by intricate embroideries on luxurious silks. "Don't get me wrong, it's a good look. Just the wrong occasion, maybe. Doesn't it get stuffy in that?"

"A friend made this for me," Zhongli said with a calm and dismissive air, as if that excused everything. If there was a touch of defensiveness to his tone, he hid it well.

Hu Tao gasped, covering her mouth. "You have friends?"

"Interesting… Do they accept orders?" Jaune asked, more intrigued by the possibility of getting clothes for himself and certain other people. The suit really was a wonder the more he looked at it. Slits that appeared useless, until one sat down and the jacket conformed perfectly to the new position without a single crease. Fabric a subdued black, catching the light of the lanterns in such ways that it resembled the undulating scales of a snake or lizard. Jaune squinted to make out the embroideries on the suit's lapels, and if he wasn't mistaken then they depicted a continuous saga, scene to scene, though where it began and ended on the jacket he could not guess.

"I do, and no, not any longer," Zhongli answered them both, ending with a wistful sigh.

Jaune caught the meaning, and winced. "Oh. Sorry."

"Don't be. No life lasts forever. He would be flattered to know that you appreciate his work."

That didn't stop the mood from sobering up for the table and people nearby. The villagers sent Zhongli careful looks, unwilling to speak lest they offend. Jaune dithered in silence as he searched for a topic that would maneuver them down lighter avenues without seeming crude. It brought about an awkward lull in the festivities for everyone.

"Awww, turn those frowns upside down! Is that any way to think of the dead?"

Except for Hu Tao, that was. She pounded the table with her palms, affecting the bearing of one greatly aggrieved that she exaggerated for effect.

"Come on, let's enjoy ourselves. Jaune, tell us a story!" she demanded.

He looked at her. "Hah?"

"What do you mean, 'hah'?" she asked, mimicking his deadpan delivery. Still seated, she planted her hands on her hips. "It's not often that villages get a show with their dinner. Look at them." She jerked her head at Fischl and Bennett, the pair growing flustered as they noticed the sudden focus on them from this corner. "Our young'uns already did their part unlike you two old fogeys, are you going to let that lie?"

"Ye—"

Hu Tao cut him off. "No! So get to it, and participate! Celebrate! Inebriate!"

A few people cheered at that last one, raising their cups. Hu Tao grinned, and motioned to them as if to say 'See? I'm doing my part'.

The mood that barely had the chance to veer into a downward turn pivoted in a new direction, and Jaune had to crack a smile at that. A person who could not take things seriously might sometimes be what the world needed. It gave him the encouragement to join in.

"So, you want to hear a story? Alright, sure," he said, looking around to see nodding heads.

Wetting his lips with a cup of water, he shifted to sit straighter. His elbows went on the rickety table, and he lowered his voice.

"Then let me tell you a tale of hate."

A sudden hush fell over the listeners. Those that had been paying less than their full attention snapped around, eyes wide. Jaune noted Zhongli pausing in drinking his tea for a brief moment, before setting the cup down altogether. They hadn't anticipated this from Jaune and, instinctively, many leaned in to better hear him. Once he had their complete focus, he elaborated.

"Hate, for that is the beast I encountered." He scanned the audience, locking gaze with one face to the next. "You think hate is a scowl, a glare. You imagine it wielding fearsome weapons of steel and fire, raining death over the land. I know it as a more personal thing.

"A foul creature of the most bad-tempered disposition."

Murmurs passed among the listeners, each guessing at what he meant. Even now, they imagined dragons. Tentacles from the deep, or ravening wolves.

They understood nothing. Jaune continued. "Early in my travels, I chanced upon a cave amidst a pitted landscape, and I explored it thinking to seek riches. Gold, perhaps. Mystical artifacts and legendary arms, certainly. Instead, as I delved into the depths of the cave, I soon discovered the remains of those who came before me. I saw enough to bury the ground beneath my feet, a carpet made of bones picked clean. I never did find treasure. Hate cares not for such things."

He brushed a hand over his neck, on the side. Some nights, he woke up and remembered the feeling of sharp fangs on his jugular.

"Our clash began as it ambushed me. When the first strike failed to bring me low, it dashed into hiding—oh, but don't think it gone. No, it lurked in the places I could not see. It watched my every move. The beast sought more than wanton violence, it was clever and knew of joy, of having me scared and helpless as I experienced the utter certainty that death comes for me. I had stepped into its hunting grounds, and I wasn't getting out. From the moment it met me, it dreamed of seizing my throat and tearing it away with its bare teeth. That is hate. That is malice."

Children moved closer to their friends or parents. Bennett clenched one hand into a fist, the boy looking ready to charge into the past and fight back the big, bad monster to save Jaune.

A villager pushed his way forward.

"What manner of beast is this, sir?" he asked, a young man quaking in his boots from anxious nerves, whose eyes yet conveyed a dream of his own adventures. Innocent eyes that have not seen the peak of the mountain.

"Its fur was as white as snow, or should I say, as white as the bones among which it lay in wait. The eyes, you should have seen the eyes, red as blood… I suspect that is its favorite color. It had ears yay long." He mimed with his hands, placing them atop his head. In the seat beside him, Hu Tao slowly tilted her head. "And nasty, big, pointy teeth, like this." He demonstrated.

"How tough was the skin? How big was it?" Bennett questioned with a frown. "Your sword's wicked sharp, so I can't imagine it not cutting the beast in half."

With the questions rolling in, Jaune shifted the way he told the story to turn it into a dialogue. "Small does not mean weak. I could have held it with my hands put together." He showed them, ignoring the way Hu Tao made a small noise in the back of her throat. "Quite impossible to hit at the speed it was going. It hopped and hopped and hopped, and all I could do was swing blindly in hope of a lucky blow."

"And you beat it?" said a villager, the girl that had served him food and drinks, as she hung on to his every word. "How?"

He looked at her. "I've learned to fight all manners of beasts, so I did what my teachers taught me. I ceased my futile flailing, and thought. Thought long, and thought hard." He tapped the side of his head. "What were its weaknesses? The large ears suggested an acute sense of hearing, perhaps I could deafen it with a loud noise? The tail, a short and stubby tuft of fur on a short and stubby body, might it provide a spot for me to grab where the beast cannot bite me?"

Hu Tao's face grew brighter with each detail, until her mouth hung wide open and she trembled with suppressed emotion.

"In the end, the plan I arrived at was to put myself on the line. It sought to get a taste of my flesh, and I shall allow it, thereby becoming the bait to a trap of my own devise. I stood in the open, and in order to draw the clever beast in, I threw away my sword."

Gasps, whispers. They couldn't believe it, and Jaune heard calls of "Idiot!" and "How brave!" in equal measure for the risk he chose to take.

"My heart was pounding in my chest," Jaune said solemnly, placing a hand over that same heart, "as I stood awaiting death. Closer and closer it came, sure of its victory. It bared its teeth in thirst, eager for my blood. With a final leap, it sprang for my throat… just as I brilliantly deduced. I reached out with my hand and CHOMP!" Those listening jerked back at the sudden noise. "I sacrificed to it my fingers. Oh, how it hurt. The pain was beyond what you can picture. Yet, at that moment I smiled." And tonight, he chuckled at the memory. "I had won. With my fingers hooked behind the teeth, the beast could not run. Lacking leverage, it could not hop out of harm's way. The battle between us then and there, with me the victor."

"And thus clear-headed thinking triumphed over blind hate," Zhongli observed, nodding at the satisfying moral to the tale.

Jaune answered simply, "Yes, it has."

"Tell us what it is, Jaune."

The commanding tone caused people to turn toward Hu Tao. Her hands were squishing her cheeks, which had grown completely red.

The corner of his lips twitched, but he fought down the impulse and replied in a neutral manner. "Hm?"

"The beast. What is it called?"

He shared a conspiratory look with her. The girl knew.

"Some refer to it by the legend left in its wake. The Beast of Caerbannog, named for the bone-strewn cave where hundreds of warriors had fallen. However…"

He stopped there. His shaking hands reached for a cup of water, holding it as if it held his salvation. He allowed the moment to drag on, milking it.

"However, you may know of it better as a bunny."

For a bit, the audience reacted with appreciation. Ohhhh, that was what it was. Of course.

Then, what he said fully hit them.

A child, not even ten years of age, summed it up best. "…Excuse me?"

At this point, Hu Tao dropped out of her seat with how hard she was laughing. Meanwhile, Jaune sat back, basking at the utterly flummoxed looks of the villagers, along with that of Bennett and Fischl.

"A bunny?" Bennett asked, his voice cracking partway through.

He nodded, and showed his hand. "And I have the scars to prove it. My fingers still hurt on rainy afternoons."

"I don't see anything," someone said.

"The scars are on my soul," he amended. "No, really, I can't see a rabbit nowadays without wanting to cook it in a pot."

Hu Tao climbed off the ground, using the table to pull herself up while wiping the tears from her eyes. "Ahhh, I knew I wasn't wrong about you, Jaune. You understand my dark, silly heart." She flashed a haughty, challenging look at the person on Jaune's other side. "Your turn, Zhongli. Top that if you can, oh famed storyteller."

Jaune now noticed the other man's change in mood, the way Zhongli looked at him with a tired gaze, fingers rapping on the table in an about-face from his earlier contented demeanor. He offered a sheepish grin, a gesture returned with stern rebuke.

"A joke," said Zhongli, never so uncouth as to spit out the words. "A fair attempt at fable, with a moral lesson, only to end with a punchline. With humor, the lowest form of theater. The Heyu Tea House would burn if such a story was performed there."

That had to be the most scathing thing he had heard from the man in their brief acquaintance.

Jaune raised a finger in objection. "It's… actually the truth, as unbelievable as it might sound."

With a click of his tongue, Zhongli slid his chair back a little and crossed one leg over the other. He tugged on his jacket lapels to straighten his suit, which seemed more habit than necessity considering the already crisp appearance of the outfit.

"Your story, while entertaining in some ways, lacks polish. Storytellers must take into account their audiences, and tailor to suit the occasion," Zhongli critiqued. "As the Director requested, I shall recount one to match yours, and it would even draw a connection with what we have discussed earlier, however tenuous. A tertiary concern, yet continuity matters in regards to a feast. Its components should form a whole.

"Last night, I spoke to you of the yakshas of yore. Let us add to this tale."

Zhongli cleared his throat, and raised his cup to his lips to take a sip of tea. The cup returned to the table.

"What knowledge of the yakshas that survives into our current era is scarce, indeed. They are remembered most for their violent temperament. Yet, that reflects just one side of the story. Their daily lives amounted to more than ceaseless war, and it is said that each yaksha had their passion.

"For Menogias, it was clothes-making."

As emphasis, the man flicked imaginary dust off the cuff of his suit. Jaune noted the difference among the villagers between the last story and this one. His had best drawn in the young, the adventurous. Zhongli captured everyone's interest.

He told the right story, perhaps. Liyue was the land the yakshas fought for. Faded legends they might be, something within the people's hearts retained the memory. What was the life of Jaune Arc compared to that?

"He loved it so, and for years Menogias honed his craft amidst the mountaintops, seeking inspiration in the formless clouds above and the coursing rivers below. His works grew into the envy of mortals, adepti, and even demons alike. In fact, the clothes he wove would likely be lauded as the height of fashion today."

A slight exaggeration, Jaune had no doubt. Fashion lived in cycles, but old was old.

"Now, let it be known that the clothes Menogias created are not always without flaws, and none knew this better than Bonanus. For you see, he doted on her like he did no other." Zhongli gave a small smile. "Rex Lapis himself had to wait while the yaksha sewed a dress for his sister in all but blood."

A gasp followed that claim, shocked and offended. Zhongli accepted the reaction with aplomb. Would it count as blasphemy to suggest that one's god stood in line to pick up his order at the tailor shop, like everybody else?

"A prized status Bonanus held, though she might disagree had anyone asked. The wild ideas that gripped her self-proclaimed older brother from time to time caused her much suffering. For example, on a day in spring, Menogias found inspiration in a waterfall and from it he gifted Bonanus with a dress. So flowing and layered was it that in the next battle it caught on her movements, leading Bonanus to roll herself into a ball, flailing as the demons she was pursuing escaped into the forest.

"Her tantrum thrown that day shook the mountain that they call home. The other yakshas fled to the valleys, and slept in the open that night for fear of a landslide."

As Jaune listened, he asked himself one question. Was Bonanus blonde, by any chance? Because this sounded like something he'd see in his house. Being the only boy, he got a lucky break, but the subject of hand-me-down dresses was serious business and had resulted in a fight on more than one occasion. (And one time, him in the dress that his sisters were fighting over.)

"It is a testament to their bond that after Bonanus expressed her grievances of the dress, Menogias took no offense. Rather, he immediately set to weaving his next project, now taking into account her opinion instead of only his own. Nothing that would hinder her movements. No more fabric than is necessary. It must be a dress for battle, it must be short.

"Menogias heeded the request to the letter. Short, Bonanus said. Short it shall be. So short was the dress in the next battle, that it rendered the demons spellbound with her mere appearance… Unfortunately, the windy day ensured that the mighty Bonanus could not move for fear of a stray breeze.

"And that was how a dress did what no demons could, and defeated a yaksha."

Zhongli finished his tale to a scandalized audience. Though, look closely and one would notice that he also garnered many eager ears. The man ignored it all to drink his tea. He then glanced at Jaune, meeting a tepid gaze.

"After all that, you ended it with a punchline?" Jaune asked.

"It's actually the truth, as unbelievable as it might sound," was Zhongli's blithe reply, mirroring Jaune's own words. His calm delivery carried a hint of a smile.

"Uh-huh, color me skeptical," Jaune said in good humor. "I have to admit, though… it is different from the impression I got when I first heard about the warlike yaksha."

Zhongli shrugged. "Rather than warlike, I believe the truth is that they lived lives full of emotions, whether that be anger or love or embarrassment on a particular day. They knew what their duty entailed, and so gave their all in each moment."

Jaune thought about it for a bit. "That's not so different from some people I can name."

He decided that he truly did like these yakshas.

The brief lull that followed the statement was broken when Hu Tao clapped her hands together.

"A fine entry by Liyue Harbor's Zhongli, to be expected of someone I hire." She stuck out her tongue as Zhongli turned toward her with a blank look. "Okay, next up… Bennett!"

The boy jolted at the mention of his name, mouth bulging with food that he had to swallow down in a hurry.

"Me?"

Hu Tao just nodded without saying anything, an evil smile stretching wide on her face.

Bennett fidgeted in place, uncomfortable with the attention turned his way. A hand went up to rub the back of his head. "A story? Uh, does one of my adventures work? Because I have a pretty good one—"

"Bennett," Fischl suddenly called out.

"Hang on, Fischl, I'm getting to it."

Fischl shook her head, blonde hair swishing. "No, Bennett—You're not choking."

The girl pointed, and Jaune realized what she meant as he followed the hand to the empty bowl in front of Bennett.

"He's not choking," Jaune echoed.

The confused villagers broke into whispers, wondering what they were talking about, but Bennett simply looked down at the rice bowl, blinking.

"I...ate it all? And I'm fine…?" he mumbled in a stupor.

"The laws that bind the firmament of this world have been broken. The sky is falling!" Fischl bemoaned, holding Oz for comfort.

Jaune wouldn't go quite that far, but it was an uncharacteristic stroke of good luck for the other boy. He cast his mind back to the day, recalling all the accidents that didn't happen to the hapless Bennett, unlike yesterday afternoon. The other boy walked without crashing into things. He failed to perform a clumsy tumble down a hill that would alert the hilichurls of the party. Hours gone since they arrived at the village, and he had yet to slip in the river even once.

Bennett must have taken the same trip down memory lane, because with a shout he pumped both fists in the air.

"I've never been this lucky before!"

Whoof. Wasn't that just sad. The boy was experiencing what others would call a normal life, and he deemed it a miracle.

Jaune shoved that morbid thought out of his mind, along with the creeping dread that the cause of Bennett's misfortune might have shifted over to him. This was a time to celebrate, and he got up to walk over to Bennett.

"Welp, now that I'm reasonably certain it won't kill you…" He summoned a bottle to hand, one made of glass so clear that it drew amazement from those around him. "You deserve a drink."

He poured the Spirytus into a cup for Bennett, then one for himself. He raised the cup high in a toast, a gesture returned by many.

They downed their drinks.

Bennett immediately started coughing up his lungs.

"Oops. I guess some things are beyond luck. Sorry, Bennett."


-o-​


Come nightfall, a new sound interrupted the peace of the village. It almost went unheard amidst the hubbub of conversations. Jaune craned his ears, and caught it in full the second time.

It was a cry for help, pitched with a forlorn plaintiveness.

The villagers surprised him. For as kind as they have been to him, they chose to go back to their homes upon hearing the plea rather than lend aid. He saw door after door shutting, the people holding their hands over their ears.

"What are they doing?" he asked nobody in particular, pausing at the fence dividing the village from the forest. Old Fong Sai, the retired adventurer, met Jaune's gaze from his place on the bridge which spans the stream. The man only gave him a weary nod, before turning away.

"Boss! Let's go!" Bennett called over his shoulder. He and Fischl have crossed into the thickets ahead of him.

"...Right." Jaune pushed the villagers' odd behavior out of mind to focus on what was important. Somewhere in the darkness, a person had encountered trouble.

The forest next to the village ran long, and uphill toward the mountain ranges. Its trees bore golden leaves where the bamboo had not overgrown, the latter forming thick groves that broke the forest into a dozen twisting paths. Bushes rustled as animals rushed away from the loud humans barreling through their habitat.

He quickly overtook the others, with them falling in to follow him. The voice that requested help had been joined by more like it, a chorus of weak and hopeless prayers. He used their constant droning to get his bearing, adjusting course when needed.

And then he heard the voices come from behind him instead of in front.

Skidding to a stop, Jaune scanned the woods with a careful eye. The scant light from the moon above, half-obscured by clouds, allowed a measure of visibility. The pair of young adventurers looped around a bamboo grove to join him. They, too, startled at the new direction of the cry for help.

"Have my ears deceived me?" Fischl asked, spinning round and round to look for a hint of people in their vicinity. Her familiar, Oz, shot off into the night in order to extend the search, while Bennett took up position back to back with the girl to cover one another. "No, my senses remain my own. I hear them, it is no fevered dream—Jaune, have you ever encountered this before?"

"Disembodied voices? Oh yeah, that's never good." Thankfully, he had a solution for that. [Blank], on~.

…Nevermind, that didn't work.

"I see something!" Bennett shouted, and they whirled toward him. He had a sword in one hand, the other pointing.

The place he indicated shone with a faded, milky light of no determinable source. Over time, it emerged more and more from among the bamboo trees, shifting and undulating to create shapes that weren't quite there. Jaune studied it closely, striving to make out a pattern. Suddenly, he found it as the formless mass grew clearer.

Two pitted holes and a gaping maw turned his blood to ice.

"Ahhh!"

"G-Ghosts!"

Bennett and Fischl screamed, hugging each other. Jaune took two big strides to stand in front of them, which caused the ghostly entity to shift its focus to him.

He shivered at the sight of the disturbing pseudo-face. Things like this were why he preferred the comfort of a nice, big wall whenever he slept. Who could ever guess what lurked in the darkness.

But tonight, that wasn't going to be a problem…

His hand mimed a sword grip, and one appeared in it an instant later. He twirled the weapon once, ending with the tip leveled at the entity. The string tied to the hilt swished back and forth, the paper talisman connected to it catching the moonlight. A deft motion with his free hand pasted a disposable version of the seal onto the steel blade.

…because Jaune and his spirit-slaying blade would save the day!

Pak!

Hu Tao chopped down on his wrist with a dainty hand shaped like a knife, making him pause before he could charge at the ghost. When that didn't lead to his sword slipping out of his grasp, the girl pouted at him as if it was his fault and not due to her noodly arms.

"Hu Tao," he muttered, gaze returning to the entity. "Not the time right now."

Unfazed, the girl poked experimentally at the paper seal adhering to his sword, then scratched at it with a black-painted nail. She bent her knees to put herself level with the talisman attached to the hilt, observing it with a critical eye.

Afterward, Jaune heard her sigh.

"Ai-yai-yai, such violent intent these fellows hold. I ought to meet the person that made them and give them a piece of my mind," Hu Tao complained.

He was more concerned with the things going on behind her. The formless entity had drifted closer, and it brought along friends. He tried to raise his sword, which earned him an annoyed look from Hu Tao.

"Stop that!" she demanded.

"You stop that!" he retorted.

Hu Tao stomped her foot. "Ugh, you are just the rudest house guest, aren't you? You're embarrassing us!"

"Miss Hu Tao," Bennett piped up behind Jaune, voice trembling. "What do mean by that? We're in the woods andtheghostsarealmostonyouahhhh—!"

And the boy was doing so well for a while there.

He would have attempted to crush the pseudo-limb grabbing onto Hu Tao's shoulder if she hadn't gotten there first. The girl gently laid her hand atop the misty substance, and Jaune's eyes widened as it sharpened into clarity as another hand. He followed it up along an arm and behind Hu Tao to see… people.

A young woman and a young man, and a little girl clinging onto their legs. Half there and half not.

"...Help us…Help…"

"Mommy…"

Hu Tao looked at the expression on his face, at the figures reflected in his eyes. She reached up, and patted his cheek.

"We didn't think to ask and they didn't want to tell the story… Why was there a new village?"

Because the old village was gone. As the clouds peeled back, the light of the moon illuminated the immediate area to let Jaune view in full the details around him.

The pile of rocks that was a well. Shattered fragments of clay pots. Paths reclaimed over the decades by the fast-growing bamboo, until almost nothing remained. His boot scuffed against the ground, and beneath a layer of dirt his heel encountered a wooden floor.

He picked out traces of homes. The corner of a house here, the remnants of a doorway there. Some spots showed signs of deliberate removal, the material extracted to be used again. Most were buried under the earth, covered by grass and flowers with the passing time. The worst of the damage seemed to have been suffered by the area that rested further up the slope. A landslide had taken the village, long ago.

Hu Tao's face scrunched in displeasure. "I'll need to have a talk with the census bureau once we're back in Liyue Harbor. It's their job to notify the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor whenever something like this happens."

She continued to grumble complaints but he didn't quite catch those, still transfixed by the family crying and beseeching for him to help them.

He worked his jaw, and after a while, managed to speak. "What do we do now?"

A rhetorical question, since he had a solution but simply wanted to avoid the idea. Killing a ghost sounded easy until he put faces to them.

In answer, Hu Tao pulled out incense sticks from who knew where, and winked at him.

"What else? I'm always prepared for a funeral ☆"


-o-​


Flowers, she had said. Flowers, he would get.

Jaune weaved his glider between the steep peaks that jutted like pillars out of the ground. The shape of the mountains here created an interesting effect on the wind, producing strong gusts that twisted and turned in unpredictable ways. Conditions which made for good flight training, not that he had the time for it.

A second pass around the area, and he spotted what he was looking for on the sheer cliffside. Upon an outcropping that measured no more than a couple of inches grew a singular green stem, from which multiple flower bulbs bloomed, tipped downward with their soft, purple petals seeming to glow under the moonlight. He angled the glider to cut back toward the location, slowing his momentum with careful blasts of the rockets on his boots.

Clinging to the side of the mountain, he cut the stem with a small knife. The knife went inside his Pocket afterward. The flower he held on for a short while longer, turning it this way and that as he enjoyed its scent.

Violetgrass…

They resembled the bluebell flowers that grew near his home, and which often carpeted the forest floor when in season. A shade darker, perhaps, but carrying the same fragrance that he hadn't known he missed until now.

Its item entry in the inventory list cited uses in cooking and, more notably, medicinal concoctions, spurring him to linger in the area to collect additional specimens for Escha. Whether the solitary nature of the plant would hinder proper cultivation, he would leave for their little gardener to figure out.

Once he had his fill of reminiscing, the flower vanished into thin air, as if it were never there.

"Okay, two more," he decided, pushing off from the rocks.

Eventually, he descended from the mountains with his bounty. Locating the right spot required a few tries, but soon he was walking along the path leading back to the meeting point, just outside the destroyed village. The stone steps here would take him up to a shrine built of wood and smooth rocks.

Signs of the others' efforts dotted the path. The foliage had been trimmed, the steps swept cleaner. Someone had stuck paper talismans of a different design than those he owned to the trees. Their presence asserted a sort of order to the wild forest—a boundary to denote a purpose to this place.

He found Hu Tao partway to the shrine, sitting alone on a boulder.

The girl barely acknowledged him, absorbed in turning her hand, again and again, to watch the Aura gleaming on her skin. Hers was a dark red, so dark that it almost became black to blend with her clothes. It reminded Jaune of the color of blood.

"Oh, you're back," she said after a bit. "I was… It's strange, don't you think? To see one's life."

"I don't usually hear it put like that," he replied, walking closer to stand at the foot of the boulder.

"The soul is the person, the body a vessel," Hu Tao explained. "Each has its proper place, and together it means we are alive. So, am I here or am I inside? Is it still a part of me, I wonder, or am I dead even while living?"

Jaune shivered, because the wind was cold and nothing else.

"Hee-hee. Sorry to have made you uncomfortable. I'll stop, I'll stop." Hu Tao stood up, and brushed down her clothes. A jump took her from the boulder to beside him, and a bright smile dispelled the previous atmosphere.

"Can I interest you in some specially-made talismans? I assure you that they would be much cozier than the ones you currently have on your sword."

Jaune chuckled at the sudden sales pitch. "I'm not really looking for 'cozy', but hey, if you can show me that they work…"

"I'll ask again some other time, then. Did you pick up the flowers?"

He summoned the bundle of Violetgrass as an answer, and Hu Tao's smile turned decidedly softer.

"Good. Come on, we shouldn't keep our clients waiting."

The two of them made their way up to the shrine. Zhongli was already there, standing with his hands clasped behind his back. Most would think the man out on a stroll given his casual air.

"An inauspicious day for a ceremony, Director," he said once they drew near. "The moon is partially obscured, and there are only strangers in attendance."

Hu Tao nodded, accepting the counsel. "I'm sure that they can forgive us for the lapse. We will just have to do our best."

Soon after, the final members of the party returned from their assigned tasks. It was time for a funeral.

As far as it went, the ceremony did not last long. At least, compared to Jaune's experiences. He lacked the understanding for much of it, and on the whole stayed kneeling along with Fischl and Bennet while Hu Tao burned incense three times, and recited a long poem, or what to him sounded like a poem. The trio took their cue from Zhongli on when to bow their heads, and to light colorful papers that caught fire fast and drifted up with the smoke.

Near the end, Hu Tao turned to them. Her demeanor was one that had bothered Jaune throughout the ceremony, so far was it from her usual mischief. She bowed to them, and he and the others hastily returned the gesture. One by one, they were requested to place offerings on the altar, composed of food from the disrupted dinner that was retrieved from the village down by the stream.

About this step, the pair from the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor had been singularly vague, leaving the selection of offerings up to each person. So when his turn came, Jaune presented what he chose with some trepidation. A bowl of rice, and a dish filled with osmanthus wine.

Here, as home, settlements took life into their own hands. Any number of calamities might strike, the chances rising higher the further out they went. Help was promised, yes, but the cities were far. Rice, wheat—the grains mattered. It was food, and another day, at the most basic level.

That, and a toast of wine in remembrance of the years this village stood… He hadn't spoken a word this whole time, and hoped this would at least convey to that family his thoughts.

He wouldn't know. They never showed themselves beyond their first appearance.

Hu Tao clapped twice, and pushed upright.

"Thank you, everyone, for your presence today," she said, with an air of finality.

The abrupt end threw Jaune for a loop. "It's over? So did it work, were the ghosts able to move on?"

A long moment ensued in which Hu Tao simply stared at him, still with that soft, sad look. The flower-shaped pupils of her eyes reflected the flickering incense flames. They rooted him in place, and in the back of his mind, unbidden questions arose that he never thought to mull on before now. What laid at the end. Where did souls go. Who will be there at his funeral.

Then, it was as if a flip switch, and Hu Tao broke out in a big smile.

"Who knows? Don't ask me, I just conduct funerals—Ooh!" She dropped a fist into an open palm. "There's time if you want to pick off the best bits of the offerings before the spooky spirits eat it all. Better hurry!"

Seriously, why did he even let her get to him in the first place?

His face met his hand. "Really don't know what I expected... And Hu Tao, no. Please, no. Show some respect."

"Pssh, whoever those lingering spirits were spent years surrounded by doom and gloom. They have to be bored of it at this point. Come on, I'll show you a traditional funerary dance, and you can help cheer them up. If they're around, that is."

The funeral director that probably shouldn't have her job glomped onto an easy target, Fischl, and pulled her to her feet. The sudden action flustered the younger girl but she went along, unwilling to dampen Hu Tao's good cheer. Bennett, with Oz on his head, soon became her second victim, with Hu Tao then using their numbers to apply pressure on Jaune to join in.

Her antics got a laugh out of him. It was said the happiest were destined for the frontier. Born to it, like none other. Hu Tao would have fit right in with home. His somber mood fell away, and after rolling his eyes and showing an appropriate amount of reluctance, he walked over to the group, hooking an arm around Zhongli to drag him along before he could escape.

"How traditional is this dance?"

"Three months! I made it up!"
