#5,111
Chapter 64: Down Where It's Wetter (Pt. 1)​


Bennett and Fischl stood at the top of the road leading down to the Yaoguang Shoal, and together they cheered.

"It's the seeea!"

Jaune left them to enjoy the moment, strolling past the pair with his hands laced behind his head, his Gallian-blue jacket rolled up to the elbows. He breathed in a lungful of the fresh ocean air, and basked in the bright sunshine. Good or bad, it always came back to the sea with him.

The Yaoguang Shoal consisted of a long, long stretch of sand filled with shallow ponds left by the tide, situated between the cliffs of the higher plateau and the open ocean. Some pools of water measured no deeper than a person's ankle, others essentially created islands cut off from the main landmass. He hadn't ever seen anything like this before, and it seemed to him a charming destination for a vacation.

In normal circumstances, that was. He frowned slightly upon spotting an area up ahead that did not appear so picturesque. At the end of the road, there should have been a simple fishing village to greet a traveler. A place where someone could rest for the night following a day of frolicking at the seashore. What laid before his eyes was a mire, a bog made brown and rough from the churned up ground, blemished by the many detritus left from the buildings that once stood here. The area saw a lot of activity today with guards dispatched from Liyue Harbor working alongside the villagers to reclaim the land.

"You know, I heard that the people here made out just fine, but I didn't expect that they'd be this energetic," he remarked.

"Their village was due for relocation, anyhow," Hu Tao said, skipping to his side and slowing down to match his pace. "On my last visit, I kept getting stories about how the foundations were slipping more and more each month, to the point that shoring them up became the local pastime. Everyone saw what was coming."

A silver lining, that. From how the Guild put it, the collapse of the village took hours, spanning from near midnight to the early morning. A slow, inexorable process giving ample warning to even the deepest sleeper, rather than a sudden calamity to swallow everything at once. The people escaped with minor injuries, along with most of their stuff. Pangs of sorrow over the loss of their homes and the memories made inside were mitigated to an extent by the knowledge that they remained alive to feel it (and, on a sorely-needed positive note after that, to begin again). Mother nature could be a wicked witch sometimes, but on this occasion she wasn't out-and-out villainous about it. Life went on.

"The funding from the city helps," Zhongli added, from his place a few paces back. "Say what you will of Ningguang and her policies, she has changed the way of Liyue."

Hu Tao stuck out her tongue. "Pffft. Ningguang is terrible. She refused my proposal for the Lantern Rite Festival three years in a row now!"

"I am sure that 'more fire' will find a receptive audience at some point," Zhongli said, indulgently.

The girl accepted the show of support without thinking deeply of it, and once she found another interesting object to occupy her time, began to skip ahead down the road while humming a merry tune. Bennett and Fischl blurred by Jaune a little later, racing after her.

Meanwhile, Zhongli drew level with him. "Well then, shall we go?"

Jaune looked up at the bright blue sky.

"Sure, let's see what today has in store for us."


-o-​


Not long after, the party entered the former fishing village and set to work. A quick glance affirmed that others had the reclamation effort well in hand, and it was not Jaune's purpose here in any case, so he asked around and a guard pointed him toward an overlook where the adventurers dispatched by the Guild based their camp. With a few days headstart over him, they would hopefully possess a wealth of information on the situation to save him time.

"Rex Lapis, deliver us from that girl…"

Those words, said in a less than discrete fashion, were the first indication for Jaune that the meeting might not go as he imagined. Hu Tao seemed to be acquainted with the speaker, because she perked right up on catching sight of them.

"Yingzhu!" Hu Tao called out, rushing up the slope to enter the camp. The place consisted of simple tents pitched around a table where the adventurers could conduct their investigative work. Three people occupied the area, and they gathered in the presence of visitors. They shared a common theme, hardy clothes in predominantly green, almost like a uniform. "Where have you been, I haven't talked to you in ages!"

The person she addressed, a woman a few years older than Jaune, returned the chirpy greeting with a tight smile. "It really is odd, isn't it, Hu Tao? I wonder why."

Her eyes scanned over their group. Aside from lingering on Zhongli, this Yingzhu regarded the rest of them with a cool air. Most of her emotions were reserved for a particular girl.

"You know her, Miss Hu Tao?" asked Bennett.

"Aw, me and everybody at the Guild go way back," Hu Tao said. Skipping up to the adventurers, she spun around to face Jaune and the others, and flourished both her hands. "Ta-da~ let me introduce you to Yingzhu, Linyang, and Honglang. They're some of the Guild's most reliable members, and they've even taken a few jobs from me over the years."

Past her shoulder, Jaune watched the uncomfortable fidgeting among the adventurers, and the scowl that passed by on Yingzhu's countenance. Whatever friendship Hu Tao thought existed between them appeared a one-sided sentiment.

Stray musings of how many coffins Hu Tao had made for this group of people to sour them on her did cross his mind, but he found that he wasn't in quite the right mood to find it funny. Odd was different from unpleasant, though perhaps that was his bias talking.

Yingzhu scoffed, and rolled her eyes. "Yeah, that's us. Now would you mind telling me what you're doing here? There aren't any bodies for you to bury. We already checked."

"Hey!" Hu Tao giggled, a hand raised to cover her mouth. "Don't say it like I'm a workaholic. I take time off, I do!"

The other woman's scowl deepened.

"Look…"

That tone rang in Jaune's ear, loud and clear. He had been on the receiving end of it from Lisa, from his mother, from various sisters, from Glynda Goodwitch, from… a lot of people. It never spelled anything good. To head off the imminent outburst, he cut into the conversation.

"Hu Tao, you're familiar with the locals, right?" he asked, and received an innocent nod from the girl.

"I drop by to play on the Yaoguang Shoal, sometimes," she explained. "You should see it at night, it's pretty. And of course, as a rare source of gossip on the happenings around Liyue Harbor, I tend to get invited over for tea while I'm in town. I have a few clients out this way, too—three coffins sold in the last year alone," Hu Tao said with a fair amount of pride.

"...Neat." It had been so nice and wholesome until that last part. "Then, how about you go talk to them for me? Just to ask if they noticed any odd details the night of the collapse, and look for things that seem unimportant they may not have thought to mention. I'll have a chat with these guys, and compare it with what you find out later. You can catch up with them afterward. What do you think?"

Hu Tao mulled on the suggestion, tapping her chin. "We~ell, I do want to check on a couple acquaintances of mine that haven't sent me letters yet. It wouldn't be a bother, would it?" she asked to make sure.

It was Fischl who answered. "Worry not, my dear. For I, Fischl, the Monstadt Guild's top investigator, shall be present in your stead to shed light upon this mystery."

"Up-and-coming, Mein Fräulein," Oz reminded. "Katheryne spoke no more than that."

Ignoring her familiar with steadfast resolve, Fischl finished her declaration by striking a pose with a hand over her eyepatch, the other pointing forward and slightly up. One of the adventurers from the Liyue branch, the sole man of the group, followed her hand to stare out to the empty sea, lost on what was happening. It got a laugh from Hu Tao.

"In that case, I'll leave things in our detective's capable hands. Be back soon!"

With that, the young woman headed down from the overlook. In her wake, Jaune heard a collective sigh from Liyue's adventuring team that raised his hackles.

"Thank you ever so much for getting rid of that weirdo," Yingzhu said once Hu Tao was out of earshot.

He held back the retort on his tongue; this was a time to play nice.

"Whatever," he said curtly.

"Let us not tarry," Fischl advised, taking the lead. "The good mistress of the harbor chapter proclaimed thou the vanguard of this crusade. Sing now to us, that we may herald an end to the malediction."

A cold wind blew through the area.

"Uhhh… What did you just say?" asked the male adventurer, whose name had already slipped Jaune's mind.

"The head of the Liyue branch, Lan," said Oz, the raven taking the confusion in stride, "has sent us to assist in determining a cause for the incident so please share your findings, is what she means."

Yingzhu grumbled, "You could have just led with that."

"Do forgive my ways," Fischl said. "As royalty, one must adhere to proper grace. Mind it not and carry on, as I shall endeavor to provide clarity."

The faces of the people looking at her suggested that she could stand to endeavor a little harder. Nevertheless, the Liyue adventurers pressed on, motioning for Jaune and the others to gather around the nearby table on which they had collated the maps and sheets of notes that was their work for the past few days.

The bulk of their investigation focused on the vicinity of the fishing village, moving outward since yesterday. At least one of them could draw, the provided sketches relaying a simple story. As far as the adventuring team could tell, a good chunk of the land had been pulled below the sea not by tide or by sand erosion, but more along the line of a sinkhole with the ground beneath the land having turned hollow over the course of an as yet unknown time frame. Crumbling sand and a high tide in the aftermath rendered the area a treacherous pit where one might slip past their neck into the earth. Signs pointed to the sinkhole following a diagonal direction, leading out to the ocean.

"A detail most curious, and enlightening," Fischl said once the Liyue adventurers explained their proof for that conclusion. She paced back and forth, hand holding her chin. "A subtle hand hides where none may tread, weaving its machinations with an industry that Snezhnaya itself can scarcely match."

"Mein Fräulein means to say…" Oz began to explain.

"That it happened under the bedrocks?" Jaune chipped in, a picture forming now that someone had guided him partway there. He leaned on the edge of the table, his back to it. "The underground space runs on an angle, meaning the shallows just outside the village wouldn't have held if the hole was too close to the sand layer up top. Whatever that triggered the collapse was being oddly professional about it."

He shared a look with the others in his party, a sense of anticipation fluttering in his chest. By now, he had brought them all onto the same page that he was looking for a yaksha. Fischl's observations strengthened the chance of his target being the one responsible for the incident, rather than a simple issue of nature taking its course. It narrowed the search down to a very small section of the coast, if the theory panned out.

Fischl gave him a big smile. "Verily, thou grasped the heart of the matter. Of course, one mystery gives rise to the next, and the question must still burn within thine mind: wherefore dost our journey proceed from here?"

"Basically, yeah," Jaune said, nodding. "Whatever did this is out on the water. Could be right by us, could be half an ocean away." And as much as the pirate's life appealed to him, he was working on a timetable.

Fischl's smile changed to (a fair attempt at) a confident smirk. "Hmph!" The girl flipped her hair dramatically. " Be assured that I, the Prinzessin der Verurteilung, have ruminated of the myriad pathways on the tapestry of fate, and—"

"Excuse me," a voice interrupted Fischl, and Jaune twisted in place to see Yingzhu on the other side of the table with a hand raised, on her face a frown. She made sure that she had Fischl's attention before taking a deep breath. Her other hand came up to pinch the bridge of her nose. "Sorry to cut you off when you're making good points, but… it'd really help if you would speak normally."

That took Fischl aback.

"Huh? I mean—Pardon?"

Yingzhu waved over her shoulder at the palace floating in the sky that was little beyond a dot at this distance. "It's just, I've met Ningguang. Real hoity-toity people don't act like you do, and it only makes you sound like you're not taking this with any seriousness."

Fischl flushed red. "N-No, that's not true!"

"See, now that's normal." The woman pointed with a finger, brightening up. "It's easy to understand and we don't waste time waiting for the bird or him to translate." The finger diverted to Jaune. "Stick to that, alright? You can play later."

Jaune opened his mouth but Bennett got there first, moving to stand by Fischl.

"You've got it wrong, miss," the younger boy said. "She isn't joking around."

The male adventurer butted in. "Kid, you can't tell me that's how she talks. It isn't how anybody talks."

"It is, if you came from the Immernachtreich," Bennett insisted, his usual carefree air giving way to a hard stare.

"The what?"

"Forget it, Honglang, they're from Mondstadt," Yingzhu said, growing from annoyed to full-blown irate as she snapped her gaze from Fischl to Bennett to Jaune, a realization dawning in her eyes. "I should have known that it wasn't Lan's idea to send a second team."

Bennett piped up, "What's that supposed to mean?"

"That there's a pattern. The nonsense that comes from that city is mindboggling."

The last of the Liyue adventurers, content to have taken a backseat to the discussion, tapped Yingzhu on the shoulder and said quietly, "Yingzhu, maybe just let it go? I get it, but you're arguing with kids."

"They—"

A piercing whistle rang out, bringing the incessant sniping to a halt. Jaune held the note for a little longer, to ensure nobody would immediately try to start up the arguments again.

"Bennett and Fischl are adventurers," he corrected that last point. He turned to lean over the table, planting his hands on its surface while looking from face to face. When Yingzhu went to reply, he glared at her and curled one hand into a fist. It drew a clear line as to which side of the dispute he stood on.

He probably should be the one making peace here, but eh, screw it.

Fischl had a way of speaking that was sometimes difficult to parse, he'd admit to the truth of that. Except, he could still understand her. The general thrust, at least. This feat demanded no great intellect or skill.

The one requirement was that a person gave an honest attempt at listening when she spoke. Listening, instead of using the time to formulate a response.

"We have too many people," he said. "None of us are getting time to think. Bennett?"

Bennett pointed at himself. "Me?"

"Yes, you. The guards down there are gearing up for some reason, I'm guessing to hunt monsters. Go and pitch in for me."

The clear reluctance in his demeanor told Jaune that Bennett wanted to do anything but leave. The other boy kept flicking his gaze toward Fischl, whose confidence had long since fled.

Bennett said, almost in a whine, "But boss, they're gonna gang up on Fischl."

And the boy couldn't let that fly, as no good teammates would.

"I've got her," Jaune assured him. "Come on, go. You'll do good there, I know it."

"...Yes, boss."

As Bennett passed behind him, Jaune turned back to the people on the other side of the table. He cocked an eyebrow, the message conveyed loud and clear. He sent one of his away first. Don't complain.

They got the point. After a small fight among themselves, Yingzhu stormed off on the excuse of scouting. The quiet that settled in her wake was uncomfortable, leaving a bad taste in everyone's mouths, but it lacked the biting air of hostility.

The remaining female adventurer broke the silence.

"She means well," she said with a weak laugh.

"I suppose so," Jaune said in as diplomatic a manner as he could. Then, he bluntly asked, "Are you going to have a problem working with Fischl?" He nodded at the girl in question, who fidgeted while looking down at the table. The hunch to her shoulders made her appear smaller, less noticeable. The universal defensive response for those prone to shyness.

A nudge got her to look at him and he showed her an encouraging smile, eventually receiving a tiny one in return.

Meanwhile, the Liyue adventurers thought over his question, and then thought about it some more. In the end, the male adventurer groaned.

"I don't exactly have a problem, but… You have to understand, you showed up with a bunch of kids and Hu Tao. It doesn't exactly bolster confidence."

"We have Zhongli, too." Even if he hasn't done much, Jaune thought darkly, glancing at the man standing apart from the meeting. With hands clasped behind his back, Zhongli stared out to sea. The coattails of his suit jacket fluttered in the breeze.

The male adventurer was about to respond, but stopped to ponder on that.

"True. That does change things."

"It does?" Jaune recovered, wiping the gawking look off his face. "I mean, you see? We're taking this seriously." He hooked an arm around Fischl, lightly rocking her. "Fischl, what was your idea earlier?"

She glanced up at him. Looked down again.

"Well, um, the notes here"—she snatched up a sheet of paper—"refer to damages along the coast."

Jaune took the sheet, and checked the map on the table. To make it easier for him, the female adventurer tapped on a series of circles drawn onto the parchment.

"The connection is pretty weak," the woman admitted. "Rocks that broke off of the cliffs, weird dips in the beach sand, things like that. We think it's related due to the presence of the same monster types, but there wasn't anything special about these areas when we poked around. Just trees and grass."

"Turn your eyes yonder, as the gentleman does," said Fischl, indicating Zhongli. She took a deep breath to steady herself, and straightened up. "Oz, my dearest vassal, take flight to the islands that you could see, and return with news for me."

"At once, Mein Fräulein."

Oz shot off into the sky. Jaune followed his progress for a little while, before turning back to Fischl.

"What are you looking for?" he asked.

"A second data point," Fischl answered. "With one, we have an enigma. Two, and we have a map."

To narrow the search area, Jaune realized. With the available information, the best they could determine was that the source originated from the sea. The big, wide sea that would take a lifetime to comb over. However, if they managed to add another point from the other side, on one of the islands dotting the coast, it would at a minimum establish a boundary. At best, they might pinpoint the location of their goal.

Using angles and stuff. Math, and one of its derivative sorceries. He wasn't very knowledgeable about the specifics.

Nevertheless, he had one thing to say to that. "Good job, Fischl!"

The compliment pushed Fischl right back to fidgeting. This time, she bounced on her heels and wore a happy expression as she did so.

While waiting for Oz, Jaune passed the time discussing with the adventurers from Liyue about the monsters that have been popping up lately in the region. The adventurers theorized that they were an evolution of the Hydro (water), or perhaps Geo (Rock), slimes and nobody could say for definite if they were a byproduct or the cause of the sinkhole here.

Before long, he got a firsthand look at them. As villagers panicked and guards formed a defensive line, a pack of slimes made their appearance at the perimeter of the village. In all honesty, they didn't do a very good job at mimicking a ravening horde, looking like scoops of chocolate ice cream.

Bennett stood at the forefront of the defenders, and to nobody's surprise, he charged headlong toward the slimes. The guards saw it as bravery, and followed on his heels.

None of them would get the honor of the first blow.

"Open the gates of annihilation.

"Burst forth, the hounds of discord."

Poised at the top of the overlook, Fischl pulled back on her bow. Electricity crackled around the tip of the arrow.

"The Immernachtreich welcomes all,

"In the quiet slumber of a moonless sky.

"Erdbeerkuchen!"

A slime blasted to smithereens marked the first casualty of the battle. In that moment, Fischl resembled nothing so much as a warrior, and the Liyue adventurers were forced to confront the fact that a so-called kid was stronger than them.

"Is it me, or does that magic spell sound different from the last time?" Jaune asked.

Fischl averted her eyes. "'Twas surely your imagination."

The last doubts about Fischl's capability were dispelled when Oz returned good news. A slew of calculations later with lines drawn on the map, and they had a likely location for the source of the incident, smack dab in the middle of the water off the shore. As to how they would get there, Jaune provided a plan.

"Since we now have confirmation of multiple entry points, we can afford to be less careful about breaking into one," he said.

Behind his back, he held a scroll. The screen glinted in the sunlight.

"So, my friend told me about this neat thing called dynamite…"

#5,133
Chapter 64: Down Where It's Wetter (Pt. 2)​


As with many of Jaune's ideas, it was undoubtedly a great one. Plentiful and cheap, the humble dynamite packed a big punch for its size if one were to believe Lisa Wilbourn. The underrated star of demolition work.

How big? Jaune must admit to a fair amount of uncertainty on that front. Naturally therefore, he adhered to the meticulous nature for which he was famed and erred on the side of caution. A delicate touch, for a delicate task. Like pruning a flower bouquet.

KABOOOOM!

Or more like, he stuffed the ground full of dynamite, really packing it deep and dense in holes all over the area, then set off the lot from a distance, come what may.

"I think it's slightly possible—maybe, perhaps—that I used too much dynamite," he said in a rare moment of epiphany, leaning on a shovel with its blade planted in the ground next to him as he watched dirt and other debris shoot high in the air. A flock of seagulls happened to be flying by, and found themselves in a sudden aerial battle against the planet. The ground quaked and plumes of smoke covered the sky, while monsters of all stripes raced through the tall grass to get away from the eruption.

"Psssh, no such thing," Hu Tao assured him, holding her own shovel. She wore a satisfied look, a healthy glow to her skin. Her experience with gravedigging had delivered a real boon in saving Jaune time. 10/10, would hire again.

Her eagerness to see fireworks, in hindsight, helped a fair bit less and bore at least half the responsibility for the situation getting out of hand, what with her egging him on.

On his other side, a stiff-faced Bennett muttered, "I know someone who might want to meet you, boss." Fischl nodded numbly along with the boy.

No idea what that was about.

After the smoke dissipated, they observed the result.

"How about that?" Jaune said. "It hasn't broken through. I guess we'll have to—"

With both hands, Hu Tao lifted her shovel over her head. An expression of glee framed her face. "Keep going?"

"You read my mind."

Soon after, another explosion rocked the land.

For whatever reason, immediately following the creation of a hole in the ground a lightning bolt tried to smote Jaune where he stood. Too bad for it, he had already darted inside the opening he made.

Four other intrepid souls descended after him into the darkness.

Until they turned on their lanterns and in Jaune's case his scroll, of course. Rule number one of spelunking for treasure and similar relics, no cave exploration without a light. That sort of mistake was how brave, handsome adventurers ran into giant scorpion monsters.


-o-​


Teams were… important.

If man was meant to fight alone, then they as a species would be bigger. Better. Faster. Stronger. They would have matured from children into absolute killing machines, to the point that no Grimm could ever stand in a person's way.

But no, man was weak and needed help. Only by banding together did they survive, and history testified to the wonders that could be accomplished by people when they threw their pitiful lot in with one another. With comrades at their side, and more to cover their back, man went on to carve out a place in this bloody, savage world.

"Bennett, watch where you're swinging that thing!"

"Yes, boss!"

Kick. Punch. Slash.

"Boss, you're boxing me in!"

"Whoops, sorry."

Stab, stab, stab.

"Here I have a match. And now, FIRE!"

"Ahhhh!"

"Dammit, Hu Tao!"

Yep. Teams were the best.

Shouting a cry, Jaune slammed his blade home within the last enemy, a slime like all the others they had encountered thus far. The strong blow popped it like a balloon to scatter pieces of it every which way, spelling its end. With that, peace returned to the area, allowing him a reprieve to prop a hand against the wall and catch his breath.

As he rested, his gaze panned across the glorious battlefield to take in the sight of a slightly singed Bennett covered in dead slime residue and Hu Tao slumped facedown on the floor with her rear pointed up, her hat askew.

"You know," he said. "I think that went pretty well. Nice work, everybody, we did it!"

Bennett and Hu Tao voiced out cheers.

Three frontline fighters… probably did not make for the optimal team composition when it came to the cramped quarters of a tunnel. No pointing fingers, but one of them was prone to setting her surroundings on fire to boot. Aura saved them from mistakes on an embarrassing number of occasions.

The important thing to remember was that they were alive and kicking at the end of it. Clearly, teamwork had proven its worth.

Further back, Fischl unnocked her arrow. A warrior, but also a worrier, she had refrained from firing a shot this whole time for fear of hitting an ally, and his advice that she just 'let loose' failed to change the attitude. She didn't seem all that sad at this lack of opportunity, however, likely having to do with the pristine state of her dainty dress as compared to their clothes following the skirmishes. Oz alighted on her shoulder now that he saw it wouldn't get in her way.

Only Zhongli enjoyed an easier time than the pair of girl and bird. Like a man out for a morning walk, he brought up the rear at a leisurely pace. Yet to lift a finger, his cave-delving experience differed greatly from the rest of them, with his fitted suit impeccable. The man's reason, whenever asked, remained an infuriating, and flattering, "I trust you to succeed."

Jaune shook out his poncho to get rid of the slime residue. Mud, if he wanted to be blunt about it. He had traded his jacket for the water- and stain-proof poncho pretty quick after learning that fact firsthand.

Mud surrounded them, forming the passage in which they traveled. It dripped from above, oozed along the walls, and pooled at their feet. The twisting path created by it followed no rhyme or reason, going down and up and left and right to build a slippery obstacle course that at times threatened to send a person flat on their rear with a misstep. Cold followed their every step.

And throughout the entire journey, one sound remained everpresent.

Squelch. Squelch. Squelch. Squelch.

"Deep puddle."

"Aiya, it almost got me. Thanks for the warning."

Squelch. Squelch. Squelch. Squelch.

The warning didn't actually matter at all beyond common courtesy. The mud got everywhere.

Yet, life was about looking for the positive side, and Jaune's giddy laughter rang out in the tunnel as he signaled the group to halt. His scroll's flashlight beamed at a section of the nearby wall. Within the muck, gold shone through. He plunged a gloved hand into the wall, pulling out a fistful of coins.

"I can't believe how much stuff is in this place!" he gushed, vanishing the coins into his Pocket before going back for more—divvying them up was a task for later. "Mora, Mora, gem, Mora, helmet, Mora, a live salmon?" He tilted his head, looking bemusedly at the flopping fish for a few seconds before tossing it over his shoulder to carry on. "Mora, Mora, aha!"

The latest bout of rummaging earned him an honest-to-goodness spear, seemingly preserved in a perfect state by the mud. Sure, it didn't look all that special except for the intertwining dragon motif, but the blade cut razor sharp and the strangely light weight to it could suit Lisa were she so inclined. He popped the weapon into his dimensional space to check over at a better time.

At this rate, he'd have to upgrade the Pocket to the next tier before the day was done.

In fact…


Ding!
[Skill] purchased.
Point balance: 58,860 - 10,000 = 48,860


[Dimensional Pockets Lv.2]
You have deeper pockets. Heck, you could fit a family of bodies in there!
p.s. At Level 2, the available inventory space measures 3m by 3m by 9m—or about 9ft by 9ft by 29ft for bizarro worlds deprived of the metric system.
p.p.s. Time does not move within the inventory space.
p.p.p.s. Ignore line. Still reserved for future patches. Any day now.


Lisa would allow the purchase if she was here, he believed. They had discussed the need to acquire it for the future, at least, and the ability paid for itself many times over thus far. A reshuffle of priorities shouldn't divert from their plans in any significant fashion.

A small pang of worry grew that he might be predicting her reaction wrong, but he shoved it aside. He'd just have to mark the purchase down as coming from his private share of the Points. No problem, no problem.

He stowed away his scroll as Zhongli walked up to the wall. The man leaned forward with chin in hand, and he plucked a coin from the mud, turning it end over end to study the markings.

After a time, there came a remark.

"My word, what a thing to find."

Jaune's ears pricked up, and he sidled closer. "Hm? What is it?"

"Many treasures of the land have been lost to the sea across the millennia, and this is proof." Zhongli's voice took on the lecturing tone of a professor. "There are some who extol Mora as a perfect, unchanging object. Those that see further than gold regard it as a catalyst, an instrument capable of becoming anything."

"I think I've heard that before," Jaune said, nodding slowly. "How does it go… Lien, ah, Mora can be an egg for breakfast, a newspaper to read over lunch, and a ride to the other side of town to grab dinner, or something."

"An apt enough description, although you might be surprised at what else it can turn into." The coin stopped flipping, with Zhongli's thumb underscoring a tiny squiggle in the etching. "Even then, what everyone tends to miss is that it also serves as a calendar. The design does not stay static. The details shift over the course of centuries. Put them side by side, and you may notice the central imprint is moving. Based on that common pattern, this coin is very old, indeed. If it is as I suspect and the structure we currently occupy was raised from the ocean floor, we may well discover more history from a variety of eras along the way."

"Weapons?" Jaune asked with a sidelong glance. "Magical relics? Glowy potions that give amazing effects? Weapons?"

Zhongli offered a mysterious little smile. "Shall we find out?"

Movements in his periphery attracted Jaune's attention. He turned that way to spy shapes in the darkness bouncing closer. Slimes, again. Standing between him and loot, though they know it not.

Baring his teeth, Jaune said, "Let's."

He charged toward the creatures, with the sound of splashing mud behind him indicating his allies following suit. Too dumb for higher thoughts (the slimes, not his allies), they met him head on.

Unlike his first fight today against these things, he refrained from speeding up to simply blast through their soft bodies with his momentum. Down that path lay hours of laundry cycles and undoubtedly a clogged drain pipe that he'd have to clear, with Lisa snickering in the background. Instead, the first slime got chopped in half by Crocea Mors without even a chance to go out in a blaze of glory, its death a sad pffft as the outer jelly-like membrane burst open to spill the mud within.

How wet dirt could give rise to life was beyond him.

Footsteps closed in behind him. Instinct screamed, and he ducked his head just as Bennett's sword sliced through the space it used to occupy to end the life of another slime. The blade had barely passed when he sprang up to stab a third enemy, a hand over his face to protect from the splash.

"Here I have a match—"

He spun on his heels, his arms waving and sweat breaking out on his brow. "Me and him have it handled, no need for that!"

And no, making a sad face wouldn't change his mind.

His open back presented too tempting a target, and a slime launched itself intending to bodyslam him, only to get shoulder-checked by Bennett. Jaune leapfrogged over the other boy to stomp down with both feet on the slime. His sword reappeared, and he whacked one of its compatriots into the wall. An ill-advised roundhouse kick at another foe splattered filth all over his leg.

His sword swung back, the crossguard tapping against that of Bennett's.

"Thanks for covering me."

"No problem."

Their shields rose up to block streams of mud spat out with the strength of pressure hoses, Bennett a split second behind due to copying him. They advanced together in formation, maintaining a steady guard until they felt the attack weaken. Then, it was open season as they rushed forward to dive within the enemy's midst. One, two, three, four, the slimes fell in quick succession to bring the fight to a close.

Or so he mistakenly assumed. One last slime had stuck to the shadows, and upon watching him de-summon his sword sensed its moment to strike, leaping for him with its beady eyes locked on his throat.

He grabbed it out of the air with little fanfare. "And what were you going to do? You have no teeth to bite me."

The slime wriggled in his grip. The outer membrane of the creature had a strange texture, sticky and not quite liquid.

"Seriously, what even are you?" he asked, holding it up for a closer look.

Sniff, sniff. Blegh.

"Condensed elemental energy," Zhongli provided, walking over along with Hu Tao. "Slimes come into being where great power dwells. The Five Yakshas certainly qualify, given their mastery of the elements." He peered at the creature with interest. "Of them, Bonanus possessed an affinity for Hydro, while Menogias held some measure control of Geo. To which do you belong, little slime?" he pondered.

"But this is mud," Bennett noted, his white-blond hair caked in the stuff. His shirt and shorts hadn't fared better after the repeated fights. "Even when Hydro and Geo slimes show up in the same place, they don't mix. They're still their own thing. Today's the first day I've ever seen these guys."

Zhongli nodded. "To have a touch of each element is to not be wholly of either. Impure, in a sense. Such a novel development signals… change, for the future of Liyue and further beyond."

"Uh-huh, that's very interesting, please tell me more," Jaune said absentmindedly, having tuned out the discussion in lieu of squishing the slime's round body with his hands and enjoying the sensation. "They're kind of adorable up close, don't you think? Almost made me wish I didn't have to fight them."

The slime spat a glob of mud into his face.

"I take that back."

Winding up his foot, he dropped the slime and gave it a swift punt. It sailed down the passageway to go splat. And that was that.

The party spared a few minutes after the fight to search the area. The slimes traveled the tunnel, and their body collected detritus in the process. Trash, mostly, but also Mora, fragments of a crystalline gem that shone with an inner glow, pretty seashells. Good stuff for a minute's work, and Jaune pocketed them all. (The seashells garnered an interested party in Hu Tao, as she was collecting them.)

Further along, he discovered a new aspect to the tunnel. What he assumed would allow a straight shot to his goal turned out to be maze, because a choice laid before him now.

"A fork in the road," he contemplated, looking at the two offshoots headed in completely opposite directions. The beam of his flashlight traveled down one, then the other. Both times, the light reached the limit of its range without revealing a hint of anything to decide their course.

"Boss!" Bennett shook him by the arm. "Boss, I think this is a proper Domain!" He caught the blank incomprehension on Jaune's face. "Oh yeah, I forgot you were from another world. A Domain… they're lost places that sometimes resurface. You never know what you'll find in them, it's an adventurer's dream!"

Now, that was heartening to hear. Professor (despite being in another universe, Jaune braced for a correction) Oobleck did so love to wax on about 'discoveries for the ages' waiting in ancient temples and jungle cities dotting the surface of Remnant, where danger went hand in hand with riches.

Heartbeat rising, he addressed their best navigator, "Fischl, what have you got for us?"

Fischl rummaged in her pack, retrieving a map that she unfurled to study. The map turned and turned, aligning the markings she had added to the parchment with their estimated location.

"The center which my forbidden eye hath divined lies due north. Thus, the left entrance should see us forward."

She looked pretty proud of that one, bouncing on her heels in expectation. Jaune gave a dutiful laugh, to her delight.

As if to mock them, the next fork had four paths. All of them led north.

"Soooo," Jaune began.

"Wait, I'm on it—I mean, spare me but a moment!" Fischl said, curtsying with grace before scrambling in a hurry for her map. She scrutinized it in hope of an answer, but soon gave up and focused on the tunnels. "Perhaps the humidity of the air would hold a clue… no, that's dumb… These kinds of puzzles usually have a hint in the room…" She cast her eyes around the area. Mud, mud, and—surprise!—mud greeted her, and her shoulders slumped. "Nevermind," she said in a small voice.

"A good try, milady," said Oz. He nipped at a stray lock of her hair, moving it back in place.

Chiming in his support, Jaune said, "Hey, don't get so down. We don't always have a logical solution. In times like this, we should go with our instinct. And you know…" He turned to the rest of the party, meeting their confident nods. They were all on the same page. "I think we have an idea of which direction is best."

He pointed at the leftmost path, Hu Tao the one next to it. Bennett had the rightmost. Zhongli went over to stand by the last tunnel, crossing his arms and leveling a steady gaze at them as if to say he would brook no argument.

A beat of silence passed.

"No, guys, you don't understand!" exclaimed Bennett. "I can smell treasure down this way!"

"You liar," Jaune said. "You told me your buddy is the one who was part wolf. The left passage is always the correct one."

Hu Tao planted her hands on her hips. "Says who?"

Those choose-your-own-adventure books he read as a kid. Which, now that he thought about it, might have been published by people that never once traveled beyond the city walls. Too late to take it back, he had to stick to his guns.

"It's basic psychology," he argued. "Everyone wants to be 'right', so the tricky person would make the right choice 'left'."

Bennett scratched his head. "Your left, or their left?"

Jaune paused. "Say that again?"

"Uh." The other boy furrowed his brow, working through his train of thought. "Because if you think about it, the center of this Domain would be the origin, right? The entrance we used is added on later." True, it was brand new. Made that very morning, in fact. "That means whoever built the Domain is looking at things from the opposite direction from us. Does that make sense?"

"Make sense?" Jaune echoed, shaking his head. "Bennett, you're a genius. We have to switch it around!"

Straight away, he moved over to the rightmost passage. Meanwhile, Bennett scurried to the left one. They then stopped in their tracks and stared at each other, question marks practically popping up above their heads.

"Why are you changing your mind?"

"I realized halfway through explaining that I was looking for the right tunnel, which is the left from this side," Bennett admitted.

Zhongli brought a hand up to massage his temples. They ignored him.

"Okay, look," Hu Tao intervened. "Since we each have a different idea, why don't we just make it simple and split up for a minute?"

Jaune shot that ridiculous notion down forthwith. "Uh, no. Doing that is how you die. The party needs to stick together… while I head down this way on my own."

Because, clearly, he could handle himself and wouldn't end up like horror movie characters.

Nobody agreed with him, thereby showing how much they trusted his leadership.

"*whisper*...Escha would have gone along with it… Nora, Ren, maybe Pyrrha… Lisa, too… Grumble, grumble, grumble…*whisper*"

It took them ten minutes and another round of arguments to finally decide on a corridor.

From there, they pressed ever onward through the many twists and turns. Sometimes their choices paid off, sometimes they didn't.

The layout of the 'Domain' adhered to no set design, looping on itself in several instances or culminating in dead-ends to force them to double back. Between four fighters, battles fought along the way saw the party enriching their pockets with little resistance, it becoming a game for them as to whose defeated foes yielded the most reward, all to stave off the rising monotony of a world filled with mud, mud, mud. Wall treasure remained a rare and elusive treat beyond the mundane Mora, not often enjoyed although always leading to much rejoicing.

One thing they recognized, the Domain was building up bigger and bigger as they moved deep under the ocean. An hour on, and the tunnels had grown more firm, with sharp angles and corners where there were once only curving lines. Structure began to assert over the slapdash construction.

It also started to get… weird. Blank stretches of the walls surrendered to messy, slanted engravings, like murals but covering the floor and ceiling, too. Formed of the same substance as everything here, the details were blurred by the soft muck to prevent them from deciphering their meaning, though that did not stop Fischl from the attempt—she seemed to have an interest in this stuff, from what Jaune could tell.

The ludicrous scale of the place truly hit home beyond that point, with the tunnels opening up so they could have sent ten people marching abreast, the ceiling above measuring two stories high.

"Did anybody have any idea at all that this was here?" Jaune asked incredulously, turning this way and that as he wandered down the passage.

"The villagers never mentioned a peep of it to me," Hu Tao said, shaking her head.

"The sea is often a mystery, and that goes for man and gods alike," Zhongli added from further back. The man had knelt down to study the muddy inscriptions on the floor. "They have learned that there are many things below the surface better left undisturbed."

"You're telling me…" Jaune said as he stopped by a lump set against the wall, Fischl joining him in looking closer at it. The bend here, the curve there—the lump resembled a person, albeit incomplete with most of it merged into the wall. Similar ones like it dotted the corridor. "Well now, that's odd."

He could have sworn it was moving.

At that time, Hu Tao called out to him. "Uhhh, Jaune? We have company."

Her tone carried a strange note, but he chalked it down to nerves. He turned away from the mud statue to look down the corridor.

"More slime? Nice. Get ready everybody, the score stands at—why does that slime have arms?"

Mud slimes didn't appear so adorable anymore when they had fully articulated, human-like arms. Unable to bounce with the additional weight, it dragged itself over the ground. The movements lacked finesse, as if the creature didn't quite understand how limbs function.

Jaune's sword popped into his grasp, with him ready to skewer the unholy abomination then and there.

It never reached that point. Something about the slime's condition made it unstable, because halfway to him it began to wobble. The tremors grew worse with the passing seconds, until the slime ceased to move forward and just lay on the ground. Its form oozed to melt into the floor.

Jaune glanced behind him. "That explains this thing. Are they how the Domain was built, do you think? Hundreds of thousands, or millions, of mud slimes adding on to it bit by bit?"

"'Tis would be the work of a thousand winters, and a most cruel existence, besides," Fischl murmured. The girl then pressed the back of her hand to her forehead, swooning. "Oh, what sovereign would torment their subjects so. As royalty, I declare, we must—"

A slime entered the passage from around the corner ahead, sprinting on two bare legs extending out from under its round body. They had the general shape of belonging to a well-built, middle-aged man.

Fischl's face twitched. "—kill it with fire."

"Milady meant that in the best of ways," Oz hastily added.

Jaune doubted it, since the girl had already pulled back on her bow. The arrow she fired absolutely roiled with arcs of electricity, bright to the point that it hurt to look at. It impacted the running slime and vaporized its legs from existence altogether.

"Rest in eternal slumber," Fisch kindly said afterward, dispelling her bow for a moment so she could place her hands together and bow.

"Don't you have to cast the spell?" Jaune asked as he admired the scorchmarks which attested to the power of that attack. Not bad at all.

Fischl gazed up at him, blinking. "Huh?"

"The spell? The chant that activates your magic?"

The girl seemed to experience a light bulb moment. "Oh! Um, t-that's right!" She struck a pose, one knee raised and a hand across her face—trying and failing to hide her reddening cheeks. "Darkness of the midnight, um… how did it go again?"

Seeing her looking ready to cry, Jaune patted her on the shoulder. "Forget I asked. Also, you're right."

He turned to the crowd of slimes spilling into the area. Even calling them slimes was a misnomer. The human features attached to them ranged from just arms or legs to the full torso, creating a scene from hell. The innocent image he had in his head of adorable blobs frolicking amidst the flower fields withered, replaced by a horror show and too many dangling bits.

"Kill it with fire. Hu Tao, you're up!"

The girl obliged, and with a twirl, a line of fire bisected the corridor to cut off the slimes. It failed to last long given the cold, wet mud, just enough for Hu Tao to summon her fiery butterflies that scattered among the enemy force. One by one, they exploded and set the slimes alight. Another spin of her staff, and a second wall of flames went up.

Jaune crashed through it, his frame encased in the Rathalos armor to dampen the heat. With the large space, he could afford to bring out his gunlance, a horizontal swing obliterating the slimes' front ranks. The backswing wiped out another line of them.

He had to admit, it was easier done when they were not cute.

A slime leapt high above its brethren. Human up to the neck and clothed in what looked like a suit of mud armor, it had a fist cocked back for a punch. Jaune considered shooting the monster out of the air, but thought better of it. Waste of a round aside, there were many ways to find out if the ocean dwelt on the other side of the wall, and cracking a hole in it with an explosive shell numbered at the bottom of the list. Instead, he propped the lance on his shoulder, and settled into a baseballer's stance.

"Homerun!" he shouted as the slime fell into range. The resulting swing took the creature's head off, the rest of the body flipping from the momentum to slam against the floor, breaking apart.

His allies had entered the fray in earnest by now. Bennett covered the opposite side of the passage from him. Even fighting alone, the boy did a good job at remembering that he wielded a shield in addition to his sword, although he often defaulted to using it as a weapon for punching rather than its intended purpose—they'd have to keep working on that. Fischl hung a few steps back from the melee. At that range, aim presented a nonissue to her, and she fired shot after shot with barely a pause in between to pull back the bowstring.

The arrows of light never ran out. Quite unfair in his opinion, that.

Butterflies continued to set everything on fire around him while he pressed ahead. It led to many of his foes collapsing before he reached them, the heat destabilizing the delicate balance that allowed their clumsy half-slime, half-people shapes to cling together. For all that they were bigger and meaner, and possessed thumbs, these new slimes posed less of a threat than their previous iterations. Those, at least, understood how to control their bodies.

Between them, the number of enemies dropped at a precipitous speed.

As the battle wound down, a particularly strange specimen rushed at him. For a brief instant, his mind registered that he was being attacked by a sumo wrestler. A blink of his eyes, and its appearance reconstituted as a very, very big slime with two fat legs and two fat arms, the round body positioned where a person's belly would be.

Moving to meet its charge, he shook his leg to dislodge some of the muck out of the rocket nozzles and engaged the trigger. The one-footed hop rotated him above the creature, upside-down. A sharp jab of the lance tip punctured its skin. He landed behind the sumo slime as it ran on, its inside squirting out as a stream until it deflated completely.

Jaune stood up and braced the gunlance on his shoulder, leaning slightly back to better balance it. He looked around at the amalgamations of slime and people that were losing their form, returning to the mud from which they were born. Some had the makings of statue-like faces, the melting of which disturbed him to no end.

"Seriously, what the heck is going on with this place?"


-o-​


"Silly-churl, billy-churl, silly-billy hilichurl~
"Frilly-churl, willy-churl, frilly-willy hilichurl~!"​

Jaune followed the singing voice, using it to orient himself amidst the cramped passageways. He soon emerged from the side tunnel, back in the wider main corridor.

The first person he saw was Hu Tao, dancing in the middle of the path as she sang. Mud splashed beneath her feet, but she paid it no mind. She seemed to be enjoying herself. Zhongli, meanwhile, watched over her with a calm expression. The man nodded to Jaune to acknowledge his return.

"How goes your excursion?" Zhongli asked.

Jaune replied with a helpless shrug. "There was nothing great in there. I found this vase, but that's all." He held up the item in question with one hand.

"Eeeeeee!"

The piercing squee caused him to wince. Moments later, his hand became empty, and in utter befuddlement he watched a happy Hu Tao hopping up and down while hugging the vase.

"I take it that's valuable?" he ventured a guess. "Is it an important relic of some sort?"

Hu Tao whirled toward him. "Even better than that. This, is a funerary urn."

Jaune wiped his hands on his pants.

Hu Tao stomped her foot, and held out the urn. "You don't understand! Inside it could have been anyone! Imagine what it has seen during its life, or while it was sitting on the ocean floor? How could you not get excited?"

He placed a finger on her forehead to push back her face, as it had gotten far too close, and motioned placatingly. "Hu Tao, calm down. It's not like you can talk to the urn."

She blinked at him. Once, twice.

"…You can't, right?"

Blink. Blink. Head tilt.

"You know what, have fun."

He left her to it, and for Zhongli to deal with, making his way toward the other members of the party to check on them. Bennett waved to him. The boy appeared to have hung out with Fischl all this time, leaning on the wall as the girl roamed back and forth studying the murals. Around this area, the engravings had straightened out to form a tidier design, giving the Domain the air of an ancient temple.

"What was…?" Bennett gestured behind Jaune.

Jaune shook his head. "I got her something she liked. Probably isn't going to be your thing, but ask her about it if you're curious. How was it here?"

"Good," Bennett answered. "None of those weird slimes attacked while you were gone, and the food you gave us was great. I'm still amazed at how much you can fit in your dimensional storage. For most people I know, we can only put away our weapons."

"Eh heh, yeah, it's a thing," Jaune said, averting his gaze. He had been keeping the particulars of his Pocket vague up until now, so when he bought lunch for the party from the Marketplace to eat in lieu of basic rations, nobody batted an eye.

"Other than that," Bennett continued, glancing at Fischl, "I'm just keeping Fischl company. The wall drawings have better details now, and she's trying to figure them out."

In a blink, Fischl stood in front of them. "And I did! Bennett, Jaune, come see this!"

"You are breaking character, Mein Fräulein," said Oz, perched on Fischl's shoulder. It fell on deaf ears. Fischl grabbed the two boys by their arms, and dragged them to a different section of the wall.

"Okay, the murals look like a mess, right?" she asked them. They nodded. "Right. Most of it doesn't flow. It's disjointed. But here"—she excitedly jabbed a finger above the group—"I found a repeating pattern. This one set of drawings is shown everywhere in the Domain!"

Jaune looked up at the mural, captured in a large square relatively free of unrelated clutter. The messy script flowed around the edges, only sometimes dipping into the space to mar the artwork.

It depicted a scene of five figures on a mountain peak, a great tree casting its shade over them. One stood head and shoulder above the other with his big frame, leaning on the tree. One napped on a tree branch. The rest sat on the grass at the base, in a small circle. A rectangle with little dots, a game board, lay between them.

"The five yakshas, lounging in peaceful respite," explained Fischl. "Unaware of the turning wheel of misfortune, and the dark future foretold. Alas, had my journey through the many centuries of my immortal life placed me there at that point in time, I would have lent them the full might of the Immernachtreich so that they may rebel against the uncaring design of the heavens."

"Milady wishes she could have done something for them, and she is also spoiling the story."

"Oz! I am not!" Fischl cried.

Eager to skirt over the accusation, she tugged on Jaune's poncho to get him to move on. The next mural, the mountain had vanished. A circle hung above two figures that had the vague features of people, somewhat smudged by the medium on which they are carved. An oscillating line underscored the scene, located near the bottom edge.

"Ahem. Here, beneath the sun, or possibly the moon… or a cloud, two yakshas met in the sky. The ancient language shrouded their identities, but we know their names as spoken by the erstwhile historian Zhongli—Bonanus and Menogias."

"What's this thing here?" Bennett asked. "These squiggles."

"Some mysteries lie beyond the distance."

Jaune parsed the statement, and nodded. Fair enough.

The next mural also included the squiggles, and the next one, too. Always, above the two figures. An object of worship?

From scene to scene, the two figures clashed. Sword-like objects flew from the first figure, the second figure retaliating with warped, twisting projectiles. They seemed evenly matched, an estimation soon proven.

"They were taken out at the same time, huh?" he said, pausing for a moment. "Then, this next scene… One of them fell. What's the line here?"

"I do believe it is the ocean." Fischl pointed at the scene after that, which depicted the line—the ocean waves—higher on the mural. In it, the second figure had dived into the water after the first.

The surface of the ocean rose higher and higher, and higher still. Soon, the entire mural took place beneath the sea. Yet, the distance between the two figures grew further apart, until the first figure sank into the depths, fading from view to leave the second alone.

"The second yaksha wasn't going in for the kill," Jaune realized.

"I think they came back to themselves. From the madness," Fischl said in a somber voice. "They wanted to save the other person, but… they couldn't find them, because the sea is too big. And here." She led him and Bennett to the next mural. "This circle, instead of swimming up for air, they made a barrier to keep out the water."

Except the water began to fill up inside the barrier, with the figure trapped within.

The last mural showed a blank stretch of wall, missing even the ever-present squiggly lines. Then, it rewound to a scene of five figures on a mountain peak, a great tree casting its shade over them, letting the entire series of events play out again.

"So ends the story of Bonanus and Menogias," a voice murmured.

Jaune turned to see that Zhongli had arrived at some unknown point. The man studied the murals with a distant air, lips pursed.

"Maybe not quite yet," Jaune said. "One of them had to have survived, otherwise the barrier wouldn't have expanded into this Domain. Both of them, if the elements of Hydro and Geo can't properly mix as you mentioned."

The other man did not answer, his attention on the scene of the Five Yakshas. The lull grew to the point it became apparent that the conversation wasn't going to continue. Jaune and the others shared a look, and shrugged their shoulders.

"Heeeey! All of you, come look at this!" Hu Tao called from the exit to the chamber up ahead. In her arms, she hugged her funerary urn.

The whimsical girl truly was a quick one, wasn't she? Always here, there, everywhere. Her chipper attitude broke their solemn mood, something Jaune silently thanked her for.

With a last look at the tale of Bonanus and Menogias, he padded after her along with the rest of the group, to her impatient urging. They entered the passage to find Hu Tao now further down the hall, and they joined her in peeking around the corner, heads stacking one by one atop each other.

Except for Zhongli, who deigned to observe their antics rather than play along.

It didn't take long for Jaune to spot what had Hu Tao so thrilled.

"Is that…?" he asked, his eyes widening.

"It is!" Hu Tao confirmed.

Halfway down the passageway, sat a treasure chest.

Secret tunnel. Ancient ruins. Money in the walls. Now, a treasure chest. This place was turning out amazing~!

Not only him and Hu Tao, Bennett and Fischl also ran to the cache. They jostled for position, crowding around it with Oz flying above trying to get a peek.

"I knew it," said Bennett. "I just knew we'd find a treasure chest. Domains are the best!"

The container rested at the center of the path. Smooth, polished wooden planks fitted together without a single flaw or crack, dry as a whistle. Metal bands secured the construction. There was a lock, but before Jaune could worry, Hu Tao unclasped the latch—it was unlocked. Too easy.

Hu Tao looked over her shoulder at him and the others. At their nods, she grinned and turned back to the chest, placing her hands on either side of the lid.

"Okay! Let's see what weahhh! Ahhhh!"

"Ssaaaa!"

That sound smashed through the fog of time and memory to root itself in Jaune's brain. As Hu Tao's entire upper half was slurped inside the treasure chest to leave her legs kicking up and down, one of his eyes developed a twitch. A name sprang to his lips.

"MIMIC!" he shouted, summoning his sword.

A tentacle whipped at him, which was new. This mimic was not the warrior poet of yore, he of the spindly limbs and creepy brawler moves. No arms, no legs, it brought a hundred sinewy ropes of flesh to the fight to serve as both limbs and weapons.

Jaune dodged the attack and rammed his sword into the lid of the mimic, burying the blade deep.

"Eeeek!"

Whoops, he almost ended Hu Tao.

"What was that just now!?" Hu Tao's butt wiggled, giving the impression that it had done the talking.

A tug on his sword couldn't dislodge the blade. Something had a tight grip on it from within the chest.

"Why are there so many tentacles? Heeeeelp!" Hu Tao cried.

Okay, probably that. He shoved the sword into his Pocket instead, summoning it back a split second later. A tentacle whacked him in that moment of vulnerability, knocking him away.

Capitalizing on what it thought was weakness, the mimic launched another feeler at him, but Zhongli was suddenly there with his spear to pin it down. The man pulled to tear off the tentacle and spun the polearm to divert the next blow, giving Jaune the opening to rush in.

Tentacles twisted together to form a huge fist that flew at him, meeting the shield that blinked into his grip. The two sides pushed against one another, neither willing to give ground.

"Ssaaa… Ssaaaaa!" the mimic hissed past the tasty morsel of Hu Tao jerky.

Jaune gasped. "Don't you dare say that about my mother!"

"You speak furniture?" Bennett yelled over, forgetting for a moment the tentacle wrapped around his waist and lifting him in the air. (Oz, the literal birdbrain, maintained focus to continue pecking at the appendage in an effort to free him.)

He couldn't answer the other boy, embroiled in fending off rapid-fire blows that were arriving from every direction. They began to overwhelm him, not by skill but by sheer number. His answer was to throw [Third Arm] behind him so that it pulled him away from the mimic.

The tentacles, tasting victory, tore through the air in pursuit.

Jaune landed with both feet on the wall, hanging off the ground, and he grinned at the approaching feelers. They never got to him with Zhongli below swiping upward with his spear, slicing through multiple of them in one fell swoop. Fischl added an Electro arrow into the mix, shocking a half dozen more limbs numb.

He saw his chance.

"Cover me," was his simple request to his allies.

The shadowy arm dispelled to leave nothing but wisps of smoke. Before he could fall, rockets engaged to carry him across the corridor. He forewent his weapons, relying on Zhongli and a newly-freed Bennett to defend his flanks. Arrows weaved around him, opening the path. A slide under the grasping tentacles put him right in front of the mimic.

The monster went ignored for the time being. Killing the thing was best left for after he took Hu Tao out of harm's way.

"You alright in there?" he called out, rapping his knuckles on the lid. A tentacle whipped above his head, tackled off-course by a raven.

Hu Tao's legs stopped at the sound of his voice, then began kicking harder. "Get me out of heeere!"

"On it!" Then, to himself. "Probably isn't too bad."

"No! It is! It really is! Please, I'm gonna barf if I stay in here any long—eep!"

Jaune ignored her squeaks, adjusting for a better grip of her waist. For leverage, he planted a foot on the chest. Realizing what he intended, Hu Tao ceased kicking to give him an easier time.

"On three, okay?" He'd assume that movement of hers meant a yes. "One… two… three!"

Jaune pulled Hu Tao toward himself, and the response was immediate.

"Ow, ow, ow, ow, you're ripping me in half!"

He rolled his eyes at that exaggeration given her Aura, but relented and let her go. Hu Tao resumed her flailing against the mimic. Despite how difficult to digest she must be turning out, the treasure chest refused to give up on eating her. It shook in mirth(?) at them.

Two tentacles thought they were being sneaky, trying to wind around him. He tied them into a knot, then said, "I'll give something else a go, Hu Tao."

"'Kaaay, not going anywhere."

Rule of Lisa. If a girl could still spare the energy to snark, she was fine.

"Ssaaa…"

Do your worst, was the clear-cut challenge Jaune (did not) heard.

His eyes narrowed. He grabbed onto the edges of the box and the lid. The mimic's hinges proved tougher than expected, supernaturally so, though failing to draw more than a small grunt as he applied strength to pry open the lid.

Once he had a big enough gap, he slipped his knee inside the chest to free up a hand, wincing at the sharp fangs pressing into him. The tentacles within the mimic made a play at dragging him in, but the fistful of Mora that he tossed into the mouth provided a fair distraction. As one would expect from a mimic, greed overruled other instincts, and gold tasted divine.

It allowed him to seize Hu Tao by her coattails and yank her out of the chest. He leapt back with her in tow, and absent his resistance, the lid of the mimic slammed shut to bite down on its own tongue. It swung open again in a scream of pain and outrage.

That opportunity, he couldn't let pass. Tossing Hu Tao (a "Thank yooou!" trailing behind her) over to Fischl, he pivoted on his heels to launch right back at the mimic. His sword appeared, and it plunged into the open mouth to skewer the very depths of the chest.

A screech shook the corridor. It found no sympathy from him and he twisted his sword to worsen the wound. A spear slammed into place beside his blade.

He shared a look with the impassive Zhongli. They nodded to one another and savagely ripped out their weapons to leave the mimic hacking up blood.

All of the tentacles tensed for a long few seconds, then fell limp. The lid of the chest tilted back, the edge hitting the ground.

The tongue shuddered and spasmed, the movements slowing as energy seeped out from the mimic, until the best it could do was breathe in ragged gasps.

His party kept their weapons raised, alert for a trick. Jaune did not bother. He had fought mimics before, and knew the signs.

The mimic let out a final hiss as it watched him striding closer.

"Ssaaa…"

Translation: You have bested me. Now my end draws near. All my life, I sought the surface. Heh. I guess such are dreams, ever beyond our grasp. Farewell to you, the better thief. Know that… that…

Mimics never die—​

"Yeah, yeah. Enough out of you." Jaune kicked the chest over, spilling out the contents. "I still remember what you said about my mother."

Not all mimics were the same. Some had class.

He left the dead mimic there to go check on Hu Tao. Beside the chew marks on her clothes and a thick coating of drool, she remained hale and hearty with the dark red glow of Aura shining on her skin.

Of course, healthy did not equal happy. Hu Tao grabbed her twintails, bringing them up to take a sniff of the frazzled locks, making a gagging noise after.

"Ueeeeh, I reek!" she complained. Fischl, who Jaune had shoved the other girl into, shared in the sentiment and visibly struggled to not react.

"There, there," Jaune said, kneeling down to pat her comfortingly on the back. Which put him at a level where the smell of the mimic's drool hit him.

Sniff, sniff. Blegh.

That earned him a very offended look from the girl.

"What? You were right." Saying that didn't aid his cause. To placate her, he brought out a towel and a water bottle to help her somewhat clean up.

Meanwhile, Bennett took on the job of searching the chest. The cry of "Boooss!" soon rang out in the passageway, with Bennett returning to them carrying an armful's worth of prizes. A cursory skim showed nothing of note, just the usual loot, except for one item.

A stopped clock.

What the hey?

Jaune was about to throw the piece of junk away, until that same mysterious little smile crossed Zhongli's lips and it prompted him to give the object a second look.

Even then, the pocket watch still did not appear very impressive. Pretty, Jaune supposed, with the red clock face and the decorative flowers. The bell attached to the watch on a string jangled a clear, melodious note pleasing to the ear. All ruined by the needles that would not tell the time.

But beyond his eyes, he had another tool at his disposal.

"Apparently, this comes in a set. Have you ever seen anything like it before?" he asked Zhongli, giving his scroll a surreptitious glance.


Summer Night's Moment

Zhongli held his chin in a thoughtful pose.

"There have always existed artifacts that bestow power. By luck or fate, they tend to never travel far from one another."

Interesting news for sure, and a new priority on the list for him to keep an eye out for. He reined in his eagerness, however. The party took precedence, and he preferred them in good shape for whatever they might face, so he called for a break, allowing everyone time to freshen up.

Hu Tao, mainly. She needed it. Blegh.

Half an hour on, the girl looked like a different person. A less chewed-on person. Her hair had been restored to a silky luster with the shampoo and water that Jaune 'just happened to have lying around', her clothes damp from a light washing—though that was nothing new for the group by this point, since all of their clothes felt damp to a degree.

They resumed their journey with a renewed buoyancy. After the thrill of battling a mimic, fights against slimes somewhat weakened in impact. They posed little challenge, or reward. Still, the party pressed on.

A deep chill settled in, right around the time Jaune realized that the corridors had steepened to direct them more down than forward. A part of him wondered if they should have taken that as a sign to turn around. Be glad for what they have gained, retire to a village and tell the story over dinner.

Because, as the slope straightened out to deposit them in the next chamber, he discovered that he seemed to have led them into a terrible place.

The ground before him writhed. A shiver went up Jaune's spine.

The illumination of the lanterns couldn't penetrate far, and the group relied on him to sweep his flashlight around for a better view of the space. Hu Tao helped out, a swing of her staff sending out her flame butterflies to fly around the cavern, shedding light over the area before dissipating.

From the uneven ground filled with pits and slopes, to the high ceiling where oozing mud coalesced in stalactites, everything moved with a pulsating rhythm. All around them, the mud roiled and churned, with shapes rising out of the muck to act out scenes and settings before abruptly collapsing in pieces.

One of the butterflies passed by a shambling figure. The flames faded away, but his flashlight replaced it to shine on the spot.

Jaune saw a person. A man, clad in tattered robes.

The blue-tinted skin and the eyes that were slightly milky could not do much to mar his features. Menogias was handsome, still. Even in death.

As the drowned yaksha wandered aimlessly, a croaking whisper echoed throughout the cavern.

"Bonanus… Bonanus, where are you…"

Again and again, he said it. "Bonanus… Bonanus, where are you…"

Suddenly, his gaze snapped to them, blinking as he looked into the light emitted by the lanterns. Intelligence resurfaced… or perhaps not. His face warped into a snarl, the mouth spouting long, sharp teeth that grind and crack against one another.

"Demons! What have you done to her!?"

Jaune summoned his sword.
