#5,320

Chapter 66: Who Am I
​


The apartment in another world felt like home.

Had he ever said that before? Probably.

And yet, at no time did that hold more truth than today. The clock struck midnight, and a roaring din allowed no sleep.

"Ooooh, what does this do? And what does that do?" a young woman marveled as she scurried from one kitchen appliance to another, her long twintails bouncing.

"That's a microwave to heat up food. Don't stick your head in it. The other is… nominally a rice cooker, that also does everything else. Don't stick your head in that, either."

"I see!"

The young woman stuck her head in it, before moving on.

She poked and prodded, oohed and ahhed. In her wake, gadgets played a disorderly song of beeps and clicks and dings, their lights flashing. She seemed to find great amusement in these effects, the eagerness to see what else laid in store for her only rising over time.

Alas, that enthusiasm stalled out with the errant press of a button.

Whiiiiiir!

The blender revved to life, wailing its unholy screech to scare the daylight out of Hu Tao. In a flash, she snatched her hand away from the controls and beat a hasty retreat to the other side of the kitchen, where she took cover behind the counter. A flat-top hat and a pair of eyes poked above the edge, observing the mechanical contraption with a wary edge in a manner not unlike that of a cat.

Nearby, Bennett rummaged among the boxes and crates of supplies to retrieve the assorted knickknacks from his bags that he had accidentally spilled all over the place, the boy apologizing whenever he knocked into something with an elbow or a container fell on his head. Every once in a while, curiosity led him to hold up a random object to ask Jaune what it was, the answers only half-heard due to the racket made by Escha as she chased after Oz with a strange glint of determination in her eyes. Bird and felyne raced round and round, scrambling from couch to table to cabinets, with Escha's fur standing on ends since she kept trying to touch the crackling electricity that formed the raven's body.

"What manner of sacred artifact is—Eep!"

And that, was Fischl discovering the dildo-bat Jaune left in the corner.

Jaune took great care to keep his face neutral, feigning unawareness. Inwardly, he cursed his past self. Of course that thing was going to come back to bite him someday.

Thankfully, Fischl was more concerned with whether anybody had seen her holding the long, veiny bat than questioning why it was there in the first place, blonde hair swishing as she whipped her head to and fro to check. Flexible silicone shook with the motion, reeling her attention back in. Her eyes reflexively roamed along its length, up and down. A beat later, it occurred to her that she was still touching the… member, at which point her face turned to a tomato red hue. One would believe the bat scalding hot to the touch with the way she cast it back to its resting place. Unfortunately, her actions hadn't been very subtle.

"Oho? What was that, Fischl, what did you just—Eep!"

And thus, the dildo-bat claimed another innocent pair of eyes.

Hu Tao could blush. Who knew?

As pandemonium reigned, Jaune stood back, giving the newcomers the freedom to carry on in much the same manner as he once did for Escha. Put in the shoes of those who lived in a different era, he imagined the apartment must resemble a sort of treasure chest, utterly irresistible. Full of discoveries beyond their wildest dreams, just waiting for them to open up and look. (Complete with a few nasty surprises ready to spring on them, because—whoops—the chest was actually a mimic.)

It would be their home for the foreseeable future. He'd prefer they saw it as a place where they could be themselves, and not a prison.

"What a… colorful group of people you've brought back," came a voice next to him.

He glanced to the side. Lisa stood there, having gone largely unnoticed by everyone else given her quiet air, her hair tousled from sleep. Silk robes hung off of one shoulder, tied loosely with a sash. She watched over the various ongoings with a saccharine smile that set his teeth on edge.

"They're great," he said quickly. "You'll love them. Now, how about some proper introductions?"

The complexion of her face had improved since last he saw her, and judging from items strewn about the room, she had at one point or another stopped spending the whole day in bed. That spelled good news for the state of her mind and heart. Yet, the book that started all the troubles remained in her firm grasp, the pages scuffed from far too much handling than was healthy. Moreover, a sense of lethargy still hung about her, dull eyes and slumped shoulders where a cheeky confidence belonged.

"I don't care. I think I'd rather—" she began, but he barreled over it to keep talking.

"Come on, let's start with our best foot forward," he said in encouragement, in part trying to push matters along before he lost the initiative. Lisa sometimes had a bit of a thing about strangers, in that they made perfectly acceptable targets for her to pry into with her powers and spill all their secrets, as opposed to the boon companions for whom she spared a measure of mercy (on occasion). Couple that with her current attitude, where she seemed just about done with it all? The sooner he moved Bennett, Fischl, and Hu Tao into the friend column, the lower the chance of words said that could never be taken back.

"Hey, all of you! Gather round for a bit. You too, Escha. I brought gifts."

Cat ears flicked, and Escha skidded to a stop. She spun to look at him with her mouth open wide, pointing to herself as if to say, for me? At his nod, she dashed over on all fours.

Hesitation set in as she came near. Thoughts of presents gave way to a different concern. Her steps slowed to a crawl, with her sending peeks around his legs.

"Jaune?" she asked with some trepidation. "You didn't bring back a dead body, did you?"

He blinked, and turned to look at what had her so worried. A coffin rested against the back of the couch, looming behind him.

"What, this? Oh, no no." He reached over, opening up the lid to show nothing inside, smiling to soothe the cat. "This is for me."

Tears began to pool at the corners of Escha's eyes. "...Jaune, are you going to die?"

Above her head, he sent a certain girl a deadpan stare, gesturing at the cat as proof that funerary-themed presents would never catch on. An unrepentant wink was the answer he received.

A sigh, and he said, "From how I hear it, everyone will someday."

"Geeze, that's a hell of a morbid thing to spring on a cat," Lisa remarked in a quiet tone.

"Gifts," he reminded them. "Let's focus on that."

Kneeling down, his hand swept over the floor, summoning flowers as he went, collected from mountains high and valleys low throughout his trip. From the wispy, pale petals of silk flowers to the ethereal glow surrounding the glaze lilies, they formed a tableau of many colors, as fresh as the very moment he picked them. Escha practically lit up at the sight, picking up an armful at once to breathe in the out of this world fragrance.

"Like them?" He got a nod. "Here, take this, too."

He passed her a seashell, a starconch shell from the Yaoguang Shoal, named for the five-pointed encrustments dotting its spiral surface. At his prompting, Escha held it up to her ear.

Confusion spread across her face, and she removed the shell, staring at it. Then, she pressed it harder to her ear. Despite the insurmountable distance, the sound of another world's ocean echoed within the shell.

He nudged her. "Cool, right?"

Escha agreed. Very cool.

By now, the newcomers had more or less formed a row in front of his little team, Bennett leaning on the dining table, Hu Tao bold and brash at the center, while Fischl lingered half a step back from them with Oz on her shoulder. For reasons unclear to him, their eyes trained on Escha with an unnerving focus, even more than an adorable and oh so fluffy long-haired cat measuring up to Jaune's thigh should garner. Still, since he deemed it as good a place to start as any, he set Lisa's presents aside for later and indicated the felyne.

"Everyone, meet Escha. A felyne, and a certified Palico of the Guild of Monster Hunters—"

"And she talks!" Fischl blurted out, unable to suppress the thought any longer.

"So does your bird," Lisa scoffed under her breath. Jaune frowned, and nudged her with an elbow. She… did not like that, judging from the glare.

Breaking off from her gaze, he turned back to Fischl. "You have Oz and I remember someone here talking with urns." That earned him a strange look from Lisa. "So yeah, I think your world has us beat on that front."

Oz the raven cleared his throat, chiming in, "You would find that most in Teyvat consider me an oddity. I cannot comment on the proclivities of Hu Tao, however." Hu Tao poked him, a mild reproach for his phrasing. A spark zapped her on contact and she hastily pulled her hand away. It made Jaune laugh as he continued speaking.

"It isn't seen as strange in Escha's world. Cats there go into battle alongside humans, and they're a deft hand at a lot of things." He jerked a thumb toward the window. "The garden is all her work, and she makes a number of devices that you might be interested in." Escha preened as he talked her up. "I visited her world a while back, and she chose to come along for the ride. Consider her your senior adventurer." That last part gained him a few dubious gazes, but it paid to establish the pecking order early on. He then addressed Fischl, who looked about ready to pounce. "She welcomes scritches, by the way."

"Always," Escha said with utmost seriousness. In a show of magnanimity, she offered up her chin, with Fischl descending at once to pet her.

"Does thou prefer this spot? Or this?" the girl asked, entranced by the soft fur. "Surely, thou art the cutest in all the land."

"You are, too!" Escha happily returned the praise, and Fischl almost died then and there.

Jaune left the pair to get acquainted, standing up. With a flourish, he introduced the girl next to him.

"And this, is Lisa Wilbourn, who also goes by Tattletale out in the field. She's my partner, and has been here since nearly the beginning of my travels."

At first glance, she must present as nothing special. A girl in need of sleep, with a sad cast to her looks that she couldn't quite conceal. Jaune wished that they could have seen her at her best, those days when she decided she was going to utterly ruin someone that deserved it.

Credits to her, she mustered an effort. A semblance of a grin, not very vulpine, appeared on her face that would fool those unfamiliar to her. A hand went on a cocked hip. "That's me. Kept him alive, gave him advice," Lisa airily listed out while checking her nails. "Handle the books, crunch the numbers. I do most of the thinking around here."

"Don't listen to her. I come up with half our plans." The risky ones that fail. "She does know a lot, though. If you have a question about how the stuff in this room works, she's the best one to ask." He was forgetting something… "Oh, right, and she has superpowers."

"Super… powers?" Hu Tao said, mulling on the term.

Jaune considered how to explain. "Think of it as a Vision, without needing a Vision. Instead, it's entirely within a person. Magic, if you want to call it that."

Understanding dawned, and she dropped a fist onto her palm. "Is that what the weird feeling in the back of my mind is? Aiya, you should have mentioned it," Hu Tao admonished, shaking her head. "I thought I caught an illness."

"Say what?"

Lisa cut in with a snort of amusement. "She's talking about [Blank] and [Mind Defense]. We bought the option to share them, remember? It would have activated when you dragged them here. How did you forget this?"

He winced, detecting the rebuke in her tone even if hidden behind a joking demeanor. In fairness, she was right that it completely passed from his mind, what with other, more pressing concerns occupying his attention.

"Okay, at least we know the cause, and it's nothing to worry about. I'll run through the details with all of you later," he told Hu Tao. His eyes narrowed. "And don't poke at it in the meantime."

He meant that as a jest, but it found a distracted audience. Hu Tao was gazing at Lisa with an inscrutable expression, one that Lisa interpreted with far better accuracy than him. It may be his imagination, but Lisa seemed to bristle.

Then, all of a sudden, the moment passed with Hu Tao breaking eye contact to beam at him.

"Too late. I already did it lots," she said. "What did you expect? You can't just leave things lying around unpoked, silly!"

He breathed a sigh. "I suppose that's just to be expected of you. Anyway, with me, this is the team as it stands. Boy, girl, cat. For various reasons, we've been going from world to world with the apartment serving as our base, although that last part should change soon."

Jaune panned his gaze around the room. Furniture, equipment, supplies, garden. The apartment had filled up over the months. Now, with three more people in the space, the cramped state of it had grown impossible to ignore.

"It's about time we find a bigger place."

"Sorry to have barged in, boss," said Bennett, catching on that, yes, their unplanned presence wasn't as trouble-free as Jaune had led them to believe while on the other side of the portal.

He waved it off. "Ahhh, quit fretting about that small stuff. It's—how does it go again, Lisa? Say lay something. Life happened. I wasn't going to leave you to get struck by lightning, and you didn't want to be there for it, either." He caught another questioning look from Lisa. "I'll explain that part later. Anyway, Bennett, you're up."

The other boy startled.

"Me?" He glanced left and right in the hopes for a volunteer to materialize out of thin air and go first. No luck, and with Jaune egging him on, he shuffled forward.

Dressed in shorts and short-sleeved shirt, Bennett could pass for a modern era boy. A person that Jaune spared a glance at, at best, on the city streets. Less colorful than others, and ordinary as they come. A fine choice to ease Lisa and Escha into the idea of new team members.

Bennett darted his eyes around, attention never staying long on any one thing. Shifting in a self-conscious manner, he said, "Okay. Right. Uhhh, something about myself. I didn't have parents, and my dad found me in the mountains."

Jaune nodded, and turned to Lisa. "That's right, and he works as…" He whipped his head back toward Bennett. "Wait, seriously?"

"Yup. It might have been inside a volcano, too."

"What an exciting start to your life," Hu Tao commented. Jaune waited for her to make a horribly bleak comment, but she only left Bennett with a simple "Good on you."

Seeming unused to remarks of that sort, Bennett rubbed the back of his head, overtaken by a bout of shyness. "Aw, thanks." The hand ran through ashen blonde hair that stuck up in a wild mess, tossed and turned by the wind without an effort at fixing it. "It's a pretty high bar for an adventure, even if I was too young to remember. To this day, I'm still trying to top it."

"Hence you joining the Adventurer's Guild at this age," Jaune reasoned. "Well, you will probably get that wish if you stick with us. Now that I can admit it without causing issues, I was downplaying those stories I told you on the road."

If the thought of being lied to offended the other boy, the promise of wilder tales of derring-do made up for it. Growing comfortable enough to regain his gutsy spark, Bennett bent at the waist in a bow directed at Jaune, Lisa, and Escha.

"I look forward to it," he declared, then turned to Lisa. "And I look forward to your guidance, miss. Boss told us a lot about you."

The remark took Lisa by surprise, but she soon recovered to offer him a sweet and soft smile. "Is that so?" A giggle invited laughter in kind. "I can see Jaune has left an impression on you."

Needless to say, everything about that rang the alarm bells in his head. She was overplaying her act, and he watched her with no small amount of concern.

"Now, who is this?" Lisa asked, and with that question she neatly seized the momentum of the conversation, leaning down to address a girl heretofore content to pamper a cat with pets, singling her out.

Where Bennett blended in, Fischl captured the eye. If she walked the city streets, people might mistake her for a student of the Huntsman Academies. An abundance of lace, frills, and fishnet compensated for the subdued purple and black colors of her dress. Very bold, in a way that contrasts her meeker moments.

Thrust into the spotlight, Fischl bloomed. Her posture straightened with aristocratic grace, and she tossed back her hair. A smirk found its way onto her lips.

(Meanwhile, the Hu Tao who was left ignored on the sideline bustled off to do her own thing, rummaging in the voluminous sleeves of her jacket. Jaune kept half an eye on her, just in case she got up to mischief.)

Fischl inhaled a breath, before introducing herself. "Among the myriad stars, one shines above all: the Immernachtreich," she said with a solemn hand placed over her heart, the eye not covered by an eyepatch closing. "I am its sovereign, Fischl, who some call the Prinzessin der Verurteilung. In my many lives, it is not often that I encounter such a manse as thine, resplendent in its mysteries yet welcoming to all guests." Eyes opened, and she swept an arm out in a grand fashion. "I extend to thee my utmost compliments!"

"Mein Fräulein means to say, you have a wonderful home and she is thankful that you have invited her to a sleepover," said the bird on her shoulder, to much sputtering from the girl.

"Oz, I am not lonely!"

"Please recall that I did not say you were, milady."

Amidst the argument between owner and pet/retainer/sentient lightning, Lisa observed the younger girl with wary focus. Her gaze lingered on the bright green of Fischl's one visible eye. Drifted to the head of blonde hair. They zeroed in on the hand ruffling and brushing through that very same hair, watching how it tucked stray locks back in their proper place.

Jaune took his hand away. "Whoops, didn't even know I was doing that."

"I don't mind," Fischl broke off from speaking with Oz to say in a small voice.

The girl maintained her long hair with great care, though its occasional frizziness due to stray zaps of her Electro powers vexed her to no end, Jaune had learned. And like a bad habit, some instincts never go away.

Having arrived at a conclusion, Lisa turned to him. "I'm sensing a certain pattern." She shooed away the hovering Hu Tao, and continued to give Jaune a dull, half-lidded stare. "Is there something you want to confess?"

"Total coincidence," he denied.

"Uh-huh," was her skeptical reply.

Fischl saved him from further scrutiny. "Indeed, it is a most incredible confluence of fate. Perhaps the blood of royalty, too, does flow in your veins to explain our similar features, Lisa. For history attests, oft have my kindred found themselves cast beyond the veil between the worlds, exiled to far-flung reaches by those that stalks fair Immernachtreich. Who can guess where they may settle?"

"Are you in the market for a little sister, Lisa?" Jaune interpreted, to Fischl's yelp of surprise. He bumped his shoulder with Lisa's, making the pitch in place of the younger girl. "She's not just an adventurer, but also an investigator for the Adventurer's Guild. Your skills kind of overlap with hers, while she and her familiar Oz make for a pretty solid guard detail. I can imagine her assisting you when we go traveling."

The falsely sweet smile once more greeted him.

"I'll think about it," Lisa demurred. "I am wondering why she is talking like that, though."

The remark jogged his memory, and Jaune snapped his fingers. "Oh yeah, I didn't tell you. Get this, she came from a different world than Bennett and Hu Tao before ending up there. An old-timey one where people still use thou and thee. Cool, isn't it?"

"Except she slips all the time," Lisa muttered. Jaune didn't quite follow what she was referring to, but he did catch the flash of hurt crossing Fischl's face.

"I think we've traveled to enough places to know that anything is possible out there in the universe, Lisa," he said, a trace of reproach coloring his words.

"Some mysteries have simple answers." Lisa dismissed the matter, turning her head. "And excuse me, but what are you doing? Please stop."

Upon being addressed, the last of the newcomers pulled back her measuring tape. She jotted down a note on a piece of paper, and that too she tucked inside her sleeve.

"Hee-hee. My apologies, dear client," said Hu Tao. Even with her flat cap, she stood a little shorter than Lisa. "Since you were so engrossed with your conversation, I thought I might use the chance to, how do you say, dig two graves with one shovel?" She pressed her palms together, and tilted her head. Her long twintails trailed nearly to the floor. "Hu Tao, the 77th Director of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor, at your service. Do you have time today to finish the fitting? My schedule has freed up, so I can squeeze you in right away."

"Did you mean that in a literal sense, or…" Jaune trailed off.

Hu Tao laughed. "Of course not! A coffin takes time if you want to do it properly. I can't just knock one out on short notice to put her in there."

Lisa opened her mouth. Closed it. She studied Hu Tao, then the nearby coffin.

With rings on her fingers, bracelets on her wrists, and painted nails, it wouldn't be unfair to call Hu Tao gaudy, and that carried over to the red irises and flower-shape pupils of her eyes. This impression clashed hard with the suit she wore that ran more along a theme of elaborate formality, creating a mess of confusion for most. In Lisa's case, the truth shone through.

"You're completely serious. This isn't a prank," she stated, earning a nod.

"My pride allows no less," said Hu Tao. "Everybody coming through my doors is offered the Wangsheng guarantee, that every body coming through my doors gets the best of care. And that starts with a proper coffin. From fine wood without a speck of rot to lacquer applied by brush and hand, our process ensures quality at each step for the last bed you will ever sleep on."

A chip cracked in her mask, and Lisa replied flatly, "I'll pass, thanks. Color me optimistic, but there's at least a few good years left in me before I turn old and decrepit."

Hu Tao sighed at the quick rejection.

"Aiya, we have a tough customer here." She walked over to Jaune's coffin. "I don't normally do this because the wrong size might lend you a mistaken impression, but since my regular stock isn't available…" Hu Tao put on a five-star service smile, and opened up the coffin lid. "Would you like to test out the product for a trial period?"

Was it strange that it annoyed him, seeing her make that offer with his coffin? It wasn't like he intended to put it to use for anything.

A beat, and Lisa reached out to gently push the lid shut. "No, really. I'm good," she insisted. A moment to think allowed her composure to reestablish, and she smiled indulgently at Hu Tao as if watching over a child, shaking her head with an air of finality. "I trust your expertise, but I actually plan to live forever."

Hu Tao scrunched her brows. "That sounds lonely."

Lonely, not blasphemous or a pipe dream. A glimpse into where her priorities lay. While his opinion ran along the same line as Lisa, Jaune thought that, maybe, he could understand where Hu Tao was coming from. To live on and on, it would be a forever full of hellos and goodbyes.

"If it works out, I'll live long enough to see us build ships that sail into space toward other galaxies," Lisa countered, shrugging her shoulders. And also making a lot of sense.

He certainly would like to experience for himself the so-called space age dreamed up in the comics. Portaling to such eras wouldn't count. The idea of it as a Remnant effort, his people's effort, held an irresistible appeal.

"Hmmm." Hu Tao tapped her chin, sending Lisa a teasing glance. "You believe that now, but just you wait until I have your coffin ready. One little lie-down and you'll be hooked, I'm sure of it. The padding I use to line the sides is to die for."

At that moment, Escha scurried over, tapping Hu Tao on the leg to get her attention.

"Are your coffins really that amazing? Will I get one?" she asked, apparently feeling left out.

Hu Tao knelt down to her eye level, and reached out to scratch Escha behind the ear. Soft purrs soon followed, with the felyne bouncing one foot in bliss.

"You do know that cats have nine lives, don't you?" said Hu Tao, her voice warm and mirthful. "Which one are you on now?"

Escha counted on her toe beans. After some hesitation, she looked up. "The first one?"

A light laugh, and Hu Tao patted the cat on the head before standing up. "Then you wouldn't be needing my services for a long time. Sorry, that's just how it is." Jaune's coffin creaked open again. "That said, you can give this one here a try if you like. It's very, very soft~" crooned the funeral director.

It should have looked endearing, but with the type of container involved all Jaune could think about were the fairy tales that featured a similar scene, with a wicked witch luring a poor, innocent soul into a trap. Escha must not have grown up with the same ones, because she was now happily ensconced inside the box and, from what he could tell, taking immense enjoyment from the plush, cushiony padding. Her eyes began to flutter shut, overcome with sleep while receiving pets from Fischl and Bennett.

Jaune took that as cue of the meeting running its course, something Lisa agreed with. The girl cleared her throat, speaking up.

"Hu Tao, Fischl, Bennett. Oz, too. Let me just say…" She met their gazes in turn, and winked. "It's wonderful to meet you. Welcome aboard."

Her words received a rousing cheer, or the best approximation of one when nobody wanted to wake up the cat. The display of friendliness led Jaune to relax.

Of course, he really should have known better than to bet on Lisa Wilbourn letting matters go. She stepped closer, into his space. At this distance, he couldn't ignore her or talk past her.

In a subdued monotone quite unlike seconds earlier, Lisa murmured, "Come with me." The voice lacked the bite of anger, sounding tired. Before he could argue, she addressed the room. "Everybody, please feel free to make yourself at home. Me and Jaune here need a moment to ourselves."

With that, Lisa spun on her heels and marched into the bathroom, leaving the door open for him.

The abrupt departure drew concern from everybody else, with much awkward shuffling. They glanced at one another to confirm that others saw it too and it hadn't been just them.

"Boss, is everything okay?" Bennett asked, hesitant.

Jaune gave them a bright smile.

"It's fine, no worries. This is about something from like days ago. As she said, make yourselves at home and I'll be back soon."

They accepted his reassurance at face value. Tension bled out of their postures, and the group broke up with the meeting's end. Escha snoozed. Oz flew off. The two adventurers began talking among themselves, discussing the fantastical room from another world with an air of marvel.

As Jaune followed after Lisa, his eyes met Hu Tao's. For one so willing to ignore the mood, she did not seem completely blind to it, sensing his uneasiness. The girl placed her hands together and performed a short bow, mouthing a quiet 'sorry' with a grimace.

He waved away the apology. They had plans, stuff got in the way, they reacted. Such was life.

C'est la vie. That was the phrase.



-o-
​


The door to the bathroom swung shut behind him, cutting out almost all sounds from beyond. Inside, the rhythm of ocean waves played from speakers, loud enough to grant conversations a measure of privacy. Lisa stood with her back to the sink, half-sitting on the long counter, a hand braced on the edge and the other clutching her book. Her silk robes still hung off of one shoulder, her hair tousled. She did not fix her disheveled appearance, nor did she speak.

Under her steady gaze, he walked over to stand beside her, an elbow planted on the gray wall so he could lean against it. There he waited.

Over time, the bathroom had evolved from its sterile, picture-perfect beginnings. Towels hung on a rack, his in green, hers in light purple. A smaller one in pink for Escha, who bathed in a small tub rather than the large shower stall that could accommodate at least two people with room to spare. A high-tech toilet claimed its own corner, the electronic screen turned on. A cord ran from it to an outlet by the sink.

A lot of good memories here, but he believed this would not be one of them.

"So, is this it?"

He almost missed that, so softly had Lisa spoken. As it was, his reply lacked much thought. He leaned down to look at her.

"What?"

Lisa studied the floor tiles. "Is this it? I couldn't carry my weight just once, I showed one little problem, and you went and got a new team? Loyal of you."

He pushed off the wall in a hurry.

"What, no. That wasn't it at all!"

Wrong answer. What even was the right answer? Her fingers curled to grip the counter, and she looked up to glare at him.

"Then, what was it? What am I supposed to think, when you decided on your own the very moment I'm not there to bring back a goth, a hick, and a cosplayer to our apartment?" she asked, with not even the semblance of a mask over her thoughts.

"She's… a funeral director," he said as a joke, hoping to lighten the mood. Wrong answer, again.

"Dressed like that? I don't think so. What's great about her, then? Or any of them? Must be special if you made out fine and dandy in that world without me."

"You were the one to push me out of the apartment, remember? Besides, it couldn't be helped—"

Bitter laughter cut him off.

"I wanted space," Lisa retorted. "Not for you to go off and do something stupid. How well do you even know them? That Fischl girl? A liar. The weirdo wants to put me in a coffin. The idiot—"

"They would have died," he said in a harsh tone, before regaining his cool. His reflection in the mirror behind the girl wore a scowl. To an extent, he anticipated less than a stellar reaction, but had thought it would be the usual annoyance, not for her to blow up on him. "Lisa, there were gods in that world, throwing down lightning like it's going out of style. It was a choice between evacuating them or digging graves."

"Why?"

He stopped short at that simple question, and Lisa continued.

"Why did these so-called gods want to kill them? Did it have anything to do with you?" Catching the way he winced, she hissed, "It did, didn't it?"

Before, he had resolved to tell her of his adventure. So now, he was resigned to the fact that he wouldn't be getting the reception he wanted.

Slumping back against the wall, he said, "On the first day there, I visited this harbor city. I went on a shopping trip. I drank tea."

"The attitude they had for you doesn't come from footing the bill for bubble tea," Lisa scoffed.

"I know." He heaved a sigh.

The possibility of lying more than he planned to do crossed his mind, but… Lisa wanted him to see her as part of the team, and he needed her to know that she already was. Right here, by his side. The one he trusted to see this harebrained idea of overturning what might well be an apocalypse.

He told the truth, or a version close to it.

"I… might have held a funeral for an undead half-god." He raised a hand before she could speak, speaking in a rush. "Half. Like, he wasn't close to the top of the food chain, and drowning to death the first time did a number on him. The risk had to have been pretty low, in my opinion, and it did give him a final rest, so all's well that ends well, I say."

Yes, he was babbling, hoping to strike on the magic words that would preempt her worries.

Quietly, softly, Lisa spoke. "And what does that have to do with anything?"

Jaune pointed to the bathroom door. "Those three? They were there, helping out. Somebody didn't like that. When I was about to leave that world, what looked like a typhoon was sweeping in, centered on us. Lightning fell nonstop. That was when Hu Tao got struck, and if I hadn't awakened her Aura earlier, you'd be meeting one less person today." No sooner had he said it that Jaune experienced a premonition. Lisa was about to focus on the wrong thing, the most inconvenient detail to his story.

"You gave them Aura."

He didn't deny it. Slowly, Lisa turned to the sink. The book dropped from her grip followed by elbows hitting the counter, and she dropped her face into her hands, massaging her temples.

"I told you," she whispered, in the manner of one barely keeping it together. "I told you, be careful of spreading that around. Do you get a kick out of being this impulsive?"

"I don't. You know that."

Her head shook back and forth. "I don't," she echoed him. "I just thought I did, and assumed that those times you said you'll do better, you wouldn't be lying to me." She whirled on him, with face red and a snarl on her lips. And trails of tears running down. "You keep doing unnecessary things, every time coming to me with a new excuse. Oh, you didn't use the word 'promise'. Oh, lives are in danger. Oh, lightning is randomly falling from the sky." Her eyes squeezed shut, hands balling into fists. "You have a hundred reasons why you don't have to listen to other people, and that makes it really, really hard to trust you, Jaune."

He flinched, her words seeming to slam into him with physical force to make him take a step back. Half a dozen protests sprang to his lips, all of them unable to gain a voice, his throat feeling so constricted that he imagined his breath cutting short.

Lisa continued, eyes opening. "If holding a funeral for the wrong person could set off one of the gods in that world, how do you think spreading Aura around will fare?"

This time, his tongue did not betray him. "That's not a fair comparison, Lisa," he argued. "You have no idea how those gods think."

"I can guess! I can connect the clues, because if you had forgotten now that you have swanky new teammates, that's my power! You marked them, and then you dragged them into your mess. It all added onto a pile of crap that made them undesirable to their world's rulers."

Could that be it? He fretted for a split second before shoving the thought aside, shooting back, "I was trying to keep them safe! In a world populated by monsters, why wouldn't I pass on the best defense for people to stay alive? It isn't my fault that a random being of omnipotent power I didn't know a lick about would take offense to me doing the same thing that worked out fine for Gallia."

"This isn't Gallia," Lisa spat out.

"I didn't know!" Jaune shouted, before amending, "Or I knew, but I thought it was a nonissue, because, again here Lisa, it was a god I hadn't even met." He rapped the wall on each word. "There's no predicting that. We go from world to world, and they're all different!"

At that, Lisa tilted her head, squinting at him. She gestured at herself. Up, down, up, down.

"That is why we research, and take it slow, and plan for contingencies—did you think I do all that for fun? Without me, the best thing you could have done was to stay put. Stay put," she stressed. "But you just…" A groan, and she made violent hand motions. "You keep talking about taking life as it comes, taking it one day at a time, except that doesn't actually work. You run from one crisis to another, always reacting until now when it bites you in the ass, because you already committed to your decision and couldn't take it back." She leaned forward to poke him in the chest, the volume of her voice rising louder and louder. "That's your problem, Jaune. It isn't anyone else's fault. Only yours."

Knock, knock.

They turned toward the door, so fast that both their necks cricked.

A lively, singsong voice drifted through from the other side.

"Hello, hello. Are you okay in there? The others are asking how you are doing, just letting you know~"

She heard, Jaune had no doubt. All of them did. His and Lisa's voices had carried further than they thought, lost as they were in snapping at one another.

The interruption led to a lull between the pair of them. He was still leaning on the wall, shoulders hunched and hands in his pocket, the posture screaming defensive. Lisa breathed hard, and pinned him with a seething glare. Hurt swirled behind her eyes.

Jaune got the impression that the past few days hadn't helped her as he hoped. Something burned within her, directed at him.

After a time, he licked his dry lips and spoke.

"I know that there are problems with how I do things. I'm not blind to it. But…"

Lisa looked about ready to go off on him again at that word. More excuses.

He waited.

Finally, curiosity got the best of her. One of her greatest flaws. "But?"

"But there is a limit to planning," he said, and exhaled a breath. "The nature of the portal is that we never have enough time, always too little information. The one constant I do know going in is that I could die."

Lisa watched him carefully. "So what? You think it makes you brave, walking into danger without a care. At some point, it becomes outright stupidity."

He shook his head. "I accept those risks, for what I can gain. It isn't thoughtless." He snorted a laugh, despite the situation. "Even though, you know, it's me."

A sneer greeted the comment. "Let me guess, you're going to tell me more of that tripe about how you had to save those poor, innocent saps, and heroics is about doing what you can for random strangers. It's all crap, Jaune. Lies people fed kids growing up that doesn't matter in the end." Tears swam in her eyes to undercut the hateful expression, and papers crinkled as she tightened her hold on her book. "Go on, tell me. What wonderful treasures have you found along the way that made the pain all worth it?"

Who was she talking to, with that faraway look? Him, but also not him, he felt.

Pondering on it, Jaune fished out his scroll. The boring, mundane one bought from a mall, special only to him.

"First of all, check out this picture of a fox I took. Lookit the lil' guy, bathing in a pond like it's his house. I got a ton of pictures on the trip." He cocked his head. "No, not cheering you up?"

His arms filled with an odd assortment of items, their bells chiming. The butt of a spear clanged against the bathroom floor, hooked in the crook of his elbow. An amulet inlaid with a gem landed on his palm.

Wings appeared on his back, feathers in the colors of the early morning sky.

"Magical artifacts, magical spear, magical powers that I still haven't figured out yet… As for this glider, how would you like to give flying a try?" He tried to smile. "See? It isn't just mushy, intangible feelings that I find in these places."

Most of the items vanished, and he moved over to Lisa to pass her the spear.

"I'm teaching you to use this, by the way." A hint, that he wanted her here.

Lisa examined the weapon from tip to tip, noting the detailed dragon motif. Lighter than its appearance suggested, a deft twirl sent it spinning around and around her wrist like a baton, an action that led Jaune to wonder where she learned that from.

The spear stopped, gripped in her hand. She looked up at him.

"Okay, it's done."

He blinked. "I hate saying this all the time, but… what? I'm missing something here."

"You screwed up, and now you've paid me to make up for it." She gave a nonchalant shrug of her shoulders, and walked past him. "What do I have to be mad about, right?"

Was that his thinking? Was that what he hoped for?

He grabbed her hand before she could touch the doorknob.

"It isn't about the spear or any of the other stuff. You were right," he blurted out.

She turned back toward him. And yeah, now he could tell that his approach had worsened the situation. Seen in a different light, carefree could also mean uncaring. Lightening the mood translated to avoiding the issue. Friendliness, to flippancy.

Her hand in his, he confessed, "More than any of that, I stayed in that world, and did what I did, because it meant I got to see something that shouldn't have been. The yaksha, the man who saved countless lives only to drown and wind up an evil spirit, his fate was to suffer forever. Actual punishment from the gods kind of deal. Ordained by the heavens, a person told me." He swallowed, heart thumping as his mouth formed the next few words. "I changed that fate."

He had done it in Gallia. In Brockton Bay. In Academy City. The world went careening down one path, until he stood in the way and forced it onto a different track.

"My actions aren't always for the better, but they also aren't always for ill. One thing I know is true, I created the story I hoped to see, and… and that means the world to me. Because of me, what could have been ended in another way. That was what I really wanted. I'm sorry."

And to that confession, Lisa laughed a hopeless, acidic laugh. Resignation and despair, in one.

"That is so typical of you."

Her lips wobbled. She blinked away tears, and brought her face close to his, close enough that he felt her breath on his skin.

Teeth bared in an unkind, vulpine grin.

"Hey Jaune?" Lisa asked sweetly. "Do you want to hear a story of 'what could have been'?"

She gave him no chance to refuse, tugging on his arm to pull him toward the sink counter, where she hopped on its surface. A hand patted beside her, inviting him to sit. Once he had done so, she made a show of making herself comfortable, shifting from one side to the other with her legs swinging off the ground. The thick sheaf of paper bound by metal rings landed on her lap, and she placed both hands atop it, clasped together.

A glance at him, and she nodded in satisfaction. He was paying attention. She leaned back, eyes kept forward.

And… she told him a story.

"There once was a girl who made her home in a city by the sea. It wasn't the happiest of lives that she led, but she stayed for her friends."

Lisa paused. Her lips twitched, and she whipped her head towards him.

"No, she stayed for the money. No, she stayed because she was forced to. No, she stayed to make a difference."

With each change to the tale, she moved her face closer and closer to him. The grin filled his vision, a rictus of humor laughing at a joke only the girl understood.

"In the end, she stayed."

Lisa pulled back, her gaze returning to the far wall. The grin softened.

"Bombs fell. The sea rose. Monster after monster crawled out from beneath the bed. She didn't let it get to her. Each and every time the troubles came, she met it head on, and after it was over, she would rebuild her home. Maybe not exactly to what it was, maybe not for the better, but she gave her all to put Humpty Dumpty back together again. Because she saw something there, and she put her life into that city until she found it.

"Hey Jaune, do you know what she found?"

This time, he didn't try to joke.

"Friends," he guessed. "Money. Her freedom. That she made a difference."

Lisa covered her mouth, giggling. "All very good guesses. Look at you, mister good listener."

She put her hand back on the book, playing with the pages by riffling through them.

"She found that she was okay."

Jaune frowned at that answer. "Just okay?"

"Hehe. Dumb, isn't it? How small. It's the truth, though. You see, she made a lot of mistakes. She did some things right, too, but it was tough balancing out the scale. Due to that, she grew into a woman different from what she imagined as a little girl, different from what she was at the start of the story. Someone she, or a version of her, would become 'just' okay with.

"But you know, I want that. Reading through the glimpses of her life, I can admit that I really, really want that. Except, on a spring day near the start of it all, a boy swept through her city and that was her story gone, that he ruined, because he took her away."

Jaune, in a quiet voice, said, "Ruined?"

He hated how small he sounded.

Lisa looked away.

"Changed," she amended. "Seeing yourself on the pages is strange. The certainty of knowing who you are. I thought this was a good direction, getting away from Brockton Bay, but… it would have forged me. I don't know who I am becoming anymore."

"Is that other life better than what you have now? It couldn't be sunshine and rainbows."

A thumb brushed over the title of the book. Worm.

"I can't rightly say. My part comes and goes; they're snippets of a larger whole. The ending wasn't that great." Her lips quivered. "I do know, at least, that there would have been a moment where I thought I was at the top of the world. It wouldn't last. A lot didn't. Life is like that. But it's a feeling I want to feel."

And that moment was gone.

For him to stand at the center of someone else's story, meant pushing them out of place.

Lisa slid off the counter. Many thoughts ran through Jaune's mind, to stop her, to apologize, to argue and say it wasn't his fault. Before all of that could come to pass, she reached out and patted him on the arm. The hand lingered, warm and kind. Then, she walked away.

He spoke aloud, to her back.

"I can't return that moment to you."

Without breaking stride, she nodded in acceptance.

He watched her go, fingers rapping on the counter. Tok. Tok. Tok.

"I can give you a new moment. Maybe not as her, or as a hero, or even as someone happy, but a moment worth living for."

Lisa stopped for a beat, thinking. She turned her head. On her lips, a ghost of a smile.

"I told a little lie. Life might not have led me there anyhow, even without you. I don't know where it started, only that her world and mine differed in small ways."

The door opened, and shut behind Lisa.

"But I'll hold you to that."
