#5,417

Chapter 67: A Place to Call Home
​


Sunlight streamed through the window curtains, heralding a new day with its soft, warm shine.

Jaune assumed, anyway.

Rather than sunlight, he woke up with darkness surrounding him on every side. A deep and tranquil silence enclosed him from the worries of the world, so comforting that it felt akin to a hug.

His internal clock informed him it had been but a few hours since he laid down, four or five at most. Yet, energy brimmed within his body, his mind reveling in the sensation of a well-rested night. He rolled one shoulder to stretch it out, marveling at the lack of a crick or pop.

He had never felt more alive.

Pushing aside the cover, the light of the morning greeted him. He sat there for a time, enjoying those first few minutes by basking in its radiant beauty. Only after braving the dark could a person truly appreciate the sunshine.

"That was… better than I thought it would be," he finally said, to nobody in particular.

A bracing lungful of air, and he was ready to meet the day, swinging up to stand on his feet.

As his gaze swept across the room, the question of why so many people were in the apartment caused him a brief moment of consternation. Then, the events of yesterday caught up, and he relaxed.

On the air mattress where he usually slept, Lisa laid with arms and legs sprawled unreservedly, Escha lying atop her stomach and using her chest as pillows. Over by the couch, Bennett snored away in an uncomfortable position, half his body falling off the edge, head pressed to the floor. Meanwhile, the bed in the corner played host to a snoozing Fischl buried beneath a blanket, with a soft smile on her lips telling of sweet dreams. Next to her was Hu Tao, twintails untied and cascading around her.

Six people, including him. Seven, with that bird there. That equaled out to a whole lotta crepes he needed to make.

Not long after, the scent of cooking wafted over the apartment.

Slices of ham sizzled in a pan, while batter turned into thin sheets of dough in another. One folded into the other, along with cheese and fried eggs, forming a mouth-watering savory crepe that joined its brethren on a plate, stacking high. A different plate carried a pile of plain crepes, meant for those who preferred the cream and fruits variety. Ingredients for a healthy smoothie waited beside the blender until a time when the machine could turn on without causing those still in bed an undue bother.

Soon, the hearty aroma of breakfast roused his companions. He could hear them shifting, the fog of sleep competing with rumbling stomachs. Noses sniffed the air, no doubt wondering from whence the heavenly scent came. He began dicing up bananas and strawberries on a cutting board just as the earliest awake padded over to the kitchen.

He believed them Lisa at first, but no. That smuggest of smug grins belonged to someone else today, stolen as the fox dozed in happy dreams. Dressed in borrowed clothing, Hu Tao resembled any other ordinary girl.

"Gooood morning!" she said, hands clasped behind her back as she swung her shoulders from side to side. "Hee-hee. How. Did. You. Sleep?"

With each word, she inched closer and closer, her face practically glowing with anticipation. He could read it in her eyes. I told you so, I told you so.

He glanced at the open coffin, his bed for the night. The discussion over who would rest where had taken a number of twists and turns, was all he would say on the matter.

"Honestly, you do good work. That was one of the best sleep I had. Somehow."

That had her beaming.

"The feel of a coffin is amazing, isn't it?" She closed her eyes, hugging herself. "That warmth, that sense of the world shrinking down to fit you. I worked really hard on the posture support, if you happened to notice it." She gave a long, sweet sigh. "All at affordable prices."

The wooden casket failed to hold a candle to the air mattress—that piece of tech was night magical. Still, it did possess a certain something beyond mere wood and fabric that he found difficult to describe.

As an amateur cook, the answer came to him in a flash. "Did you make it with love?"

"With a saw," she corrected. "And lots of lacquer. Everything is better with lacquer."

Ah.

Hu Tao lingered in the vicinity as he prepared their meal, using this chance to watch how a person went about operating the various appliances the proper way. She also tried to pinch slices of banana, only to be rebuffed on each attempt by a flick to the back of her hand. It would take a better food thief than her to pilfer morsels from him, for he grew up with the best.

She did get her sneaky bites in, once he set her to the task of dicing the fruits. His mother taught him that trick, through firsthand experience if nothing else. Those willing to help out in the kitchen were allowed their rewards.

In any case, with that part taken care of, he could focus on the frying—

"Oh. Lisa."

Jaune stepped back from the girl he almost crashed into. At what point had she arrived, he did not know, but she looked like she had just rolled out of bed, hair mussed and silk robes askew.

"G'mning," she grumbled, barely coherent.

That marked the extent of their talk, the both of them falling into a silence of awkward shifting and eyes that never meet. Jaune found an avid interest in the pans on the stove, mechanically cooking crepes with the excuse that they couldn't be left to burn. A part of him hoped for some space, another took heart that she had interacted with him.

One crepe, two crepes, three crepes, four crepes, five crepes, six crepes, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven…

"The bathroom is free," he finally said. An inoffensive remark that shouldn't hurt anyone.

Out of the corner of his eyes, the head of blonde hair shook.

"Nah, I'll help out," Lisa muttered.

He turned to her with a flutter in his chest. Was she… trying to mend bridges? He couldn't rightly recall another occasion where she had done it first. Most times, if not each time, it fell to him.

"Do you want to learn how to flip crepes?"

"Mm, maybe. Is it hard?"

"Not at all." He scooted to the side. "Come over here. Now, you have Aura, so there's no need to worry about burns…"

And on it went, the spaces within the silence filling with innocuous comments that strung together to create a conversation. They kept it related to the cooking, and tried for simple gestures here and there to establish their old rhythm. Lisa learned the dish he liked; he got to see her smile.

"Ooh, that looks fun. Can I give it a go?"

"You're a little behind the times, so better not. I wouldn't want this complicated modern tech to confuse you."

"..."

"..."

Lisa and Hu Tao seemed to be getting along like sisters, too. A good morning all around.

By the time they sat down for a meal, it would not be incorrect to think everything had, if not returned to normal, then pretended as such.

With the extra people, breakfast in the apartment enjoyed a louder time of it than most days. A look across the table revealed the morning birds from the night owls. Escha belonged to the former, bright-eyed and bushy-tailed as she competed with Bennett, the pair scarfing down their food with gusto. Fischl, unlike them, stayed in somewhat of a daze, poking at her plate with a fork and missing half the time, while Oz plucked and tucked her hair to straighten it out. Lisa had no feathery pet to provide the same service, and so stuck to a comb. A cup of coffee helped her fight back the pull of sleep.

As the meal wound down, the mood gave way for serious business.

Not really.

"Six people. One bathroom. The situation cannot hold," Lisa stated, looking from person to person.

Of all the impetus to get their plans moving, it had to be this issue.

"We can mess about with this and that solution, but the simplest answer is one we've been bouncing around." She looked at him. "Are we agreed?"

The decision came down to him and her, not anyone else. The cat cared little of their destination, the rest of them too new to provide input. Jaune nodded to the question.

"Good. Give me the phone."

"Scroll," he countered.

"..."

The Company scroll exchanged hands. He did not comment on her missed timing.

Before Lisa had the chance to find out from the device, he admitted a certain problem, "I spent some of the Points. It was just from my own share."

She noticed his tone, the careful mannerisms. A glance at the screen confirmed how much he was understating it with that 'some'. He prepared for an argument, but none came.

"Got it." Lisa left the many issues unsaid, breaking out the laptop. She booted it up. "That's going to change things. Puts the kibosh on the accelerated start we wanted." She navigated to a document, a list that she had made extensive notes in. From energetic Bennett to drowsy Fischl, everyone gathered around to watch the enigmatic machine along with Lisa's sorcerous workings (spreadsheets). "A little higher in terms of danger, less in the loot rating. It might be more difficult, or even impossible, for us to get a return on the world beyond restocking everyday supplies."

Despite himself, he flinched upon hearing the assessment. His actions had crippled them, by Lisa's reckoning. Hard not to feel guilty about that.

"We'll make do, and I'll find ways to fix it," he said. "How does it affect the other criteria? Do you still see any places you recognize?"

Lisa hummed, delaying an answer as she scrolled past world after world in an infinite catalog. Until, she stopped on one. "This universe was on my list. I know the starting location and it's a pretty good spot to put down roots, especially if we hit a good year." She checked her spreadsheet. "Ratings… pretty survivable, not totally empty. It ticks our biggest concerns. I think we have a winner."

"It's not Grand Blue, is it?"

"No."

"Great." Meeting a different version of a friend, he experienced it before and had enough of that already. It wouldn't end well, was the lesson he learned.

"Uh, boss, boss lady? What's going on?" Bennett asked, scratching his head, expressing the sentiment shared by the rest of the newcomers.

Jaune looked up from the laptop, a tad miffed that the other boy had promoted Lisa to a new title. Because he earned his from fighting monsters and watching out for his dear junior. What had Lisa done? Hmph!

"What's going on is that all of you are about to get your trial by fire," he said, and snickered at the sudden apprehensiveness to their faces, Lisa joining him with a none-too-kind smirk slipping out. A lightbulb blinked on above Escha's head a second later, to make three smug countenances arrayed before Bennett, Hu tao, Fischl, and Oz.

"Now, who wants to go to another universe?"

Surprisingly, every hand went up. Intrepid, curious, or just plain stupid, whichever the case, they weren't backing down from the challenge.

Time to head on, toward a new world.



-o-
​


"Aiya, why is it so loud?" Hu Tao said, eyes scrunched shut and hands over her ears. She peeked out from under her eyelashes, trying to get used to the deluge of stimulation.

That was one down.

Hands on hips, Jaune looked around. "This many cars will do that. All the people, too. Whoa, there's a lot." He felt a tug on his sleeve. Fischl had been staying close to the group, unwilling to drift off like Bennett.

"The odor emanating from the nether realms forebodes an imminent cataclysm," she said, fully on guard. "Should we be worried?"

That was two down.

He pointed at her. "Good question. Not even the docks of Vale come close to this stench. Lisa?"

"That's just how it is, you'll get used to it. Whatever, not important… Everybody, welcome to New York City!"

New York, New York. Their (possible) new base.

What a busy place.

Vehicles packed the streets, gridlocked worse than he had ever seen. They honked their horns together in a chorus of misery and rage. People walked at a near running pace, eyes locked forward as if they all had someplace to be, often forming together in a tide that tossed about the unfortunate stragglers who failed to keep up. The sheer numbers gave rise to an amount of litter that boggled the mind, plus a thousand scents to assault the senses.

Beyond that, though?

Wow.

"Boss, how is any of this possible?" Bennett maintained his composure well. His voice only cracked at the end. The boy's head was tipped back to look up, up, up at the skyscrapers looming above them.

Jaune had no answers for him, except, "Earth's crazy like that."

Academy city. Seoul. Now, here. The pattern held across distance and time. Unchecked by the Grimm threat, the many Earths out there bloomed without limits. The concrete jungle of New York put Vale's to shame. It almost felt hard to breathe with how the city seemed to block out the world.

While the party gawked, the sole native (in spirit) among them left their little circle and moved toward a newsstand, gleaning for information from the papers, the vendor, the customers, and probably a dozen other little details that nobody but she could put together in a coherent picture.

Aaand, she stole somebody's wallet. Dammit, Lisa.

"Was that necessary?" he remarked as she rejoined the group, a hotdog in one hand, newspaper in the other, bought with her ill-gotten gains.

"Would you rather we wander around as homeless beggars? Because that's stupid. Besides, he deserved it." Lisa caught the skepticism on his face. She scrunched her nose, displeased. "What? Don't you trust me?"

Jaune backpedaled. "I do. I just, you know, wanted to hear your reasoning. Forget it."

One moment, things seemed fine. The next, an argument looked about primed to blow. He didn't know where the shaky ground between them might collapse.

Someone nudged him in the side.

"Care to let us in on the joke?" Hu Tao asked, popping her head around him. "It sounded like Lisa here took something she shouldn't." No judgment colored her eyes, not yet. Still, it occurred to Jaune that he hadn't taken the measure of his new companions in regard to certain matters. The lapse would require easing into, over the coming days.

"I haven't told you this," he said, motioning at Lisa, "but her mind makes her possibly the best detective you'll ever meet. If she says that person is evil, chances are, he is."

That drew the notice of Fischl, who ceased her gawping to step out from behind Jaune. "The best detective? A bold claim, my erstwhile landlord. Many have enjoyed such a reputation, only to find it a mistaken pride. Even I, Fischl, would hesitate to seize that lofty title."

Lisa giggled, a sweet and lovely sound, leaning in to tap Fischl on the nose like she thought they were close.

"Awww, is that a challenge I hear? Now, while I always welcome that…" Her finger trailed down to catch Fischl under the chin, tilting her head up and locking their gazes together, their face inches apart. In the same friendly tone, she continued. "You have to ask yourself, Fischl, if that really is your name, whether you've learned enough of the clues to solve the mystery. If so, I don't see why we shouldn't give it a shot." Another giggle, as she separated from the younger girl, who shrank away.

Jaune resisted the urge to facepalm.

Dominance, asserted. Dammit, Lisa. Again.

"H-How astute, a-and I shall treasure thine wisdom. Yes, perhaps such a game would be better served on a more opportune occasion." Fischl hiccuped. "A duel as ours needs not interfere with your search for a new home." Her eyes swam, and Fischl looked everywhere except at Lisa. "In fact, allow me to host you for a most splendiferous tea party, where we may exchange tales of past cases and clash wits at our leisure. In private."

"No comment," said Oz on her shoulder, who also struggled to meet anyone's eyes. A scrap of fabric tied to him like a hood hid his electrifying physiology from the people passing by, lending him the mere impression of a very exotic bird.

A wide grin grew on Lisa. "That's what I thought you'd say." She turned away from Fischl, dismissing the matter and the girl, to offer Jaune a hotdog while keeping the newspaper for herself. "Authentic New York cuisine. Give it a taste."

"...Thanks? I'm not sure what brought this on, but I'll take it."

He nibbled on the food, finding nothing out of the ordinary compared to a regular hotdog. They used beef instead of pork, maybe. Lisa seemed to expect an actual review, however, so he muttered a few praises to placate her before offering it to the others. Escha and Oz both dove for it, the pretense of normal animals nearly forgotten.

A couple of people stopped to record the scene. None of them appeared overly amazed, amused at best, so Jaune chalked it down as them expressing a passing interest. A few of the phones turned toward the human side of their group due to the fanciful clothes among some of their members, murmurings of 'Is there a cosplay event today?' and 'Are they models?' passing from lips to lips. Those were a bit too prying, prompting him to turn his back to them.

"I've been to NYC, like, twice in my life," Lisa mentioned absentmindedly as she skimmed the news articles. "Both times as a kid. First thing I always do, I get a hotdog. It's part of the experience."

Welp, now he felt guilty for not enjoying the hotdog more. Lisa recited that piece of knowledge with faint traces of innocence, her voice that of someone who had heard of the mystical land of New York from others, and believed it.

"Anyway, from what I can tell, this world suits our needs perfectly. I'm seeing articles on the economy, celebrity marriages, football scores. Boring things. Safe things. There's a couple of weird bigfoot yeti stuff that's out of place, but they're all kept to the back pages where relevance goes to die, sooo—oh, I almost forgot. We're in the year 2022."

"Yeah, that number means nothing to me. What day is it?"

"Wednesday."

That, he had a reference for. Nothing happens on Wednesday.

Out of habit, he checked the time on his scroll. It provided no useful information, of course. The scroll went back in his pocket, while he turned to the sky, judging for a rough estimate.

"We're, what, around noon right now?"

"10:30-ish," Lisa provided.

"Nice. Real estate offices should be open, then." With a thought, his Pocket pinged back to him the presence of the sphere-like device sitting inside the dimensional space. An anchor, it came with their purchase of a permanent access to this world. Activating it would move the portal from the dingy gap deep inside an alley and hidden behind a dumpster to wherever he set the sphere. "You think we can get a place by nightfall?"

"You wish. A vacation rental on a Japanese island was one thing. They didn't have any real way to confirm the authenticity of our fake IDs, "she said, referring to the customizable cards they got from Aleister Crowley back in Academy City. "Property deals in the big city will check us for a proper background. We'll need a whole lot more than a driver's license."

"Are there not temporary hostels?" Hu Tao chimed in. "Slip a fellow a few extra Mora, ask nicely, and I'm confident we can secure accommodation without trouble."

"Ew," was Lisa's opinion. "You can do that if you want to. I'd rather not end up in some skeevy 'hotel' with an organ-trading gang bashing down the door to ruin my beauty sleep."

Jaune's eyes narrowed. "Is that likely?"

"Ehhh." Lisa waggled her hand in a 'maybe' gesture.

If they slept here tonight, he'd lay down a few traps just in case. Not for his sake, but for the intruders who would otherwise find themselves facing a Huntsman with a sword.

"Public order must leave a lot to be desired, then," Hu Tao mused. "Let's keep it in mind." She directed that comment to Fischl and Bennett, getting nods in return.

"Be careful swinging your staff," he warned her, but Lisa barged in with different advice.

"Don't bring your weapons into it at all! That's not normal here. I don't see indications of superpowers or Aura, which pretty much guarantees us as the strongest people around. Unless you have a solid case of self-defense, it's enough to beat them to a pulp with your fists. More than that invites scrutiny."

Bennett and Fischl appeared none too sad about that, agreeing without a fuss. He, on the other hand, lamented the prospect of a swordless, de-lanced, ungunned existence. Still, better this than having Grimm at their doorstep.

"Alright, fine," he said. "Identity first, house hunting second. Put people in hospitals, not graves." Hu Tao was inconsolable. "We'll figure out the best way to trade the gold for local money somewhere along the way. Tell me you have an idea."

"When do I not?" Lisa answered in an airy tone. "We're in a city. And a city always has an underground. I'll go and check the usual places."

"Got it. What are the chances we'll see fighting?" His hand flexed, limbering up for battles to come.

"In a library? Low."

He stared at her in askance, before understanding dawned. "You know, I was under the impression of it being an actual underground, with a shady barman and stone cold serial killers lurking in the dark corners, but then I realized how silly that sounds."

"What century are you from? I'm just going online."

"Useful thing, the inter-net. My Remnant's version can't do half of the stuff you get up to. You sure you won't need me there?"

"I highly doubt it, but if you're feeling like picking up a book…"

The tepid look on his face provided her the answer. There were times to read, on rainy evenings and whatnot. Today called for something more active. He had energy to burn.

Hang on, when even was the last time he read a book?

To his deliberate silence, Lisa nodded and continued. "Yeah, I thought so. You can stay around here if you like. Chill out for a while, and keep an eye on the kiddies—"

"Wait!" Fischl interrupted.

She missed the flash of displeasure that slipped through Lisa's friendly demeanor. Jaune could get away with cutting Lisa off, because he was adorable. And while Fischl could perhaps claim the same, she hadn't the weeks and months with which to endear the supervillainess. Without him interceding by miming for Lisa to let it go, Lisa might well have sniped a comment at the younger girl.

The oblivious Fischl gamely pressed on. "A library?" Her eyes sparkled at the word. "May I go with you? Please?" She clasped her hands to her chest, sighing. "Ohhh, to wander the halls of knowledge of an entirely different world, why, I shan't pass up the chance."

"Mein Fräulein is dying ("Did someone say 'dying'?" "Figuratively, Miss Hu Tao.") to find a series to read, since her favorite author has not released a new volume in quite some time," said Oz.

Hearing that, Jaune placed his thumb on the scale. "Lisa? Why not take her along? It isn't a bad idea. She could learn a lot from you."

Lisa pointed a finger at him, a retort on her lips. The finger then curled back, and she held her chin in thought. Jaune saw his opening, lightly nudging Fischl to direct over to Lisa's side. With her joyfully ensconced next to the older girl, it would take a monster to rebuff Fischl at this point.

As for himself, Jaune stepped back, and hooked an arm around Bennett's neck. "Yo. Want to stick with me?"

"Sure thing, boss! I'll probably get lost trying to navigate this place, otherwise." He scanned their surroundings, still with that same look of awe. "There's just… so much."

Lisa's gaze went from her side, which now included Hu Tao, to theirs. "Boys and girls, then?"

"Nah," Jaune said, shaking his head. Crouching down, he petted Escha. "Join my team, Escha. I'm thinking we're going to hit a park. Stretch our legs, get fresh air." Do some combat training—I probably shouldn't be keeping that from Lisa. "Do some combat training. Maybe explore the neighborhood. It should keep us occupied for a few hours."

"Combat training?" The beginning of a scowl formed on Lisa's face. "You can put that off. This isn't a good time for it."

"No."

"Excuse me?"

His hand came up to massage his neck. He maintained the smile. "This kind of thing is important. Bennett's a decent fighter, but he could be even better. Since our styles are so similar, I have a few tips that he'll need if he's to follow us around to the places we go. Bennett, what's your feeling on becoming stronger?"

"Well… Adventuring is rough work, and I'll take any chances I have to be prepared." Convinced, he nodded. "Yeah, I'm with you."

He turned back to Lisa. "See? I'm letting you know because I don't want you to see it as a nasty surprise, that's all. I'm still doing it."

Lisa regarded him coolly for a bit, before rolling her eyes.

"Find a secluded spot with lots of trees. If anyone stumbles on you, tell them you're LARPing and get out of there."

"Sounds good. And hey, call me if you need anything. I'll come running."

All the plans in the world didn't mean much with no directions. A couple of fruitless attempts at waving down pedestrians later, Lisa went back to the hotdog stand. Seven hotdogs got her a step-by-step guide to reach a library, one for a park, and a request for a date. She ignored that last one.

Prior to splitting up, Jaune leaned in for a small word.

"Is Fischl not who she says she is? Do we have an impostor among us?"

Lisa pursed her lips, mulling on her answer. "It's… unclear. That girl answers to the name like it was her own, but when she refers to herself as Fischl, it doesn't always ring with the truth. Her mouth tries to shape a different letter before she catches it."

"Huh. Maybe ask her about it when you're at the library." He raised a finger to stop her from leaving. "Don't push too hard. Let's not make her cry."

"I won't. Who do take me for?"

"Lisa Wilbourn," he deadpanned, as if that said it all.



-o-
​


"Woe be upon ye!"

Jaune gawked at the raggedy stranger encountered on the trail. "Is that a prophecy? Wow! Hey, can you tell me what I'm facing? What kind of monster is it? When—hey, wait! Where are you going?"

Sadly, the man wanted no more part of it, of him, hurrying off with bundles of pamphlets held in his arms.

"Jaune, Jaune, what was that guy talking about?" Escha asked once their group was alone again.

"I don't know, Escha, but I wished I did. Ah well, I'm sure I can handle whatever it is. Come on, let's move further in."

They continued down the trail, one of the many twisting paths running through a wooded area smack dab in the middle of New York City. Apparently, people called it the Ramble, part of the city's Central Park. Escha and Bennett went ahead of him, racing each other and often disappearing among the trees to follow whatever had caught their fancy.

The paths here traced back and forth to form an intricate maze, and the deeper Jaune traveled, the fewer people he met. With the trees blocking the views of the buildings in the distance, it gave him the sense of having taken a step out beyond the walls, into the wilds.

Even if it was an illusion on this occasion, he enjoyed the feeling, recalling the day he stood at the gates of his hometown, and the day he stood in front of a portal to a new world. His people had given up a lot for the sake of safety, but the call to adventure, the desire to wander and roam, it surely dwelt within them still, as it did for him.

Or maybe that was just the delusion of a small town boy looking for more than a small town end.

He soon settled on a promising spot, a flat stretch of rocky terrain set off the trail. Copses of trees provided a measure of privacy, though he deemed it a needless precaution. They hadn't met another soul for quite some time. He directed Bennett to stand opposite him, and then the training began.

First thing, he summoned the malfunctioning shield of Crocea Mors from his Pocket, tossing it to Bennett to use in place of his own.

"Better that you have that while we train," he said, arming himself. "My sword doesn't have a workable scabbard at the moment that I can use to blunt the impact, so it'd slice right through your wooden shield. I'll pick up a new one for you soon."

"Thanks, boss." Bennett studied the emblem on the surface. "I like the design." He strapped the shield to his arm, testing the weight. "Is it supposed to be this heavy?"

"You jumped from nothing to wood to metal. It is only heavy in your mind."

"Whoa, that's so deep," Bennett said, eyes shining. Nearby, Escha marveled at his sage wisdom.

It was nice to be appreciated. Lisa would have laughed at him for spouting that drivel.

His blade spun in lazy circles as he considered how to proceed from here. Should he set his student to performing drills? Run down the list of various tips and tricks he learned from experience about combat, so Bennett wouldn't suffer them in turn? In the end, he chose neither.

"Bennett, this is up to you. I can go easy, or I can put you through the training regimen cooked up by a friend of mine. To warn you, it will be harder."

The other boy answered without a pause, "Give me the second option." He saluted with his sword. "I'll smash through it!"

With a laugh, Jaune pointed at Bennett.

"I like that enthusiasm. Keep it up, and get ready."

Bennett laughed, too. "Aw, thanks, Boss—" His eyes bulged out, and he whipped the shield above his head.

WHAM!

Stone shook, and birds in the surroundings took flight en masse. The overhead swing sent Bennett crashing to the ground, knees buckling until he was folded flat against the rocky surface they stood on.

Jaune backed away. By the time Bennett managed to sit up and peer over the rim of the shield, the boy saw Jaune with his sword idly swinging at the empty air, a bright and happy smile on his face.

"Now, I know what you're thinking: Am I just beating you up?" Jaune said. "It's called the Pyrrha method, and trust me, it works. You need to understand why a shield is needed. There's no better teacher for that than live combat. It lets you measure your progress." He averted his gaze. "Also, I've been missing a sparring partner and Escha refuses to step up."

Crouched in a ball off to the side, Escha peeked through her paws at them. The moment his gaze fell on her, silent question beaming across the distance, she frantically shook her head and covered her eyes again. The heartless felyne spared not a speck of concern for her junior, giving Bennett up for dead.

Bennett muttered something under his breath.

Jaune leaned forward. "What was that?"

Resolute eyes looked up at him.

"I'm not done yet!" Bennett cried, and scrambled to his feet, charging in with sword aloft.

And that was how, three for three, the Teyvat bunch suffered woe today.

Jaune went easy—

No, he lied. He went predictable on Bennett. Big swings, telegraphed blows. He left aside the tricks of his trade, those tools he learned to incorporate in active battle, in lieu of the enhanced strength from various sources, employing moves that allowed Bennett plenty of time to respond.

In relative terms. He cheated whenever the other boy seemed to figure out his rhythm. Bennett might not even realize how fast he himself was moving as he struggled to keep pace.

Throughout the spar, Jaune watched. His sword struck from the left, from the right, over and under, to test how well did the other boy maintain his defenses. Hardly ever the same attack twice in a row, sometimes exactly that to observe the way Bennett's footwork fared while in motion. He pushed, and judged if Bennett had a grasp of when to break off and when to commit, could the boy hold his own in a prolonged exchange. This first round, he wanted to assess what he was working with.

More than that, he needed to know. What would Bennett do, when facing an insurmountable opponent.

"You're not half bad," Jaune praised. "Hands down, you would have thrashed the me from half a year ago."

"Thanks, boss!" Bennett gasped, bracing for a kick that sent him skidding backward. Without a pause, he threw himself back into the fray. And thus, Jaune learned the core of him.

Single-minded determination. The trait that shone through in the sweat-soaked, half-dead boy.

Their time in Teyvat had not been a lie. Bennett was just that way.

Pyrrha would have both admired and scolded the young adventurer for it. Jaune followed her lead, in a fashion.

His fist cracked against Bennett's chin, faster than Bennett could get his shield in place. A foot placed on the shield, he pressed it down to Bennett's chest, applying pressure to hold the boy in place.

As Bennett turned red in the face from exertion, Jaune rested his blade on one shoulder.

"You didn't give up. I like that. Still, you really should have changed tactics a while ago." Raising his voice, he addressed their audience. "What would you have done, Escha?"

The felyne, sitting on her haunches, held a paw under her chin.

"Not be there?"

"Fair enough."

"And then, and then, I'll throw a boomerang!"

Jaune turned back to his opponent. "See, Bennett? The cat has a plan. Why don't you?" He removed his foot, extending a hand to help Bennett up. "Believe me when I tell you this, because I have the same problem even now, the urge to rush in straight on is best done with a big cannon on your side. Or a cute girl that can summon stars who you can hide behind."

Bennett blinked. "Wait… You're not telling me to stop?"

It was Jaune's turn to be taken aback.

"What, no. Would be damn weird if I told you that and then go on to do it myself. Like I said, find a big cannon." He swapped his sword for the gunlance as a demonstration. "Or a cute girl," he repeated.

"With a big cannon?"

"You know it."

Bennett took the lesson to heart, immediately mulling on the idea. His face flushed.

"I- um. Maybe. In the future."

Ahh, the innocence of youth, unbeholden to one's libido. That wouldn't last.

"I still can't help but feel like this lesson is somehow off."

"Excuse me, are you doubting Pyrrha Nikos, blond trainer extraordinaire?"

"N-No."

Jaune pretended to eye him with suspicion, before shrugging. "Eh, I wouldn't blame you if you did. You've never met her." And Jaune doubted her, too, on other matters. "Anyway, with that, I think we'll wrap up our first session early. You look like you need the rest."

Bennett dropped to the ground in relief.

Jaune joined him, sitting with his legs crossed. Escha scurried over, climbing to sit on his shoulders, preferring the high place. Water bottles appeared, and was passed to everyone.

For a while, they kicked back and basked in the daylight. Autumn had just begun to set in, here. It hit that perfect moment of cool breezes and warm sunshine, where a mind could become lost in the minutes, the afternoon passing with that sense of foreverness.

An indeterminate amount of time later, Jaune broke the silence.

Scooting closer to Bennett, he said, "Since we have the chance, can you help me figure out this Vision thing?" He turned his palm up.

A trinket appeared, an amulet of a flowery motif, with three petals. Lisa called it a fleur-de-lis. Set within the metal casing, a gem glimmered in gold, its surface bearing a pattern of interlocking lines, resembling a puzzle.

It felt right, sitting in his hand. He tossed it up and down, the catches done without a need for him to even look. It would be there, of that he was utterly certain.

"Having one means I have magical powers, right? Nothing seems to be popping up, though."

He had tried to shoot fireballs to no avail. Rubbed the trinket to a shine, and found no genie. As far as his many tests could discern, its purpose was to serve as an interesting paperweight.

Bennett withdrew his own Vision, a red gem, presenting it side by side with Jaune's.

"I'm not really any kind of expert, so I can only go by my own experience. Mine's a Pyro Vision, while yours look like a Geo. I can conjure fire on my sword—"

"Just your sword."

"Yeah, it sounds weird, I get it. But when I fight, it seems… right." Bennett waffled a bit, grappling for the best way to put his explanation into words. "I feel this heat, here in my chest." He tapped his knuckles to his heart. "It'd start pounding in my head, like a heartbeat that becomes louder and louder the harder I fight. Then I shout it out, and the world explodes at the point of my sword." He turned sheepish, scratching his cheek. "That wasn't very helpful, was it?"

Jaune waved it off.

"It helps plenty. Gives me a starting point to work from, at least." Emotions, instincts, the proper headspace… That stuff didn't need a college degree. His prospects looked bright.

Bennett cracked a smile. "I'm glad. I guess what it comes down to is that I really, really wanted it to work, and it did."

The Nora method, his favorite. The thought occurred to him that that girl would adore this kid, what with his explodey sword.

"Maybe it's the same for you," suggested Bennett. "Except with a Geo type."

"Rocks?" Jaune said.

"Rocks," the other boy confirmed.

Rocks…

He grabbed a stray pebble, throwing it into the woods.

Did that count as him casting a rockball? Probably not.

In his pants pocket, a song played to interrupt them. His ringtone. He fished out the phone, singing under his breath.

"You're my soda pop—yello?"

"My little soda pop~ Fuck, now it's stuck in my head. Thanks, Jaune."

"Lisa, what's up?"

"Ceiling, sky, bird, vampires."

"Oh haha, you're so—one of these is not like the others." He blinked. "Are you in trouble?"

Over the line, he heard the crash and din of many falling objects.

"We have a stalemate situation going on. I might have sorta, maybe, busted open a local vampire conspiracy."

Why did she get to have all the fun?

"Honestly, they're a bit of a disappointment, just a bunch of hipsters from a nearby college—NYU—stalking the public library for victims. Too bad this time the bite didn't take. The problem is, they think they have to silence us because we're now witnesses to their scheme—do NOT start a fire here!"

"Hi, Hu Tao," Jaune called out.

"Heeeey~!"

"Come on, get back to building the book fort! Go, go, go! Anyway, they walk in sunlight with lame sunglasses and sunscreen, and there's a good three dozen in their little gang. Killing them is… hard. They're not what I expected. A little too human, if you catch my drift. Come do your thing."

His thing. What a nice and safe way to put it. Jaune turned to the others.

"Bennett, Escha. We've got trouble. Follow me." They wasted no time, not even Bennett who stared at the phone as if it were alien technology, following him as he dashed into the trees.

"Hey, no rush. Like I said, we're in a stalemate. Keep your abilities under wraps."

A straight line through the woods brought them outside the Ramble, and from there they cut out to the city streets. At Lisa's direction, he flagged a taxi. The state of traffic in this less busy area meant it beat running the whole distance. Despite himself, Bennett resembled a kid on his birthday throughout the experience, giddy at being inside the magical carriage.

The taxi took them southward until they were a couple of blocks away from their destination. A sudden deadlock of vehicles ahead prevented the driver from pushing any further. Jaune and company left the taxi there, paying with the stolen paper bills Lisa had, with quite a bit of forethought he now admitted, insisted he took in case of expenses and emergencies.

The reason for the traffic jam became apparent as he pushed through a crowd of people. A line of police tape blocked off the avenue, preventing cars and bystanders from approaching an impressive edifice of marble.

The library stood out amidst the modern high rises. Fluted columns and arches lent the building the air of a temple, sculptures of robed figures gazing down from above. Statues depicting lions decorated the steps leading up to the entrance.

Large banners on the side of the building advertised upcoming events—book signings, symposiums, and so on. Re-imagining Dracula for Normies, said one that featured a pale man with fangs.

Three police vehicles bolstered the cordon, their harried officers running to and fro to keep the situation in hand. Down the street, more police cars blocked off the library from the side, an uphill task as there was a whole lot of building space to secure. One policeman stood near the crowd, speaking into a handheld radio. Agitated, he neglected to moderate his volume, and Jaune listened in.

"—our backup? Who knows what those freaks are getting up to? You know what they're like!" the officer shouted to the person on the line. His scowl then deepened. "Oh, who cares about their politically correct bullshit? They're freaks, them and all the others!"

Judging by the many, many phones recording the conversation, a lot of people, if not care, then at least were eager to post that conversation on social media for the world to hear. Jaune foresaw troubles in that man's future.

The officer's eyes snapped to him as he raised the line of tape up, and passed through. Training took over, and the man's hand hovered over the holster at his side.

"Sir, I'm going to need you to move back behind the line," he said in a voice that brooked no argument. His gaze scanned Jaune head to toe, a measure of apprehensiveness entering his features as he had to look up for them to be eye to eye.

Ignoring the command, Jaune presented a friendly demeanor, smiling. "About that, I need to get into that library there."

The officer stared at him like he had two heads.

"This is an ongoing police matter. Nobody is getting in or out." Then, in a lower, more strained tone, the man said, "Did you not hear what is happening here!? Vampires are in the library. Vampires!"

"I can handle it," Jaune assured him. "Look, there are people I know inside. I'll just go in and pick them up, then I'll get out of your hair." That failed to convince the man, if anything cementing his opinion that Jaune was out of his mind.

When one tactic did not work, try another. Blunt honesty took the loss today, stepping aside for quick thinking and showmanship.

"In fact," Jaune said, pitching his voice to a confident boom. "Since I'm heading inside anyway, I might as well take care of the problem for you." His hands swept out wide. "After all, I… and my team… have a fair amount of experience dealing with unordinary opponents. Not two nights ago, we put an undead to rest. From creatures of the deep, to zombies and ghouls, I've seen it all, and lived to tell the tale."

Skepticism colored the officer's features, but Jaune spotted it, that glimmer of hope. The officer did not enjoy this situation, did not like the vampires. And here Jaune was, boasting that he could resolve it.

"What are you, some kind of monster hunter?" the officer asked, trying for an indifferent scoff, and failing. Had the man truly doubted, he wouldn't give Jaune the time of day.

Jaune glanced at Escha, and decided to roll with it.

"The correct term is Monster Hunter, with caps. Yes, I can hear the difference."

Below, Escha puffed up in pride.

The officer gave him a long, evaluating look, lingering on the sword tied to his hip with a strap, a sword that the man no doubt would swear had not been there before. He balked upon realizing what it was, gripping his gun hard. Harder, as the officer noticed Bennett had followed Jaune's example at some unknown point. No longer a pair of harmless civilians, the people in front of the officer now presented a threat.

The question was: to who?

In the end, the policeman turned his head to speak into his radio. A hurried conversation ensued between him and the person on the line.

A minute later, he stepped aside, waving Jaune through. With a nod, Jaune grabbed Bennett by the back of his collar and dragged him along, rescuing him from the teenagers who had co-opted the boy for their selfies.

The officer left him with one instruction. Dead or alive. His boss back at the station did not care which.

The two boys and the cat ascended the steps to one of the doors. Jaune opened it without hesitation, summoning a shield and entering with it raised, his sword primed for a stab.

The lobby better suited a palace than a book repository, with its high ceiling and engravings on the wall. Marble busts sat in alcoves. A grand staircase led to a second-floor balcony.

He contacted Lisa through their phones. "Where are you?"

"Third floor, reading room." He heard a fwip sound. Lisa had shot at something.

[Third Arm] latched to the railings above, and with Escha clinging to his back, the arm pulled Jaune to the second floor. Down below, the sound of Bennett's boots rang out on the marble steps. Jaune was already on the third floor before the other boy cleared the first staircase.

A plaque on the wall directed him to the reading room. Its doors stood ajar, from which a clamoring din drifted outward. Jaune strode inside, and found a scene of pandemonium.

Desks laid overturned, the books knocked off shelves. People ran to and fro, chased by lightning. The sunglasses they wore worked against them, from time to time sending them crashing to the floor as they tripped on an obstacle. They shouted at each other, suggesting what to do, assigning blame, their sharp fangs glinting.

At the center of the room stood the statue of a man, some sort of actor or poet reading from a page in one hand, the other upturned and held aloft, a bird on his shoulder.

Above that, a different raven circled, raining down bolts of electricity and weaving on graceful wings through the books thrown by the vampires.

Of his many foes, Oz doggedly chased two in particular.

"Get away from me! I saw what it did to George when he helped you!" shouted one of them to the other, as they passed a smoking, twitching fellow. Dressed in black same as all the vampires were, the woman tried to break off and leave her companion to his fate, but he stuck to her like a cockroach, finding safety in numbers.

"It's not my fault!" that man wailed.

"You were supposed to nibble!"

"That's the problem! I couldn't! She had this weird force field thing, I'm not even sure what species she is supposed to be!"

"Yeah well, good job, you made her bird angry, you idiot!"

"C'mon, don't lose your head—"

Shing!

The man stopped speaking mid-sentence, mouth flapping and shut without a throat to form the sounds. His head flew in an arc, tumbling end over end. It landed on the statue of the poet, right on the open palm.

The eyes of the head rolled around until it found him. The vampire mouthed something suspiciously like "Oh look, a cat," before crumpling to ash. The room fell deathly quiet in his wake. In a series of jerky, halting motions, the vampires turned to Jaune.

"He just killed Benny…"

"Oh crap."

That concise summary found many believers, creating a chorus that flowed from one end of the room to the other, echoing off the vaulted ceiling. Bennett entered the scene in the middle of it, and grew very confused as a result.

Confusion became consternation after a vampire lunged for Jaune, and he rammed his sword down the reedy man's throat. As Jaune shook off the ashes on his blade, Bennett gulped for air.

"What? Something wrong?" Jaune asked once he noticed the odd response.

"You didn't even blink. Just like the Guild bounty hunters…" A vampire ambushed Bennett from a balcony above their heads that Jaune had missed on arrival, and the boy whipped his sword upward, still in its scabbard, to clobber the college student/bloodsucker. This time, the vampire survived, knocked unconscious.

"My job," Jaune explained with a shrug. "Will it be a problem?"

Bennett looked down at his sword. "I should be the one saying that. Is it okay that I've never killed anyone before?"

Jaune thought about it.

He repeated his answer.

"My job."

Nobody else's. As it should be. He didn't need people who would kill at the drop of a hat. Really, it was the other way around. His companions offered him perspectives he never considered.

"Now." He pointed his sword ahead. "Who's next—"

"Oh my god, I didn't sign up for this!"

"It's a library. This was supposed to be easy prey!"

"Help, help! Police!"

Courage fled, and the vampires were not far behind. They may dress like assassins, but their attitudes spoke more of stylish goths, out looking for trouble and finding too much. There was a reason they hunted in a place made for quiet, studious types. They ran pell-mell every which way, booking for the exits and even leaping to the windows set up high, crashing through the glass to escape. Any method, to not be in a room with him.

How hurtful. Left behind, Jaune sniffled.

Oz alighted on his shoulder, and patted him comfortingly on the head with its wing. The bird guided him and the others to a corner of the room between two shelves, where tables, book carts, and books had erected a barricade. A number of vampires snoozed in front of it, sleep darts sticking out of their skin.

Lisa poked her head out of the book fort.

Jaune looked around at the mess, then at her.

"You know, I guess I was wrong. Things do happen on Wednesday."


Author's Notes: Jaune and Lisa, dead broke once again.
