#5,514

Chapter 68: A Land of Opportunity
​


The police commissioner enjoyed his cigars, and so did all his friends. A haze of wispy gray smoke enveloped the room, the old-timey office of rich carpets and muted beige walls resembling a misty night on the streets of Vale.

As the odd one out, Jaune tried to not let it get to him. The police officers from the library brought him in as a guest on instructions from their boss, this man. Sour things here, and that status might change to detainee. Or more likely, suspect-at-large.

It amounted to a lot of sitting around, sipping a cup of subpar tea as the people in the room told him stories.

Not their stories. Not 'exactly' their stories. They would be absent, otherwise.

"That was the last I ever saw of Tommy," one said, finishing his tale as smoke curled around him. Jaune couldn't see him, or the others, very well from his spot in the plush armchair set before the commissioner's desk. He had asked who they were, these men and women, and was still waiting on that answer. "Walked out of prom with the prettiest girl we ever did see, and out of our lives. I check back with his family, sometimes, until his case went cold."

With a scoff, the man settled back into his seat. A short period of silence followed, as it had done a few times now. A part of the ritual, almost, before somebody else took the spotlight, and on it went, this… whatever this was.

The police commissioner, a fat man in a fine suit, seemed to sense his waning attention and motioned for the others to cease their talking. They took cue from the man, diverting their activities toward studying Jaune with an unnerving focus, puffing on their cigars or taking a drink of their whiskey glass. The scrutiny gave him the uncomfortable impression that he was sitting in front of a panel of judges.

He glanced around the room. With the glass cabinet full of expensive-looking bottles, the pool table, and the occupants, the place had the air of a private club. Newspaper clippings the commissioner deemed worthy of recollection decorated the wall, the smoky haze blurring the words and pictures. A trophy depicting a football quarterback rested on the desk, taking pride of place—either a son, or the man himself in a bygone age before the big meals and cigar-damaged lungs. Near it, a picture in a frame, rotated to face the room so everyone can admire the sight of the commissioner holding a hunting rifle while posing next to his quarry.

He couldn't quite make out what kind of animal it was. Not a deer. Not a moose. Not boar, nor bear. An odd creature defined by what it was not. His gaze returned to the man behind the desk, who had yet to voice the thoughts on his mind.

Well, if Lisa had ever taught him anything, it would be the importance of seizing the initiative in a conversation. It paid to have the first word, the last word, all the words at a moment like this.

Clearing his throat, he said, "So, I guess we might as well cut to the chase. Someone told me before I came in that my killing of the vampires who attacked my friends could be… problematic?"

He phrased it nice and polite, framing the situation just right to deflect the blame. Life taught him a few bad lessons, and they stuck. He should probably feel ashamed about that, except, uh, he was also pretty sure he didn't want to go to jail (and wouldn't) or break out of a police station (the reason why he wouldn't go to jail).

The hasty research Lisa had done on the way over, via a phone taken from a tranquilized vampire, revealed a little more on the situation in this world. The back pages of the newspaper that morning hadn't been as irrelevant as she dismissed at first. That bigfoot yeti thing did exist (or had, until the last known one died decades back with only rumors of sightings remaining), and alongside it came a whole host of other mythical species, still alive and strong, if small in numbers. They lived among people nowadays, with IDs and everything.

Records, domiciles, all the stuff that made a citizen. Therein lay the problem.

Apparently, what he did could be considered a crime around here, with a good enough lawyer. A fact that might have somewhat changed his approach to subduing the vampires had he known—aw, who was he kidding? They tried killing his friends, and he answered in the time-honored tradition of "No, you."

"Vampires?" The commissioner said, balking. Or appeared to, anyway. "What vampires? The only ones we have are in lockup."

Well, okay then. Not such a big problem after all.

Laughter sprang up around him, every person there joining in. He assumed that he was the joke at first, but they winked at him when he turned his head to look, inviting him to laugh along with them.

"Be careful with your words, boy," one said, wagging his finger at Jaune. "Don't go admitting to things you haven't done."

Jaune frowned. "I don't quite understand."

The police commissioner found that very amusing, chuckling as he beckoned for Jaune to lean closer. He quieted the room once more, and spoke in a stage whisper.

"There's a set of little-known statutes, and it's best that it stays that way to not upset the status quo, so mum's the word, alright? Anyway, a couple rules still on the books put you in the clear, and that's the end of it as far as I'm concerned."

That brought up a number of questions, chief of which was this: Had Lisa been wrong?

"These rules, they allow me to kill with impunity?"

"More the line of… deniability," said the commissioner. "Their kind has tried, but they never managed to repeal the old laws. How can they? It protects them, too, and the crimes they commit."

"Exists within its framework," a voice murmured.

"Was there when it was signed," said another, darkly smiling. "They agreed."

The commissioner nodded to his colleagues, taking a puff of his cigar and holding it between two fingers as he blew a smoke ring. "Now, it won't surprise me none if there's some grumbling from that crowd about whether you've taken the proper legal steps, but with how my friend there is spinning it?" He pointed to an old man with a hawkish nose, who mimed tipping his hat. "Nobody is asking the wrong questions. You've slain monsters."

Monsters. The inflection the police commissioner put into that word sounded familiar to Jaune's ears. It mirrored how he understood the term. A beast did not always have scales and breathed fire. Some might pass him by on an evening walk without receiving a glance.

It dawned on him, and he'd have to tell Lisa later, that this word operated on different rules than what the girl was used to, even if the geography stayed the same. Closer to his side of things.

The commissioner placed the cigar back in his mouth. He chewed on the end, speaking around it. "A lot of missing person reports make their way across my desk because of their lot. So if one of them goes missing? Well, that's because of them, too. You understand what I'm saying?"

Jaune sat back in his chair, eyes drifting to the ceiling in thought. "Yeah. Yeah, I think I do."

"Good, I see a bright future for a boy like you, especially if you're intending to keep at this line of work. You might even see me throwing a few jobs your way in the days to come. Been too long since we had one of your sort."

"My sort?"

The many faces in the room grinned at him, the commissioner's widest among them.

"Why, monster hunters."

No caps. Typical.



-o-
​


A step outside the door, and the old—quaint, even—trappings of the police commissioner's office gave way to the sleek grays of a modern workplace. Policemen walked to and fro in a state of perpetual hurry, their pace akin to a run in other circumstances. A few spared Jaune a glance, with eyebrows raising at the sight of him shaking hands with the police commissioner before the door shut.

Free to leave, he retraced the route he took, down an elevator and across a lobby. Perhaps the military cut of the Gallian jacket had something to do with it, for the people in the building accepted his presence as natural. He leaned into that to avoid being waylaid. Walk with purpose, look the part, and a person like him could well blend in with the blur of faces.

Lisa was the only one waiting to greet him. She lingered on the steps to the station, half-sitting on the stone balustrade with her arms crossed. Her gaze snapped to him before the door could fully open.

"Hey. Where are the others?" he said, descending the steps.

"Cafe across the street," she replied in a clipped tone, her impatience becoming clear as she changed the subject. "So? How did it go?"

"Good, I think. I'm walking free, and I might have had a job interview."

That earned him her full, undivided attention. He reported further on the happenings within the commissioner's office at her eager prompting. Except, as the recounting proceeded along, her frown grew and grew until she outright cursed. By the end, she was stomping her feet and clutching her hair.

"I could have gotten us an actual deal!" she raged. "Found dirt on all the people in there, run this town. Why did I miss this, uuugh!"

Jaune scratched his head, glancing around to make sure nobody had overheard those remarks. "I'm a little concerned about half the stuff you mentioned, but… yeah, it would have been great with you in there. Too bad you destroyed that secretary. The commissioner was kind of miffed about that."

"She deserved it, talking to me like she did," Lisa insisted. "The only reason she has a job is because she's fucking her boss!"

Although he already somewhat guessed, according to Lisa's suppositions the police commissioner and his friends must count among the upper echelon of New York City. Influential, with wealth in spades. Those for whom the phrase 'movers and shakers' applied.

Yes, Lisa had the right of it. Their team would be running this town by now, had she stayed her tongue for a minute longer.

Zero chance, in other words.

"Next time," he comforted her, guiding her away from the station and toward the crosswalk at the intersection. No point standing around when they could regroup with the rest of their team, and grab a coffee along with it. "They mentioned passing jobs on to me, so I will probably meet them again."

Lisa's wallowing lessened at the news, features overtaken by a calculating look. "Right. That's right, there's opportunity here." She shook a finger at him. "You're providing a service that other people can't. That makes you super valuable."

He held up a hand, stopping her short.

"Before I agree to anything, I have to ask. Were they telling me the truth? We're no strangers to this. Remember Crowley?"

A scowl flitted across Lisa's face at the mention of that man, prompting her to think long and hard. Their conversation went on hold, and she was soon lost to her research. The phone she stole from a vampire saw one query followed by the next, building out a clearer picture. In no hurry, Jaune watched the clouds, leaving the girl to do what she did best.

The pedestrian lights were taking forever, anyway. He stood on the sidewalk corner, one foot tapping as cars streamed by.

After working it through, Lisa waggled her hand in a 'so-so' gesture. "Ehhh. They made their side look more sympathetic than it really is, but I can confirm some of their claims. This world doesn't realize it, but the amount of people going missing is way higher than normal… smaller count of murders than Earth Bet, though, for whatever reason," she added as an aside.

"You suspect that the vampires are killing off humans, then," Jaune guessed. "In places where people don't pay attention to."

Creatures lurking in the dark, feasting on innocents. More and more, it reminded him of home, in a bad way.

"Them, or any of the dozens of known species. On the other hand, the yetis are gone, the minotaurs are gone, and I highly doubt they vanished into thin air."

She cocked an eyebrow in a way that conveyed she knew for 100% certainty they had not, and he would be stupid if he did not take her at her word. All that, with one twitch of a muscle.

He was getting pretty good at this.

"What they've told you back in that room speaks to a lot of tension simmering," Lisa concluded. A grin broke through. "That means they are seeing genuine use in you, which offers us security."

The lights turned, and they crossed the wide avenue. Five lanes of traffic rumbled their engines, the drivers glaring at them as if they had been personally responsible for the red stop light. Past the long window of the cafe, he spotted Escha with her face plastered to the cold glass. Fischl was petting her, and she shyly waved at them.

"Of course," Lisa piped up when he opened the door to the cafe, "you do realize that they'll want you to go to war against the supernatural, right?"

He paused at the threshold, and looked back at her. Through her, to the city where people went about their peaceful days.

"No, thanks. I'm in it to hunt monsters."



-o-
​


A car traveled down the highway, under the pale circle that was the unbroken full moon. On either side, faint lights of houses stretched into the woods, along rivers, up mountains.

Jaune craned his neck to watch it all, this magical land. The wind whipped up his hair every which way, a rat's nest after it was done. Still, he sat on the open window of the car with a hand on the grab handle for balance, savoring each second of the hours-long drive.

It had been easy to hear about. To look at on a map. A kingdom that spanned from sea to sea, filled with people. Lisa had laughed at him, and decided that he needed to know the place he had ended up in, this America where on and on the road went, seeming to never end.

Exits from the highway led into towns and cities, homes and streets lit up bright. Lisa had detoured into one, just to let him see. He took a picture of it.

Eventually, he heard Lisa calling, and climbed back inside to drop onto a worn seat. The beat-up clunker of a sedan they bought from a dodgy car shop didn't boast much in the way of frills, but it had cupholders for their drinks, a radio playing a soft beat, and a chair with room for him to stretch his legs. Good enough to journey up north, and might open the doors for them to better things in America.

"We're close," Lisa informed him, tapping the navigation screen on the stolen phone. "Tinmouth is the next exit."

The trip involved more than a simple adventure, or he would have brought the other along. They had business to conduct of the less than aboveboard kind. Before the vampire attack, Lisa managed to compile a list of contacts offering the services they were looking for. New identities, documents and backgrounds both. The top of the list was one Kurt Volkov, who promised the goods ready to go that very night, had they the payment.

A gold coin rolled across his knuckles, flicked forward and caught on the upraised palm.

Their car peeled off the highway onto a smaller road, which soon placed them in a sleepy rural settlement. Houses sat far apart on farm plots, with barns and silos a typical feature. They hit the town center, a smattering of buildings comprising a single street. This time of night, only a few other cars were on the road. Outsiders, Lisa pointed to the metal plates on the back as an explanation, acting as if it was obvious. The locals would be in bed. They drove out of the town center and deeper into the woods.

"Are you sure we're going the right way?" he asked after a while. He stuck his head out the window, peering into the dark. "This isn't what I imagine when I think of a forger. Normally, they're in the cities. Best ones operate behind a front, like a nightclub."

"How do you—oh, right, I forgot that you're tapped into that crowd." Lisa shook her head, sighing as if to lament the company she kept.

"Don't make it sound like I'm a career criminal," Jaune retorted. "It was a one-time thing."

Tonk, tonk went her nails on the navigation screen again. "Is it?"

"This one doesn't count." He averted his eyes. "It's… for a good cause?"

Lisa snickered. "Have you ever heard of ethical egoism, Jaune?" She turned the wheel to divert them onto a dirt road.

"I don't think so."

"Heheh. Well, just know that it is very ethical. Super ethical, even." The car slowed down. "Oh hey, I bet that's it up ahead."

Trees gave way to open space, the dirt road leading them to a large tract of farmland. Harvest season had yet to arrive for the fields of corn, the stalks standing tall as they dried in the cool air. A two-story farmhouse rested up ahead, a home lovingly painted in red with an oversized doghouse beside the steps. The covered porch wrapped around the building, with a big yellow box of a car parked on one side. Lisa brought their car to a rest next to that vehicle, and turned off the engine.

He reached for the handle of the car door, but Lisa stopped him.

"Alright, quick gameplan. First thing to know, this guy will try to stiff us."

His hand retracted, and he turned to better face her. "You always pick the best people to work with. What gave him away?" No point asking if she was certain. If she said so, then the forger would.

"His email. How people word them matters, and his was filled with aggressive language. He confirmed the price twice, fixated on it. The first email took an hour for a reply, second one returned in ten minutes. He's hard up for money and is hoping to jack it higher at the table, with threats if we don't agree."

Which neatly explained his presence on this trip. Intimidation was the game, and while he didn't have the right face for the job, the ability to lift a man one-handed went far.

"Sword, or no sword?" he asked.

Lisa rolled her eyes, and patted him on the shoulder. "Oh man, you have so much to learn. Us Americans just aren't that afraid of bladed weapons these days. Try a firearm, instead. Nothing like a big ole gun to get through a wannabe mobster's head to not mess with you."

That didn't make any sense to him. Hacked to death or shot to death, either way, you were dead. Still, he supposed Lisa knew Earth better than him, and so he nodded.

"Sounds simple enough. Need me to put on an act?"

"No. Stand behind me and let me do the talking."

A simple division of responsibility. Her to spin a yarn, him to look pretty. The usual, really.

Plan set, they exited the vehicle. Ruhm appeared to hand, lifted to rest on his shoulder. The lights were on in the house, with lamps illuminating the porch, and he moved to the side to see if he could glimpse anybody within, spotting a TV playing a sports game in front of an empty armchair. Their contact was home, at least, and likely on his way to the door.

Jaune took a few steps toward the house, halting when he heard the sigh. He turned around to find that Lisa hadn't moved.

The girl stood next to the car, head tilted back and eyes closed. A breeze blew strands of her hair out of place, but she didn't mind it and didn't seem aware of him, idly running a hand over the car hood as she breathed in the night air.

"Lisa?" he called back, and his voice woke her. She opened her eyes to look at him.

"I like this," she declared, with a soft smile on her lips.

He checked their surroundings. "Lisa the farmer, huh? I have to admit, that never occurred to me." The same soft smile answered him. "Not that, then?"

She shook her head, walking around the car. Her hip bumped against him in passing.

"Figure it out. But not tonight. C'mon, let's go meet the mark."

A confusing person, as always. She looked… happy.

As they approached the front steps, Jaune heard the sliding of locks and bolts. Moments later, the door to the house opened. Light streamed out, with a figure appearing at the threshold.

"Hello!" the figure said, his voice deep and booming. "Welcome!"

"Jaune, shoot him."

A lot happened in a short time. Lisa's smile turned plastic. The clouds peeled back to reveal the pale celestial body above. He spun to her, a question on his lips. And Kurt Volkov stepped out into the moonlight.

The sound of snapping bones alerted Jaune that the situation had gone wrong. Very, very wrong.

Volkov screamed out in pain, yet kept a grin on his face. There was something to that grin, a sharpness that set Jaune's teeth on edge. It reminded him of the dark woods, of Grimm.

Yellow entered Volkov's eyes, before, with another snap, he hunched over. Despite the bright illumination, his form grew darker, and bigger. His limbs bent and twisted in sickening ways, developing new joints. The tracksuit he wore strained, then ripped apart entirely. Claws scraped the wooden porch, tearing gashes.

What rose up was no man, but a wolf.

It threw back its head, and howled—

Bang.

The bullet tore through the jaw, shattering it, and the bloodcurdling howl ended up as more of a yip. It hadn't fallen, however, so Jaune pulled the trigger again, sending another bullet straight into the wolf's heart, then a third into the same spot.

Volkov keeled over, dead. His large frame hit the porch with a resounding crash that cracked the floorboards. In his wake, silence returned to the surroundings.

"Holy crap, Volkov is a werewolf!"

Until Lisa broke it.

"Was," Jaune corrected, snapping out of his stupor to come closer and nudge the hulking body with a foot. "Yep, dead as a doorknob."

Fur of a deep brown had overtaken Volkov. The remnants of his face showed an elongated snout, with feral eyes that in death retained a sense of hunger. Not much of a human remained.

"What was his deal? I thought you said he wanted to stiff us for money."

Hearing the accusation in his tone, Lisa spluttered, "In a way, he was gonna!" Her gaze flicked to the side. "He just… would have eaten us to do it rather than make threats. How was I supposed to know that he was a werewolf? That part didn't get advertised, and the forgery business was legit—" Lisa froze solid. "But it was a full moon!" she cried, as the truth dawned on her.

Proof, if proof was needed, that Lisa did not know everything. She had considered every logical possibility, predicted the many scenarios. Then, bam!

Werewolf.

"Also, would you please stop poking at him?" she added, sounding put out that he hadn't given her revelation its proper due.

"Come on, this is fascinating." He shifted the body over. "Terrifying, too. He resembles a Beowolf Grimm. See the back legs here? Practically identical."

How deep did the similarities go? Because research into the internals of a Grimm never got far, due to them vanishing to smoke. With Volkov, that could change. The mystery might finally have an answer.

"Stop poking at him," Lisa commanded in a harder voice.

He waved her off. "Lisa, I am standing on the cusp of life-changing discoveries here. This may be the breakthrough my world is looking for. I… I have to take the body. For science."

"Uh-huh. Is that so? That's very interesting, Jaune." Lisa seemed to mean it, too. "But I'm more concerned about the other werewolves right now."

His brows furrowed, and he turned to her. "Other werewolves? What other—"

His gaze drifted past her to the figures crawling out of the corn fields. Growls emitted from their throats, low and threatening. The baleful yellow of their eyes were locked onto the dearly departed Volkov.

"Ah, them." He stopped poking the body. "They don't look pleased."

"Try apoplectic. They want to tear you limb from limb, and food doesn't come into the equation. Volkov. He was their leader. Pack leader. Wolves see their pack as family. With these numbers, it's a whole clan with him the patriarch. And you killed him."

"What's this 'you' business, Gossip Girl?" Jaune stepped up beside her, aiming his rifle as a warning for the werewolves to back off. Not that it worked. "We are in this together."

Oddly, she seemed quite happy with that.

The new werewolves came in various hues, and different sizes. Their normal clothes hung off them in tatters, strips of fabric stretched across their tall frames. They stalked over the grounds, twitching whenever his rifle pointed their way but continuing to advance. It suggested that some measure of intelligence still dwell within their heads, not at all the brutish beasts he hoped for.

A clattering from above led him to peer upward. The snarling visage of a wolf glared down at him from the roof.

"Would you look at that? They understand that combat is three-dimensional."

Quick as a flash, he jerked his rifle up and fired off a shot, the bullet slamming home in the werewolf's eye. Its falling body marked the start of the battle.

Dozens of howls harmonized into a war cry, and the creatures broke into a loping charge. Lisa took cover behind him as he let loose on the trigger. With the car midway between them and the werewolves, escape wasn't in the cards.

Bang!

"...was supposed to be a game of hunting…"

Bang!

"...picked any other day, nothing would…"

Bang!

"...are coming. Mechanic, doctor, housewife, priest, they're embedded at all levels…"

Bang!

She talked, he killed. They split the job neatly. His clip ran empty right around the time the werewolf from the roof got up, his last shot spent for a point-blank blast straight down its throat. By then, the werewolves had reached close quarters. Pushing Lisa back into the wall, he traded Ruhm for Red Rook. With both hands, he swung the gunlance to smack a leaping werewolf in the midriff, folding it in half and launching it over the heads of its brethren.

That didn't kill it, though. Same went for a lot of the bullets he fired. Werewolves bled from the holes in their head, their chest, their throat. They wheezed and stumbled, untold damage wreaked within. Yet, they advanced, and he couldn't move anywhere lest it left Lisa undefended.

Boom!

Now, that shot made them pause for a split second. The gunlance shell had struck a werewolf in the face, and blasted the entire head to smithereens. No shrugging that one off.

Of course, it also sent them to new heights of rage. The howls deafened the fields and forests for miles around.

[Third Arm] reached out, grabbing one werewolf and pulling it toward him so that the beast careened into a second werewolf. The tip of the lance slipped between its rib cage to skewer both upon the pole. The lance disappeared, replaced by Crocea Mors as he spun and lobbed off the hand of a third that had been lunging for Lisa. That werewolf screamed, and snapped out its other hand to slap him away, its claws raking his chest.

He hit the wall of the house. Wood crunched behind him at the impact from a blow whose strength did not fit the werewolf's lanky arm. Beside him, Lisa shot a sleep dart that jabbed into the werewolf's shoulder to little effect. The monster leapt, jaws opened wide and aimed at Jaune's neck.

Jaune shoved the shield for Red Rook between the rows of teeth, wedging it open. A twist of his arm, a pivot of the heels, and he threw the werewolf against the ground. His blade descended to remove its head, then flicked upward to slice a nasty gash on the next arrival, right between the nose to fill the nostrils with blood. That werewolf went near insane, lashing out in a frenzy that caught its allies more than doing anything to him and Lisa.

Their noses were keen, and the scent of blood had a particular effect on them. Good to know.

"They have a sense of smell akin to dogs, and blood specifically riles them up. It might be the iron content."

"Thanks for the tip, Lisa." He made no mention of his own earlier deduction.

With how many werewolves there were, they had gotten close by now, way too close. Before they could pile on, he pulled Lisa into a hug and lashed [Third Arm] to the edge of the roof. The shadowy limb stretched like a bungee cord, then contracted to yank them into the air. Rockets engaged beneath his feet to help him move faster. The pair landed on the sloped surface, finding temporary reprieve.

A head peeked above the edge. Boom! It was gone. More took its place, vaulting up and sinking in their claws into the shingles to maintain balance.

A flashbomb, fashioned from the innards of a flash bug, popped into his hand.

"Lisa, close your eyes."

Night turned to day, and he launched forward, tearing through the blinded werewolves as a whirlwind, slicing left and right before shoving their bleeding forms off the roof. Hitting the edge, he jumped, the rockets launching him into a flip that carried him back to the top of the roof where Lisa crouched with a hand holding on to the chimney.

"They're not all that tough," he assured her. Angry roars and the sound of fighting below brought a satisfied smile to his face. He sat down on the roof. "And now they're sightless, frenzied, and in close quarters with one another. It's over."

Not believing him, Lisa stayed on her guard. Her face was pale as she listened to the slaughter.

Over time, however, she gleaned the general direction things were headed, and joined him in getting comfortable. The occasional werewolf popped up, but they lacked the semi-organized charge of previous, and found themselves dispatched by him in quick order. The rest remained locked in combat, the pack turning on itself even after the effects of the flashbomb dissipated. There might have been a killer of a pack member up here, but so were there killers down there, violence begetting violence as they killed and were killed in turn.

"I'm going to have to remember this tactic," he said in idle thought. He caught the disturbed look on Lisa. "What?"

"...Nothing. That's a good idea. I guess I just didn't expect it from you." A wan smile, and she added, "You really are a Hunstman. A Monster Hunter."

He didn't get what she meant, but… "I am, and don't you forget it."

Lisa sighed, dropping her face in her hands. "Vampires. Werewolves. What the fuck is even my life?"

"I'd call it a very exciting time," he said with a laugh. "A shame the deal was a trap, though. Tonight's not our night, huh?"

"Tomorrow's a new day. I have more names on the list that we can contact. Next one is further north, but back over the state line in New York. A Lupa Lykos, from Lake Placid."

"Sounds like a plan. Let's take the others along this time. Make a trip of it."

Lisa agreed. And with that, they sat back to wait out the battle.

As werewolves warred, Jaune's gaze turned upward. For a time, he said nothing, simply watching the good moon on the rise.


Author's Notes: What a peaceful world, until Jaune decided to make it less so.

Not quite an epic battle, but that's the vibe, I suppose. He is the big fish in a small pond here.

Time for a new world, methinks. Can't get bogged down with basebuilding. It's best in bits and pieces.

#5,598

Chapter 69: A Farmboy from Kansas
​


A soaked Jaune Arc dragged himself out of the water, dressed only in his boxer briefs. His hand came up to tear off the slim, compact rebreather he wore, revealing the beaming smile on his face at a job well done. The lake at his back was on fire. On fire, with a section of it dyed red due to the blood.

It… had been a long night.

He walked past Hu Tao's sitting form on the pier, clapping her upon the shoulder in silent thanks for her stellar assistance. 10/10 would tap her when he needed it again. Platonically speaking.

Hu Tao seemed too preoccupied to acknowledge the gesture, however. Because, whoops, he was still mostly naked with the rest of his clothes sitting in his Pocket so that they wouldn't hinder his movements underwater. A hasty apology and he continued on, all too aware of her eyes on his back.

The police had arrived at some point prior, the flashing lights of their patrol cars illuminating the secluded clearing in which the house sat. The fire must have drawn them here, or maybe the explosions from the bomb barrels did it. A fair number eyed him with a measure of wariness, at a guess due to them catching the tail end of the last ten minutes. He spotted officers over by the driveway lugging computer equipment out of a side entrance, and a small part of him winced at what it meant for his group's prospects of legal identities in America—no good deeds went unpunished, it seemed. Near there, another pair of policemen directed an elderly woman into the back of a squad car while she wailed for her fallen god.

In a twist that nobody could have possibly foreseen, Lupa Lykos turned out to be a werewolf.

Yes, right on the heels of the person yesterday. What were the chances?

Anyway, her arrest had precisely nothing to do with that.

A sweet lady with a particular set of skills from her younger days, Lupa Lykos pursued a slew of less-than-legal side gigs to keep afloat in her twilight years. Since the full moon had passed, the werewolf side never emerged beyond a set of long fingernails that she used to cut a taut string while they talked. He would even dare to say that they hit it off.

The elaborate series of dominoes, see-saws, pressure plates, tipping garden gnomes, a large rock, and the swinging log hidden above the entrance of her home that sent him sailing into the lake… was a different story. Especially once the aforementioned rock hit the water surface to rouse the bus-sized monster lurking beneath Lake Wrongfully Named. 'Sacrificed by a cultist to feed their god' could now go on his bingo card.

Hunting that giant crocodile had almost felt like fighting dragons again, but underwater. Good times.

He weaved through the various ongoings, the police giving him a wide berth. Over by the porch, Lisa chatted with an officer, and snippets of their conversation reached his ears upon his approach. Quite a tale, she told. Full of plausible reasons for the presence of him, her, and the others on the property that the uniformed woman could jot down in her report. Knowing winks passed between them as they reinterpreted events in a way that did not so much paint a picture as it painted over the picture.

Lies, Lies, and more lies. Yet, with everybody in on the game, it caused no harm and smoothed out the proceedings. The police received their answer to—and this was judging by the field of bones he found at the bottom of the lake—a ludicrous amount of unsolved cases that the force could claim the credit for, thus guaranteeing hefty appreciation from the public at large and a budget increase in the near future. In return, they saw no cause to look too deeply into the how and who of the meddling kids that cracked the mystery.

He let Lisa work her magic, lingering a short distance away so that he could scan the area for other members of his team. Last he checked, Bennett had been helping Escha plant her bomb barrels on canoes, shoving the traps into the lake for him to lead the crocodile toward. The pair must have made themselves scarce before the police got here. Lisa's decision, most likely. She did mention that the hunting etiquette from his and Escha's worlds might find pushback from local authorities.

Fischl, he found through Oz. The raven kept circling a tall tree planted next to the house, and among its autumn leaves Jaune spied a lithe form hidden on standby, close enough to provide backup for the girl below should the situation called for it. Nobody else had noticed her yet, and he made a subtle wiggle of his hand to greet her.

The tree shook, and Fischl appeared within view for a split second before vanishing again. If he was not mistaken, she had just slipped and fell from her perch. The why escaped him, until he caught the repeated sidelong glances sent his way from the police officer as she asked Lisa increasingly inane questions to draw out the conversation.

Right. Clothes. Better get on that soon.

Lisa agreed with the sentiment. "Put some pants on!" she ordered him after shooing away the officer.

He gave a helpless shrug as he walked over to join her. "As I recall, you were the one telling me to cool it with my abilities before they sic a nu-cleah weapon on me." From context clues and prior experience, a nu-cleah weapon translated to 'sexy, silver-haired angel with a big cannon'. He… wouldn't call that a bad thing, depending. "Unless you can find a pair of jeans lying around here, I'm out of luck."

"I—" Lisa paused, biting her lips as she looked him up and down. "Oh whatever, do as you like. Anyway, good job dealing with that crocodile. I wish you had been quieter about it, but what's done is done."

"Hey, now. You can do better than that," said Jaune, fishing for compliments. He planted his fists on his hips. "Did you catch the rodeo with me standing on its back? And the flip at the end? I got an amazing picture out of it to remember that thing by."

Lisa nodded along. Then, with a roll of her eyes, she cut in snidely, "Yeeeah, and alerting the cops with your antics nixed our chances of using her files to put together a set of IDs ourselves."

At that revelation, his mood sank like a stone. His gaze turned to the van that the officers were filling up with evidence.

"I did notice them grabbing her stuff. Is there nothing we can do? Maybe if we claim it as spoils…" The look on her face told him enough.

"Nope, and trust me, I tried. This incident is going to make headlines, and the police aren't risking anything to jeopardize that. My usual methods won't cut it. Nothing short of me blackmailing the entire department, that is." Her eyebrows waggled. Hint, hint.

He blanched, holding up his hands to stop her. "Let's not go that far. We aren't desperate."

"In that case, it's on to the next forger for us. I'm positive this one won't be a werewolf."

And she had been right about that. It definitely was not a werewolf.

That person did not pan out, for… reasons. Or lived, for… reasons. The same fate befell the one after them. He kept suggesting they find a contact inside New York City, to break the pattern, but Lisa insisted that the city—the Big Apple, she called it—was too hot to handle at their level. That they would be stepping on toes.

So, Jaune pressed on, and in the days that followed he began to internalize the lessons.

The sun sat high in the sky as Jaune walked up the gravel driveway to a simple one-story home. It was midmorning in the town of Sleepy Hollow, a time sure to annoy any vampires and make them think twice about fighting outside their element, while neutering werewolves altogether. It did zilch for wendigos and invisible people, but that was where good sharp steel came into play. His knuckles rapped on the door, three soft beats rounded out with a louder finale.

Afterward, a deliberate step back and to the left cleared him some room. It left plenty of space for him and Bennett, who stood toward the right of the door, to work with. At this angle, they both could summon their weapons and have a clear shot at any possible aggressor charging out of the house. The distance between them also split the attention, reducing the risk of an instant knockout via snaky gorgon stares—that had been a fun ten minutes of doing absolutely nothing until Hu Tao rescued them—or mechanical contraptions involving sawblades and acid—a fun ten minutes of chasing a mad inventor through his horror house of deathtraps to rescue Oz from a fate as a living battery.

Footsteps inside informed him of the homeowner's approach, sharpening his instincts to a state of alert. Plans of engagement played within his mind, three to start that might develop into specific strategies depending on who opened that door. Each one began with a smile, because friendliness could always make a difference.

Also, it made people let their guards down.

The footsteps ended directly on the other side of the door, and Jaune imagined the person studying him through the peephole. Whatever they found must have satisfied, for they stepped back and unlatched the lock. The door swung open.

A young man not far from his own age ducked his head in greeting.

"Hi there! What can I do for you?"

Jaune eyed the young man for a brief moment before answering. The jeans and t-shirt lacked strands of loose fur. No hat, so no nest of snakes waiting to be unleashed. Short sleeves displayed spindly arms that spoke of less exercise than doctors advised, although he hesitated to dismiss their threat outright—it did not preclude muscle enhancements from a transformation.

Finally, he spoke up. "Good morning, I'm here to pick up the papers. You might remember a certain AllSeeingEye on the inter-net? I'm the person they were talking about."

The young man brightened, recognizing Lisa's handle.

"Perfect! I was afraid you were random solicitors for a minute there." The forger turned to the side, hands going for something out of view to cause Jaune and Bennett to tense up. A needless worry, as he returned with a small stack of folders, placing it in Jaune's grip. "Here you are, five sets of IDs with the full premium work, digital files in the USB drive there. Plus two more for your pets. First time I had an order for that one, I can tell you that… What's wrong?"

Jaune stared at the young man. Looked down at the folders. Looked up again.

The sequence of events did not compute, leaving him stranded in a situation for which he held no frame of reference. In some small way, reality had broken.

He swallowed his spit. "That's it?" he asked, a tremble in his voice. It couldn't be so simple. It couldn't. "Are you a werewolf?" he pressed. "A shapeshifter? Dullahan? C'mon, you can tell me."

The forger gave him an odd look.

"Uhhh, no?"

"What about a scientist?" Bennett chimed in. The acid that dissolved his clothing had left its mark on the boy. Poor Fischl still couldn't look him in the eyes, even a day later.

The man scratched his head, brows furrowing. "Guys, what is this about?"

Jaune and Bennett shared a glance, both forced to come to grips with the fact that they were having a normal interaction with a person. In a flash, big smiles appeared on their faces and they turned back to the forger.

"Nothing. No problems here," Bennett said.

"Thank you for your time," Jaune added, passing the folders over for Bennett to hold. "Let me get your payment."

He rummaged around in his poncho, pretending to search for money while summoning it from his Pocket. Since the money he won from the Super Reality Climax deathgame didn't match the local version of the dollar, and gold proved a cumbersome tool here, his team had hit up pawnshops along their routes all over New York and the neighboring regions to trade in their wealth. Courtesy of his partner's negotiations, the stash had grown to a sizable sum over the course of the week in exchange for very little gold. His hand withdrew a stack of bills that had the forger's eyes going wide.

The man licked his lips. "That's, wow. You walking with that much cash in your pockets? You guys must be some high rollers, huh?"

"Something like that. I—"

The forger whipped out a handgun tucked behind his back. "Give me every"—Jaune grabbed him by the wrist, twisting it onto itself and hearing a snap—"yaaargh!"

Earth people could be so fragile. A kick sent the man sprawling, the handgun falling to hit the floor with a clatter. Crocea Mors appeared in Jaune's grip as he advanced inside the house.

"Boss?"

He vanished the weapon, and turned his head to show Bennett a friendly look.

Bennett and Fischl resembled Lisa in a certain aspect, shying away from the idea of him putting a backstabbing, double-dealing scoundrel in the ground. The giant crocodile had been fine, the werewolves confused them, and anything more human than those got him a worried side-eye. Even Hu Tao, who expressed understanding, balked at his answers to the hypotheticals posed over dinner by a Lisa who had wasted no time reinforcing her lessons on Earth norms once she spotted allies.

Before, he could dismiss it as Lisa's quirks. Now…

The people around him saw something wrong in him, and that thought disturbed Jaune to no end.

Movements at the corner of his vision drew his notice, just in time for the forger to pull the trigger on the gun he had retrieved. A victorious grin split the man's face, wiped off as the bullet slammed into a glowing force field, manifested to protect Jaune from harm.

Not his Aura. This field extended away from his body, a sphere shaped of swirling golden light. He had managed to work out one aspect of the Geo Vision, at least, and saw the potential right off the bat. The shield activated on command and could survive a fair amount of damage before crumbling, always coming back after a little while ready for use again. The best part, he did not experience the phantom pain that went with blows to his Aura.

The bullet ricocheted off the Geo shield and flew back at the forger, who had no time to react as it sliced a shallow line of his cheek, the brush with death freezing him in place. Hearing the screech that escaped his mouth, one would think him struck by a mortal wound. He cringed on himself, covering his face with his arms to ward off further attacks.

Not that Jaune did anything in that second half beyond standing there. He whistled, stepping closer to the puddle of cold sweat that was a man and taking a knee beside him. "Lucky break. Are you good?"

The forger mumbled an incoherent string of babble. Jaune looked to Bennett for help, getting a shrug.

"I'll take that as a yes," he decided. "So… we're not here to hurt you." The other man's stiff-faced whimper conveyed his disbelief, and Jaune's gaze darted to the broken wrist. "Much," he amended. An idea struck him, born of the awareness that this had been the tamest encounter with a forger thus far. "In fact, we'll even give you a ring for other jobs in the future and pay a fair price for it, assuming you don't try any more silly tricks. Deal?"

No response.

"I think he's passing out," Bennett commented.

"I almost prefer the werewolves," Jaune grumbled as a needle syringe popped into existence, and he plunged the stimpak into the man's shoulder.

Fear turned to awe as the forger witnessed his injuries recovering, the miracle healing doing a better job persuading the man to agree to their new arrangement than Jaune ever could. Eyes shining, the young man inquired about the 'magic juice' and its potential to let a person skip hospital visits—a costly affair, according to him.

The forger very much liked the answers he got, and his about-face was a marvel to behold. Star customers, they now were, if their group kept the witchcraft coming. Jaune left the house under odd circumstances, with the person who tried to shoot him waving goodbye and telling him to return any time.

A win for forgiveness, he supposed.

A leaf through the folders as he walked down the driveway confirmed the items Lisa wanted, and the file on him sounded quite convincing in his amateur view.

Jaune Arc was now a farmboy, raised honest if unaware of the world in the corn fields of Kansas. Faded membership cards fraying at the edges for gyms, dojos, and shooting ranges wove a backstory of training from an early age in hopes of entering the military, with him falling into the Monster Hunting gig to make ends meet after the family farm went under. A few years on, and now the farmboy held dreams of making it big in the city. His old plans of a uniform and a medal never panned out.

Call him optimistic, but the identity should pass muster in most circumstances. The crafted details were tight and coherent, giving people what they expected to see. It excused his ignorance of most things regarding Earth, and on the surface explained away his survival against the various beings he met in the past couple of days.

Nobody who looked into his background would believe him an alien from another world. Just a normal boy from Kansas, with an extraordinary future ahead of him.

As he walked by a bush on the side of the path, a bird popped out of it, followed by a head of blonde hair covered by a fashionable lace bonnet which served as the raven's perch. The lookout for their group, Fischl had her bow at the ready.

"Art thou safe?" fretted the girl, fingers tapping a rapid, nervous beat on her bow. "I heard the infernal noise of a 'gonne,' but you appeared hale at a distance and gave me no signal…"

"All fine," Jaune reassured her, waving for her to fall into step with him. "We worked it out with the guy. Here, check this out."

He passed her the folder marked with her name, Fischl von Luftschloss Narfidort. Bennett received his, too, and the two adventurers perused the story of their alternate egos with keen enthusiasm as they strolled along the road. A peek over their shoulders allowed him to glean some of the highlights.

Childhood friends, school records up to date until last month, logged volunteering hours at no doubt defunct local programs, bird rearing license. Ordinary civilians living their lives, the pages blared. Nothing to see here, move along.

"What do you think?" he asked.

Fischl opened her mouth, but the overeager Bennett got there first. Unbeknownst to the boy, she stepped aside and pretended that she had intended to give him the floor all along.

"I don't get this part," Bennett said, pointing to a page. "Do you know what it means?"

Jaune scanned the paper, parsing the unfamiliar terms and almost alien format. "Exemption to draft, it means you're resilient to the wind," he stated very confidently.

"Ohhhh," said Bennett. He studied his own arm. "I am pretty hardy." He looked up. "It's like you know everything, boss."

"Heh heh. Yeah."

He couldn't meet that earnest gaze, lest he admitted the truth. Anxious to change the subject, he directed his attention to his other companion.

"What about you, Fischl? How are you finding your new identity?"

Fischl gave a theatrical scoff, and skipped ahead of the group so that she could strike a pose. Her modern yet somehow dated dress lent her a doll-like quality, but she made it work, the frilly skirt flaring in the breeze as she planted her legs apart. Her hand pulled the bonnet low over her eyes.

"It captures but a mote, a mote, of mine true self. Adequate as a cover, perhaps, if rather lacking as compared to my majesty." She released her hat to wave in a dismissive manner. "It is no matter, for my shining tale is written in the stars. So long as you understand this, I am satisfied."

"Milady protests the lack of accolades and certifications to her name," said Oz. "Especially the award she once won in a writing contest. She was promised its inclusion in the documents."

"You're kidding!" Jaune said, taking her file to rifle through the pages. "That forger must have forgotten it. Let's go back and complain!"

Fischl stepped in front of him, waving both arms in a panic. "Wait, no!" She coughed. "I mean, there is no need to concern ourselves with the minor details. Why, I shall simply regard this as my chance to begin anew." Surer now, she smiled. "Yes, that is the way. My pen will take the world by storm, unbound from preconception… Can you help me sign up for a contest when I'm ready, i-if it isn't too much trouble?"

"I suppose, yes. That should be easy enough," he said. "I'll bet Lisa can put together a list of the ones nearby."

Fischl fidgeted, heels worrying against the ground. "I would really prefer that nothing tries to eat me when I go to submit my story."

Fair point. "Alright. For you, I'll venture into the inter-net. Just know that while Lisa has been a bit off her game recently, she did come through for us in the end today." He glanced at the folders. "And on that note, I should probably call to update her."

As they resumed their journey across the small town of Sleepy Hollow, he flipped open his phone and rang up the first (and only) entry. Lisa picked up on the third ring, as was her habit.

"Who dis?"

Jaune rolled his eyes. "Is it ever not me?"

"A girl can hope." Ouch. "Alright, no joke, how did it go?" she asked with a trace of resignation.

With a grin, he delivered the good news. "I have it. Our IDs."

A pause on the line. Then, "...You're serious. How many people are dead?"

"None. Oh, but I did break his wrist."

Over the line, he heard Lisa exhale a breath. Like the world had just made sense again.

"Dare I ask what species they were this time?"

"Human."

"Ahhh, the old reliable. Plain greed did it, I assume?" She did not wait for him to answer. "Send me the following from my file: driver's license, social security number, passport, and the fake utility bills that should be included. I've got all my ducks in a row, and that should let me set up everything."

He found the documents without issue, as the forger had oh so helpfully stuck them together with a paper clip. Picture after picture appeared in their text chat. Lisa had already started working on her end, the rapid click-clacking of a computer keyboard filling the empty space in their conversation. Jaune kept an ear open as he chatted with the two kids on his side.

They took turns regaling him of their adventures over the week. New sights, new scenes, this world presented fresh grounds in every aspect to them, and during the moments when they did not accompany him, they had spent it exploring far and wide. From taking the subway train to visiting the department store, trying out foods to getting roped into playing basketball, they received an eclectic mix of modern life experiences that strung together with hardly a semblance of structure.

Of course, not everything had gone well.

"I thought those carriages were supposed to stop at red lights," Bennett said, recounting his near collision with a car. "At least, that's what boss lady told me. And it was definitely a red light, but the person inside yelled at me." He hung his head. "So I must have done something wrong, but I don't know what."

Where to begin, to explain driving behavior? An entire evolution of the human mindset, built around an invention that had yet to arrive for Mondstadt. More than that, the sheer meanness on display in New York City overwhelmed the worst he ever saw in Vale. He had no good answers.

"I'd guess that it was a really bad day for them. I doubt everyone is like that. Remember the people at the cafe?"

Bennett's face flushed at the memory, and he looked away. "That was somehow worse."

Heh. Beauty standards across time and space was a funny thing, and it seemed to be hitting the newcomers as hard as it did him. Despite swapping for modern and mundane clothing, the pair still stood out in a crowd with the intensity of a lighthouse on a dark night, and even now drew gawking looks from the pedestrians.

"A model. Has to be. The dress is peak Japanese street fashion."

"What's she doing in Sleepy Hollow, then?"

"It fits, don't it?"

"That boy in the windbreaker is for sure a popstar."

"Canadian, you can just tell. Bieber Fever is back, god save us all."

"The tall one with them..."

On and on went the whispers, withstood by the pair to poor success. Their bright red faces led to outright sighs from various lovestruck teens.

"Bank account is done," reported Lisa. "Once it finalizes and we deposit money in there, I'll book somewhere we can stay longer term and we'll see about a phone plan for everybody. How do you feel about this place?"

A series of chiming bells emanated from the phone. He opened the text chat to a slew of photos, and the others gathered around to ooh and ahh with him over their prospective lodgings, a log cabin of great size set amidst a snowy landscape.

"It has all the amenities. Internet, hot water, full kitchen… Including the apartment, we would have five beds and three showers. I'm thinking of reserving it for a month, and then we can see how we go from there."

One detail of note stuck out to him, the lack of the concrete jungle. "This doesn't look much like New York City."

"The Catskills," she explained. "A few hours out. I've checked and a decent property in the city costs a lot. The top floor penthouse of my dreams will come after I study the market and put our cash to work. For now… Well, at the same rate and with less scrutiny, we can live in a sweet vacation rental where nobody bothers us, or rent a dingy unit with paper thin walls between us and our neighbors. Think about that."

A short discussion among the trio present, and Lisa found unanimous support. New York's bright lights had its charm, but a break from the noise, the odor, the… the whole cauldron of sensory overload, sounded pretty ideal. Months of living away from Vale got Jaune used to the peace and quiet, and that was how he preferred it to stay, with this world existing as a reprieve from his hectic days.

He would take the Big Apple in small bites.

"Glad you see it my way," Lisa smugly announced.

"How long is this going to take, would you say?"

"Mmm, about a week for everything to clear."

"That's time enough for us to earn some Points. What do you think, Lisa? Up for a trip?"

His grip tightened on the phone as he waited for her reply. And when she did, he pumped a fist to the sky.

"Why not? I can use the distraction. Not today, though. Drop by the library and we'll go grab a late lunch. I'm feeling up for a good burger, with ice cream by the riverside."

"You got it. Be there in ten."

"Pick up Hu Tao while you're at it?"

He cocked his head, having been unaware of this development. "Where is she?"

"She learned there's a big name in the funeral and cemetery business operating around here, and went ballistic. I think she headed for the local graveyard. Kept yammering about market research and outreach and group rates. Tell me honestly, Jaune. Does she have a screw loose?"

He considered the question, and what he knew of Hu Tao. His mind went to the last few months starting from when his life upended. The answer sprang to his lips.

"Nah. She fits right in."



-o-
​


David Martinez woke up in the morning, feeling like a trillion eddies.
