Chapter 70: Just Another Night City Gig
​


David Martinez woke up in the morning, feeling like a trillion eddies.

Maybe more. The news he watched last night said inflation went up again.

He interfaced with the home assistant program, cybernetic eyes flashing blue, to shut off the alarm before it could blare, with minutes to spare. The day was early yet, the dim orange glow of the sun barely cresting over the skyscraper-filled horizon, competing with the eternal neon lights of Night City, California.

For the Japantown penthouse he earned from his work as a mercenary, that put the time at around six AM. It would not be too far off to call this a mark of how high he had moved on up in the world. Before, by the point he saw real daylight he already had to leave for classes. Placing his hands behind his head, David laid back to enjoy the fruits of his efforts for a little while longer.

The penthouse stayed cold even during the summer, another mark of his success. Used to be that a short payment on his family's subscription to the ventilation system would turn the old apartment unit into an airless oven until his mom figured something out. If only she could see him now, because now he set the temperature at a constant and comfortable 50 degrees. All-natural external cooling for the various chrome stowed within his body, from the Gorilla Armsᵀᴹ that had replaced his original meat, to the cyberoptics, to the neural processor embedded along his spine, to the neural port implanted in his skull since young that was the crux to making the whole setup work. He used to find the metal grafted into him cold, but they ran hot these days for some reason.

Probably because he had broken them in. They were a part of him now, hot as the blood pumping through his veins.

Useless thoughts were blown from his mind and his mood skyrocketed to new heights, like always, as he felt the sudden warmth of Lucy. With the weight of his frame, the bed tilted to his side, making her lithe form roll right up against him. Curled under the blanket, she still slept, the nanotech pigment-dyes of her techhair catching the light from the window to glitter in shades of an iridescent rainbow. Her soft breaths broke the silence of the room.

He drank in the sight of her. On his face, a smile grew. The one she said looked dopey. What did he do to deserve her, he asked himself every day, and would never know. If the sun symbolized his success, then she was the moon, his dream come true.

Not bad for a boy from Santo Domingo, David would say.

If he could just lay here forever…

But he had to go higher still. No time to waste.

With great care, he slipped out of bed to leave Lucy undisturbed. His heart squeezed tight as her hands roamed the sheets, grabbing his pillow and hugging it to her chest.

A quick trip to the bathroom to wash his face and change into a pair of running shorts, and he went down the stairs to the penthouse's main floor. The sheer amount of space got to him, even now. Slowly, it was filling up with signs of his and Lucy's life together over the last few months. Pictures and various knickknacks they bought on their trips out together, plus trophies from his gigs. The small memories.

He skipped breakfast for the time being, heading for the door which slid aside in a whisper-smooth motion to deposit him in a clean, carpeted hallway. The elevator sat further down the passage, properly reinforced for guys like him so he did not have to take the long, long staircase to the bottom floor. He appreciated that.

The trip down, he spent shuffling priorities. Who to contact, where to roam. How many jobs could he and his people knock over during the week given their condition. Leading a crew in Night City took more than good aim and a big gun.

A ding, and the elevator doors opened to the lobby. David stepped forward, and lost in his head, he almost slammed into a wall of boxes and paper bags with two legs sticking out from below. Only by shifting to the side at the last second did he prevent a crash, and in a great bout of charity he squeezed past and put a hand into the elevator to keep it open, allowing the person to enter.

"Thanks!" the walking tank of cardboard said over their shoulder, but David was already off on his way.

Good deed for the day, done.

David left the towering megabuilding, stepping out into the dirty, grimy street that numbered one of many in the Westbrook district. The hell to his heaven, a constant reminder that while he might live at the top, he still wallowed at the bottom. He spared a moment for a deep, bracing breath. The odor of Japantown was a fine mix of grease, sex, and trash that never failed to punch him in the face to wake him up.

Even in the early morning, this part of the city buzzed with activity. Here, corpos low on the rung dragged their feet along the street, either ordered to go in early or ordered to work all last night. There, poor suckers barely making rent with dead-end menial jobs hurried to their shift before they lost it to someone else. Late night revelers stumbled home, faces slack, not quite lucid. And the tourists, they did what tourists always did.

Gonkily gonking like the gonks they were. Gonk.

No matter who, they turned toward him on instinct as he jogged by, attention riveted like small critters in the presence of something dangerous. Hard to blame them, as his looming bulk measured head and shoulders above other pedestrians, and without a shirt, everyone saw the metal on him. His cyberware set him apart, as sleek as anything the corpos might afford while tougher and heavier than their soft lives could ever stand to carry. The sort of deadly chrome that only elite members of the Tyger Claws gang went for around here, except those guys stayed well out of his way, so that sent a certain message.

It said that David Martinez was an edgerunner. A real edgerunner. Built different.

His route took him a short distance south past the bars and storefronts and pachinko parlors, past the Yagami Market where he often grabbed dinner. The underpasses cast deep shadows that he plunged into without fear, hugging the underbelly of Japantown to reach the border with Charter Hill. Today, as ever, the NCPD maintained a heavy presence here. A thin blue line meant not to keep the law but to heckle people who looked too poor to fit in with the upscale residential areas.

David found it amusing that they stood on the street corners, side by side with the joytoys plying their trade. Both sucked the corpos' dicks, but only one of them he respected.

He ignored the badges, and the badges pretended to have grime in their eyes. Once in Charter Hill, a hop over the highway barrier dropped him into the elevated park set above Gold Niwaki Plaza, his very own free membership card to the private sanctuary. The place enjoyed fresh(er) air than Japantown courtesy of industrial purifiers that blew all the bad air away (and straight into Japantown), with flights of steps that provided a good warmup. He always liked spending the first part of his workout just jogging up, down, up, down to clear his head. This morning saw more locals trying to keep pace with him, running ragged until they inevitably threw in the towel one by one. It did not bring a smile to his face, at all.

Ten minutes, the exercise ran. No more, no less. He refused to get comfortable in either direction.

A jump over the edge returned him to the street level, where cleanly swept roads stretched on for block after block in a pristine state, an alien world in the view of most people living in the city. His boots pounded the pavement, never stopping, breathing in through his nose and out through his mouth. The new set of Synth-lungs inside him performed as advertised, moving the oxygen into his blood at peak efficiency—4.5% higher than his old model, at the very minimum. He cut a line across Charter Hill in record time, before heading up to skirt by North Oak. The top of the Night, some call it.

Good views there, he heard, but the outermost road was as close as he tread to the neighborhood. The private security force would shoot him before he made it halfway up the hill.

As he put the area behind him, a Trauma Team AV flew above his head, the flying box of a vehicle gleaming in white and red. Fair bet a bigshot overdosed on whatever hot new designer drug they passed around at the legendary North Oak parties and needed evac to the hospital, their premium membership package ensuring dispatch from the very moment their heart rate skipped a beat out of tune.

It hurt less now, catching sight of Trauma Team around. He could breathe, and think about that day without punching a wall. The pilots, the EMTs… they played by the rules, and he was an idiot believing for a second they would have saved his mom. Life since then taught him better. The only person he could rely on was himself.

A loop around the northernmost side of the Westbrook district put him back in the glitz and glam of Japantown.

And, back to Lucy.

He told a lie. She was someone he could rely on, too.

Life is good, mom. I'm climbing.



-o-
​


The holocall came in as he was eating breakfast with Lucy. Nothing like Kiroshi cyberoptics beaming the avatar face of an old woman into a person's retinas when they were about to kiss their girlfriend to make the stomach churn. A name flashed obnoxiously bright to alert him, just in case he might not have noticed the interruption. Rogue Amendiares had business with him, and her voice blared in his ears.

Rogue: Early and bright, kid. Got a gig for you. Get to work.

You could ask first : David​

But why would she? The Queen of the Fixers did not beg. David understood that and he remembered the absolute bitch of a time he had trying to get into her good graces, professional-wise, so he sent another message. The blurb of thought converted to text alongside the audio.

Send the detes : David​

In Night City, it paid to advertise reliability.

"Rebecca needs 'help' again?" Lucy asked once he closed out the conversation. She had caught the glow to his eyes that indicated a call, and with their lovey-dovey game on hold sat back in her chair to sip at her kale smoothie. Had he a Trauma Team subscription, his mental crash at her adorable pout would have sent them scrambling to evac him.

David shook his head as he returned to his meal, a big protein bowl of EEZYBEEF and RealFruit held together by a sticky heaping of soy paste. A complete breakfast, for all his morning nutrient needs.

Through a mouthful, he answered Lucy, "Nah, Rebecca's fine. Her dryer wasn't even malfunctioning last time so I don't know what she was on about. This was Rouge, from the Afterlife bar. She had a tip on my next job."

A better way of saying the queen spoke and he rolled over like a dog. Some people, you just did not mess with, because they earned that right through the life they walked.

The data package chose that moment to download over the holocall connection, and he began reading up on the gig. "I'll have to set off soon. A freelance journalist working with Network 54 got a scoop, then lost a scoop. Flatlined with a bullet to the back of his head. Rouge thinks he had something ugly on an Arasaka exec, and they took issue with that."

"Sounds real enough," Lucy said with a scowl. "N54's a Militech shill. They would have paid good eddy to put a stain on Arasaka's lovely silk suit."

David nodded. "The twist is, the journalist placed everything he discovered in a dead drop." Lucy opened her mouth, and he preempted the question he knew she would ask. "Not on the net, Lucy. Down in meatspace where the rest of us cavemen live. He must have been afraid of a netrunner like you plucking the info out of his head." That got a wry chuckle from her. "Anyway, the head of N54's regional office wants the data so he can blare it from the rooftops."

Lucy practically lit up at that. She had a… thing about Arasaka. He never got the whole story there, but he held no love for the corporation either, so it all worked out.

She hated Arasaka. He hated Arasaka. They had the best sex whenever he came home after his crew gave those bastards a kick in the teeth. What more did he need to know?

His large hand scooped up the protein bowl and he inhaled the last half of the chunky goop, afterward pounding a fist to his metal chest with a resounding clang to help the food go down.

"You are going to choke one of these days if you keep that up," Lucy chided, before taking the straw out of her smoothie and slamming back the entire thing in a mirror to him. David's eyebrows rose. Rarely did his girlfriend act with that kind of ill grace at the dining table.

Hoooot.

"Let's get to it, then," Lucy said, standing up.

David could not believe his ears, and he scrambled to follow her to the kitchen. As she dropped the cup into the sink to let the autowasher deal with it, he gawped like an idiot, like a gonk.

"You're coming with?"

"I'm not returning to the crew." The firmness of her tone doused his excitement a little. Not completely, because she continued. "But I could… be in the area. See this done right."

He would take it. With a whoop, David grabbed Lucy by the hands and swung her around. Laughter filled his home.

Close to noon, his crew rolled up to the meeting spot in their Chevillon Emperor SUV. Falco, their wheelman, sat in the driver's seat as usual and signaled David through the glass in greeting with the clacking metal fingers of his cyberarm. The dandy very quickly found himself shoved against the door by Rebecca so she could wave at David.

The diminutive girl did not leave it at that, bouncing out of the car to come greet him.

"David! What's new, choom?" she called over with a smile, one of her oversized Gorilla Armᵀᴹ raised high.

Grinning, David offered his own chromed hand, and Rebecca slammed their metal palms together in a certified Gorilla Armᵀᴹ low-five that sent shockwaves through their bodies.

"A fat stack of eddies in our accounts, if it goes well," he said, pretending to shake out the hand in pain, to her laughter. "Didn't you read my text?"

Rebecca made a face. "Bleh, you know I trust you with that boring stuff. Just point me to the target and I'll make with the bang-bang."

She ran a finger over the iron strapped to her waist, another absolute monstrosity of a cannon that she must have bought while he was not looking. Spray-painted in hot garish pink, just for the extra. Rebecca then spotted the girl hidden behind David's bulk.

"Wait, is that—" She zoomed around him. "Lucy!"

The others had also discovered the addition to today's gig. Falco poked his head out of the car window, an eyebrow raised. In the back, the crew's netrunner, Kiwi, leaned forward in her seat, the blonde woman's expression muted as ever behind the red mask she wore—not that taking it off would change anything.

"Rebecca, hey," Lucy said softly, before looking to the side.

Rebecca was having none of it, darting into her view again. "Are you back with us? No, before that, where have you been? David was worried sick for you!"

David flinched. He told Lucy it would be a bad idea to hide the fact they were living together. He told her.

"I know," said Lucy, contrite and not all faking it either. "There were things I had to do alone. Are. I'm not exactly coming back yet. This is to… observe."

The answer displeased Rebecca, who waved her arms wildly. "The fuck does that mean?"

A gesture from him quieted her. "Let it be, Rebecca," he said, voice firm to brook no disagreement. "We have a job to do, and extra help we can trust is welcome. Lucy isn't taking a cut on this, either." Then, kinder, he soothed her. "Look at it as a chance to remind her what we're about, and leave a good impression."

He sweated as Rebecca narrowed her eyes, and thumbed her shotgun.

"Oh, I'll leave an impression, alright," she spat. "A few hundred of 'em, all over her. I didn't forget that you ran out on us, Lucy, and if you don't have any intention of ever coming back, that makes you a traitor."

The most violent way of saying 'I miss you and I want to hang out again' ever. David breathed a sigh of relief as Rebecca stomped off to reenter the car, and after sharing a look with Lucy, they followed her. He held the door open as she got in, then dropped into a free spot in the semicircle bench seat that took up most of the back of the vehicle.

"Bring Your Gal to Work Day, David?" Falco said in lieu of a hello, pulling away from the curb. He asked for no direction, a sign that at least one person in David's crew bothered to read the file. Their armored ride headed toward Northside, one bad part of town among many. Hey, we're better than the Pacifica combat zone, was their motto.

"C'mooon, don't you give me lip, too," David joked.

As he chatted with Falco, he did not miss the glowing eyes on both Lucy and Kiwi. The two netrunners' talks flowed faster than his, without a sound. During a lull, he brought them into the conversation.

"Kiwi, what have you turned up on our target?"

Around the car, everybody put their business faces on. One moment of acting serious, so that they could later go wild without it screwing the team over.

"Your buddy has a sense of humor," Kiwi reported. "He hid his tracks well, but he went out of his way to pass by the defunct WNS station in Watson, where he vanished off the net for close to ten minutes. Good odds that the datashard is hidden inside."

David chuckled. "In Arasaka's own mouthpiece. Nice find, Kiwi. That saved us days of searching. Rebecca, you've kept your ears to the ground—"

"Is that a short joke, gonk?" Rebecca growled, and the possibility of him getting shot skyrocketed.

"You've been around," he amended, leaning away from the muzzle of a revolver she had yanked out of her puffy jacket, "so do you know who's controlling that area this week? Claws, or Maelstrom?"

"Ehhh." Rebecca rested her chin on an oversized finger, thinking on it. "Neither, if I remember right. The last war in Watson cost them. Dumbasses pulled back to lick their wounds before the next one. I know the station, and it should be in the gap they left."

"Cold zone, then," David mused. "Best kind."

"Not necessarily," Kiwi interrupted, drawing his attention. She was looking out the window, idly tapping a finger on the handrest. Often a sign that she was less certain of something than she liked. "Word on the vine is that Wakako is sending people up that way. Timeframe and general location matches. Not a peep on the NCPD comms about another incident."

David furrowed his brows. "Meaning their gig could be the same one we're on but from a different player, you're suggesting? Anybody we know?" The life of an edgerunner—a mercenary, a solo, a street samurai—often pitched a person against others in the biz, people who shared a glass one evening going on to blast one another with their iron the next night. The nature of the game, David understood that, but he relaxed a touch as Kiwi shook her head.

"Not much on them. Gotta be new. Did two jobs for Wakako, and that's only rumors because none of her usual solos were tapped for those. They're noobs."

"They survived two jobs for Wakako," Lucy chimed in. "That counts for something."

David reached over, squeezing her hand. "Lucy's right. That old lady is particular. If this crew failed the first gig, their second would have been a death sentence in all but name."

Kiwi frowned behind her mask, but ultimately nodded to acknowledge the point.

"So either it was and they succeeded against the odds, or she thought they could handle themselves," said Kiwi. "That explains it. A bit. Because the second job was a big score. The kind that we get."

It should have gone to their crew, the thought passed between them all.

With those revelations in mind, their plan took shape. They were dealing with street samurai, or ones with the chops to reach that status. Harder opposition in some ways, easier in others.

Quickest solution? In this scene, reputation carried you far, and David's crew had built a solid cred for themselves. He might just ask the other team to step aside, and fifty-fifty shot it ended right there. Nobody wanted to mess with David Martinez.

Now, he was not blind. A solid cred also translated to 'if I flatline these guys then my fame goes to the moon'. So, he proposed to his team backup plans A, B, and C. Otherwise known as Mister Left, Mister Right, and Miss Rebecca. This earned him loud and spirited support from one member of the team—three guesses who—plus agreement from the rest.

"That's literally our usual op," Kiwi pointed out. At the front, Falco grunted.

"And it hasn't failed yet," David replied with calm, to Rebecca's cheers. He loved how she always got his back.

Glancing at Lucy, his heart fluttered he cooly winked. Her soft smile at the scene inside the car told him she still remembered the old days. And someday, someday soon, she would rejoin the crew. He just knew it.

At his request, Kiwi retrieved the schematics of the WNS station and dropped it onto a datapad. Step by step, they set up the scenario. Him through the front entrance, Rebecca from the back. Easy pincer if things go hot, with Kiwi outside playing overwatch and, if their luck holds, maybe jacking into the building's subnet through the maintenance access port on the roof. Years of neglect would have killed most of the tech inside, but zombie electronics popped up in the most unlikely places, and had their uses in the hands of a good netrunner. They had two of those today, for excellent odds.

Wrapping up, he reminded his team to check their loadout. Rebecca seized the chance to show off her new shotgun, gushing over its specs. He listened with half an ear while retrieving a set of revolvers from a gun compartment. Precision with a dash of power, along with a proper heft that would let him pistol whip a man through a wall, if needed. He stowed them in holsters strapped under his armpits.

The car rolled to a halt just outside the WNS station, and every single one of their plans went out the window.

"Empty?" David asked to make sure. "You're joking."

"N-ope," said Kiwi, eyes aglow and directed at the building. "My scans are picking up a few lights on, a couple appliances they forgot to unplug when they shut the place down. Not one piece of cyberware, anywhere. Nobody's inside."

"She's right," Lucy added on. "My own search routines are turning up blank."

Hot damn, how about that?

"The other team didn't already get what they came for and left, did they?" Rebecca asked.

Kiwi shook her head. "I'm checking interface logs and handshake procedures. Most recent contact with the subnet was days ago. The journalist, is my bet. Since then, it's been dead quiet."

"Good enough for me," David said, and he kicked open the car door. "Rebecca, Kiwi, let's just walk in. No point wasting time. Falco, keep that engine purring." He flicked his fingers in a salute at Lucy, sending a quick text with a thought.

Brb : David​

Lucy: K.

True love.

Kiwi's quickhack sent the doors to the news station sliding aside for them to enter without breaking stride. The lobby featured a reception desk and a vending machine, and they started there, sifting for hidden caches. A datashard measured the size of a fingernail, but a dead drop would have some kind of marking to set it apart.

On a whim, he looked behind the TV screen mounted to the wall, one that still displayed the WNS logo in big, bold font. No go.

"Find anything?" he checked with his crew, getting shrugs in reply. "Let's head in deeper."

The door on the back wall led to a hallway cluttered up with junk, splitting off into other parts of the building. Posters hung on the wall, announcing programs canceled years ago, their hosts and actors faded to irrelevance.

Rebecca peeked around the corner ahead, and groaned. "More hallways. This is going to take foreveeer."

He clapped her on the shoulder, gentle so as to not bowl her over.

"The journalist didn't stay long and he was trying to be clever. It's going to stick out like a sore thumb."

They split up, with Rebecca and Kiwi heading one way, him another. So while they got the boring old offices and break rooms, he roamed through a storage area for stage set pieces filled with creepy mannequins that somebody had left standing around.

Uh-huh, no idea what was up with that.

The mannequins faced the coffee machines, or grouped around as if holding conversations, half-hidden in the gloom. One laid on a couch as if napping. Two were hidden in a closet, faces pressed together. David spent more time keeping an eye on the mannequins than he did searching for the dead drop. As he ventured deeper into the building, he swore they moved when he was not looking.

No matter how much chrome a man chipped in, he could recognize when he was in a horror movie setting. If he had his revolvers raised and fingers on a hair trigger, then it was out of the manly desire to shoot a ghost in the face, and not from fear.

A clattering noise almost saw him emptying his entire clip.

But then, he listened a little more, and he realized that it sure sounded like a person up ahead in that room there. People, he could deal with, and David padded over to the doorway.

The newsroom studio stabbed him in the heart with its familiarity. He and his mom must have watched the evening report taped from this very place, because he remembered that backdrop, with the brownish-red smudge at the top corner that, for years, nobody ever bothered to scrub away. That carelessness might explain why the office was shut down.

Damn, what was the anchorwoman's name? He thought she was so pretty back then.

The person David heard was being less than subtle, and remained oblivious to his presence. Off the bat, David resolved to kill him for his chrome. Because wow, wow, wow his cyberlegs had a flight function.

No, no. Hang on. He was a man of conviction, and not the rap sheet kind. He could stand to make a fair offer first. Pretty please chop off your legs for me, I have money.

The solo, for he had to be one, floated near the ceiling, jets of fire streaming from the bottom of his feet in defiance of gravity. If he had other chrome, it was less obvious, hidden under baggy pants and some kind of bootleg Trauma Team merch, a rain poncho in their colors. David stayed back to observe him, watching the guy fiddle with a spotlight hanging high above.

His eyes narrowed as he spied the 'X' painted on the side of the light. His suspicion received confirmation a moment later.

"I got it! It's here!" The solo suddenly cut off the flight function, dropping like a rock. David's desire for those cyberware shot up as he saw it in action, quick activation bursts slowing the descent to give the impression that the guy was walking on the air. Landing, the solo brandished a small chip held between his fingers. "Lisa, look, it really was here—Lisa? Hey, where did you go?"

A song played, emanating from the solo, who reached in his pocket to retrieve a phone.

The sight of that device reminded David of something. Hadn't Kiwi and Lucy both agreed that nobody else was in the building?

"Lisa, hey—wait, what?"

The solo spun around, locking eyes with David.

A man's face said a lot about him. This one was a corpo fucker coming down from on high, he could just tell. Skin soft as a baby's, without the blemishes of a real life. The full suite of biosculpting for that unnaturally handsome look. Cyberware so artful that it seemed like there was nothing there, daddy's money at work.

It reminded him of Katsuo. Of Arasaka Academy. Of—!

David breathed in, and out. His heart rate steadied.

Another tick mark in the 'kill' column. Nothing more, nothing less. It did not decide his course. He was a reasonable man. He had to stay cool.

Putting up a smile, David stepped out of the gloom. He raised a hand in greeting, showing that it was empty—a sign of peace.

"Nice flying, choom," he said. "Whaddya got in your hand there?"

The corpo playing at being a solo looked ridiculous, one hand pinching the datashard, the other clapping a clunky phone to his ear. Those things faded out of fashion for a reason, and no real edgerunner would ever consider using them. One hand occupied was a hand not holding a gun.

Head cocked, the corpo seemed to be listening to the person on the other end of the call. He then glanced down at the datashard, before hiding it behind his back.

"Nothing," the corpo said, unconvincingly.

David almost felt for the guy. This gonk seemed green as grass. He had to remind himself that it was almost 100% a front, what with corpo parents raising their kids to be ruthless snakes.

"Tell you what," said David. "Let's do business. We can both walk away happy. You give me that datashard there, and I'll pay you in your currency of choice. Eddies, or a favor. An invite into the Afterlife isn't out of the equation."

A rich kid would not blink at money, but if he read this guy right, then the mention of the Afterlife should have him salivating. Why would a corpo put on the trappings of a solo? To live the life, and experience what no braindance could emulate. A central part of that involved setting foot in the greatest edgerunner bar of Night City, the Afterlife where legends the likes of Morgan Blackhand and Andrew Weyland once frequented.

"No, I'm good. Thanks for the offer, though."

Aaand this one was the worst sort. A brat born fifty floors up who thought they earned what they had by their own two hands, and expected to do the same in the solo scene.

Also, thanked twice in one day? Man, he was becoming a regular samaritan, wasn't he?

Too bad he probably had to flatline this fool.

"I need that datashard—"

"So do I."

David growled under his breath. He spent years at Arasaka Academy with everything he tried to say cut off by entitled corpo brats, and this idiot decided to slam that button with both hands.

"I need that datashard," he repeated. "And I am going to get that datashard. Hand it over, or I'll let metal do the talking."

David read the guy's answer from his stance before he could speak a word, and in one smooth motion pulled his revolvers out of their holsters.

Bang, bang, his iron sang. End of story.

The corpo brat walked it off.

No, really. David blinked his eyes, wondering whether his model of Kiroshi cyberoptics had a design glitch they neglected to mention, and if he should lodge a complaint. But no, the guy was standing upright, rubbing a spot over his heart and frowning.

His comms blared, the message coming in at the speed of thought.

Rebecca: David! That you?

Kiwi: What are you shooting at? I don't see anything.

Lucy: David? David, are you okay?

Rebecca: We going hot?

I just—whatwhatthefuckingshitshit : David​

David dove behind the cover of the newsroom desk, cursing his glitching Kiroshis as the others shouted their alarm in his ears. A spark of electricity danced up and down his leg, a bullet lodged within the cyberware. All throughout, he played back the memory, trying to figure out where the weirdass rifle that the gonk was firing one-handed even came from.

A netrunning quickhack. Had to be. Shut down his optics for a split second to make him think it magic.

…If the guy could do that, then he could have destroyed the Kiroshis outright. The corpo had style, if nothing else.

He heard the jets of fire. The clue gave him ample warning, his experience as an edgerunner springing to the fore. He aimed his revolvers up, waiting for his target to—where the fuck was the corpo keeping that sword!?

The direction had been correct, the distance less so. The corpo showed himself within swinging range, a sword like something out of a 2020 fantasy vid stabbing down. David fired a round as he rolled aside and to his feet, and this time he saw it clear as day the bullet plinking off the corpo's skin like David just shot a Samson borg.

It just didn't make sense.

"Why do everybody and their mother keep trying to kill me?" the corpo called out, darting after David as David attempted to clear some room, searing the floor beneath with blasts of fire that sent him zooming forward.

The maneuver practically invited a bullet to the face. Despite the previous failure, David obliged with another bid, full-bore overkill with his metal limbs shifting to reveal the cannons stowed within his forearms, his wrists turning to hold his guns sideways.

Two Projectile Launch Systems armed with rockets. Two .42-caliber Malorian Overture revolvers. A meatgrinder special. The room shook as he let loose.

Out of nowhere, a shield appeared to cover the corpo, comprising huge red lizard scales that David refused to believe belong to something real. The bullets bounced off it, as useless as blanks. The rockets struck, and the corpo showcased top-line reflex boosters, shaking his shield side to side in a quick movement to bat the rockets off-course, sending them to detonate on the newsroom wall far behind him.

It just didn't make sense.

Rockets had momentum. Weight. They were bullets writ large.

But the guy stayed standing. His legs had shifted at the moment of impact, bracing against the force. Somehow, that kept him exactly where he was instead of blasting him off his feet.

David had heard of 'steeling yourself', but excuse me, what the fuck?

Rebecca: Kiwi's down!

His blood ran cold.

Is she alive!? : David​

Lucy popped into the comms.

Lucy: Vital signs a go. Melatonin and adenosin spike parallels the effect of sedatives.

Rebecca: She's dead asleep!

He ducked under a sword swipe, releasing one of his guns to throw a pulverizing uppercut into the corpo's sternum, drawing a grunt. A grunt. Instead of, ya know, guts exploding everywhere.

The corpo retaliated by seizing David by the collar and slamming his head into David's face.

Crack!

David saw stars. He had less subdermal armor in his skull than elsewhere, Lucy disliking the idea of his face changing. In other words, he had some, and he felt them dent from the blow.

As he stumbled back, David saw the corpo kick out low, catching David's revolver in the crook of his foot. In a blink, the gun vanished.

What just happened? : David​

He had thought that to himself, but within his rattling head, the comms sent it off as a message. Rebecca took it as something different, a question to her.

Rebecca: A netrunner got her. A good one. Better than Kiwi. Threw a dart from ambush and hacked our optics, made us see them as a cat!

Lucy: Not possible. Not mid-fight. That kind of detail work needs a dive.

Rebecca: Well, that's what happened!

A… cat?

A barrage of gunfire wracked the building, sounding far off.

Rebecca: Die, die, die you fucking pussy!

David had no time to absorb this development. A flicker, a trick of the light, and the corpo's shield was gone, the rifle in its place. How, how, how, his mind screamed. His eyes belonged under somebody else's control, and it freaked him.

The next trick arrived. Prior to shooting, the corpo made a gesture with his hand, and shadows engulfed David's vision. A gravitational effect—some prototype cyberware he had never even heard of—yanked him off-balance, preventing him from escaping.

His other senses worked fine. He heard the sound of fire, and so spun around. His arms snapped up, protecting his core, too late as the bullet slipped between. It crashed against his chest, and David fiercely grinned.

Still alive.

The armor plating on his chest cost a pretty eddy, and proved its worth yet again. More bullets struck his arms, nicking the metal but failing to punch through.

"Tough luck, gonk!" he shouted in the darkness, rushing forward. "I'm built different!"

Light returned, the shadows fading as he rammed into the corpo, and he strove to trample him underfoot. At first, it worked, the corpo knocked back and carried along by David's charge. Then, he did that weird bracing of his legs again, and David found his stampede grinding to a halt. Over the top of his fists, he met a pair of calm blue eyes.

Then, David felt his chromed-up body being pushed back.

It just didn't make sense.

The sheer amount of cyberware required for the corpo to do the things he did, it rivaled David's own if not belonging to a different class altogether. Except, chrome went deeper than the skin. The corpo's lungs needed the strength to handle the strain of his tech, strength that came from augmentation which added its own load to the neural processor. His heart, reinforced. His stomach, reinforced. His damn liver, reinforced. More load, more stress, more stress to deal with the stress.

He should have been teetering on cyberpsychosis, not looking cool as a cucumber right back at David.

Evac Kiwi, Rebecca. I'll hand this : David
...Rebecca? : David​

Lucy: David… The netrunner got her too. I'm heading in.

His heart leapt to his throat.

No! Lucy, stay out of there! : David​

She did not answer, and David knew she would not listen. Lucy left the team, but she loved them. Loved him.

David wanted her back on the crew, but not like this. Not with a corpo freak of nature and his netrunning ninja pushing their backs against the wall. He had to end it in the span of time it took for her to leave the car and make it inside.

And he would.

Calm overtook him. David flipped a mental switch, and his body jerked.

Heat. Light. Sparks in his brain. A roaring in his chest. His limbs were set afire.

Sandevistan.

In a still world, David moved. In the space of a breath, he stepped aside to walk past his opponent's outstretched arms, grab him by his clothes, flipped him onto the floor, mounted him, and pounded a synthetic-muscled, shape-memory alloyed Gorilla Armᵀᴹ fist into the bastard's face. A microsecond later, the next punch landed, his other fist already cocked back.

One. Two. One, two. Onetwoonetwoonetwoonetwo—

His knuckles smacked against a force field. That was the only word for it. The accelerated perception caused by the Sandy cyberware implanted inside him reached its limit, and as colors bled back into the world, David stared in utter incomprehension at the golden sphere encasing the corpo, whose head lay embedded in a hole in the ground. The force field had shoved David back against the newsroom desk, pinning him and giving the corpo space. His mind blanked as he watched the guy rolled to his feet and pulled a giant stick out of his ass.

The thing was a huge chunk of metal, with gun parts shoved in it. Covered in those fake red lizard scales.

David then heard the tinkling chime of bells. A mask popped over the corpo's face, depicting a cat or… or a fox, and David was suddenly reminded of that Japantown legend. Not the solo kind, but the myth about animal spirits haunting the land that people hawked around come a festival.

People like Wakako the fixer.

"Set effect, huh?" muttered the fox. The corpo. Whatever he was. "Let's test it out."

Darkness, literal darkness, seized hold of David's leg right before he activated the Sandevistan again. All of the momentum he put in moving aside encountered just enough resistance, and his ankle twisted. He exited Sandy time with a cry of pain.

The huge chunk of metal rushed up to meet him.

Wham!



-o-
​


David came to, lodged in the ceiling of the newsroom studio. Blood ran down his dangling limbs, traveling over the metal to drip to the floor. A small red pool had formed during his bout of unconsciousness.

The corpo was long gone from the look of it, the datashard nowhere in sight. David could not care less that he had failed the job. Through the fog that blanketed his mind, a name sprang to his lips.

"Lucy… Lucy…"

Lucy… Lucy… : David​

Lucy: David?

Tears fell alongside his blood. She had answered his prayer.

Are you okay? Please tell me you're okay : David​

Lucy: I am. Alive. Good. Rebecca good. Kiwi good.

David blinked. Lucy sounded off. Like a Kiwi.


Are you really? : David​


Lucy: David, I saw them walk by. Boy. Girl. Cat-shape thing. I hacked. Tried. Nothing. No face. No ID.
Lucy: No chrome.

It just didn't make sense.

...We got whooped by a bunch of cripples? : David​

Lucy: They had phones. Connected nowhere. Tech weird… Mpshpsm…

Lucy, what's wrong? Lucy? : David​

Lucy: Just sleepy… nighty… night…

David could breathe again.

"Fucking ninja. Fucking corpo." Relief washed over him, and he barked out a shaky laugh. His metal-grafted ribs screamed in protest. "Cats, foxes, experimental cyberwares out the ears, and motherfucking Arasaka."

He said it like a slur, and he meant it as a slur. Were they really involved? He wasn't sure, but when in doubt, blame Arasaka.

The one thing he did know?

"Time to chrome the fuck up."


Author's Notes: There were a lot of good guesses on who Jaune and co would fight in this world, from the Maelstrom gang to Adam Smasher, but… the idea I had way back when was that I really, really wanted to pit Jaune's crew against David's crew. And then pit David's crew against Jaune's crew. And then—

Basically, I want to see them beat the everloving stuffing out of each other, escalating all the while.

#5,850

Chapter 71: Just Another Night City Solo
​


2076.

Night City, California.

A city by the coast, at which many roads converged. The last place where the sun would set. They called it the City of Dreams.

As Jaune watched the skyline from his balcony, he found the title an easy one to believe in. Up here, he saw the vision, what it was meant to be. Up here, they had not taken away the blue sky.

…The holographic streams of ads beamed toward the heavens somewhat detracted from the picture, though.

"Have you ever thought, 'Man, I need to get bigger?' Then boy do I—"

"Not interested," said Jaune to the massive hologram billboard. The image itself floated in thin air a hundred yards away, but the technology behind the ad allowed it to pinpoint him and transmit sound across the intervening space to whisper the sales pitch right in his ears. The ad 'heard' his rejection, but theirs was a stubborn sort and with a flicker the billboard now portrayed a different product. Naked flesh greeted him, wrapped around a pole.

"Looking for a good time? Come play, my lord. You virtual girlfriends await—"

'Not interested," he repeated, groaning.

Unwilling to let the ads run roughshod over his day, he turned around so that the algorithms could no longer read his face, his reactions. Would not analyze his age to match it with the proper demographic, playing with averages and statistics to guess a young man's interests.

What he wanted, truly wanted, was a simple thing. Jaune rested his back against the balcony, head tilted up to enjoy the morning's light… and the quiet. After three days of staying in this world, he had come to rely on the penthouse apartment as his oasis of calm in the bustling metropolis of Night City. A time to unwind before heading out for work to earn his daily bread (and then some). The noise far below reached him as the memory of sound, barely there and lost amidst the wind.

Koi fish swam in the small decorative pond by his side. A handful of food crumbs sent them into a frenzy, the water surface broken by their merry splashes. He ignored the fact that one more fish had gone missing since last night, which surely had no connection to the poorly-swept ashes of a spent fire hidden under the potted bonsai plant in that corner there. A certain cat deserved the right to midnight snacks.

A peaceful sleep, and a full belly. A place like this counted as a luxury in Night City from how he understood it, beyond the means of most. Doubly so for a boy without a bank account stored in his skull.

He heard a soft hiss as the door to the balcony nudged aside. From within, Escha stuck her head out. Her face scrunched as she got a whiff of the open air.

"Jaune, Jaune, Lisa is calling—a… achoo!"

"Good morning, Escha. Still not used to the California air yet?"

An emphatic shake of the head was her answer, the felyne snuffling her nose. She darted back inside, beckoning with her little paw. Jaune laughed as he followed her. The glass door slid shut behind him.

"Sometimes, I wish I had a human's nose," Escha said wistfully, padding off toward the window where a warm spot in the sunshine awaited with a good view overlooking the city.

Lisa had set their expectations high, waxing on and on about the perfect Cali weather, the fresh sea breeze, the beach life… a whole host of upsides to their destination. The girl ate her words pretty quick once they actually arrived and she discovered a city unlike any place in America she knew.

Funny, but also disappointing. Seeing Tattletale (Bikini Ver.) again would have been a treat.

Instead, he got Tattletale (Neurotic Ver.) sitting on the couch with her bloodshot eyes riveted on the TV, hunched over her little project, a piece of paper set on the low table that she scribbled in with feverish concentration. Slovenly dressed in pajamas, she bounced a jittery knee as she listened to the person on the screen. Halfway through the man's spiel, a decisive stroke of her pen scratched a line on the paper out of existence, new information replacing them written on the margins. She spared him a look, crooking her finger, and he walked over.

The apartment featured a lot of space, divided between a main floor and a mezzanine level where the bed was located, connected by a curving staircase. Meant for two but built for six, it suited their needs, the boisterousness of their daily lives given room to breathe without grating on nerves, at least for the time being. It let each of them do their own thing.

The couch, though. Everybody loved that, and he passed by a disheveled head of blonde hair on his way to Lisa.

"Fischl, hey," he said, pausing. "Had a good sleep?"

Said girl mumbled an incoherent reply, and curled into the corner of the couch to softly snooze. Multiple nights of staying up late had taken their toll on Fischl. He could not blame her, because he suffered the same problem. There was just too much to see around here.

Hand planted on the back of the couch, he swung over to land beside Lisa. His shoulder bumped against hers, followed by the briefest glance as he judged her reaction to that. She did not seem to mind the gesture, and the tense knot in his stomach uncoiled as soon as it had formed. Things between them have been going well, recently.

Then again, these last few days saw her far more preoccupied with something other than him. Since it fascinated her so, Jaune gave the TV show a chance to catch his interest. The technical jargon firing back and forth lost him in mere seconds. The performance of this cyberware implant outpaced that model because of this, that, and the other factor, trading off with such and such drawbacks. It could put a man to sleep, listening to this stuff.

"What's got you in such a tizzy?" he asked.

Lisa shushed him. "Busy. Need you to buy me breakfast. Eggs, bacon, toast, avocado. A glass of orange juice."

"Anything else for your order, ma'am?" he said archly, an eyebrow raised. "You know, we can just eat the food here. It won't kill us." Shifting, he stretched out on the couch and withdrew the Company scroll from his pants pocket. A series of taps put him in the food section of the Marketplace, where he perused the options.

"Says you. I know what's in them," Lisa shot back, her airy tone lacking heat. Her pen circled a spot on the paper three times, signaling its importance. Then, with a final stroke, she slapped the pen onto the low table. "Done!"

"What is?" Jaune asked as he began setting out the ready-made meals he bought. From the mezzanine level above, the whooshing sound of a sword swinging through the air redoubled in speed as a hungry Bennett rushed to complete his exercises, while Oz flew down from his perch in the chandelier to peck at his own dish of bird seeds with gusto.

Despite her growling stomach, Lisa focused on him, too hyped up to leave his question alone. She brandished the piece of paper in his face. Pure nonsense they were, to his eyes. Still, a few words popped out, underlined or circled depending on a system of organization known only to Lisa.

Arasaka-brand Cyberdeck. Camillo RAM Manager. Ex-Disk. Memory Boost. Monowire.

In short, cyberware.

The futuristic Night City offered an amazing variety of plunder, enough to dazzle his eyes with the steadily climbing Points balance on the scroll. The guns featured neat gimmicks like electromagnetic tech and homing bullets that put them a step above mundane arms. Escha climbed onto the low wall, turning to face them. "Won't they catch us coming if they can see in the dark? We have to be extra sneaky-sneaky."

"Do we want to?" Jaune countered. "I can just charge in. Break into the back and start storing everything in sight."

Tattletale elbowed him, nixing the idea. "I wish it was that easy. The second group aren't run-of-the-mill gangsters. Walking gait says daily training, likely corporate mercenaries with a clear playbook. See that one? His buddies might be getting out, but the driver is staying inside the van with the engine running. Hand movement, he just locked the doors. Ready on a moment's notice to delta."

He checked through his own binoculars. "Good point, Tattletale. Alright, stealth it is. And look at you, picking up the local lingo."

Tattletale refused to look at him. Her face under the low light was tinged red. "What can I say? They speak my language."

"Heh. Okay then, let's figure out how we'll delta in there… What?"

"Never say that word again. You use it all wrong."

Jaune sighed. There was no pleasing some people. Escha patted him on the head in sympathy.

Their plan took shape. Tattletale remained behind, keeping an eye on the convo between 6th Street and their contact. At her signal, he would dive in from the one direction that the gang neglected to cover, the sky above. A simple approach with few points of failure. Now, they were just waiting for the contact to remove themselves and leave only the gang to deal with.

As for Escha…

In the middle of banking the glider around to perform another lazy circle, Jaune scanned the ground below for hint of a white furball. "Where is she now?"

"Steadily getting there," reported Tattletale through the phone looped around his neck with a string. "Roving patrols are slowing her down. A cat is worth a fortune in this day and age. A glimpse of her, and they'll call up their full roster to comb over the area."

Escha's job involved the backup plan of infiltrating the van to knock out the driver and unlock the doors, her more diminutive frame well-suited to the task. Succeed, and Jaune could enter and drive away before anybody had the chance to react.

"Dammit."

"What?"

"They brought out a metal case. 6th street wanted to check the goods. Experimental rifles. Ballistics. Smart bullet capabilities? No, that's not important. Gotta pick those up before you leave if you want to stick to the contract."

The screech of tires signaled further complications.

As Tattletale shouted in his ears about newcomers to the party, a car smashed through the chainlink fence separating the parking lot from a side alley. A boxy thing decked out in thick armor, its wheels locked to swing the entire frame around, smashing into gang members to crush them beneath its bulk, coming to a halt between the people present and the gray van.

Half a beat was all it took for 6th Street and the mercenaries to light up the area in a firestorm of bullets. Not everybody operated on the same page, with the members of each turning weapons on their counterpart, having assumed this new development a betrayal. Bodies dropped in quick succession.

"Fuck, I'm gonna puke again—Wait, I remember that SUV. It was parked near the WNS station yesterday. The license plate is identical."

Bullets chipped and scratched the SUV, but its armor held against the onslaught. Then, the people inside jumped out, and the shootout began in earnest.

Jaune frowned as he swooped lower, spying a yellow jacket that pinged his memory. "And I remember that big guy with the quaffed hairdo."

He watched the door to the gray van opening, the mercenary inside leaning out with a handgun. A strange flicker, and his arm lopped off at the elbow. A lithe figure exited the SUV to seize him and yank him from the vehicle, taking his place at the wheels.

"Tattletale, the plan's shot. I'm heading in."

The bald eagle would go hungry. Problem was, he might, too. Vultures had come out to play.

The glider on his back folded in, letting him fall. Near the ground, he twisted to point his feet downward, landing with a loud slam right in front of the 6th Street lieutenant who had been handling the negotiations. A punch to his gut dropped him like a sack of grains.

The man's counterpart spun around at the noise, squeezing down the trigger of his weapon, one of the very same experimental rifles they haggled over. The three-shot burst blew past Jaune's ear. He grabbed the rifle, tugging it toward himself with such strength that it threw the mercenary over his head to land yards away in a heap. Without another person touching the weapon, it disappeared into his Pocket. The contents of the case followed suit without a pause as gunfire concentrated on his position in retaliation. He armored up to help weather the impacts, retreating to cover behind the rusty frame of a car long dead. The gang members hiding there fell quiet in short order.

"Caught our strays, Tattletale. Only the van now."

"It's escaping. Don't give it the chance!"

"On it."

A smoke grenade hit the ground to blur his movements from cyberoptics, and he darted from cover on a beeline for the gray van. That did not work as well as he hoped, with more bullets than was comfortable hitting his back to send him stumbling. A golden dome manifested to protect him, and he pressed on, using the abandoned cars in the lot to break their line of sight.

Ahead, the solo from yesterday stood in his way, and upon noticing him, a wide and eager grin overtook the young man's features.

"You! I was hoping to find you again, you corpo bastard!"

Jaune paused for a beat, studying him. "Is it me or are you bigger than I remember?"

The answer arrived in the form of a massive machine gun that the other boy swung off his back to hold with both hands. The Geo barrier caved under the resulting barrage, with the shield to Crocea Mors appearing right on time to block the powerful impacts that rattled his arm.

"David!" Jaune heard someone shout. "Give me cover fire, what are you doing?"

"Not now, Rebecca! Got a gonk to flatline!"

The bold claim fell somewhat flat as [Third Arm] pulled Jaune into close range, and his sword sliced the machine gun in half with one swing. A twirl, and the sword descended to do the same with the young man.

A pair of oversized mechanical arms got there first, grabbing the boy's head and pulling him into the SUV. As his blade whiffed air, Jaune got a glimpse of a very short girl with bluish pale skin slapping her teammate on the head in chiding. She stuck her tongue out at him as the car lurched forward. Tires squealed on the asphalt, with the SUV shooting off side by side with the gray van.

"Jaune, after them!"

The remaining 6th Street and mercenaries had turned their guns onto Jaune, and they stared with mouths agape as he took to the air, shedding his armor and weapons to blast across the parking lot. The convoy of vehicles hit the street with him not far behind, glider unfolding to help him stay aloft.

The cars were picking up speed, though. He had no time to waste. Ruhm filled his hands, and he fired off a barrage.

The bullets struck asphalt, and nothing else.

"Come on, hit the wheels! The wheels!" He yelled at… well, at himself. At his marksmanship ability, whose wonderful aim worked right until the bullets left the barrel. After that, simple physics ruled the day. With fast-moving targets, that meant a series of embarrassing misses as he resorted to putting actual firearm lessons to use in order to lead the shots. A couple dings and nicks did little to stop the cars, and with a frustrated cry he ceased the fruitless endeavor in lieu of chasing after them—a shorter distance might see him fare better, was his thinking.

The attack had alerted the group of a pursuer, however. A panel on top of the SUV slid aside and a figure in a familiar yellow jacket appeared, mismatched pair of revolvers at the ready.

The glider folded one wing, and Jaune rolled to the side in midair in order to avoid the incoming gunfire. The convoy seized the chance while he was distracted to adjust course, turning sharply at a corner.

He had been hoping for that. Firing off his rockets at full power, he launched over the buildings lining the road. The shortcut placed him on a diagonal path, a straight course to his target. In fact, he moved ahead of them.

Yellow Jacket scanned the sky in the entirely wrong direction. At his waist, the shortie with the ghostly-pale look likewise peeked out of the open sunroof.

"Did we lose him?" she asked her partner.

With a grin, Jaune landed on the car roof, where he answered her.

"Haha, n—"

Pain flared in his back. He stared at the night sky.

"—ope… What the heck just happened?"

He swung to sit up, and found himself face to face with the pile of muscles that was Yellow Jacket. The other boy was climbing to his feet, having fallen onto the road the same as Jaune. Behind him, the convoy continued to put distance between them.

"Oh no," Jaune said with a groan, "It's that weird effect again. But at least I can deal with y—"

The solo vanished.

"—ou and that is just not fair."

His gaze bounced from one side of the street to the other, before focusing on the convoy to see the mercenary swinging onto the roof of the gray van.

"So unfair," he repeated.

"Get it, kid! Go after them!"

Jaune turned his head. He had an audience. Pedestrians on the sidewalk had cleared space to avoid the altercation, but they watched in rapt attention. Eyes glowed with beeping red lights, recording the scene.

No quiet spectators, they. The people jeered and laughed, hooted and hollered. The common throughline? They wanted him to keep going, because edgerunners made for the best entertainment.

"Mad, all of you," Jaune said as he scrambled to his feet, and gave chase through the air.

His vantage point allowed him a view past the convoy. The sight caused him to wince.

"Tattletale. I have eyes on them, but I'm not sure I can catch up," he reported. "They've hit a main street. From here, it could take them halfway across the city. My rocket batteries won't last."

"Shoot out their wheels."

"I tried. Didn't work then, won't work now with all the other cars on the road. A stray shot could kill a lot of people."

"Good call. You can't get in close? What am I talking about, of course you can't. Your top speed isn't close to theirs on a straight road."

A brief silence had him listening to static.

"Do your best, I'm already on my way."

His best amounted to not much. A formidable distance had formed between him and the convoy, increasing with the passing seconds. His curses rang out in the night as he coaxed his boots to somehow fly faster, mustering all his willpower to the maximum.

That… was less effective than he liked.

Then, Tattletale's voice returned.

"Gimme a landmark. Whatever's biggest."

He asked no question, immediately searching around.

"Megabuilding H6 is at my 1 o'clock, facing city center. There's also—"

"No need. I know where you are. Bank right to two streets over. See our car?"

It did not take long for him to spot the tricked-out, neon-lit eyesore that they 'borrowed' from a gangster on a previous job. Seconds later, he touched down on its roof, grabbing the edge of the window to poke his head inside. Tattletale had the steering wheels in a death grip, eyes locked on the road. Escha, meanwhile, sat in the passenger seat and seemed to be enjoying the car ride immensely. She waved to him, and he waved back.

"Nice work, Tattletale. Stick to this road and it should put us on—"

"Don't talk to me. Focusing. Oh god, this is way too fast."

"Fair enough."

He clung to the car as they entered the wider avenue, with Tattletale ignoring the lights to plunge across five lanes. She weaved between the oncoming vehicles with a level of skill he envied, screaming at the top of her lungs.

Something told him Tattletale had not planned any of that.

Whatever the case, they now rode on the same street as the convoy. Pinpointing them was not difficult, since their two frontliners of Yellow Jacket and Little Girl laid in wait for him atop their respective rides.

They began shooting at him as Tattletale closed in, and Jaune climbed forward to the hood of the car, raising a golden Geo dome around him that protected the windshield at his back. The bullets that did not miss struck without doing much harm.

But that had not been the attack he should have worried about. Their car suddenly went haywire, the wipers activating, radio blaring a roaring rock song. From his phone, he heard Tattletale swearing.

"Their netrunner hacked into our car! They're seizing control bit by bit—damn, damn, damn, they're cutting the power!"

"Peel off the road!" Jaune commanded. "At this distance, I can make it. Escha, on me!"

The car went dark. As it drifted back, he launched into the sky with Escha clinging to his leg to hitch a ride. Gunfire tracked him to stop his pursuit, futile as he threw out [Third Arm] to latch onto the SUV. Zipping across the space, he lunged for the short girl.

A shotgun blast shattered the Geo dome, and he blanched as she ducked under his arms to then shove the barrel of her gun into his mouth.

"Eat lead, motherfucker!" she cried.

A fluffy furball tackled the girl before her oversized metal finger could pull the trigger, and with a yelp, the thrashing pair fell inside the SUV. Jaune gasped a thank-you to Escha, his heart running a mile a minute.

Gunshots rang out from within the vehicle. The short girl must be firing blind, because holes appeared all over the SUV, with the man behind the wheels screaming at 'Rebecca' to stop wrecking his baby.

A blonde woman wearing a facemask focused on him, pointing a handgun at his face as he reached in to help Escha. He batted her hand aside, causing her to cry out in pain.

A big metal slug slammed into his ribs, and almost threw him off the car roof. Jaune bit back a yell, shoving the blonde away and turning toward the shooter.

Yellow jacket, hanging to the side of the gray van, shouted at him, "Pick on someone your own size, corpo!"

The SUV swerved to avoid a car ahead, widening the distance between them. It then swung back into the lane so that Jaune and the other boy were now inches apart.

"Gladly!" Jaune shouted back. "You stole what I was about to steal, so I'm stea—"

He was sitting on the curb.

"—ling it back and DAMMIT!"

He slapped the ground, growling as he tracked the speeding convoy. Yellow jacket thumbed his nose at him as he sat with legs swinging off the edge of the van, for whatever reason spurting two streams of blood from his nostrils.

Over on the SUV, the shortie popped out of the sunroof, one scratched-up metallic arm wound back. She threw a yowling felyne over the road, forcing Jaune to scramble to catch her before a passing car did.

The distraction cemented their escape, and his last sight of them was of the small girl flipping him off. Then, they vanished into the depths of the city.

Night City had taken the measure of Jaune Arc, and adapted.


Author's Notes: A day where nothing went right for Lisa Wilbourn. Heh.
