Chapter 72: Just Another Night City Pub
​


Day or night, the Afterlife was always the place to be.

Everyone knew it, whether they worked from the highest office in Arasaka Tower or dug for trash in the deepest and darkest corner of Pacifica. People from all corners of the city whispered about the things that went on inside the bar. Children were born from the womb with its name on their lips. A constant gaggle of groupies hung around outside the doors, begging for somebody allowed in to take them along as a plus one. Corpos threw bribes at the doorman, and always looked lost as money failed to speak for the first time in their lives.

Even if they snagged an invite, it would only last them the night. Come morning, the bouncer kicked them out like yesterday's trash.

The real way to gain entry was to pick up a gun. Then you go out into Night City, and you run.

Through the gangs, through the corps. Take the jobs, earn those eddies. Chrome it up. Be somebody.

Because all edgerunners were bound for the Afterlife.

He should know.

David lounged in his usual booth with the tiredness of a man coming home after a long day. A couple of Valentino toughs had occupied the circular couch and low table until they saw his crew arrive, and now the team enjoyed a corner of the room to themselves. He had an arm draped on the back of the seat, Lucy sitting beside him.

Located in a former morgue with ice-cold fridge tech still running full blast, the bar gave its patrons a rare taste of winter, but nobody would think this looking at Lucy. She had shed her jacket to leave only her netrunner leotard and a pair of shorts. Her breath fogged in the air as she fussed over him and generally being her adorable self. Above them, the speakers played a thumping beat, background noise for a dozen different conversations as the mercs of the Afterlife jockeyed for an audience, regaling friends and strangers of their recent gigs before the rumor mill—or worse, the corpo media—got there first. Some laughed, some cried, a toast was raised to those who never made it home.

On most occasions, he would be right there with them to share the straight detes of his night, but wow, did activating the Sandevistan four times in a handful of minutes take it out of man. The closest to socializing he could manage about now involved giving the ceiling a blank stare, one foot tapping the metal floor in idle restlessness to show everybody that he was still alive. His stomach rumbled, but the snack plates on the table went untouched. He just was not feeling it.

"I could have taken him," he muttered to himself.

Lucy heard him, and she shifted to stand on the seat with her knees which put them eye to eye. She looked like she wanted to slap him. "If you ever see that man again, you delta. Got me? If we hadn't brought you to that ripperdoc yesterday… If Rebecca didn't pull you out of the way today…"

"C'mon, I was caught off-guard for a second," he said. His sluggish mind began picking up steam, rousing from its stupor as he thought more and more about the corpo. "I've replayed the fight a hundred times. Did you see him blocking bullets with those shields?"

"Yeeeah?" From her face, Lucy seemed to miss the implication. So, he clarified.

"It means he would have died without them. His chrome is strong, but they don't make him invincible. There's a limit." And he knew, knew, that limits existed to be overcome.

By an edgerunner, not the corpo. The corpo was supposed to die in this scenario.

The voice of Kiwi broke into their conversation.

"It isn't chrome," she said. With her personal link cable jacked into a tablet, her eyes glowed blue rather than the usual yellow and red. "I wasn't being jammed. He didn't counterhack my cyberoptics and wipe my memories. If he could, we would have bigger problems. Keep telling you, he doesn't have a single ounce of cyberware in him."

A piece of cloth covered Kiwi's mouth over her mask, falling down like a veil. The cat-themed corporate ninja had damaged said mask during the fight inside their car, and it now needed repair before Kiwi was comfortable wearing it in public again. Occasionally, a bendy straw went under the veil so she could sip at a can of Nicola.

An idle thought lurking at the back of his mind suggested he convince Lucy to wear something like that. Just around the penthouse. For no reason.

The patent ridiculousness of Kiwi's claim, a claim parroted by Lucy, drew him out of the sudden reverie before he fell too deep in it.

"He had a forcefield generator," he argued. "I've listened to your theory on bone lacing and skin weaves, but bioware doesn't explain half the things he did."

"David, girls, give it a rest!"

A tray hit their table to cut them off, slammed down with unnecessary force. Rebecca had returned from the bar, and she passed out the second round of drinks before plopping herself onto the bench with him as her backrest.

"We finished the gig and made out like bandits," she said, lifting her mug of beer. "This is a time to celebrate, gonks!"

They could all agree with that sentiment, at least. A smile played on his lips as he raised his glass and clinked it with the others in a toast. The taste of Ab-synth then hit his throat.

Terrible as always. It was the price he paid to avoid the carbonated beer (without touching the fruity cocktails).

Over the rim of the glass, he panned his gaze over the bar. Cubicles set in the walls that once stored bodies poured their cold fog into the room, granting the space an eerie, almost mystical feel. On the opposite side of the room from him, Rogue Amendiares held court with her people, the Queen of the Afterlife granting the favored few with the kind of gigs that had the rest of the solos present salivating. In secluded corners, lesser fixers called on promising mercs to gather a crew. In this city, there was always a score to settle, or an angle to play.

Other edgerunners not caught up in biz filled the booths and tables, well on their way to making it another rowdy night. A game of throwing knives at a picture of the mayor had begun, inevitably dragging politics into it and devolving into an argument. The constant posturing common to their line of business sped matters along, but guns stayed in their holsters. For now.

The bartender, Claire, nodded to him from behind the long counter, the centerpiece of the Afterlife where many a legend had graced and many a drink bearing their names had been served. On a nearby stool, Falco drowned his sorrows in a bottle, the getaway driver running a hand over the new bald spot on his head. Torn off by the same person responsible for Kiwi's busted mask, this crippling injury had devastated the mustachioed dandy. David resolved to pay for the man's hair graft appointment, a gift for his stellar driving earlier.

A blink of his eyes, and it was like nothing had ever changed. He saw Pilar at the center of the floor, amusing people with his antics. Rebecca tried her best to fill that role nowadays, but she could never bear to go all-out making a fool of herself like her brother. A booming laugh rang out over the air, and David turned toward Maine. The man winked at him, leaning on the booth with his girlfriend Dorio under one arm. The two hulking brutes had no sense and little qualms, openly groping one another.

The images faded as David took a hit of his immunosuppressants, the needle depositing a cocktail of chemicals into his bloodstream. They got to work, and the side effects left empty places where his friends once stood.

He never liked how the drug kills his daydreams. He could have gone without the stuff, honestly, but it made the adjustment process with his new implants smoother, and if he wanted to add more cyberware by tomorrow? Then the current spike in load gotta simmer down, or the doc would get on his case.

Not that the reinforced joints helped him much today. The strength to lift a heavy machine gun as if it were a pistol, and none of it mattered when the corpo sliced the firearm to ribbons. He should have punched the gonk during their dive off the car, even if it would do fuck all.

The drink glass shattered in his hand.

"David! The hell, dude?" Rebecca yelped, the others jumping at the sudden commotion.

He motioned with his hands, placating his teammates. "My bad, I forgot my own strength." He checked his palm. The artificial skin was thankfully too tough to break, but the alcohol clung to it. "What a waste of eddies... Can you get me another glass?"

"What do I look like, your maid?" spat Rebecca, flipping him off. In the same breath, she shouted toward the bar counter. "Hey, Claire! Can we get a rag? And a baby bottle for this idiot while you're at it, too!"

"Rebecca, cool it. He doesn't need this right now," Lucy admonished, frowning hard.

"Oh, puh-lease, sister," said Rebecca, slumping down to lay over his lap so she could look up at Lucy. "This is just some tough love. Right, Davey-boy?" The attitude then dialed back a notch as she peered closely at him. "Really, though. What's going on? You're gloomier than usual."

"It's nothing."

In tandem, Lucy and Rebecca exhaled a long breath at the response, with Rebecca muttering, "Of fucking course."

"Don't give me that," Lucy said to him. "Anybody can see that you're distracted. Even Rebecca noticed."

The other girl immediately snapped back, "Hey! What are you trying to say?"

"That you can't take a hint." Lucy leveled a sharp glare at her friend.

Their bickering ceased as he opened his mouth. He did not speak at first, pondering on the right way to put it. His troubles began and ended with one cause, the corpo who he had beaten today. The issue was, why did it continue to bother him?

He took in the sight of his crew. Of them, he and Lucy made it out just fine. Falco lost a tuft of his hair—okay, whatever, he would live. Kiwi and Rebecca were a different matter. Their run-in with the ninja left cuts and bite marks all over their bodies now covered by bandages, with staples holding it together where the skin was less than organic. The metal Gorilla Arms Rebecca used had inches-thick armor plating, and they looked like someone took a katana to them, with an actual dent in one spot.

"The corpo is still out there," David finally said. "Him and his ninja. I have to think about what it means for us if we run into him on a job again. I can't lose you all."

Lucy interjected, "The chances of that—"

"Twice in two days, Lucy. You tell me what those odds are. He's targeting us." He sighed as his girlfriend fell quiet. "You and Kiwi don't have any way to touch him. Me and Rebecca, we're scratching him. We won today by running with our tails tucked between our legs. It…. I don't feel like it's a win."

His hand curled into a fist, the finger joints clicking one by one. He imagined it impacting the other man's face, how he would crumple to the floor. That was what victory looked like to him. Boxers in the ring, the stronger person standing tall at the end. The kind of win that had meaning.

If only corpos were ever willing to make it a fair fight.

"We need to be prepared. We need to look back and learn, instead of pretending it won't screw us over in the future." They seemed very unconvinced, for some reason, giving him deadpan stares. Still, he pressed on. "And if I'm right… I'm not alone in this, am I? What have you got for us, Kiwi?"

At that, he and the others peered across the booth to where Kiwi sat all by her lonesome. The woman weathered their scrutiny with cool aplomb, quietly sipping her cola. Those familiar with her saw through the act for what it was. Kiwi wanted to drag out the moment. The sadist.

A beat later, the corners of her eyes crinkled. David was certain she would be smirking had she been able to. Unjacking from the tablet, she turned it toward them to reveal the various notes and data points she had managed to compile, including a digital rendition of the corpo himself. David would recognize that smarmy grin anywhere.

Kiwi tapped the screen, and the standing figure shifted to one of the corpo charging ahead with sword in hand. That soon changed to one with him crouched, which triggered a side image of him from up close, a POV take that David realized came from Kiwi at the moment she encountered the man.

Good old, reliable Kiwi. Even in the midst of a car chase, she kept her head in the game and did exactly what a netrunner should, working the data in their favor. She never let him down.

The woman leaned back in her seat, satisfied with their impressed looks. "Small disclaimer. Got less than I'd like. But I managed to record his facial profile..."

David waved her comment away. For two hours' work, she had nothing to be humble about. Some netrunners took days. "Good, so—" He paused as Kiwi continued talking.

"His voice... The shape of his blue eyes..." Kiwi manipulated the screen, showcasing each feature. "Height. Estimated weight. Favored side. Muscle definition."

"Uh, Kiwi?"

"Walking gait. Hand size."

"Kiwi."

"Di—"

David reached over the table, clamping onto Kiwi's wrist. "Okay, we get the idea! Good work. Great, even. Can you please move on? What did you do with that data?"

"Ran it through the NCPD system. Duh," Kiwi snarked, shrugging off his grip. David gave it a second to makes sure she would not veer off the rails again, before backing off. "Then through databases maintained by contacts of mine. Roughly accounts for most of NUSA and the Free States, plus Nairobi."

Rebecca blinked, and raised her head off his lap. "Why Nairobi?" She then balked at the judging gazes leveled at her from all sides. "What? I'm serious. What's there?" Her confusion grew and grew in the face of their silence. "Am I out of the loop? Are you guys just fucking with me?" As per usual, her attitude quickly changed to a burning fury, and she plunged a hand into the depths of her jacket to search for a gun. "Tell me or I'll light you up!"

David pressed a hand on her to hold her still and left the gung-ho gunner to rage her heart out, familiar by now with how her short fuse tended to run out of steam in minutes. Meanwhile, Kiwi pulled different files onto the screen. Blank pages after blank pages greeted them.

"He doesn't have a criminal history of any kind. No school records. No media rep. Doesn't do porn braindances, either."

"What kind of searches were you doing, again?"

Kiwi ignored the question. "Far as it goes, we got a ghost that popped up within the last week or so."

A few videos and blog posts slid into view. Lucy sprang forward as she zeroed in on one in particular.

"Wait, he was caught up in that?"

"If by that you mean he walked in and somehow flatlined every side involved, then yes. Some people think the fixer Wakako was behind it, others are saying the incident was the one to put him on her radar. I'm leaning toward the latter."

"I'm surprised he's alive," Lucy said. "Tyger Claws normally wouldn't let something like this slide. They've killed for less."

Kiwi scoffed, "Tell that to him. Anyway, since then he's been accepting jobs from Wakako, with sporadic sightings of him in Japantown."

Right on David's doorstep. Who woulda thunk?

"Unfair is what it is," Rebecca grumbled. "It took me years before the old lady hired me, and this guy gets it in a day? Gonk better watch his back down dark alleys. I see his face, I'll shoot it like… BLAM BLAM! And then—"

The pop-ups closed out one by one to leave a single image of the corpo, frozen in time as he glared down at Kiwi with the night sky at his back. A name underscored the picture.

Johnny.

For reasons he could not quite explain, within David's heart there screamed a roaring beat and a guitar riff.

Another set of files appeared, taking up a corner. "His partner, same deal," said Kiwi. "No trace in the system."

Rebecca took leave from making threats against her new nemesis Johnny to comment. "Because she's a fucking cat!"

David opened his mouth. Closed it. He looked at Kiwi while pointing a finger at Rebecca.

"...That isn't far off the mark," Kiwi admitted. "The ninja pretending she was a cat? A little further down the crazy column than we thought. No hologram involved. She's an exotic, a human biosculpted to be a cat."

"Do people still do that?" Lucy wondered.

A gleam entered Kiwi's eyes, and she sat up straight. "They do. Mostly in Europe. Where bioware is popular."

An intake of breath, and Lucy spun toward David. At the same time, they both shouted.

"That's it!"

"Maybe," Kiwi said, to burst their bubble. "Working theory is your guy either had a full identity wipe or came from overseas. Which complicates things. Dead end unless we have the eddies."

A glance at Falco jogged his memory.

"There was a third member, a driver."

"Didn't get a good look. Decent driving skill, I guess. What more is there to say? That one is no big deal," Kiwi casually dismissed with a haughty sniff.

"Yeah, Falco's way better," Rebecca agreed. "Creeping up on a netrunner in an unshielded car? They probably hired her off the street."

David frowned, crossing his arms as one foot tapped the metal floor. Tonk, tonk, tonk, tonk, tonk.

"How certain are we of that?" he said, feeling restless. His intuition was pinging something fierce, and in this business a man ignored his gut at his own peril. "What if we can use her? Let's look at it from every angle."

Lucy's hand swept in front of him, cutting him off. "Later, David. We have company." She nodded her head to indicate beyond their table.

"I'm hurt, Lucy. Truly. Don't you trust me to be here?"

Claire sauntered up to them, hefting a small tray. A deep, heartfelt sigh of grief was followed by a snicker, and the bartender set down a glass in front of David.

"Another round for our superstar," she said, winking at him. "And a rag to wipe with. Ab-synth sticks like nothing else once it gets in the seams of your cyberware, so you better clean that off soon." The bartender gestured at his hand.

"'Preciate it, Claire," David said, taking the rag.

The piece of cloth stretched taut, caught between their grips.

"Ah-ah. Nothing's free in Night City, David," Claire admonished. "You and your crew wouldn't mind doing me a small favor, would you?" The woman did not give him time to answer either way, releasing the rag to jerk a thumb over her shoulder. "See what that's about for me? Before I have to get involved."

Everybody at the table poked their heads around Claire to look behind her. After a moment, David spoke.

"Since when did you let kids in here?"

"How old are you again?"

"Shhh."

David averted his gaze, and sipped his drink. Unimportant details aside, he understood Claire's problem. Among the rowdy crowd, there strode a set of anomalies. More than just kids, these were tourists wandering around the Afterlife. The bar's owner, Rogue, hired the toughest, meanest sonuvabitch she could find to man the entrance, just to prevent this exact scenario.

They dressed wrong. Walked wrong. Gawked at every little thing like for the first time. Anybody with eyes could see that they did not belong.

The boy had this gormless face that begged for someone to scam him. He stumbled through the room on two left feet and, worse, apologized for it. The mercs he tripped into watched with bemused expressions the string of sorrys and thank yous that came out of the boy's mouth.

The girl behind him, now, she drew even more attention. The dainty steps, the fancy dress, the actual bird sitting on her shoulder… Everything about her screamed rich princess come down from an ivory tower. The bouncer at the door should have barred her from entering on general principles, because she was liable to start a fight with how many people were suddenly calculating the price of her ransom. A lot of mercs could be less than choosy about how they made their eddies.

"I'm getting the picture, Claire," David said, shaking his head. "Those idiots are gonna die."

"That's the same thought I had. Deal with it, hon? My customers are waiting."

As Claire hurried back to work, David turned to his teammate.

"Becca, round them up for me? Let's do our good deed for the day."

His teammate groaned at the request but listened to it anyway. She slid out of the booth and padded off toward the tourists, grumbling all the while. People in her path found themselves unceremoniously elbowed aside, often in very vulnerable spots due to her short height.

One person made way for her, politely taking a step to the left to avoid Rebecca before they collided. This simple act clued David in that they might have overlooked a third member to the little group.

The girl appeared a couple of years older than the other two, or maybe that was just the more mature air about her as she studied the bar with a keen gaze. That said, she outpaced them in plain weirdness. Darting from place to place, the girl would listen to conversations between solos one moment then in the next stick her head inside the morgue cabinets, afterward nodding to herself as if she had solved a mystery. The flat-top hat she wore sported a strange wooden tile on the front, the logo on it failing to match any brand, corp, gang, or trend David recognized.

The oddest thing was the way people seemed to not notice her.

But she did notice them.

Her eyes passed over their table, then snapped back to their group to meet their stares. Pupils shaped like flowers blinked once, twice. Then, the girl smiled.

"Why is she coming over here?" Lucy asked, squinting in suspicion. "She better not be a David fangirl."

As she reached the table, the girl put her hands together, the billowing sleeves overlapping. A bow followed, respectful and oddly formal.

"Greetings, all. Might I have a moment of your time?"

David and his teammates glanced at one another. Kiwi mimed a flapping mouth with her hand, the suggestion clear. Keeping this one out of trouble would be easy enough, at least. Just let her yap.

"Uhhhh… okay?" he answered.

The girl beamed. Up close, her unnatural beauty became all the more apparent, and it raised David's hackles a little. Rich folks and their biosculpting ways.

"I am Hu Tao," the girl said, bowing again. "The 77th Director of the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor. A pleasure to meet you before you go on your way." She stopped there, giving them an expectant gaze.

"I'm David," he replied, with the others following suit to provide introductions. "You said you were with a… funeral parlor?"

Strike one. He did not enjoy thinking about funerals.

The girl, Hu Tao, nodded. "Yes, and I am here seeking the answer to a simple question: are you fine with this as your 'afterlife'?"

A single thought passed through his mind. Oh crap, someone's angling to open a new edgerunner bar, Rogue is going to kill this girl.

Lucy leaned around him. "What do you mean?"

No, Lucy. Don't encourage the nut!

"I'm glad you asked," said Hu Tao, smoothly sliding into the booth without an invitation to sit across from him. Her long hair almost brushed the floor until she gathered them up in her arms. "Can I get you something? A drink? Some snacks? No? Straight to business, then. I commend your eagerness."

Crossing one leg over the other, she scanned them up and down.

"You see, I could not help but notice the rough shape that many of your compatriots are in."

The girl indicated the room with an airy wave of her hand, encompassing both Kiwi's state and the blood splatters on his clothes, but also the many other signs of battle that the edgerunners of the Afterlife wore like a badge of honor. As if to agree, a crew of mercs rushed into the room, carrying a wounded teammate. They dropped him onto the pool table and began attempting to resuscitate him, their leader on a call with Trauma Team.

"The times are tough, aren't they?" Hu Tao said.

David shrugged. "Part of the job. If somebody can't take it, maybe they should quit."

"Oh no, no, no!" said the girl, sighing. "Who are we to dictate their life? No, let each live to their fullest, following their own paths wherever it may lead… And it is that very destination which concerns me."

Okay, she lost him. Kiwi, however, narrowed her eyes.

"The Afterlife."

"Exactly."

"I'd mind what I say, if I were you," Kiwi advised. "Here, the walls have ears."

"And mine won't." Hu Tao leaned forward and lowered her voice, and as she spoke, she poked the table for emphasis. "Just straight wood. Handmade custom. Guaranteed to satisfy your needs."

He felt like he had been thinking this a lot lately, but… what the hell was going on?

"Drugs," Lucy whispered in his ear.

"That's she's on, or that she's offering?" he muttered back.

"Yes."

He had his doubts on that, because as the girl continued to talk, the possibility just did not make sense. Granted, nothing about this did.

"How will your weary bones rest in this freezing box? Brrr!" Hu Tao hugged herself and exaggerated a shiver. Then, she clapped her hands over her ears. "What kind of sleep are you going to get with this much noise?" She shook her head. "Ai-yai-yai, it's impossible!"

Despite himself, a smile grew on his face. The corners of Kiwi's eyes crinkled in that mouthless smirk of hers, and even Lucy snickered.

The girl was just so bad at this.

When did she think they were, 1977? If she wanted to make a sales pitch, then she missed every element of a good ad. The gun firing in the air, the naked babes in the background, and so on. The attention-grabbers.

And then it stopped being funny, because he figured out what she was selling.

"Your mortal body deserves better for its service. More than that, you deserve reassurance." She waved at the room again. "Standing in line? A keeper at the door? Is this what they have demanded your money for all this time? I doubt this establishment even has a retrieval service should you meet your untimely end outside the premises."

Strike two. He did not like people selling him funeral packages.

"Wait a minute," David growled. "Who said anything about me dying?"

Hu Tao cocked her head, bewildered at the interruption. "Were we not, dear customer? Is that not the reason all of you are waiting here for, in case you succumbed to your wounds tonight and needed a burial?"

"No!"

"Oh," said Hu Tao in a small voice. A second glance at their surroundings, and understanding began to dawn for her. "So… I will go out on a limb here and guess that this isn't a quirky funeral parlor." They need not answer. She read the truth from their faces, and thereafter slumped over to bang her head on the table. "What is it going to take to sell a coffin around here?" she whined miserably.

Strike—nah, scratch that. Whether it be in this life or the next, David Martinez did not enjoy seeing a woman cry.

"If it makes you feel better, nobody actually buries a dead body nowadays."

"It doesn't…"

Welp, he tried.

Rebecca saved them from the awkward mood. Her brash self held no concept of reading the room, and she charged into the conversation with the delicacy of a Maxtac strike squad, her mission half-complete with a blonde in tow.

"Guys! You gotta listen to this chick talk, she's hilarious!"

"Unhand me, pale demoness of the abyss! I am not your entertainment!"

Rebecca shoved her captive in front of them, and slapped away the bird trying to peck her eyes out. "Come on, princess," she urged, elbowing the younger (but taller) girl in her side. "Tell them what you told me. Who are you again?"

Rather than complying, the kid looked ready to cry, and David realized he had a crisis on his hands. Reputation meant the world in this business. An edgerunner known for slaughtering corpos and goons in droves was a solo headed for the top. An edgerunner that ransomed men, women, and children for a quick buck was a dangerous man to watch. An edgerunner who bullied kids for their candies got flatlined and double-tapped by the entire bar. They were mercs with class, thank you. Keep it professional!

Yet, before he could intervene, the dainty girl gritted her teeth. Defiance flashed in her eye as she set her feet apart. A hand went up to cover her eyepatch, the other pointing to the ceiling.

The air around her changed. Surer, with confidence born from spite.

"H-Hark! You stand in the presence of Fischl, the Prinzessin der Verurteilung, sovereign of fair Immernachtreich! Bow your head in supplication, for salvation comes!"

"Bahahahahahaha!"

All of the girl's confidence vanished as she watched Rebecca roll on the floor, laughing her heart out. Barring Hu Tao who applauded, everybody at the table plus everybody within earshot struggled to not point and laugh.

Look, some people were just very bullyable.

And then the bird let loose an EMP blast, and they all stopped laughing.

Arcs of electricity framed the dainty princess. They bounced along the metal floor to send tough, scarred mercs stumbling back, with Rebecca screeching in a panic as she rolled, and continued rolling, to avoid getting zapped. The bird revealed its artificial nature, spreading its wings and seeming to grow three sizes as it hovered behind the girl named Fischl. A violet glow had overtaken her one visible eye, trailing sparks as she turned her head to glare from face to face.

Guns left their holsters before their owners even realized it. The kind of crazy gonk that would drop an EMP grenade in the middle of a conversation…

A laugh cut through the tension, rough and loud. The Queen of the Afterlife had her head thrown back, cackling at the sight of her mercs running scared. An indulgent wave of her hand rendered judgment upon the fool who dared to start a fight with a dozen solos.

…someone like that belonged here.

"Fischl, are you okay!?"

A boy squeezed through the crowd, and ran up to the girl. He put up his fists, standing back to back with her like they were about to throw down with everybody in a bar brawl. These kids had spunk, if nothing else.

"It's fine," David called out, shifting position to hide how he had scrambled away from the EMP. "It's cool. Nobody's got a problem here, ain't that right?"

He looked around, gesturing for the other crews and solos to ease off. With Rogue and now his voice added to the scale, it snuffed out the budding hostilities. Guns returned to their holsters, and ruffled feathers settled down.

Thus, he proved the old adage that it paid to build rep.

The only one he worried about was his own teammate, Rebecca. A grenade in her own right. The beaming grin on her face as she hopped to her feet told him he could relax.

"That bird is fucking nova, girl!" Rebecca cried, slapping Fischl on the back as if the earlier situation never happened. "Where did you get it? Because I'm thinking, right, I'm thinking we gather a whole flock of them to release at the dashi parade. Make it a show!"

The dainty girl's head tilted to the side. "Oz is… nova? Is that good?"

Rebecca stared askance.

"Yeah, it's good. You must be real sheltered, huh?"

Sheltered was right. He knew corpo kids sucked ass when it came to modern slang, but this girl took the cake. Still, he must admit. Rebecca had it right.

That bird was fucking nova.

"You ever thrown a knife, princess?" Rebecca asked, already warming up to the other crazy girl in the room. Leaning on her, she wrapped an arm around Fischl.

"Yes."

"Well, you're gonna—hold up, what?" His teammate blinked, staring slack-jawed.

"She has pretty amazing aim," the boy next to Fischl provided. Rebecca turned to him, an ever-widening grin stretching her lips.

"This gets better and better. So what about you, kid?"

"I… once took a man's finger off at fifty paces."

As Rebecca shouted about corpo kids and surprises, David listened to the quieter conversation between the two blonds.

"I thought you said you could never win a game at the Mondstadt fair because you always miss the targets."

"He was standing behind me."

This sounded like a disaster in the making. David made no move to stop it beyond checking the location of the knife-throwing target, and he sent Rebecca and her new friends off with a smile. Surely nothing bad would happen. If it did, Rebecca could handle herself.

If she couldn't, then Rogue would intervene.

If she won't, the other solos were going to step in.

If they didn't, they had a funeral director on-site.

Not his problem.

A giggle from across the table drew his notice. Hu Tao softly laughed, covering her lips with her fingers, gaze trailing after Rebecca.

"A lively person, that one. I know a few people who could stand to meet her." Propping her chin, she leaned on the table, casting her gaze over the uproarious crowd. Somewhere in there, a man screamed, likely from a knife wound. "I supposed this kind of 'afterlife' isn't such an insult to the real thing."

"It's never boring," he offered.

"That's true. Charter Hill is so much more interesting than I gave it credit for."

Lucy frowned, confused and being all cute about it. "Charter Hill? We're in Little China."

Hu Tao gave Lucy a blank stare for a few seconds, completely silent.

"...Oh," she finally said.

The girl looked to the left, then the right, then launched to her feet. Placing her hands together, she bowed to them.

"It has been a pleasure, but please excuse me. Something has come up."

With that, Hu Tao dashed away in a blur.

"Oh no. Oh no. Oh no. Fischl, Bennett, we have to go! Please don't tell Jaune about thiiiis!"

Jaune, what a weird name.

Watching the strange girl disappear into the depths of the Afterlife, David, too, pushed off from his seat. The others thought it was a signal for them to leave, but he bade them to not get up. Lucy could stand to hang out with the girls, and maybe mend bridges.

As for him, he just felt a little peckish, that was all. No need to make a fuss. A bowl of noodles should hit the spot.



-o-
​


The doors to the apartment slid shut behind Jaune with a soft click. He pressed his ear to it, and for a minute strained to listen if anybody had awoken.

No.

Good.

He padded down the hallway to call the elevator. Soon, he stepped out onto the street where a soft rain fell upon the city.

Life carried on even past midnight, with too many faces to count. They did not let the rain bother them. Somewhere, gunshots rang out, followed by the sound of police sirens. Just another Night City story to tell.

Jaune stood at the entrance of the apartment building for a while to center himself. Once the noise and lights ceased to overwhelm his senses, he set out into the alleys of Japantown. Neon colors lit the way.

Barely inside, a person stepped out of the shadows to put a gun to his head.

"Give me everything you got or I'll shoot, motherf—gack!"

The mugger dropped like a sack of potatoes.

"I'm not your mother. Ooh, and what a nice umbrella."

Jaune walked away from the altercation with a pep in his steps, twirling his newest gun in one hand while cradling an umbrella on his shoulder. Droplets of rain struck the transparent canopy, and reflected light from the glowing neon ribs to form a cascading waterfall of colors.

There was a reason he warned the others to stay out of the alleys, and it was the same reason he took them every chance he got. Bad things happened here.

In no time at all, he spied a familiar sign. Jig-Jig Street.

A feeling of heaviness settled within his chest. Perhaps he should have told Lisa about what he was doing. No, he definitely had to, but he also knew what her answer was going to be. She had made her opinions clear.

But…

He just could not take it anymore. The curiosity, the urge, was near irresistible.

Jaune strode by the sign, and crossed the street. A flight of stairs put him at his destination.

Here, flickering holograms created the twisting branches of a garden to cast everything in a cherry pink glow. Stalls made of steel and plastic scaffolding laid out in a haphazard pattern, and from behind their counters the entrepreneurs of Japantown shouted and waved to those passing by.

Cherry Blossom Market. Where the petals eternally fell yet never touch the earth.

They sold junk. They sold dreams. Above all…

The scent of sizzling oil tickled his nose, tinged with a sweet and piquant aroma.

Above all, they sold slop.

Complete, utter slop. A certain girl deemed it unfit for animals, let alone humans. It looked good, though, and Jaune really wanted to know what the food here tasted like.

Look out, Night City. A gourmet had arrived.

#6,091

Chapter 74: Just Another Night City Beat'em Up
​


A hundred red lanterns glowed in the night, illuminating the Cherry Blossom Market.

A dome of glass protected its visitors from the rain, the soft pitter-patter lost among the bustling pedestrian traffic under a gray sky. Jaune walked through the crowd with his nose raised high in the air to breathe in the scent of cooking, for which there were many. The narrow paths between the stalls put all they had to offer on display.

Even with a single bowl of ramen, each cook put their own spin on it to stand out from the rest. Kebabs ran the gamut from spicy to sweet to the 'orgiatic vinegar chili-infused' special recipe. The possibilities seemed endless, a culinary feast for the senses.

Eager to partake in the food of the future, he soon stopped by a booth and paid for a meal.

"...Excuse me, there's a bug in my mashed potatoes."

"There's a potato in your mashed bugs?"

Oh boy.

Jaune and the cook stared at one another unblinking, neither quite able to comprehend the nonsense that the other person was spouting. The eye contact broke as the next customer stepped in front of Jaune, leaving him alone with the small paper cup he bought, it dawning on him with a creeping dread that he should have read the menu more closely.

'Mashed Tater(ish)' sounded to him like a kooky name that a person came up with to attract customers. Haha, no, the cricket leg poking out of the mound of food corrected that mistaken notion. It was in fact a disclaimer, or a threat. He had a vague inkling of it going in, but wow, Lisa had not been kidding.

Gingerly, he scooped up a spoonful of the stuff and held it closer for inspection. The electric mixer did a pretty good job rendering almost everything down to a fine consistency, with what he assumed was food coloring to bleach the resulting goop and grant it the appearance of a familiar dish. A naive person might then believe the small dark chunks a result of the cook seasoning the dish with black pepper and bits of bacon. To help sell the happy delusion, a generous heaping of gravy atop the so-called tater obscured its true nature. Crushed flakes added an extra flair to the meal, like what the fancy restaurants did to steaks with gold shavings.

Crushed flakes of what, the cook never said. At a glance, it resembled… um… well… more of those alternative protein sources, let's call it.

Now, he liked to imagine himself as the adventurous type, but it seemed the world wanted to challenge that with a simple question: could he put his money where his mouth was, and put a cricket in his mouth? The thought that waiting any longer would lead to the meal losing heat, and him eating cold dead bugs, spurred him to action.

"Nothing for it, then," he said, and quickly chomped down on the spoon before he lost his nerves. Chewing would mean more time spent thinking about it, so he swallowed the food right away.

The sensation as it traveled down to his stomach insisted to his mind that this was soft, fluffy mashed potatoes. The gritty texture of the bacon pieces really elevated an otherwise mundane recipe. Flavor-wise, the gravy carried the whole thing on its back with this rich, deep note of earthiness he had never before tasted.

In a way, the dish defied his expectations. He had prepared his heart for mere slop, ready and willing to toss it aside should it prove inedible. Faced with the fact that he could stand to eat this as long as he closed his eyes, he considered the actual outcome a worse one, because he did so hate to waste food.

"Yo man, how is it?" the cook called over, taking a moment out of serving customers to give him a thumbs-up. "Good?"

Jaune answered the cook with a stiff smile, and hoped it did not come out too obviously as a grimace. Also, that he did not have bugs stuck in his teeth.

The experience taught him the value of caution. Clearly, the Night City palate spanned a wide range of flavors and ingredients. Not to say this was a bad thing, only that a person new to the local cuisine might find it an acquired taste, to be taken in small bites. Very, very small bites.

Which was why, after he had eaten as much of the mashed tater as he could stomach (the bug juices collected at the bottom), he opted for a safer choice on the next go-round.

"Franchise chains. That's the ticket," he assured himself as he waited in line with others for a store set in the corner of the night market.

In other circumstances and to anybody else, he would decry this decision as a cop-out. Visiting the big city then making a beeline for plain fast food, in his opinion, wasted the opportunity. It risked turning a person boring, and the last thing Jaune Arc wanted to be was boring. Still, tonight warranted an exception, at least until he worked up the nerves to branch out.

Upon reaching the front of the line, he placed his order.

A slice of cheese pizza. No way to go wrong here.

True to the name of the restaurant, it cost him one whole eddie for the meal. For a buck-a-slice. The supreme value boggled the mind and forgave a lot of downsides, such as how the pizza came out thinner than pictured on the menu sign. After all, cheap prices added a spice of its own. Other than that, the pizza appeared perfect, the cheese turning just a little brown from its time in the oven with the crust achieving that wonderful balance of softness and crunch.

He bit into the pizza, and chewed with relish.

Seconds later, the chewing stopped. The bite of pizza in his mouth slowly moved from one side to the other. Then, he tried to let it sit so that the flavors seeped onto his tongue. Or perhaps he should say, flavor. Singular.

Swallowing the food down, he mused aloud, "Am I… eating the pizza box?"

He picked at the cheese, lifting it up as if he might find an entirely new pizza inside the pizza-shaped container. But no, what he saw was what he got.

The tomato sauce seemed to be ketchup. A local version, too sweet with a lingering sourness. It made up the best part of the pizza, a bar so low it was buried in the ground. The dough tasted of nothing, a holder for the bland cheese that was already rapidly cooling in the night air, congealing into a sticky mucus-like goo.

The bugs tasted better than this.

His next bite turned out no better than the first. It would not be wrong to describe the pizza as melting on the tongue, for its various components fell apart at prompt speed once it landed in his mouth. Decomposing, he thought.

To him, that was the worst part. In return for this assault on his palate, somewhere along the way to his stomach the morsel of food vanished, mixing with saliva to become thin gruel that failed to sate a person's hunger.

He ate the pizza, and just felt bad afterward.

Gazing up at the sign, 'Buck-a-Slice', Jaune decided then and there that them charging an eddie for this was no fair deal, but daylight robbery. That first-hand look into the level of quality he could expect from Night City franchise chains convinced him to beat a hasty retreat toward the independent food stalls. Chances were, these guys would have to eat whatever they failed to sell at the end of the day, a wonderful incentive to keep their food from hitting the true rock bottom. If he could not rely on their skill at cooking, then let him trust their sense of self-preservation.

The search for better fares carried him deeper into the night market. He touched nothing, not this time. His original mistake had been one of carelessness, his second laziness. Now, he applied those lessons, combing over the signs and menus with a keen eye before ever dreaming to place an order, often spending a minute or two peeking into the cooking areas.

In the process, he discovered a secret. The cooks were improvising their sauces and spices from things like snack tubes of flavored jelly, pouring them over the food. It made for interesting combinations, albeit shallow. The flavors went skin-deep. That knowledge led him to ignore dishes touted as special recipes, and instead looked for dishes whose intrinsic value shone due to the ingredients themselves.

What did that pretentious yammering (that he read in a magazine) even mean?

Su. Shi.

A popular dish, sushi in the Cherry Blossom Market featured three distinct styles, judging from what he saw. Vending machine, prepackaged on a shelf, and made by hand. The first, he disregarded at once. The very idea sounded bad, considering expiration dates. The sushi on the shelves were a step up from that, but the impersonal feel of the plastic boxes lost his interest. That left the last and most expensive option. The rave reviews from customers leaving the sushi stand persuaded him to give it a chance.

Plastic chairs set next to a counter allowed customers to sit down. Jaune grabbed one, and with elbows resting on the counter, he watched the chef perform her magic. Most of the prep work was already done, with thin cuts of fish stored in a container that she retrieved from a fridge. The same went for the rice. Cleverly, she had shaped them beforehand to save time, and they stacked in neat rows within a big tub. A deft hand arranged the ingredients in a hypnotic dance of fingers, the chef showing off her years of experience. Soon, a colorful spread of sushi sat in front of him on a plate, fit for a picture. The fish roe looked a little mushy, but the fatty and succulent slices of tuna made up for it.

A second packet of soy sauce, the chef informed him, would cost extra. He was far less willing to pay for that. Oh, well.

Chopsticks in hand, he chose neither roe nor tuna as the opener. That honor went to the piece topped with egg omelette.

Squeak!

Jaune stopped mid-bite and drew away from the sushi, staring at it in suspicion.

"Something wrong, mister? Ya ain't eating," the chef said, with Jaune mutely waving away the concern in reply.

Giving it a second go, he nibbled at the fried egg to confirm he had not imagined the rubbery texture. What a strange way to cook an omelette, and something he might look further into later. He dusted off the egg sushi, then moved on to the salmon and tuna. Yes, both. One after the other, to strike the newest tally mark in that eternal contest to decide which fish reigned supreme as the king of sushi.

First, salmon. Its soft, smooth flesh went down easy, the taste subtle. He could hardly detect the smell of fish, which was one of the reasons he always enjoyed salmon sushi. Prepared well, it became a dish that suited the tongues of beginners and connoisseurs alike.

He then tried the tuna, bracing himself for a sharper, fishier flavor. Tuna, cheap tuna in particular, often featured a harsher note than salmon. Its intensity was not for everyone, and the firmer texture created a different mouthfeel. Yet, on this occasion, he had been wrong. As befitting the highest quality tuna, its soft and smooth flesh went down easy, practically melting on his tongue—waaaait a minute.

A theory popped into his head, born from a sudden sense of deja vu. Heart sinking, he plucked another piece of salmon sushi and scarfed it down, and did the same to a second tuna sushi. He paused for a beat, before reaching for mackerel, followed by octopus. Shrimp was next. Roe. Surf clam.

The speed at which he ate impressed the chef.

"You must love your sushi! How about another order, special price? Five percent off," she said with a greedy glint to her smile.

The chef had the wrong idea, and Jaune refused the offer. He studied the half-eaten piece of surf clam, the consistency of which felt a lot softer than what he remembered clams being. And, strangely, while eating it he tasted the salmon earlier. Along with the tuna, the shrimp, and all the rest.

The sushi came in different colors, but tasted nearly the same. He would bet Crocea Mors they shared an underlying ingredient that had nothing to do with the names put on them.

SCOP. Had to be. The ads on the TV and billboards proclaimed it the miracle food, able to transform into anything* a person cared to eat through the use of additives. Lisa told him it was worms in a can.

And no, he never found the accompanying note to the asterisk.

"So, this is it in action, huh? I guess the ads lied to me," he said, working through the plate of sushi and dissecting it for signs of a difference between the species mimicked by the SCOP. There was enough of a fishy smell to make a person think of seafood instead of, for example, a cow. Something got added to toughen the octopus and clam meat, sort of. It crumbled apart with too little resistance to be real.

Except, the other customers of the shop gushed over the authentic flavor, contrasting it to the plebeian vending machine version that lacked a master's touch. He suspected they never had the actual thing to compare with.

What a world. No wonder they went in for sauces so hard.

After that meal, he continued to wander the night market, tasting food here and there with somewhat cooled spirits. Fake meat aside, it did fascinate him how well the stuff reacted to cooking. Grill it, boil it, fry it, the SCOP-made ingredients sizzled and browned in a believable way, for all purposes behaving as the food they pretended to be. It lent to the illusion that the 'turkish' chicken kebab he bought from this stall was a completely separate style of cuisine from the 'chinese' pork dumplings from that stall. Here, they believed more in the art of seeming than the truth.

The music was real, though. The clothes and electronics, too. Cherry Blossom Market sold things other than food, and in between tastings, he explored the world of the future.

Souvenir knickknacks turned out mostly the same as in any universe, overpriced and poor in quality. Yet at one booth, a lucky cat figurine with one paw raised ended up in his pocket despite him swearing he would not get conned into buying junk.

Another stall carried a selection of data tablets. The prices on them drew him in, until he overheard a customer grill the vendor over how many viruses and spying programs were embedded in the devices. Very little, the vendor bragged, which was not an assuring answer to Jaune. That place, he left alone.

At a record store, he gave the old man behind the counter a minor seizure when he admitted he had never heard of the band Samurai. This faraway look overtook the old man's face for close to a minute before he snapped out of it. Jaune's sympathy waned at that point, because the old man turned around to act in an insufferable manner, talking about kids today and their terrible music. He refrained from telling the old man Samurai wasn't all that, in his opinion. Too angry and bitter, unlike the styles of Remnant, and scratches on the ears. He was half-tempted to play the man a couple of the songs stored in his scroll, but in the end departed from the store on good terms after a not-totally-voluntary listening session of the band's greatest hits, a pounding rock song screaming at his back and a t-shirt in hand that he intended to foist onto Bennett.

Whispers followed him. Had been, all this time.

"Look, that's the guy! The solo!"

The words passed in one ear and out the other, at first. Unused to the term, he assumed people were referring to someone else. However, the chatter around him refused to ease off, and the suspicious behavior finally clued him in that they were talking about him.

Cherry Blossom Market lay at the heart of Japantown, a place where Tyger Claws roamed unopposed. A small rally of them with their tricked-out motorcycles took place at the road adjacent to the night market, and they were rather riled up tonight, not so quick to avert their eyes as he looked their way. He wished he could explain it as him building a good rapport with them, but the sneers they try to hide said otherwise, and the video playing on tablets in their hands likely had something to do with it. A sneaky glance over a nearby person's shoulder revealed a familiar face on the screen. His own.

Mere hours, and somebody had collated the videos recording his chase of Yellow Jacket and his crew to create a continuous montage, set to music. The slapstick sort, paired with wacky sound effects when he seemingly teleported from the top of a moving vehicle to lying flat on the road. Slowed-down replays showed the buff edgerunner tackling him and slamming him into the asphalt with nary a response on his part, the video zooming in on his face in the aftermath with a sad trombone sound effect.

Some were talking about his flying and expressed amazement at him withstanding a bullet to his gut. They said his chrome had to be so 'preem'. But, overwhelmingly, his flops dominated the discussion, the "Wah-wah-wah-waaaaah!" playing from many speakers at once. Everybody loved to laugh at the loser.

Ahhh, the nostalgia~ The situation reminded him of back in Beacon. Man, he forgot how much he hated this kind of thing.

He had no intention of running away from the ridicule, of course. Him stepping behind the relative privacy of a noodle stand's curtains was all about trying out food. Yep.

In lieu of a menu, the shop's counter doubled as a display case that highlighted the items available, with prices beside them. A quick glance, and he spoke to the person staffing the kitchen.

"I'll have the soy sauce ramen with tofu and... and mixed green colors?" He shook off his confusion. "Extra firm noodles."

"You got it, boss. Coming right up."

As the cook bustled off, he settled down on a seat. The noodle stand rested at the end of the path, allowing it to take up the corner and command two lanes of customer traffic. At the moment, he had a whole side of the shop to himself and intended to enjoy it, kicking out his legs to lounge in comfort.

All of his movements ceased as his eyes met that of a solo. Of Yellow Jacket.

Sitting at the other counter, the edgerunner did likewise, strings of ramen hanging from his mouth. A long period of silence ensued between the two of them, while in the background, money started exchanging hands among the sharp-eyed observers.

Then, they both launched to their feet.

"You!" / "Motherfucker!"

"Where did you even come from?" / "Were you following me?"

"No, before that—" / "Wait, that's not important—"

"Gimme the van back!" / "Fight me!"

Clack. The cook placed a bowl of soy sauce ramen, piping hot and fully cooked in the span of seconds, on the counter in front of Jaune. He and Yellow Jacket stared at it, with the latter then looking to his own bowl. The edgerunner's stomach rumbled.

"After," Jaune suggested.

"Agreed," the edgerunner instantly replied. "But once we're done, I'm pounding you into the dirt."

They sat down.

"You can try," Jaune said, separating a set of disposable chopsticks then using it to stir the broth. Steam wafted off the ramen bowl in waves. "Maybe if you make it a fair fight and don't run away this time."

The declaration lacked bite, because as the ramen entered his mouth, he grimaced. Extra firm noodles meant something different here, evidently. More akin to the consistency of leather shoe laces.

He seriously considered spitting it out.

Across the food stand, the edgerunner scoffed at him. "Problem with your ramen? Does it not suit your delicate tongue, your majesty?" The other boy's hulking frame was forcing him to hunch over his noodles. With practiced hands, he twirled the ramen on his chopsticks and slurped it up, afterward pointing the chopsticks at Jaune. "The view from the top of that mountain must be nice if you can't see how real people live anymore. A corpo like you don't get to talk about fairness."

Jaune swallowed the noodles. "A corpo? I'm not—" He shook his head. "Okay, seriously, you can't even see the mountain I'm on. No joke, but you're kind of out of your depths here. I'm not opposed to talking about this peacefully, you know."

"We can, after I flatline you," spat Yellow Jacket.

Flatline meant kill. Thus, that was the end of that, so far as Jaune was concerned.

The noodle stand quieted down, with the clinking of utensils the only sound left for the next few minutes. As Jaune ate, he studied the other boy with a curious eye, and absent the frantic actions of hours ago, he confirmed an earlier assessment. Yellow Jacket had grown bigger since their encounter at the WNS station, and it was not just a simple matter of height. Arms, legs, torso… Everything seemed off, like somebody took him and stretched him a few inches longer on a rack, then filled him with even more muscles to smooth out the proportions. His chair certainly protested the immense weight pressing down on it.

Cyberware? Unless the guy was into some BDSM medieval torture play, then that seemed the likeliest answer. He really should have paid more attention to those catalogues Lisa kept waving in his face, then he might have a better idea of what upgrades Yellow Jacket made to himself. In his defense, he was nowhere near as gung-ho about inserting metal rods and screws inside his body as she was.

It did not matter much, he supposed. Capture Yellow Jacket, and he stood a fair chance of learning where the edgerunners stashed the shipment of arms. Four hours or so meant it must not have gotten far. He could still turn the night around.

For the sake of that possibility, he would stick around and see where things led. Even if it was a little awkward sitting across from an enemy like this.

"You know," Jaune said after a while, in between bites. "The noodles aren't that bad. Way too salty, but at least I haven't seen a bug in the soup yet."

"Wow. I bet they're over the moon about that backhanded compliment, you pampered brat… But yeah, Yagami does the tastiest noodles in Night City, bar none," Yellow Jacket replied.

Despite the animosity, they shared a slight smile.

The first strike.

Jaune stared off into the empty air, his chopsticks idly stirring the murky ramen broth. Final review: nowhere close to the best ramen he ever ate, not by a long shot. Needless to say, the food tour was a bust. The night market boasted no hidden gems, only poor choices.

"...Urp!"

Why is it suddenly hurting so much ahhhhh!

Not leaving, no. That would be too reasonable. David felt like a king. Two fighters entered the ring, and in the end one stood tall: David Martinez, long may he reign.

Playing to the crowd, he shadow-boxed from atop the vending machine. Pop, pop, pop, a knockout blow, ladies and gentlemen. Spirits soaring higher than the sun, he unholstered his revolver and fired a round over the audience.

They loved it, cheering him harder than for any rockerboy. He was on top of the world.

His grin died with a whimper hearing the screech of metal on metal behind him. Cold sweat poured down his neck as money stopped exchanging hands within the crowd. Living in Night City, a person learned to heed the signs and read the wind better than any mystic soothsayer.

When the bets had not settled, it meant the fight was still on.

Johnny walked out of the broken market stall, expression haggard yet seemingly none the worse for wear beneath the dirt and stains. Between one stride and the next, a suit of armor sprang from nowhere to encase him from head to toe, a thing of shaped metal and crimson scales glistening in the lantern light. It belonged in a fantasy novel, or on the ancient fields of honor. A relic of an era that never was.

"What is it going to take to keep you down?" David cried, holding his head in disbelief. The people around him parted like the tide, none willing to get dragged into the fight.

The corpo did not reply. The forcefield appeared, shading his armor in gold. A guard put up to ward against the next Sandevistan-powered punch. The other boy had learned his lesson.

David unslung the shotgun stowed behind his back. One shot could reset the board, opening up a chance once again for his ace in the hole.

That armor, on the other hand, added a complication. He had watched it withstand a barrage from a dozen 6th Street goons, making it the equivalent of a forcefield in its own right.

Looked pretty heavy, though.

"Fuck NUSA, then, I guess. We do it like the nomads," David muttered. "Whoo…" he added in monotone, unable to muster the enthusiasm of earlier. Lifting his shotgun, he fired a round to reopen hostilities.

The bold challenge earned him hearty approval from his fans. Less so, when he hopped off the vending machine and darted into concealment. David ignored their jeers, ducking low as he focused on presenting an inconspicuous profile, a hard task for someone of his size.

He disliked the indirect approach, but only an idiot charged an armored tank straight on. The way to beat a tin can was to open it up and get at the soft meat inside.

His route traced a circuit around the corpo, weaving between the tables and stalls. Cyberoptic low-vision mode helped him avoid the glass bottles and metal objects strewn about the place that might give his position away, the footfalls further drowned out by the music playing from speakers somewhere.

Catchy tune. Chromatic rock wasn't his thing, but he kinda knew this particular song from hearing snippets here and there, and quietly sang along to the lyrics under his breath.

Now, if he was right—

A metal slug punched through the wall on his right, zip past his face, and continued on into the food stand located on the other side of the path. It struck the oven there, and lit the whole place up in an explosion. Flames engulfed the adjacent stalls, starting a wild blaze.

Frozen in his tracks, David's mouth hung open mid-squeak. Mutely, he brought up a hand to feel his nose, recalling the sensation of the fist-sized round brushing by, coming away with a bit of blood. That… had been much too close.

His heart thundered in his chest as he waited, guns at the ready, for the corpo to show. Sneaking closer, he peered into it.

David much preferred the raging, raving lunatic types. He knew where he stood with them.

Johnny was coming here.

He wasted no time, bolting from the area to seek a better firing position. A dive took him over a counter, and he came back up with his shotgun braced on the flat surface. The muzzle swayed to cover likely avenues of approach, with David alert for the slightest movement.

Hearing the clamoring din coming from inside the booths next to him, a distinct sense of worry grew.
