Unarmed and chased by an undying monster. He really was in a movie. Unfortunately, they cast him in the wrong genre. Had he the choice, he would not have signed up for horror.

Breaking out into the open, he frantically searched for a Budget Arms weapon vending machine. The brand sold plastic junk masquerading as a gun, but this was a textbook case for why they had customers.

Lo and behold, one laid a mere few steps from him, ready and willing to arm anybody off the street.

David surged forward, only to have his foot pulled out from under him.

He hit the ground hard, though his armor plating rendered it harmless. What was less harmless was the grip Johnny had on him with his long, creepy tentacle. The previous attack must have angered him something fierce, because he practically vibrated in place.

"You're going nowhere. Get over here!" the corpo shouted, and the arm began to retract, dragging David with it.

David scrambled to grab onto the vending machine, missing by the barest of brushes. His fingers scraped long furrows in the concrete as he struggled against the unrelenting pull of the weaponized darkness.

Tears sprang to his eyes at how close he had been, how well he was doing this whole time. The vending machine grew further and further away, and with it went any hope he had.

Until the roar of a motorcycle engine cut through the night.

As David turned his gaze to the sky, the vehicle shot over the edge of the upper level above Cherry Blossom Market, gleaming in violet and gold. It flew down the staircase with its wheels spinning in the air, unbound by roads. On its back rode a vision of beauty, iridescent locks of hair floating in the breeze. From behind her, twin shotguns aimed Johnny's way, letting loose.

Lucy had arrived, with Rebecca in tow. They hit the ground running, tires screeching on the concrete. One hacking, one blasting.

He could face the whole world, for he had his crew.



-o-
​


A tear rolled down Jaune's cheek. He had been so close to ending it. Every passing second, he regretted not bailing from the fight in the first place. Pride and street cred did not count for much to a man on the brink of his sanity.

Rather than dodging, he allowed the shotgun pellets to knock him over. Frankly, it was easier that way. Each step he now took resisted him, his body a bundle of tensed-up nerves stiff as a board.

He didn't really want to die, though. Yet.

Backup had arrived for Yellow Jacket, and Jaune took their measure while crawling upright. The short one with arms like a gorilla—he was pretty sure they called her Rebecca—carried a lot of guns, and prior experience told him she was a deft hand with them. She had passed a stubby assault rifle to the big guy, so he could expect twice the firepower aimed his way.

The other woman went unarmed. A bare-knuckle brawler?

The woman's eyes briefly glowed, and a stovetop near Jaune bloomed into a fireball that knocked him off-balanced. Her allies used the chance to spray him with a barrage of bullets, the rounds plinking off the two shields he summoned to protect his body.

A witch. Got it.

"Bahaha! Hahahahaha!"

The one named Rebecca laughed like a maniac as she fired her guns, resisting Yellow Jacket's urging to find cover.

"Firefight on a Friday night, playing my fucking jam? Oh, Davey, you know me so well!" she shouted to be heard over the din by the man at her side. Her ghost-pale skin showed an outright blush, each pull of the trigger accompanied by a euphoric gasp. She saw this as the time of her life. "Hey, gonk!" She yelled to Jaune. "You gonna sit on your ass all day? Make this a little exciting, why dontcha?"

"I mean, if you insist…" Jaune said, unheard.

"Ahahahaha—oh, fuck!"

Time seemed to slow down as the trigger-happy maniac's expression morphed from a gleeful smile to open-mouthed surprise, diving to the side as [Third Arm] flung him across the intervening space. It quickly transformed to a look of focus, and she fired at his figure passing by. On his other side, Yellow Jacket held the second woman in his arms, turning to shield her with his body.

Jaune landed, rolled, whimpered at the flips his stomach was doing, then rushed at the edgerunners again. They scattered before him, hoping to surround and pin him down. He chased after the closest, Rebecca. His hand reached out, and Yellow Jacket jumped in between to head him off.

For such a big guy, the solo could move damn fast, but Jaune didn't mind, because he now had him right where he wanted him. He snapped out a punch, cracking him across the chin.

The metal he felt under the other boy's skin saved him from a shattered jaw. Yellow jacket rolled with the momentum, weaving his body in the manner of a boxer to regain his stance and launch a retaliatory blow. Jaune batted it aside, surprised yet again by just how heavy the arm was.

Cyberware messed with his judgment in little ways like that. Which person had enhanced endurance, and which would simply die from a light tap? Was so-and-so a strongman or a jumping kangaroo with a sword? It wreaked havoc in planning his approach to a battle, leading to mistakes that tended to get him a lot of wary side-eyes afterward.

Well, this case presented less of an issue now that he had clashed with him a few times. In many ways, fighting the solo was like fighting Ruby Rose. In other words, effectiveness was not conducive to victory.

…Okay, so, he never won against Ruby Rose, obviously. It was a working theory he had going into the Vytal Tournament that never saw the light of day. Anywho, the point stood. There might be stark differences in size, but at the core, their strengths and weaknesses shared common lines.

Up close, Jaune enjoyed the advantage, as evidenced by the one-two combo he just threw that had Yellow Jacket seeing stars. He added a knee for good measure, jumping to slam it into the other boy's chest and leaving him gasping for air.

Part of that turned out to be an act, and the solo attempted to retaliate in kind with an uppercut. The split second to brace himself meant that the fist failed to budge Jaune all that much, and he made the other boy pay for it with a gut punch that permanently dented his armored abs. Now, the solo gasped for air in truth, and at this range, his allies dared not shoot lest they hit their own side, granting Jaune impunity to continue beating the daylight out of him.

Throughout, he watched carefully, maintaining a steady rhythm that did not push his opponent too far. Yellow Jacket had to believe he stood a chance in this contest. That he could overcome the situation by punching back. Because…

Seeing his chance, Jaune shoved the edgerunner away to gain the space needed for his sword. He summoned it to hand, and without ceremony swung the blade to chop off Yellow Jacket's head, ending the battle once and for all.

The edgerunner's form blinked out of existence, an afterimage that had tricked Jaune's eyes. Immediately, he called on the Geo shield. It flickered on then broke apart, which told him enough. He did not even have the time to sigh before a megaton punch sent him rocketing across the night market, bouncing on the concrete like a pebble on a water's surface. The sheer force of it threw him clear to the edge of the plaza, stopping only when he slammed into the fleet of parked Tyger Claws motorcycles, to their owners' distraught wails.

Buried under the bikes, Jaune finished his sigh. He saw that coming.

Give the Ruby Rose type a moment to collect themselves, or even too big a spike in their sense of danger, and they would resort to their trump card. Superspeed pretty much turned a person into a teleporter, and he did so hate fighting teleporters.

And now the battle had shifted back to a long-range gunfight, where his 'marksmanship' had proven deficient as of late. One would think the ability to put a bullet where he aimed it was the entirety of the concept, but no. He swore to keep the next shipment of smart bullets his team came across, no matter how much they could sell them for.

He realized that he had a problem on his hand when the motorcycles around him began turning on one by one. More than that, their engines revved up to unholy levels of noise, the warning gauges beeping in alarm. It occurred to him that one of the edgerunners, the witch with her magical techno powers, had demonstrated not long ago with ample clarity what she could do with a machine.

The beeping grew louder. Jaune engaged his rocket boots and bugged out at top speed.

In his wake, Tyger Claws bemoaned the loss of their bikes, while everyone else in the audience celebrated another fireworks show. The force of the explosion knocked him out of the sky, and thereafter he sat on his butt to watch the pretty colors, distracted for a moment from the dark, eternal curse that was ripping him apart from the inside, the endless benighted torment for which there was no escape.

*gurgle*

Fuel ignited. Neon underglow lights burst, spraying fragments across the ground. Painted metal warp from intense heat, melting like ice. The motorcycles played out a drum roll with their detonations.

Technology sure was scary.

A niggling thought did the equivalent of jumping up and down, waving its arms. Jaune looked around him, taking in the booths stuffed full of kitchenware, used electronics, computer screens and so on.

Wasn't he… completely surrounded by technology right now?

The witch answered him by waking the night market. Lights blinked on and gas stoves hissed, absent of a human's guiding hand. TV screens flickered with the image of eyes, rolling in their sockets until they stopped on him.

He gave a nervous chuckle, and waved.

The chime of an incoming text defused his rising consternation. What good timing. Yellow Jacket thought his team would save him, but Jaune had friends of his own. With all haste, he withdrew his phone from his pocket.

Annoying Blonde N.8: ^._.^

Um, what?

"Meow!"

A mighty warcry pierced the air. From on high, The Meowsterious Cato Cat—nearly unrecognizable as Escha due to her mask—leapt into the battle, her entrance heralded by a string of curses from Rebecca as she received a faceful of wet cat, damp from the rain. The two went down in a tangle of limbs, falling out of view.

Not the foe he was worried about, but he would take it. Besides, that meant Lisa must be around here somewhere to help out.

Ding!

Annoying Blonde N.8: I told you so!

Yep. She was here.

Annoying Blonde N.8: You ate the local junk, didn't you?
You got food poisoning, silly man.
Annoying Blonde N.8: I told you so!

Jaune let out a resigned breath, and typed his response.

Sorry :Jaune​

A bullet shattered the ground by his side. Yellow Jacket had found him, no doubt pointed to him by the witch. He laid down a stream of gunfire, sending Jaune rolling into cover behind a vending machine. It had yet to start beeping or smoking, so he assumed it would remain safe for at least a few more seconds. The phone continued chiming in the meantime, clamoring for his attention.

Annoying Blonde N.8: lol
Annoying Blonde N.8: I could say a lot right now.
Annoying Blonde N.8: But I won't.
Annoying Blonde N.8: Don't have to.
Annoying Blonde N.8: lol

Stop laughing :Jaune​

The phone notified him of a call, and he picked it up. The first thing he heard, Lisa laughing at him. Because of course she was.

Then, more honestly, she asked, "Are you hurt?"

"They knocked me around a bit, but that was all. The food poisoning is worse," he reported with a small smile, suppressing a grimace. "The big one can hit hard when he activates that superspeed cyberware."

"It's called a Sandevistan, although he's using it oddly. The ones on the market don't function exactly the same according to videos. Also, does that mean he already used it?"

"That's right. Twice, maybe three times?"

"And that's, what, adding on top of the last four? Geeze, he shouldn't even be alive. People can activate it once or twice a day at most. It melts their brain if they try for more. Yeah, there's definitely something up with his cyberware, or with him. A supersoldier program, maybe. That'll make him either a deserter or an escaped lab rat. He has combat training. Has to be a deserter, then."

"Later, Lisa," he cut in before Lisa fell further into the throes of her rambling analysis. Fascinating as they may be, their importance to the situation at hand was rather questionable. "Give me something I can work with."

"That girl with the rainbow hair seems close to him. There could be something between them, methinks."

"I could have sworn we've had a talk before about hostages and puppies."

"This one is a combatant. She knows the score."

The vending machine his back was resting against began rattling and whirring on its own, the metal heating up.

"Fair enough. Still…" Jaune looped the phone strap around his neck and tucked it below his armor, then dashed out of hiding. Instantly, bullets flew at him, as if waiting for the exact moment the witch flushed him into the open. He brought up his shield to deflect the brunt of it as Lisa's voice chirped over the line.

"Oh, fine. Bait them out. I want to get a look at what I'm dealing with."

Cue him running through a minefield. Lisa did not seem to register what her request entailed, as the witch orchestrated a symphony of fire and shrapnel to stall his advance through the tight confines of the market stalls. Under the woman's direction, an innocuous cart delivered a payload in the form of a half-repaired washer straight to him, exploding as he vaulted over it. Ovens overloaded and went up in flames from the other side of walls, vaporizing the thin sheet metal in an attempt to catch him unaware. To his favor, the area lacked anything with the oomph to put the actual hurt on him, only allowing Yellow Jacket and the witch to stay a step ahead in this game of cat and mouse. The occasional flashes of white fur and ghost-pale skin amid the ever more derelict night market told him that the duel between their diminutive teammates was being spared the same treatment.

"I see them. Ooh, that big fella don't look so good."

"Yeah," Jaune gasped out. All this moving around was playing hell on him, but he was not going to admit that to Lisa. "Before you got here I gave him what for and beat him like a drum."

"Not what I mean, and you don't have room to talk. Try not to vomit, tough guy," she scoffed. "No, I think the Sandevistan is taking a toll on him. Some of his injuries won't make sense, otherwise."

His mind seized on that tidbit, and took off running. "If I bait him—"

"Into using it more—" Lisa jumped in, fighting to be the one voicing the plan.

Jaune finished, "He'll drop dead on his own!"

"Or fall unconscious. Let's not plot murder, yeah? Take the next right, he's to your two o'clock." Lisa then cursed. "We've got incoming drones. Police markings. The netrunner must have hacked into them… But when did she get the chance, and where…"

Wherever Lisa was hiding, she remained safe, devolving into mutters as the new complication descended on the Night Market. The boxy, darkly-painted objects streamed down the staircases in floating swarms, dozens of them converging to then head straight for Jaune, opening fire with in-built guns.

He summoned a random firearm from his stash, shooting with barely a glance over his shoulder. One, two, three, they fell out of the sky, and he could almost see the moment the netrunner gave them a new command. The drones performed a simultaneous jerky motion, then scattered apart, weaving patterns in the air to present harder targets. He tried taking them out anyway, meeting much less success, and the drones' return fire forced him into cover, harrying his steps as he blindly combed the night market for his foes.

"Left!"

The order came out of nowhere, but he followed it without thought. Lisa had been right, of course. His keen eyes spied the movements in the shadows, and he pounced.

"GOT… you?"

Angular, catlike eyes of red and yellow bore into him, vaguely pinging his memories. Knocked down, the woman laid below him on her elbows, her face close to his and their legs tangled together. She was rather tall, he noticed. Taller than him, even.

But she was not the big, buff man he was looking for.

"Sorry, wrong person," he said, and it dawned on him with growing horror that this woman might well have been trapped inside the night market due to his fight with Yellow Jacket.

Her answer was a soft "Ah!" as she winced at the tight grip he had on her upper arm, prompting him to release her with haste. His eyebrows furrowed at the electronic twang he heard in her voice, which drew his attention to a particular detail.

The woman wore a veil, one that had flipped aside during their collision. And beneath…

"S-Stop, don't look," the woman muttered, covering her mouth with a hand and averting her gaze.

Now it became Jaune's turn to wince, feeling like a heel. Beneath the veil was a broken and mangled mask. A gap in it revealed no lips or teeth, but a gaping hole, with metal lining the inside from the roof of her mouth to the bottom of her throat, cyberware replacement for a devastating injury.

"It isn't a bad thing," he said, although that was just him finding words to make her feel better. "Sorry, again. I didn't mean to get you caught up in this."

The woman sighed. "Yeah… I'm sorry, too."

A drone smacked him on the back of the head, throwing him over the woman to land on his back. By the time he got his bearing and looked up, she was already gone.

"Sandevistan just activated. I don't know what you did, but good job, Jaune!"

His mouth fell open.

"Wait a minute, I remember her! She's one of them!"



-o-
​


David exited the still world, ready to keel over. Lucy was watching, though, so he propped a hand against a shelf to hold himself upright, and swallowed the glob of blood in his mouth. Nothing he could do about the nosebleed but to gamely press on.

"It's okay, you're safe now, Kiwi," he said, smiling at his newly-rescued teammate.

Kiwi simply grunted, looking none too happy. But then, that was normal for her.

The two of them ducked low, joining Lucy behind the counter of an electronics repair shop, right under the nose of their opponent. Outside, fire raged, and David watched with envy as Johnny took to the sky, shedding his armor to fight the drones in their domain.

"Did…" He rubbed his eyes. "Did he just pull out a motorcycle?"

Kiwi rapped the side of her head with her knuckles, as if that would reset her cyberoptics. Lucy, meanwhile, dropped a fist onto her palm.

"So that's why the signal for a bunch of them disappeared!"

The heavy motorcycle fell, crushing the drones flying beneath before Lucy's previous command detonated it to wipe out a few more. Johnny rode the blast, flinging himself into a group of drones, swinging that sword of his to cut them apart.

David cursed. "He's going through them fast. Do we have more?"

"Nope," said Kiwi. "Also, Falco couldn't lose our tail, so NCPD will be on us in about two minutes."

"What, why?" Lucy asked. She then facepalmed. "Because you didn't hide your tracks when stealing the drones."

Kiwi shrugged at her. "You ran out the doors with the keys to my bike, saying, and I quote, 'Hurry up and bring everything, my hubby is in trouble!' So I hurried."

"I didn't say that last part... but thank you." Lucy hid her embarrassment by seizing control of a drone, overloading it before sending it careening into the corpo.

Kiwi looked around. "Where's Rebecca?"

A computer screen flickered on, courtesy of Lucy. It connected to a camera sitting over the night market, zoomed in on a short girl with twintails rolling on the ground while hugging a very grumpy cat. On her face, a bright and innocent smile.

Not the epic showdown he expected.

"She seems fine, aaaand video saved," Lucy said. "Anyway, let's worry about ourselves. Time to delta?"

David shook his head, and got up on a knee. "No. He's weakened, I can tell. See how he keeps messing up?" He pointed at the aerial battle, where a mistimed dodge led to a collision between Johnny and a drone. A mistake that could happen to anyone, except David knew for a fact that the corpo was better than that. "Everything we did has added up. I need to hit him now, and put him down for good."

"You're not in a state to say that," Lucy replied. It killed him to hear the hopeless note in her voice, like she didn't believe in him, but then she jumped to her feet, and the wild grin on her face told him that she would stand with him all the way. "Kiwi, I'm borrowing your drones. Gonna soften him up." Her eyes flashed red, and under her command, the police drones fell into a frenzy, bombarding the corpo with suicidal abandon. "David, he's coming down. You—"

"Already ahead of you," David said, and he stepped into the still world where no sound existed.

He loved it here. The quiet. The dark. The unmoving people. It was lonely, but a good sort of lonely, and in this time between the moments, there was no pain. The world waited for him with the patience of a mother.

His route traced the edge of the plaza, then cut into the path that Johnny was on. Upside-down and locked in combat with the drones a mere few feet off the ground, the other boy made for easy pickings. David pushed at his chrome to eke out a little more momentum. He wanted this to hurt.

Thirty steps. Twenty. Ten. Five—Are those eddies on the ground?

What drove him to stop and pick up the money bills, he would continue to ask until his last days. They were already in his hands before he thought about it, and he only realized the mistake once the colors around him began to bleed at the edges. Pain returned, tearing at him from every direction as the damage to his muscles caught up from behind. Time was up.

The first thing that happened upon David returning to normal speed, was Johnny cracking a smile.

The second thing? Shadows grabbing him, as the smile turned cold.

"Get baited, idiot!" Johnny shouted, and yanked David forward. Their foreheads collided, flesh to metal, hard enough that David thought he felt a shockwave around them. His vision dimmed for a second, the Kiroshi cyberoptics stuttering, and he dropped like a sack of scop with Johnny hitting the concrete beside him.

They both held their heads and rolled on the ground, oddly in sync. Once David had blinked the stars out of his eyes, he surged to his feet to find Johnny doing the same. With not a moment to waste, he swung his fist.

The reinforced knuckles of his Gorilla Arms smashed against a golden shield, while Johnny's fist punched past the barrier like it was never there, connecting with David's nose. A sharp crack, and it gave way under the blow.

Johnny threw a follow-up punch to capitalize on the momentum, but strong as he was, his technique left a lot to be desired. David traced its path and diverted it aside, directing the arm between them to leave Johnny's entire side open. A quick three-shot combo had the corpo doubling over for David to aim a soccer kick at his face.

Bonk!

"Jesus!" David hissed through his teeth, clutching the foot that had just bounced off Johnny's chin without even budging him. Hell, the kick might have done more damage to his foot than it did that smarmy face.

Recovered, Johnny rushed at him, a bright glow leaving his eyes. An implacable arm seized David by the jacket to swing him with the ease of a child's toy, slamming him against ground with enough force that he bounced. A stomp to his chest drove David back down, another crashing into his face to make him stay down.

A brief lull ensued, the two of them breathing hard. The shoe sitting on his face ground against his skin, and past it he met the blue-eyed glare of the corpo… which, if he was being honest, failed to look all that intimidating.

"You give up yet?" his opponent asked, sounding stressed.

His jaw clenched, frustration building. He didn't want to admit it, but the winner of this bare-knuckle brawl had been decided.

So, clearly, he was left with no choice but to whip out the revolver tucked inside his jacket and unload a round right to Johnny's balls.

A shrill cry pierced the night.

Johnny fell, tears streaming from his eyes. David, meanwhile, climbed to his feet at an unhurried pace and leveled his revolver at the corpo.

"You cheater!" Johnny gasped, curling into a ball.

"We were playing by rules?" David asked blithely.

In Night City, one objective mattered: living to see the morning. Beyond that, anything goes.

He would not die here. Not due to him deciding on a whim to go out for a damn bowl of ramen.

That thought spurred him to pull the trigger, and a bullet slammed into the side of Johnny's head.

Johnny outright laughed. "...Have to do better than that…"

David obliged him, taking aim at his chest now.

A sliver of light pierced his revolver, going in one side and out the other. He had barely registered it when the projectile exploded with electricity.

A scream tore from his throat as his arm went haywire, the connected nerves set afire. His fingers spasmed, twisting in a psychedelic dance without his control, the revolver dropping to hit the concrete. The Projectile Launch System activated on its own, the metal panels glitching out to repeatedly open and shut, catching on the cannon.

And then Johnny kicked him in the balls.

David spat a mouthful of blood, and dropped to his knees. As he laid in a heap, he saw through the tears Johnny getting up. The other boy spoke to the empty air, likely on a holocall, for whatever reason not leaving it as thoughts.

"Lisa, nice timing. Was that—hey, Fischl, thanks for the save. How did you know we were here?"

Fischl, Fischl. The name echoed in his mind. He had heard it before.

"Well, I'm glad you were passing by, then. The cops are coming? Right, I'll be there in a bit."

David frowned. He was hearing the other side of the conversation, if faintly. Were they… using phones?

"What, no, I wasn't planning to kill him. Why would you say that? He's a what? Okay, okay, fine, I'm going."

Johnny sounded very guilty, to David's ears. The corpo shifted on his heels, and in the direction he faced, a number of figures were waving to him from the top of a staircase. David squinted his eyes, striving to make them out over the distance.

A cold pit opened in his stomach.

No.

He should have known. He should have smelled the trap a mile off. There was even a moment where he noticed the dead giveaway, that specific biosculpting process that gave them their unnaturally natural looks.

Fischl, Bennett, Hu Tao. Those tourists he met in the Afterlife… were working with the enemy.

That motherfucker Johnny had been playing him all night long.

Chapter 74: Just Another Night City Day Off
​


Jaune's day began with a quiet morning.

"Bleeeeeeegh!"

As quiet as a person experiencing a case of food poisoning could manage, at any rate. With his face directed over a toilet bowl, the boy who had earned himself the title of Valkyria, the Hunter of the Deviljho, a full-fledged Huntsman (of the Axel Branch Adventurer Guild and, yes, he was cheating and, no, Ozpin could pry the job off his cold dead corpse) shook like a leaf in the wind, his expression a drawn and haggard thing parched for water. Night City cuisine had claimed another victim.

"Looks like that's it for now," Lisa declared in an all too chipper voice, muffled behind the gas mask she bought. Dramatic, but Jaune was in no position to complain about it since she had a hold of him and could decide to drop him at any point. "Ready, Bennett?"

"Yes, boss lady!"

"It's Lisa. Lisaaaa," the girl corrected, faintly chuckling. "We're all friends here."

Bennett nodded. "Got it, boss Lisa."

"Better."

So it wasn't the 'boss' part she objected to.

Together, the two of them hoisted him upright and helped him walk out of the bathroom. The worst of his illness passed a few hours back, but a few minor symptoms persisted, among them a dizzy spell whenever he walked and a bit of weakness barely worth mentioning. He did not, and still did not, believe it affected him to any great degree, but his explanation of that obvious fact had been rather undercut by him stumbling and banging his head against the wall the last time they let go. Now, firm grips guided him across a tiled floor to the long couch where Escha just finished arranging pillows for him to lie on.

The felyne waved to them while looking very proud, and she climbed on the backrest as they approached. The quiet giggles she hid beneath her paws told him she found all of this quite amusing, another silly human thing that the felyne physique apparently bypassed altogether. Or maybe this was what happened when a person ate dinosaur meat chock-full of bioenergy from day one, that it granted them bellies of iron.

For her mockery, Jaune laid a curse upon her. May your tummy ache from too much ice cream.

Past the oblivious cat, soothing daylight streamed into the room from a bright, cloudy sky to denote the late morning. After the events of last night, which from the tale his companions told included more than just his misadventure, none of them objected to taking it easy today. On the balcony, Fischl reclined on a chaise lounge while reading a book she brought from their previous world, with Oz perched on her shoulder and following along. Something, something Philosopher's Stone. Inside, Hu Tao had taken over a corner of the room for her arts and crafts project. Stacks of freshly bought wooden planks leaned against the wall, awaiting her delicate touch. Hearing the grave news that he was suffering in poor health had lit a fire in her, albeit not in a direction he enjoyed.

Lisa settled him on the couch, handing him a glass of water that he sipped at, and after fixing the pillow under his head she plonked herself down beside it to join him in watching the news. They passed the time chitchatting about inconsequential matters, to the sound of a saw cutting into wood.

In a testament to the hectic nature of Night City, his actions warranted merely a small mention tucked among a rapid-fire list of events that the news anchor touched on.

"Our Japantown correspondent reported of a rampage past midnight in Cherry Blossom Market, where rowdy street gangs once again gave in to their destructive impulses. The event in question, of which we can only speculate involved the use of brandless drugs, caused devastation to the livelihood of honest Night City citizens. Remember, viewers: say no to drugs if you never saw it on a billboard."

The news anchor shook his head as if to lament the sheer inhumanity of it all, before moving on.

"In other news, efforts to curb the unlicensed use of public city spaces within Japantown in anticipation of the upcoming Aratama-Matsuri Festival is continuing at scheduled pace. Organizers from Arasaka Corporation have assured our station that those refusing to comply with the city ordinance may instead deal with the full force of NCPD ordnance." The man chuckled at his own joke. "I don't know about you folks at home, but I will certainly appreciate the improved view at the dashi parade!"

"I hadn't even thought about that…" Jaune muttered dully, as the TV flickered to the next segment.

Lisa turned to him, half-listening. "Hmm?"

"I did a number on that night market. Nah, scratch that, I reduced it to scraps."

"Given the garbage they pass off as food, I'm confident the people of Night City will send you a thank you note."

"Maybe," he said, giving a small, humorless laugh that died quick, "but the workers there were making their living from it. Doesn't that mean I ruined them, like the news reported?"

On the other end of the L-shape couch, Bennett grimaced. "Well…"

Lisa cleared her throat, cutting the boy off.

"I wouldn't trust the news here, if I were you." She indicated the TV with a derisive air. "That thing? That endless stream of contradictory nonsense wrapped up in a pearly smile? They said it because their sponsor wanted them to, because violent thugs in the street means that you can stomp down harder for a stupid parade."

Was that the aim? He would love to believe so, that it was all theater. It made for a convenient narrative.

He fidgeted, uncomfortable with that thought. "It doesn't change the situation on the ground, though, I feel. Most of the place was on fire when we left." Those shops will be back up and running in no time. As for fault, people would tell you the other guy holds more responsibility for it ending up this way, and look how he and his crew ran from the cops."

Jaune opened his mouth to reply, then stopped and thought it over before speaking a word. Seeing no point in arguing, he said, "Yeah, sure. Let's hear it." I'll drop by Cherry Blossom Market on my own time.

He has a reputation as Night City's best mercenary, or edgerunner or whatever, for those tapped into that scene. Pretty much the guy to hire to deal with your problems."

To somebody at the top of the game, having that kind of threat roaming in the same territory makes for a dicey situation."

Thus putting them almost inevitably on a collision course.

"...Today's a good day… I can feel it…"

"What are you up to, now?" he interjected.

Lisa grinned at him.

Let's go chip in!"

That sentiment was shared among their entire group, whether human, cat, or bird.

A couple of steps later, it struck him. "Hang on a minute, did you just catch a serial killer?"

"Without even trying. Some days I wake up and think my power is a curse, but then I remember I'm fucking Sherlock Holmes." Lisa sighed. "And I deserve something for the trouble. C'mon, you're not getting out of it this time. The future called, and it wants you in neokitsch."

They departed, leaving colorful Japantown for the towers of steel and corridors of smooth glass found in its more upscale neighbor. The journey took longer on foot, but they were in no rush that they needed a taxi. It gave everybody the chance to see the sights, for good or ill.

Upscale meant shiny. It did not wholly translate to safe. Scammers elevated their game from junk to art, doing their hardest to bump into their group while carrying expensive-looking vases or paintings. A businessman dressed sharply in gray used a briefcase handcuffed to his wrist as a bludgeon to deck a thief in the face. Solos escaped from an office building, beaten back by gun-toting employees. Something was broken in Night City, and Jaune did not have a clue how to fix it.

To those living at this height, the happenings down there must seem so very small, while the floors above loomed impossibly high.

"The money dries up before it can trickle down," Lisa explained without explaining. A turn at the end of the bridge, and she led the way into the shop.

The place screamed class, with white marble floors and a fancy chandelier. Mannequins posed on staged daises took up most of the space; divans and champagne glasses to accompany the gold dresses, or posters of fast bikes to go with the meticulously-designed streetwear. Store clerks roamed their hunting ground, stalking the customers from behind the displays and forming veritable packs around the wealthiest of them.

The person stationed at the entrance took one look at their group, and seemed torn on whether to welcome them or kick them to the curb. His eyes flicked from one face to another, then darted to their outfits, notably the jeans and t-shirt Jaune wore under his jacket. The cat squatting on the floor threw an additional wrench into his thought process. The man settled for a plastic smile.

Lisa replied without missing a beat. "Deposit, please."

She fished out a fat stack of eddies from her purse, slapping it on the counter and smirking as the store clerk changed his tune in a flash. The employee now sported a face bright and eager, fawning over them as if to skirt over the previous attitude. In his view, they had proven they belonged here.

Since Lisa had a better handle on this kind of social niceties, Jaune left it to her and turned to the others.

"Okay, all. Lisa's buying, so go pick out whatever you like." He panned his gaze over the store, then grimaced. Too rich for him. Anxiety rising. "If you need me, I'll be in that corner."

Together, they—plus a likewise flustered Fischl—beat a hasty retreat to a small, deserted section of the store. Let Lisa have her fun with the silks and gold-lined fineries. He appreciated more the brightly, almost Huntsman-esque aesthetic that he so often saw on the Night City streets. The style was something called kitsch, and he had to say, he liked it. Clothes that made people feel happy just wearing them, quirky and very 'you'.

"What do you think?" he asked the others after pulling a jacket off the rack. Neon orange. Mmmm.

Chapter 75: Just Another Night City Nine to Five
​


Jaune placed down the last stack of wooden planks, piling them neatly at the side of the plaza. With that done, he turned around with a beaming smile.

"This should be a good amount," he said to the vendors of Cherry Blossom Market, looking from one bright(ish) face to the next. Barely-concealed anticipation passed among them, the assembled crowd no doubt chomping at the bit to start the rebuilding. Not one to disappoint them, he kept it short. His fist punched into the air.

"Alright, everybody! Ready to start putting up your new stalls? I bet we can get it done by the afternoon if we work together!"

Those rousing words carried across the plaza… and then just sort of petered out, met by silence. Glances passed between the vendors. One of them cleared his throat and stepped forward.

"Aaactually, we have it covered from here," he said, the sentiment earning immediate support.

"Yeah, yeah, that's right," said a second.

"No need for you to trouble yourself, mister."

Jaune lowered his fist, uncertain of how to take the tepid response. People around here tended not to mind free labor, something that had roped him into a number of shenanigans. This sudden turnabout was a departure from the usual. He looked from the pile of materials, then back to them.

"Are you sure?" he asked. "I'm pretty handy with simple construction work."

A storm of protest rained on him from all sides.

"No no no no! Leaving it like that is fine!"

"Thank you, we have it from here."

"Genuine fucking wood—"

"You've done more than enough, choom!"

"We'll help them out, don't you worry!"

The vendors of Cherry Market Street paused at that last sentence, turning to the bystander who had voiced the offer. Many faces in the crowd near that person were nodding up and down, eager to pitch in, with smiles all around.

"...Right, what they said," agreed a stall owner. Reaching down, she grabbed one of the hammers that Jaune provided. Others followed suit with the crowbars and saws.

Ahhh, such camaraderie. A community coming together, supporting their neighbors. It brought a tear to his eyes.

And okay, he could understand why they preferred he did not stick around any longer than he needed to, what with him being one half of the reason the night market got thrashed. A good chunk of the people he met found deep entertainment in his actions, referring to it as 'nova' and even clapping him on the back for it. Another group, however, had seemed very nervous at his presence, packing up the scraps of metal and cloth they were using to repair their stalls like they thought he was somehow coming back to kick a sand castle over a second time.

Night City, like Vale, had a fondness for their duels. But, only up to a point. He had pushed past the line, becoming… scary.

That sobering thought encouraged him to leave while the going was good. After bidding farewell, Jaune climbed the steps to the upper road to depart from Cherry Blossom Market. He hoped he would have a chance to come back again.

"Johnny-san."

A familiar face awaited him at the top of the steps, a man with glowing lines tattooed on his skin to form the snarling face of a tiger, dressed in red and green. The Tyger Claw subordinate bowed deeply, hands clasped together. As ever, sweat poured down his face. It seemed to be a constant with the ganger.

"Hey, you!" Jaune greeted him with good cheer, while deftly hiding the fact he had no idea what the man's name was in such a manner that nobody could possibly realize it. "What's up, buddy? I haven't seen you in two days, how have you been?"

"Er, good?" The man did not sound sure, and quickly moved on, gesturing with both hands across the road. "She, that is, Wakako would like a word."

Jaune looked past him, and his expression slipped into a grimace for a brief second. How wonderful, another trip down rowdy Jig-Jig Street. Early in the morning, and the place carried on like it was midnight. Deals took place in the open, business not at all hidden in the mouths of alleys. Never change, Jig-Jig Street.

"Got it," he said. "I've been meaning to catch up with her on some personal stuff anyway, so this is good timing." Speaking of rowdy, was it him or were things getting pretty loud back at the market? Eh, probably construction work had started. He clapped the Tyger Claw on the shoulder, stopping him from leaving. "Oh right, have you eaten breakfast yet? Know any place around here that won't make a man sick? Yeah? Lead on, my friend!"

An unsatisfying yet safe breakfast in an upscale restaurant later, Jaune approached the open doors of a gaming parlor. He walked past the clickclacking pachinko machines, nodded a greeting to the security guard whose back was glued to the wall, and swept the curtains aside to enter Wakako's office with its decor that tried to evoke the sense of Japan yet was subtly off-tune. Wakako, as ever, surrounded herself in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tray near her elbow filled with the discarded ends. The old woman looked up as he entered, and smiled a crooked-tooth smile.

"Ah, my solo. You always come when called. If only my boys could be the same."

A quick glance around the room confirmed that Hu Tao was not hanging around, so Jaune pulled out the rickety chair in front of the desk and sat down. From an inner pocket of his jacket, but really from the dimensional space he walked around with, he withdrew a simple pouch containing tea leaves that he passed over to the fixer. The old woman pounced on the gift without hesitation.

"Are your sons doing well?" he asked for politeness's sake.

Wakako waved her hand in a dismissive manner while stowing away her new batch of tea leaves. "You know boys."

Answer enough, so far as it went with the fixer. For all that she liked to make mention of her children, Wakako had a certain attitude regarding them from what Jaune could glean. The rules she set down ensured her sons never stepped too far out of line. Otherwise, they would do what they do, and reap what they sow. He had yet to hear her say their names.

Once the old woman had resettled into her seat, she took a drag of her cigarette.

"How are you finding your apartment? Is the view from your window still to your liking?" She gave him a steady look, expectant.

Right, this game again. Jaune racked his brain for a good response.

"The soundproofing could use some work. I think I might have heard a person screaming in the night."

"There is always someone screaming in the night." Wakako tutted in good humor. "Bah. You are a poor hand at this. Give me the rude child any day. She is disagreeable, but I would enjoy negotiating the rent with her."

Jaune did not grant that idea much serious thought. Wakako and Lisa should never again be put in a room together, period. As for rent, considering the cut she got from the jobs they did for her, the fixer was making bank off of a place that had been going vacant between tenants. The woman had no real reason to complain, doing it simply for the sake of formalities and customs Jaune knew not.

He chitchatted with the old lady for a while, mainly listening to her talk. Today, Wakako went on about the tourists who would pour into Japantown for every big event, the next day leaving the locals holding the trash bags. She had strong opinions on the matter, and seemed to relish expounding on this to a person unfamiliar to the scene. He received quite a spiel on the proper way to sort and dispose of garbage, as a result.

Some time in, he finally found a chance to segue toward a different subject.

"Have you found one yet?" he asked. "A blacksmith, I mean."

That earned him a roll of the eyes. "A 'blacksmith', he says." A flick, and cigarette ash fell into the tray by Wakako's side. "I have a contact in the outskirts of the city. A workshop that asks no questions and is familiar with fancy toys. They will see you at a time of your convenience. Tell the little messenger attending you. He will guide you there."

Now that was news he wanted to hear!

"Sweet. Thank you, Wa—"

"Any costs incurred, they lie between the two of you. My fee is paid. My part in this is done."

Jaune deflated. Way to put a damper on things, bringing money into it.

He thanked her anyway, and the old woman accepted it as her due. She then cleared her throat, sliding a tablet in front of her that she swiped open.

"On to other matters, I have here a selection of requests. You and your crew are in high demand. Most are frivolous, not worth the pay. They wish to see the flying solo of Japantown. They believe you are a conman."

Jaune grumbled under his breath for a bit about the unfairness of that assumption, before speaking up. "You usually have an idea of which ones I should take. Any thoughts?"

His question earned him a satisfied nod from the fixer. Respect was something he knew she valued, even beyond money, and it hurt him none to show her a bit of deference. And wow, did he wish that sounded less manipulative of him.

"Let's see now," Wakako mused. "If you are after quick eddies, another fixer is willing to front a payment in exchange for a meeting."

"It's Faraday, isn't it?" he deadpanned. "Pass, please."

Wakako gave him a thin smile that told of her own annoyance with the man. Did Faraday bark orders to her like she was a dog when he talks to her, too? The old woman seemed to relish sweeping the message away on her tablet.

"Then, let us talk of birds," said Wakako.

He wondered if that was her habit of speaking in metaphors acting up again. A sharp look from her quelled those words before they could slip out. Instead, he folded his hands in his lap and sat up straight to present the image of an innocent schoolboy whose transcripts absolutely were real, eager to learn. (He had a lot of practice with that one.)

"Birds are not seen anymore in Night City, for good or ill," Wakako said. "These days, something else has taken their place in the majestic sky. In many ways, I enjoy them more than I did the birds."

Wakako stubbed out her cigarette, burned down to the little end. She lit another stick immediately, taking a drag and puffing out a curl of smoke.

"Aerodynes fly high above the hustle and bustle of the streets. They deliver cargo too important to risk in transit. Sometimes goods, sometimes documents, sometimes corpo executives on the way to lunch. Always there will be people calling on me, and I in turn calling on my solos, to liberate the treasures these golden geese hold. Today, it shall be a little different. A client wishes to destroy a shipment of proprietary technology they lost track of. At the least, make sure the shipment does not enter the hands of the recipient."

Proprietary technology? Consider his interest thoroughly piqued. Uncommon goods often commanded higher price tags.

The fixer noted his sudden enthusiasm, and she waved him down with a lazy gesture.

"I do not think you will find anything of note. The label is an excuse. What our client truly wish to bury is the past."

He pondered that. "I… don't quite understand," Jaune said, brows furrowed.

Wakako answered him with a chuckle. The mirth did not reach her old, tired gaze.

"Someday, you will. Night City changes in the blink of an eye, and nothing hurts so much as the memory of days gone by."



-o-
​


"What are those things? They're massive."

Standing atop an office building near city center, Jaune looked out over the urban sprawl, a hand shading his eyes. At the moment, his gaze was locked on the sliver of horizon visible between the skyscrapers, at the place where the ocean met the Night City docks.

Ships had brought something new from across the sea. Great, big carvings of beasts, and elegant structures resembling houses. Mechanical cranes transported them with care onto solid ground.

He heard only silence from the person he addressed, and he turned around to find Tattletale curled into a ball near his feet, clinging onto the parapet step with a death grip as she poked her head over the edge. Decked out in her new costume, the girl had lost her gung-ho attitude to now shiver like a leaf in the wind.

"We are really high up," Tattletale murmured, slowly blinking behind the smooth, futuristic visor that had replaced her domino mask.

"Uh-huh. It's so cool,"Jaune gushed, a fluttering sensation in his chest. One thing he especially liked about this world, its cities went up and up. With the wind in his hair and the sky so near, he felt free as a bird. What a thrill.

"Not the word I'd use…"

The supervillainess seized up at the sound of his boots scraping on the concrete, and hunched into herself even harder.

"Don't you dare poke me!" she hissed. "If I fall, I will haunt you!"

Jaune rolled his eyes. Not everyone was like her, thank you. He knelt down, placing a hand on her back where it rubbed in soothing patterns.

"Relax. Even if you fell, I've got two, maybe three ways to get you out of going splat."

His reassurance achieved little effect beyond Tattletale sticking her lower lip out in a sulk. Still, despite the glare she sent his way, she did not snap at him and allowed his hand to continue while she observed the world beneath through wary, half-squinted eyes. He refrained from telling her that she very much resembled a cat to him right now, what with the posture and the thin collar around her neck.

Er, choker. Not collar. And these were back rubs, definitely not pets.

*Pet, pet, pet, pet*

Tattletale stretched in a very cat-like manner, in no way enjoying the attention.

The two of them continued to laze around, passing the time waiting for their mark by pointing out interesting sights. In the current era, life had moved upward. Holographic ads encircled buildings, beaming their message both to the populace miles out, and inward to the office workers and residents of the towers. Higher still, private rooftop gardens created a different world from those living below, one calmer and more gentle. Meanwhile, windows offered a view into life at the top, from ballrooms to golden statues. Quite a few had the personal effects or artworks arranged to face the glass, presumably on the assumption that people would be peeking in as Jaune and Tattletale were doing. What better way to enjoy one's wealth, than to stoke the envy of one's peers. Tattletale pointed to the rooms that went in total darkness as places of actual note, the activities within too sensitive for prying eyes.

To break up the static scenery, aerodynes—AVs—took to the air with the sky as their road, weaving between the dense skyscrapers unimpeded by the gridlocked traffic on the streets. The flying vehicles bore a distinct resemblance to cars, only with jet engines in place of wheels. Some went for the sleek look, meant for passengers, while others had a clunky feel to them, rectangular boxes built for the rougher work of cargo hauling.

What a fascinating place. He could sit here watching it all for hours. A shame, then, that the peaceful time soon came to an end.

"I think that's ours there," Tattletale informed him, pointing at a small shape banking around a glass building. A glance at a tablet left lying near her, and she nodded. "Correct place, not too early, not too late. Looks like Gandalf is behind the wheels."

Literally who?

Jaune climbed to his feet, and helped Tattletale up before returning his attention to the approaching AV. In his head, he ran through the steps of the plan over and over. The timing was key.

Tattletale tugged on his arm. "Oh, hang on. You have a bit of dirt on you." She began patting him down. "Just there, and here—stay still, you."

"I should put you in this suit," Jaune groused, swiping at her hands to stop her copping a feel. Oh sure, he totally had that much dirt smudged on him from sitting down.

"Don't be silly."

The aircraft they sought measured a little wider and longer than a van, and as it drifted closer to their position, the thing turned out to be rather basic in make. Its purpose was to move cargo, with no frills. The route that the AV took should be, and appeared to be, carrying it on course to somewhere below their vantage point.

A cursory search of the net would suggest that midair heists of AVs were by no means impossible, but neither were they common. It took a crazy kind of solo to jump off a building hoping to land on what was, in practical terms, a tiny stretch of smooth metal floating in the sky. For most, the choice came down to making a play at either the loading or unloading point. On the other side of the playing field, the corporations operating these flights had long adapted to the ways of mercenaries and rival corps, and considered it standard practice to set strong guard presences at the two locations, always turning the endeavor into a bloody affair.

Jaune planned to skew those statistics a little, today. Without any warning or windup, folded cloth wings quietly appeared on his back. He placed a foot on the parapet.

"Ready, Tattletale?"

"..."

"You could stay back."

Her answer to that suggestion was immediate. "Fuck that. We're pulling a heist. This is, like, my whole thing."

"I figured you'd say that," he said, not unkindly.

Tattletale had insisted on attending the heist. The problem was, her practice time on Fischl's wind glider up until now clocked in at about an hour spread over several days, at a much shorter height. A tall ask, then, to put her a hundred floors up with small room for mistakes. She had been nowhere near ready for this job to spring on her.

Hence, a little creativeness had been called for: he could carry her. They would not fly, or even glide, but a controlled fall was within his capability.

"In that case…" Jaune spread his arms wide, motioning for a hug. "Come on, then. We've got an airship to catch." Noting the clear hesitation remaining on her face, he adjusted his approach. Annoying Blondes had their weaknesses. "You don't want to hear that Escha's team succeeded while we called it quits, do you?"

The reminder swayed her some. He could tell.

Escha, upon hearing that the job did not exactly require their full lineup, had requested for responsibilities of her own. Thus was born the Escha Expeditionary Team. A bit of wheedling had gotten Wakako to hand him a simple courier job that he felt comfortable passing along to the cat plus her two subordinates, Fischl and Bennett. They were pretty much guaranteed to complete it, just like how Tattletale would definitely hear all about their day later.

With great reluctance, the supervillainess scooted over to him, stripping off her jacket and passing it to him for safekeeping. The garment vanished into his Pocket, and she allowed him to hug her body close. To reassure her, he made doubly certain that he had a good grip of her. After all, she was not the only person concerned about this plan. The last thing he wanted was for Tattletale to slip and plummet out of the sky.

"Jaune, you're grabbing my ass."

"Oh now it's a problem."

Tattletale gave a shrug, and wound her arms around his neck. "I was just saying. Carry on."

With a hop, she wrapped her legs around him to lock behind his waist, entrusting all her weight to his frame. Her grip tightened as he shifted closer to the ledge. Far, far, far below them rested the hard pavement, and Tattletale hissed at the brief glimpse she got of it, her nerves wavering.

"Remember, we want to land parallel to its flight path," she told him in a near babble. "That gives us the longest possible runway to bleed off the momentum. If you can match its speed then all the better, otherwise—"

"Hey."

He stopped her.

"I got this," he said, losing his unserious tone. His forehead pressed against hers. "You trust me, right?"

Tattletale bit her lip. Looked to the side. Made a real show of thinking on the question.

A lot of it came down to him eyeballing the needed calculations. Math. Jaune Arc. Yes, it did not bolster confidence.

But then, life was in the doing. Through experience, if nothing else, he had gotten quite good at his landing strategies.

In the end, she left it to him.

The moment finally arrived. The AV weaved between this building and the one opposite, closer to his side in what one might imagine would be the right lane of traffic if there was a dividing line. Fire sparked beneath his boots in anticipation.

Under his breath, Jaune muttered to himself, "Yo ho ho, I'm a sky pirate."

And as Tattletale burst out laughing, he jumped right over the edge. The actual experience of it cut through the girl's worries. She let out a whoop, screaming her thrill in his ear.

The air whipped around them as they plummeted twenty floors down in the blink of an eye. Before Tattletale's sense of terror could reassert itself, the wings of the glider unfurled. The colors of dancing sunlight fluttered in the wind.

With the weight of two people, they hardly slowed down, but the barest ounce of control let Jaune angle in the right direction. Twin jets of flames spewed from the rocket boots, and the air caught beneath the glider wings. The straight drop took on a new vector. Behind the windows, the faces of those who had spotted the falling pair underwent a marked change, the office workers springing out of their chairs to gawk as what they thought was another Night City tragedy turned into an act of pure daring and wonder.

The quickest thinkers saw their trajectory, where that would carry them, and put it together. Jaune read it on their lips, a name loved and feared by Night City in equal measure.

Edgerunners.

He was set to hit the AV on an angle, and his approach could be no finer. A featherlight step brought him in contact with the aerodyne. Wasting little time, a knife appeared in his hand that he slammed into the roof of the aircraft to serve as an anchor. The vehicle was not even hitting 30mph, but after he set her down, Tattletale latched onto the knife handle with a deathgrip, flattening her body to the aerodyne while urging him to get them inside.

Balanced on the aircraft, he summoned his sword to shove it through a gap between the door and the main body. As Tattletale watched on with no small amount of fascination, a light overtook Jaune's vision, his strength growing beyond its limit to pry open the door in one motion using the sword as a lever, in the process breaking the locks and mechanisms to leave the heavy panel dangling on the one remaining hinge. It was then a simple matter to swing inside, with Tattletale in tow screaming at her sudden and disorienting relocation.

They hurtled into the aircraft cabin. Jaune followed through on the momentum to slide across the floor and end up on a knee. Tattletale, meanwhile, managed to turn her graceless flop into a roll that took her upright, a maneuver that surprised no one more than herself.

Her lips twisted into an assured smirk, shown to the whole wide world. Hips cocked, the girl gave an arrogant toss of her long blonde hair.

"Easy-peasy!"

Jaune's tepid gaze went ignored.

"W-Whuh—How—"

The pilot, a man dressed in t-shirt, slacks, and a high-tech helmet with too many eyes, struggled to comprehend their presence. His hands remained on the controls, a complicated mess of switches and dials, to keep the aircraft steady, but his focus was all on them with his mouth flapping open and shut.

As Tattletale looked toward the pilot, she swiped a small button on the side of her visor, activating a preprogrammed effect. The visor grew more opaque, while numbers and letters scrolled down the cyberglass.

What made it cyber? Nobody would say.

She looked good in it, and that seemed to be what mattered. The symbol of an eye emblazoned across her chest, shaded in a subtly different purple, reflected the ambient light to create a shimmering effect, grabbing attention.

"Don't mind us, we're here to recover a few misplaced things," she declared in a chipper tone, shooing the pilot away. "We'll find what we need and delta. Wouldn't even take five minutes."

With the size of the AV, it really would be a quick in and out. The gray interiors of the aircraft held little of note. Two pilot seats, one filled and one not, along with a number of metal containers secured in place with clasps on the floor.

"You can't!" The pilot cried. "It's… You…" His bearing grew firm, the man seeming to snap to rigid attention. "Zetatech Aerodyne Rule 1 dash 3, all Zetatech flights will operate at the sole discretion of Zetatech policy, superseding local, federal, and anarchist laws. No personnel, including officers of the law, may enter, inspect, or otherwise interfere with Zetatech cargo in transit. You are in violation of the aforementioned statute, and are hereby ordered to remove yourself from the craft at once."

Jaune stared askance at the man. "Are you trying to rule-lawyer this whole situation away? 'Remove myself', am I supposed to just stroll off the ledge?" He poked his head out the open door. "I mean, I can survive it, but for anybody else you're basically telling them to go die."

"Zetatech Aerodyne Rule—"

Apparently, yes. Unauthorized intruders were obligated to commit suicide according to company policy, and Jaune had better be prepared for a lawsuit if he did not follow this very reasonable order. Good to know.

"Give him some slack, Jaune," Tattletale snarked. "He has to say all that stuff if he wants to shoot us. Kinda dumb, but it's policy so what can you do?"

The pilot, faced with their continued defiance against all proper laws of gods and men, took one hand off the controls to whip out a handgun at Tattletale.

A blade tickled his throat.

"I wouldn't do that if I were you," Jaune said, sword raised, eyeing the firearm. A stubby thing, called a Lexington if he recalled right. He had sold enough of that model to know that it was not the best gun around. "The two of us are protected against bullets. I doubt you are bladeproof. Just drive, alright?"

The pilot glanced at the front window, where the AV continued to follow its route with minimal input. The man licked his lips.

"The regulations—"

"Says there should be two pilots," Tattletale spoke over him. Her gaze roamed the cabin, absorbing the details, to end up at the back half of the vehicle. "Where's your partner? Did you never have one assigned, or were they laid off and now you have to do the job of two people? It really goes to show that rules are there to be broken."

A flicker of hesitation passed over the pilot's face, and though Tattletale should not be able to see it, a grin grew on her face. She drifted over to the containers, checking out the electronic panels attached to the crates.

"Overlook it this once," Tattletale suggested over her shoulder. "After all, the important thing is to stay safe and alive. You're not doing anything bad," she stressed. "Think of it as… joining the game."

Her honeyed words juxtaposed the sword Jaune held, the carrot to the stick. The handgun wavered. The pilot looked resigned, yet relieved, at the prospect of a peaceful resolution, no matter the form.

Then, his eyes flew wide.

"Wait, no, don't touch that!" he yelled at Tattletale, who had confidently punched in a set of numbers on the container lock. The lid popped open right as an alarm blared throughout the cabin, the sound deafening in the small space.

"What is that?" Jaune asked loudly, a hand on his ear.

Tattletale, outraged, kicked the container she opened. "The stupid thing is set to go off on any attempt to put the password, not only when you put in the wrong one! Dammit!"

"Now that's just unsporting," he commiserated.

Suddenly, the alarm cut out. There was an electronic chime. The front window grew staticky, with a screen then appearing on the glass to show the head and shoulders of an older man with salt-and-pepper hair.

The scowling visage roared, "What the hell is going on here?"

"S-Sir!" The pilot quailed. "I was—"

"Smith, you have exactly ten seconds to explain yourself, and you had better pray I don't fire you on the spot!"

Whatever threat Jaune posed to the pilot, it had nothing on the man on the screen. The pilot was near blubbering. Jaune mentally filed the new person as a bigshot, and squinted to make out the title on the nametag.

"Wait a minute, are you his manager?" Tattletale asked, her head popping over his shoulder. She began snickering. "Oh my god, you are!"

A small bigshot, then. The guy a person complained to about the bad service.

Tattletale gave the screen a dismissive wave. "Yeah, we can ignore him. He talks big but he's, like, two rungs from the bottom on the corporate ladder. Nobody important. Help me carry this stuff, Jaune."

"Sure thing," he said, putting the matter behind him.

The clear lack of deference seemed to set the manager off, the man launching into a tirade about company policies and their violations thereof, which further convinced Jaune to tune him out. As a courtesy to the pilot, he flicked his sword toward the handgun, slicing it in half. Hopefully, this would make it hard for the pilot to catch flak, given that he had tried to subdue the intruders and was outmatched.

Clang. Clang. The AV lurched, throwing everybody off-balance. Tattletale braced against a container, while Jaune grabbed one of the handles hanging off the aircraft's wall.

"What is it now?" he asked, to nobody in particular.

The answer arrived in the short, twin-tailed package of Rebecca the edgerunner. The girl swung into the opening Jaune made, toting a shotgun. A loud boom resounded as she fired a round in the ceiling of the vehicle, blasting a bunch of holes in the metal.

"Okay, gonks!" she gleefully shouted in a very strange, exaggerated dialect. "Hands up, cuz I'm da captain now—Bweh!"

A small figure flew out of the AV, and out of sight, trailed only by a fading "Oh fuuuuu—!"

David Martinez ducked his head upside-down into the cabin, mouth agape in horror. He found Jaune with his foot still raised.

Jaune gave a shrug. "Her or me."

Faster than he could follow, the edgerunner now brandished a handcannon, one that he had already fired. A bullet hit Jaune between the eyes to knock him dizzy. A second struck his side, having tried to get at Tattletale who he hid with his frame.

A third splattered the pilot's brain across the window and control board. The aerodyne began to list, lurching harder as Martinez jumped off into thin air, diving after his teammate.

Jaune could not catch what happened to the other boy, by this time already rushing toward the front. He grimaced at the grisly sight of the pilot. There was no saving him.

"Not how I saw it go down," he muttered in apology, for all the good that it did the dead man who could not hear him. His eyes then scanned over the controls, and at where the AV was currently heading after being knocked off course.

The roads of Night City stretched out before him. Underpasses, overpasses, the complicated network resembled a ball of tangled strings. Typical of the locals, the cars drove like maniacs. There were… a lot of cars.

"Tattletale! Can you make sense of this?" he called out. The girl stumbled over the uneven footing to join him.

"Oh, ew!"

Daintily picking her way forward, Tattletale dropped into the copilot seat where she tried her best to observe the dead pilot's side of the controls without getting sick. Her hands hovered for a bit atop the many buttons and knobs.

"Should be this," she flicked a switch. A joystick extended from a compartment. "And these." Three buttons were hit in succession, after which she pulled back on the joystick. The floor of the cabin drew even. "Uh-oh," Tattletale then blurted out, to set off his every warning bell.

"...What do you mean, 'uh-oh'?"

"Everything just seized up." Tattletale shut her eyes as the AV banked hard toward the ground, forcing Jaune to grip the headrest to stay upright. "Oh, that's real funny. Perfect. Fucking asshole."

That clued him in, and Jaune snapped his head up to glare at the screen that still broadcasted the manager. The man's impassive face stared right back.

"Do you mind?" Jaune asked through gritted teeth, sweeping a hand at the dashboard. When the expression changed not one iota, his tone grew a touch more… annoyed. "It's going to hit the highway."

The manager finally cracked a smile, satisfaction written clear across it. He took the time to adjust his suit's jacket, sitting back in his chair.

"That certainly sounds like a problem. For you, that is. The hijacker clause in our insurance policy covers this eventuality. I would have to check, but I do believe the compensation amount outweighs the value of both that AV model and its inventory by a multiple of… My word, I might even see a bonus come from this." The man nodded to Jaune. "Truly, thank you."

The screen winked out, leaving Jaune's reflection.

"That complete, utter—" He stopped, shaking off the rising anger to speak in a rush. "Tattletale, can we send a message to evacuate the people down there?"

"We have a minute at best," she pointed out. "No way it'd happen, even if they give me the time of day. Bail?"

"No! Well, yes, but before that there has to be something… we can… oh." He stared at the dead pilot. "Ohhh."

Tattletale slapped a hand over her eyes. "Obvious answer is obvious." She climbed out of the copilot seat, holding tightly onto him to stay in contact. "Grab the containers, first. No need to be subtle anymore."

"On it."

With a last look at the pilot, he moved at speed toward the back with Tattletale in tow, his hands held outward. They gently brushed over the metal crates, which one by one vanished into thin air.

Once done, he withdrew a device from the pocket of his pants, passing it to Tattletale. As she navigated through the menus, he gathered her in his arms.

"Ready?" she asked.

He slapped his hand on the side of the AV. "Ready."

Seconds from hitting the highway, the aerodyne blinked out of existence. The only trace of it was a boy and a girl hanging in midair, borne on a set of wings. Below, people looked up from their cars, some still screaming because they had been about to die.

The pilot's remains slammed into the windshields of one of the cars, cracking the glass.

Jaune winced. Hu Tao... was going to get some work from him.



-o-
​


Later, hours later, the question occurred to them.

"What did we get, anyway?" asked Tattletale.

Jaune mentally pinged his Pocket, the shapes of the many new objects inside flashing by his mind.

"Huh," was all he said.

He withdrew one of the items for study, before putting it on his companion's head.

Tattletale's eyes went up to the high-tech headphones she now wore and the two feline, almost fox-like, ears protruding from the top.

"Huh," she echoed.

There was a little logo stenciled on the side of the headphones.

Danger Gal.
