#6,650

Chapter 76: Just Another Night City Level Up
​


His hand shook, an accident that could happen to anyone.

The pair of chopsticks David was holding slipped out of his grip. Luckily, his fumbling lunge for the utensils managed to recover them before they fell over the side of the ripperchair, saving them from coming in contact with the blood-streaked floor. Most of it was his, but still. Ick.

He sat up again, and found himself looking into Lucy's stiff, anxious face. His girl was halfway out of her seat, her hands reaching forward.

She worried too much. But then, he did worry her too much.

"I'm fine, Luce," he said with a crooked smile, the one she liked. "Not used to eating with one arm, that's all. Doc will take care of it soon enough."

The chair creaked under him as he leaned back. It barely held his weight. The thing should have been replaced ages ago, he kept telling Doc, bound for the great heavenly garbage heap outside Night City. A medical tray on a stand next to the chair served as David's dining table. Its awkward position forced him to twist his body further than was comfortable.

With the chopsticks, he picked up strands of noodles from the instant ramen cup, blowing to cool them before gulping down the lot. Lucy watched him eat, her chin between her hands. The TV over by the wall of the dingy basement that Doc called a clinic filled in for the lack of conversation.

"It's a bird, it's an aerodyne, no, it's just another Night City jumper. Yaaawn, amiright? What you might find hard to believe is that this one didn't go splat on the pavement. Walls are just roads, my viewers—"

He listened with half an ear, seeing no need for the details when he had been there in person. They mentioned a name. Someone died at the scene.

His hand shook.

"—continues unabated with smoke visible from all across the city. Thus far, no winner had stepped forward with the so-called 'furred feline' reportedly seen out and about in Reconciliation Park. If you're in the mood for a scavenger hunt, head up there today and join the fun! Don't forget your guns!"

David tuned out the program to scarf down the last half of his cup of ramen. Just as he was slurping up the dregs of the salty broth, he heard the door at the top of the steps leading down here squeak open. Familiar footfalls announced the return of Rebecca and Kiwi from their trip to the vending machine, the shorter of the pair bringing back another glorious serving of the food of the gods. Said teammate proceeded to fuss over him with the same kind of spirit Lucy possess, popping the lid and pouring in the Real* Moisture pack for him like he was a baby that needed spoon-feeding. Lucy made a sneaky play for his chopsticks, intending that very act. A soft smile, gone all too soon, passed her lips as he hid the two sticks behind his back.

Kiwi, meanwhile, stalked over to a low shelf so that she could lean on it and act surly.

"Here you go, hero~" Rebecca stressed the last bit, sweet as sugar, as she moved to his side. She hadn't stopped calling him that since their little escapade. To be honest, it was kinda embarrassing. Sent chills up his spine every time. After setting down the food, she placed her head near his chest to listen hard for his heartbeat.

Thumpthump. Thumpthump.

"It sounds better now… I think?" she said, not very certain. "Lucy, c'mere and check this gonk out."

He would have thrown a quip back at her for that, something witty, but his stomach rumbled to tell him that he had better start eating or there would be trouble. There was a lot of energy to replenish. Chipping in took its pound of flesh.

Worth it, of course, and not because it gave him an excuse to pig out on cup noodles. Every ounce the scalpel carved away had put more in, and made him better. As he ate, power thrummed under his skin. It felt like a furnace inside him. He had never felt so alive as when blood pumped through his second heart.

Heh. Since he needed repairs and was going to get cut open anyway, why not put in more work, right?

Even Lucy couldn't argue that. Hell, once she heard what he wanted, she had grown downright eager to see it done. She thought this stuff would help keep him living, and so didn't give him those sad eyes.

They were on adjacent pages, then, if not the exact same one.

A lot of theories floated on the net when it came to the Sandevistan. Nothing captured the people's imagination quite like that nifty piece of chrome (except for cyberdecks, but netrunners were weirdos about it). For years, people dedicated pages after pages to its limitations, and how to eke out another second in the timeless world of accelerated perception. Everybody had their own opinion on what chrome might complement the piece, not to mention the ones who advocated for meditation or mystical breathing techniques or what have you. A good dozen lists of 'builds' existed that their owners swore should work if it was ever put in practice. Some of those ideas had… inspired David.

Of course, his Sandevistan was a prototype for a reason. Other people didn't push their body like this, and didn't have as much room to work with. What went once for others went double, triple for him. It forced, and allowed, him to modify his approach. When people pointed out that the Sandy duration was partly bottlenecked by oxygen intake, and that a set of Synthlungs could only get so efficient as long as the other parts of a man stayed 'ganic, he figured it was a better fit to install a whole Second Heart cyberware rather than a simple Blood Pump. And then he put in the Blood Pump as a backup, too, because both of them working together sounded perfect for what he had in mind.

Ramp up, ramp up, get that blood flowing beyond the limits, oxygen pumping to the max, his limbs ready to work, then hit the switch to make him go.

Admittedly, all theory. Machine specs and projections from gonks on dodgy message boards, half of them pretending they had speedware, the other half pretending they did not. Some of the models they discussed had been taken out of production years ago, bicycles compared to his Quadra muscle car of a Sandy. The future was now, and trying it out was gonna be fan-fucking-tastic.

"Hey, David," Kiwi suddenly called out, to make his head jerk up and waking him from his daydreams. "Are we going to talk about what happened or what?"

Before he could ask what she meant, Lucy cut in between them, a little too quick to leap from her chair. "You mean the disappearing AV mystery? God, you wouldn't believe how crazy some of the arguments have gotten in the forums—"

"No," Kiwi said, sounding quite, quite blunt. "I'm referring to the dead pilot with his head blown off. We all heard the gunshots over the comms, even with Rebecca shouting in our ears."

"Fuck you, I was falling like a bajillion floors straight to the ground!" Rebecca flipped Kiwi off.

Kiwi deigned the gesture not worth responding to beyond a withering look, after which she directed her attention again to David. Her eyes had narrowed to two thin, suspicious lines.

"Was it him that did it?" she pressed, no need to ask who. The electronic twang created by her voice assistance cyberware added a dryness David found difficult to tell was intended or not.

He fidgeted, too aware that even Lucy and Rebecca were waiting for his answer, despite them arraying themselves to side with him over their other teammate. Nor was he blind to the fact that Kiwi had given him an out. He could push the blame onto the corpo and his joytoy.

"No, it was…" His hearts seized up. "It was me."

The room fell quiet for a beat. Everybody was looking at him, he could feel their eyes prickling on his skin.

Kiwi broke the somber moment. "Knew it hadn't been him."

Lucy bristled.

"The pilot was a threat. David did what he had to do." She alternated her gaze between Rebecca and Kiwi, trying to appear firm. His Lucy had her habits, though. She couldn't hide her anxiety from him. "Look, it was better that he at least tried something to stop Johnny and his crew from taking the AV, instead of nothing at all. We're mercs. Remember what Maine always said? Our reputation matters."

"Y-Yeah!" Rebecca chimed in. "And I kinda needed the dummy to hurry up back there, so I'm pretty damn grateful." She shot Kiwi a weak glare, her heart not in it.

They were on his side. He knew that. He loved that. The problem was…

The problem was Kiwi looking so fucking satisfied. The netrunner stood there with her arms crossed, staring at him, not even trying to hide the smug superiority. The gall, to judge him when she always stayed far back from the action. She didn't get that he had to do it. He had to!

He had to?

His hand shook. Then, and now.

"—could stand to show a little more basic empathy," Lucy was admonishing Kiwi.

Kiwi's shoulders moved up an inch, then back down. Placid eyes swept to the side, at the TV. "He screwed up. He should tell us why. End of story."

The sudden bout of rage quelled, leaving him strangely empty. David couldn't muster the energy to retort, and so busied with his food, louder than was polite to make it clear he was taking a break from his part in the conversation. Once the empty styrofoam cup hit the table, he forced the topic to steer down more comfortable avenues.

"New gig's waiting for us," he said.

Rebecca, who he already informed alongside Lucy, seized on the subject. "Yo, about that. I was hoping to check with you on something."

"Shoot. But not literally."

Always had to specify, with Rebecca.

Rebecca nodded. "Right, so… What's Faraday playing at? Protection? Guarding? We don't do that crap."

"For the money he's paying? We definitely will."

"Excuse me," Kiwi said, raising a hand. "Mind starting from the beginning?"

David shifted to a better position to talk. "You weren't there when I got the call. Faraday has a client that wants us to run security. They have a package bogged down mid-transit. We'll sit on it until they arrange a pickup."

"Sounds corpo," Kiwi stated the obvious. "What's in the package?"

He wasn't the only person to catch the look on her face, but he spoke for them all. "Kiwi, don't even think about it," he warned. "We don't fuck with our fixer, we don't fuck with our client. They're paying us to keep the shipment safe. It's not on us to check what's inside."

Kiwi gave him an unrepentant shrug. "No harm in looking," she said, already pulling a tablet from inside her coat to no doubt ferret out all she could.

That curiosity was really going to get her in trouble someday. To distract her, he sent the deets on the job. Her eyes flashed blue, the data package received then redirected to her tablet. She swiped on the screen.

"Damn."

Kiwi delivered the remark in monotone, which understated it a fair bit. David nodded. Damn, indeed.

"Yup. Faraday's having us set up in a decommissioned factory. It used to have big contracts with Arasaka before the Fourth Corporate War or something, until that stint with Arasaka getting kicked off the continent. They left their security systems intact."

Even with that, he had had to spend a good ten minutes convincing Lucy that they were not working for the Japanese conglomerate. And if they were, they had just been handed a blank check to wreck the building. She really liked the second bit.

He continued. "The factory did a bunch of hush-hush stuff, apparently, with the protections to match. Faraday had a netrunner grab the codes for us to activate the defenses."

Kiwi was deep into the documents. "Turrets, drones—ooh, a mech."

'What?" Rebecca piped up, as eager as David was when he caught that detail. She vacated her seat in a blink, rushing over to Kiwi where she stood on tiptoes to catch a glimpse of the screen. "Whoa, you weren't kidding! Do they even need us?"

Kiwi explained, "The thing's designed for a pilot—"

"Dibs," Rebecca said at once.

"Lucy or Kiwi will take that job," David corrected. "The exoskeleton is meant for moving cargo, so it can't hold a gun. I'd rather rely on you with your shotty, and keep the robot back in case we have to relocate the shipment. It's a big shipment." Which would also give an excuse for him to put a suit of armor between Lucy (or Kiwi, but he was mostly concerned with Lucy) and anybody sniffing around.

Rebecca was beaming.

"Does make me wonder what all this is for," Kiwi remarked.

"Faraday told me he didn't know for sure, but he expects people to crash the party the longer it goes on, and doesn't think the low-leveled mercs he had stationed there would cut it," David replied. "We'll prepare for the usual Watson suspects. Scav gangs, Maelstrom, corpo soldiers..." A dark look crossed his expression. "But I have a feeling in my gut that it won't be so simple."

He studied his teammates, from one face to another, and he liked what he saw there. Lucy clenched her hands in front of her chest and returned his look with a steady gaze; she was with him, all the way. Rebecca also seemed raring to go another round against a certain team of wannabe mercs, playing with one of her guns that she had pulled out from inside her oversized jacket. Kiwi… Okay, maybe Kiwi's reaction was a bit different from the others, but she knew to be professional on the job.

A little later, a new set of footsteps rang out on the concrete staircase leading to the basement. David and his team were a few minutes into planning their approach to the gig, going over positions and chokepoints, when Doc entered the room. Someday, the ripperdoc would tell David his name, and David would probably default to calling him Doc anyway out of habit, a real tearjerker moment for the movies. For now, whatever they had was working well enough, especially when the man carried with him a long, sleek cyberarm. Unlike the usual fares he stocked, this one gleamed with a polished sheen.

"Oh, preem, Doc!" David praised, sitting up straight. "Now that's what I'm talking about!"

He was wondering where the guy went for him to be away so long. His missing arm had been itching something fierce. Now that he was here, maybe Doc would finally connect the nerves running from his spine to his feet that'd let him hop off this chair for five minutes.

Had anybody ever noted in the specs that a set of Fortified Ankles could counteract a lot of force in a pinch, but turn brittle as glass as a result? Or that ramming an arm into the side of a building and letting it scrape to generate friction would work up to a point, and also grind it down to a bloody stump? Yeah well, he learned that stuff firsthand.

God, he didn't even mean to make that pun.

In contrast to David's enthusiasm, the ripperdoc merely spat a gob of spit right onto the floor. It splattered on the tiles, making the place a little cleaner.

"If you have any sense, you wouldn'ta be saying that," the man sneered, but in a friendly(?) way. Doc sneered at everybody. The backalley surgeon smoothed his goatee, observing David from head to toe before indicating the cyberarm he was holding. "Listen, Davey. How about you slow down on this one, eh? Make sure it's the model you want. The load—"

David laughed, unsurprised. "Come on, Doc, are you seriously gonna try to jack the price higher after you strapped the armless man to your chair? It's always 'the load' with you."

A soft hand caressed his shoulder, rubbing soothingly to calm him down. Lucy pecked him on the cheek as he looked at her.

"David, hang on, it's fine. We can hear what he has to say, can't we? You don't have to follow his advice but he's done this for a long time." She sniffed in disdain at their surroundings. "Even if your associate could use work. And integrity. And ethics."

"Ah, blow it outta your ears, girlie," Doc shot back, before leering. "Or better yet, you can blow…" His voice trailed off as he looked beyond her toward David. A bead of sweat dropped down his cheek. "Never mind, then."

David snorted. "Stay classy, Doc."

It wasn't quite a warning, but close. The man raised his arms—both the ones attached to him, and the cyberarm—in surrender with a roll of his eyes.

"I musta removed your sense of humor at some point, 'cause you can't take a joke no more," Doc grumbled under his breath, edging around them.

By then, Lucy had ceased paying attention to the ripperdoc, turning back to David. Perhaps she saw something in his eyes, because her smile faded. He quickly grabbed her hand, and now was his turn to run his thumb in circles on her skin.

"I get it, Lucy. You think I'm going too hard. And yeah, it looks like a lot, but you have to remember that I lost three pieces of cyberware," he explained. "Those will just be replacements. I'm really only up by two. The Second Heart and Blood Pump." He jerked his head at Doc. "And he knows damn well that's no problem for me. You don't have to worry."

Off to the side, Doc scoffed. The man hooked the metal arm on one of the racks set near the ripperchair, and stood there for a little while, seeming lost in thought. A hand went up to hold his forehead, pinching and massaging them. Then, Doc came to a decision, and walked over to David while breathing out an exasperated sigh.

"Davey, gonk, it don't work like that." He tapped David on the foot, knee, stomach, chest, and nose in quick succession. "You are up a few dozen pieces a' chrome. A fuckton this week alone. It never go away. You lose the last arm? Whoop-de-doo. Your flesh, your nerves, they don't understand this new arm. As far as your body know, you put in an arm and now you put in another arm. Like a fucking messed-up octopus."

"Sooo, what will all the new chrome today do to the load?" Rebecca asked from over by Kiwi, no longer looking very confident about this.

"Who the fuck knows," was Doc's blunt answer.

To that…

Well, to that David could only grin, because it sounded like a challenge.

"I can take it, Doc. I'm built different."

His hand shook, he was so excited.

A car roared down the desert road under the bright sunshine, a cloud of dust whipping up in its wake.

The scenery passed by in a homogeneous blur, rolling plains of scrubs and sand with the occasional pit stop. The road begged for maintenance, cracked in places, but the car's shock absorbers handled that like a dream.

"Aaaaaahahaha! Go faster!" cried the thrilled voice of a young girl, and she whooped in joy as Jaune stepped harder on the pedal to grant that very wish.

Uncaring of danger, Fischl sat on the open window of the passenger side, hanging onto the car for balance as she tilted back her head to bask in the warm day. Her long blonde hair streamed behind her, a tousled mess after almost an hour into their highway drive. The destination they had been aiming for lay on the outskirts of town, way back there, but one look at the open road beyond the city, and adventure had beckoned with its siren call.

As the driver, Jaune couldn't stick his head out the window, which was a shame. Still, with the window rolled down and a catchy as hell tune playing on the radio, he was enjoying his time. He kept one hand on the wheel, the other hanging off the side of the car.

Tucked between him and Fischl, Oz the raven called out, "I am glad you are feeling better, milady, but perhaps we should slow down? A fall could be disastrous."

"Whaaaat?" Fischl called back, unable to hear over the wind.

The bird heaved a sigh, and Jaune switched hands on the wheel to reach over to pat him on the back. It left a tingling sensation dancing on his fingers afterward.

"Oh, let her have her fun, Oz."

At the start of the drive, Fischl had been rather sulky. From what he gathered, it had to do with Bennett and Hu Tao heading off without her, talking about fire this and fire that—a subject the zappy electric girl could only contribute to in a limited capacity. Jaune had yet to mention to her that Lisa was taking them to a police seminar course on fires, their dangers, and how to commit arson in a responsible manner. Something about learning caution. It really was not as glamorous an adventure as she seemed to think.

Jaune looked to the passenger side, where Fischl continued to scream and laugh with carefree abandon, waving to every car that they happened to pass by.

Yeah, she got over it.

A while later, they pulled into a parking lot of a bustling car shop, where they continued sitting in the sedan a little longer in order to sing along with the song that was playing on the radio. Even Oz got in on it. "...I don't wanna kno~ow!" they finished the final line in chorus.

The shop itself was loud and unsafe, with a whole lot of junk parts lying around to trip over. Sparks flew as welders worked, sizzling on a pockmarked floor. Still, the cool shade of the interior space was a welcomed reprieve after their time in the sunshine. Jaune strode past the various ongoings, ignoring the people huddling together and pointing him out to their friends. Beside him, Fischl turned her head every which way to take in the sights while Oz perched on her shoulder, picking at her windswept hair with its beak to neaten them.

A corner of the room was taken up by other projects beside the cars. Small machinery and neon signs, mostly. Jaune figured that place would be what he was looking for, and headed over.

The grouchy old man there reminded him of Wakako.

"This is what you waste my time on?" The old man, the owner of the shop, waved his hand at the shield lying on the table. Specifically, at a fault in the mechanism visible from the back of the shield. Warped by the heat of a laser beam produced a Valkyria's fiery Aura, the metal along what should have been a smooth ridge had grown misshapen to lock the gears tight.

"So you can fix it, then?" Jaune asked hopefully. He got a roll of the eyes for the question.

"Bah! Are your muscles for show?" the man mocked. "Back in my day, we handled crap like this ourselves. Only when it's in ten different pieces with half the screws missing, and only then, do we bother somebody else. Kids these days, I swear." As he complained, the old man grabbed a hammer and a chisel.

Jaune tried to interrupt, raising his hands. "Whoa, hang on. That's not going to work!"

His warning went ignored. The old man scoffed, turning back to the mechashift shield half of Crocea Mors.

"What good is buying a fancy toy if all you can do is break it? Nothing, that's what. The hell even is this thing anyway? Half of it doesn't make a lick of sense."

The man elbowed Jaune back to get some room, sending him a glare. For his age, the shop owner kept in scarily good shape, and an arm bulging with corded muscles rose high in the air with the hammer in its grip. It came down in a swift, unhesitating motion.

*CLANG*

"Jesus—!"

As he awkwardly scratched his cheek, Jaune watched the old man scream a slew of invective through clenched teeth. The hammer lay on the floor, the chisel bent in half, with the old man holding a shaking and reddened hand. The spot on the shield he had tried to beat flat experienced zero changes to its shape.

"I warned you," Jaune said, receiving an admonishing look from Fischl who was helping to soothe the old man.

"What is that thing made of, kid!?"

"Some decent steel, some magical ores. The usual stuff." He didn't bother hiding it, because...

"Ugh, you are just reeking of corpo bullshit. This a new product coming out? A prototype, maybe? Ah, whatever. I'll crack it."

"I… would rather you didn't? I brought it here to have it repaired, you know."

"Shut up and follow me, wiseass."

The owner of the shop brought them to a backroom, a big space equipped with heavy machinery. A few, he recognized. His world had them. Others looked more at home in sci-fi comics, with robotic arms tipped with saw blades, drills, and other miscellaneous functions. One by one, they awoke with the flip of a switch.

"The price I quoted you?" The old man secured the shield onto a bench with clamps, and strapped a set of goggles over his eyes. "I'm tripling that—"

"Sure thing." Money was no object if it could put his shield to rights. He loved that thing.

"For a start," the old man finished the sentence. "Any of my stuff wears out on this mystery metal of yours and you'll be paying for that, too. They weren't meant for moon rocks or whatever."

Jaune considered the state of his wallet, and the expensive-looking equipment. He cringed hard, but ultimately nodded.

"I'll take that bet."

A clanking cacophony soon filled the workshop, along with curses and wails. Broken bits of tools began to litter the floor. Jaune's bill ticked upward at a steady pace.

To get his mind away from the looming expenditure, Jaune brought his companions out to the back of the building, past the fences. A quick talk with one of the employees on break, plus money to grease the grease monkey's palm, had provided him with a set of targets crafted from scrap metal and painted with concentric circles. He set them at different distances out in the sandy waste they called the Badlands.

"Alright, that should be good enough," Jaune said after planting the last one and returning to the others. "Fischl, I leave myself in your hands."

The girl preened, chin tilted up and hands on her hips. She seemed quite taken with the idea of being the teacher this time around.

"Why certainly," she said, tossing her hair with a flick of her hand, "and I must commend you for your keen wisdom. Magic is only as powerful as its practitioner, and relying upon its whimsy an inevitably doomed foolishness. The boon of felicity oft wears thin at the most inconvenient of times. True skill shall guide you much further."

Jaune snapped a salute. "Yes, ma'am!"

Fischl squirmed, delighted.

"A-Ahem. In any case, you have done well to come to me. In all the lands, ne'er would you find another legendary marksman as I." She walked to the side, giving him plenty of space. "Let us commence with a trial. Fear not, for I shan't judge you harshly." She pointed at the furthest target, took another look at him, then changed her mind and moved it over to one of the easier ones. "Bring forth thy weapon of choice, and empty its quiver into the target over yonder. Do not use your so-called 'marksmanship' magic."

Heeding the order, Jaune whipped out his hand. A double-action revolver with a proper heft to it materialized, and he let it sing.

Blam, blam, blam, blamblam, blam!

"Heh."

The revolver spun in lazy circles, twirled around his index finger. Jaune closed his eyes, a satisfied smile on his lips.

Fischl piped up from her spot, ""My word! Oz, doth mine eyes deceive me?"

"No, Mein Fräulein. It has indeed, as they say, struck the eye of the bull."

"How splendid, Jaune! Why, I could not have done it better myself!" Then, after a beat. "A shame about the other five bolts…"

Yeah. Sigh.

"You don't have to say it. I wanted to ask you for tips on leading my shots, but it's looking like I have more problems than that."

Fischl held her chin in thought. "Well…" The girl coaxed him into a shooting stance, walking around and around him to study his form. "I do not understand much of this 'gonne' thing you use, so I can scarcely comment on the proper technique." She stopped before him. "That said, what I did see was a lack of rhythm."

"Rhythm?" He cocked his head.

"Yes. Here, allow me to demonstrate."

An ornate bow resembling a raven's dark wings appeared in her hands, and she turned to face the targets. With a deep breath, Fischl set into motion. Like always, she moved like no archer Jaune had ever seen.

A ballet twirl, and the bow drew back, letting loose. The arrow punctured the closest target, dead center on the bullet hole Jaune made. Her heels then slid apart, with Fischl dropping to a knee with one leg stretched forward. At the lowest point, the bowstring tugged back and snapped with a melodic note, almost like a harpstring. An arrow found its way to the second target. Fischl was already up in the air with a hop. Her body rotated a full circle, bow drawn. The bow swept from left to right, and the moment the arrowhead lined up with the furthest bullseye, she let it fly. Thwack, the distant sound reached them.

Fischl landed on the ground to a wave of applause, and after dismissing her bow she curtsied in the direction of Jaune and Oz. A charming smile lit up her face.

"Rhythm," she said. "We stand on a stage, and each battle is our performance. This is the way I have learned my craft." Her hands fidgeted together as she struggled to find the words to explain herself better.

"You barely seem to be aiming," Jaune observed. "Are you sure you aren't using magic?"

"I assure you, it is a result of tireless practice," Oz chimed in. "Milady was very insistent that her archery must look as impressive as possible to an audience."

"Oz, cease thy prattling!" Fischl squeaked, red creeping onto her cheeks.

Haltingly, the girl expressed to him how the dance-like movements served their purpose, allowing her just the right amount of time to calculate the variables that went into shooting an arrow, without overthinking it. The swiftness of the dance keyed her to certain shooting positions, whose short window forced her to commit, no chance to second–guess. In all, they formed an artificial mix of pressures to stimulate action, and as a result brought about maximum focus. She deliberately made things more difficult as part of her approach to archery.

Confidence lay at its core. Fischl moved as a dancer on a stage, and so believed she was a dancer on a stage. She centered herself through the performance.

Jaune wasn't about to do anything like that, the beginner that he was, but it did give him a point to start from. He spent the next hour under Fischl's guidance, learning the principles of shooting as taught by a princess and her bird. A curriculum he suspected would not be found in any official program or school of thought.

He managed to clip a target with two bullets. It might have been an accident.

And then, it was his turn to be the teacher.

"Both hands stay on the gun, alright? It isn't the same as with a bow," he said to his student as she aimed down the sights of the revolver. Her stance was probably far from picture-perfect, considering he wasn't that sure on what a correct gun-handling stance looked like, but it served well enough. Aura meant that recoil factored a little less in the equation unless they were talking about a proper, two-handed cannon of a rifle.

Fischl had flipped up her eyepatch to unleash her forbidden eye. It should see her learning speed improve manifolds, from the explanation he got. Not to mention a better aim due to what she called acute prescience, in her words a metaphysical ability inherent to her bloodline that lets her extrapolate the myriad paths a projectile might take several seconds into the future.

It sounded like aiming, but apparently was not.

Blam!

The bullet pinged off a target.

"YES!" Fischl cheered, throwing her hands in the air. "I did it! Jaune, did you see!? I got it on the first try!"

"Good shot," he praised. "It looks like your skill at archery is translating well to this. How did the gun feel? Not too strange?"

The girl shook her head, still bouncing on her heels and over the moon.

"It's a little heavy, and I can't help but sense an anger harbored within this metal shell, but I am confident I can bind the 'gonne' to my will. Soon, you shall watch me 'lay down fire' and 'pop a cap' with the best of them!"

"...Where did you learn those phrases?"

"On the streets. Why?"

Fischl seemed to be taking to modern life quickly. That was good, he supposed.

"Although… these guns are very loud, aren't they?" Fischl said with a small frown, rubbing an ear.

Jaune smacked a hand to his forehead. "Oh, right. So, you're probably going to get used to that. I did. Until then, give this a try."

With a gesture, a set of headphones popped into existence, and he placed it on her head.

Fischl blinked at him, before her eyes trailed upward.

"I have a bunch of these, and I've no idea what to do with them. Take one."

The cat ears atop Fischl's head twitched.


Author's Notes: Yeah, sure, that's totally how the Sandevistan works and David shooting up his veins with that much blood and accelerating them isn't going to backfire in any way.
.
And in Brockton Bay, Vista the hero whined and raged, for she sensed that somewhere out there a responsible adult had just handed a gun to a little blonde girl, and that girl wasn't her.

#6,804

Chapter 77: Just Another Night City No Good End
​


An arrow made of light arced across the field.

It struck a security turret installed at the entrance of a sprawling, windowless complex set in an industrial park that had seen better days. Unable to pierce the metal plating, it did nothing to stop the contraption from spewing bullets at the trespassers huddled behind a low wall. That was, until the arrow exploded in a shower of electrifying sparks that wreaked havoc all throughout the mechanical device's internals. A hiss, a soft pop, and the turret fell dead with little fanfare, hanging limply from the ceiling as it shared in the fate of its brothers.

Fischl might have struck a pose at this point, surely a cool one… but unfortunately for her, half her audience were already in motion. Jaune and Bennett raced across the yard toward the building's entrance. The exterior of the place was nothing to write home about, worn down and surrounded by empty lots that saw not a single sign of life. Its doors laid wide open, a trap if Jaune ever saw one.

He dove straight into it. Bennett followed half a step behind. Jaune had the Red Rook shield strapped to his arm while the other boy wielded the shield to Crocea Mors, which provided him better protection than his wooden buckler. They entered a large room with a squat ceiling, barren save for a counter on the opposite side and a few concrete pillars. Of the light fixtures, one remained working, down to its last leg with a flickering bulb. Something moved in the gloom.

"Left," Jaune called out.

"Right!" Bennett answered.

They peeled off to their respective directions, with Jaune shaking his head at the obvious mistake Bennett just committed. Always, always go left. He had no time to admonish the other boy, as not a second later bullets slammed into the floor where they had previously stood. They each found cover behind one of the concrete pillars.

Above them, cameras tracked their progress. The outside, too, had been lousy with them. Stealth had gone out the window since minute one due to that. The question on Jaune's mind now was, who looked back at him from the other side? He could practically feel the hostile, hateful gaze behind the lens watching his every move.

A flash of movement occurred at the corner of his eye. He whipped around, but by that point, a certain felyne hitching a ride on his back had sprung into action, leaping through the air to latch onto the figure.

"Jaune! It's one of those weird-weird people!" the cat reported after getting a closer look.

"A robot," he corrected, kicking out to tilt the muzzle of the gun that the humanoid robot was holding toward the ceiling. "It's just a toy. Have fun, Escha!"

With a smack of her boomerang, the head of the mechanical soldier snapped to the side. Escha then went to town on the unliving foe. A distance away, Bennett was dispatching his own robot.

Jaune left them to it, tilting his chin down to speak into the phone hanging off his neck, needing to shout as streams of bullets crashed against the pillar at his back. "Tattletale, we're in the lobby. You can start moving up but take care, alright?" He peeked out of cover, and quickly pulled back his head as concrete shattered under a spray of lead. "A squad of robots is heading for us, and there were two waiting next to the door to shoot anybody coming in."

The voice of his partner came over the line, sounding all too smug. "An ambush? That sounds too sophisticated for an automated defense system. Another fixer must have managed to pull together a guard detail for the cargo. I told you so."

"Excuse me, did I disagree when you brought it up back then?" he retorted good-naturedly. Most would find his attitude too chipper for the situation he was in. "Anyway, the turrets have a clear sight of the door, so I'll take care of them—"

"Up, bup, bup. Hold it, mister!" Tattletale scolded. "Remember your role. Leave the right person to do the right job. Fischl, go."

Time passed. The pillar behind him slowly turned from a thick, heavy column to a skinny stick ready to collapse. Jaune hummed a tune under his breath as he waited, the clanking footsteps of the robots growing ever louder.

He then heard Tattletale's tinny voice coming over the phone, as if she was holding a conversation with someone else.

"Maybe you can, I dunno, shorten the chant? Just a little? No rush or anything."

"Oh shoot, is that what Fischl is doing?" he asked. "You really should have put her on speakers so we don't miss it."

An arrow crackling with electricity lanced past the entrance to punctuate the statement. One of the turrets promptly fried from the inside, while Fischl's back hit the pillar next to Bennett. She had a new arrow nocked in her bow. Oz flew into the room, weaving around the pillars to present a difficult target, and that was all the distraction she needed to take out the second turret with another shocking blast. Jaune saw his opening to charge out of cover, [Third Arm] sending him right into the robots' midst. They fell in short order, sliced to pieces.

The door at the far end slid open, and a new squad trooped in with guns blazing. The bottom edge of his shield hit the ground, with him hunkering behind it to weather the hail of bullets.

"Oz," he yelled. "Divebomb them for me!"

None of the robots aimed for the raven. Unlike the turrets, their targeting program or however they determined a threat seemed to not yet register the bird as a foe, and Oz used that advantage to the fullest. His wings tucked in and he swooped down to the height of their red cyclops eyes, where he unleashed a storm of electricity. Many of the robots very quickly began to stutter and spasm, emitting smoke. The remaining ones turned toward Oz, a chance for Jaune to zip into range.

His shield vanished to let him grab one by the head. It refused to enter his Pocket, so he threw it at another unit, skewering both on his sword. Summoning a spare handgun, he shot the furthest robot from him. Two rounds plinked off the thing's chest, one missed entirely, with a fourth tearing through the face to destroy it for good. An arrow took the last robot offline, with it twitching in place until he bisected it from head to navel.

He tried popping the broken heap into his Pocket, and this time it worked. He tossed the scraps aside again.

"We have a door open, Tattletale," he said over line. "Looks like it leads to the main building, not the offices. Do you think we should go that route?"

Tattletale's voice came from behind him, the girl having entered the room at the tail end of the fight. "We might as well." She checked their surroundings for further threats before striding closer to him. His eyes flicked up to her fox ears, then back to her face. She probably hadn't noticed, right? "If there are people protecting our target, then they won't leave it lying around out here. That data server is probably being kept in the deepest parts. Watch out, though."

Behind her visor, Tattletale's eyes narrowed as she squinted at the space past the doors.

"That's a pretty long hallway with no obstructions, and I'm seeing old bullet marks on the wall and floor."

Jaune got the point she was driving at. "They have more defenses set up, then. Maybe all throughout the building. Noted."

He limbered up, and walked right in.

As warned, a single step into the hallway and two security turrets deployed from the ceiling. They had twin barrels extending out of a complicated arrangement that bore little resemblance to a gun. Painted black, each was stamped with the Arasaka brand.

He could have shot them both out before they got going, via a quick application of his wonderful 'marksmanship'. He opted instead to advance with his shield raised to draw fire, leaving his team to handle the rest. They did not disappoint, twin explosions ringing out not even a second apart to destroy the two turrets.

"Nice work, Fischl," he called back in praise.

But then, upon turning around, his smile slipped off his face. Above his team, a panel was in the middle of sliding open. It shared the same raised plate design as the other turret cubbyholes, attached to the ceiling and difficult to spot in the low light.

Now that was just devious.

Tattletale stole the warning from his lips. "Up!" she cried, and near instantly Bennett jumped. The boy understood nothing of the reason, had not even looked until he was halfway to the ceiling. Once he caught sight of the turret, he rammed his sword into the mechanism, and with a whine the turret powered down in a flawless execution.

"Ghhh!"

Bennett tugged on his sword, to no avail. It was stuck fast in the turret. The boy continued to hang several feet off the ground, kicking his legs. All that effort led nowhere, and he soon gave up to dangle limply off the sword handle. Below, Tattletale pointed and laughed.

A flawless execution with a slight hiccup when sticking the landing, then. All told, Jaune marked it down as a success. Half the point of accepting this job was to let Bennett and Fischl get a taste of the work he was doing around here, and moreover to learn how to deal with modern world threats. In his view, they were excelling at it in a splendid fashion.

The hallway limited itself to one entrance and one exit. Given little choice, they headed into the next room where they found a factory floor. Of sorts.

The space was about the size of a Beacon classroom, occupied by a row of office desks on one end with factory equipment on the other. The equipment and its accompanying conveyor belts appeared entirely self-contained.

"What were they even making here?" Jaune asked. He might not understand much about business, but he thought the point of automation was to scale bigger.

Tattletale wandered over to the conveyor belt, peeking into the opening where the belt fed into the machine. "Specialized parts, I would think. Maybe ghost guns. Didn't you say that they were contracted for military work, according to Wakako? Keep an eye out for anything valuable."

Jaune placed his hand on one of the machines. "Does this count?"

Tattletale rummaged through her belt for the Company scroll.

"Ehhhh, it's not showing up." She gave the bottom of the machine a light kick. "I guess because it's bolted to the floor and counts as part of the building."

Probably was not worth much, anyway. Losing interest, Jaune turned away, in the process summoning a gun and with hardly a thought unloading the whole clip into the security turret that was sneakily extending out of its cubbyhole. He spotted a camera in the corner swiveling to track him. Feeling cheeky, he blew it a kiss.

On the other side of a set of metal doors came the steady footsteps of mechanical soldiers. This time, he did not wait for them to arrive.

"Hey, Bennett. Want to do something cool?" A mental ping to his Pocket, and a small, cylindrical can popped into his hand as Bennett scurried closer.

"You know it, boss! What are we doing?" The boy eyed the door, and shifted his grip on his sword, ready for battle. He then blinked as Jaune snatched away the weapon, trading it for the can. "Um…"

"When I open the door, all you need to do is throw this. I already activated it, so don't hold on for too long, alright?"

Another "Ummm…" indicated Bennett's enthusiastic reply. Probably.

"Get ready, and 3! 2! 1!"

Jaune pulled on the door handle to reveal a host of glowing red eyes staring right at Bennett. Poor, weaponless Bennett, who in great alarm immediately lobbed the object given to him, which went to show that everybody no matter the era they live in had the natural instinct to set things on fire dwelling within their heart. The door shut right as the grenade engulfed the robots in an explosion. A light rumble rattled the door frame.

After waiting a few seconds, Jaune cracked the door open and stuck his head out to check the state of the corridor.

"Huh, looks like we have a few left," he said, studying the half-broken scraps trying to move. The scene rather creeped him out, what with the torsos dragging across the ground and the shambling headless bodies. Another grenade appeared. "Hey, Fischl. Want to do something cool?"

The robots ceased moving soon after that.

Room after room, corridor after corridor, they delved deeper into the factory. The building's defenses folded under their advance. The layout of the place worked in their favor, containing encounters to small skirmishes that never managed the level of firepower needed to overwhelm them.

Meanwhile, the robots made for great practice dummies, clearly inhuman foes that Fischl and Bennett could fire a gun at without much qualms. Jaune didn't think he could get them to point those weapons at a person with any serious intent, though; Tattletale was teaching them to shoot for the knees.

"We're in a combat situation, that makes them my students. Butt out, please."

"You're biased, so no."

"Can I have one?" Escha asked.

""No way!"" exclaimed both Jaune and Tattletale.

The felyne grumbled and sulked off to hang out with Fischl instead of them.

"Well, now I feel guilty."

"Don't you dare cave. She's faking it," Tattletale revealed, before shoving him around the corner to face a hail of bullets. He returned a minute later to wave everyone forward. "Anyway, something is strange about all of this."

"In what way?" he asked, leading the party down a corridor with doors on one side. Glass windows allowed him to look within the offices. The personal effects had been taken away in a rather hasty fashion, with a fair amount of papers and assorted other pieces of junk strewn about. The furniture remained intact, with computers sitting on desks, the chairs pushed in.

Tattletale indicated a computer, which seemed to have booted up from a reset. "How about the fact that the whole place is active. At first I thought they used the location because it was convenient, and maybe hacked their way into gaining some control, but no, they fully turned on the building to power the defenses. For the utilities to still work in an 'abandoned' factory? That takes more than a bit of finders keepers could arrange."

"They own the factory," he guessed. "Whoever is paying for this security team, I mean."

"Exactly. Combine that with everything you destroyed and the cost for a group of mercs, it adds up to a pretty hefty bill. What is in that data server that is worth so much?"

"Maybe we'll get an answer somewhere ahead."

They did not.

Somebody had moved the unit.

"You've got to be kidding me," Jaune groaned, studying the spot Tattletale pointed out. The dust there showed the outline of a rectangle on the tiles, left not long ago. The dimensions of it compared to that of a refrigerator, perhaps.

"It's been barely five minutes since they evacuated," Tattletale informed him.

Further away, Fischl gestured to a series of cracks on the floor leading out of the room they were in and toward a different part of the factory. "Our thief surely harbors the fell strength of a dozen men, for the artifact we have long sought after sits heavy upon their shoulders."

"Or maybe they're a fatty," suggested Tattletale as she pushed up from a kneeling position to scan the room, a central control hub of some kind populated by banks of computer monitors. The air in here measured several degrees lower than elsewhere in the building, likely to help cool the row of computer hardware stacked along one wall. Her gaze focused on one monitor in particular. "It was part of the plan," she remarked softly. "They weren't confident in facing us head on, so they deployed forces to draw us in the direction they wanted. That lets them predict what time we will arrive."

"And thus, the craven fools were able to vanish into the darkness," Fischl chimed in. A sigh, and she pressed the back of her wrist to her forehead. "Alas, hubris shall spell their end. To the sovereign of Immernachtreich, the dark is but another shade of light. Mine eye sees all."

Contrary to the solemn tone, Fischl struggled to hide her eagerness. The girl drifted over to the set of footprints, fidgeting as she waited for someone to follow after her. She was sorely disappointed as Tattletale ignored her to head toward a glowing monitor.

"This is the computer they were using," Tattletale pointed out. "This controls the security system, at least from here."

The idea struck him. "We can trace their route on the cameras!"

"Ideally, yeah." Tattletale leaned down to look at the screen. "It looks like they logged out. Hehe, that's cute, thinking it'll work."

Her eyes roamed the work station around the computer. She opened a drawer, glancing inside. A bullet casing rested next to the keyboard that she played with.

"Military type, obviously. Who else to run security? Strict organization of drawer, knows opsec. No cameras in the room, they're the paranoid type. The password is more likely to be randomized and not a date or name, but chances are good there's a pattern if they—he has to input a complicated string of text from memory every day for opsec. Southpaw, so we all know what that means."

Jaune raised a finger in objection. "I don't. What does it mean?"

"Shoosh. I'm working. Q or W to start. First pattern, authoritative yet brusque personality means he'll want to make it snappy but not so short that it feels like he's dumb. Letter-letter-letter-number-letter lets him remember it as a word, and if the first string ends with Y, then it won't repeat but shifts to the right. Worn down key, it is Y. Bullet casing suggests sniper. Q-a-R-2-Y, quarry, it makes him feel strong. Then, next one has to be a number, 8 or 9, never 0. It's 8. Number of kills, maybe? Creepy. No, wait, he quit the army young. He feels guilty. 9."

Bennett sidled over to Jaune. "Is she… okay?"

"She does that, don't worry about it," he answered airily, quite engrossed as he listened to what appeared at first to be a stream of nonsense. "I'll explain to you what a password is later, but trust me, she's practically weaving a magic spell right now."

Leaning on the adjacent desk, he watched the login box on the screen fill up one by one with characters. Escha climbed on the table to poke her head in and catch a view of what was happening, oohing and ahhing despite not understanding anything going on here. She almost fell off the edge as the screen performed an abrupt change to display a series of programs and windows.

"Q-a-R-2-Y-9-u-N-D. Quarry gunned. He could have at least made it difficult," Tattletale 'complained' to him, and with the fox ears on her head, her grin looked decidedly vulpine. Her glances lingered, and Jaune knew just what she was expecting.

"That was amazing!" he exclaimed, applauding. Frantic signals with his eyes got the others to follow suit, piling on praises for her feat of hacking. Tattletale basked in it without a lick of shame.

A toss of her hair, and she began manipulating the various windows. Turrets shut down. Robots returned to standby. Cameras blinked out one after another as she narrowed down the route taken by the person transporting the data server unit.

A stuttering on the screen brought her efforts to a grounding halt. Tattletale ceased tapping the keyboard, and hearing her curse under her breath put him on alert.

"What happened?" he asked.

"Everything I've shut down is turning back on. Somebody else is in the system. A netrunner." The screen then blurred with how fast the blinking, flashing windows opened and closed. Tattletale slammed her hand on the keyboard, doing jack all. "I knew they abandoned this place too easily."

A cartoonish icon appeared, superimposed over the ongoing tasks. Jaune spotted the angular, feline-like eyes first, then the tongue sticking out in mockery. The overall shape resembled a smiley face, except…

He leaned over for a closer look, putting his face before the screen.

"Is that a slice of kiwi?"

The icon vanished in a blink of an eye, swapped to a camera view. It seemed to be from a computer monitor, because he could see two people looking back from the other side.

"Kiwi, what the hell? Why did you do that!?"

"...Hi."

Jaune glanced over to the woman with iridescent hair, Lucy, who looked quite panicked with sweat running down her brow as she berated the person front and center on the screen. That person, who Jaune ran into earlier in the week and was identified in Tattletale's briefing as a netrunner named Kiwi, ignored her teammate. She shared the same angular yellow eyes with red irises as the earlier cartoon icon, but there was no mocking tongue blowing a raspberry. Instead, a mask covered the woman's lower face. Red, to match the coat she wore.

The last time he saw her, she had been rather distressed about her broken mask. There was none of that unease now with the facepiece repaired. It registered to Jaune that she had been addressing him.

Tattletale facepalmed as he raised his hand in a small wave.

"Hi?"

A shove to budge him aside, and Tattletale reclaimed some room for herself in front of the computer. Her attitude changed from one moment to the next, falsely cheerful.

"Hey there! Martinez's crew contracted with the other side of this job, then? I don't suppose we can come to a compromise? Those robots had to cost a pretty penny- a pretty eddie."

This subject appeared to put Lucy back on steadier footing. Through a difficult expression, she scoffed. "Too bad, but we're not the ones paying for it. There's an entire army of them that we can throw at you. Look, you get how it works. Here's our offer: you call it quits, and we let you walk out of here alive."

A laugh was the answer she got. "I can smell the lies even from here," Tattletale crooned. "How many of the robots did my team take out of commission? 25%? 50%? More. You're not in a very good position, are you?" She raised her voice to be better heard. "You can park that data server where you've got it now and take a hike, and I'll tell my partner here to not shove a sword up your ass. That's my counteroffer."

At the crass tone, Lucy frowned. She replied, likewise increasing her volume, "What a joke." A boxy object floated into view, a police drone. The point was made. They had more where that came from.

Tattletale did not see it as such. A roll of her eyes conveyed her disdain, or at least the appearance of disdain.

"You'd need hundreds"—her grin widened—"and you don't have hundreds. But there's still a decent-sized force, isn't there? You have to have a place to put them. Where, oh where, could you be? And where is your boytoy? I didn't catch news of him croaking after his trip, but it had to have been a close call."

On the screen, Lucy stiffened. "He's fine," was her instant reply. Her arms then crossed, and she recovered her composure to give Tattletale a smirk. "Nothing people do can keep him off his feet for long. David is amazing like that. Look down on him and he might just flatline you one of these days."

As Lucy spoke, Tattletale's expression shifted to a more contemplative one. "What's—" She paused, and tried again. "What's the deal with him? I can tell when something is up, and—" She stopped once more, now turning to the side. "Jaune, can you pretty please shut up and focus?"

Jaune and Kiwi broke off their budding conversation about the upcoming festival, which according to Kiwi had some very good food if you knew where to find them. The rapport he was trying to build, which could have seen an actual compromise come about between their two teams in this situation, died in a fire. He sent Tattletale an annoyed look for that. On her end, Kiwi mirrored the action with her teammate, who had taken a grip of Kiwi's shoulder.

Tattletale feigned wiping sweat from her brow, and turned back to the screen. "Ahh, blessed silence. Seriously, how many packs of smokes do you have to go through to fuck up your voice like that?"

"Tattletale!" Jaune snapped. Around the room, the rest of his team jolted at the sudden harsh note. Of course, it bore little fruit with the supervillainess, who had faced bigger and badder than him.

"What? I can't be the only one weirded out—wait a minute." Tattletale pressed her face closer to the screen. "Oh. Oh geeze, my bad." She sounded contrite…ish. No, not really. "Sooo, I hear medical technology is pretty good these days."

Now was Jaune's turn to facepalm, with Bennett and Fischl cringing. Even Escha covered her eyes.

"I am so sorry, please don't mind her," he said. "And Tattletale, it's not our business. Don't pry into it."

He didn't dare look at the woman on the screen. Only, when Kiwi spoke, he heard no anger or sadness in her artificial voice.

"You… didn't tell her?"

"About your mouth?" One of his hands waved aimlessly, the other continuing to cradle his head. "It wouldn't feel right after seeing you hide it like that. There's already the chance of us killing each other, no need to make the grudge personal." That was reserved for things that needed to be dead.

"Huh."

Kiwi leaned forward to draw his attention, and propped a hand under her chin as she studied him. Her eyes narrowed, lacking rancor.

"I have to agree with you, even if some among my team don't care to. 'Don't take it personally' is pretty much rule two in the merc business," she remarked, brushing her hair behind an ear.

He perked up. "Really?"

That was a first in this world. People got so angry over the littlest thing.

"Mmhm. Less hassle that way." Was it him, or was Kiwi fidgeting? "So, look, I wouldn't be opposed to… working off any bad feelings between our teams with you, if it helps. For the sake of our teams."

Slowly, Jaune tilted his head. The way Kiwi phrased that did not sound very innocent.

Behind Kiwi, Lucy facepalmed, the third person to do so in as many minutes. With a flash of light from her eyes, the computer screen went blank to leave Jaune staring into his reflection.

"I think she was offering to have sex with me."

"Goddammit, Jaune. Her job is to kill you. How do you even get into this situation?"

"Don't ask me! I literally said two sentences to her before today!"



-o-
​


Unfortunately, when he next faced the edgerunners, it was not someone so agreeable as Kiwi that he ran into. A shotgun blast smashed into his shield the very moment he kicked open the door to the main factory floor of the sprawling complex. Over the edge of the shield, he spied the woman called Rebecca situated in a cold, damp room filled with factory equipment and conveyor belts, an angry, fun-sized package ready to take it out on him. In addition to her, robots scattered across the floor and the upper catwalk. Drones swarmed like bugs in the air. Every single one was facing in his direction.

There was a reason he put the others, and especially the new members of his team, far back for this one. With confirmation of who was in the building, he had made the executive decision to change their approach. Humor faded away, and Jaune marched into the room drawing his sword.

A kick against the floor activated his rockets, putting him high above as drones and robots unloaded their combined arsenal to obliterate the spot where he once stood, the noise rattling the room. Among them, Rebecca was the fastest to track him, dropping on her back to aim that oversized shotgun rifle she favored his way. The gun roared, the bullets smashing through the drones in between her and Jaune in order to reach him. By then, he was already gone, diving into the thickest grouping of robots.

He landed on one, driving it into the concrete with both feet. His sword whipped out to slice through a trio of its brethren, more raw strength than technique. Amidst the crush of metallic bodies, defense was unnecessary, and his shield popped away to let him grab one of the robots by the arm. With a shout, he swung it as a club, bashing it into another target and reducing both to scraps. Kicking out to break a leg, he rolled that robot over his back to block incoming fire from the drones above. A thought toward his Pocket, and a grenade now balanced on the tip of his boot. He flicked it upward.

The resulting explosion wiped out a number of drones, and unbalanced many more. Their parts rained down on the room.

"Oh fuck, oh fuck! David, where are you?" Rebecca shouted, speaking to the empty air. "Get over here already, choom!" She punctuated that with another shotgun blast. Jaune willed the Geo shield into being to take the brunt of the attack, the rest of it cracking harmlessly against a suit of armor that vanished as suddenly as it had appeared on him. [Third Arm] launched out to slingshot him at her, and Rebecca yelped, diving behind a piece of factory equipment. He arrived to find her scurrying under a conveyor belt, the last thing he saw her hand flipping him the bird before she ducked out of sight.

His problems extended to more than just her, so he put the edgerunner aside. Staying with the momentum, he crashed into a robot to bring the both of them to the floor, rolling to launch into the air on his rocket boots. Crocea Mors sliced through a slew of drones with little resistance. Up here, he had no cover and his opponents punished him for it. Jaune armored up again as a wall of bullets slammed into him. Something told him it wasn't Kiwi operating these guys.

His back hit the ground. He bounced, rolled, turned that into more momentum that sent him shooting behind the cover of hardy factory equipment. A second later, he emerged from the other side, armorless so as to not encumber, the rifle Ruhm in his grip. A reckless burst of gunfire unerringly found their marks, cutting down many of the robots stationed on the catwalk. He never slowed for a single moment. Faster, faster, faster was the thought at the forefront of his mind. In quick succession, broken metal sparked, detonated, or fell silent where they stood. There might someday be an age of machine warfare, but that wasn't today, nor here.

Rebecca soon resurfaced with her shotgun steadied over the top of a cutting machine. A juke left got her to pull the trigger, a shadowy arm tugging him to the right let him evade without a scratch. Ruhm swung around, forcing her back into hiding. Bang, bang, the rounds struck metal.

The phone around his neck crackled. "Jaune, are you still okay on your own in there?" Tattletale asked, trying for a carefree tone. "Should we come in?"

Sliding into cover at the center of the room, he said in between shallow, rapid breaths, "The most troublesome one hasn't shown up yet. Give it a minute. I want their attention on me."

The strange humming sound that drones emitted gave him early notice of their approach. Twirling Ruhm, he locked it into position with the barrel straight up and began blasting the things as they showed their presence. Some missed, some found their mark. The bullets pierced straight through this side of the Geo shield he erected yet those that were fired at him stopped short, a quirk he had come to appreciate. Over the phone, Tattletale whined about him giving her tinnitus one of these days.

Her voice faded to the background as darkness fell over Jaune.
