His casual demeanor dropped like a mask as he heard a soft electronic tone, along with the click of the door lock. In the relative quiet of the apartment, the sound was deafening and not in a good way. He shared a look with Lisa who had noticed the same problem.

They all used physical keys. Nobody in their group had the cyberware needed for the scanner.

A few quick strides put him at the balcony overlooking the main floor of the apartment. His eyes were rooted to the corner that led to the entrance foyer. Soon enough, two people skulked into the room. He recognized them.

Boy, those small details along the way that did not concern him sure seemed relevant now. The edgerunners, Lucy and Rebecca, had infiltrated his base. Last he heard of them, the former had navigated through a wall via her robot with the latter in her arms, escaping after his team pulled their punches.

"How wonderful," he said in a tired voice as he drew a sword from the empty air and swung one foot up to step on the banister, before that grew to a shout. "Fine, then! Here we go again—!"

"Wait, wait, wait!" Lucy yelled, throwing her hands up.

Beside her, Rebecca dropped her weapons, all of them, a pile of guns pouring out of her jacket to land at her feet. Sweat dripped down her face, the young woman grimacing hard as she added her voice to the mix.

"Truce, you crazy gonk! Truce!"

Jaune hesitated, looking from one face to the other. Those guns didn't say truce.

That point turned moot as a head poked around the corner, twin-tails trailing near to the floor. More voices from out in the hallway announced the return of the apartment's inhabitants.

"Oh! Do we have guests?" asked Hu Tao. "I'll get the tea."



-o-
​


Steam rose from the teacups set on the living room table. The ones in front of the intruders went untouched. All of them, from Jaune to the cat to Lucy, had arranged themselves on or around the couch. The edgerunners occupied the shorter end of the L-shaped seat, everybody else at the other. Escha hid under the low table, glaring up at Rebecca and hissing whenever the short woman tried to reach for her. Outside the windows, rainclouds had rolled in.

The conversation had been rather stilted up until now. Jaune kept his hand shaped to summon a sword and swing for the neck. These two things might be related.

"Sooo," Lisa began. She had stowed away her headphones. "What's up with your boytoy?"

How nice, that he could rely on Lisa to ferret out the pesky details. His gaze fell to the familiar yellow jacket that Lucy was clutching to her chest with a white-knuckle grip. The last time he saw the garment, David Martinez had thrown it off then punched him in the face.

Lucy worked her jaw, likely having trouble finding the right words. Strands of her iridescent hair shimmered under the light as she fidgeted back and forth.

"I need your help," she finally said in a small voice.

"To?" Jaune asked.

His response seemed to embolden her. She looked up, eyes flashing with determination.

"To save David!"

"…No. Is this a prank?"

Aaand now the edgerunner was curling in on herself again, all sad and stuff. But then, what did she expect? Jaune looked at Lisa, getting back a shrug. He subtly gestured at the intruders. His partner in crime (and adventure, but mostly crime) squinted at him, suspecting that he intended to foist the work onto her, which he was, but since it was her wheelhouse she went along with it. As Lisa got started on coaxing more information out of Lucy, he picked up a teacup and took a sip.

As he did, he glanced to the side. Eyes with pupils in the shape of flowers stared back at him. Hu Tao hovered behind the couch, and had been doing strange things ever since he sat down. Like now, for instance, where she brought her face close to his neck to take a sniff of him.

"Hu Tao, is there any reason why you did that? Do I stink?" he asked, a little concerned.

"You smell… different."

He flinched, understanding exactly what she referred to. A quick look at Lisa, and he made up a lie on the spot. "That must be the sweat. I was running through a few exercises earlier and didn't get a chance to shower off."

"That might be it," Hu Tao agreed, although she did not sound convinced. She also continued to linger nearby. Sniff, sniff. The girl puzzled over the scent on him.

Past her, he caught the sheepish gazes of Bennett and Fischl. Clearly, their show of mercy the other day hadn't panned out so well, and they knew it. The two resembled him and his sisters when they'd bunch together in solidarity after getting into trouble as they waited for a rebuke from their parents. He thought of what his parents would do. He put on a reassuring smile, and waved it off.

They had performed an undoubtedly good act, with good intentions. The world just decided to kick their teeth in for it, was all.

They were also trying to wave at Rebecca when they thought he wasn't looking. A gesture the edgerunner returned with her big, metal hands. That part seemed less forgivable, but ehhh, whatever. Strangers were just friends you haven't met yet. Your friend meeting a stranger who turned out to be your enemy despite you two having that mutual friend might be somewhere on that chart. Overthinking it would just confuse him.

"You have got to be kidding me."

Lisa's incredulous tone drew him back into the conversation with the edgerunners. She had a hand gripping her forehead, and stared at Lucy without blinking.

"The whole time?" she asked. "No. That's not possible. I would have noticed. We would have ran into each other. You can't seriously tell me you were living on this same floor!"

Pardon?

"Preach it, bitch," Rebecca said, throwing her hands to the sky. The short woman had also turned in her seat to glare at Lucy. "My beautiful, sweet, kind-hearted self spent months freaking out over a certain someone and it turns out she was living the high life! Like, what the fuck, amiright?"

"Rebecca, I already told you—"

Lisa cut in, addressing Rebecca. "And shacking up with your guy, too? That had to sting."

"He… He's not my guy," Rebecca said with a fluster, before recovering. "But at least I wouldn't have tried to shoot my shot so often if they just told me they were still together! Now I look like a homewrecker!"

"What a bitch!"

"Yeah!"

No, he was pretty sure that Lisa was the homewrecker at the moment. Two minutes in and she had fractured the duo. Not to a great extent, perhaps, but enough to seed doubts that could play them against each other. All with a smile on her face.

Sometimes, his friend was kind of scary.

"Look," Lucy said, hard at work corralling her emotions before she snapped. "That isn't the point. I knew you were living literally three doors down from us, and I kept that secret. I could have told David, but I didn't!"

Lisa raised a finger to object. "Because he'll come calling and then die, let's get that straight. You did it for his sake, not ours."

Jaune nodded. Martinez would have eaten the sharp end of a sword had he set foot in here. Yup, yup.

"We can have many reasons for the things we do," said Lucy. The young woman hugged the yellow jacket tighter. "I wanted him to be happy. I want him to live. Please, I can pay."

"I'm going to regret asking this, but what are you talking about?" Jaune said. "Where did the guy disappear to? And where's Kiwi, anyway?"

Any semblance of composure Lucy managed to cultivate suddenly cracked into pieces. Her eyes burned with a red-hot anger, and she looked out the window to a towering spire in the distance. "They got to him," she spat, scowling hard. "Arasaka."

To that, Jaune could only say one thing.

"And Kiwi?"

Hey, if he had to pick who to focus on between the two, it might as well be the person he actually held a decent chat with.

Evidently, Lucy didn't share the sentiment, so while she sat there seething at him for his uncaring attitude, Rebecca was the one to answer. "Kiwi's out in Corpo Plaza. She told us she'll pursue our current leads while we talk to you."

"Leads, huh?" Lisa pondered. "You act like you're certain it was Arasaka despite not being there. You caught it on a camera playback, then? The place was lousy with them." She crossed her legs, propping her chin on a hand as she observed the edgerunners. Unlike him, she treated them with far less hostility. For the most part, curiosity held the reins.

Lucy nodded. "They sent a retrieval team. Their netrunner shut down half of David's implants in the span of two seconds. Then… They…"

"They put a bullet in him when he wouldn't show his belly like a dog," Rebecca growled. Jaune noticed that her fingers were twitching involuntarily, miming the act of firing a gun as she thought of the people who took her friend away.

He rather felt that he had a good grasp on her type by now. A bomb with a faulty fuse. A Biri-Biri girl, as a certain ordinary high school boy would call it.

"Corpo rats had to bring their special forces. They knew David would fuck them all up, otherwise," she said.

Yeah, right. The guy was likelier to keel over dead than take a swing. The amount of blood he had lost at that point shouldn't even fit inside a person. Jaune let the comment pass by, however. It served little purpose to burst her bubble, and he had something else he wanted to know.

"I don't really see why they nabbed him at all," he said. "Oh, and do try Hu Tao's tea. It's delicious."

The sooner they finished, the sooner he had an excuse to usher them out the door. Hu Tao gave him a surreptitious poke for that, cottoning on to his game. She took the matter of hospitality more seriously than him.

Lucy and Rebecca shared a look. It was quick, but hard to miss.

"That's… a secret," Lucy said.

Lisa scoffed, and stood up.

"Welp, that's that, then. Good luck."

One would think Lucy teleported with how fast she sprang to her feet. Hands out, she motioned for Lisa to wait. "Okay! Okay! He—David—he is special." The young woman turned to Jaune, silently begging him to keep listening. "His compatibility with cyberware is higher than anyone I have ever seen."

The picture grew clearer and clearer over the next few minutes as Lucy talked on. In a world where metal was power, prestige, profit, products, David Martinez counted as one in a million. The holy grail, to borrow a phrase. Unlocking the possibilities hidden in his DNA could usher in a new era of robotics. A future where everyone was chromed to the gills, and paid for the privilege.

A private army of cyborgs to depose competitors, or nations. A new, untapped market ripe for expansion. Name it, and that was the hope David represented to the corporations aware of him.

And by unlocking, Lucy made it clear that she meant dissection. The corporations were famed for their brutal approach to furthering scientific progress. David Martinez would die on an operating table, screaming.

It couldn't have happened to a better guy. Jaune then chastised himself for that thought. His personal feelings aside, he noted the pale faces around him. The image Lucy had put in their heads was a grisly one. Certain factions within Arasaka had been known to cut up children if he was to believe the netrunner. Lisa didn't flag it as a lie, which spoke volumes.

Lucy was paying close attention to him. She spotted his reluctance. Or, rather, his animosity with her leader. Fumbling in a bag she had brought along, she pulled out a fistful of small computer chips. Datashards, they call it here.

"I can pay," she said, and poured the money shards onto the table, where they bounced in all directions, clinking against the teacups and falling off the edge. Two more handfuls joined it, along with stacks of paper eddies. She plugged one of the shards into a slot on her neck, an act that will never not freak him out with how carefree the people in this world were about it. Her eyes flickered blue, denoting the transfer of data. She ejected the chip and slapped it down on the table afterward. "The entirety of my bank accounts. Every stash of eddies I hid in my home. Everything I own. It's yours if you save him."

The desperation bled through. They colored her every action, each line of worry on her face. It began to register for him that, oh, she was being dead serious on requesting their help.

It weirded him out, and made him want to turn her down even harder. Frankly, he was more preoccupied with that whole child abduction and mutilation bit. Who did he have to talk to, to find out where that was happening? Who did he have to shove a sword through?

"Sorry—"

"Please!" Lucy bowed her head.

"I don't trust you," he said, giving up the pretense of politeness. Lucy flinched, and Rebecca glared at him. The latter deflated rather quickly, grousing in a way that told him she found the comment rather fair. She shoved a shotgun in his mouth, he kicked her out of an aircraft. That sort of impression stuck around.

"They don't need us, anyway," Lisa remarked, studying the pile of money on the table. "If each shard has even an average of a couple thousands, what they have here can hire a lot of people."

Lucy shook her head. "Arasaka plans to take David out of the country within the week. There isn't enough time to jump through the usual hoops. More than that, it's Arasaka! Other mercs won't cut it. It has to be you." She stared hard at him. "You're David's rival. The only other solo in Night City strong enough to think of taking a corp head-on. And…" Here, she hesitated. Her voice, when she spoke, held a note of wonder. " And you're the man who flies. You can do anything."

There was a hush, lasting a beat. The silence rang in their ears.

Some of the tension bled out of Lucy.

"David… He's a good man, deep down," she said, gaze drifting to the jacket. She played with it, running a thumb over the plasticky fabric. Before Jaune could refute that claim, she continued. "You didn't hear how he talked that night you chased after us on the highway. He was tucked in bed, and he wouldn't sleep. He just went on and on to me about the flying man, and whether you could fly to the moon." She cracked a smile, wistful and sad. "He was like the goofy kid I fell in love with, way back when. He hates you, but he also admires you."

Jaune recalled a head splattered against a cockpit wall. "You and I must have met different Davids. That goofy kid murders people with a smile."

The wistful mien faded, and Lucy just looked miserable. "He has his reasons."

"Need better ones," Jaune muttered under his breath.

Rebecca overheard him, and grew furious in a heartbeat. Swinging upright, she pointed an oversized finger at him. "Fuck you! The guy crawled out of a hole, okay? We all did. Sorry it offends your hoity-toity sensibilities!"

"Becca, stop it. We're not here to fight." Lucy tried to pull her back in her seat.

Rebecca did not, and whirled on her ally. "I can't stand him! He doesn't know anything about David!" She turned and flipped him the bird. "Corpo kid with your fucking organic bananas and clean air and… and… all that stuff! It's so easy, people like you always say." Her voice pitched higher, mocking. "There's never a need for violence. We have rules. Why don't those poor people just eat cake instead of shit? He did what we all had to, breaking pieces of ourselves to make it another day. What would you know about that?"

It shouldn't have bothered him. Yet, something in him rebelled at Rebecca's condescending attitude, and he jumped to his feet, leaning over the table to glare at her dead in the eyes. "I'm carrying my entire world on my shoulders. Do you think that is easy?" A fist punched against the table. Rebecca cringed back. "I'm going to die in a ditch one of these days and it will all go to hell. I have every reason to be a horrible person, not least for my life, and still I have to try and be someone my parents could be proud of. So, yeah, from where I'm standing his excuses don't cut it."

"Alright, cool it!" Lisa commanded, pushing in between them. She placed a hand on his chest, trying to move him back, and after a brief moment of hesitation, he relented. That earned him a quick smile from her. He sat down, a storm in his heart, with Hu Tao proceeding to massage his shoulders, urging him to drink his tea and relax. On Rebecca's part, the young woman looked from Lisa to Lucy, then threw herself back into her seat, fuming. Under the table, Escha bristled at her, fur standing on ends.

The conversation stalled out for a good minute. The people on his side were sending him glances. He slowly registered what he had let slip, that thought lurking in the depths of his mind which dogged his every step, and his cheeks burned with embarrassment.

Jaune knew, better than anyone, that he was still not good enough.

But… that wasn't what other people thought, was it?

"I need you," Lucy weakly pleaded. She couldn't look him in the eye, once more bowing her head.

He wanted to just say yes. Someone was counting on him, like he was a hero. They believed him more than he was, and it drew out such a heady feeling within him.

Instead, he barked out, "Why?"

"You're the man who flies," Lucy repeated, then elaborated further. "Arasaka has a plan on how to move David out of Night City. It's the parade floats. They travel along the same route each year, high up and at the center of Arasaka security forces. After making a circuit of the festival, the floats load right onto a boat and ship back to Japan. He'll be on one of them."

Something about that sounded off to him, but he left it alone for now. He pointed with the hand holding his teacup.

"Let me see if I have this right. You're asking me to drop in during the middle of the festival, straight into an army's worth of soldiers, and break him out?"

She nodded. Her lips trembled. "Once he is across the ocean, there is nothing we can do. Arasaka will ensure he never sees the light of day again. This is our only chance."

Hesitantly, Bennett raised his hand to interrupt. "With a glider, it's possible. The buildings here go up forever. Me and you can jump off and reach him pretty easily. Between us, I bet we can hold him up long enough to let him land safely on the ground."

"The interwoven web of this city forms a maze cast in the everdarkness," Fischl reminded them. "Where lost souls may vanish with the morning light."

"The many alleys offer a suitable escape route, should you wish to lose your pursuers," Oz interpreted.

Fischl made an offended sound. "My retainer, please do not diminish my contributions so. My very words carry with them power, voiced in the true manner of reality."

"Indubitably, Mein Fräulein. Apologies."

"Did that bird just clucking talk?"

They ignored Rebecca's question, to her impotent raging. Plus her joke, but that was a given since it was awful and deserving of no recognition, only shame.

Besides, with Escha and even Hu Tao chiming in with suggestions, people were starting to get ahead of themselves. He had to nip that in the bud.

"My team will talk it over," he said curtly, and everyone fell quiet to listen. "After that, we'll get back to you."

Lucy looked like she was ready to argue. Lisa jumped in, reaching over to pat the other woman on the knee.

"Hey, heeey. Relax. You have a friend in me. I'll try to convince him. He's a big softie, but he also has to worry about the good of the team. You get it, right?"

She shared a look with him. Lisa was making him out as the bad guy in this situation, except both of them understood the truth of the matter. They were of a like mind about this request.

Blinded by hope, Lucy grabbed Lisa's hand. "Thank you! Thank you so much!" She spun toward him, ready to do the same, but Lisa headed it off.

"Go home," she ordered. "Sleep. You need it. The world is going to look different in the morning."

"Yes, I—Rebecca, let's get out of their hair. Sleep can wait. I have to dive into the net first. There's so much to do!"

Her newfound liveliness bordered on the manic. Lucy practically dragged Rebecca from the apartment, turning around every few steps to bow and thank them again. Her money stayed on the table. In her head, it was a done deal.

For some of the people remaining in the room, it did appear so. Bennett was happy. Escha, too. Being heroes and saving lives appealed to them. Jaune didn't have the heart to tell them that, for the most part, Lisa said those things to get the desperate women who were not in any state of mind to accept no for an answer out of the apartment.

Fischl's contemplative demeanor was interesting, however. Jaune asked her about it as he stood at the entrance watching the edgerunners walk down the hall and enter another apartment unit.

"David is… scary," she said. Aside from him, she had been the one with the best chance to observe Martinez the other day. She saw the cracks, and what lay beneath.

He patted her on the shoulder, and shepherded her back inside. Lisa passed by her to join him at the foyer. They spoke quietly.

"What do we do?" he said.

"You got us into this. Figure it out."

"I vote we turn them down. Move out if we want to avoid a fight. We have enough to book a hotel, I'm sure."

Lisa chuckled. "You understand me so well." Then, she blew a raspberry. "The problem is everyone else. I don't think the timing of those two showing up was a coincidence. They were hoping to lean on their prior connections with Hu Tao and the others. Escha, too. Kitty cat complains about the short one, but she doesn't have much of a mean streak."

Jaune tsked, a hand coming up to rub his temples. "They played us like fiddles, then. Did you notice…"

"That the story is off? Duh. If David Martinez is so important, why did Arasaka go for this convoluted plan of using a parade float as a prison transport?"

As Wakako had told him, airships were what people sprang for when moving important cargo. The Arasaka Corporation could have stolen David out of the country the very same day they brought him in.

"Because David is not the target," said a new voice.

Jaune and Lisa both blinked, then poked their heads out the open door.

A tall figure stood just outside, leaning on the wall. Kiwi, the netrunner. She had her thumbs hooked in her pockets, back subtly arched with her chin tilted up in a striking pose. Her height lent her the image of a fashion model on a magazine cover.

She spoke in a bored tone.

"Hi."

"...Hi?"

"So, are you going to invite me in?"


-o-
​

This time, there were only three people gathered on the couch. Despite the increased space, they sat close together. Very close.

Lisa leaning on him and Kiwi's hip bumping against his, close.

Their new guest showed no inclination to change that state of affair. She took her tea in a glass, with ice cubes plus a straw. The end of the straw tucked through one of the vents on her mask to let her drink, although Jaune had no idea how that worked. A sip, and she gave an appreciative hum.

She then placed the glass back on the table, and shifted in her seat to make herself more comfortable. Jaune grew quite aware of how soft her thigh felt.

He broke the ice. "Lucy said you were in center city."

"I lied to her."

"Ah."

A liar? What a horrible person. How could people do that, just lie to someone?

"It's about you. It was always about you," Kiwi remarked. One leg crossed over the other, and much like the friend she lied to, she looked out the window at a tall tower.

It took him a moment to get it.

"I'm Arasaka's real target."

Kiwi nodded. "That job in the factory was supposed to be when they grab you. It looked like they intended for my team to soften you up. Explains why they handed us so many toys."

"I knew it!" Lisa interjected. "I knew the expenses didn't add up. What about the previous jobs? We meet way too often for it to be mere chance."

"Not sure, but it's likely." Kiwi looked at him, and her eyes narrowed in that 'smile without a smile' way of hers. "I think you confused them with the things you do. They had to keep hiring us in order to study you and figure out a plan."

And their plan was David Martinez. Too bad he fumbled it.

"David is the second prize," Kiwi said when he noted that. "They posted watchers on the fight, and when he ran away out the factory, they had seconds to make a decision. After that… Well, you know how corpos are. The division dealing with you two ran a cost-benefit analysis. You won out, he became a pawn. They're now going for broke. It hinges on a conclusion they had about you."

That sounded rather ominous. He straightened in his seat, focusing on Kiwi. "Which is?"

"They think you're a bleeding heart brute. You don't hurt innocent people."

On his other side, Lisa wiggled her hand. "Slightly off."

Kiwi shrugged, and sipped her drink. "Doesn't matter. They're running with it and designing the playing field with that in mind. This is good tea, by the way."

"Thank you!" Hu Tao called down from the upper floor in a bright voice. That reminded Jaune to drink from his own cup. Throughout, he mulled on what Kiwi said.

"The festival?" he guessed. "The parade floats that your friend was talking about." That earned him another not-smile.

"Yes, although the name is a misnomer. They are more akin to barges with rockets strapped on. Now, imagine the buildings lining the road as the mountains, filled with caves where their soldiers hide. Below is the river, an endless crowd of people that they wager you would not touch. Their analysts have made a comprehensive report on you, from your armaments to your habits. An entire psychological profile to predict your actions in this scenario."

With a flash of light from her eyes, the TV turned on. Files popped open one by one. Photos of him flying, shooting, fighting over the course of a week and a half. Pages after pages of text accompanied the pictures.

"You stole these?" he asked.

"Thought you might appreciate it."

He laughed. "I do, thanks for that. It'd be nice to confirm what they know." And what they didn't.

Kiwi mumbled something he couldn't catch, and moved on before he asked about it. She began highlighting pieces of the text, the relevant notes to paint for him a picture of the situation. Helpfully, a diagram of the festival route was included on the screen, letting him see how the vertical terrain of the area would box him in, with his hypothetical placement on a parade float opening him up for Arasaka forces to attack from multiple angles—frankly, all the angles. In addition, the multi-tiered nature of the area, with balconies dotting up and down the buildings to be filled with festival-goers, limited his ability to bring firearms to bear lest stray shots land in the crowd.

Indeed, it was a trap, top to bottom. All they needed left was to put him inside the cage.

"Lucy lied to us," he muttered, a harsh fire flickering to life within him. His voice came out as a hiss. "She would have turned around and stabbed me in the back had I helped her out."

Kiwi, hesitant, spoke with care. "In a way, yes. My teammate got her information from a fixer named Faraday—"

In unison, Jaune and Lisa facepalmed.

"Faraday!"

"Of course, it's that weasel. Didn't I tell you he's trouble, Jaune?"

"When you're right, you're right."

"Stupid Faraday!"

Kiwi made a noise that might have been a chuckle, and waited for them to finish. "He is tied into this. He works for Arasaka, now. Maybe. He was supposed to give you to them on a platter. Using pretty face Lucy to lay bait is the last ditch plan he came up with."

"And Lucy is in on it?" he asked.

"That's harder to say," Kiwi answered, shrugging. "The details he passed to her are incomplete, but knowing her, she would have learned parts of the truth from diving into the Arasaka subnet, enough to suspect there is more to the situation."

"But so long as it allows her to rescue David, she would do it," Lisa concluded, before narrowing her eyes at Kiwi. "It does beg the question, though, on how it is you found out so much more than her. As if someone had told all of it to you."

The implication hit him at the same time Kiwi replied.

"Faraday brought me into the real plan. He figured I'd go for it. Paid me to betray my team and help them capture Lucy as well as you and David," Kiwi admitted.

Flabbergasted, Jaune stared at her. "You're serious."

"I am. And he was right," she said without a hint of reticence. "I will betray my team. By telling you everything so that you aren't caught in the trap." She jerked a thumb over her shoulder. "Leave Night City. Use the festival as cover."

He had only a brief moment to parse that before Kiwi surprised him. She replaced her drink glass, and in one smooth motion left her seat to stride for the door. The whole time, she refused to look at him. Her entire demeanor screamed that her business here was done.

He caught a sliver of the myriad emotions playing out on her face as it turned away, and he moved. A lunge captured her hand in his own, causing Kiwi to stop in her tracks. She whirled around. All of a sudden, she carried the attitude of one out of their depths, tense and shifty. Despite being taller than him, she looked small. And worried. Reluctant to leave, but determined to.

"What about you?" he asked, an alarm ringing in his head. "People go on and on to me about the dangers of crossing a corp. What happens now that you've ruined Faraday's plan? Arasaka's plan?"

"...I'll figure something out," Kiwi deflected. She lightly tugged on her hand to see if she could slip out of his grip. Her eyes rose to meet his own, and she held his gaze with a silent question.

What are you doing?

He didn't even know. What a mess.

Lucy asked for his help, and planned to betray him. Quite a surprise to spring on a person. Except, she had never been on his side. Her reason was simple. She was almost too upfront about it. She wanted to save her teammate. The man she loves. Someone who was counting on her, Jaune's life be damned.

That wasn't an easy act for him to forgive from a friend, let alone a stranger. He would have turned his back on her. It would eat at him, he couldn't even blame her, but he'd see it done.

In came Kiwi to throw a spanner in the works. Everybody's works. A traitor to her team. A traitor twice over, today. There was a word for that. Scum.

She did it for his sake.

He.. truly hated this complicated stuff. He wished it was simple.

Simple, he mused.

"Kiwi, what will happen to you after you go out that door and I don't show up to the festival?"

The woman affected a bored facade, cocking an eyebrow. "Who cares? You just stay away, 'kay?"

"Good luck with that," Lisa grumbled. The girl had remained on the couch, and she was pinching the bridge of her nose, appearing exasperated. Once again, she read him like a book. He took heart that she hadn't spoken out against him.

Kiwi balked, losing her cool. "What? Why? Did I not explain the situation clearly enough?"

In place of a reply, Lisa gestured to Jaune, who sheepishly scratched his cheek as Kiwi glared at him.

"Well… forewarned is forearmed. Now that I know, I can prepare for trouble," he said.

"It's Arasaka," Kiwi retorted, speaking slowly as if to a child. "You should be running back to Europe. Today. Now." She flicked her hand at him. "Why are you still here? Shoo. Shoo."

Jaune barked out a laugh. His head tilted back, looking to the ceiling as he gathered his thoughts.

Within his mind, he straightened out the mess. He ran through the options, the risks and the rewards. The cost of doing the smart thing, and the cost of doing the stupid thing. Or rather…

"Because it's a simple thing," he said. "Because I'm not a good person, as much as I want to be. I don't see the world fairly. A man dies in an aircraft, and it is a sad thing, but life's like that sometimes. A girl burns down a city to reunite with the boy she loves, and I think it's a romantic thing, even if I hate them." He laughed again. "And then there's you. The one who's going to die for doing the right thing."

His eyes fell on Kiwi once more. Blue, meeting red.

"Yeah, I think I can fight for you," he said, nodding to himself. "I'll walk into that trap to make sure nobody could blame you."

He then heaved a rueful sigh.

"Much as I dislike him, it looks like I'm going to rescue David Martinez."


Author's Notes: As stories often do, it comes back to the same three beats.
The knight. The dragon. The princess.
Jaune. Arasaka. David Martinez.
...Wait.
I had an image of Jaune and David teaming up to rescue their people from Arasaka at one point, and for some reason my entire being rebelled against it. There was no way I could see for them to work together like that. And if they try, they were obviously going to die.

Then, on a whim, I put 'David's team' in place of 'David', and suddenly it sounded plausible. Funny, that.

Bring Kiwi to the portal? No! Go throw hands with an army!
I wonder how Lisa feels about that. In a way, he's taking her wishes to heart. In another, he's being an idiot because of it.

#7,174

Chapter 79: Just Another Night City Call to Arms
​


Neon lights marked his destination. They framed an innocuous staircase, dark and drab, where old graffiti painted the walls in psychedelic patterns. Half-dead overhead bulbs cast much of it in shadows. Sketchy? Yes, sketchy was the word Jaune was looking for. An altogether unpleasant hovel that made one question why people waited to go inside.

The line was short, but did not lack for passion. They all had this yearning look on their faces as if there was no place else they'd rather be. The line never once moved.

The instructions Jaune got told him to skip the line. Ignore them, and they would not stop him. Leery as he was, he gave it a shot, leading the way for his team. Sure enough, the moment people saw their group they squashed themselves against the wall without a single word from his lips. Some tried to peek under the 'I❤️NC' cap he bought off a street stall, but he passed them too quickly for that. He went down the steps first, with Escha dangling off his back. Bennett and Fischl trooped in after him; people were all agog, pointing at the raven on Fischl's shoulder. Hu Tao brought up the rear.

The staircase landing opened to… to a maintenance tunnel or something, although that was clearly not its purpose. Concrete gave way to a metal floor, with exposed piping running along the wall and ceiling, all vibrating to a thumping beat emanating from ahead. There, a burly man stood. His mouth was pressed in a thin line, and he let his hand do all the talking. A stop gesture, followed by a spin of the finger and a shooing motion. No matter how much people begged, this was invariably their answer. Not a soul shall pass.

The bouncer guarded a set of double doors made of thick glass on a metal frame. Fogged up, everything behind it blurred in indistinct colors. Jaune approached the man, walking under an archway decorated with a single word.

Afterlife.

The solo's bar. The place where all edgerunners were bound, or so they say.

The people down here were whispering now, having noticed him. Had to be an edgerunner, had to be, he kept hearing. Nobody else would skip the line like that, bold as brass. A few got a clear peek of his face. A name sprang to their lips, not his but close enough. They knew none other, and he hadn't been here before. That last part apparently meant something. Excitement grew with the passing seconds. All eyes turned from him to the bouncer.

On his part, the burly man looked impassive as ever, not even blinking as Bennett waved brightly to him. He eyed Jaune up and down, then pressed a finger to the side of his head in this world's gesture for 'I'm on a call right now', speaking quietly to someone not present. A nod and the call ended, after which the bouncer stepped aside, waving him through. The doors slid apart to give those waiting in line a glimpse of their paradise. A cold wave washed over Jaune as he strode inside.

The bar was chilly. Vents on the walls blew in a winter's frost that dug through the skin, causing the room to feel perpetually on the wrong side of comfort. It bore a marked effect on the patrons, and on him. Each bracing breath he took sharpened the senses. It made him want to fight. It made him want to dance.

Music blasted from hidden speakers, seeming to come out of the very walls. It muted the clanging of his boots on the floor. Everything was of a sleek metal finish, reflecting the lights to cast the windowless space in a bright ambience. Removing his hat, he spun on his heels to take it all in.

Hehe. They had those holographic projectors here, the ones with the strippers. He sold a bunch of them to the Marketplace the other day. Someone, somewhere, loved them.

"Whoa! Is that Johnny?"

Who said it he could not tell, and it did not matter. The cry was taken up by many more, spreading through the room. It brought the inhabitants of the Afterlife into focus.

Leather jackets were in vogue, the same with cybernetic eyes. Most sported additional chrome, to varying degrees. They seemed a rough and tumble lot, brash attitudes screaming they were ready to throw hands at the drop of a hat.

The mercs occupying the tables and booths along the walls refused to merely stand or sit, oh no. They lounged. They posed. Each table resembled a movie poster, the team arrayed to show their best side. Advertising, Jaune realized once he saw a woman with an eyepatch join one table and the people there all crowded around her, a fixer finding her crew.

The fixer happened to glance in his direction, and their eyes met. He could almost see the calculations grinding behind her gaze, before she shook her head and turned away. The crew at her table visibly relaxed, their livelihood safe from the depredation of fixer-stealing blondies.

The other mercs, their job unthreatened at the moment by his presence, took far more interest in him. Those with experience, or were just good at keeping their cool, assessed him out of the corner of their periphery while sipping their drinks. To a one, they would look at his hip to try and find a weapon, a shared habit among their profession. Each had a plan on how to kill him, no doubt.

As for the excitable majority, they pointed and whispered and gawked with bright eyes full of awe. They seemed torn between rushing at him and keeping their distance. Snippets of their conversation reached his ears as he walked toward the bar. His first visit, they kept saying. Flyboy, they called him. Firewalker. Goldstep. Twinkletoes. A story in the making, the title still in flux. It struck him how… glad they were to see him here, like he had come home to where he belonged.

Erm. Minus those Tyger Claws over there who had jumped to take cover behind the couch they were sitting on, crying. Then again, that was normal behavior for them in his experience.

"First impression looks good," he said quietly, scanning the crowd. "Okay, gang. Stick to the plan. Hu Tao, Bennett, Fischl. You've been here before. Go and mingle. Let them know that I'm with you. Escha, look for Tattletale. She should be with Kiwi. I'll head to the bar."

They had to make it appeared natural, of course. Image mattered, as Tattletale unnecessarily warned him. It was better that the team moved on his command than on their own, so he made a show of casually shooing everyone off.

Once he was alone, he walked over to the bar counter.

"Well, well, well, it's Johnny himself!" said the bartender as he sat down on a tall, short-backed stool. "I really didn't think Rogue would let you in. Claire, by the way."

The long counter occupied pride of place at the very center of the room, wrapping around to face multiple walls. Behind it, the bar hosted a large selection of bottles, and rather than sitting on shelves they were stored in small yet deep cabinets. He had heard the story from his friends who came here before, so he was at least somewhat prepared to see the repurposed mortuary drawers which in a bygone era would have held the bodies of the dead. Still, how… morbid.

As for the bartender, a brunette with a friendly smile, he noted the way she commanded the space behind the counter with the confidence of royalty. That Rogue person she talked about was supposed to be the owner of the club, but from her demeanor he got the sense that Claire was the ringmaster of this little circus.

"Nice to meetcha, Claire!" he answered her with the same good cheer she showed him. "I'm Jaune—Johnny, though I guess that's not news. What was that about Rouge? I'm not somehow in trouble already, am I?" He cracked a sheepish grin. The chances were never zero for him to screw something up without his knowing.

Claire shook her head, waving it off. "It's fine. You're in, so you're in. Just keep your head down for a bit to show you're not a troublemaker, and she'll warm up to you in no time."

"Really?"

"No, not really. It's Rogue." Claire shrugged, as if that explained it all. Jaune assumed she intended it as a joke, and laughed.

He couldn't follow that advice, anyway.

Off on one side of the room, Jaune spotted a familiar silhouette, clothed in purple. It accompanied a tall figure in red. He left them alone. His work was here, to be seen and heard. It was all part of the plan. He learned the steps to it in a place called Yuell.

"It's not all because of you, though," said Claire. "She's been peeved all week. Those projectors of ours"—a jerk of her head indicated the hologram strippers—"are getting old and she put in a new order a while ago. The problem is, somebody keeps stealing the shipment before it gets here."

…Oh. Oh no.

"That's awful! How could they?" he said, sweating bullets.

"Right? A lot of horny bastards here are looking to introduce their knuckles to whoever is responsible. Anyway, it's not for you to worry about. What will you be having, hon? I can mix pretty much everything you might fancy."

People were leaning forward. Why were they leaning forward? Was this a test? A dozen ears pricked up to listen in, making him feel rather put on the spot.

"Spirytus—ah, I mean, I'm not really familiar with the drinks around here," he said. Or drinks in general, he thought. "Something… mellow, I guess." The opposite of Spirytus or 'oolong tea', in other words.

The bartender hmmed under her breath. Her eyes went to the ceiling as she pondered the request. "What do they like in Europe?"

Don't ask him. He wouldn't know.

Her expression then brightened, and she snapped her fingers. "Champagne. It fits." She began striding back and forth to snatch things off the shelves without even looking. "Then, if we go light on the gin, harder on the syrup…no, let's take a can of..."

As the woman busied behind the counter, Jaune leaned back in his chair, one leg swinging below to affect an easygoing air. Friendly, and inviting. It did not take long for another customer of the bar to take the bait.

The merc who approached was of a height with Jaune were he to stand, older by maybe half a decade with vague Japanese features. He dressed in the dark, no-nonsense clothes that on Earth meant he was prepared for combat. The goofy grin spelled good intentions, however.

"Not even two weeks. That's gotta be a record for getting in here," the man said, setting his glass on the counter and leaning against the bar. A handgun hung off his belt. "You're crazy, you know that?"

Jaune blinked. "I am?"

"You've been butting heads with David Martinez! Goddamn, buddy. You picked the biggest guy in the room and you punched him in the face!" With a laugh, the man held out his hand. "Welcome to the Afterlife, Johnny. I'm Mike."

"Tiny Mike," Claire said, returning to the counter.

"Claire!" Tiny Mike squawked.

"Hey, you earned your nickname. Wear it with pride."

Claire set a drink in front of Jaune. It came in a tall champagne flute, a bubbly mixture with two tones—a predominantly pale yellow capped with neon green foam. He was no connoisseur, but that didn't look right.

"This is…" he began, puzzling on how to put it.

"My take on a French 75," Claire said, as if that meant anything to him. "Champagne and gin. A dash of Realfruit lime for your fancy-smancy corpo roots and sugar* syrup, with one part ChroManticore Lime to mellow it out further but still give it a kick."

Those were certainly words. What was that asterisk about, anyway?

Jaune gave the cocktail a try under the careful gaze of the bartender. Soon, he was humming in appreciation. The drink went down like juice, refreshing and rather fizzy. The chroma-whatsit must have been a cola.

"Well?" asked Claire.

"I can see it becoming a favorite of mine, that's for sure," Jaune gave his verdict to the bartender's smug satisfaction.

Tiny Mike leaned in, peering at the glass with interest. "That's yours then, is it?" he said, the meaning admittedly passing over Jaune's head. Claire chided him, something about bad luck.

Over the rim of his glass, Jaune observed the room and he soon deemed the time right. The patrons of the bar were paying attention, but the ice had been broken. Tiny Mike and Claire had as good as vouched for him, marking him as one of their own. He took another sip, then set the glass on the counter.

"I hear that if you want to gather a crew, you go to the Afterlife," he said in a casual fashion, to the near instant hush of his surroundings.

"Y-Yeah, that's right. The best of the best in Night City comes here, everybody knows that. Why? You recruiting?" Tiny Mike said, his stupor a mirror of many faces. The man had jolted out of his easygoing pose, and his demeanor bore an eagerness that hadn't been there before.

"For one job, yes," Jaune confirmed. "A real big score."

That got them to sit up.

"Are you serious!?" Tiny Mike nearly squeed. A cough, and he recovered his composure. Or at least put up a facade of it. "Well, don't be shy. What's the deets, brother? A merc's gotta know what he's getting into before he commits to a cause."

Fair enough. Jaune nodded in respect to the sentiment. "Days ago, the Arasaka Corporation abducted David Martinez. They ambushed him while he was down."

If his previous comment got them to sit up, then this one put them on their feet. A roar of voices blasted over him, hollering about how that couldn't be, expressing their disbelief. More than one person regarded him with suspicion, thinking he had something to do with it. That was alright. He dispelled those misgivings with a single sentence.

"Tonight, I'm going to bust him out."

Eyes on me, eyes on me, he thought. Yuell had taught him a lesson in star power. People were stronger than they knew, and would jump into a fight no matter how impossible if only they had someone to stand at the front for them to follow. Here, there were two names to rally around.

He was the rising star. The one with the momentum, the pictures in the news. That counted for a lot.

But Martinez? He was the face of the Afterlife, a son of Night City. That counted for more.

He could already tell the ones itching to sign up. Younger faces. Fresher faces. The dreamers and hotshots following in Martinez's footsteps, swept up in Jaune's hype. They formed a small contingent in this exclusive club that favored veterans, but their foolish hearts guided their decision.

As for those with more experience, they were a bit more reticent. A certain problem loomed large in their minds.

"You, Johnny, are taking on Arasaka," Tiny Mike stated in a strange tone of voice. His eyes darted around, and his cheeks puffed up as he blew out a breath. "Cool. Cool, cool, cool." All of a sudden, being associated with Jaune seemed like a very risky endeavor for him.

"Weren't you two guys enemies?" Claire asked, more bewildered by the fact that he of all people came forward with this proposal.

"We sure are," he answered. He retrieved his cocktail to take a sip, then idly swirled the glass as he looked around. "You hit the nail on the head, Claire. It was us two. Between me and him. Arasaka had no rights to stick their beak into our business. But now that they did… What was it that you said, Mike? 'Pick the biggest guy in the room, and punch him in the face'? That's what I'm doing here. It's what I want you for. The story of David Martinez doesn't get to end like this."

Would he sway them, he decided not to wait to find out. With a flourish of his free hand, a small hill of datashards and eddie bills appeared on the bar counter. Loose pieces cascaded down as rivers, spilling out over the flat surface. The small fortune, and the magic trick, left people gawking.

Lucy offered everything she owned, and since he wouldn't be staying here much longer, Jaune had added earnings from various jobs, back alley reverse-shakedowns, and that time Lisa bet on his underground fighting ring matches into the pot. He plucked a datashard from the pile and flicked the small chip over to Tiny Mike. The amount on it should be about the same as all the others after he asked Kiwi to even out the various sums. As for the result, well, Tiny Mike's shaky hand slid the shard into the slot on his neck (ew!) while his colleagues watched on, and he soon whistled at the number he discovered there. The calculations ran in his head, with him then nodding to confirm that Jaune had one more gun on his side.

Kiwi had drilled a simple concept into his head earlier. He couldn't say he agreed, but hey, she was the one who lived here. Her wisdom was this: edgerunners… liked getting paid. Pretty words only went so far when the news kept lying, the corporations kept lying, the politicians kept lying day in and day out.

So, if he wanted these rebels to fight for a cause, he better show them the money.

On the other side of the room, Tattletale and Kiwi both gave him a thumbs-up. They had gathered a small group of recruits between them. Next to the pair, Lucy showed a stiff, nervous smile. She meant him to be a sacrifice, fighting and falling as a distraction for her to slip away with her man. Now she caught an inkling of his plan, and unfortunately for her, she was already on the ride.

This solo had no intentions of going at it alone.



-o-
​


Tattletale was in fine form, in Jaune's opinion.

"It will work. It's a lot harder to spot a person in the air than one would think, especially when you can spoof the cyberware scans," she explained to the room at large. "Meanwhile, the coolant spray will get his temperature down, and coupled with the sheer heat of that many people gathered together plus all the lights, it should mask his approach from infrared well enough to give him a few more seconds to work with."

She slapped her hand down on the pool table, going right through the holographic map projected on its surface by the device installed in the ceiling. (She was very taken with this piece of tech and advocated stealing a set for themselves.)

"And when he's coming down, I want every scrap of stolen fireworks going off. Screen, screen, screen, people. The snipers they post out there are gonna be blinded by the time we're done, while everybody else will think it's part of the festivities. So remember to touch base with squad E and squad 5, for your explosive needs, 'kay? Any questions?"

A hand rose.

Tattletale stabbed a finger in that direction. "You in the back, from team Alphabet Soup."

A few mercs moved aside, revealing a woman in her thirties with signs of heavy augmentation in her arms. The woman scratched her head.

"I have just the one…. Who are you?"

Tattletale growled. "Oh for the love of—" She beckoned, and Jaune helped her climb on the pool table where she cupped her hands like a megaphone. "I'm a part of Johnny's team! Got that? I'm part of the team! I said this already!"

Somewhere within the assembled crowd, on team Number Salad's side of things, another voice called out, "Yeah well, I never saw you in the videos!"

"I'm his netrunner. If you can see me, there's a problem!" raged the teenage supervillainess.

Kiwi fake-coughed something that sounded suspiciously like 'liar', earning herself a glower from the girl standing on the table.

"What?" said Kiwi. "You guess computer passwords through a game of Cluedo. You're good, but you're not a netrunner by any definition of the word."

That comment set Tattletale off on another round of asserting dominance over everyone in the vicinity, to much tears and grief. Jaune spent this time committing the current iteration of the map to memory, while also keeping an eye on Lucy who for the past ten minutes had been gazing off into the distance with a thousand-yard stare.

The people Lucy helped to gather at the start of this were saboteurs. Netrunners that she knew and advocated for. She had a whole plan of scrambling communications, before setting fires and explosions in multiple places to draw Arasaka forces away from the parade. Depending on how much of Arasaka's intentions she was aware of, this would either be a swift and expedient strategy, or a lie she was selling to excuse throwing him and him alone into the lion's den.

She hadn't expected him to tap additional people for the rescue. Or for the adventurer duo to bring in the friends they made from their last visit to the Afterlife, who brought their friends. Even Hu Tao managed to rope a couple of suckers into it. Apparently, she provided them with coffins at a discount for deaths in the family.

Lucy also hadn't expected to see Tattletale start kicking people out, the supervillainess citing that she could detect their bad intentions and prying way too far into their secrets (including but not limited to whistleblowing tendencies, cowardice, and sexual diseases). Now, Lucy appeared to be living in terror of showing the slightest traitorous thought lest Tattletale called her out on it.

As for the map, it had grown ever more complicated as time went on. The parade would take place on Japantown's largest thoroughfare, where haphazard building codes had led to two solid walls of impossible heights filled in with rooftop plazas and bridges. Behind the windows lay rooms teeming with hidden security forces who were armed better than the Atlas military given what he was seeing in front of his eyes. From sniper nests to robotic drones the size of Imperial tanks to what Kiwi suspected might be corporate ninjas given the messages she intercepted between Faraday and his Arasaka contact, the map glowed in the crimson red color of their foe.

Corporate ninjas were not actual ninjas, to his disappointment. They posed many times the danger, however.

Pockets highlighted in green denoted civilian spaces. Lo and behold, extra viewing areas had opened up at the last minute, so he could look forward to waving at them all from a parade float.

"You okay there, Jaune?" asked Tattletale as she hopped back down to the floor.

"Just perfect," he said, faking it hard.

Tattletale squinted at him. "Uh-huh. If you say so. Anywho, it's your turn to report. How did it go with Wakako?"


"I named you after a fool, and hoped for you to die. I knew you'd bring trouble."
​

Jaune heaved a long breath. "Wakako will do as I ask. She owes me that much." He looked down at the map, despondent at the memory. "You were right, by the way."

Tattletale read the whole of the story from his eyes. Uncannily for her, she did not say that she told him so.

There was apparently a saying in Night City, that people remembered a legend by how they die.

The fixer had been in on it, accepting work from Arasaka to pit him against Martinez's crew. She excused it by saying that one did not live long by refusing Arasaka, yet she was far too happy to milk their purse for all it was worth. Would she have backstabbed him in a worse way, given time? He dreaded the answer to that.

He still struggled to understand the full implication of what the old woman meant, the things she spoke to his back as he walked away. But in the end, it was clear that she never saw him as he thought she did.

A hand came to rest on his shoulder. Kiwi was peering at him with an impassive gaze. "If you like, I can hack her implants. Give her a really bad day," she said in a soft, almost sympathetic tone. The actual words leaned more toward ice-cold, though.

Jaune gave a short laugh, and shook his head. "No need. I owe her some, despite it all." He cocked his head, and his smile grew more genuine. "You know, that guy doesn't deserve a teammate as kind as you."

"Stop it…" Kiwi demurred, turning away from him.

He shook off his malaise and returned his attention to the briefing, addressing Tattletale. "Have you figured out which float Martinez will be on?"

Tattletale let out a frustrated noise. "I'm getting there. We have ten options to choose from... Technically, there's also a bunch of smaller sub-floats, but their positions wouldn't make sense."

"He's got to be in the middle," said an edgerunner on the other side of the pool table. "Every convoy I've ever intercepted has their valuables in the middle car."

Tattletale waggled her hand in an iffy gesture. "I'd agree with you, but if the lineup stays the same as in the brochure, then that float provides too much cover. They will want him in a nice open space. The second, third, and seventh float from the front is a better bet."

"This is too complicated," someone complained. "We should raid them before they load him on."

"If you know where they're keeping him, do tell us," said Kiwi drily.

"It's not a big deal, at any rate," Tattletale added. "This step can remain flexible until go-time. I'll just have to scope it out during the parade. What you should concern yourself with is what happens after my partner here lands." She bumped him with her hips. "Every Arasaka soldier in play will converge on him."

Tiny Mike nodded. "And that's when we strike."

"Some of you," Tattletale corrected, and jerked her thumb at Jaune. "Remember that our best card is him. Free him up to do his thing and he's a one-man army. He'll get Martinez out of there, and he'll get you out of there."

It did his ego wonders, the way the people around him seemed to take that at face value. They believed. And when he opened his mouth to speak, they stopped to listen.

"Do try to make some noise, though," he said with a mild grin. "It's a festival, after all."

That got him a round of chuckles. The nature of edgerunners, on the whole, was of one loud song screamed into a microphone. Making noise was what they did best.

He kept the actual reason close to heart, which is that the bigger the mess he caused, the better Kiwi's part in it could fade to the background. This entire endeavor was a balancing act of taking plausible steps for someone in his position without alerting Arasaka that he was privy to insider knowledge, while utterly humiliating them. In an ideal world, the architects behind the scheme were going to face the kind of trouble from their bosses that made revenge against Kiwi an inconsequential priority. Perhaps then she would be free to go her own way.

"Your squad leaders have the checklist of objectives I handed out," Tattletale reminded them all, while Kiwi fiddled with the hologram. Emblems of the various edgerunner crews populated the map, with arrows showing the directions they should go. Colors pulsed to highlight obstacles they could expect to meet. "I will field questions later but go over it with them, and be sure you know what we're asking. Outside of that, anything goes."

"That's all fine and good," said a woman who had slipped her way forward to study the map. "But what about the endgame? The exfil? This entire op is a bust if that David kid can't get away."

"Johhny has it handled, right?" Tiny Mike said, and mimed a pair of flapping wings.

"Going up might seem expedient for a guy that can fly, but it limits options," the woman, an older lady with punkish hair, replied. "You don't want to get caught on a rooftop with no way off."

"I can't drag his fat butt up there anyhow," Jaune further provided. "Going down is no good either, so long as the crowd remains on the scene. A descent would draw fire that could get some people hurt."

The woman snorted, as did Tiny Mike. "Try everybody dead. Arasaka isn't known for their careful regard toward collateral damage."

"Is that true, though?" Jaune asked with a wince. "They would be causing a massacre. That's insane."

Kiwi shrugged, chiming in, "Bribe the police to clear the bodies. Direct the news to blame it on you and David. Business as usual."

"Blame me for what, not standing still to get shot? How does that make sense?"

"It doesn't, but they'll do it anyway and everyone will believe it. Even those who were at the festival."

An edgerunner grumbled. "News literacy's been in the crapper since 2050." He seemed to be speaking from experience, the way he swiped a finger over the scars on his face.

Neither down nor up, unless circumstances aligned. That left one path open if Jaune was inclined toward escaping.

"Your best bet is to go through the buildings," the old woman said. "Prepare breaching charges, because they're built back to back for blocks, and the one you find yourself in might only exit out at a bad location. Always have a contingency. The more horizontal distance you put between yourself and a pursuer, the better."

Jaune gave her a grateful nod. "Thanks for the advice, old-timer—" He paused as Kiwi nudged him.

"Don't call her old," she hurriedly whispered. "That's Rogue Amendiares. She'll kick us out in a heartbeat if we annoy her."

He blinked, and turned his gaze back toward the old, ahem, the finely-aged woman.

"Wait a minute, you own the Afterlife? What are you doing over here?" he asked her.

The woman had her scars that she wore with pride. Her clothes suited a person that needed to spring into action at any moment, with chrome armor built into her body. She might have been a solo once upon a time. She stood like one.

Rogue thought on his question, panning her gaze from one face to the next. "For my amusement, I reckon. When I heard that half my mercs were setting out to bail their choom from a megacorp, it sounded like a lark."

He might be the better liar between them, because for him, her words did not ring with the truth. Her voice was sad and sweet, and a little lost. She must have noticed it, too, for she pressed on.

"I figured you bunch of cyberpunks could use some advice on how to avoid a real afterlife."

Jaune leaned on the table, and tilted his head to the side.

"A cyber-wha?"

The term was unfamiliar. Yet, its meaning was somehow not. He saw the answer all around him. The ones bought, and the ones starstruck. Those who carried a chip on their shoulder against the megacorps, and those chasing a dream. They went from shifty looks and tense stances, to something more certain.

The mistress of the Afterlife responded with a wry smirk.

"An idiot, 'Johnny'. It means an idiot."

"Well," Jaune said. "That's not making me feel very confident."

Rogue Amendiares just laughed, on and on.

For Night City, this festival would be one to remember.

Expect either two chapters next week, or one big chapter at the end.
