One way or another, they met in the Afterlife.

They hadn't ended up here to lick their wounds, though a corner of the bar did turn into a clinic to treat the injured. No, the edgerunners returned victorious and with that came celebration. The mother of all parties was taking place in the underground club to shake the building above. Music, alcohol, and fistfights counted as the starters, with more to come.

Some cried as they danced. Not everyone made it out alive, and the curious rituals of edgerunners for a fallen friend was a thing Jaune only partly understood, but went all in for. As they had won, as their comrades had gone out in a glorious end, the place of the living was to party on as if each day was their last. In Night City, it might well be.

Maybe not in the same way, this time.

As the running news report on the overhead screens around the room could attest, the Aratama-Matsuri Festival had taken a turn nobody foresaw. The scene of hero Adam Smasher heroically mounting a heroic defense of valuable Arasaka Corporation property against anarchic terrorists played out again and again over the airwaves, reaching every corner of the city, and beyond. Whether anybody believed the official story, which flip-flopped about five times thus far before settling on the current iteration, was beside the point. Adam Smasher had been a war asset, a boogeyman, an investment, and a symbol wrapped up into one.

A Legend.

Jaune hadn't known back then what he had done. The world, in a small way, shook from the aftershocks of his actions.

And he should probably bug out before the consequences drop on his head, or so the general sentiment went. Half the mercs in attendance would be doing that very same thing with the rising of the sun. In the gun-for-hire business, a successful gig often meant a period of lying low, and this job? Whoo, boy. Rogue Amendiares was busy organizing a whooole lot of exfil packages in between her drinking away half of the bar's stock.

The Queen of Fixers seemed quite giddy, even though she'd have to contract newbies for her jobs around the city for a good while. There was a story there.

But those were concerns for tomorrow. Tonight, they lived it up.

"Lisa, hey~" Jaune said happily, dropping onto a seat at the bar and slinging his arm around his partner's shoulder. The girl leaned into it, a red glow to her face, well on her way to tipsy.

"Hey, 'Johnny'," she replied with a light laugh. "Having fun?"

He gave an emphatic nod. "I used to not think much of the music here, but it's growing on me."

"Mmhm. Fischl seems to agree."

Said girl was on the dance floor with the edgerunner named Rebecca, headbanging to a song with her hands in the air. The princess from another world had gathered a court of followers. If Jaune was not mistaken, some of them had adopted her manner of speech and poses, teaching her in return of rockstars and devil horns.

"What happened to her minder?" he wondered.

Tattletale jerked her thumb in the opposite direction of Fischl. Jaune followed it to see Oz and Escha being fed snacks. Bennett was also on that side, joking around with mercs who ruffled his hair and egged him on to throw a dart at a target.

Struck by an idle thought, Jaune scanned the room, searching for the last member of their group. He frowned as he saw her drinking tea at one of the booths set along the wall. Not because he had any problems with teas or booths or walls, as that would be kind of nuts, but because of her companion. Wakako had taken leave of her office to partake in the festivities, teacup in one hand and cigarette in the other. His eyes met hers, and the old woman stubbornly stared him down. Then, Lucy sat down at the booth, and Jaune decided to move on before he had another person glaring at him. There were better things he could be doing with his time.

"You know…" he said, his voice dropping to a low, husky whisper. As hoped, it sent a shiver through Lisa. She gazed up at him, studying his face, and—

"Nope."

Jaune paused, eyes blinking blankly. "Nope?"

Tattletale, rapidly sobering, put up both her hands in surrender. "Nope," she confirmed, and pushed away from the table. "I know this pattern. I know what you're thinking. I wanna be able to walk tomorrow, thank you."

"Oh puh-lease, you got this."

"I do not, in fact, got this."

With that, the girl grabbed her drink glass and waded into the crowd, leaving Jaune alone at the bar.

"Fucking oof," said the person who took her seat.

"Oh, shut it," Jaune grumbled to David Martinez, before raising an eyebrow. "Hang on a minute, should you be up and about?" As Claire the bartender placed a glass in front of the edgerunner, he continued. "Or drinking? This definitely looks unsafe."

The other boy waved away the concern. "It's no problem. Doc gave the go ahead."

The random bits and bobs dangling outside of Martinez to serve as makeshift replacement for broken functions within his body suggested that this 'doc' should have his license revoked. Jaune was pretty sure he saw a beating heart among them, but didn't want to look again to check. The boy still lacked an arm, and a mess of fluid bags and tubes pumped chemicals and new blood into the edgerunner's metal chest, keeping him in a somewhat stable state.

Martinez sipped his drink. Jaune could tell there was a question on his mind, but given no prompts for further conversation, he followed the example and left it alone for now. The fizzy champagne cocktail Claire made for him went down rather easily, and as he finished one, he signaled for another. The two of them quietly sat there for a while, taking in the ambience of the party.

"How do you do it, Johnny?" Martinez finally said.

Jaune turned his head. "Hm?"

The other boy was staring into his cup, expression maudlin with one foot swinging below the barstool. His gaze had drifted to a booth by the wall, locked on a certain girl.

"It's just… You kept going," Martinez blurted out in a rush. "You kept your team in one piece. You took on everybody. You do crazy things without batting an eye. And after all that, you won. You won," he repeated as a hopeless whisper. Where I didn't, went the unspoken words.

Jaune thought on how best to answer, and summed it up succinctly.

"I cheat."

Something, something, powers from another world and all that.

The answer did not seem to please Martinez, however. The boy gave a groan, and slumped over the table. "I don't mean your fancy chrome. They're not what did it. I thought they were in the beginning, but more metal didn't save me, or Maine, or Adam Smasher." He gestured with his one remaining arm, up and down to indicate everything about him. "They didn't unfuck my screwed-up life."

Now, Jaune understood what the other boy was saying. A disbelieving laugh slipped out of him, and he pointed at himself. "You think I have it together?"

Martinez raised his head.

"Don't you?"

Jaune scoffed and leaned an elbow on the bar counter. Taking up his cocktail by the thin stem, he studied the contents within as he contemplated a response. The cold vapors of the Afterlife had frosted the surface, catching the neon lights and reflecting it into the pale gold champagne to form a kaleidoscope of colors, like broken glass. He tipped back the cocktail. The drink landed smoothly.

The stem spun between his fingers as he spoke.

"If that's true, then why do I sometimes feel like a mess of a person? I feel like I'm as lost as anyone. I think I'm walking forward, yet I've ended up so far from home. I've hurt so, so many people along the way and I tell myself that was alright. Where am I going? What am I doing? I never know for sure."

He released a long sigh, and turned from the glass to look at the other boy.

"Tell me, David, how do you see anything but another idiot?"

David Martinez squeezed his hand into a fist, looking down at his lap. And in that moment, Jaune got the sense that this boy, out of everyone in this world or any other, saw the truth at its clearest.

"Would you do it any differently?" said that boy.

Do it better, do it right. Change what led him here. Change the him who stood here.

There was a reason he didn't deserve to be in Beacon.

"Not on your life. But I wish I didn't regret it."

Martinez nodded, and in tandem the two raised their glasses in the air. They drank to the better version of themselves that never were.

The party raged on, as if it could stave off tomorrow. David Martinez bade leave to go and pull his lover onto the dance floor, while others dragged Jaune into giving yet another recounting of the night's events. Their paths did not cross again, though they never said goodbye.

He joined in on the dancing once a particularly good number began to play, but there was an odd feeling dwelling in his chest as he did so. The feeling was always there when it came to dancing. He taught Fischl a few moves, and Bennett, too. He tried to snag Tattletale in a dance a few times, but she kept cheekily sticking out her tongue before giving him the slip.

Little wonder, then, that he ended up heading back to the bar alone. The occasion called for a drink.

It was during this time that a voice reached his ears.

"Hi, stranger."

Jaune turned, and smiled. "Don't say that, Kiwi. I'll be glad to call you a friend. Here, sit down." He offered her the seat next to him. "What brings you around?"

"Thanks. And your… friend, Lisa, mentioned you could use the company."

Kiwi settled on the seat and placed her order with the bartender, but Jaune didn't get to hear it amid all the commotion. His companion had to lean toward his side of the counter for them to talk. She, just like each person who had taken part in his plan, had been grilled and grilled for details until she was sick of it, so they steered the conversation to lighter subjects. From the nitty-gritty of netrunning, of which the Net apparently had a whole digital rendition of the world that people like Kiwi can walk into, to some of the sights he had seen on his journey, disguised as that convenient and fantastical land they call Europe. Where cats talk and blondies fly.

"I heard you're setting out tomorrow," Kiwi said during a lull.

He nodded, a little tipsily. "Yuuup. With the festival over, that's pretty much it for me here, and with most of the blame for that fiasco falling on my end, Rogue suggested I leave before Arasaka can finish putting together an investigation." Which was really corporate double-speak for 'a punitive force intended for the holistic task of asset retrieval and/or liquidation of all liabilities'. It was a fascinating language, excelling in economy of meaning. "Aren't you heading out soon, too? David mentioned something about Africa."

"Nairobi, yes," Kiwi confirmed. "But that's only for him and Lucy. Maybe Rebecca, too. They picked it because it has a space program."

Oh yeah, people were colonizing the moon here. That was just wild.

"What about you?"

Kiwi waved her hand dismissively. "The moon is nice to look at. Slaving away for the chance to stand on a barren rock doesn't interest me as much. Since the team is disbanded, I figured I can set out on my own." She mulled on it. "I think I'll visit Asia, or… or Europe. Maybe we'll see each other out there."

Jaune put on a bright face, nodding. They wouldn't, he wanted to tell her.

Kiwi fidgeted, and Jaune experienced a premonition. The woman crossed her arms on the table, resting her head on them as she stared at him, blinking her feline-like eyes.

"Or I can just skip the detours," she said. "Can I convince you to take me along?"

He winced slightly, looking straight ahead. "That's… a bigger ask than you know."

Kiwi waited for a long beat, watching him.

"A shame," she said in the end. "But then again, we have all night. Who knows where it may lead."

Those cryptic words went unaddressed as the bartender interrupted their conversation to set down a drink in front of Kiwi, who sat up to accept the glass. Jaune peeked at the simple amber liquid contained within, garnished with a chili to add flair. Plus a straw.

"Ever had one?" Kiwi asked him upon noticing his curiosity, and he shook his head. "Really? You've never tried a Johnny Silverhand?"

He shook his head once more. "No. Cool name, though. Why does it sound familiar?" he wondered.

Kiwi blinked slowly. "You don't know? I just assumed he was your namesake. It was a popular one for a while."

"I'm not from around here, you know that," he said with an easygoing shrug.

"Huh."

Kiwi tapped the counter with a finger, thinking, before turning her body more toward him. Her long legs uncrossed and crossed again. She propped her chin with an arm on the table while playing with the plastic straw in her glass.

"Well, if you're curious, do you have time for a story?" she said.

Jaune held his drink up in a toast.

"Like you've said, we have all night."

Something flashed in Kiwi's eyes. He could have imagined it, but in this world, it could also be the blue glow of a net search or money transfer or whatever.

"We do, don't we?" said Kiwi. "Alright, how about this? Let's trade a few stories." She tilted her head, her eyes becoming half-lidded. "And maybe later, I can show you this spiderweb tattoo I have. It's pretty neat."

It sounded like a fine time. Jaune answered by clinking their glasses together.

He sat back in his seat, as Kiwi cleared her throat and began to recount the tale of a Legend.

"The year was 2023, and Night City was the place to be. Then, one evening, a man named Johnny burst through the doors of the Afterlife…"

The chill soaked into his skin. He would know this cold anywhere.

Jaune opened his eyes to sightless sky of the Void.

His bed had become a slab of unyielding rock with little comfort to be had. Jutting spires formed a canopy at his back, while the stone floor transformed mere steps from the bed to become the concrete of a highrise rooftop. The roof was empty but for a lone figure standing opposite him, right up against the ledge. The young man dressed in a drab brown coat was peering over the side of the building, his toes precariously teetering over the empty air.

Jaune stepped off the bed, and walked across the roof. The sound of his footsteps on the concrete led him to realize that he was wearing his boots, and his Gallian-blue jacket. In a dream, this would be the point he woke up.

New details emerged as he approached the Outsider. Islands in the Void, bearing upon their backs not quite a city, but pieces of one fitting together in an incomplete jigsaw puzzle. The tables and chairs of a meeting room. An office placed up high. Cubicles and break rooms. Sections of a bridge led nowhere, carrying cars that came from nowhere.

Jaune could picture from these fragments the entire length of the bridge, the sound of honking horns and the fumes from the exhaust. He saw Night City everywhere he looked. He stepped up on the ledge beside the Outsider, and directed his gaze down. Far, far below, there was a city street with still figures in mid-stride, another scene transplanted from reality. A person down there was looking up at him.

"It's been a while," he said as a greeting. "I almost thought you'd forgotten me."

The Outsider spoke without looking at him. "Never, Jaune. You are as interesting to me as the day we met. You give things perspective."

"Oh." Jaune rubbed the back of his neck. "That's flattering… I think."

A rumble passed through the stillness. Islands sank, and others rose. Different scenes, different people. The day continued in Night City, stone by stone. The person looking up at Jaune had stepped aside, and now looked down at the pavement. There was nothing there.

"What a busy place," The Outsider said. "So large. So small. I see each of their lives. They call it the daily grind, and my, how it grinds."

"They seem to do okay," Jaune argued without heat, for he knew it as a lie. He had seen those tired faces walking by. Hurrying, hurrying, without time to stop. For him, it had been an adventure. They lived there.

The Outsider voiced the words in his mind for him. "You stand where few could. Some days, you face Leviathan. And some days, you are Leviathan. Perspective, as I said." He returned his attention to the scene. "I believe I am supposed to pity them, yet I do not. It may be why we met today."

Jaune frowned. "You mean, you didn't bring me here?"

"No." The Outsider cocked his head. "Not in the way that you think. The scene before us holds no significance were you not here as witness. And thus, you are. You give it shape. You give it meaning."

Those pitch black eyes bore into him.

"Tell me, what do you see? What do you feel, you mess of a person?"

The Outsider often professed to Jaune of a boredom so total that the barest modicum of emotion sometimes lie beyond him. On occasions, and this was one such, Jaune caught a glimpse into what that truly entailed, of the desperation behind the impassive countenance that wished to know what it was like to be human.

So, he peered out over the city, and gave it his full consideration.

He first saw the shape of the whole. The buildings and roads formed by the scenes blending together. The smokestacks of the factories spewing their smoke, and Arasaka Tower. He saw Night City.

But it was just a name.

His eyes were playing tricks on him, for the longer he looked, the more he picked out of the individual moments. Scenes that he swore had not been there until he focused on them.

There, was Cherry Blossom Market. They had rebuilt it better than ever, although the only bits of wood present in the construction were the new signboards hanging above each stall.

And there! Wakako was sitting in her office, the one at the back of a pachinko parlor. She had a new solo standing at attention before her desk, who she probably wouldn't invite for tea. They lacked the flair he liked to think he brought to the job. Or maybe that was his ego talking.

With those as reference points, he sought out the familiar places, tracing the paths created by his steps. His gaze drifted up a tower, up, up, up to an apartment unit with a balcony. The excitement of spotting his lodgings for the past couple of weeks faded as he discovered it had a new tenant, a well-to-do corpo working on a computer.

Suddenly uncertain, he continued on. He found the machine shop on the outskirts of the city, where an old man was engrossed in his next project. The targets out back had fallen down with nobody to pick it up.

A car was riding past the shop, carrying David Martinez and his crew. What lay beyond on that road, Jaune did not see. There was only the Void from this side of things. They never looked back at the city.

Back and forth, back and forth. His eyes flew over the paths he trod until he came to the urban ravine which had hosted the festival, and where a Legend fell. Its road was spotless, thick with cars and pedestrians. For them, today was another day, same as the last and same as tomorrow. The daily grind pressed on. It was as if nothing ever happened.

He was rather taken aback by the feeling surging within him at this sight. He couldn't quite put a word to it. A red-hot, indignant anger swelled at the forefront, seconded by the sensation of standing beside a plunging cliff. And… melancholia, behind it all.

There had been something here. A hundred disparate souls throwing in their lot, risking themselves for a small yet wonderful purpose. To save a life. Did that not have meaning? Could that not shine forevermore as a light in the dark?

Jaune looked far and long, and he saw nothing of him. How strange, that that mattered so much. In lieu of an answer to the Outsider's question, he asked one of his own.

"Will they forget me?"

Then again, perhaps for the Outsider that served as an answer in and of itself.

"Everything fades, Jaune," the Outsider said.

Jaune thought of what the young man with dark eyes truly wanted from him, the thing he called perspective. Scale was unimportant. The god needed no deep thoughts or philosophical musings. He expected no grand views that would encapsulate Night City in a neat pithy quote.

In the end, the bitterness revealed within a small and insignificant being was what drew the Outsider's curious gaze.

"They will remember you in the little places."

Jaune opened his eyes, only then realizing he had closed them in the first place. He turned to the Outsider, who looked back at him. Directly, at him.

"Everything fades, Jaune," the Outsider repeated the earlier sentiment. "Even now, the truths are mixed with lies. Your story is changing with each retelling. Those events you lived through will continue to distort, tear apart, and reshape until one day you would not even recognize the man within the tale, the you that they wished you were.

"But they will remember you in the little places, in little ways."

A gloved hand casually pointed ahead, and Jaune's gaze followed where it led. The islands within the Void were sparse there. He made out a brick wall, some graffiti. Not much else.

"Would-be killers walk carefully down the dark alleys of Japantown, while the honest laborer ventures with surer steps. Imitators take up your colors, some to enact violence and some to stop it depending on where they heard your name. The red and white herald bloody days, and peaceful nights."

The Outsider directed Jaune's attention eastward to the desert.

"Out in the Badlands, a young man learns the tale of a hero, and of a call to arms. He sets his sight on the city in the distance."

This time, he pointed to the west.

"Within Arasaka tower, a woman watched her mighty masters scream and rage, and very carefully hid a smile. She thanked the Butcher of 2076 for the fine show."

The gloved hand moved south.

"In a Heywood bar, a solo finds a new gun for his cause, and a new fire. They were going to the Afterlife, whatever it took."

Jaune's heart thundered in his chest, for with the places that the Outsider showed him, he had begun to discern an oddity amid the islands within the Void. Scenes that did not fit within the tableau, a hidden pattern that, with a shift in perspective, moved to the forefront.

A blink of the eyes, and it sharpened into stark clarity from the blades of grass to the clouds in the sky. A city behind the city, a small place of little note that never really mattered in the grand schemes of things, yet meant so much to him.

The rubble had been cleared from the cobblestone roads. Workers climbed among the beams of new houses being raised. Trucks chugged along the street, bearing new goods to fill the shelves of market stalls. Children played games at the base of a myrtle tree in bloom, while on a hill the bell towers of the university stood tall.

Springtime had arrived again, and Yuell was rebuilding.

Familiar faces stood out to him. Walter wore an apron as he cooked in a restaurant kitchen, still with a pair of sunglasses covering his eyes. Dark-haired Magari was exiting a shop, a stack of books in her arms. Nearby, Marina stopped to rest in the shade of a statue. She no longer wore a military uniform, and her casual set of clothes clashed hard with the futuristic rifle slung over a shoulder.

Jaune laughed at the statue. That hadn't been there before.

It depicted a trio of people, and right off the bat he did not recognize one of them. A man in a dandy suit lurking behind the others, fedora on his head tipped low in a manner that obscured the features of his face. The kind of figure that came to mind when one thought of a spy.

The second person was a girl. No, a woman, with curves to die for. Her sculptor had put in the work to make that clear. Her grin could have melted hearts and sparked wars. She held a radio set in one hand, a military coat draped over her shoulders.

The third… The third was true to life. Smaller in a way, as a result. He liked how they made his smile.

Beyond the statues and the city, far past the clouds, Jaune thought he saw something in the air flying across the blue sky.

He drank in the sight. At which point the steps appear, he failed to notice, but they were there when he looked. They led down to a bar counter lined with neon lights, where the Outsider had already occupied a seat.

Still with his attention on the city in the distance, Jaune descended the steps. The Outsider had a drink, an actual drink, in his hand, although not one that Jaune recognized from the Afterlife menu. A shocking blue base crowned with a fizzy layer in bright yellow, served on the rocks. A cocktail sword stuck out of the glass. A more familiar glass sat in front of the empty barstool next to him. Jaune took that one.

"They will remember you in the little places, in little ways," said the Outsider.

Jaune glanced at the menu, toward the bottom where the bartender had added a new item to the list. Its name was a play on the drink favored by the Legend who fought Night City and made it out alive.

The Johnny 76. A year to remember.

He raised the glass high and clinked it to his companion's in a toast.

In Night City, it was the best ending a solo could hope for.



A large van drove up a mountain road, winding its way through the forest. The trees grew tall and thick here, and an unseasonal snowstorm had coated the world in a blanket of blinding white. The strong winds gently rocked the car to make it drift from one side to the other.

The van rounded the last bend, breaking out of the forest gloom and into a clearing where its destination came into view. A log house stood at the end of the lane, two stories high with a balcony on the second floor. It sat upon a hill, next to a small lake that glittered in the late morning sun. The occupants of the van oohed and ahhed at the picturesque scene. Located an hour's drive from New York City, this tranquil respite would be their new lodgings for a while, a place where the strange peculiarities about them could pass without remark as they continued their extraordinary days.

The front doors of the log house opened to a bright and airy room, with the floor-to-ceiling glass window overlooking the lake letting in the sunlight.

"Dibs on the biggest bedroom."

The one sentence heralded bedlam. Suddenly, everybody was clamoring to get inside.

"You wish, Hu Tao. I'm the one who rented this place, so that means the biggest bedroom belongs to me!"

"I want my own room! I want my own room!"

"Well, I care not for size and merely request that my private chambers be aligned with my element, for it should be calamitous indeed were the glaring light of mine ancient enemy to sear away my powers during my repose."

"Milady, you must learn to wake up early one of these days. The sun is good for you."

"Is there a bedroom that isn't attached to anything structurally important? I'll take that one, please."

In moments, the log cabin became a loud, boisterous place thundering with activity. Jaune had to smile. Now, it felt like a home.

Before he followed the others in, he looked back.

"Hey, are you coming?"

"Hm? Oh. Yes, in a bit."

"Is something wrong?"

"Nothing. It's just… this is my first time seeing snow. It's beautiful."


Author's Notes: Another adventure comes to a close, and a new one begins. But never let it be said that any of them didn't matter.

"I really want to bring back that rabbit one of these days."
–the idle musing of a writer who would like to see the main character cry.

The Johnny 76 - A French 75 with lighter notes. That, and a story. It was a year to remember.

#7,778

Chapter 81: The Thing That Goes Bump in the Night
​


Jaune laid in blissful darkness, heart and mind becalmed. He had just settled down to rest.

This moment seemed to last barely a blink of an eye before he heard a gentle rapping above. Then came the sound of wood scraping on wood. A crack of light pierced his sanctuary. Peering beyond it, he found the faces of his friends waiting for him.

There were far fewer than seen in his dreams. But for now, that was alright. It ached a little less, each day.

Jaune sat up, stretching with a yawn. He accepted the hand Lisa offered to pull him from the coffin where he slept. Outside the window, the sun was shining.

To the new morning awaiting him, he put on a smile and said, "Hello again."



-o-
​


The log cabin boasted an open floor plan on the first level, without any real divide between living room, dining room, or kitchen. A room suited for a house party were one so inclined, it measured more than twice the size of the apartment, the portal to which was now anchored to an empty stretch of wall next to the kitchen. Having that much usable space was, honestly, a little disorienting.

Jaune spent his first morning there decluttering the old apartment, putting boxes of supplies, tools, and various knickknacks he picked up in his travels to a proper place. Clothes went into wardrobes in separate rooms on the second floor. Weapons were stowed on shelves in the garage. The garden of herbs and mushrooms stayed where they were for the moment, as most of them did not fare well in a winter chill. Same deal with the bugs. The apartment soon grew comfortable again, perfect for someone—him, but disputed by Lisa—to claim as their bedroom. With help from the others, he was down to the last few items after not even an hour.

The task would have gone even faster had he done it by himself, since he could load it up into his Pocket for ease of transport, but he wasn't going to tell Escha, Bennett, or Fischl that. They had been so eager to lend a hand, and in any case it made for a decent team activity that would familiarize them with the house and where the different supplies were stored.

As for those uninterested in that, they were off doing their own thing.

"So, what do you think of the 'inter-net' here?" Jaune asked as he walked by the long couch facing the TV and the floor-to-ceiling window. The half-full drum of volatile whale oil on his shoulder sloshed with each step.

"Workable."

A smile popped to his lips at that, and he moved on to set the drum inside a storage trunk where nobody would touch it without cause. The oil served as a propellant in the wristbows Lisa favored, and had lasted for a long while with how sparingly the supervillainess ventured into combat. Now, it saw better use as an enhancer for Escha's explosive barrels, which had led to the container emptying out at a much faster rate. They would need to find a substitute at some point. Or hunt a whale, but Lisa told him that wouldn't fly here.

Speaking of whom…

On his way back he passed the dining table, where he paused to peek over Lisa's shoulders. The dizzying amounts of charts and texts on the laptop screen in front of her made his eyes go blurry at once. Certain words managed to jump out to him, however. Dispersion field. Personal realities and vectors. Quantum, quantum, and more quantum. He might be able to take a guess at the meaning for some of those, but as a whole they were utterly confounding to his unscientific mind.

"I thought you were going to start small," he said.

Without looking at him, Lisa crossed her arms and sat back in her chair. A small, frustrated noise slipped out from between her lips.

"A girl can dream, can't she? I just want to check how viable the major developments from Academy City are to this Earth. They have people here pulling billions in investments for one startup idea. Stock trading looks like a kid's game compared to that…"

"And you couldn't resist playing in the big leagues," he finished the thought. He leaned down more, putting his face next to hers to study the various texts. Nope, still unreadable. "What's the problem, then?" he ventured instead.

Lisa scoffed. "Half of the underlying concepts tying these research papers together don't exist yet. It looks fake, and it'd take us years to prove it even if we got a team of scientists working to bridge the gap." She paused, and raised a finger. "And yeah, okay, that probably wouldn't stop us from making bank anyway, but if we want to pull this off over the long term, then scamming investors right off the bat would just come back to bite us."

Jaune considered reminding her that 'billions' could fund their operations for decades and beyond, but the part about cheating people out of their money did indeed leave a bad taste in his mouth. They should be robbing from those who deserve it, fair and square, as honest criminals were supposed to.

…Some days, he wondered what had become of his life.

At that moment, the cleaning robot rolled by. The device spun round and round as it scooped up every speck of dirt its scanner could detect. Somehow, it was going twice as fast as usual, on several occasions teetering on the verge of tipping over with how hard it took a turn, adding to the general chaos of moving house by tripping up everybody else. Bennett spilled a box of tools and instantly the robot was there to try and suck up a hammer in its intake vent.

It seemed almost happy if such a thing was possible for a geometric cylinder, zooming back and forth between the two dwellings.

He pointed the robot out for Lisa. "What about that?"

"I'm not going into business selling stupid roombas, Jaune. People already have that here." Lisa leveled a harsh glare at the laptop. "Give me something with more oomph, will you?" she demanded.

The laptop sat there, smugly silent.

Jaune patted Lisa on the shoulder to comfort her, trying to convey all his warmth. "Well, don't get discouraged because if there's anything I know about you, it's that you'll always figure out a problem. Maybe you can try and hit a good middle ground—"

"I already have five ideas that can go to market if we pull together enough seed money for prototypes."

"Give me back my worries. I thought you were in actual trouble."

"You just don't get it," Lisa complained with a sigh. "At a ballpark estimate, they'll only net us ten to fifty millions in the first few years."

The absolute tragedy.

He turned away, shaking his head and giving the matter its proper due—which was none. In any case, all this talk of business was pinging something in his memories. As Escha padded over to request leave to explore the surrounding forest, which soon led to the felyne racing out the doors with Bennett and Fischl in tow, he thought and thought about it until it suddenly clicked into place. He tapped Lisa with a finger to regain her attention.

"By the way… If you do plan to start a company, can you take some time to help Hu Tao with the paperwork for hers, too?"

There was a gasp, and Hu Tao poked her head into the room through the portal. "You remember!"

"How could I not?" he said, looking a lot more confident than he felt.

"For the humble coffin-seller, business is always booming."

"Are you certain that your cough is just the flu? It can always be a sign of something worse!"

"Would you like to hear more about our couples promotion?"

"Silly-churl, billy-churl, silly-billy hilichurl~!"
​
…Okay, so that last one was fine, but still. A funeral business operating with Hu Tao's brand of enthusiasm continued to confuse him in many ways. Was there a demand for it? Hu Tao seemed dead set that there was, boasting about the enormous boosts in sales after she took over the Wangsheng Funeral Parlor.

What did that translate to in hard numbers? Don't ask. Enormous, she assured him.

"And don't forget," said Hu Tao as she fully entered this side, toying with a lock of hair, a bright smile blooming, "you have to visit a cemetery with me this week."

Right, that. Jaune gave Hu Tao a stiff nod, showing none of his doubts behind a stoic demeanor. No point regretting it now, his careless promise to help her scope out the competition guaranteed that he would be knee-deep in that mess given time. The cemetery must grow, or whatever.

"Bring a shovel," she added.

His composure snapped like a twig. "But why!?"

Hu Tao snickered. "Oh please, don't you fret. It isn't like we will be digging anybody out of their grave."

Oh, thank goodness. His hand went to his chest, and he was just about to sigh in relief when Lisa chimed in on the conversation.

"What's with the oddly specific emphasis?" she asked.

That astute observation quickly led to many side-eyes directed at Hu Tao, not only from Jaune and Lisa but also from everybody else in the room. They waited for her answer.

"Gasp!" said Hu Tao, very ungasply-like, as she dropped a fist onto a palm. "Would you look at the time? Welp, back to work. Hm, hm, hm~"

Thus, singing a tune, she skipped away to leave naught but questions in her wake.

For a long while, neither Jaune nor Lisa spoke, the pair gazing after the whimsical(suspicious?) funeral director in silence. Then, Lisa nudged him in the ribs.

"You're dealing with that."

"Yeah, yeah. I complain but it's not like I mind, you know?"

"She did have a point on one thing, though," Lisa added with a sparkling grin. "Check the time, Jaune. You should get going unless you want to be late on your first official day of work."

Jaune froze for a beat, before hurrying to pull out his scroll. The time was 11:30, nearing noon.

He absolutely did not giggle and hop up and down like a little kid on his birthday.

"Good call, Lisa. Can you take care of everyone while I'm gone? I'll try to be back by tomorrow," he said in a rush. "Where's my sword? No. No! I'm taking the gunlance!"

They had discussed this matter already so it was no great imposition on her, of course, but he figured he should ask anyhow. Lisa gave him a casual wave of dismissal as her answer, bidding him good luck as he raced out the door. There was a pep in his step absent these last few days.

And really, who could blame him?

A Huntsman had to eat, and the call had come in.

There was a monster that needed slaying.



-o-
​


Jaune stepped off his ride at the edge of town.

The motorcycle driver then roared away, traveling down a road she had never been to see new sights and new scenes, her long coat trailing in the wind. He watched the bike until it dipped out of sight, around a bend where pine trees grew.

Now alone, he swung his attention back to the coastal town named Mystic.

On Remnant, it would have been a brave thing. The twin danger of sea and land posed no small trifle, demanding the kind of defenses afforded to a proper city. Outside of the main capitals, Argus was the example that came to mind. The Mountain Glenn that never fell.

The novelty hadn't worn off yet, that such places were nothing special on Earth. He still found it quite wonderful. Here in this small town, the buildings had had time to grow old, seen in how the houses sagged with age. In the way creeping vines clung to the faded paint of brick walls, undisturbed in the many years since they lay down roots. He took a moment to breathe in the fresh sea air before setting off into the town.

The dreary weather over on this side was a far cry from the clear skies of the New York mountains, with the afternoon sun obscured by clouds. Most everyone stayed indoors, and only the occasional vehicle would pass by. The cars tended to go in one direction to what he supposed would be the center street of Mystic. Certainly, the buildings looked better kept there. He walked at a steady pace, taking it all in, waving at the few pedestrians out and about.

They did not wave back, and in fact gathered together in small groups as if for strength of numbers, where they watched him and muttered among themselves. In time, he grew very aware of the unfriendly gazes sent his way by them and other locals through the windows of shops and homes. Something had them spooked.

A monster on the prowl could do that, but… No, that wasn't quite right.

The directions on his phone led him to a diner, the exterior in silver with the black-and-white checkered pattern. Some things stayed the same no matter what world one lived on.

The reception waiting for him within mirrored the same earlier attitude that he had begun to believe was the norm here. An unwelcoming suspicion that marked a clear divide between 'us' and 'the outsider'. The afternoon crowd consisted of a few customers sitting in the booths, plus one leaning on the counter.

The latter was dressed in police uniform, and had been speaking to the portly owner of the diner. His eyes immediately fell to the sword strapped to Jaune's hip. The police officer would be the contact that the text mentioned, Jaune presumed. Out came his phone as he approached them, the message on the screen serving as a shield.

"Hi there! Jaune Arc, monster hunter for hire." Ooh, it sounded even better aloud. "Were you the person to put in the request?"

One would think he just zapped them all with the way everybody in the room jolted.

"You're the fella the commissioner recommended?" said the police officer. An older man with a gut, he looked Jaune up and down with some skepticism. "But you're just a kid! I asked him for help, not to send a sacrifice!"

"I'm the best in the business," Jaune asserted, painting on a veneer of confidence to sell the boast.

And it wasn't that much of a lie, even. The profession, from what Lisa dug up, had always been an unpopular one existing in the periphery of history. It had something to do with how the tales of monster hunters here often ended with 'and then they die horribly.' He was alive and full of enthusiasm, which was more than most could say. Those qualities counted in his books.

Jaune Arc. #1 (unlicensed) Huntsman. Accept no substitute.

The police officer held his chin, brow creased in a frown. "I don't know…"

A fist pounded a table. When Jaune turned that way, a customer had stood up.

"Don't screw with us, Parris. We can't take this anymore, something has to be done! Good folks are going missing!"

Murmurs of "Do your job!" and "Better him than us!" passed around the diner in the wake of those sentiments. The tide of popular opinion was definitely against the officer. Jaune, as the one their callous remarks addressed, threw his voice into the mix.

"Yeah! Better me than them! Let the monster eat my face, will you? It's only right!"

The whole room went dead silent, with all eyes on him like he sprouted another head. Weird, he was just repeating what they said.

With a tsk, the police officer spoke, "Fine, alright. It's your funeral, what do I care?" He slumped against the counter. "Just get rid of what's been killing people, and you'll get paid."

Jaune nodded. "I will do my best. What's the monster?"

"Dunno."

"Where is its lair?"

"Dunno."

"...Aren't you a police officer?"

"Dun—" The man coughed. "I am, but it's not my job to deal with that stuff. I want to keep living."

Troublesome, although not insurmountable. Tracking the target came part and parcel with the job. One whiff of the right clue by the olfactory sensor and he'd be on that monster in a heartbeat.

A chuckle from across the counter drew his attention. The portly owner of the diner was shaking his head, arms crossed.

"Come on, buddy," he said to the officer. "We all know where the thing's hiding. It's the mansion."

The police officer grimaced. "Bill, there's no evidence. If I tell him that, it's on my ass if anything goes wrong."

But it was evidence enough for the townspeople, who took that as their cue to jump into the conversation and inform Jaune all about the mansion on the cliff. How unnatural it was. How strange people would gather at the place every summer over the years, gaunt figures garbed in black, out and about at times when decent folks should be in bed. Of the unholy screams in the middle of the day, and spates of bad luck for the neighbors.

"Swarms of black cats, each June. Don't know where they come from."

"From them."

"Evil, you can see it in their eyes."

"Must be a werewolf that's doing this. I saw one once. Ferocious thing. A monster."

"It's no monster. We're under a curse from that mansion, mark my word."

"We ought to do something. Nothing good comes from outsiders. Present company excepted, of course."

"Of course," Jaune deadpanned.

He refrained from telling them what he really thought, that they were a superstitious lot willing to string up innocent people for peace of mind. So what if someone's house wasn't up to their standards, it didn't mean the ones who owned the place were evil… aaand nevermind.

From where he stood on the sidewalk, the mansion rose in the distance. It sat upon the cliffs right outside the town, at the end of the lane past normal if boring rows of identical houses. Painted black, steeples and towers made it resemble a castle.

Left at that, it didn't seem so bad. Almost picturesque, in the fading evening light.

The nearer he got to the mansion, the fewer animals he saw. The closest homes to the property line appeared to have been abandoned for a long time, with For Sale signs planted in yards overgrown with weeds. He stopped at the gates to study the interesting skull pattern on the wrought iron, where mistakes in the forging warped the skulls into faces wracked by agony. The wailing winds of this area sounded like the screams of the damned, and they carried with them the faint scent of rot from the fish dashed upon the rocks below. 'Sat upon the cliffs' was the nicer way of saying the building was poised to plunge into the sea given an excuse.

Not the best location to spend the summer, in short. If it wasn't haunted, he'd eat his boots.

He gave the gate a tentative push. It swung open with a long, low creak to grant him access. A gulp, and he ventured forth into the unknown—

Bright and cheery music chose that moment to play from his phone, snapping apart the tension. Suddenly, the birds were chirping, the sun was shining, and life looked beautiful.

Fischl: Jaune, what would you like to eat?
Fischl: I will try to order food through the phone tonight!
Fischl: I have decided that we will eat pizza!
Fischl: Lisa said I can.

"I guess this is Lisa's next lesson for her," Jaune said, reading the messages.

With actual identities in this world now, Lisa had put the team on a phone plan, and along with it introduced to them the wonderful world of texting. Some had taken to it better than others. Hu Tao, for one, was spamming him exclusively in emojis. Meanwhile, Bennett's texts suffered constant typos.

Sorry, Fischl. I won't be back today :Jaune​

Fischl: Yes, I know.
Fischl: But I want to make sure you have food waiting when you come back.
Fischl: Good luck!

The disconnect between Fischl's normal manner of speech and her texts continued to throw him for a loop. He chalked it down to her unfamiliarity with the format. That she sounded so proud of doing something so mundane made him smile.

He sent in his order (extra pepperoni) along with a grinning face emoji that Fischl promptly copied. Then, the phone returned to the pocket of his pants, and he put his serious face back on to climb his way up the path to the mansion.

Not a blade of grass stirred on either side of the cobblestone path. The whole lawn was dead. As he ascended the porch steps, Jaune felt a twinge bugging at his eyes, this… deep sense of unease whenever he looked at the doors that were too tall and the windows set a tiny bit uneven. He soon realized that the entire place was like that, built subtly out of tune. A person could go mad seeing it everyday.

A bell hung off the door, and he pulled on the cord to make it ring in case somebody was on the premises. The chimes sound off, dulled to give it a solemn note.

"Be right there!" a voice called out, to his shock. According to the people of Mystic, the owners only ever dropped by in the summer for their mysterious reasons. This was late autumn.

The entrance featured a peephole, and he leaned forward to try and peer inside before pulling back. A second later, the doors yanked open to a kindly woman of middle years in a gingham dress who looked rather confused at his presence.

"What can I do for you, dearie?" she said.

Jaune inclined his head in a polite bow. "I'm sorry for bothering you, ma'am, but I was asked to check up on the house… I didn't realize that someone was living here. Are you a relative of the family?"

He hoped the lady bought the story, because he sounded suspicious as hell right now. Not that he spoke a single lie, of course.

"Oh no, bless you, but I'm just the housekeeper. Come in, come in."

Infiltration, success.

He followed the housekeeper into a wide corridor. Like the outside, the interior of the mansion looked old and dark with long shadows cloaking the corners. The furniture wasn't cheap, though. He had gained a knack for spotting that sort of thing with the places he had been, even if his tastes remained somewhat questionable. The design choices spelled out M-O-N-E-Y.

And yet, for all the pomp, it had the air of home. Pictures hung across the walls, too many and too eclectic to be for show. Jaune passed from one frame to the next, studying the colorful(?) ensemble as they spent their days at the beach (it was raining), or hiking in the forest (it was still raining). A person had loved their family, taking every chance to commemorate them on a camera. Through these memories, it was like he could see into the very heart of the people that lived here.

"What a dour-looking girl," he concluded.

The housekeeper laughed. "Don't let the pictures fool you. She's a darling. Just a bit goth, that's all."

As expected of a longtime employee. They would know better than him.

Guided into a kitchen that appeared much more modern compared to the rest of the house (but still in black, obviously), he took a seat at the breakfast table. It turned out to be the best decision of his life, as the kindly woman then placed before him a plate of chocolate chip cookies baked to crumbly perfection. The housekeeper, whose name was Clarice, joined him at the table and listened to his story in rapt attention, gasping as he informed her that there might be a monster on the loose in Mystic. Apparently, she kept to herself for the most part, hence her ignorance of the rumors around town.

"It's typical, if you ask me," the housekeeper said with a sigh once the tale was finished. "Never a how do you do."

Jaune nodded, mouth stuffed full with cookies. The nerves of some people.

"Never an offer of help, never a care for those who don't fit in," she continued. Jaune kept nodding, feeling quite incensed himself. His blood was up, the hair on the back of his neck standing. "If you ask me, something ought to be done about them."

He stopped nodding, and pried away his hand from the handle of his sword to raise a finger in objection. "Ehhh, I wouldn't go that far."

That brought the housekeeper up short. She blinked a few times, before sagging in her seat. "Of course, dearie. I don't know what came over me."

"Happens to all of us." He then cleared his throat, tugging at his collar. "Speaking of help, would you like me to sort those out for you?" He pointed to the bags of fresh groceries sitting on the floor near the rear door, then rapped his knuckles against the big fridge at his back that he could have walked inside if he wanted to. The housekeeper must have forgotten about it altogether, and jerked upright at the reminder.

"There's no need for that, I can do it later. Please, sit."

"It's really no trouble," he insisted. Honestly, he should have offered beforehand given that he intruded on this woman's day. In his defense, the cookies distracted him. Yes, it was a poor excuse—

"I said it's fine!"

Jaune reeled in his seat, taken aback by the way the woman had suddenly snapped. Her hand on the table was clenched a fist, and for a second, she looked so, so angry. He thought he must have stepped on a landmine somehow, but over groceries?

Then, in a blink, she returned to herself and was all apologies.

"Don't know what came over me, don't know what came over me," she kept telling him.

And what could he say to that, except, "It's alright, that was on me for imposing." Searching for a change in topic, he pulled the plate on the table closer. "Have I told you how amazing these cookies are? Because they're amazing."

The compliments to her cooking soothed the upset housekeeper.

"I truly am sorry, dearie. Medications, you know. And the weather here has me out of sorts."

That, Jaune could agree with. The climate here seemed to not agree with him either, for his skin had gone clammy. An unsettled sensation in his chest, too, refused to go away.

He tugged at his jacket. "Is it too cold? Do you need this?"

"Oh no, thank you. I'll just go grab my stole from upstairs."

That might be for the best, now that he thought about it. The jacket was of fine quality, but as the stiff padding and the armor plates woven underneath could attest, the maker of the garment built it to stave off a drive-by rather than the late autumn chill. He slipped the jacket back on as the housekeeper went upstairs via a small set of stairs connected to the corner of the kitchen.

A child of the modern era, it took about ten seconds for him to have his phone out. The inter-net of Earth had nothing on the scrollnet, and he would stick by that opinion, but there was a lot to learn. All monsters had their weaknesses, even if it was a sword to the face, and a spare moment that could be put toward studying those was time well spent.

Deciding whether a story was a tall tale or held a grain of truth did pose a problem. He was halfway convinced that they had curses and rituals here, esoteric stuff that could really screw up his day. Vampires seemed to vary in strength, and might not even be the same species. Some could sparkle? That was a book series, however, so for now he chalked it down as vampire propaganda to hide their real vulnerabilities.

After a while, though, his gaze moved away from the screen and drifted over to the grocery bags.

He could help. It literally would cost him no more than a minute.

Getting up, he crossed the kitchen.

The back door is askew.

Jaune mulled on that thought, his hand slowing as it reached for the handles of a shopping bag. The house was designed to offend the senses, but he did not believe this part to carry the same deliberateness. If anything, somebody tried to hide the damage to the hinges by slipping a rock under the door.

The doorknob is hanging loose, bent until it broke.

A clattering noise from above jolted him into a state of alert. The back door rested next to the staircase, and with a step to the left he leaned in to peer up the steps.

"Miss Clarice?"

No one answered. He sidled past the grocery bags, and began climbing the staircase.

The top of the steps opened up to a long corridor. It had seen better days, with cobwebs strung all over and the air of general neglect. The high ceiling lent it a cold, cavernous feel.

"Miss Clarice, are you okay?" he called out in a loud voice that echoed in the corridor, trying in vain to pierce the gloom. Again, he did not get a response from the woman, or anyone else.

His eyes narrowed, and purposeful strides carried him to the nearest room where he opened the door. An empty bedroom greeted him, coated in a layer of dust that was disturbed only by his actions. He tsked under his breath and moved on. The portraits in the corridor seemed to follow him with their eyes.

Signs of a forced entry, and the housekeeper now missing. That spelled nothing good.

It did not necessarily suggest monsters in the night, however. This was all too human.

Cobwebs brushed the back of his neck. He shook his head to clear it away, before entering the next room. Then the next, and the next, searching for a sign of life.

The door to the fifth room was locked. Without hesitation, he twisted the knob hard enough for it to break. A push, and the door swung open.

Snap. Whoosh!

Jaune, bemused, brought a hand up to rub his smarting nose. He then leaned into the room, turning to the side to where a massive pendulum blade shaped like a crescent moon was coming back the other way. His head tilted back, letting the blade slice through the air where his face had been.

"Ummm…"

He took in the room, a girl's bedroom with a four poster bed decorated like it should scream pink except it was all in black. The daughter lived here, at a guess. Dodging around the pendulum trap, he stepped inside.

Something clicked beneath his heel. A crossbow bolt slammed into the floor from above.

"I'll come back."

If the housekeeper had gone in here, then she'd be needing Hu Tao's services instead of his. How did the intruder have time to set up these diabolical traps, though? He could only be thankful that it was him who sprung them and not the housekeeper or, goodness, the poor goth girl whose room that belonged to.

Still… Things weren't adding up. He reentered the hall, thinking hard.

The housekeeper. Fresh groceries. He walked in through the front doors. Why was it important that he walked in through the front doors? Forced entry. Fresh groceries.

Cobweb brushed the back of his neck again. Impatiently, he waved it away.

It was important that he used the front doors, because he never saw anybody enter before him on his approach to the mansion. Which meant that the housekeeper had to have entered through the back entrance. The one that a person had broken into.

Thus followed a question. Was she really a housekeeper?

Lisa was going to laugh at him if she found out about this. Now that the thought occurred to him, it seemed the most obvious thing in the world. He should have seen it from the beginning. Jaune sighed, tilting back his head.

Two yellowed, bulbous eyes stared directly at him from above.

He "Ummm…" once again, but harder.

A gangly creature dangled from the rafters. It had the ugliest face he ever did see, a mouth full of fangs and eyes of uneven sizes on a leathery skin stretched too taut. Clawed toes allowed it to grip into a wooden beam with its feet, and in this manner held its whole body up off the ground. Thin, bony arms extended downward, ending in two sets of long fingers that were delicately looping around Jaune's throat.

Jaune beamed.

The problem turned out to be a monster, after all!

Now that he had discovered it, the creature abandoned all pretense of subterfuge. Roaring, it squeezed its fingers tight in an attempt to strangle him.

He reached up, grabbing the monster by the arm, and pulled the entire thing down from the rafters. The wooden beam cracked as sharp claws carved great gouges on the way out. The creature hit the floor with a resounding crash.

"You're the one responsible for the disappearances in Mystic, aren't you? What did you do with the housekeeper?" Jaune asked, placing a foot on its chest. The monster screeched, strings of saliva spewing from its mouth. That ceased as Jaune clocked it right between its eyes with his fist. "The housekeeper!" he insisted, pressing down harder.

The monster chose instead to take wild swipes at him, the attacks batted aside as he matched it strength for strength. His sword leapt from his hip to his hand and he raised it above his head. If it couldn't understand him, then he saw no point in reasoning with it. Either the housekeeper was alive and stashed somewhere, or she had already been killed—maybe eaten, in the worst case.

The sight of the naked blade sent the monster into a frenzy. With a great effort, it twisted to throw him off, in a flash scampering to its feet to stand just outside sword range with back hunched, arms trailing to the floor. There was a cunning dwelling inside that head, for the baleful glare it directed at Jaune conveyed outright hatred.

"Raaagh!" it screamed, seizing a marble bust sitting on a console table and lobbing the object at him. The piece of decor, depicting a portly mustachioed face, met Jaune's hand and vanished into his Pocket as he advanced toward the monster. The table flew at him next, gone in a blink. The monster's eyes widened, and it shifted back half a step. A tremble passed through its body.

He watched its posture. With a number of exits available, a being that was so afraid would have run. That it stayed must mean it had a plan. The creature was faking it.

The smile never left his face as sharp claws plunged past him, missing his head by a hair as he turned his body aside to evade the blow. Below the monster's outstretched arm, his sword lashed out to swipe a deep cut on its abdomen.

Blood spilled on the floor, and the creature roared in pain as it clutched at the wound. It stumbled back, while Jaune just kept walking forward.

The monster looked at him. At his demeanor, at his eager smile. Something clicked within its mind. The creature spun around and booked it.

Where was it going to go? Its lair? Its lair with maybe the housekeeper there? Jaune gave chase to find out.

The lumbering gait of the monster was deceptively quick, in a large part due to the strong arms propelling it forward. In seconds, it had reached the end of the hall, where it chanced a look over its shoulder.

He was right behind it, sword prepped for a stab. The creature made a strange half-screech, half-gurgle, and to save itself threw its body out the window to avoid the attack. One of its hands seized the ledge above, pulling it up to the third floor in a shower of glass.

A moment later, Jaune followed the monster out into the air, rocket boots engaging to reverse his course and shooting him through the same upper floor window it used. He landed inside a luxurious suite with silken covers on the bed, a hot tub in the corner. Neither hid the monster, which had vanished from view.

Odd, that. He had expected it to retaliate the instant he entered the room, as befitting the ambush tactics it seemed to favor. The door to the bedroom remained undisturbed, so it must still be in the suite.

"Come out, come out, wherever you are~" he sang while scanning his surroundings, alert for shifting movements in the darkened space.

A shape emerged in the gloom as he moved around. A cabinet with its doors laid open, capped with the visage of a woman. Jaune peered closer at the insides of the cabinet, and had to stop short, because wow, what kind of sick bedroom games were you supposed to do with that? Somebody can't settle for whips and candle wax anymore? How even did—

Ahem.

Now was not the time to wonder why the owners of the mansion decorated their bedroom with an iron maiden. Those questions were best left for later. By the police.

No, the better thing to wonder about would be: did that iron maiden just move?

The heavy object tore strips off the floor as it surged forward, shoved from behind the monster. The iron spikes within loomed in Jaune's vision, the doors ready to close on him.

A light hop, and the iron maiden passed beneath his feet.

"Rargh!?"

The monster equivalent of an 'uh-oh', Jaune would guess.

"You really are wily," he said with a measure of admiration, and swapped out his sword for the gunlance. Momentum did the rest, with him slamming the thick length of metal and scales down on the creature, crushing it into the floor.

Its hardiness was no joke, as it barely laid prone for a second before trying to lunge at him.

So, he lifted the lance up and brought it down again. The monster screamed as bones gave way under the force of the blow, and lashed out wildly in desperation as he repeated the motion.

Whack!

It tried to get up.

Whack!

It tried to get up.

Whack!

It ceased trying to get up.

"Phew!"

Jaune settled the lance on a shoulder, and wiped his brow at a job well done. Evil had been vanquished.

Beneath him, the monster stirred weakly.

"...After all that, you're not dead? Man, that deserves respect."

The monster lifted its head, peering up at him with watery eyes.

"Once I kill you, I should hit up a library."

The monster dropped limply back onto the floor. It made a noise as Jaune raised the lance for the last time, one that sounded halfway to a word.

Jaune frowned. "What was that?"

Did the thing just diss him as a final parting shot?

"Wad arp…" The gaping maw full of fangs bulged and caved, and it took a little longer for Jaune to understand that the skin, the flesh, the bone themselves were changing before his eyes. The monster's form reduced in size to a half, then a quarter of its former bulk. The leathery skin pinkened, and claws grew short until fingernails replaced them.

In the end, the creature vanished to leave housekeeper Clarice in its place.

"I said, what are you, you freak?" she snarled through a mouthful of blood.

Jaune retorted, "Uh, excuse me, I don't think you have any room to talk. Seriously, what even are you?"



-o-
​


Human enough, that was what the woman was. It ultimately changed his approach, and he spent another half an hour in the mansion waiting in the kitchen with her trussed up for transport. For the last couple of minutes, sirens had been growing louder and louder. The police were on their way.

He never learned what manner of being was the creature she turned into, as the woman had soon lost consciousness from her injuries. It did, however, become clear once he pondered more on the poor state of the mansion that she was no housekeeper. The empty vacation home where locals were reluctant to visit made for a good lair. The only mystery left concerning her involved confirming whether she had been behind the spate of missing townsfolk, a job for the police to perform.

As Jaune leaned back in his chair to get comfortable, his foot struck something below. The sound of the object rolling across the floor led him to look beneath the table.

It was a tomato. His gaze went to the bags of groceries, finding that one of them had tipped over. Probably when he skirted by it to go up the stairs earlier. Getting to his feet, he moved around the kitchen to pick up the scattered foodstuff.

He had already done enough damage to the house. The owners didn't need to come back to have rotten food and mold everywhere. With his arms full, he walked over and used a foot to kick open the big fridge that he could have walked into if he wanted to.

Or that somebody could put multiple people into.

I don't think I can eat anything for a while. :Jaune​

Fischl: But I already ordered!
