#7,987

Chapter 82: The Peaceful Dead
​


The arrest of Clarice the fake housekeeper made the papers. The local police force took the credit. A picture of the officer from the diner shaking hands with the mayor of Mystic featured on the front page, while Jaune's part in the incident was relegated to being a nameless, out-of-town consultant brought in to provide assistance. He sounded rather unimportant if one went by the articles.

His name was making the rounds in higher circles, or so New York City's police commissioner assured him. The places that needed him would find their messages delivered. In the meantime, obscurity provided a cover for him to work in the gray lines between the new and old laws of the land.

Good enough, in his books. The job was done, and people would sleep a little easier at night. And so, he moved on while pretending that he did not wish for the applause of the crowd.

A day passed, then two, without him embarking on a new trip. He spent most of this time running errands, bringing back a whole slew of expensive computer equipment. Lisa, meanwhile, arranged for the kind of net service that she claimed could rival an office highrise. Basically, everything they needed to start exploring the possibility of putting the netrunning skills of 2076 to the interconnected global network of a different worldline's 2022. How that complicated mess of an investment would pan out… Well, Jaune was optimistic and Lisa was muttering about world domination. Early results had been deemed 'workable', after all.

The biggest hurdle right now involved something called a USB cord. Standards could change a lot in fifty years, apparently. He didn't understand much of it. Not his wheelhouse. He left the solution to members of the team better suited for the task.

Other than that, it was business as usual. He trained, he rested. He familiarized himself with the lay of the land. Escha made for fine company as they dove deep into the woods.

He also watched with great care the trio of Bennett, Fischl, and Hu Tao to determine how their stint in Night City was affecting them, and what their thoughts might be on entering the different worlds alongside him. They were standing at the same place he stood not all that long ago, having taken a first step on a journey filled with farewells. He expected that it would not be for everyone.

Then again…

Maybe I'm worrying too much, Jaune thought as rowdy cheers shook the log cabin.

"Cenaraph, the Dark Divine Star, destiny lies within thine grasp. Soar, in the name of the Prinzessin!"

Both fists pumping, Fischl shouted encouragement to her champion. Opposite her, Bennett knelt one knee on the wooden floor, biting his nails as he watched the lead between him and her narrowed. Others in the crew surrounded the hallowed arena, calling out to their respective contestants in this sport of kings, the grand game of bitterbug racing.

Bitterbugs were beetles taken from Escha's world, colored in a vivid blue and measuring the size of a person's hand. They made good potion ingredients. Sedentary by nature, a glob of sweet honey would nevertheless get the lazy bums moving, and a few weeks under the care of Escha had grown their population to the point that she could spare specimens to stage a full racing match between everyone. After a bit of a rough start involving an open window and Bennett tripping over his feet that threatened to unleash the entire cage of them onto this world, seven bitterbugs now vied for victory on a long yoga mat placed at the center of the living room.

Jaune hated to admit it, but the mysterious challenger who some called the Dark Divine Star (Normal-rarity) posed a mighty foe. The bitterbug fighting under Fischl's banner harbored a strong sense of focus to compensate for a diminutive stature that should have placed it at dead last. A quality it displayed as six stubby legs beat a perfect straight line, nudging aside Better-Than-Scop (Normal-rarity) whose master barely gave it a thought, then seizing the lead from Bennett's Wild Charger (Normal-rarity) just as the biggest beetle on the field grew distracted and began drifting sideways.

"Cenaraph, goooooo!"

However, the young girl's triumphant cry was short-lived.

"As we practiced," Hu Tao said, making her move with a complicated hand sign, "Zhongbee!"

Chittering wingbeats answered her command. Hu Tao, with ten minutes' work, had retaught her bitterbug the mechanics of flight, and Zhongbee (5-star Legendary-rarity) leapt high into the air. Such was the might it exuded that Lisa immediately screamed bloody murder and dove behind Jaune for cover.

"What the fuck, Hu Tao? Ew, ew, ew!"

"Lisa, the bugs are harmless. It's okay," Jaune said.

"It most certainly is not!" cried Lisa as she grabbed the hem of his shirt to pull it over her head, her idea of protection from the flying bitterbug that was zigzagging above them instead of going for the honey at the finish line.

Judging by the satisfied nods Hu Tao was giving, that girl saw this as a perfectly acceptable outcome. A successful prank, accidental or not, was its own reward.

"Why did I even agree to let us raise them?" Lisa lamented. "Those things are gonna to escape one of these days, and in a few generations New York will be worse than Australia!"

"Oh look, I think you're winning," chirped Hu Tao.

Lisa poked her head out from behind him, all smiles. ""Wait, really? Whoo! You go, Skitter!"

Skitter (Mythic Prismatic-rarity) was another worthy contender standing in Jaune's way. Selected for the perfect combination of traits to turn it into a monster among bitterbugs, it had deigned to give its competitors a ten second headstart. Out of sheer arrogance like its master, presumably. Yet, that time was up, and it now zoomed forward—insofar that the species could, at any rate. Cenaraph stood not a chance, trampled beneath as Skitter climbed over it to become the leader of the pack.

The new state of play drew a soft tch from Jaune's lips, and he looked to Buggy, the Indomitable Steed (Normal-rarity) in order to gauge its progress, his mind grasping for a strategy. The race was coming to a head, but one good move could still flip the leaderboard upside-down.

…Unlike Lisa's bug, the little fella he chose was facing the wrong direction and moving away from the honey prize, thus achieving negative progress.

"This game sucks," he concluded.

"I dunno, it's kind of growing on me," Lisa mused.

"You're only saying that because you're in first place."

Her reply to that was to stick out her tongue. Sure in her victory, she ceased paying attention to the race, pulling out her phone to fiddle with as she leaned on his back. She had been spending a lot more time on it these days, now that there was someone on the team as tech savvy as her and could text at the speed of thought. Did it matter that the two were about a foot apart behind him, and therefore could have saved time and effort by just speaking aloud? Not to them.

In any case, Jaune hid a mischievous smile for that lack of attentiveness portended a tantrum on the horizon. A twitching pair of cat ears grew ever more animated as the race drew down to the wire. Victory was at hand, but not for who Lisa thought.

A bitterbug crossed the finish line, and the room exploded into cheers and applause.

"And the winner is… Escha!"

"I won, I won!" cried the felyne jubilantly. She scrambled off her place on Fischl's lap to grab Bitter-bitter (Rare-rarity), swinging the bug around and around in celebration. The rest of the blue bitterbugs scattered to avoid the dancing giant in their midst.

"How?" squawked an indignant Lisa, phone tossed to the side. "My pick was the best one. The thing had longer legs, more stamina, it was smart…" The list went on and on, betraying the level of depth Lisa had put into something she outwardly derided as 'a kid's game'.

The greatest Thinker powers in the universe—her words, not his—failed to account for one variable.

"This one eats a lot," said Escha, hugging the bug to her chest, "and it loves honey."

Jaune recalled that Escha had been the one to set up the course, including the bait at the end.

From whom did the cat learn that sort of deviousness? She wasn't this sly before.

Lisa raged and raged, looking for all the world like the teenage girl she was. How much of it was real and how much of it was fake, he wondered if she'd ever tell.



In the sky, there shone a blue moon. These were the last days of autumn, and the wintry chill bit deep in the late hours. A layer of mist covered the ground in dull tones of gray. On such a night, two figures stood before a set of wrought iron gates, under a flickering lamp.

The shorter of the pair stretched her arms above her head, and let out a sweet sigh.

"What a night to be alive, don't you think?" said Hu Tao.

Jaune looked around, hands in his pockets. The world was quiet here, with the faint lights of houses at a far remove. The one car parked in the vicinity belonged to them.

"Not quite how I would put it," he said, walking over to the gates and peering inside.

Past the entrance, headstones lay in neat rows. They had lamps here and there, not enough for the acres and acres that stretched on without end. The stars and the bright moon provided illumination for the most part, their soft light casting the mist in an otherworldly glow. This cemetery on the outskirts of a small city, not far from a certain log cabin in the mountains, was the resting place for many souls.

"I'm surprised they're still open at this hour." He reached out to tug on the gate. It refused to budge. "Hang on a minute…"

Hu Tao peeked around him. "Oh? Like I thought. Looks like they're closed, after all."

"You knew that beforehand?" He turned his head, cocking an eyebrow. He might have felt more annoyed if he hadn't experienced for himself her many nonsensical actions up until now. "What did we even come here for, then?"

"The right atmosphere is important, silly. Everybody knows that the best time for snooping is after dark," Hu Tao admonished him with a tap on his nose.

What she intended was not hard to guess, given that hint. The girl separated from him to walk along the fence that enclosed the graveyard, running a hand over the row of tall iron bars. Stopping at one, she braced a foot on the fence and hoisted herself up.

"Breaking in, huh?" said Jaune. Sometimes, he had to wonder why his life was filled with troublemakers. Beside the fact that he fit right in with them, of course.

A burst of rocket fire brought him to the top of the fence, feet placed between the pointy spear tips capping the bars. Then, a hop put him back on the ground inside the cemetery, on a wide foot path that led deeper into the field. Only once done did it strike him how natural such maneuvers had become for him, as simple as breathing.

Hu Tao took a little longer, relying on her own physical strength supported by the enhancement of Aura, but soon she was swinging a leg over the fence. A wide and lively smile shone down on Jaune.

"You really did just go along with it," she said. "I knew you were the right choice for this, my accomplice!"

He gave a slight raise of his shoulders and said, somewhat mildly, "I've had practice."

His answer pleased her, if going by the way her demeanor softened. With a "Hup!" she brought her other leg over, and pushed off from the fence. In a bout of mischief very reminiscent of Annoying Blondes, she aimed her landing toward him, no doubt expecting him to panic.

Yet, before he even finished considering which way to dodge, Hu Tao's progress halted with an abrupt jerk. Her expression froze, with Jaune getting a glimpse of a rare sight—a Hu Tao whose prank had backfired.

"Eh?"

He winced as the girl's momentum redirected straight into the fence, her face banging against the bars. From where he stood, he could see the back of her coat had been caught on one of the iron spikes, with Hu Tao now dangling from it in the manner of caught prey, limbs hanging loosely below her with her hat askew. On her face was a most confused look.

"Eh? Eh?" she kept repeating, trying to twist around. "Why am I stuck? What's the big idea?"

A brief struggle left her facing the other way and no freer than before. By then, Jaune could restrain himself no longer.

"Bahahahahaha!" It mattered little that Hu Tao was glaring at him, he fell on his rear, pointing and laughing.

"Quit making fun of me and help!" Hu Tao roared in a furor of flailing arms and legs, accomplishing nothing of note but to make him laugh harder.

Gasping for air, he rummaged in a pocket. "Just a second. I want to get a picture of this."

"It's tearing! It's tearing! Ahhhh, this coat was expensive!"

"There, hold that pose."

*Snap*



-o-
​


He got Hu Tao down safely, albeit with not all her dignity intact. The next few minutes saw her hopping up and down, trying to grab at the scroll that he held high above her head. At one point, she was almost climbing on him, all teary-eyed.

Still, he refused to budge on preserving the memory. Moments like these were worth it.

"Hmph! Make a note, assistant. There will be no fences at our cemetery, or at least no fences with sharp poke-y things sticking out. It should be easy to sneak into. Why in the world would anybody want to keep people out of a graveyard? The whole point is to put them in!"

It seemed her nature was not one of holding grudges, for Hu Tao was back to her cheerful self in a flash, skipping along the paved stone path as she cracked jokes. Well, he hoped they were jokes at any rate. There was a shovel in his Pocket that he still didn't know what to do with.

"Is that why we're here, to look for ideas?" he asked during a moment of quiet.

Hu Tao tilted her head. "Of course. What else would we be doing?"

To be honest, he thought she wanted to dig up dirt on the competition and shut them down. That was the kind of plan Lisa would go for.

"Different places have different funerary rituals and customs. America seems to follow the Mondstadt style rather than Liyue's, so I may have to adjust my approach... Also, it's been days since I've had a chance to go out and scare people." Hu Tao covered her mouth with the oversized sleeves of her coat. "Huhuhu. I hope we meet someone tonight."

Oh, right. There was that side to her, too.

"Most people tend to stay away from places like this after dark," he pointed out, gesturing around them.

No reply came, however, for Hu Tao had already darted away. She frolicked among the graves as if this were a field of flowers, studying the headstones, the words inscribed on them, humming all the while. Jaune followed at a distance, observing this strange girl.

Lisa, Escha, the others? He understood them to varying degrees. They were all chasing something, from power to adventure to the pure wonder of living in a new world. He had an inkling of how to cheer them up and make them happy. What he could give them.

Hu Tao followed her own whims most days, and he was content to let it be so. But…

He joined her by a grave close to the path, where she knelt to brush aside the overgrown weeds and vines. Once she was done, she wiped the sweat off her forehead, uncaring that dirt had gotten on her clothes.

It would be nice, he thought, to see what those eyes see.

The cemetery went on forever, yet spanned no more than a few yards away at a time. The mist made it impossible to see further, swept by wind to turn Jaune's surroundings into a landscape of swirling gray.

As they continued on, he and Hu Tao never quite walked side by side. Every few minutes, her attention would fixate on a new thing, with her rushing off at the drop of a hat. Sometimes he scrambled after her, and sometimes he left her alone. They both led to one outcome, laughter sounding like bells and wind chimes. He got the impression that nothing he did would ever truly bother the girl for long.

He found it oddly comforting, and over time he ceased to pay mind to Hu Tao. Either she would be here, or she would be elsewhere.

His footsteps on the paved stones grew to be his one constant companion in this eerie world of only two living souls, echoing for longer than it should. Section by section, he came to recognize a pattern to the cemetery, a grid where everything adhered to a certain symmetry. The main paths ran at perfect right angles to one another, the side trails grouped in threes between the bigger intersections. Simple headstones at the edges gave way to box tombs sitting pretty with little engravings and filigrees, then to mausoleums bunched together to tower above everything else. Very neat. Very tidy.

"Very bo~ring!" complained Hu Tao, in one of the rare moments where she stuck by him. "Did you notice? Did you? There isn't a single tree here! And would it kill them to build a pagoda?" Crossing her arms, she continued to grumble under her breath about the changes she would make to the design to better serve the dead. The living too, but mostly the dead.

If she expected him to agree, she was disappointed. "I kind of like it this way," he said as he peeked through the open entrance of a mausoleum. Urns lined the walls, with a single tomb at the center of the room. A shiver ran up his spine. 'Like' was a strong word in regards to any aspect of a graveyard. "A predictable layout means I won't get lost. And let me tell you, that's a really important consideration for me. You have no idea."

Just slightly, Hu Tao's shoulders slumped down.

"But isn't a sense of mystery important, too?" she asked him. "How are the spirits going to scare anyone like this? Or play hide and seek?"

"...Are there ghosts here?" That budding worry faded as he studied her face. "There aren't. Phew."

He would keep the stack of paper talismans close to hand, though. Just in case.

Especially as Hu Tao took it as a challenge, dashing into one of the side alleys between the mausoleums without a second thought. Her vow to bring 'local voices' and 'pillars of the community' into the conversation echoed off the tombs. The dark corners seemed to bother her none.

Whether the spot of empty air she brought back was a ghost or not, Jaune decided to leave it to her to determine. He certainly saw nothing. Bowing his head and apologizing to a spirit he couldn't perceive for denying its existence did feel a bit ridiculous, although it improved Hu Tao's mood so he refrained from commenting further on the subject. Even if her snickering behind her sleeves made him suspect that she was playing a prank on him.

"There wasn't a ghost," she later admitted on her own. "Not a single one. That's the reason I wanted to visit, because I thought the person running this place was doing something right and everybody had gone ahead. It turns out that the spirits just don't like it here."

She pointed out to him the cramped confines of the mausoleum district, where no empty lots or even a blade of green grass remained. The layers of moss and mushrooms that grew due to the lacking sunlight. The sense of sameness to the tombs, simple concrete walls adorned by the barest of ornamentation.

The owner ran the graveyard as a mere business. Where was the duty, Hu Tao raged.

"Every grave is a wish. 'Remember me'," she insisted to him.

And that, at least, he understood.

Hu Tao led him, unerringly, to the very center of the cemetery. Her goal, all this while. They were to engage in a spot of… nonmalicious mischief, let's call it. With the shovel resting on a shoulder, Jaune mulled on the request, deeming it several levels better than his fear that they would be robbing graves tonight.

Before that, though, he had to consider how to handle the group in front of him.

Hu Tao was right. Dead people do hang out in cemeteries. Or undead, in this case.

They melted out of the shadows one by one, pale figures dressed in the deepest black congregating around a leader who sat on a box tomb with the air of a king. Their casual attitudes—grinning, chatting—belied a tension that screamed of danger, of predators barely restrained from ripping their prey apart. Despite it being nighttime, many wore sunglasses. That last one was a definitive sign of their species, in his notes.

Their leader cracked a debonair smirk, revealing a sharp fang to clinch Jaune's suspicions.

"O'er the last divide, from whence the sparrows of clipped wings fly, come a question not oft asked."

Jaune and Hu Tao looked at each other, then back to the vampire.

"What?" Jaune said.

The vampire's expression slipped for a fraction of a second. "Not that one." He then cleared his throat, and continued as if he hadn't said that. "What is death, is the question not oft asked."

"I don't know, giving the answer outright like that…"

"Shhh. The fellow is trying, Jaune."

A twitch developed on the vampire's brow, quickly hidden as he stood up to his feet. "Alas, blood anoints blood in a river run dry. Not all souls will reach paradise."

"Again, what?"

He thought he was maybe getting it, but nope, he was still lost. Anyway, given that they were talking like Fischl, it lent credence to the notion that vampires had royal lines in their society. That could also link to their level of power, if he considered the many legends of Count Dracula he came across during his readings.

He might have to go all-out for this.

"Benighted curs, torn from the light. Come to join, come to die, and rise again…" As the vampire waxed on without end, one of his cohorts split from the background to sidle over. She whispered into his ear behind her hand, throwing quick glances toward Jaune. The leader of the group began to trail off.

"What? He what?"

*Whisper, whisper, whisper*

"With a what!?"

*Whisper, whisper, whisper*

The conversation ended, leaving the vampires looking even paler than Jaune thought possible for their normal sallow parlor. There was some shoving and jostling among them that worked out to everyone standing in a line, where they politely owed their heads low.

"We're heading out now. Sorry to bother you," said the leader of the vampires, his previous tone entirely absent.

"Classes in the morning. You know how it is," another vampire chimed in. "Gotta bet up bright and early. Boy, do I love sunlight, puppies, and blood bags."

"Mmmm. There's nothing more tasty than blood willingly donated through legal blood drives. You wouldn't catch me twice-dead drinking anything else."

The line of vampires voiced various other excuses as they power-walked into the night without a backward glance. The moment they were out of his sight, Jaune heard them break into a run. In no time at all, peace and quiet returned to the cemetery. Barring Hu Tao who was pounding a fist against a mausoleum wall, laughing her heart out.

"Those vampires from the library back then must have spread the news around," Jaune mused, scratching his cheek.

"You sure left an impression," Hu Tao said.

She skipped over to the vampires' previous hangout spot, humming a carefree tune. With a look around, and a frown, she cleaned the area of empty beer bottles and potato chip bags, getting him to pitch in by vanishing them into his Pocket for later disposal. Once that was done, she directed him to pry up a loose piece of paving stone to get at the dirt underneath, and while he dug a shallow hole, she went rummaging through the surprising amount of pockets in her coat.

"Aha!" Hu Tao held a packet of store-bought seeds up in triumph.

The sight of it reassured Jaune for certain.

"You know," he said, planting the shovel and leaning on it, "I really am glad we weren't here to steal a body."

"You didn't believe me the first time, huh?" Hu Tao groused in faux-anger. She squatted down, sprinkling the seeds into the hole. Jaune passed her a filled drinking bottle from his supplies afterward so that she could water them.

"What kind of seeds are they, anyway?"

Hu Tao tapped the flower branch adhered to her hat. "Plum trees. My favorite! Spirits back home sometimes rest under their shade before they go on their way, so we might meet a few here one day." She looked up, showing him a beatific smile. "Wouldn't it be nice?"

Maybe he didn't understand this strange girl, but he wanted to. That was the thought in Jaune's mind as he watched Hu Tao plant life in a dead place.

Gazing down at her with soft eyes, he answered.

"Hell no!"


Author's Notes: True mastery of the sword is ending a battle without ever drawing the blade. This… probably isn't it, though.

#8,206

Chapter 83: The Howling Beast of the Castle
​

The peaceful morning that day shattered with a loud crash, sending cats and blondes into a panic.

It wouldn't be the first time something like that had happened this week, so they settled down rather quickly. A few days in, and everybody had grown familiar with the new place, and the new routine. The rowdy, unrestrained, and wildly haphazard routine that made Lisa thankful they did not have neighbors, because it would have lost her the rental deposit before the week was up.

A look outside the window revealed the cause of the disturbance, a big old robot lying flat by the snowy lakeside with the shockwaves from its fall causing ripples across the sparkling blue water surface. The two arms were wriggling in a futile effort to climb upright, while its legs performed a walking motion in the air. Behind the glass canopy sat the pilot, Jaune, who struggled for all he was worth to regain control of the mech.

"Come on, come on, come on," he griped, turning and twisting in his seat. "Work, you stupid lump of metal."

Clearly, none of this was his fault. The seller provided him a defective product. He was the victim.

He gave it another go by swinging both arms back to slap the ground, which from how he imagined it would send the AMP suit surging to its feet in a deft show of strength and acrobatics. Instead, the mech's hands sank deep into the earth to clog up the joints with mud. Meanwhile, the lower half was still trying to walk into the sky. His face burned redder with each new failed maneuver, all the more so given the additional spectators now watching from the house.

"Natural human-like motions, my foot," he said, tempted to give the mech a whack to see if that'd reset the thing to proper function.

A grinning face came into view above his prone form, upside-down. Lisa planted a hand on a cocked hip as she leaned over the glass, here to spend her precious time that could be used to earn her millions with him.

Her words, not his. He was pretty sure she wanted a chance to laugh in his face.

"Told ya to study the manual," she chirped. It sounded snide and much too sugary, and were it anyone else, Jaune would have read into it to take offense.

He grimaced (some might say he pouted, but no). "I did!"

He went over the manual twice, in fact. The first time to study the basics of the AMP suit, then a second time when he didn't understand any of it. The person who published that booklet deserved all the misfortune headed for them, because they had concocted the most singularly useless set of instructions Jaune had ever seen. Whenever it could stand to give the technical jargon a rest, it instead harped on about how piloting came down to 'feel'. He was supposed to 'employ best judgment'. What did that even mean?

At least he wasn't alone in this. There were scribbles on the margins of the manual from the person the mech once belonged to, crashing out over the same issues. The last page sported a couple of bullet holes from it.

Whatever, he just had to put in more effort. It was all in the arms. Unlike the legs which followed a complicated structure of pre-programmed routines operated by foot pedals, the AMP suit (somewhat) matched the mechanical arms up with the pilot's own movements. That afforded him a lot more control of the mech's upper half.

He closed his eyes, and counted down from ten to regain his composure. Then, his eyes flew open.

"Ahhhhhhh!" he shouted with renewed efforts, mustering all his might! He wasn't about to lose to this mech!

Unfortunately, effort was for meat and bones. The flailing robotic limbs shoved and shoved, yet the only result was the mech suit rocking to one side then the other like an overturned turtle. A minute of that saw him sinking another foot deeper into the ground.

"Done?" Lisa asked once he stopped moving.

Pride bruised, he nodded. The mech powered down.

"Yeah, I'm done."

"Then, get out so I can take a crack at it. Honestly, you only have yourself to blame, trying to brute force something like this." Lisa shook her head, hands spread as if to say 'what can you do'. "Did it ever occur to you that a Thinker might be the solution for cerebral work?"

He paused the middle of unbuckling the various safety belts, and shot a suspicious squint up at Lisa.

"Are you calling me dumb?"

"Nuh-uh. I would never."

That quick answer was rather undercut by Lisa pointedly looking away from him. The glass canopy sprang free to let him climb out, and he seized the chance to poke Lisa's side in passing, drawing out a yelp from her. Now it became her turn to glare at him as she dropped into the pilot seat.

His boots hit the soft snow, and he made a bit of distance from the mech so as to not be struck by an errant limb. The arms were the size of his torso, able to exert a lot of force, and with Lisa at the helm, who could say for sure what might happen. He anticipated untold damage to the surroundings, with her maybe walking into the lake and needing rescue.

The mech powered up again. Through the glass, he saw Lisa shifting in the seat to get comfortable before slipping her arms inside the harness rig that would read her motion inputs and copy it to the mech. The process wasn't an exact one-to-one, which had been the part to give him the most trouble. Move an inch, and it felt like the robot took a mile. He found it very unintuitive, not at all fun.

Lisa… seemed to be faring better. She limbered up the arms, shoulders digging into the ground as they rolled, then brought a hand in front of the glass to count on the fingers. One, two, three, four, five; the fingers fluttered in a wave. Thus satisfied with the equipment's performance, Lisa braced her palms on the snow and slowly raised the AMP suit off the ground. Meanwhile, she was also doing something with the foot pedals that got the robot's legs moonwalking back under the torso. Ten seconds, all told, and she was smirking at him from an upright mech.

Jaune gawked, in total awe at her precise control. He cupped his hands like a megaphone, and called out, "How!?"

But Lisa simply doubled down on her smug, and set the robot to pacing back and forth. The steps began clumsy, yet in no time grew firm and sure to speak of experience that she shouldn't have. It raised a small suspicion for Jaune that something more was going on here, and he observed the mech with a close eye as it stopped in front of him, putting up its fists to shadow box. Crisp punches snapped across the air, as fluid as any flesh and blood human.

He watched the show for a while, timing the punches. Then, once he had gotten the rhythm down, he jumped to squat atop one of the fists. It put him face to face with the girl behind the glass, who paused with the arm raised to serve as his perch.

"Did the Scholar class let you learn that?" he asked, tilting his head. "You're way too good at it for your first time."

Her smirk deepened. The speakers on the mech crackled as Lisa's voice came through.

"Aw, you figured it out," she whined, pretending to sulk. She unhooked her arm from the harness to reach inside her top and pulled out her Adventurer Card from who knew where she had stowed it, brandishing the card between two fingers. "Yeah, stuff like this is a cinch when you can [Speed Read] and [Memorize] and [Visualize] to help in the process. I can probably learn the basics of whatever I feel like in a couple of days if I put my mind to it. Even that glider of yours."

Jaune shielded his eyes, for his partner suddenly looked twice as bright and reliable. With just the right set of circumstances, Lisa had become an incomparable existence, a do-anything girl.

Wait, no, that sounded wrong.

"Buying the base skill for [Piloting] from the Marketplace was one of my better ideas, too," Lisa added. Her gaze drifted to the side. "Right up there with upgrading it to the second level."

He blinked, needing a second for the words to finally hit him. Once it did, he lunged halfway up the mechanical arm, jabbing an accusing finger at the cockpit.

"You cheated! There was a Skill like that!?"

Lisa stuck out her tongue, then said, "You're only mad because you didn't think of it first."

No, duh! He should have bought it for himself ahhhhh!

"Let me get the scroll for a sec," he said, motioning with his hand. Riding a mech was the dream of humankind. He had no intention of passing up a chance like that.

Unfortunately, Lisa did not share the sentiment. She squirmed in her seat, turning to cover from view a pocket on her tight jeans.

"I don't think so, mister." She wagged a finger at him. "Since I already bought the original copy on the phone, if you want it you'd have to pay for the skill share option and that's just a waste of Points."

"I don't know, I think that's a price I'm willing to—"

"Besides," she continued, "it's not really cheating when I understand the underlying concepts, unlike you. All it did for me was skip the practice time needed to pick up the second-nature instincts. If I lose the Skill tomorrow, I can still operate the suit. You'd just be deadweight in that scenario."

Because he might run the risk of becoming deadweight, he should stay as deadweight. Something about that logic didn't seem to hold up to scrutiny, and he said so.

"Not what I meant; I'm saying that you should stick to items as much as you can, we can at least trust those," was Lisa's adamant reply, the same one that had them training daily instead of buying the upgrades which would have bypassed the need. And while he agreed with that to an extent…

"You'd sound more convincing if you hadn't done the complete opposite of that."

"Aaanyway, it's a matter of filling out the different roles," Lisa noted, bulldozing over his point. "You're never gonna sit in this thing in a fight. No, you'd be flying around out there swinging your sword. That's the part you play best."

That… was fair, he had to admit. A big robot did not mesh easily into his current repertoire. Adjusting to it meant shutting out most of what he could do.

Ummm, but why did it feel like she was leading him by the nose?

"You aren't exactly the best suited to work our heavy weaponry either," he said, though without much heat, more arguing with her because that was just what they did. By now, Lisa had turned the mech to face the lake, with him flipping around and lying back on the outstretched arm to enjoy the bracing mountain breeze, one leg swinging off his resting place. "I can't see you firing that big rifle that came with the suit."

"Eh, true, that part is a work-in-process. But I look at this suit as more of a mobile command center, in any case," Lisa explained. "What do you think?"

He pondered on that, the idea of Lisa in a thick suit of armor where nobody could hurt her while she did her talking. Yes, it held an undeniable appeal, especially given the sheer rage she tended to induce in their foes. And allies. And bystanders.

Honestly, she needed all the protection she could get.

He brought his arm around to rap his knuckles against the glass canopy. "I guess that depends on how tough this is."

"It's pretty decent."

His hand clenched into a fist, with him pulling it back. "We'll see about that."

Lisa cringed in her pilot seat, pressing against the backrest. "Stop, you maniac! Do you know how strong you are now? You'll kill me!"

He relented, and Lisa heaved a relieved sigh, smoothing her chest.

"Look, I can judge the specs just fine," she assured him. "It can take a bullet, at least."

Jaune summoned his gunlance. Lisa was once more pressed flat to her chair.

"Not that bullet!"

"You are so fussy," Jaune complained.




Good luck. Do your best. We're praying for your victory.

The words of the men of the castle rang hollow, for as honest as these sentiments were, a greater wish engulfed them under its shadow. Crystallized within thousands, and resounding to their every heartbeat.

Get. Wrecked. Idiot.

Jaune pretended it did not bother him, accelerating across the air to better leave it all behind. None of it should matter right now. For him, there was the sky, the wind in his hair. A foe, over there. One girl cheering him on.

He needed nothing more.

The person in the far distance turned toward him, detecting his presence despite the space in between them. With the ocean waves crashing at his back, he cut a mighty figure as he unslung a bow and drew the string in perfect form.

Yet, it was merely a bow. The sandy plain from there to here posed a greater obstacle to the weapon than anything he might do, so Jaune paid it little worry. This time he had, the calm before the storm, would be better spent clearing his mind and centering himself for the coming battle. The one whose composure broke first would be the one to fall, it was oft said.

For a moment, the wailing winds that blew over these sandy shores fell to a murmur. The bowstring loosened with a crisp snap that carried across the battlefield, and from it an arrow streaked above the blood-tinged dunes as a blur. A respectable if not very impressive speed, as arrows were for those who lived in a world of guns. Jaune could follow it with his eyes, and wasn't that just a damning insult as to the threat it presented to him?

The problem began at about a hundred yards out, the point where it occurred to Jaune that the projectile looked awfully big for an arrow, and seemed to stay on a straight trajectory without ever wavering. The swirls of displaced air around it was rather concerning, too.

Ahead of the arrow, there arrived a sound. It bore into his ears, into the depths of his mind. A sound that he would remember always. Screeeeeeeee- WHOOSH!

He jerked his head out of the way as an entire spear lanced past, the force of it picking him up and whipping him around to leave him tumbling through the air. More akin to a cannon than small arms, it wouldn't have ended with just a bit of an ache had it struck dead on. An explosion rang out behind him, way back toward the fortifications, as the arrow slammed against a thick stone wall. He got a glimpse of the aftermath in the middle of trying to steady his glider. There didn't used to be another entrance on those balconies, if he recalled right.

What monstrous strength.

Regaining control took some doing, and lost him half his altitude in the attempt. Afterward, he stuck to flying at an angle while keeping a wary eye on the bow. The people at the castle had told him he would be facing their greatest warrior, and now, he had an idea of what that entailed. It went a lot further than the outdated liveries and simple blacksmithing he saw from the rank and file soldiers would let on.

So, when the figure in the distance grabbed a handful of spears to put in the bow, Jaune made no assumptions and was ready for any or all of them to reach his position.

He was slightly less ready for that handful to grow into a rain of hundreds of spears falling in a column to blot out the sun. His glider banked hard to one side, and he kicked his rocket boots on full blast to avoid catching a spear in the head. And then he had to avoid catching a spear in the head again… And again, and again…

"Why are they following meeeee!?" Jaune yelled as he zigzagged toward the ground, the raining arrows behind him changing trajectory in physics-defying fashion to give chase. The landscape below him churned and roiled from repeated impacts that were akin to a stampede of wild horses, turning unrecognizable. With no time to consider his landing, he slammed into a sand dune to go cartwheeling over the top and down the side, his body rolling on as the ground evened out to throw sand every which way, inches from impalement at any given moment.

His journey came to an end with him flat on his back half-buried in the beach. The last spear impaled a spot inches from his face, where it quivered with the residual energy left within the shaft.

Jaune laid there, staring at the spear, heart thundering. He hadn't gotten a chance to make an opening move yet, and the fight already went off-kilter. Arrows that multiplied? How did that even work?

The prospect of a second volley gunning for him got him moving. Groaning at the phantom aches and bruises that Aura hadn't healed yet, he pushed up on his hands.

"Huh? Where did he go?" he said, looking around the empty plain.

No sooner had he asked it, a rumble shook the land. The sand around him turned warm, while an oppressive heat licked at the back of his neck. Jaune looked up as the world tinted in a violet light.

He needed a couple of seconds to fully comprehend what that rock growing larger and larger in his vision was about. His eyes slowly widened to two big circles, and his mouth fell open.

"H-Hang on, I thought they said you were a warrior, why are you using magic?" Jaune's voice grew progressively higher. "Hold up. Time out. Can we talk about this? Wait, wait, wait, wait, wait!"

Astride the meteor bearing down upon Jaune, a beast that was once a man howled at the sky.


Universe: Elden Ring. Location: Redmane Castle of the Lands Between.
Event: The Festival of Radahn


-o-
​

Jaune dragged his sorry carcass out of the surf. Once he had cleared the waterline, he flopped down to sit on the shores at the foot of the castle. Tugging at his boot, he pulled it off and tipped it upside-down to dump onto the rocks the seawater collected inside, shaking it to get the flecks of sand out.

Behind him, the metal chains of a crude, archaic elevator rattled as a platform descended down to his level. Out of it Lisa daintily skipped, moving over to his side. She scanned him from head to toe first before looking across the small inlet separating them from the sandy plain where the mindless beast that people called General Radahn endlessly roamed.

"Some date, huh, Jaune?" she asked in a casual manner. "Soooo, changed your mind on dipping out yet?"

He jerked his head to indicate that same Radahn. "We could, but did you see the bow he had on him? That thing ought to sell for a pretty sum."

"Say that after you actually get within arm's reach of him."

Jaune wilted. "Yeah..."

One festival on the heel of another, it had seemed like fate to him. When a person was on a roll of good luck, they had to keep going, right? Most of that kerfuffle in Night City came about as a result of his own making, so his thinking was that if they stayed out of trouble, this new place could well be a stress-free vacation destination to Lisa and him, with maybe some good stuff lying around for the taking. Thus, even with the danger rating associated with it, he leapt on the chance.

A warped sky streaked in red and the wasteland beyond the castle attested to how well that decision turned out. Caelid was a dying land, ravaged by a scourge disease. Apparently, among other things, it turned all the cute little doggies into dinosaurs. That sounded pretty awesome right up until a watchman on the wall pointed one out for him.

"From now on, we're blacklisting anything with 'festival' in it," Lisa demanded. "They're never what they say they are. Bunch of liars."

That, he found hard to argue with, and they might as well blacklist Elden Ring along with it. Seriously, he still wasn't over the dino-dog. The rabid, festering monstrosity needed cleansing by fire.

Jaune slipped his boot back on as he continued to listen to Lisa's grumbling, and walked with her to the wooden elevator. A signal to the soldier stationed at the top got the rickety contraption moving. For a medieval society, it was quite ingenious that they managed to approximate a convenience from his time; although, he supposed an elevator was a system of weights and pulleys at its core, and those have been around practically forever.

The higher elevation granted Jaune a better view of the battlefield he escaped from. Strewn with broken banners and corpses long dead, those grounds caged the single remaining combatant still upright through the use of high walls and tall cliffs that muted sights, deafened sounds. The might of the prisoner rendered any direct methods of containing him futile. He stayed inside so long as nothing outside caught the attention of his deteriorated mind.

Jaune had thought the stress on such a containment strategy to be an exaggeration. No longer. Now, the thick walls of the castle didn't seem enough.

The elevator reached the top of the battlements, grinding to a halt at the keep that laid in the highest part of the castle, at the very back. A series of clicks rang out as latches secured the platform in place. A person was already waiting for the two of them here, stroking his long beard with a cheerful smile on his face. Someone whom Jaune was not so good at dealing with, an elder.

"Ohoho! The plucky lad returns, eh?" The jolly old man, thin frame clad in worn and patchwork armor, chuckled as he clapped Jaune on the shoulder. "By the by, how did you find the mettle of General Radahn?"

He sounded entirely too happy for a man whose stated purpose was to bring an end to his former comrade, the mad Radahn. Jaune looked down at his own filthy, water-logged form and back up to the castellan of Castle Redmane.

"You know, Jerren, it would have been really nice if you warned me beforehand that your old boss could summon a meteor—ahem, excuse me, must have been a cough." Jaune changed his tone to something less caustic. "I almost had him."

The old man, Jerren, passed him a knowing look. "The greatest armies of the land broke upon his sword. Diminished as Radahn may be after all this time, it will take the gathered champions of far and wide to have a hope of slaying him. Of course, you are welcome to try again as many times as you dare before the festival begins." His gaze beneath the hood he wore narrowed, the general air of dottiness peeling back as he jabbed a finger at Jaune in warning. "So long as you remember honor."

Jaune avoided the glare, scratching his cheek and awkwardly glancing at Lisa for help—no luck there. Him firing a shot with his rifle, Ruhm, from the castle walls had nearly set off a revolt among the soldiers stationed at Redmane. Radahn could play with giant rocks dropped from the sky, but just try to hit him from a safe distance and suddenly this Jaune Arc fellow was taking it one step too far.

"I'll keep it in mind," he said, and bade farewell to the castellan. He followed Lisa out of the keep, headed for the main courtyard that laid below.

They hadn't even cleared the first set of steps before someone else accosted them. A hulking figure leapt down from a higher platform, joining them on the staircase.

"You survived! I guess you are not all talk, Jaune Arc!" bellowed the figure. His tone held a hint of a growl, though by no means was he angry. It had more to do with his wolfish maw and wolfish eyes and wolfish ears—a general wolfiness to the warrior who stood a good three heads taller than Jaune.

"Blaidd, you saw the show?" Jaune said, and braced for the congratulatory slap on the back which would have sent him flying otherwise. A wolfman, not a werewolf, Blaidd nevertheless exhibited an inhuman level of strength, something Jaune found out for himself upon their first meeting.

"From beginning to ignominious end." Blaidd pointed up. "That tower there afforded me a fine view. How you can fly, I know mistress R- milady would love to hear…" That mysterious 'milady' again. A person whose name might get the warrior in trouble if spoken aloud, or so Lisa had gleaned. "Bah, no matter, you have bought us important information about the battle to come, news that must be spread to our fellow champions. It will be a fine chance for us to make their acquaintance. Come!"

A friendly sort, Blaidd. Jaune was glad that his sword had missed the guy's throat hours earlier. In his defense, a wolfman opening his mouth to say hello bore an uncanny resemblance to a werewolf trying to eat someone's face off.

The wolfman led them down another flight of steps. Away from the inner sanctum, activity began to pick up with soldiers marching to and fro, chests puffed up to display their surcoats emblazoned with the image of a lion. Those who were stationed at the defenses watched their group closely.

"It's been bothering me, but why are all the ballistas facing the wrong way?" he mused aloud.

Castle Redmane followed a tiered structure, one section stacked atop another, growing smaller in area as it went. It bristled with medieval traps and artillery. One would expect them, then, to point that outside the walls, maybe at the Radahn problem, but no. All were aimed at… well, at the place Jaune was headed to, hence his concern.

Lisa opened her mouth to answer, yet Blaidd got there first, his rugged baritone crowding out Lisa's more delicate voice.

"Haha! Away from the general, you mean? Radahn has his enemies even to this day who would see him brought low as a quarry rather than a warrior. A final humiliation as vengeance. More fool them, but such is their reason."

Spotting her chance, Lisa chimed in, "It doesn't help that there are a bunch of outsiders in the castle right now, half of them famed for their strength of arms. Give them a reason and the castle might fall in a day—"

"Too right!" Blaidd agreed, cutting her off. The wolfman then hunched low to put his face at their level. He glanced around, eyeing a soldier in worn armor as the man hurried by. "And you did not hear this from me, but there's good odds at least a few are spies from other forces. Ears everywhere, listening in. After all, Radahn holds a shard of the mighty Elden Ring—"

Lisa jumped back into the conversation, shooting Blaidd a glare for good measure. "Which means defeating Radahn lets a person grab a piece of his power, right?" she half-guessed, half-declared. "That makes him quite the prize—"

Blaidd took over. "I'd call that an understatement. With how well-hidden the remaining holders of the shards are, the road to the Erdtree for those seeking to rule must pass through here," he said, unaware of the girl now making strangling motions behind him. Lisa did not seem to like Blaidd much, which Jaune supposed might stem from her difficulty reading into a wolf on two legs with her powers, plus the wide breadth of familiarity the man held with the various ongoings around these parts making him an excellent guide.

With a final step, they arrived at their destination. The main courtyard of the fortress, staging ground for a war… and a celebration. Today, the line blurred between the two.

Here, the champions had assembled to make their preparations, to mingle with both old friends and sworn enemies, all grievances put aside in the face of a greater purpose. Rough hemp ropes crisscrossed above their heads, upon which hung the weapons of the champions who came before, fallen to Radahn.

Nipping at their heels were those seeking to make a profit, peddlers and stalls set up along the walls to form a bustling market. Jaune had given the traders a cursory glance thus far, but he intended to visit them in earnest soon. Many sold food, while others touted artifacts and good luck talismans—some of which might even work. As befitting a martial event, weapons took center stage, and he had already spotted a number of items that seemed to go beyond the mundane. Swords that crackled with esoteric energies, and axes made from no material he recognized. With luck, he would find a decent shield to bring back for Bennett as a souvenir, and something for himself.

Also, they were big on faith here. He could finally talk to a priest and maybe get some help making heads or tails out of the scrolls that Solaire gifted him way back when. He wouldn't mind the ability to throw lightning bolts around, just saying.

That was a matter best left for later, though.

"See him? That's Great Horned Tragoth." Blaidd indicated a man whose armor was wrapped in a pair of huge, ram-like horns. "Many a questing Tarnished owed their lives to his assistance. Ah! And over there we have Okina of the Land of Reeds." He pointed at a samurai, now. One wearing a wooden mask depicting a snarling old man. "His stories are but rumors, and bloody ones at that. Yet, if even half of them are true, then he has crossed blades with legends in his time."

The people around him were too interesting for him to spend his time shopping. The best in the land had answered Jerren's call, and days would need to pass before their deeds were fully listed out.

Strong, he kept hearing. Skilled and battle-hardened, masters of the art of combat. He could learn a thing or two, or ten, if he played his cards right.

Despite being well out of earshot, the samurai turned his head to fix his gaze on their group, thumb running over the handle of his katana. Lisa promptly took a step to the side to hide behind Jaune's frame.

"He wants to kill us along with everybody in the courtyard," she informed him.

"It would not surprise me. Strength manifests in different, often repugnant, ways," Blaidd said. "Still, he abides by the truce. I won't worry about him until this is all over." The corner of his mouth twitched, and his tail wagged back and forth. "I understand him, a little. All these warriors in one place… it gets your blood boiling for a fight, does it not?"

Jaune nodded at once. "I get you. I might not know them like you, but I want to." How they fought, what they've done. There was a whole wide world filled with knights and heroes and villains, with barely any time for him to listen to their tales.

"Look there, that's the fellow I told you about," said Blaidd, nudging him. "Iron Fist Alexander, a fine warrior making his name. He'll go far, mark my word."

Jaune eagerly looked where the wolfman gestured, searching for the person. That soon grew into confusion.

"Am I crazy, or is nobody there?" / "Am I crazy, or is that cooking pot moving?"

He glanced at Lisa, who was rubbing her eyes and squinting hard at a big clay cauldron set up near the tables and benches for eating, a little further past the spot Blaidd indicated. The thing could cook for an army, tall as him and wide enough to fit a dozen of him inside. It was also just sitting there, as pots were wont to do.

"...Do you want my honest opinion?" he asked.

"Shut up, it was rhetorical," Lisa shot back. "That pot is moving."

He placed a palm on her forehead to check if she had a fever. She shoved the hand away and glared at him.

Blaidd was the one to interrupt their little staring contest, seizing Jaune by the shoulder and turning him around. The wolfish maw perked up in a clear smile.

"Never mind that, you two. The gate is lifting again."

A portcullis gate separated the castle from the outer buildings, kept shut most hours. The traders were unable to use it, forced to move their goods via a system of pulleys on the wall or via the side entrances like the servants. The inconvenience had to do with ceremony. The soldiers of Redmane would open it only for one reason right now.

Chains rattled as the gate rose. On the other side stood a figure cast in shadow.

"Another champion has come to join us, and I would recognize that scent anywhere." Blaidd's tail resembled a fan with how fast it was swinging. "He is here."

Jaune whipped his head up to look at his new acquaintance, and had to resist shouting. "He? You mean, the one you said is closest to becoming the Elden Lord? The man that defeated Godrick the Grafted and Rennala of the Full Moon?"

In this place, nobody went without a title. Always 'the-' or 'of-' something. It made him a little jealous. He wouldn't mind one of his own.

"Yes, him," Blaidd confirmed, and Jaune pumped a fist.

He had been waiting for this ever since the wolfman regaled him of recent happenings. A new wind was sweeping over the Lands Between, a time of legends not seen since centuries ago, and Jaune arrived right on time to watch it unfold.

Sometimes, he just had to come right out and say it. Circumstances aside, he loved traveling between worlds.

Next to him, Lisa heaved an indulgent sigh, knowing exactly what was going through his mind. She crossed her arms and bumped him with her hips, waving for him to go ahead. He heard her mutter under her breath, "Stupid boys…"

The gate settled into place with a final clang, and the newest champion stepped through.

Aseo, the—

"It is him," howled Blaidd. "Aseo, the Naked Parry King!"

Jaune balked. "Wait, what? That's seriously his nickname?"

In the wasteland they call the Caelid Wilds, the champions had gathered from far and wide. And once more, the Festival of Radahn commenced in earnest.


Author's Notes: It still gets me that the official comic for Elden Ring is a humorous take on it all.
Here, well, I'll be mixing it with the tone of the game, but on the whole, Jaune's and Lisa's presence in this place is better served by a dash of humor. They're going to need it.

Anyway, might be writing other stuff, might be playing through Elden Ring for realsies this time. Let's see how the week goes.
