#8,537

Chapter 86: The Rock that Falls
​

"Peh! Peh!" Jaune woke up to a mouthful of sand, in darkness with the world pressing down around him.

Terror lanced through the bleary fog of his consciousness. Spitting and coughing, he thrashed about in a bid for freedom with no idea of which way was up or down. In a frenzy, his foot kicked out.

"Oof!"

That sound. That so very human sound. It became his guiding star, and he dug hard to break from his prison. With a final push of effort, the sand dune he was buried inside burst apart.

The first thing to greet him was one of the late afternoon's fading beams of sunlight reflecting off an egg-shaped head.

"Ahhh, dammit! Patches, is that you!?" he shouted, slapping his hands over his watering eyes. Dimly, he noted a catchy song about soda pops playing from the phone hanging around his neck.

He then paused, growing aware of something strange. His toes wiggled in his sock, feeling the warm ground beneath his sole.

"Hang on now, why's my boot off?"

Laid out on the ground, clutching his belly and groaning in pain, Patches cracked an eye open. The man went stock still for a second, before perking up. "Oh… Oh, look who's alive! I was, uh, trying to help! You wouldn't believe how stuck you were in that sand. Why, I almost threw my back out when that boot slipped from you. Heh heh heh."

Jaune wiped at his eyes to get the sand out, regretting it immediately. Summoning a water bottle, he splashed the contents over his face. "What are you even doing here, Patches? This isn't any place for a merchant."

Nothing about his surroundings looked familiar. The sand blew every which way, drifting down like snow. Titanic impacts had reshaped the land with new dunes, new craters, the broken meteorites strewn across the beach giving off a heat haze. The beach might have previously passed for a vacation destination… if one squinted really hard… and pretended to not see the dead bodies, and ignored the smell, and… okay, so the analogy broke down pretty fast, but there was at least the notion of redeeming features like a nice view for people to argue about. Now, what remained was just Caelid Wasteland 2, Rot Harder edition.

He tried to get up only for Patches to quickly grab him and pull him low. The man motioned him to stay down, sweat breaking out on his skin.

"Careful! Careful, now! Wouldn't want the old dog to sniff us out and drop another rock on our noggins, do we? Both feet in the grave and the oaf still has the vision of a stormhawk!"

The peddler poked his head up over the shallow dune to peek around while Jaune put his shoes on. All the while, his phone continued to ring, and the newest call ran its course as he fumbled for the device. Barely a second, and the ringtone started again before he could dial the number back.

"Yello?" he said tiredly.

"You—!" The voice on the line dropped for a moment, then came back. "Oh, hey, you finally returned my calls. What, too shy to talk to me?"

Jaune turned away from Patches to get a bit of privacy from the wide-eyed look the man was giving him and the phone. "Is that why you're calling me? Because I'll hang up."

"You won't," she challenged.

"Try me." Then, with more seriousness, he said, "What is the situation, Lisa?"

Where was everybody…

Her sudden silence told more than words ever could. He heard a sigh over the line, and when next she spoke, Lisa's meek tone revealed her true demeanor beneath the jokes and bravado.

"Over eighty percent casualties. They're saying the whole thing's a bust back here in the castle."

Jaune's eyes fell shut, and he held back a hiss. In a way, he had already expected it. The red sands of the beach had looked wetter than he remembered. Not all those upturned bodies, crushed and broken, were from the fallen of yesteryear.

"The survivors are laying low. I can see some of them from here. Where are you?"

He checked on Radahn's position, and chanced a wave of his hand in the air. The motion provided enough of a prompt for Lisa to find him, and she immediately chided him for going so far in. As if he had a real choice in that. One did not get time to think in the game of dodging meteors.

With Lisa serving as lookout on the high wall, he was able to gain a bird's eye-view of the situation. The closest group of champions huddled just yards away from him, and it heartened him to hear their names from Lisa's lips.

"Jaune, you're going the wrong way," Lisa deadpanned, once she realized that he was heading toward that group instead of the safety of the castle.

"I know what I'm doing." Sort of. If running was to be the play, then they were all running with nobody stuck behind. Cowardice by committee, one might call it.

"Jaaaune," Lisa growled warningly.

"Lisaaa." He turned toward Patches. "Stay low, and follow me. We'll meet up with the others."

Patches nodded, gripping tight onto a spear and tower shield in determination. "Go. Trusty Patches will be right behind you."

That made Jaune smile. He brought up his shield, the very one bought from the man before him, and clinked it together with Patches's own in camaraderie.

"Let's go, then," he said, turning to look ahead, his stance shifting to a runner's starting posture.

It put him in the perfect position for an impact to his rump to send him sprawling into the open. By the time he lifted his head out of the sand, Patches was a glint of reflected sunlight off a bald head in the distance, racing for the elevator.

Meanwhile, Radahn was staring dead-on at Jaune, bow in hand.

"Aha. Ahaha…" Jaune gulped.

As he scrambled over dunes and craters while dodging spears launched like arrows, Jaune swore to kill Patches once this was over.

Ruhm saw the light of day, and a brief exchange ensued between him and Radahn. Bullets weren't as easy to avoid as arrows, and in the span of seconds, half a clip emptied in the demigod.

One would think that'd end it.

"He's alive."

"What do you mean, he's alive!?" Jaune shouted into the phone as he ran unevenly over the sands. "I shot his face off! How did he survive that?"

"Magic."

Jaune ducked under an arrow, the projectile whiffing inches above his head. Despite it never touching him, an immense weight pressed him down until his feet were buried in the soft ground. He tore free, shooting into the air on a blast of rocketfire.

"I'm starting to hate that word," he said, swinging Ruhm around, firing onehanded. The rounds struck Radahn's helm, and this time he paid a close eye to the result, accepting a glancing blow on his Carian shield as the price.

The bullets behaved in an odd manner once they reached the General, diverting downward sharply to glance off the armor, penetrating far too shallow even when they hit. The ones that met flesh in place of metal saw similar effects.

"So, his gravity magic can work in such a way."

That hadn't come from Lisa. A hand seized Jaune and pulled him into cover, where he almost put a round into the beastly visage of a wolf baring its fang at him.

"I was smiling," said Blaidd.

"Sorry."

A projectile hit the dune they hid behind with a loud boom, scattering a cloud of sand over them and the other champions present, a merry band made up of his acquaintances for the most part. A samurai, a jar, a priestess, a no longer naked man, and a Tragoth, all laid snug in a dip in the ground. The one named Therolina was weaving a spell to alleviate her companions' wounds.

Jaune flopped down in an open spot as more impacts shook the area to awaken uncomfortable memories of an artillery bombardment, ending up beside the one person he didn't recognize.

"Jaune, is that an onion next to you? What the heck?"

The knight in a… rotund set of armor heard the comment, and thankfully laughed rather than take offense. Twinkling eyes peered out at Jaune from under a wide-brimmed helm that resembled a sunhat, searching for where Lisa's voice emanated from.

"Your sharp tongue cuts to the quick, young lady, but do not discount my armor as a joke, oh no! An onion has layers!" His gaze then settled on Jaune's. "Wherefore does your company hide her form? Not here, I hope. These shores are not exactly welcoming to us, as you may have surmised."

The calm demeanor of the knight, and frankly of everybody chilling in this hole of theirs, helped ease Jaune's heartbeat that was running a mile a minute. The niggling thought of being in a hole filling up with sand like a burial grave faded to its own small corner, where it could traumatize him at a better time, leaving room for polite introductions. Because obviously that was the most important thing to consider.

"Lionel the Lionhearted, father to Fia." said the jovial knight.

"Jaune Arc, title pending." Was he supposed to know who Fia was?

The bombardment began to peter out. Lisa gave a report from up top that Radahn had engaged a different group of champions, wiping them out wholesale. His deteriorated mind recalled naught of blondes and wolves, and after everyone still alive remained where they were, making not a peep, a shaky sense of peace soon returned to the shore.

Once Jaune relayed Lisa's words, Blaidd asked in a quiet voice, "Did you, perchance, see what happened to the others?"

Jaune's lips drew a thin line.

Blaidd leaned back on the dune, head hanging low. "That… Yes, that's how this has to be. Nothing less, for Radahn."

"The numbers were a mistake," Tragoth said. "It would have worked. It would have worked, and his instincts knew it. Even in rot, he remembers war. None knew more of tactics and odds than him."

"And gravity sorcery," Blaidd bemoaned. "I suppose it was a foregone conclusion before we ever started. We were damn fools."

Aseo chimed in, "What even is gravity anymore? He's plain cheating at this point!" Next to him, Jaune's head rapidly nodded up and down in agreement.

"Calling meteors, empowering his attacks, and now negating damage?" Jaune listed out. "I didn't think his control of magic was to that extent."

For almost a minute, the group laid there in their half-buried grave. The same thoughts surely ran through their minds, the full implications of what it meant to challenge a god.

"They call him the Starscourge Radahn," Blaidd finally said, shifting to sit up. "War is his blood, but… sorcery flows through the heart of Caria, and this is no different for its General."

He pointed above them.

"See that there, those stars in the sky?"

The assembled champions turned their gazes upward. At the height of twilight, the darkening sky had become a canvas awashed in a million little gems. They shone down upon the world, so far removed from the dirty, bloody struggles of mere mortals.

"It's pretty," Jaune said.

The wolfman glanced at him. "The stars move, you know."

"No, they don't."

Jaune quickly covered the phone speakers. Blaidd chuckled without humor, his usual friendly demeanor blunted.

"They do, and their movements guide our fates."

A romantic way of thinking about it. Only, Blaidd didn't seem like he was being poetic. The wolfman brushed the sand off his armor.

"The stars move," he began again. "And for a long time, that was the natural way of things. Until one day, Radahn challenged them with gravity sorcery. Through it, he held back the sky, and has done so ever since his youth."

Aseo jolted to a sitting position. "You're not serious, are you? All of them? But there's like"—he began counting—"one, two, three, lots of them!"

Jaune also doubted the notion. If Blaidd told the truth, then Radahn could have squished them like a bug with a gesture, none of this bow and arrow nonsense. A few of the others voiced similar opinions.

Tragoth, though. "Radahn remembers war, and he remembers honor," he said, to which Blaidd nodded.

"He'd give us a fair fight now, I wager," the wolfman mused. "With a sorry lot like ours, the need for grand sorceries would not even occur to him."

Jaune quietly asked Lisa her take on it.

"Something's off with the sky," she admitted. "Now that he pointed them out, I can sorta tell those stars are wonky. They don't shine properly, or they're too bright. Too close, and… and they're shaking?"

Her vague ramblings gave him all the evidence he needed to believe it. If Lisa was buying the story, then it had to be true.

Radahn was holding the stars in place. It didn't make any sense, the scale of it beyond imagination. Challenging the General had been a fool's game from the beginning, and once that realization hit them, well, the champions assembled here grew quite thoughtful, indeed.

Because, seen in a different light, it suggested something curious. The majority of Radahn's efforts was at the moment directed elsewhere. How much of his magic did fighting stars take? 50%? 90%? They were facing a weakened foe, the weakest he might ever be.

If there ever was a time for man and god to meet on the field of battle, it was now.

Jaune looked up at Blaidd. "What are our chances?"

In answer, the wolfman pushed off of the ground. His blade left its scabbard, drawing an elegant line through the air as it swept high in a swordsman's salute. To Radahn, and to the fallen.

"Why even ask, my friend. I'm terrible with numbers."

And honestly? Jaune was, too.


-o-
​

As they strode over the sand toward their opponent, Jaune and the others hashed out their strategy. A mindless Radahn was not a helpless Radahn, and certainly not a survivable Radahn to anyone here unless they went in with a better plan than the original 'we'll run up and poke him with a sword' brand of genius.

They were still doing that, of course. Just in a smarter way. Seven heads put together should come up with something workable, was their optimistic assumption.

"So hey, Aura—"

"We'll need a decoy," Lionel the Lionhearted urged, glossing over Jaune's umpteenth offer of saving their hide. "A lure to which the good General would direct his aim while the rest of our team closes in, taking him totally by surprise. Never you worry, I volunteer for the task."

Okina immediately shook his head. "No, me. I am faster."

"My armor is sturdy," the heavy-plated Tragoth reminded them. "If anyone is to withstand a blow from his mighty arm, it should be me."

Blaidd, Alexander, even Therolina… each champion offered to be the decoy. Sacrifice, might be the better term. All their suppositions about Radahn were only that, mere guesses on how he would react. They assumed that he'd keep to a code in a one-on-one. A single meteor at the most, instead of a dozen.

Two combatants hadn't thrown their lot into the ring. Jaune sent a glance toward Aseo, the other odd person out. He got the same look in return. A silent acknowledgement passed between them. Neither were willing to be the last man to volunteer, that'd make them a coward.

The slightest twitch of Aseo's lips, and Jaune launched his preemptive bid.

"How about—" / "I could—"

"Perfect!" said Great Horned Tragoth. "We'll leave it to you two to decide among yourselves!"

They had been tricked.

With every pair of eyes on them, there was no backing out now. Jaune sidled up next to Aseo, speaking quickly.

"I have an idea."

"It's going to be me, isn't it?" Aseo said, morose.

"What? No. I'm saying we both go. Split his attention in two directions."

"Where's the catch?"

"There isn't one."

The deeply skeptical look Aseo leveled at him caused pity to rise within Jaune. This poor bastard tended to end up with the short end of the stick, was the impression he got. It took some more convincing, but in the end, Jaune brought the other man on board.

Especially after he explained the concept of dibs. They were risking their lives beyond the call of duty, that should count for something. That bow Radahn carried around was his, no ifs, ands, or buts.

Radahn's endless wandering soon brought his gaze in their direction, and the plan commenced. Jaune broke into a run with Aseo on his heels, hot sand kicking up behind them.

His rocket boots engaged to drag him into the sky, where three dimensions of movement opened up for him to contend with any attack. The Rathalos armor swapped for the glider which snapped to existence on his back, its wings unfurling. He spared a moment before flying off to check back on Aseo and see how he would approach the task, hearing a sharp whistle pierce the air.

A ghostly steed faded in from the empty aether, its form growing solid as Aseo leapt astride the saddle in a smooth maneuver. Beast and man shot forward at an impressive speed, putting distance from the other champions. Not to be outdone, Jaune raced alongside them. They had Radahn's full attention on them now, their brave charge an unmistakable challenge.

From behind them drifted Tragoth's voice. "Prepare for…!"

"What?" Jaune called out over a shoulder. Radahn was drawing back the string on his bow and Jaune kept a careful eye on that, with little room for hosting conversations with the others.

"He's…!"

Jaune flew down beside Aseo. "Are you catching that?"

"Something about bringing the pain?" Aseo said, scratching his head. Below, his horse neighed as if to correct him. Neither man paid attention to the horse, however. Since it was a horse.

"Hell yeah, we are." Jaune put out a fist, and Aseo bumped it with his knuckles.

Another shout, this time many in one. It coincided with the General letting loose an arrow.

"Watch for Radahn's Rain!"

The arrow vanished high above them. A rumble followed, and even though the day was not yet fully turned into night, darkness swept over the beach. A shade cast by countless falling spears.

"Ah," said Jaune. "That skill."

With not much time, he nudged Aseo by the shoulder.

"Fifty-fifty odds. Good luck if it's you."

The other man nodded. "Same. See you on the other side."

Jaune had reported on his first clash with Radahn to the champions, and so they knew to an extent what the skill entailed. Its most dangerous feature was the tracking of the target.

The solution to that seemed simple. They just had to split up, with Jaune banking left and the horse carrying Aseo turning hard to the right.

The column of spears smoothly separated down the middle, each half chasing after a quarry.

"This isn't fair ahhhhh!"

"I'm gonna die ahhhhh!"

What part of this was gravity!? The panicked cries of two poor souls echoed for miles.

In the midst of running away—hang on, no.
In the midst of bravely charging in a lateral fashion, Jaune pulled out his own magic to retaliate. A metal tube landed in his hands, the trigger pulled in a split second as he relied all on 'marksmanship' to guide his aim—he was neither in position, or had the time, for proper shooting. A missile burst forth from the rocket launcher, streaking toward Radahn. What happened to it after that, he missed, more concerned with dodging a spear that had gotten way too close to hitting the back of his pants.

He did catch the trails of light that Aseo was firing from a stave while on horseback. Forced to stay on the ground unlike him, the champion struggled to keep even a step ahead of the raining projectiles, yet wove magic in every spare moment. Shards of crystalline energy peppered Radahn and his surroundings, working stupendously as a distraction to occupy the General—the others were moving up without a single impediment.

That single-minded focus proved Aseo's undoing. Juggling the different tasks, he reacted too late to an arrow Radahn sent at him. Swirling with gravity magic, the bolt flashed across the distance trailing light like a laserbeam, fast as a bullet. There was nothing anyone could have done.

Aseo gripped the collar of his surcoat as an explosion bloomed around his form. Smoke and sand obscured Jaune's last glimpse of him.

"No," Jaune muttered.

"Jaune… He's gone."

He was not listening. "No, no, no!" His voice rose higher with each cry, until he was screaming. "Just die with dignity, won't you?"

"Uhhh. Excuse me?"

Fwoosh! A horse galloped out of the cloud of smoke, a figure riding on its back. Pale, sweaty skin gleamed in the twilight, loincloth majestically(?) flapping in the wind. The Naked Parry King had dodged a certain death.

Yet, at what cost?

"Ewwww!" Lisa screeched over the phone. "Why do you make the weirdest friends?"

"He's not my friend," Jaune tried to deny, hand held beside his face to shade his eyes. "I don't know him."

Thankfully, the champion in question donned his clothes once out of danger, dressing while in motion with unnatural ease as the rain of spears let up. It told of ceaseless practice to the point of mastery, to baffle both the blond onsite and the blonde at the castle.

Jaune had no chance to dwell on it, though. He was in the thick of it now, closing in on Radahn, near enough to peer into the mad eyes of the demigod towering at the height of a Goliath Grimm.

A blank calm existed within that madness. Radahn feared him not. Not his guns, not his flying. The battlefield was his domain.

In no hurry, the demigod slung the bow over a shoulder and drew his swords. Twin blades each bigger than a grown man. He slammed them together, creating a loud boom that shook the air and relayed a message.

Come.

His challengers obliged.

Jaune overshot the demigod on his glider, baiting a swing of the sword to squeeze out one last second of distraction. He then dropped, trading glider for armor to hit the sand with a heavy roll, reversing course in an instant to lunge at the turning Radahn with Crocea Mors. On the other side, the main force arrived to launch their own attacks. They had Radahn surrounded in a classic pincer maneuver.

It went wrong almost immediately.

He saw flesh. He stabbed at flesh. Simple.

The twin swords slammed into the ground in front of him, stopping him cold. And, wow, did Radahn look angry now.

"Did you really try to kill his horse?" Blaidd shouted.

Radahn pulled up his swords, and swept them before him in a frenzy, forcing Jaune to scramble backward out of harm's way.

"Horse?" Jaune shouted back. "What ho—There's a horse!"

The scrawny, gray thing stood below Radahn, and was the fleshy bit that Jaune had nearly managed to stab. The demigod outmeasured it by several magnitudes, to the point that he sat astride the horse with both feet planted in the ground. It looked almost comical, the giant man and his tiny, tiny horsie.

"That sickly steed is his dear companion!" Blaidd explained while chasing after Radahn, who was in turn chasing after Jaune. "Once Radahn outgrew it, he learned gravity sorcery in order to adjust his own weight so that he would never have to abandon his beloved friend!"

"What the hell, that's so sweet!"

"Isn't it just? So don't touch the horse or you might provoke him into blowing up the entire world!"

Lisa was outright cooing over the line, never mind that her beloved friend (himself, he was talking about himself) was fighting for his life. The others, meanwhile, looked at him like he was some sort of monster. The only one not giving him grief was the horse he almost murdered.

An enraged Radahn rampaging about worked against their favor, though. They needed him in one place, carefully managed and attacked on all sides.

Ducking under one of the swords, Jaune came back up with shield aloft, hoping to stop Radahn in his tracks.

An oversized blade crashed onto him in the very next second, pulverizing the Geo sphere that appeared and vanished in the blink of an eye. Heavy as a Valkyria's lance, heavier even, weighed down with magic until his arms were shaking in an effort to hold it back. The fanciful thought of parrying the blade vanished as all he could do was endure, his legs sinking into the soft terrain.

A glow briefly overtook him, easing the strain enough for him to dip to one side, letting the sword skid off the surface of the shield. The ground next to him blew apart from the resulting impact, covering him in sand.

Through squinted eyes, he glimpsed a new entrant in this duel of two. Aseo leapt off his horse, sword brandished and somersaulting in the air to build momentum. The blade slashed down dead center on Radahn's helm.

"Uweh?"

The odd sound slipped from Aseo as his sword skittered off the helm on an angle, a small nick left on the metal. The man crashed facefirst to the ground not far from Jaune, having given no thought to a landing strategy.

Salvation came for him in the form of their allies, who attacked Radahn at that time. Alexander crashed into the General's back, bringing the full might of the secret spinning jar arts. Clay ground on armor until it sparked fire.

"Get up, Aseo! Now is our chance!" the jar encouraged. As Radahn engaged him in combat, a shadow slipped past him. The swirl of a fur cloak coalesced in Blaidd, who swung his blade in a blistering combo.

"Alexander, do not stay still. Make way for the others," the wolfman said with poise as he weaved between Radahn's attacks. Taking his own advice, a backstep allowed a new combatant to enter the fray.

Okina of the Land of Reeds glided over the sand with a long katana in his right hand and a shorter blade in his left, his quick steps carrying him from the ground to Radahn's knee, then past the demigod without a pause. Only once he was done did skin split and the sound of metal on metal rang. Flecks of golden armor broke off to fly in the air, and blood spilled from the thin spaces between the armor plates.

The samurai hissed in dismay. "Too poor by half."

Jaune darted past him, mustering his full strength to divert the heavy slash of a sword. The wounds left on Radahn slowed him down not a bit, superficial to a one. An unimpressive outcome given Okina's masterful display of swordsmanship, so he could understand the frustration. But then, Radahn was plain cheating with his sorcery.

"Hit harder!" he advised.

The solution was simple. Just break through. Stronger than Radahn's altered gravity could counteract, and faster than he could redirect.

Jaune swapped his sword for the gunlance, propped atop his shield driven in the ground. A pull of the trigger, and the world heard the sound of a gong as the explosive shell smacked against Radahn's helm. Fire bloomed to engulf his head, his entire body rattling from the blow.

For a second, Jaune thought that did it. The snarling visage of the General appearing out of the smoke doused that hope. [Third Arm] yanked him backward, the twin swords missing him by less than an inch. The blade rammed into the earth, embedding deep. Jaune saw his opportunity, seizing it to lunge forward.

The swords blasted apart the sand as it came back up, giving him a whack that sent him sailing over the other champions' heads.

Short bursts of the rockets helped him regain control. He landed on the sand with a good view of absolute beatdown Radahn was laying on his allies. The twin swords were no longer swords, the surface encrusted in a layer of rocks to turn them into clubs. Each swing that connected with a fighter resulted in a harsh impact that blew them away, scattering the airtight formation that had, they foolishly assumed, locked the General in place.

"Magic?" he asked.

"Magic," Lisa confirmed. "Don't even try to block it. You'll lose."

"Always with the vote of confidence, aren't you?"

Diving back into the fight, he listened as best he could to Lisa's running commentary. Where the most damage had been done that he should aim for, where their allies were and what they needed of him. He bought time for the others to recover.

Radahn's style of fighting grew clearer as Jaune baited him back into a duel of two. His mind remembered the little tricks he loved in life, magic and might woven together in seamless flow. A slash would lead to a stab, to a wave of crackling energy that warped the ground and forced Jaune to take to the air. A gesture then, and unseen forces would pull him in for a finishing blow. With a warning from Lisa each time, Jaune held on through it all.

As the champions returned to the fight, Radahn redoubled his efforts to get rid of Jaune. The sickly steed that Jaune wasn't allowed to kill surged after him, keeping Radahn always in range.

To that, Jaune adopted the tactics of a gnat. Some would call it the style of Huntsmen, the counter to a foe that did not know to stop.

The rocks on Radahn's swords crumbled in the middle of a swing, transforming a slow and deliberate attack into a lightning quick lunge. Jaune turned aside right in time to let the blades sail past, then kicked into the air with a burst of rocketfire.

Launched to the height of Radahn's head, he whipped a foot across his unprotected face. The heat forced Radahn to shut his eyes, a prime opportunity that Jaune would not miss. His sword swung for the exposed throat.

A surge of gravity pulled his blade off-course, scoring a deep gouge on the breastplate below, inches from where he aimed it. Miles, in terms of combat. The same fate befell Aseo, whose overhead slash scratched the side of the helm.

Geo energy swirled around him, pushing away one of Radahn's massive arms, a chance for Jaune to engage his boots to flip up and over the General. Below, Lionel the Lionhearted and Great Horned Tragoth launched simultaneous attacks on the back of Radahn in a bid to knock him off his horse. Hammer and sword drove into his sides, while Jaune harried the demigod with gunfire from above.

As the others broke off from the assault, Jaune latched [Third Arm] onto Radahn, pulling forward to end up sitting on his shoulders. Instead of sword or gunlance, a simple knife he used for miscellaneous tasks appeared in his hand. A twirl reversed his grip on it, with him then driving the knife into Radahn's face.

He could feel the invisible barrier working against the knife, weakening the blow. Clutching the weapon with both hands, he gritted his teeth and pushed through the resistance.

Radahn screamed as the tip of the knife pierced his eyeball, sinking in at a glacial pace. Bringing his swords together, he reared back his head.

"Incoming!"

"Got it!" Jaune shouted, leaping off Radahn as the demigod bashed those blades against his own head.

The General wasn't done, however, thrashing about to lay waste to his surroundings with no regards to tactics or reason, consumed by a base anger. Alexander raced into that storm, shielding Tragoth and Lionel with his body as he pulled them to safety. Meanwhile, Aseo stripped, dressed, and stripped again in a desperate effort to escape harm.

Healing light washed over Jaune, an unnecessary but kind gesture from Therolina the Fingermaiden that he acknowledged with a quick salute. From there, he stayed in the air to search for an opening. They had Radahn on the ropes, and now was no time to let up.

He didn't have to look for long. The half-blinded demigod, in his frenzy, lost sight of his prey. The moment he paused in his onslaught to peer about, half a dozen swords were upon him.

"Stay to his left!" Jaune called out and followed his own advice, joining Aseo in pinning down one of Radahn's arms. One went high, the other low, their blades seeking purchase in the elbow joint where the armor was weaker. A wide sweep of Radahn's sword beat them back, others taking their place.

Gravity energy began to gather around Radahn. Faced with a choice of retreat or pressing on, an agreement passed between the combatants without the need of words. They'd risk it for one more strike, one more chance to end the whole thing.

They paid for it.

The blast took them all, a blunt wave of physical force that ripped them from the ground and tossed them every which way. Champions rained down on the sand. In a flash, the tide had turned.

Jaune landed on his back yards from where he was, groaning as the strange sensation of being squeezed flat passed. He looked up in time to see a giant clay jar falling upon him.

"Holy—erk!" Anything else he said came out as muffled whimpers, crushed beneath his ally's great weight.

Alexander did not seem to notice that the jar was sitting on him. "Oh, I say. I felt that one. Jars were not made to fly."

"Owww…"

"What the? Jaune Arc, what are you doing down there? Hang on now, just let me roll off of you."

"Owww…"

"This is harder than I thought," the jar admitted, arms and legs flailing in the air. Jaune had no idea what was inside the jar, but it weighed a ton. "If you would just give me a little push, perhaps that would do it—Ah! Aseo, help! Help!"

Laying in the dark, Jaune heard Aseo's reply from nearby.

"Alexander? Why is it that whenever we meet, you're stuck somewhere and I have to shove your butt free?"

Despite his grumbling, Aseo joined in on the effort, and soon Alexander was able to regain his footing. Jaune crawled out of the hole he was buried in, taking gulps of the blessed fresh air as he looked around.

Everybody had withstood that attack, albeit to varying degrees of success. Okina needed healing, something Therolina tended to. Lionel, on the other hand, made it out well enough thanks to his round-shaped armor, while Tragoth was already standing up.

The one person missing in this picture… was the demigod.

The world tinged in a violet glow.

"Uh-oh," Jaune said. "I know this one."

He looked up. A star was falling from the sky. Its name was Radahn.

"Everybody, take cover!"

The champions ran pell-mell, like ants from a kicked nest. They had little options. There was nowhere to hide on this beach.

Scrambling upright, Jaune summoned shields in both hands, and drew on Geo to encase him in its protective embrace. The shields slammed into place, propped on the ground.

Aseo braced his shield right next to the ones Jaune set up. They shared a look.

"Are you kidding? You'll die," Jaune said.

"I have a skill for this," Aseo assured him. "I just have to endure!" he yelled that last word.

An immense heat heralded Radahn striking the ground. The resulting blast made the earlier one look downright puny, changing the direction of the wind and blanketing the beach with the glow of gravity. Sand and old battlefield remains kicked up in the air, and stayed there floating in the grips of magic.

The explosion swept over Jaune's position. Light pulsed around him, steadying his stance. Aseo had no such power, yet he clenched his jaw and weathered the pressure with cool-headed calm.

Or… no, he didn't. As the blast dissipated, the Naked Parry King sank to his knees. Sand had scraped across his skin like knives, tearing wounds. Breathing hard, he leaned on his shield to let it help him not fall.

Of the champions, Aseo was the only one to remain somewhat upright. The others laid flat on the ground, limbs shaking if moving at all. From Tragoth to Lionel to Therolina, none had been able to escape unscathed.

A slew of healing potions popped out of Jaune's Pocket. He uncorked the first and poured it on the coughing Aseo. Then, since he lacked his reliable Palico support, he began lobbing the potions to the rest.

"They're medicine to heal you," he said. "Hurry and take it, he'll be back for another round soon!"

His phone crackled, and Lisa's voice came through over the line. "No, Jaune. It's over."

He opened his mouth to protest, but a bugle call sounded out to interrupt him. A long and mournful note drifting from the castle to its surroundings. It was the furthest thing from the music of war, or victory.

"That's them sounding the retreat. The mood in the castle is that this is it. They don't think you guys can go on anymore."

"Hah? What kind of talk is that? We got this!" Jaune asserted.

He wasn't close to done. In the past couple of months, he had faced worse than this and came out on top. Or survived it, at least.

"Look around, silly man. The others are barely holding on, and it's pretty clear to the soldiers that Radahn won't die. Time to go."

Steadfastly, Jaune refused to look at the champions he had fought alongside. They'd get up, he just knew it.

A groan from Blaidd, a small distance away to Jaune's left, drew his and Aseo's attention. The lively glint to that wolf's eyes was gone. He shivered at the sight of Radahn, half-obscured in the smoke and dust. If Jaune didn't know better, he would call it fear.

"She isn't wrong," said the wolfman. His big ears must have caught the conversation. "Sorry, Aseo. I know you needed that Great Rune, but…" Blaidd dropped his head back on the sand. "I guess this is all we amount to. A sorry lot of nobodies in a world of gods, too big for our britches—gack!"

The healing potion Jaune threw had conked the wolfman right on the nose, with Blaidd now rolling around on the ground screaming curses at him.

"Don't give me that," Jaune urged him. "We made him bleed, and what bleeds can die. What was all that you said about honor, huh?"

"Can't eat honor, I thought I told you that," Lisa chimed in. "Looks like they're starting to realize it, too. Anyway, that stuff doesn't have anything to do with you, does it?"

A pang of hurt shot through him, though he gave no outward sign. Lisa was never one to think deeply of her sharp tongue, she didn't mean it. That was what he told himself.

As if to convince them, and his own heart, he drove his sword into the ground to act as leverage for him to climb up to his feet. The aftermath of Radahn's falling star was dispersing, the General regaining his vision. The first thing he would see, was Jaune in a fighting stance with weapons in hand.

"Okay, sure," he said. "We're a sorry lot. But is that so bad? I've been in this spot before. I don't think it's hopeless yet. This isn't even in the top three of scary things I've fought," he boasted to psych himself up.

"Ha! And you were doing so well up until then!" a new voice cut in.

Jaune whipped his head around, but the owner of the voice made it moot by stepping past him.

"Jerren?" he asked, gawking. "Should you be here?"

"I have some fight left in me," said Castellan Jerren. The old man clapped Jaune on the shoulder, squeezing it as a friend would. He carried a greatsword with a wavy blade, propped like a cane. "I have served under the banner of the good General in ages past, and let me tell you, not a day went by back then that did not scare me shitless. The demigods are honorable, grand, inspiring, and also mad as a basket of kittens. My friend fought the stars. The stars."

Well, when he put it like that…

"By the by, he would have liked you," the old man commented.

Jaune pointed at his chin. "Me?"

Jerren nodded, before his gaze lowered to Aseo. "You, too. And the wolf and the jar and all the rest. He loved mortals. No matter how many fell, another always stepped forward ready to challenge monsters and gods." The castellan chuckled, and with a grunt, heaved the sword in his hand up to prop it on top of a shoulder. "We know not of any other way."

Maybe that was what they call honor. Jaune thought that he would like to find out.

He turned and looked at the others, gauged their expressions and offered a hand. He found someone to accept it, Aseo the most serious he had ever seen today. The champions likewise helped one another stand, even if there were groans and whines. The last one to get up would be forever labeled a coward and a weakling, not fools like the rest. They settled in a ragtag line arrayed before General Radahn. For one more try.

Pieces on the board with no hand to guide them, each going along their path. Once the smoke cleared, Radahn found not one of them missing.

"Forward!" shouted Jerren, sword pointed ahead.

And the champions heeded his call.

As Jerren took the field, something within Radahn seemed to recognize him. He focused on the old man more than he would most, although that was the extent of it. The rot had taken the last traces of friendship, and what remained was the beastly desire of violence. The demigod spurred his horse, and charged at the castellan with swords brandished aloft.

The castellan set his greatsword flame and met the bull rush with a well-placed slash under the arm. Spinning with the motion allowed him to deal with the demigod's followup.

He held his own for perhaps four seconds, all told. Plenty, to prove he belonged in this company. As he fell back before the heavy attacks, Jaune relieved him of his place.

Rocks began to swirl around Radahn, giving those close quarters another angle to contend with. One would have smashed into Jaune from the side, but Tragoth intercepted with a mighty swing of his hammer to ground it to dust, leaving Jaune free to slam his gunlance home and—boomboomboomboom!—land a fullburst barrage straight against Radahn's chest.

The force of the bombardment dented the golden breastplate and rocked the General, but he ultimately kept his balance through his mastery of gravity. The same mastery that sent him and his horse jumping high above the combatants, and come down with his swords chopping like guillotines.

The simultaneous clang of three swords meeting Radahn's two rang in the clearest note. Jaune, Aseo, and Blaidd strained their muscles as they held back the immense, and increasing, weight of the massive slabs of metal. Another champion, Lionel, lanced past them with his blade. That hit was no good, skidding off-target.

"Do not let him have a single second of reprieve," Castellan Jerren counseled. "He will have all the rest he wants after he is in the dirt!"

"Are you two really friends?" Jaune ground out, knees starting to buckle from what felt like the weight of a mountain.

"The fool had the gall to go and die while owing me money! I shall never forgive him!"

Best friends, then.

On an agreed signal ("Last one out is a pancake!"), the three fighters blocking Radahn leapt aside then converged again. Jaune led the way, stomping on Radahn's sword and springing high to stab at his exposed face. The General jerked his head out of the way, but immediately had to deal with Aseo who had followed in Jaune's steps, then Blaidd after that. The same relentless onslaught that was so hard for others to withstand, used against himself.

And they were not the end. Okina climbed atop Alexander, standing on the lid of the jar to gain height where he swiped furiously at Radahn, countering him blow for blow, parrying sword with sword through sheer stubborn will. Tragoth kept him safe, his giant stone hammer spinning with the force of a whirlwind.

Like ants, they rushed at the demigod. Biting, biting, always biting. The raging beast was beset on all sides. Whenever it lashed out, it bled.

"Jaune," Lisa piped up as he raced in to shield Alexander from being cracked open with a sword cut. "Just to confirm, the gravitational force layered on Radahn's armor is directing everything downward, right?"

He deflected the first sword into the ground, and pulled the exhausted Okina off the jar to avoid decapitation. "I think? To be honest, I'm a little preoccupied at the moment!"

Too tightly grouped, the samurai and him were sitting ducks. They scattered in opposite directions, dodging the flying rocks Radahn sent after them.

"It is, and I was only making you feel included. Whatever, it means that he likely has a weakness to attacks from above. They'll do full damage so long as they aren't redirected."

Jaune furrowed his brow in thought, and backpedaled out of range. Tragoth smoothly took his place without complaints.

"I think Aseo was aiming for that," Jaune said, replaying bits of the battle that he remembered. "Although maybe he didn't outright realize it."

The idea that the Naked Parry King of all people had been on the same wavelength as her displeased Lisa greatly, judging by the angry spluttering happening on the other end of the call.

Still, the information put the situation in perspective. They were trying to overpower the defensive layer through sheer strength or skill, which worked up to a point. It followed the strategy of death from a thousand paper cuts, traded for stamina and a whole lot of risk for his allies.

Everyone hoped for a decisive blow. If Lisa's conclusion proved correct, then they had found their chink in the armor. Fighting gravity was a losing proposition. So, don't. A strike from the top would see them victorious.

'So long as they aren't redirected' were the operating words.

"Guys! Guys! Team meeting!" Jaune yelled at the top of his lungs.

"Ahaha, you're hilarious," Aseo yelled back mockingly, pausing his words to gasp for air. "We're busy dying here, Jaune!"

"Speak aloud, young man!" Jerren encouraged. "Speak proud and without hesitation. The fool has not his wits left to overhear our plans! Like a dog, howling at the sky!"

Radahn threw one of his rocks at Jerren, forcing him to duck low.

"'Twas a coincidence," the old man insisted.

Jaune quickly relayed the amazing idea. "We will drop a rock on him, see how he likes it."

"...That's it?" Lionel the Lionhearted twisted around to look at Jaune, the incredulity showing throwing despite the full suit of armor. The lapse in attention nearly got him impaled on Radahn's sword, had not Blaidd got there first to knock him aside.

"No, look, it's a really big rock." He demonstrated for their benefit, summoning the boulder.

Tragoth performed a spit-take. "Why is there so much blood on it? What the heck is wrong with you?"

"Eh? Eh?" Jaune motioned with his hands. There was no way they could deny the lethality of this thing, it looked like it killed a village. (They did seem to be questioning his sanity, given the new light they saw him in.)

Those not in immediate danger from Radahn deliberated on the matter. Those who were in danger—Aseo, mainly—had a more succinct opinion.

"You know what, let's just do it!" Aseo screamed to the others.

And yet, he seemed to be doing quite fine, rolling across the ground one step ahead of Radahn to avoid being chopped apart. An agile flip and a piercing whistle, and he now zigzagged through a field of falling rocks on a spectral steed, circling around and around Radahn while shooting shards of magic.

The amount of clothes on him was vanishing one by one as time went on, though. Traded for power, one might imagine.

"Your plan is worth a shot," Blaidd said. "Go. We'll keep Aseo alive to deal with Radahn."

"We're in this together, right? I'm not soloing him, right?"

Jaune threw a salute to their sacrifice as glider wings snapped open on his back. "You have to pin him down. No mistakes, okay? He'll know to watch out for it after the first time!"

"Waaaait!"

Even in a world of magic, people neglected to look up in the thick of battle. But once they had cause to, it'd be something they would check for. The time he spent buzzing around Radahn's head might have already ruined the whole trick.

So, when he took off, he went high. Higher than the tallest tower of the castle with the wind screeching in his ears, only leveling out at the point where none would count him as a participant of the battle. Whatever happened down there, it was up to them.

The calculations involved with dropping a pebble from the height of a skyscraper and hoping for it to hit an actual target… was slightly beyond him. They didn't teach this in Huntsman school. Thankfully, he had Lisa, who cheated the whole thing. She had taken on the task of keeping an eye on the position of Radahn, the progress of the champions in keeping the demigod in place, the wind and dust and humidity or any other factor that came into it. He was just the hand to her will.

"Not yet," reported his spotter.

"I know."

"Not yet!"

"I know!"

The waiting was the hard part. As the minutes flew by, he started to grow antsy watching his allies. Alexander was easy to spot with his shape, the jar tackling Radahn as hard as he could only to be dragged along by the demigod and his horse. A person fell like a puppet with its strings cut, he didn't know who. Some damn fool had stripped naked and was taunting Radahn with a dance. Who could that be?

The sound of Lisa's voice was a balm for his nerves, cutting through his unease.

"Now, do it now!"

Some might doubt her, pose questions and demand evidence. For him, the action he took was simpler. She had done all he asked, he was sure of it. Now was his turn. The boulder popped into existence, high in the sky.

No fancy robots or superpowers needed here. In the eternal game of bashing each other's heads in, the humble rock would always make its return. The old reliable.

The boulder hung there for a second, and an eternity.

Was Lisa behind it, or had they just known? The drums rolled, shaking the shore. The bugles sounded again from the Redmane wall. This time, they sang with a triumphant note. They sang a song of war, of Radahn.

The rock fell.

It was no star, yet it decided the fate of the world.


-o-
​

The cold moon shone upon the world, its soft light a comfort to all.

Jaune sat atop the castle wall, beside Lisa, at a remove from the party raging below them. It was only getting more rowdy and welcoming as time went on, but this corner where the world was quiet suited them fine.

Tonight was a night of shooting stars.

They crossed the sky, sometimes several at once, free from the chains that bound them for an age. It portended to the Lands Between that fate was on the move, but for the two of them… Well, it was just a pretty light show. The prettiest of the places they had known.

Many of the stars flew toward the north, where a golden glow bathed the land in its warmth. That glow came from a tree, a tree that had not always been there. It appeared to him some time after the battle, and Jaune had doubted his eyes at first until Lisa told him that she saw it, too.

Because… that tree was the world. He could describe it no other way. It lived beyond an ocean, beyond the mountains, yet a person at this castle could trace the grooves on its trunk with the naked eye. Its branches covered the horizon, the falling leaves mistaken for stars.

All thoughts of merriment and drinks could not hold a candle to simply sitting here under a canvas of shooting stars, Lisa's head resting on his shoulder, watching this wonder he would never see again.

"Okay, I'll admit it," Lisa drawled. "This almost made it all worth the trouble."

He cracked a smile, glancing down at her. "Almost?"

"Don't even, mister. You didn't have to go and put yourself in danger today, did you?" She nudged him with her elbow. "Did you?" she chided, exasperated.

"I…"

He thought on the question, even though it needed no answer. He thought of the people he met today and their earnest hopes, and what he could give them. He thought of honor.

"I think I did," he said, and tilted back his head to enjoy the breeze. "Because today was another day where I want to be better than I am."

Down below, the castle soldiers had broken out the finer vintage. Aseo was chugging straight from a barrel now, locked in a contest with Alexander. A jar had lips, after all, so obviously it could drink. How delightfully nonsensical.

Jaune's gaze met with a wolf's, who made to wave him over before seeing the person by his side. A knowing smirk, and nothing smirked like a wolf, grew on his face as he nodded and turned away, motioning for others to not bother the pair. Jaune would have his peace for a while.

A hundred shooting stars racing across in the sky. Jaune sat on the wall with one leg swinging, a friend by his side. Nothing more needed to be said. It was a perfect night, and no mistake.

Exactly why they came here in the first place, even if there were some hiccups along the way.

"...Hey, know what I'm thinking? We can ask for a ton of freebies from the merchants right now and they'll probably give it to us. Not to mention what the champions owe you. That Blaidd is hiding good stuff, I just know it."

"Lisa."

"The soldiers, too. I'll bet we can talk our way into the armory!"

"Lisa, please."

"Where did everybody go? Guys, I brought presents!"

That was the first thing Jaune said after he passed through the portal, and returned to their rented log cabin. Mere days since they moved in and it already felt like home, but an empty home was no home at all.

Calling out to the upper floor, he received not a single answer.

Lisa tugged on his sleeve, head cocked to crane an ear upward. "I think I hear something outside."

He led the way out onto the porch, where Lisa's words were proven correct. Not that she got to enjoy that fact, as she at once gagged at the sight before them.

A deer was strung up on a wooden frame, expertly killed with a cut throat, belly slit and its blood draining into a bucket. A fluffy ball of fur climbed about the carcass, hard at work with a sharp knife clutched in a paw.

Nearby, Hu Tao watched Escha skin the deer with fascinated eyes. Dressed casually in neokitsch fashion, she looked nothing like a funeral director, an observation that would earn outrage if he told her.

Hu Tao noticed the pair of them, and a smile lit up on her face. She scurried over.

"You're finally back! How was your day trip?" she asked.

He mulled on the series of events that led to him bashing a god on the head with a rock. "It's a long story, I'll tell you about it later. Anyway, where's everybody?"

"Uh…"

The fidgeting boded nothing good.

"Fischl and Bennett went to the library in town," Hu Tao began, only to be interrupted by a paling Lisa.

"You let them drive?" the blonde whispered.

Hu Tao frantically waved her hands in denial. "Ohnono, they took bicycles. They're doing fine, there's no problem with them. But, um."

"What?"

"Well, it's a funny story…" The girl trailed off.

Something seemed to have clicked for Lisa, that great detective, because she started looking around the area.

"The motorcycle isn't here."

Lisa was referring to the yellow motorcycle often parked beside their car. An ARCH Nazaré model taken from Night City, its absence wasn't exactly a cause for concern, given the owner's wanderlust. Yet, judging by the awkward way Hu Tao scratched her cheek, that was the very problem she was bringing forward.

"Uh-huh," Hu Tao confirmed. "It's impounded in a place called Iowa right now."

Lisa yelped, "That's like a thousand miles from here. What the heck is that girl doing?"

Chapter 87: Small Town Mischief
​

He felt the need, the need for speed.

Where street lights blurred, and the tires screamed. The open road at 2AM was meant for nothing else.

The car he drove blasted down the highway, a thousand miles put to the wheels with one of Escha's energy drinks staving off the fatigue of his previous trip. The day-night cycle of different worlds had aligned in a most screwy fashion, him coming back from a Caelid midnight to the New York afternoon and yet to get any sleep. The price for that would come due in the hours ahead, once the potion lost effect.

He rolled into the small town of Poltergeist as the only person on its empty streets. The stores he passed had their lights off, even the ones that sold liquor, with people's cars parked in the driveway of their homes that were spaced out a shade too far from one another and surrounded by trees. He got the impression that this sleepy place kept to itself, and wasn't one for a lively club scene after dark.

The town center spanned a single street, short and sweet. A thousand times had he walked its length without ever setting foot here. Gods, did it feel familiar.

He found the police station in no time. It was the closest building to the church that sat dead center at the end of the avenue. The sign over the door said sheriff, but he figured that amounted to the same thing. Better, even. A lot of settlements in Vale, usually the ones further out like his that didn't get much support from the city, would elect one of their own to the position and that worked well enough to cover the day to day affairs of their small population. A dedicated police department was a sign that a settlement had hit the big times.

So far as he knew, a sheriff's main job involved tossing drunks into the lockup on a Friday night to sleep off a bender, where they couldn't make other people feel mad, sad, or bad. Their second, and rarer, job had to do with deputizing the townsfolk to deal with the occasional problem as a community.

Ideally beforehand, often during or after. That part tended to end up rather slapdash, as things go. His father always said that the way the city did it was better.

Whatever the case, experience growing up told him that a sheriff in a place like this blurred the line between cold, impersonal authority and the everyday normal. Someone who kept the law, yet might be happy to settle a matter with a friendly conversation or a delicious apple pie. That suited him just fine, tonight.

The squat, blocky building that the office occupied still had its lights on, and the doors opened with a push. A warm enough welcome in his books. Walking in, he found a room that was almost too sparse with a desk and a couple of filing cabinets resting at the back wall, a TV hanging in the corner next to the entrance. Tidy, though. The floor tiles squeaked under his boots, sparkling clean.

"Hi there!" he chirped to the older man sitting behind the desk, whose badge announced him as a deputy rather than the actual sheriff.

So, the overworked one that didn't get to have delicious apple pie. Uh-oh.

No, no. Let's not jump to conclusions.

He affected a cheery, if somewhat stiff, mien. "I'm here to see about a girl and her bike?"

"You're with the freak? Great, just great."

Well, they sure were off to a swimming start.

"I mean, I could leave her here if that's what you really want. You're the one who'd have to wait on her hand and foot. She has a doctor's note."

Thus hath he spake the magic words.

Kind of. It took some more doing to gain entry to the jail cells, given that he was itching for a fight after the oh so friendly opening shot and the deputy pretty much dared him to do it out of a twisted desire to relieve his own boredom. The night shift did strange things to people. Still, the promise of a problem gone from his sight convinced the deputy to come around even if Jaune got the impression that the man wasn't fully willing to leave it at that.

With a jangle of keys, the deputy opened the door to a short hallway while continuing their conversation, which had reached a particularly vexing impasse. "You can't tell me that's natural," he insisted. "It sticks to her face and won't come off. Prosthetic, my foot."

"I showed you the paperwork," Jaune said, following the man in. "She had an accident. Let's stop talking about it, okay?"

"Yeah, yeah, it'd be a real tearjerker, if it's true. And she should've had all of that on her in the first place, along with her ID." The deputy smacked the sheet of paper he held, the one printed with a copy of a driver's license and passport that was both brand new yet dated years ago. "Don't think I didn't notice the fake name or that we had nothing on her in the system until you showed up. What do laws even mean anymore…"

The deputy was not the only person unhappy. Lisa had complained to no end as she paid extra to expedite the documents and the various other services offered by their favorite forger to corroborate an identity. A rushed job meant a slipshod job, and the next week would see Lisa double-, triple-checking to make sure the cracks that the forger papered over to get these IDs out the door would not come back to bite them all.

A problem for tomorrow, in his mind. Tonight was about getting their friend her freedom.

The short hallway granted access to two big jail cells secured by simple mechanical locks, one on either side of the passage. The cell on his left lay empty, but the cell on the right played host to a single occupant. A tall, leggy blonde dressed in red, sitting on a long bench with one leg crossed over the other, whose indifferent demeanor changed as she spotted him. In a flash, she was on her feet and striding across the room, and once in front of him raised her hand to give him a small wave.

"Hi."

Jaune leaned on the steel bars of the cell, and smiled bright.

"Hey, Kiwi. How's life in this strange new world?"


-o-
​

"'s not my fault."

"Sure."

"If they didn't want me speeding, they shouldn't have built a thousand miles of paved road."

"Ooh yes, I completely get that. It's so cool, huh?"

"What was I supposed to do, not take it at maximum speed?"

"I couldn't have said it better myself."

Had the sheriff deputy heard the conversation Jaune and Kiwi were having as they waited in his office, he would likely throw Kiwi back in her cell, and Jaune with her. The man adhered to an alien perspective, though. One of law and order, and roads without wonder. He didn't understand what Jaune and Kiwi saw.

If Jaune had time, he would do what Kiwi did in a heartbeat, traveling as far and as fast as his ride could go. Coast to coast, north to south, back and forth. Simply because it was possible. What a dream it would be, the complete command of the land.

"Anyway, are you really alright? You were in here for, what, almost a day?" Jaune asked, propping an elbow on the armrest of his chair as he bonelessly leaned his head toward Kiwi's side. The deputy had provided them with stiff wooden chairs, but underestimated a young man's ability to lounge on any uncomfortable surfaces if he thought it would look cool. Still, he hadn't been the one stuck in a room for hours with a cold metal bench to sit on, hence his worries.

"Wasn't too bad. They can't stop me texting with Hu Tao, and Lisa after she got back," Kiwi said, then mimed a gun aimed at her head. "Watching the paint peel off the wall did get boring. Glad you're here."

"Once we're out, I'll find us a place to rest for the night so you can sleep on something soft. I wasn't impressed with that jail cell."

Kiwi shrugged, affecting a nonchalant air. "Whatever. I can sleep on a rock."

They chatted for a while longer, until the deputy came back into the room from a side door. Over his shoulder, he carried a bulky duffel bag that he soon dropped on the floor beside his desk.

"Your things. Check it to make sure it's all there if you want."

Despite the brusqueness that told all and sundry he couldn't be bothered to care, the deputy's eyebrow arched when Kiwi pulled the bag into her lap and began going through the contents right in front of his face. She even counted the money in the wallet to make sure he hadn't stolen any, not trusting the officer one bit. The implication of that earned her a glare from the man as he shuffled over to sit on an old office chair built for a younger, skinnier version of him from days long past. The chair creaked as he kicked his feet on the table to get comfortable.

His actions screamed that he was the king of this castle, and in a way it was true. According to him, the real sheriff held the full authority, but also operated from the main office located several towns over, the department to which they belong stretched thin across a thing called a 'county'.

"Your bike will take a little longer to return," the deputy added.

"How much to change your mind?" asked Kiwi without missing a beat, zipping up her bag now that her inspection was done.

Rather than arresting them for the blatant attempt at bribery, the sheriff deputy barked a humorless laugh to confirm everything Jaune suspected. Kiwi's release had been too easy, too smooth. It turned out that there was a catch.

"You." The deputy pointed to him. "You're Jaune Arc, right? The monster hunter."

"With caps, but yes."

"..."

The man went to retort, then seemed to think better of it and shook his head.

"Why do I always have to deal with the weirdos?" he muttered, hand reaching out for a glass bottle on the desk. On a closer look, the label was for a root beer, and not alcohol.

Working the night shift sober, what an honest man. And yet, for his law-abiding ways, as his fingers closed on the bottle his one comfort suddenly slipped from his grasp. Before anything could be done, it fell to the floor where it smashed into a million pieces with the content spilled across the tiles. Kiwi winced at the noise, looking annoyed.

The deputy took a deep breath. Then, a second one.

Jaune gazed at this man who was about to snap, and very carefully said, "Would you like me to go get you another bottle? My treat. There has to be a convenience store still open somewhere around here."

"No," the deputy growled. "This is fine." It was clearly not. "Just the poltergeist."

"?"

"It's a saying around these parts," the deputy explained.

Jaune hmmed. "Is that how the town got its name? I had wondered."

That got the deputy snorting in a rare bout of amusement, rolling his eyes. "Used to be called Chelsea until twenty years back. Damn fool mayor thought it would bring the tourists if we go all in, like that'd ever happen." The deputy glanced at the broken bottle, and seemed to decide that it was a problem for later, a choice that didn't impress Kiwi much as she inched her seat away from the mess before it could reach her shoes. "I hear you're the foremost human expert in… dealing… with that side of things."

News was spreading fast. How much of it was the police commissioner in New York talking him up, Jaune wanted to know. And why.

Then again, a reputation mattered, carrying a person far. Unearned or otherwise.

"I've solved a few cases. It could have been touch and go once or twice, so I wouldn't call myself the absolute best in the business," Jaune said, humbly.

He could be forgiven for trying to fish compliments, right? He certainly didn't get enough of it from Lisa. This Jaune Arc was a flower that bloomed with praise.

"That's not the story I hear," the deputy refuted, and held up his phone. On the screen, Jaune's own face peered back at him, attached to a document that he couldn't quite read from his seat. "A friend of a friend tells me you're the one to call when it comes to strange matters afoot. I'm far from the only small town deputy with those troubles, but unlike the rest I reckon I have something you need."

"A monster in exchange for the bike?" Jaune ventured, receiving a nod.

Well, well, well. That made this business.

If Kiwi had an issue with her motorcycle being used by the deputy as leverage, she did not show it. In fact, she grew outright invested, leaning forward in her seat to make it clear she was part of the conversation. The life of an edgerunner revolved around moments like these, Jaune figured. It must have felt like home.

"I'm willing to listen, but only that. No promises," he hedged. "Tell me more about the problem first."

The deputy cleared his throat and straightened up, trying and failing to hide his relief. "What do you know about the town of Poltergeist?"

To that, Jaune spread his hands to show his complete ignorance, and Kiwi beside him mirrored the gesture. One lived on another planet, and the other a different history. The deputy might as well ask them if they had been to the moon.

"...I don't blame you, there are bigger places in Iowa," the deputy said once he noted their blank looks. Rapping his fingers on the table, he blew a long sigh. "We're unlucky, is the thing. A two-hundred-year run of bad luck that follows everybody like a bad smell. That's what I want you for."

"To fight bad luck?" Jaune said, and he began to wonder if this was a prank. He looked toward Kiwi, receiving no help there. She was as lost as him. "I don't know what to tell you, honestly. That sounds a little beyond my range of services, and anyway a case of butterfingers doesn't necessarily mean someone cursed your bloodline."

"This is more than—" The deputy visibly held himself back, and sagged in his seat. "We get that sort of skepticism a lot from outsiders. But, look, I'm not crazy and there is nothing natural about this. The dinner plate industry probably owes their whole profit margin from us with how many we break. Stuff goes missing so often that people just live with it nowadays." He gestured at the mess on the floor. "And that?"

Before he could elaborate, a soft click sounded out and the heat which blew into the room from the vents cut out to immediately plunge them several degrees colder. A flicker passed over the deputy's face, rage and fear all rolled into one.

"Typical Tuesday, we call it. Goddamnit."

"It looks like the thermostat is shut off," Jaune noted. "Maybe it jumped? Did you have the Dust—the fuel restocked recently?" He made to get up to turn it back on, but the deputy waved him away.

"Restocked, my foot. It runs on public gas, kid. We're not that out in the sticks," the officer grumbled as he pushed off his creaky office chair, ambling over to the wall to fiddle with the electronic panel.

With him distracted, Jaune whispered to Kiwi under his breath.

"That wasn't you, right?"

The netrunner shook her head.

And he doubted that just any random person on the street would have the ability to remotely hack into technology the way she did. The situation was a little outside the norm, then. Maybe not enough to count as definitive proof of evil spirits and such, but considering that he was at the moment living in a world of vampires, werewolves, and other things that go bump in the night, the deputy's woes could be a sign of supernatural involvement if one squinted hard.

"That was a brand new thermostat," the deputy said as he walked back to his desk. "I had the electrical lines checked three times over the last six months. It. Keeps. Happening." Sitting down, he dropped his head in his lap. "Way back when, people blamed the bad luck on a poltergeist, a little mischief maker, and the name stuck for next two centuries. But something's changed, because the act stopped being funny somewhere along the way. Now, cars on the highway are blowing their wheels on rocks the size of people's head. Drivers wind up stuck for hours if they're lucky, unconscious with their possessions gone when they wake if they're not."

Jaune blinked, taken aback because that suddenly sounded more like bandit activities than ghostly pranks. The escalation curve appeared rather extreme, too, and rife with a kind of motive all too human.

"What happened to their wallets?" Kiwi cut in.

"Emptied. Personally, I think it's a witch, not that you'd catch me dead looking in them woods to find out."

Jaune frowned. "You have no problem sending me, though."

"Of course! You're the one to call, aren't you?"

He mulled on it, before turning to Kiwi. "It's your bike, so what do you think? You feel up to catching a ghost?"

The thermostat clicked off again. This time, a soft giggle accompanied the cold wind blowing in from the crack below the entrance doors.


-o-
​

"Sorry."

Kiwi's abrupt apology made Jaune look up from the text he just sent to Lisa updating on their circumstances. It might have been a step too far to imagine that his partner stayed up, heart all aflutter, waiting for a call, but she did appreciate knowing things as they happened.

We booked a motel for the night. :Jaune

"Is this about the bike?" he said to Kiwi. "Hey, don't even worry about it. This lets us get it back without a fuss and deal with the town's troubles, too. I call that a win."

One thing he liked about Kiwi, she didn't dwell on such matters after they had each said their piece. Giving him a nod, she unlocked the door to the old motel room they rented, the only motel in town that was located beside the likewise only gas station in town, next to the exit leading onto the highway. There was a hint there, same as how every room was vacant until they arrived.

The door gave Kiwi a bit of trouble at first, refusing to budge, so she braced her shoulder against its worn surface and shoved harder. Enhanced with Aura, her strength prevailed to send it flying open with a crash that shook the room.

Kiwi daintily held the door open for Jaune as he turned his attention back to his phone.
