Jaune shut off his phone screen, closing it on that last clumsy message. The nuances of texting slang was a deep and complicated affair that still eluded many of those in their group chat. Scroll further up, and a good half of messages would be incomprehensible to someone from his world as a conversation, decades of texting conventions crammed into a few days with people figuring it out as they go. He couldn't explain why, but it left a strange feeling in his chest.

"They were worried about you," he said, to Kiwi's immediate bashful groan.

"Too much of a fuss. I would have taken care of it even if you didn't come."

As they strode into their quarters, a single look from Kiwi turned on the TV sitting above a stand, now blaring a program on the riveting all-day, all-night observation of Iowa weather patterns. A curious glance at Kiwi got her to explain.

"Force of habit," she said with a shrug. "It garbles our talks to people in the next room. You can't trust motels."

"Tell me honestly… Could you have broken out of that jail any time you felt like it?"

A nod. "The locks on the cell had a computer override to open in an emergency. A quickhack would deal with it faster than you can blink."

Yeah, that figured. Her brand of hackery amounted to magic from his view.

Kiwi paused to look around the room, scrunching her nose at the stains on the carpet. Jaune, meanwhile, was more concerned with the ugly pattern on the drapes. Polka-dots, and brown on yellow? Of the many faults one could say of this drab motel room, that was its greatest offense.

"Not that I was keen to become a fugitive," Kiwi added. "That would have been more trouble than it's worth."

"Fair enough," he said as he moved over to the beds. "Are computers still giving you trouble?" That had been the project she was working on when last they spoke, the holy grail with which she would… take over the world, or something.

"A little."

Listening to Kiwi, the Night City Net was akin to a second city. A full landscape formed from a sea of data laid over reality, stapled in place by a set of underlying rules that made up its bedrock. Passwords were gates, security programs as the guards. Break on through, and the world was hers.

"Here, they're… wisps," she said, gesturing with her hands to better explain. "The connections aren't woven together, and they're weak. I can work a TV." She demonstrated again, flipping the power for the TV on and off. "But the lights above us are completely dark to me."

"Because they're not linked to a computer," Jaune guessed.

"Right... It's quiet, this world. I like it."

Kiwi tilted her head, thinking.

"That said, I am looking into that Internet of Things concept that's floating around. It might be the key to setting up a real Cyberspace here. Without the AIs this time."

All that to say, at the moment she might just as well explode a computer as hack into the software.

"If I hooked my cyberdeck up to it, that would be different!" she protested, rummaging in her bag to show him the tablet she often carried around. "I already got most of my programs working safely that way!"

"I mean, I pretty much have no choice but to believe you. Looking up a cooking recipe is about the extent of what I know how to do."

A sweep of his hand dropped Kiwi's duffel bag on her bed, a selection of daily necessities on his, and food and drinks on the small nightstand between them. Right away, Kiwi snatched up a cup of smoothie, tucking the straw in one of the slits on her mask. She sat down down on the edge of Jaune's bed and happily drank up the strawberry-banana goodness that she had grown addicted to as of late.

Night City smoothies were made of scop. He wasn't sure how to feel about that, and had simply resorted to buying up as many fruits as he could for Kiwi to throw into a blender.

Including kiwi. She hadn't been amused.

Jaune flopped down beside Kiwi, his back hitting the mattress. The day—two days, really—was finally catching up to him. Rough and lumpy as the bed was, it felt like heaven, and soon his eyes began to flutter shut—

*fwissssh*

"Kiwi, did you turn on the bathroom sink?"

"A sink is not connected to internet," Kiwi deadpanned. Jaune, groaning at the interruption to his beauty rest, rolled to his feet.

He walked into the bathroom, flicking on the light. The space wore the same drab coat as the rest of the motel, dated and faded if somewhat well-maintained. Water was running from the faucet. He turned the handles, and the flow ceased.

"Our ghost, you think?" Kiwi asked, having twisted her body on the bed to follow him with her gaze, now half lying down with the tails of her coat thrown aside, stretching like a cat.

"Hard to tell for sure. Could be poltergeist, could be—"

*fwissssh*

"—loose parts."

The handles had turned by themselves behind his back. He shut them off again, and this time waited for a few seconds to see what would happen next.

*click*

The heat to the room cut out.

"Kiwi?"

"On it."

His companion did not move, but the thermostat flicked back on and the vents resumed blowing.

For, like, two seconds.

*click*

"I swear, I just saw the button move," said Kiwi.

Which confirmed that they did not have a hacker on the loose when it came to devices being manipulated. The same force was acting on everything in the town of Poltergeist.

*fwissssh*

*click*

*fwissssh*

*click*

*fwissssh*

*click*

Yeah, no. He wasn't going to play this game. The best way to stop a prank was to just not react.

"I don't mind letting the water run," he said. "It'd all go back to the earth, anyway. I won't lose sleep over it."

"The motel provided us with thick blankets. I'm starting to see why," Kiwi replied.

Of a like mind, they settled in for the night. The empty smoothie cup went in the trash, and their possessions returned to Jaune's Pocket to keep anyone from messing with them. Each took a quick shower while uncomfortably aware that they might have a voyeur, before crawling into their respective beds with the covers rolled tight around their bodies for warmth.

The late fall weather wasn't that cold. They could bear it. And the sound of running water was almost soothing. It didn't take long for them to fall asleep, unbothered by monsters, pranks, and bad luck. Hearts steady, and at peace.

More fool them, to assume it would end at that. Barely a blink of an eye, two at most, and a scream pierced the night.

…Make that morning. My, did time fly.

Sunlight filtered into the room through the crack between the curtains as Jaune surged from his bed, poised to bring out his full arsenal and start swinging. When he looked, Kiwi was already awake, and his sluggish thoughts pulled together to inform him that it had been her who screamed.

It likely had to do with the spray of red blood splattered all over her bed, and the dead rabbit strewn about on her lap. Someone had taken a knife to the poor animal.

"What the fuck is this thing?" Kiwi rasped, pressed against the wall while nudging the rabbit with her foot to get it away.

"...You haven't seen a bunny before?" What a blessed existence.

A wet, sticky sensation drew his gaze to his own blanket, where a raccoon lay in much the same state as the rabbit. Jaune winced at the blank eyes staring dead straight at him.

"That deputy wasn't wrong," he muttered. "There's nothing funny about this."

And what was the message? That he was a raccoon? A fat little raccoon?

That he was some sort of pest who kept getting into other people's property, ignoring how he wasn't welcome, digging through trash and hoarding junk, making a mess of things, gorging himself on food, going rabid at the drop of—

Fuck.

Mischief was afoot in the town of Poltergeist, cruel and mean.

Chapter 88: Breakfast with Poltergeists
​

The investigation opened, as investigations often did, with a query.

A good detective knew to ask questions. Knew to adapt to the circumstances as they arise, and kept to the straight facts of the case. In this manner, mysteries great and small would be dragged into the light of day.

"Can I knock this off my bill? It was the poltergeist that did it."

Questions like these probably didn't count, though.

"Oh, mister. I'm so sorry to hear that… But no."

The receptionist of the motel appeared very familiar with the antics that went on around here, and thus was quite sympathetic to his plight. Just not that sympathetic. The sheets soaked in animal blood were a lost cause, and the same went for Jaune's wallet as he paid the cleaning fee. 0/10, never coming back again.

No, that sounded too harsh. An 8/10 would more than do to show his displeasure. How will they ever recover from this?

A fitting end for a place with such terrible memories.

Jaune exited the quaint motel lobby with its kind but unhelpful receptionist, stepping out into the cold late morning. The climate here wasn't yet like the New York mountains with its snow, but give it a few weeks and it would get there. The fallen leaves that blew past him were borne on a bracing, chilly wind that did wonders to wake a person up, and led him to pull his Gallian-blue jacket tighter around his body. He didn't mind these kinds of days that were perfect for cozying up with friends at a cafe.

"How did it go?" asked a person waiting for him in front of the motel.

The keen interest Kiwi held for the ancient world of 2022 stopped short at dealing with customer service, and so the woman had left the matter up to him while she visited the nearby gas station convenience store for a pack of smokes. She was now back in the same spot where they last parted, leaning on one of the columns supporting the walkway roof with thumbs hooked into the belt loops of her pants and a foot tapping the ground. With the tails of her leather trench coat flapping in the wind, she resembled a detective more than he ever did. One might imagine that her earlier freakout never happened, looking at that bored expression on her face.

"Well, I bring grave news. There's a hundred fifty dollars I'm not getting back," Jaune reported.

"The tragedy."

Cruel indifference, thy name was Kiwi. Then again, his complaint also lacked any true regret behind it. A hundred and fifty in cash felt both like a big number and nothing at all these days, so used was he to either destitution or noveau riche status depending on what world he ended up in. The impression that the paper bills used locally seemed less than real to his eyes had a big part to do with it, too. He kept enough on hand to manage the odd expense, but had a hard time seeing their value in the way he would the beautiful Remnant Lien with its shiny colors. (No, this bias had nothing to with a latent magpie tendency. Shut up, Lisa.)

In any case, his capture of the Monster of Mystic Mansion—great headline, a crying shame that it came from a gossip rag—had earned him a goodly sum to soften monetary concerns. This was not even touching on the amount Lisa provided him as operating funds after pawning off part of their gold reserves. Say what one will, she kept him in style.

"Other than that," he continued, because he hadn't wasted that time for nothing, "the guy let me look at the camera that watched the parking lot and it caught an odd thing last night, right at the edge. A dead rabbit and a dead raccoon floated by themselves across the ground for a bit before passing out of sight."

"Gas station over there had more cameras set up," Kiwi nonchalantly provided. "Angle wasn't great, but I did watch the door to our room open by itself."

Fact of the case #1: The culprit had to move objects through space, rather than summoning them from the ether.

Going for a pack of smokes. Sure, Kiwi. It seemed this detective had made the right choice in a trusty assistant. He gave her a thumbs-up as thanks for the help, which she acknowledged with a subtle nod.

What did an unseen prankster look like, when nobody was watching. That was the question he wanted an answer for, and as he led the way to the dumpster parked on the side of the motel, he pondered the conundrum of an entity with no body for him to stab with his holy sword of exorcism (Crocea Mors with a dozen paper talismans slapped to it). The deputy had suspected vile witchery. Jaune leaned more toward spirits. People way back when called it a poltergeist, and he was working on the assumption that they knew what they were talking about.

And the appearance of spirits, ghosts, and other spectral sorts mattered a lot, if one believed a certain funeral director. Were they to appear as they did in life, then he could in most circumstances take it as a good sign that they weren't far off from their nature as ordinary people. Someone he could maybe talk to and hash things out in peace. Tattered, bloody robes and a monstrous face filled with fangs or such details, on the other hand, might be a cause for worry. "A grudge reflects as a mirror," Hu Tao had warned him over the phone.

Tattletale, when she took over the call, had questioned whether the roots of their trouble lay in the supernatural at all. She just thought it was a person with superpowers. An esper or the like.

Sometimes, he wondered if she understood what 'supernatural' even meant. The blind spots of living in an unordinary world, he supposed. It was rough, being the normal one in their duo.

"What's our next step, then?" Kiwi asked as Jaune opened the trash bin and dumped the bloody mess of blankets and animals inside. Her piercing stare lent him the uncomfortable feeling that he was facing a test.

"We're not giving up this early if that's what you're wondering, so don't go eyeing that impound lot just yet," he said, and got to enjoy Kiwi's awkward shuffling as he nailed her intentions down pat. "What would you do in this situation back in Night City? Have you ever done an investigation job, or is it always guns blazing with your crew?"

"Is that how you remember me? Stupid David, and stupid Maine who taught him. Ugh." Kiwi pinched the bridge of her nose. "If I was looking for someone, I'd scour the cameras in the area, same as you had done. Tap an info broker if the mark is the elusive type." A tch, and she averted her gaze. "Hard to say what I can offer here, now that I think about it."

This place must look like the caveman era to her. Incomprehensible, to an extent.

"That's a little different from how the Huntsman Academies teach it, but I suppose we operate in different environments for the most part. If we ever go monster hunting in New York City, you'll be the one I count on," he said as encouragement. "As for the boonies… I figure we can give the methods of my profession a shot."

In one aspect, tracking a Grimm was a matter of following the footprints and broken branches into the the deep, dark woods, and through that a Huntsman might learn of a Grimm's shape and size to pinpoint the species to which their quarry belonged. The other method was simpler, and often just as reliable. Beacon had a reason for teaching its students to begin their searches within a settlement, before venturing outward.

People had eyes to see, and mouths that did so love to talk.

The center of Poltergeist lay not far away, well within walking distance. Jaune and Kiwi found they were of a like mind in that they thought the brisk morning too nice to miss out on, soon strolling side by side over the paved cobblestone streets of this charming little town.

It sounded so simple when he put it like that, glossing over how Kiwi took strides like this was the city, all in a hurry. He, meanwhile, had naturally blended into his nostalgic surroundings with the ambling saunter he learned from family and neighbors growing up. A minute or more passed in starts and stops as they tried to fit each other's pace before something seemed to click into place, and they were suddenly moving in sync.

For a time, their footsteps formed the only conversation between them, mingling with the chirping of birds and the dry leaves crunching beneath their boots. With a different companion from the norm, the chatter that Jaune kept expecting never came. Kiwi enjoyed the quiet, from what he could tell.

More people began to appear as they approached their destination, often journeying in the same direction to where the buildings grew less secluded and homes gave way to businesses. It was here that Jaune witnessed his second prank of the day.

*beep, beeeeep!*

The honking of a horn heralded a car barreling down the road. Nothing surprising, as far as it went, until one noticed the absence of a driver behind the wheels. At once, Jaune sprang into action.

"We have to stop that car! Someone could get hurt!"

"Why?"

Kiwi's question brought him up short. He paused in the middle of taking off in flight, turning around to gawk at her. His hands made a frantic series of movements toward the car moving down the street to convey to her the obvious urgency of the problem.

"You've never seen a driverless car, have you?" Kiwi asked, quirking an eyebrow.

"What is this sorcery of which you speak? Are you saying that isn't the poltergeist?"

Kiwi let out a wry chuckle, and looked back to the car as it turned the corner to vanish from view. "If it is, then it should quit with the pranks and start a taxi service. It obeyed traffic lights and speed limits. That's better than me."

"..."

It wasn't that Jaune had nothing to say, he just didn't want to incriminate himself. Because yes, that poltergeist absolutely drove safer than him.

"We had something like that, back home," Kiwi continued. "Once it starts doing donuts at intersections, then I'd worry."

"..."

Again, not incriminating himself.

Fact of the case #2: Jaune is a gonk driver The two-hundred-year-old culprit knows the rules of the road.

Jaune glared at Kiwi as he sent the revision to the group chat. She pretended to ignore him, but he could tell from the narrowing of her eyes that she was smirking without a smirk. More than one prankster was on his case today.

The place with the most people gathered turned out to be the diner, somewhat predictably. As in many a small town, it served as a hub for the community of Poltergeist, complete with coffee and delicious food for the customers to enjoy while they traded gossip. The restaurant opened early, at seven AM on the dot according to the sign, and business was booming by ten.

What about work? It'd get done when it gets done, was the prevailing mood. Jaune even spotted a group of teenagers roughhousing on his way in, athletes from the jerseys they wore and the skillful throws of an oval football back and forth. Neither they nor the adults in the room seemed particularly concerned with school hours.

The pair of them received a lot of looks with their entrance, with the local populace tracking their progress through the restaurant out of the corner of their eyes even while continuing to talk with one another. They even managed to drag a few of the people sitting at the long counter away from the game playing on the TV screen. It might have to do with the sword hanging on his hip, or how Kiwi cut a daunting figure standing taller than most with her red leather coat and metal mask spelling serious business.

Yeah, no, it was probably the sword. Good luck to them, getting him to take it off. A proper Huntsman announced his presence with the tools of his trade so that others knew to look for him in times of trouble. Besides, who could ever guess when danger will strike.

Like, say, right here and right now.

The world slowed down, and alarm bells rang in his head. He watched with a detached sense of awareness as the waiter passing near him took a tumble. The tray that the young man held upended to deliver an assortment of food, piping hot just out from the kitchen, straight at him. Five plates, heavy on the meats, eggs, and potatoes. Two pots of coffee. Perhaps it was a sign that he still needed training, because of all the crucial details that could have leapt out to him on this occasion, his lightning-quick analysis prioritized those tidbits as the clearly relevant items to keep in mind. Mmmm, bacon.

The burst of amusement within his chest didn't have the time to show on his face. Shifting on the heels of his boots, Jaune pivoted aside to avoid the plates. A mid-motion bend at the waist let him flick the tip of his sword behind and upward to intercept a dish that would have struck Kiwi, knocking the cheesy, greasy omelette off-course to join the rest of the serving tray's worth of breakfast in splattering across the tiles. For a brief moment, the sound of shattering ceramic drowned out the restaurant's hubbub and every pair of eyes snapped in their direction.

"Oh geeze, that darn poltergeist!"

The odd cry that the waiter shouted in the wake of the incident leaned more toward an excuse rather than a sorry, carrying with it a note of both frustration and resignation. Yet, those words were accepted by all and sundry as if they explained everything about the situation, with the other customers taking it as their cue to promptly return to their own affairs. The actual apology came after the waiter realized that these two strangers, being outsiders to the town, would be unfamiliar with its common sayings.

"I'm so, so, so, so sorry!"

Too many so's, but it was sincere. Jaune listened to the waiter with half an ear, preoccupied with the scene over the young man's shoulder where an unseen artist drew a crude picture on the fogged out window near a family of four eating their meal. The children pointed it out, laughing in the way of boys. Their parents barely gave it attention, the slight downturn of their lips the only sign that they found it a bother. He filed that in the back of his mind for later.

The hostess directed the waiter to pick up after himself, then led Jaune and Kiwi off to their booth. On her face she wore a service smile, sturdy as armor even as behind her the young man hissed and yelped while burning his fingers on the sizzling-hot foodstuff until someone brought him a towel.

*crash!*

The woman winced.

"Here are your menus, your waiter will be by shortly."

What a professional. Jaune resolved then to trouble the staff as little as possible. They had enough on their plate. A scarcity of plates, for one. He settled into the booth, needing to scoot in deeper after Kiwi decided that she would also be sitting on this side.

Once the hostess was gone, Kiwi leaned in to speak with a quiet tone into his ear. "On the way here, a girl was trying to enter the restroom and the door kept jamming on her. Coincidence? I think not."

Milder than the 'prank' to befall them, to the point that it could genuinely be an accident. Yet, taken together with his own observations, Jaune considered it pretty conclusive.

Fact of the case #3: Multiple instances of poltergeist behavior occurred at the same time.

Bennett: Boss
Wy do u kep doing tat?
What is ths?

Jaune paused in the middle of typing. His gaze darted to the icons in the corner of the app, checking for those who were online.

Where's Lisa? :Jaune​

Bennett: shes sleeping
Evrybdy is. Just me Oz n Echa is up

"What the—Whatever happened to helping us with the case!?" Jaune yelped.

"Behold, David… Our rival outfit," Kiwi drawled, her eyes never leaving the menu.

Kiwi: Pet the bird for me, kid.

Bennett: Yes maaam

"What?" said Kiwi once she noticed him staring at her. "I like that bird." She turned the menu toward him. "Look, they have smoothies."

Indeed, they did. Made with farm-fresh fruits, too, the menu touted. The price threw him for a loop, given that the produce came from a nearby orchard and by conventional logic should cost the restaurant less than importing from elsewhere. But, eh, board game money and all that. Jaune urged Kiwi to get one, hoping to try it out for himself. He liked fruits.

The waiter arrived, and they placed their orders. An orange, banana, and pineapple smoothie for Kiwi and pancakes with plenty of maple syrup for him. No mishaps this time, though the day was early yet.

While they waited, he got an update from Bennett on the happenings at home, written in typo-ridden verse that hurt the eyes—Bennett's enthusiasm for telling a story often outpaced his typing speed, to the detriment of coherence. Most of those who stayed up late last night had crashed come morning with the exception of Escha, who tended to nap at any spare moment and therefore suffered less for it. Apparently, the trio of Lisa, Fischl, and Hu Tao were sprawled out on the long couch in the central living room, leaving Bennett on the hook to clean up after them when he should be learning to use the Carian Knight's Shield that Jaune passed to him.

Bennett: But boss
These clues…

I know :Jaune
The answer is clear as day.​

He had already figured it out back when he sent that third item.

"It's a witch!" he declared.

Kiwi balked, momentarily knocked out of her cool composure. "What? No. There's more than one culprit."

Or that.

"That was my second guess," he said, speaking nothing but the truth.

Kiwi said nothing.

"Okay, maybe I jumped the gun a bit," Jaune admitted. "In my defense, Lisa showed me that Mickey Mouse cartoon with the magic spell and all the brooms. Neither you or me came from worlds with wizards. We can't rule out that magic is able to work on a big scale."

"You're missing the point," Kiwi refuted. "The level of severity differs between incidents. Some cause disgust and some are outright violent. Some are mindful of laws, others threaten injury. They have no coherent throughline. Simplest answer, these actions are taken independently of one another."

Jaune raised a finger to object, then retracted the finger as he gave Kiwi's point more thought.

"Huh."

He had vaguely registered that detail already, but failed to make the connection before now.

There's more than one culprit. :Jaune​

Bennett: I ws goin to say
its a wtch

The validation. In triumph, he pressed the screen of his phone in Kiwi's face.

Kiwi rolled her eyes. "I'm learning more and more about you every day."

"Good things?"

"...Let's go with that." She brushed a lock of hair out of her eyes, tucking it behind an ear. "You have your moments. You make me laugh if nothing else."

Oh yeah, they were BFFs. Jaune leaned back in his seat, smiling from ear to ear.

The waiter brought their food to the table, and other than Jaune batting aside the knife that 'slipped' from the serving tray to 'fall' in a manner reminiscent of a serial killer's stab as the waiter placed down his stack of pancakes, they received no great trouble. Him smothering his pancakes twice over in syrup garnered more consternation from people in the vicinity than anything the poltergeist had done. Even he had to admit that it was a terrible habit to have learned from his Beacon days, excusable only in that he'd be working that off through training. Granted, after witnessing Lisa's small appetite on many occasions, he also often suspected the people of his world lucked out on bodies that burned through food like a smelting furnace when compared to some of these other places. Born to eat, the Remnant man.

A picture of their meal ended up in the group chat, another entry to the gallery that he and others had contributed to over a number of days. He also texted Bennett to let everyone else keep on sleeping. This case was best left as a side activity for them while they focused on their own thing. Lisa, for one, had enough on her plate between growing their finances, putting together a coherent plan to debut computer software a generation ahead of current local versions, finalizing Hu Tao's business application with the state (finding the perfect plot of land for a cemetery was still on the docket), and teaching Fischl to type on a keyboard instead of writing by hand in notebooks. Busy, busy, busy, that little worker bee. Jaune had it easy compared to her, tasked with worming his way into the good graces of society simply by living the dream.

He parted with Bennett on a warning that they'd be sparring upon his return to New York. That should light a fire under him.

"Oh fuck~!"

The first sip of her smoothie, and Kiwi seemed just about ready to fall in love. Among other things. The moans that escaped her lips made a young couple at a table near them flush to the roots of their hair.

Jaune managed to talk his way into a gulp of the drink, and discovered a tasty if still within the realm of the ordinary concoction. Sweet, with a strong citrus note. Miles better than scop, he'd readily admit.

His pancakes? Perfection. Each bite melted in his mouth. Soft and fluffy, syrup soaked to the very center.

He probably shouldn't have talked it up to Kiwi. She was eyeing the syrup bottle with an intent gleam to her gaze that worried him.

Well, that was fine. Their antics calmed the other customers, which suited their purpose. Normal people eating normal meals, mask and sword notwithstanding. That was them.

And as the locals grew comfortable with their presence, Jaune began to broach conversation with those nearest them, starting with comments on the weather and the food. Subjects that anybody could get it eternal argument of pancakes versus waffles reignited for the millionth time because of him.

The old couple in the next table over proved the most welcoming of his company, and it was with them that he pried in depth on the history of the town and, of course, the poltergeist problem.

"Oh, I wouldn't call it a problem, dear," the old woman, who along with her husband were florists, tittered in mirth. "It's charming! Why, I still remember some of the pranks from my childhood even after all these years."

The old man beside her seemed about to make a comment, but decided to remain quiet in the end and busied himself with his phone while his wife talked on. The fingers clutching tight onto the device told of a different opinion on the matter. His forearm sported bandages. His wife had to know the cause, but… it clashed with her fond memories, didn't it?

"It's hard to believe you were called in for this," the old woman said. "I had no idea that a monster hunter was an actual profession!"

Cocking his head, Jaune said, "I never mentioned that I was a monster hunter."

She waved her hand. "Everybody knows, dear. I heard it from my friend who heard it from that Paul boy that works up at the motel who got the story straight from our sheriff deputy."

He forgot that small towns were like this. That he was like this. The time that trading group stopped by his home, he was racing against the other kids to be first to deliver the news to the mayor. Ah, the nostalgia…

A tight grip on the back of his jacket brought his trip down memory lane to an abrupt end.

Kiwi yanked him toward her side, and an object flashed by his face to hit the table. Jaune's hand extended to scoop the football on the bounce before it could do more than send the utensils clattering, safely resolving the issue. This time, there was no mystery to solve, since the guilty expressions shared between the jersey-clad teenagers on the other side of the restaurant attested enough as to the culprits.

One among them had been in the middle of trying to intercept the ball, clearly failing that, and he rubbed the back of his head in sheepishness as he ran over to their table.

"Sorry, Mister Wells, Missus Wells. Bad case of the butterfingers, y'know? Darn poltergeist."

The old lady snorted. "I hope that gets cured by game day, young man. We're counting on you to do our town proud."

"I'll do my best," said the boy, and he mimed a catching motion at Jaune.

The ball sailed across the space between them, landing in the teenager's hands with a loud smack. In seconds, he was back with his friends, the rambunctious bunch carrying on with no indication that they had learned any sort of lesson from the incident.

"Sweet boy," said the old lady.

Jaune pointed after the teenager. "Him?"

The old lady nodded. "James Griffin, he's a sweetheart. His family is a big name around here. Not all that rich or anything, but they have been with the town since forever." The woman placed a hand over her heart. "I thought I had this nagging feeling that you seemed familiar. You two could be brothers, the way you act. That's why I know you'd do right by the poltergeist."

If she had any idea of the things he had done on his other monster hunting jobs, she wouldn't say that. There was a headless gorgon buried in New Hampshire, a mad scientist with no hands in Massachusetts, and a Kurt Volkov now a bloody smear next to a corn field in Vermont.

Jaune smiled, and echoed someone else's earlier sentiment. "I will do my best." He clapped a hand on Kiwi's back. "Got all the help I need right here."

Kiwi might not be Lisa, but she was reliable in her own way. Maybe somebody from Night City made for a good person to watch one's back. They were always looking over their shoulders.

The light fixture above dropped to smash against his head, its fragments showering over him. He kept on smiling.

The old woman grew rather more reticent at that, while the old man cracked a small grin. The restaurant staff rushed over at that point to bring a close to their little chat.

He got what he needed, anyway. The old man had angled his phone screen at him there at the end, open to a text box in a messaging app. In it were written a few short sentences that marked his next destination.

Griffin Manor in the woods. Odd ducks.

Why did these things always involve a mansion?

#8,777

Chapter 89: Under the Mask
​

The motel marked the closest point to the highway, and the exit out of this small town. Griffin Manor, meanwhile, laid in the complete opposite direction, buried miles deep behind the rural fields within the thorny bramble woods. There was a message there, if Jaune ever saw one. Leave me alone.

A vacationing tourist to Poltergeist—they exist, locals alleged with insistent tones—might well miss the landmark altogether, since navigation systems for cars did not even note the road leading to the property. The only reason Jaune trusted the tip provided by the old man back at the diner enough to act on it was due to Kiwi grabbing a satellite image, a photo taken from an unmanned craft sent high into the sky, off of the inter-net to confirm that a house existed at the location. It spoke of a desire for privacy that bordered on hermit tendencies. In any case, Jaune had his heading and he drove out there without further delay, traveling as the noontime sun hung high in the sky.

A long, gently curving road and the wind in his hair. There was nothing like it in all the universe.

His van later rolled to a stop some distance out from his destination. A little past the winding driveway that presumably ran up to the house, around a bend to put the vehicle out of sight.

During the trip over, he had debated at length with Kiwi on the merits of sneaking their way into the manor. The netrunner saw this option as a matter of course, used to the idea of going where she was not welcome and taking what was not hers. Her words, not his, and the unflattering if somewhat honest summation of the merc business that paralleled certain personal experiences of his own would keep him up at night, he could already tell. On his part, he preferred the simpler approach of walking through the entrance, because if he was going to go where he was not welcome and take what was not his, then the least he could do was be sporting about it and look them in the eye as he lied to their face.

…Jaune wanted to say that this side of him had its roots in the company he kept, but no, it was him. Before the Li- of Lisa ever entered his life.

The reminder that that girl was not here to help him talk his way in further took the wind out of his sail. Sure, he could spin a fair yarn in his unbiased opinion, but convincing a brothel madame that he was there for a good time was an altogether different situation from convincing somebody to let him into their home; the Golden Cat wanted him inside it, him and his money. In the end, he and Kiwi decided that they would at least scope out the area before resorting to knocks on the door.

She kept insisting that he'd get shot. Because edgerunners that use the front doors tended to get shot.

"Good," Jaune said as he got out of the car. "We call that evidence."

Please shoot him.

"God, you solos…" Kiwi left him with that cryptic remark, and the two of them set out over the uneven ground.

Up a hill and through the bushes, the estate came into view. Squeezed in between tall trees that loomed high overhead to cast the entirety of it in shadows, the four-story building looked quite unimpressive at first glance despite its grand size. Stately yet neglected, its heyday belonging to an era passed. The paint had peeled in places, with cracks in the bricks here and there.

Jaune studied the area while crawling amid the shrubberies. A small farm plot behind the home had gone unharvested, the crops planted in the soil breaking containment to cover the manor grounds in their vines. Some manner of pumpkin that grew bigger than the usual, now trapping the expensive modern conveniences scattered about, like the snazzy BBQ grill with its eight burners, between their bulk.

"They were rich, once," said Kiwi, moving with her gaze fixed on the tablet screen in her hands.

Not moving well, mind you. He had to save her from falling twice already, catching her in his arms before her face could smash against the ground. Multitasking shenanigans like that might work on the city streets, but out here? Ha.

Unaware of her clumsiness and the careful watch Jaune had to maintain behind her, Kiwi continued. "The Griffin name used to get attached to a lot of the town's events, some of the charities. Less in recent decades."

"Coinciding with the mean turn in the pranks, perhaps?" he asked leadingly. Having found a good spot by a thick berry bush, he settled down with Kiwi hiding next to him.

She gave a small shake of her head. "No way to tell. Local newspaper must be a fan. It's all tongue-in-cheek puns about the friendly neighborhood ghost." Kiwi scoffed. "I think they're still hoping to make Poltergeist a national attraction."

"Hey now, they have a chance," Jaune said in defense of fellow small-towners, which earned him a tepid gaze from the woman. "Anyway, money could be a motive, then? 'I put everything into this town, now I'm poor, it's all your fault'?" He turned the thought over in his head. "Hmmm, doesn't quite fit. That James Griffin fella back at the diner seemed to be on good terms with everyone."

"You're serious."

"No, this is a thought experiment. Remember? But yes, if it somehow applies to reality, then I am happy with giving that choice. It's not like I need to stab somebody to call it a job well done. I want people to live in peace, that's it."

He dropped the leg that was resting on his knee. The metal edge of the boot hit the floor with a sharp clank that the carpet hardly muffled, as he sat up straight.

"On the other hand, we could go at it the traditional way," he offered, and jerked a thumb over his shoulder. "In which case, why don't you get the person behind me out of the room? Because I'll beat you up, but not your family. It's a line that keeps us from becoming monsters, don't you think?"

Ooh, there was the guilt. If Griffin had hoped to not give the game away, he should have kept his gaze steady.

"Of course, if they attack me with that vase floating above my head, then all bets are off."

A small smile flickered at the edge of Griffin's mouth, and Jaune knew he had him. The lines drawn in the sand were forming a picture, and the beginning of understanding. He hadn't come to this town with fire.

"Must we fight?" Griffin ventured.

Jaune flourished a hand. "Up to you."

"A drink is more my speed," the man admitted. The focus of his gaze shifted a bit to Jaune's right. "Sweetie?"

From that direction, Jaune heard a sound akin to something sucked through a tube. His head turned, and in the corner of his vision he caught the moment that the empty space beside him filled in with a full person. A girl with the same beige fashion sense as the man sitting in the other armchair. The daughter, then. Her bugged-out eyes stared at Jaune's face without seeming to blink, like he was a scary monster.

Because to her, he would be. Fuuuuuu—

Jaune poked his sword with the tip of his finger, popping it into his Pocket. He then smiled and waved, hoping to project a nonthreatening image.

If anything, that terrified Herbert's daughter even more. Which wasn't great, as when the door to the room flew open with a bang and Kiwi marched in with her hands up and a dozen floating knives aimed at her head, the person holding her hostage saw the stricken expression on the girl's face.

"Hurt her and I will kill this bitch!" shouted the woman, whom Jaune recognized as Herbert's wife from the family portraits.

Kiwi waved at Jaune with one of the hands she had up. "Hi."

The phone he left lying on the table vibrated, the screen lighting up.

Kiwi: I handled it.
Mystery solved.

"Fuck a duck," Herbert Griffin groaned, leaping to his feet as he motioned to Jaune for calm. "Can we talk about this?"

Jaune seized his collars in a flash, and cocked back a fist. "Put those knives down and we'll see."

One of the windows blew in, and a young man in a football jersey leapt through the opening.

"Dad!" The boy whirled on Jaune, outstretched hand wiggling strange patterns with its fingers. "Let him go, you bastard!"

"What's he, then?" Jaune asked the man in his grip, who vanished from view until Jaune shook him and he turned visible again. "Invisible or telekinetic?"

"Witch."

Jaune perked up. "No lie? Your son is a witch? Wait, what do we even call a witch boy, a wizard?"

"Still a witch," Griffin provided.

"Huh. Look at that, I learned something new. You know, there's this manual I'm trying to put together…"


-o-
​

"It's taken care of," Jaune declared. "Probably."

The sheriff deputy leveled a dubious stare at him. Next to him, Herbert Griffin piped up.

"I assure you, officer. Our young friend has the problem well in hand."

"It was poltergeists?"

"Yeah, let's go with that," Jaune said.

Griffin shot him a glare as the deputy contemplated the situation now that a respected voice of the community had added his opinion to the mix. The evening breeze with its chill soaking through to the skin hurried the process along, which was fortunate as it led the deputy to overlook the bandages wrapped around Herbert Griffin's abdomen where a recent stab wound had been healed. In the end, the deputy nodded and held out to Jaune a hand.

"It's not what I asked for, but it's more than I expected. A stupid prank here and there isn't so bad if nobody gets hurt. I'll give my buddy a call and you can have your bike back shortly."

Jaune winced. "Could you go back to the normal you?"

"What do you mean?" The deputy asked, frowning. "This is me."

"But you're not crabby."

"Keep talking smack like that and I'll throw you in a cell."

"Oh good, you're fine." He smoothed his chest, relieved.

He parted from the two men, who in turn left to go on their way. The deputy toward a group of concerned citizens that clamored for an answer, and Griffin to his family whose anxious faces peered out of the diner's window.

Jaune's last glimpse of that family, they seemed glad to see him go.

Unhurried strides carried him further down the road, where Kiwi stood waiting next to the van. The netrunner had had a rougher time of it in Griffin Manor from what he could piece together, not that she would admit it. She continued to regard the faces in the diner with suspicion.

"Loose threads have a habit of coming back to haunt a person," she later remarked, as they loaded her beloved bike onto the back of the van. "Normally, I'd recommend a clean break."

He was very leery of what she meant by that.

"The Griffin family is the closest thing they have to a leader. The 'poltergeists' will listen to them better than they would me," Jaune said. He passed Kiwi a couple of straps, helping her to secure the bike in place before the two of them climbed into the car seats.

"You think so?"

"They'll have to. Anyway, I could give a shot at rooting them out, but I can never be sure if I got them all, can I?"

Through the car window, his gaze roamed over the various groups of spectators that were peeking at them while trying to act like they weren't, and he guessed at how many of them were not what they appeared. Or were present, but he could not see. An impossible game as, to a one, they looked like people he would pass by on the street without a second glance.

A community hidden within a community, was the way he heard it explained. Blending in, living the same lives. That was the bargain struck, though one party never knew it. Where the troublemaking began, nobody had a definite answer for him. He suspected it came from the Griffin family itself. A dash of resentment combined with extraordinary powers, and the poltergeist was born.

"You can be a liar and a thief, but so long as you remember that we're all in it together, that we have to be there for each other, then you would have a place to call home. I think they've forgotten that."

The poltergeists were playing with fire, risking discovery with every prank. It was a matter of time until everything came to tears.

Maybe he was better off not knowing how this story ends.

He shifted gears, and pressed on the pedal. "They'll just have to figure it out for themselves."

And the van rumbled off into the sunset.


The Jaune Arc's Manual for Aspiring Monster Hunters


Entry #9: The invisible people
Attributes: Physical creature
A human in every way, only able to turn transparent at will.
Hunting behavior: Motivated by human wants. Completely undetectable by sight in invisible state. Employs ambush tactics and weaponry. Defaults to turning invisible as an escape method.
Habitat: Human dwellings
Identifiers:
1) Floating objects in the vicinity (their clothes turn with them, but not a flower vase? How does that work?)
2) Sounds and scents without sources
3) Blood regains color once separated
Optimal approach: stab with a sword


Entry #10: Telekinetic espers
Attributes: Physical creature
A human in every way, only able to move objects with their mind
Hunting behavior: Motivated by human wants. Employs objects in the environment as projectiles. Immobilizes victims in the air.
Stands still in combat (lol).
Habitat: Human dwellings
Identifiers:
1) Floating objects in the vicinity
2) Hand gesture (Habit, or necessity?)
3) Facial contortions (Use of power requires effort?)
Optimal approach: Work in progress, fight ended too quickly


Entry #11: Witches
Attributes: Physical creature
A human in every way, only able to commit foul witchery
Hunting behavior: Motivated by human wants. Employs objects in the environment as projectiles, but with magic. Immobilizes victims in the air, but with magic.
Stands still in combat (lol).
Habitat: Human dwellings
Identifiers:
1) Floating objects in the vicinity, but magically
2) Hand gestures
3) Glowing eyes
4) Biting own fingers to draw blood
5) Facial contortions (I believe this was entirely for effect, needs further confirmation)
Optimal approach: Work in progress, fight ended too quickly

Chapter 90: The King and All His Men
​


The peaceful mountains of New York had seen a lot of noise as of late, and the day after Jaune returned home was no different. Nothing woke up the mind and body quite like the sound of clashing swords, along with the sweat from a good workout.

A good workout, for him, involved a blade lancing for his throat.

To which, he stepped aside. Crocea Mors then whistled through the air, swatting the attack away with little effort. The flat of the blade served as a club with which Jaune smacked down the shield held by his opponent. He followed it up by planting a solid kick against Bennett's chest that was now left wide open. A cry, and the other blond boy went stumbling back with his arms windmilling.

"Stay light on your feet," Jaune advised. Rather than pressing the advantage, he paused in his tracks, twirling his sword in a lazy circle as he waited for Bennett to catch his balance. "There's a time to be a turtle and a time to be a rabbit."

Bennett, recovering, took a moment to consider that statement then tilted his head. "What does that mean, exactly?"

"Beats me. The person who trained with me, she used to say it in these situations." Of course, with him as the one getting his face bashed in. "I think it's about how you have to know when to be cool and watch what your opponent is doing, and when to go for a brutal all-out onslaught with no holds barred. Just like how turtles and rabbits behave in the wild."

"Boss, what kind of rabbits have you met?"

"They're not as innocent as they try to look, Bennett," Jaune insisted. He brandished his blade again. "Come on, one more time."

He advanced on his opponent, going slower than he would in a real fight with his movements predictable and the grip on his sword light. A spar, especially as the person teaching, wasn't about winning. That Pyrrha nevertheless whooped him in every single one came down to the difference in their abilities, rather than intent.

His sword somewhat mimicked the same set of actions as the previous engagement. First, a slice at the shins to make Bennett hop back and get him already thinking about dodging, changing to a stronger blow that hammered at Bennett's new shield to rattle his arm. Anti-magical properties or not, the Carian Shield functioned as nothing more than a chunk of metal against mundane, physical attacks. A reliable partner to those who wield it, if heavy. Its unfamiliar weight dragged Bennett's arm down.

Crocea Mors then rose high. It caught the light of the morning sun, glinting brightly.

Bennett had more than proven that he could perform a proper guard. Practiced well on how to dodge. The area that needed honing was his judgment, because appearances could be deceiving. A normal-looking boy like Jaune might hide a strength beyond mere arm muscles, a danger surpassing steel blades. Perhaps he could move mountains and fire laser cannonblasts. Some of the things waiting out there in the universe were just that unfair, and Jaune's usual approach to testing out an opponent by taking it on the chin was not for everybody.

In the case of Bennett, his eyes gave him away but it was a start. Jaune grinned, and his sword descended even as he watched Bennett dive aside, because it was important to play along and show a learning person what success looked like. The blade whiffed air to drive its tip into the dirt with a heavy thunk that smashed apart the ground in a small area, missing entirely. One would mistake Bennett for having won the Vytal Tournament, the way he cheered.

"Good!" Jaune praised. "Remember that a shield is just one option. You used to be a rabbit, I've taught you the habits of a turtle, now we're going to find that middle ground."

Down on one knee, the panting Bennett beamed. "Yes, boss!"

"Now, let's kick it up a notch."

"Wait, what?"

Jaune stomped the ground on an angle. Flames ignited under his heel, propelling him to the side in a flash. His other foot then kicked out, rockets firing to divert his momentum in a new direction. A final burst stopped him in place right in front of a Bennett woozy from trying to keep up with his quicksteps, where he lanced out with a boot.

Wham!

Bennett went flying end over end, hitting the ground with a loud cry.

Adrenaline receded, and Jaune lowered his foot. "Oh, uh, did I go too hard?"

"Why the chest again!?" groaned the prone Bennett, proving that he was just fine.

"Sorry. I've been picking up a few skills on my travels lately." ...And wanted to show them off.

He returned his shield to scabbard form, and stowed his sword to signal a reprieve in their bout. Walking over, he offered a hand and helped pull Bennett upright. The two boys dusted themselves off.

The glass door up on the raised deck overlooking the lake slid aside, and the person who had been watching them for a while now gave them a wave.

"Boys, it's time to eat. I ordered delivery!" Lisa called out.

Jaune called back, "No, it's training time. Get over here, Lisa."

One would have thought he laid down a death sentence. Lisa went from standing there smiling to vanishing through the doors in a split second, a fading "Screw thaaat!" following in her wake. Her quick escape rather demonstrated his point that the training had been good for her, not that she would ever admit to such. Her pesky superintuition powers had sussed out that the moment she acknowledged it, he would up the load as per the Nikos's Endless Training Hell (patent still pending) regimen.

"Damn, she got away," he said, looking at the door left open. "Oh, well. She'd be the one paying for it in the next session. I could use something to eat, anyway."

"Ooh, boss, are you gonna break out your smoothie stash? That stuff was great."

"Ask Kiwi. Unlike us, she literally lives on it. Alright, let's go have breakfast. Then, I'll take you to go hunt something."

There was no training like live practice. With big, sharp teeth.


-o-
​

"Are we there yet? My arms are so tiiiired!" a voice said.

"Quit your whining and keep pushing the car," said another.

A third chimed in. "Guys, maybe we can take a break. We've been at this for an hour."

"And it'll be hours yet. Now, push," the second one again ordered.

"I can switch out with someone to let them steer in ten minutes, as we have agreed. Steady on, chaps." And that made four, for a merry band.

Jaune cracked open an eye beneath the brim of a cheap baseball cap, squinting from the intense sunlight that the shade of a dead tree hardly quell. The couch that someone had thrown out on the side of the road was just as lumpy as when he first laid down on it for a nap, and he groaned as he sat up, massaging his shoulder. A water bottle, wonderfully cold, appeared in his hand which he gulped from with relish. Around him, a dry, arid landscape stretched on as far as the eyes could see.

A peek over the back of the couch allowed him a view of the road that cut through the desert. The busiest highway in the region, it received an average of two cars per hour. He had been informed that this was the peak season for travelers.

There had been a war, to be fair. They were signing an accord or something to formally end it this week, it was all over the radio. A soon to be peaceful world, he found himself in.

The affairs of the region, let alone kingdoms, had not much to do with the four young men currently pushing an unresponsive car along the road. Theirs was a more immediate concern of thirst, exhaustion, and other silent killers of life in the desert. One of them sat in the driver seat in order to steer, looking about to have a heatstroke, while the others burned their hands and shoulders on the hot metal of the convertible as they moved it step by step, also looking about to have a heatstroke. Little wonder, as they were to a one decked out in stylish black, a most ill-advised color for the locale.

Well, now. He couldn't just leave them there, could he?

Vaulting over the lumpy couch, Jaune waved his hand to catch their attention. "Hey! Need a little help there?" he offered.

The four young men whipped their heads his way, displaying a range of reactions. The two younger-looking ones (which was still about his age if not older by a few years) seemed happy for a distraction to give them a break. The man behind the steering wheel behaved in a more muted manner, pushing his glasses higher on the bridge of his nose as he turned in the seat. The big guy walking around with his shirt unbuttoned peered at Jaune with narrowing eyes.

Jaune spotted a flicker in that gaze, a quick glance to his hip and up again. Checking for a weapon, he would wager. He didn't mind it, as he had also clocked the very obvious slab of metal welded onto a handle propped on the backseat of the convertible, within the big man's reach, and the pair of handguns strapped to one of the younger guys, a skinny blond.

Said skinny blond scratched his head, then pointed at Jaune. "Hang on, where did you come from? We haven't seen anybody for hours. Did you just teleport in?" He spoke very fast, the words slightly blurring together in that excitable way Jaune often experienced with Nora.

"A good question," said the man in the driver seat. "Although I do believe our stranger here had employed a more mundane method than your imagination might suggest, Prompto."

While also a blond, the man's hair ran more to brown. The posh manner of speech put together with the well-fitted suit he had on lent him the impression of a rich person.

"Were you resting on that couch at your back?" this man asked.

Jaune nodded with a smile. "Got it in one. What's the problem with your car? Is it the engine?" He pointed ahead of them on the road. "There's a pit stop that way with a car shop. I came from there on a hunt and am going to head back there anyway, so I don't mind helping you out, if you like."

The four men shared looks, holding an entire conversation with just their eyes, their gestures, and a series of grunts. Manly grunts, Jaune imagined they would insist.

Finally, the big guy raised his voice as their representative. "I think we're good, pal."

Clearly, the conversation could have used actual vocabulary because that was not the conclusion some of the others thought they had arrived at. The skinny blond—Prompto, he believed it was—scrambled in front of the bigger man with his hands up.

"Gladiolus, my man. My brother from another mother. Let's think about this. The guy wants to help us, and I for one want to be helped. I say we welcome him with open arms."

"Need water? I have a few bottles," Jaune added, summoning them from under his poncho in a token attempt at making it look natural. His dimensional pocket kept the bottles in a preserved state, meaning that they remained as cold as when he first retrieved them from the fridge at the pit stop's supply store. Thus, everyone present took notice of the condensation on the bottles' surface, beads of water that promised an oh so refreshing sip.

The last among the four, the dour and sort of broody one, raised his hand. "He has my vote."

The person at the front gave a small laugh. "The man with the one vote has spoken. Come, Gladiolus. An extra pair of hands will end our ordeal all the sooner. Noct, time to take the steering wheel."

Gladiolus tched, still not quite convinced, but motioned for Jaune to step closer.

One by one, Jaune tossed the water bottles to each of the four. Prompto, whom Jaune suspected had a streak of hyperness, gulped the contents of his bottle down to the last drop before the rest even cracked open the caps for theirs, sighing in relief once done. The others chided him for it, although they visibly had to contain themselves from following in his example after their own first sip.

The one they called Noct had relocated to the driver seat by the time Jaune took position at the rear of the convertible. The person that replaced him there offered out a hand, and introduced himself as Jaune gripped it in a handshake.

"Ignis."

"Jaune."

The posh man indicated the others in turn. "And these luckless fellows you see before you are Gladiolus, Prompto, and Noctis." Sorry, but 'the big guy', 'the skinny blond', and 'mister broodypants' were what Jaune already filed them away as. "I really must thank you for the assistance. We were on something of a holiday, and wouldn't you believe it, not half a day from the city our ride gave out on us. The pit stop is ahead, you say?"

Jaune was in the middle of touching the car with the tips of his gloved fingers, testing out how hot the metal felt to the touch. Enough to cook eggs on, in this scorching desert heat. He could see why they had such trouble.

It was tolerable, though. His hands formed into fists, the less sensitive knuckles bracing on the car's trunk. The other young men got into position, with Ignis on his left, the big Gladiolus squeezed in on his right, and skinny Prompto on the far side. With a heave, the car began moving again.

"The place isn't far," Jaune confirmed. "Less than an hour from here." Ten minutes if he ran or flew, honestly.

"That would be the Hammerhead, then," said Ignis, to which Jaune nodded. "I suppose we may still call today a success. It was to be the first destination in our journey, albeit as a quick stop before we go on our way." His glasses glinted in the sunlight. "The owner would know us."

Jaune blinked, taken aback. "You're friends with cranky old Cid?" he asked with a touch of incredulity. The memory of getting bonked on the head for literally no reason late yesterday afternoon flashed back into his mind.

Gladiolus turned his head, suddenly interjecting, "You've met him?"

"Yes? I had to dodge a wrench." After the first one hit him, but let's not talk about his failures.

"Hm."

And now the big guy was sharing another glance with Ignis. What was that about?

Jaune did not get a chance to ask, as Gladiolus tapped a fist to his shoulder. "Forgot to mention this, but thanks for the help," the man said.

"...Sure thing."

They were odd people, all told. Not that he had room to talk.

For a few minutes, the convertible rolled along with little in the way of conversation. Grunts of effort filled the silence, inadequately. It got awkward fast, and Jaune spent much of that time pondering on how best to proceed.

"So," he finally said, settling on the question that burned brightest in his mind. "Are you guys, like, a boy band or something?"

Noctis, at the front, spluttered. "A boy band!?"

The others, meanwhile, broke out in guffaws. It seemed to be mostly at the expense of Noctis, whose vehement denials spewed forth in short order.

"Do we look like vapid pretty boys?" demanded the young man in the driver seat, tightening his grip on the steering wheel.

Let's see. Tight black pants. Fingerless gloves. Gelled hair. An androgynous face on your part…

"Not even a little," Jaune said, to the belief of nobody present.

"It's his face, isn't it?" Gladiolus said.

"No way!"

Ignis sent him a look, too perceptive by half. "Oh yes, it's the face. He is lying through his teeth," he informed his cohorts. "And no, the glasses aren't the reason I am smart."

"I didn't say anything."

"And yet, you said it all. You are either a master actor… or a true fool." Ignis chuckled. "I suppose that is as good an endorsement as any."

Jaune narrowed his eyes, because he was starting to smell something awfully fishy. "What's that mean, then?"

More shared glances, more silent convos he was not privy to. Ignis was the one to speak for the rest.

"We neglected to mention one detail about our band of vacationers." He nodded toward the front of the car, where Noctis sighed and turned in the seat to look back at them. The broody young man's face took on a different cast. Stern, and almost…

"Allow me to introduce," Ignis began, sweeping a hand out toward his friend, "the crown prince and heir to the throne of Lucis, Noctis Lucis Caelum."

If they thought he would be impressed, they were sorely disappointed. This made the third royalty he had met in his life, alongside little Emily Kaldwin and not-as-little Fischl of Immernachtreichs. He sure was going places.

Aaand that would explain several incongruities in these guys' actions, including why Prompto kept brushing his fingers over his handguns when he thought Jaune wasn't looking. Someone had been on lookout, prepared to shoot at the slightest sign of aggression against the royal personage. They as a group likely suspected him of being a bandit or an assassin until he brought up meeting the owner of Hammerhead station. All of a sudden, their close proximity spoke less of an easy sense of camaraderie, and more like them trying to box him in.

One realization sparked another, and Jaune whirled on the skinny blond. "Were you taste-testing that water for poison? Holy crap, dude!"

Prompto winced, doubly so as Noctis went all wide-eyed in shock. "Nature of the job," he said, shrugging.

"There is never a need for you to do that, Prompto," the prince insisted.

Jaune's concern lay with a different issue. "You drank the whole bottle! I'm pretty sure that's not how people do it!"

A sip, right? They took a sip and detected poison through the flavor, not chug it down and hope they wouldn't keel over dead.

Ignis raised a hand. "Lest you imagine us heartless, if I truly believed the water poisoned I would have stopped him. As the prince's retinue and personal friends, we look out for one another."

"And keep each other in check," Gladiolus added. "Prompto, get your hands back on that bumper!"

"Come on, he's doing fine on his own, Gladi-man!"

At that, Jaune looked down to discover he had been pushing the car on his own with just Gladiolus helping out. Even then, the big guy was trying to keep up with his pace rather than managing to add any real strength to it.

"Doesn't matter," said Gladiolus to his fellow… bodyguard? "Man's going out of his way to pitch in. We don't take advantage of that. Besides, this is good training," he asserted, to put an end to the matter.

"You sure?" Jaune asked. "Because I do have a method that would let us walk freely to the pit stop and still take the car along."

"…It's good training," Gladiolus repeated.

The desire to say blow it and just give up rang strong in his tone, but Jaune refrained from pointing it out in respect to a man's stubborn determination.

In this manner, they continued on down the road. From strangers to acquaintances, to perhaps friends. It took only a whim, and an offer of help.

Even if it was a lesson he already knew, he could learn from that. Again and again.


-o-
​

The Hammerhead pit stop carried everything that a traveler needed. A gas station, a supply store, a diner for good eats, a car shop, camping trailers where one could put up for the night, and, of course, a weapon merchant. Strangely enough, the most popular part of the place was the car shop with its headache-inducing din at all odd hours.

Prooobably because it had Cindy Aurum.

"Howdy, y'all… Goodness! What did you do to this poor thing!"

Sweet girl, if car-obsessed and already waist deep under the hood of the convertible Jaune brought in. Cindy Aurum wasn't one for chatting about swords or monsters like normal girls, but he had long grown inured to that quirk through his travels and didn't hold it against his acquaintance in the same way that she didn't give him grief over tuning out any talks about wheel tires and transmissions. They each stayed in their lane.

Noctis and his friends went gaga for her right off the bat.

"We did not!" Noctis protested.

Jaune pointed at the scene of Prompto hanging onto Cindy's every word with hearts in his eyes.

"Him, notwithstanding," Noctis amended.

"Yep. Let me talk business with her first, then you guys can go back to drooling over her."

He left Noctis to splutter, walking over to the crew's busted car. He did not check out Cindy's long and tanned legs, nor her shapely rear in her jeans shorts as she bent over with one foot kicked up to fiddle with the car's internals. Certainly not. The princely cries of "Hypocrite!" and "You're as bad as the rest of us!" washed off him like rain.

"Cindy," he called out to get her attention. "Your request is done."

In a flash, Cindy Aurum stood in front of him, wiping grease stains off on a towel that hung from her hips. There was already some stuck on her short blonde hair to promise more to follow throughout the day, and she grumbled over it for a second before a sunny demeanor returned to her face.

"Didja find the part?" she asked with a twang to her voice, her body almost vibrating as she leaned in. Pretty green eyes blinked innocently at him.

Once again, his poncho performed its function as a magic show prop, letting him pull an entire car muffler and exhaust out of its depths. That drew a bit of shock from the peanut gallery, but he had learned that the best way to avoid pointed questions was to gamely forge on, and so passed the part over to its new owner who gushed like he had given her a whole bouquet of flowers.

"Holy Chocobos!" Cindy yelped. No, he didn't understand what that meant, but he breathed a little easier as Cindy stepped back. "It exists! It really exists, the legendary… You didn't just rip 'er right out of the car, didja?"

"Of course not," Jaune lied. The woman gave him a flat stare. "So, about my payment?"

Whilst in deep suspicion, Cindy fished inside the pockets of her jeans shorts to pull out out a stack of bills that by all rights shouldn't have fit in there and made Jaune wonder if she had a dimensional hole of her own. As the first person he talked to in this world, the woman had through her many retrieval requests turned out to be one of his best sources for funds over the last day, funds he intended to promptly spend over at the weapon trucks—they were like food trucks, but with more stabby swords.

Before relinquishing the money, Cindy glanced around with a frown. "Whatever happened to Bennett? Shouldn't the lil' fella be with you?"

"I sent him off to get more of those Mesmenir unicorn-things that Takka wanted while I went to hunt the Dualhorns. That cook's shopping list is getting a bit ridiculous, if I'm being honest with you." He noticed the look on Cindy's face. "What?"

"You made that poor boy go out into the desert alone!?"

"Who do you take me for? I would never. I have Escha watching over him."

"A cat," Cindy deadpanned.

"A very smart cat," he corrected.

Cindy threw her hands in the air, which did interesting things when one was wearing a bikini top. "I can't believe you." The woman slapped the money into his palm. "I swear, if a single hair on that sweetie's head is hurt, I will give you such a talking to."

"He'll be fiiiine," Jaune flipped through the stack of bills, making a show of being able to calculate the sum from just a glance. (He couldn't, and would take it on trust.) "Anyway, do you have more jobs for me?"

"I ain't got no right sayin' this, but maybe you should slow down. All work and no play is no way to live." Cindy watched him for a second, then shrugged. "Suit yourself, though. This isn't really a job so much as a tip. You remember that hunter you found for me last night?"

"How is he now?"

"He's awake, just… not all there. Gets real scared at every lil' noise, and you should've seen him freak out this morning when he saw Escha outside his window. Funny thing is, he keeps circlin' back to how he regrets ever using 'that damn store'. Could be a black market's gone up around these parts."

Jaune looked out over the miles and miles of nothing, then back at Cindy. Cindy planted her hands on her hips.

"Now what exactly are you tryin' to imply, mister?"

A tumbleweed rolled through the space between them, borne on a lonely breeze. It rather proved his point.

Black markets needed customers to begin with, the demand to the supply. Otherwise, it was just a bunch of ne'er-do-wells twirling their mustaches while sitting around jobless. Still, it could be a lead worth checking out if only to satisfy his curiosity. The site where he found the hunter with one foot in the grave had contained an awful lot of blood along with a slew of dead wildlife, none of which seemed the right size to have done it to the man or each other. There was a story there.

Rather than mentioning his half-thoughts and suppositions to Cindy Aurum, he put up his hands in surrender.

"Yeah, that's what I thought," said Cindy in good humor, shooing him away.

As the woman turned to speak with the prince and his entourage, who were totally not posing like a boy band all this time, Jaune threw the group a lazy salute over his shoulder and took his leave. He beat a beeline for the two trucks sitting nearby in the parking lot, whose open doors at the back displayed a range of sharp implements and firearms. The people and vehicles there were unfamiliar to him, not those he dealt with the last time he swung by. He considered that a good thing, as he could hope for new stock.

The whole stay here had been rather odd. He was making money with which he bought weaponry to later sell, all of it done in an absolutely legal and mostly drama-free fashion, even if for small sums compared to some of the paydays he had. An honest living, he could almost say.

With permission from the vendors, he perused the wares on display with a close eye, often running a finger over the blade or testing the grip of a gun. None were what he would call legendary treasures, given the multiple copies hanging on the racks. But in a world teeming with hostile creatures in the day and daemons roaming in the night, travelers on the road expected quality arms as a matter of course. Swords, spears, guns, and more rolled out of factories with each passing hour, offered in shops across the world. Weapon merchants on the move filled the supply niche outside the cities, selling at rest stops like Hammerhead station. It made for a big industry with profits galore, plus a bottom-line guarantee: a brand that cheaped out was a brand with all its customers dead and unable to buy the season's hottest new lineup.

"A Storm Lance? I haven't seen one of these before," Jaune mused, and he read the accompanying placard to the ornate, techy-looking spear. "Oooh, and it sends out a shock when I stab?"

"For the hungry hunter that wants to tenderize the meat before the prey's even dead," the weapon seller advertised.

Jaune shoved a fistful of paper bills at the vendor. "Shut up and take my money."

A wonderful purchase, in his opinion. The level of manufacturing here appealed to him, proper arms forged with modern techniques. Zappy diodes and flame ignition systems created a mirror, or perhaps a different branch, to the Remnant mechashift, with simple but solid attachments that provided a number of effects to better kill a ravening monster dead. His only complaint was that he couldn't commission a custom order to retrofit his gear. In the same way that a black market operated best with a healthy population, a weaponsmith surely wasn't something he would find just chilling out in the vicinity of a roadside pit stop.

"It'll cost how much?" someone cried.

The sheer disbelief in those shouted words momentarily drew Jaune's attention back to the not-boy band and their conversation with Cindy Aurum. The pair of glasses that Ignis wore had slipped down to the tip of his nose, and threatened to fall off altogether as he stared at the estimate sheet in his hand. His companions, crowded around to peek over his shoulder, likewise blanched at the number on the paper.

"Yeah, you boys did a number on that beaut," Cindy said, shaking her head. "Still, it shouldn't be too steep a price for a royal prince… or maybe not," she amended as their expressions registered to her.

Ignis coughed into his hand, and drew himself up to regain some of his dignified bearing. "My apologies. this trip was meant as something of a… a learning experience for our prince. I don't suppose we can work out an alternative arrangement?"

In other words, they didn't bring enough money and now faced bankruptcy within a day of leaving home. Man, did that feel familiar.

Cindy pondered that, tapping a finger to her chin. "An alternative arrangement, huh? That's a great idea!"

Everybody perked up.

"Oh shoot, but I ain't sure if we got anythin' left for you to do. Somebody else stopped on by and took care of all that, hahaha…"

And now, despair again.

"Who is this job-hogging bastard?" demanded Gladiolus.

Me.

Prompto punched the air. "They should have left some for the rest of us! Everybody has to eat! If I ever meet this person, I'm letting them have it!"

It was me, Jaune Arc.

"Jaune, can you believe this!?" Noctis said, happening to notice his gaze.

He nodded at once, pulling together an outraged mien. "Yeah, totally!"

Once the prince turned away, Jaune frantically tried to catch Cindy's eyes. He made shushing motions at her behind the group, to which the mechanic mimed zipping her lips in understanding.

In every universe, the fight for the daily bread was a cruel and bloody affair.

Event: The Start of the Journey
